en: Oṃ.
The *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.
Homage to the Buddha! [This work follows] the characteristics of the three sages as they appear in the *Bhāṣā*.
Puruṣottamadeva composes this concise treatise.

Now begins the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*). [This applies] to worldly [words], by means of a grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that involves the conceptual division into base and suffix and possesses both general and specific characteristics, since there is no other way [to achieve this]. The instruction of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of their sequential arrangement and for the application of markers (*anubandha*). Both of these are for the sake of technical names (*saṃjñā*). And the technical name is for the sake of the efficient operation of the treatise through brevity. The instruction of the vowel *a* as "open" (*vivṛta*) is for the purpose of including the vowel *ā*. Now begins the section on the abbreviated terms (*pratyāhāra*).

1. *aiuṇ* | 2. *ṛḷk* | 3. *eoṅ* | 4. *aiauc* | 5. *hayavaraṭ* | 6. *laṇ* | 7. *ña ma ṅa ṇa na m* | 8. *jha bha ñ* | 9. *gha ḍha dha ṣ* | 10. *ja ba ga ḍa da ś* | 11. *kha pha cha ṭha tha ca ṭa ta v* | 12. *ka pa y* | 13. *śa ṣa sa r* | 14. *hal*. These are the *pratyāhāra*s (abbreviations). Having taught these letters beginning with *a* in their proper sequence, [the author] appends at the end those beginning with *ṇ*, which bear the designation *it*, for the purpose of forming abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*). Therein, by means of the fourteen *anubandha*s (indicatory letters) beginning with *ṇ*, in their respective order: One, three, and again one; four, one, three, and three.
"One, two, six, likewise one, four, five, and six"—thus [the Pratyāhāras are formed].

*Aṇ*, *ak*, *ik*, *uk*; *eṅ*; *ac*, *ic*, *ec*, *aic*; *aṭ*; *aṇ*, *iṇ*, *yaṇ*; *am*, *yam*, *ṅam*; *yañ*; *jhaṣ*, *bhaṣ*; *aś*, *haś*, *vaś*, *jhaś*, *jaś*, and again *vaś*; *chav*; *yay*, *may*, *jhay*, *khay*; *yar*, *jhar*, *khar*, *śar*; *al*, *hal*, *val*, *ral*, *jhal*, *śal*. Thus there are forty-one Pratyāhāras. With the addition of *uraṇ raparaḥ*, *cayo dvitīyāḥ śari pauṣkarasādeḥ*, and *ñamantāḍḍaḥ*, they become forty-four.
Now begins the first chapter: *vṛddhir ādaic*.
The sounds *ā*, *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au* shall be designated as *vṛddhi*.
*a*, *e*, and *o* are designated as *guṇa*.
Furthermore, the sounds *e* and *o* are designated as *guṇa*.
[And] *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* (along with their corresponding long vowels) are designated as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

Those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that have not been specified [by other rules] are to be understood as occurring in the place of *ika* alone. By the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, *guṇa* is substituted for the *aṅga*. Examples: *cetā*, *hotā*, *stotā*, *bhavitā*, *taritā*. By the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, *vṛddhi* is substituted [for *ika*]. Examples: *acaṣīt*, *ahauṣīt*, *astāvīt*, *alāvīt*, *akārṣīt*. [Question: How is it that *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *saḥ* are formed? [Answer: Because they are not denoted by the term *guṇa-vṛddhi*. By the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke*, [the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* does not take place] when there is the elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*) before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

A portion of a root is [treated as] a root. When an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix that causes the elision of a root is present, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that would otherwise apply do not take place. Examples: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*. [This applies] when there is the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix after a root ending in *ac* (a vowel), such as in *pacādi* derivatives.
[The rule] "of an *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) applies here as well: e.g., *abhāji*, *rāgaḥ*.
And [the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* applies] before *kṅit* suffixes.

When a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix is the cause, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that would otherwise apply do not take place. Examples with a *kit* suffix: *citam*, *stutam*, *bhuktam*, *kṛtam*, *sṛṣṭaḥ*. Examples with a *ṅit* suffix: *cinutaḥ*, *cinvanti*; *kurutaḥ*, *kurvanti*; *mṛṣṭaḥ*, *mṛjanti*, *mamṛjuḥ*. Question: How is it that we have *mārjanti* and *mamārju*? Answer: For the root *mṛj*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel (*saṃkrama*) other than 'a', the *vṛddhi* substitution is optionally desired. However, by means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it is compulsory in certain cases—such as *tundaparimṛjaḥ*.
[The rule] *dīdhīvevīṭām* [prohibits *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for the roots *dīdhī*, *vevī*, and the *iṭ* augment].

The roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* are Vedic; there shall be no *guṇa* for the augment *iṭ*. [Examples: *akaṇiṣam*, *araṇiṣam*. Here, in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *mip*, the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel is prohibited.
"Consonants that follow one another without an intervening vowel are called *saṃyoga* (conjunction)."
The conjunction of contiguous [sounds] is called *saṃyoga*. "Agni" is in the masculine. "Strī" is feminine. That which is articulated through both the mouth and the nose is *anunāsika* (nasalized).

A phoneme that is articulated through both the mouth and the nose shall be designated as nasal (anunāsika). Examples: *am̐*, *ām̐*, *oṃ*, and the letters *ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m*. [The nasalization is seen in] *dadhiṃ*.
Those sounds which have the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and the same internal effort (*prayatna*) are homogeneous (*savarṇa*).

Those sounds whose place of articulation (such as the palate) and effort (such as *spṛṣṭatā*—contact) are identical shall be designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another. A letter of a class (*varga*) is homogeneous with another letter of that same class. Vowels (*ac*) are homogeneous with those of their own place of articulation. For an *anusvāra*, when followed by a semivowel (*yay*), there is substitution by the following homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). Examples: *śaṅkitā*, *kuṇḍitā*. In the rule "a long vowel replaces a short *ak* vowel before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), examples are: *daṇḍāgram*, *khaṭvāgram*. It should be stated that the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* are homogeneous with each other. Example: *hotṛ* + *ḷkāraḥ* = *hotṝkāraḥ*. Since there is no long form of *ḷ*, [the substitute] is *ṛ*.
Neither *a* nor *jhal* [are considered *sthāna* and *ādeśa* in the same manner].

Vowels that are not *aja* (i.e., other than *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*) do not bear the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another. Examples: *daṇḍahastaḥ*, *dadhi śītam*, *vaipāśī matsyaḥ*, *ānaḍuhaṃ carma*. In these cases, the elision (*lopa*) governed by the rule *yasyeti ca* does not occur.
Furthermore, dual endings containing *ī*, *ū*, or *e* are designated as *pragṛhya*.

A dual-number ending that ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *agnī imau* (these two fires), *vāyū atra* (these two winds here), *khaṭve iha* (these two beds here), *pacete iha* (these two cook here). Some say that a prohibition must be stated for words such as *maṇīva*; others say that this *v* occurs in the sense of *iva* (like). Examples: *maṇīva* (like two jewels), *dampatīva* (like a husband and wife). [The rule] *adaso māt* [applies next].

The vowels *ī*, *ū*, and *e* following the *m* of *adas-* shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *amī atra*; *amū āsāte*. Why "following *m*" (*māt*)? [Consider: *amuke'tra*. Why "*adas-*"? [Consider: *śamyatra*.
The rule *śe śe* is a portion of the Veda; it is a substitute for case-endings (*sup*).
A single-vowel particle that is not a part of a verbal root is called *nipāta*.

A single *nipāta* (particle) is designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *a apakarṣa* ("bring it closer"), *u uttiṣṭha* ("stand up"), *ā evaṃ manyase* ("do you think so?"), *ā evaṃ kilaitat* ("is it really so?"). Why say "not *āṅ*"? [Observe: *ā uṣṇam oṣṇam* ("slightly warm"). One should know that this *ā* is marked with the *ṅ* (i.e., *āṅ*) when it signifies slightness (*īṣadartha*), connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), or the limits of a range (*maryādābhividhi*). However, when used for a sentence (*vākya*) or recollection (*smaraṇa*), it is not marked with *ṅ* (*aṅit*). 1. *ā* [is *pragṛhya*] when it signifies slightness, connection with an action, or the limit-inclusive [range];
one should know that this *ā* is marked with *ṅ* (*āṅ*), except when it occurs in a sentence or in recollection, where it is unmarked (*aṅit*).
Thus it was said.
A particle ending in *o* shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *aho aham*, *utāho iti*.
According to Śākalya, this applies in the vocative case when it is not a Vedic (*anārṣa*) usage.

According to the opinion of Śākalya, that which has the designation *pragṛhya* shall remain as such when followed by /i/ or /ī/, provided it occurs in the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*). For example: *bhāno* (vocative of *bhānu*), whereas according to others it would be *bhānav*.
Why "in the vocative"? Consider: *gavity ayam āha* ("He said 'go'"). The phrase "not being a Vedic archaism" (*anārṣa*) was employed in the previous rule (*ekavṛtti*).
[Now follows: *uñaḥ*.
According to the opinion of Śākalya, the vowel *u* followed by *it* (a consonant) shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. Thus: *u* (according to others, *vi*);
and *ūm̐*.

According to the opinion of Śākalya, *u*, *ī*, and *ū* are optionally substituted [for the final vowel of a word ending in -as]. That is to say: *ūm* (is substituted for *as*), *u* (is substituted), and according to others, *v* (is substituted).
Furthermore, the vowels *ī* and *ū* are also [substituted] when they stand in the sense of the locative case.
The rule *īdūtau ca* belongs to the portion concerning Vedic meters (*chandas*). That which is called *pragṛhya* has been explained.
The roots *dā* (to give), *dhā* (to place), and *dāp* (to cut) [are treated as having a long vowel in the Vedic subjunctive].

The roots *dā* (to give), *do* (to cut), *deṅ* (to purify), *dhā* (to place), and *dheṭ* (to suck) shall be designated as *ghu*. [Examples: *praṇidadāti*, *praṇidadhāti*. Why is it said "not *dāp*"? [To ensure] it does not apply to *dāp* (to purify) and *dai* (to cleanse). [Examples: *dātaṃ dhānyam* (threshed grain), *avadātaṃ vastram* (a clean cloth).
[Pāṇini 1.1.21: "In a single entity, [an operation] is like that which applies to the beginning and the end."

In the absence of a companion, an operation is extended [to it] as if it possessed both an initial and a final element. [The augment] *iṭ* follows roots beginning with *val*. [Examples: *alāviṣuḥ*. In the case of vowels beginning with *a*, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* [substitute for *i* and *u*]. [Examples: *śriyau*, *bhruvau*. When there is the status of having a final element, the suffix *yat* follows a stem ending in a vowel. [Example: *adhyeyam*. It should be stated that "with respect to a single entity, it is as if it possessed a designation. He will state a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the rule "for the first monosyllabic [root], two [are substituted]. Just as in this case [the root] *jāgṛ* [becomes] *jajāgāra*, so too [does] *iṇ* [become] *iyāya* and *ṛ* [become] *āra*. He will state the substitution of *ṣ* in the rule "in place of [the *s* of] an affix or a substitute. Just as in this case [the root] *pac* [becomes] *pakṣyati*, so too [does it become] *apākṣīt*. The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*.

These two [suffixes, *tarap* and *tamap*, when applied to words ending in short *i*] shall be designated as *gha*. Examples: *kumāritarā*, *kumāritamā*, *gauritamā*. [In these cases,] the short vowel is substituted by the rule *gharūpa-*. The words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* are designated as *saṃkhyā* (numerals).

*Bahu* and *gaṇa* have the sense of "abundant. *Vatu* and *ḍati* are suffixes. These [words formed with those suffixes] shall be designated as *saṃkhyā*. Examples: *bahukṛtvaḥ*, *gaṇakṛtvaḥ*, *gaṇaśaḥ*, *tāvatkṛtvaḥ*, *katidhā*.
Words ending in *ṣ* or *n* are called *ṣaṭ*; likewise those ending in *ḍati*.

Numerals ending in *ṣ* or *n*, as well as those ending in the suffix *ḍati*, shall bear the technical designation *ṣaṭ*. [Examples: "There are six; look at them," or "five, seven, nine, ten men"; "eleven"; "eighteen. "How many are there? "Look at how many! [In these cases,] by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jas*, *śas*, and *su*.
The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*.
These two are designated as *niṣṭhā*. Examples: *bhinnaḥ*, *bhinnavān*. The words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

All words beginning with *sarva* shall be designated as *sarvanāman* (pronouns). Examples: *sarvasmai*, *sarvasmāt*; *viśvasmai*, *viśvasmāt*. The word *ubha* is restricted to the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Elsewhere, it takes the form *ubhaya*. The suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*, as well as *itara*, *anya*, and *anyatara* [are also *sarvanāman*]. However, the word *tva*, which is a synonym for *anya*, is not included. *Nema*—meaning "half"—is excluded from this category. *Sama*, *siman*, *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, *adhara*, *sva*, *antara*, *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, *etad*, *idam*, *adas*, *eka*, *dvi*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, *bhavat*, and *kim* [are also *sarvanāman*]. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound that is a directional compound (*dik-samāsa*), [the designation of these as *sarvanāman*] is optional.

In a *dig-bahuvrīhi* (compound denoting direction), the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) may optionally apply. For example: *uttarapūrvasyai* or *uttarapūrvāyai*. [Exception: Not in a *bahuvrīhi* [in general].

In a *bahuvrīhi*, that designation does not exist. For example: *priyaviśvāya dehi* ("Give to the one for whom the universe is dear"). Here, the substitution of *smāi* does not occur. Examples: *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* ("one whose father is you") and *matkapitṛkaḥ* ("one whose father is me").

The suffix *akac* does not occur before the final vowel (*ṭi*) when used in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*) and so forth; rather, only *ka* occurs as prescribed by the rule *prāgivāt kaḥ*. This applies in a *tṛtīyā*-compound.

In this case, the technical designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) does not apply. For example: *māsapūrvāya dehi* ("Give to one who is preceded by a month"). Because of the explicit mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) [in the rule], it also applies to a sentence: *māsena pūrvāya* ("To one who is earlier by a month").
And in a *dvandva* compound, that designation does not apply. [This includes] the compounds of *pūrva* and *apara*, and of *katara* and *katama*.
In the case of the *jas* ending, it is optional.
In a *dvandva* compound, that [term] may optionally be a *sarvanāman* when followed by the suffix *jas*. For example: *katarakatame* or *katarakatamāḥ*.

The words *prathama*, *carama*, those ending in *tayaP*, *alpa*, *ardha*, *katipaya*, and *nema* are also optionally *sarvanāman*s when followed by *jas*. For example: *prathame* or *prathamāḥ*; *carame* or *caramāḥ*; *dvitaye* or *dvitayāḥ*; *dvaye* or *dvayāḥ*; *alpe* or *alpāḥ*, and so forth.

The terms *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* are optionally called pronouns (*sarvanāman*) when used in the sense of relative position (*vyavasthā*) and when they are not proper names (*asaṃjñā*). In the nominative plural (*jasi*), they may take either the masculine or feminine form: *pūrve* or *pūrvāḥ*; *pare* or *parāḥ*. Why "in the sense of relative position"? Consider: *dakṣiṇāś chātrāḥ* ("the southern students"), which means "the proficient ones. Why "when not a proper name"? Consider: *uttarāḥ kuravaḥ* ("the Northern Kurus," a specific region). The term *sva* [is optionally a pronoun] except when it denotes kinsmen or wealth.

The word *sva* may optionally be called a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when followed by the suffix *jas*. Examples: *sve gāvaḥ* (one's own cows) or *svā gāvaḥ*. Why is it said "when not denoting kinsmen or wealth"? [Because in those cases it is not optional. Example: *svā jñātayaḥ* (one's own kinsmen); *prabhūtāḥ svā dīyante* (abundant property is being given). The word *antara*, when used in the sense of being outside (*bahiryoga*) or as an undergarment (*upasaṃvyāna*), may optionally be called a pronoun when followed by the suffix *jas*. In the sense of being outside: *antare* or *antarā gṛhāḥ*; the meaning is "houses situated outside the village. In the sense of an undergarment (the lower cloth): *antare* or *antarā śāṭakāḥ*; the meaning is "cloths that are to be worn around the body."

It should be stated that [the word] *apuri* [is used]. [For example: *antarāyāṃ puri vasati* ("he lives in the middle of the city"). This is because [the word *puri*] would otherwise fall under the category of *sarvādi* (beginning with *sarva*).

Within the section concerning the optional rule (*vā-prakaraṇa*), an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *tīya* when it has the marker *ṅit*: *dvitīyasmai* or *dvitīyāya*. "The indeclinables (*avyaya*) consist of those beginning with *svara* and the particles (*nipāta*)."

The particles beginning with *svar* and the other [groups] are called indeclinables (*avyaya*). *svar*, *prātar*, *antar*, *uccais*, *nīcais*, *divā*, *bahis*, *svayam*, *mṛṣā*, *he*, *hai*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *addhā*, *kam*, *śam*, *sārddham*, *samam*, *saha*, *śubham*, *svasti*, *asti*. The particles expressing frequency are: *ca*, *vā*, *iva*, *vai*, *eva*, *iha*, *iti*. The distinction is that the *svar*-group consists of denoters (*vācaka*), while the *ca*-group consists of illuminators (*dyotaka*). That which remains unchanged across the three genders, all case-endings, and all numbers is called an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

A *taddhita* suffix that does not take all case-endings is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). That *taddhita* from which no case-ending arises shall be an indeclinable: *tataḥ*, *yatra*, *vinā*, *nānā*; [the suffixes] beginning with *tasil* and ending with *edhāc*; *kṛtvasuc* and *suc*; *śas* and *tas*; *ḍāc*; *tham* and *uthāl*; *dā* and *hil*; those having the sense of *cvī*; [the suffix] *ām* after *kim*, *etiṅ*, and indeclinables when expressing excellence of substance, as in *kintarām*; *vati*; as in *brāhmaṇavat*; and a *kṛt* suffix ending in *m* or *j*.

A word ending in *m* (the accusative singular suffix) is an indeclinable when used as a gerundive particle. Examples: *kartum*, *svāduṅkāram*, *svapoṣam puṣṭaḥ*, *irhāñcakre*. A word ending in *ej* (the suffix *eñ*) is an indeclinable in the Vedic language (*chandasa*). The suffixes *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun* are also indeclinables. Examples: *kṛtvā*, *prakṛtya*. The suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
And the *avyayībhāva* [is also indeclinable].

A compound called *avyayībhāva* shall be an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Examples are *upāgni* and *pratyagni*. In this case, the purpose of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is simply for the elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending]. There is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating that it does not take the suffixes *na*, *akac*, and so forth. The indeclinables have been explained. Now, *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix].

The augment *suṭ* is applied to the neuter [stem] before the endings *jaś* and *śas*. For non-neuter [stems], *suṭ* is also called *sarvanāmasthāna*. [Examples of] *śi*: *kuṇḍāni*, *dadhīni*. [Examples of] *suṭ*: *rājā*, *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*; *rājānam*, *rājānau*. [Examples of] *sīmā*: *sīmā*, *sīmānau*. Why "of the non-neuter"? [To exclude cases like: *sāmanī*, *dhāmanī*.
The option (*vibhāṣā*) applies according to the rule "or not" (*na vā*).

The meaning of the two words *na* and *vā* shall be designated as *vibhāṣā*. An option (*vikalpa*) operates in a domain made equivalent by a prohibition. The purpose of an "option-bothways" (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*) is as follows: for example, "there is optionally (*vibhāṣā*) vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *śvi*": *śuśāva*, *śiśvāya*; *śuśuvatuḥ*, *śiśviyatuḥ*.
[In this case, the rule] "the semivowel (*ig*) is the vocalization of a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*)" [applies].

An *ik* vowel that occurs in place of a *yaṇ* sound—whether it has already occurred or is yet to occur—is called *saṃprasāraṇa*. Examples: *iṣṭam*, *uptam*, *gṛhītam*, *auhyata*, *auyata*. Now, with reference to the rule concerning the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*), he says:
"The markers *ṭ* and *k* belong to the beginning and the end [respectively].
That which is marked with *ṭ* becomes the beginning of what is mentioned in the genitive; that which is marked with *k* becomes its end. Examples: *lavitā*, *bhīṣayate*.
*Mid* follows after the final vowel among the vowels.

*Mid* occurs after the last vowel in the midst of vowels. Examples: *payāṃsi*, *siñcati*, *ruṇaddhi*. They desire the augment *num* before the final letter of the root *masj*. This is for the purpose of [avoiding] the elision of the *anubandha* and the first letter of a *saṃyoga*. Examples: *maṅktā*, *magnaḥ*.
When a short vowel is substituted, an *ik* vowel takes the place of an *ec* vowel.

In place of an *ec* vowel (*e*, *ai*, *o*), only a short *ig* vowel (*i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*) is substituted. Examples: *atiri kulam*, *atinu kulam*, *upagu*. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes "in place of" (*sthāne-yoga*). When it is not connected [to another word], that is, when its relationship is unexpressed, the genitive should be understood as signifying "in place of. Examples: from *as-* comes *bhṛ-*; *bhavitā*. From *brū-* comes *vac-*; *vaktā*. Why "when not connected"? Consider: *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*—"after the root *guh*, when preceded by a penultimate *u*, [the substitution of *ū* occurs]. Examples: *upagūhayati*, *nigūhayati*.

*sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*: When several substitutes are possible, that which is most similar to the original (*antaratama*) shall be the substitute. Regarding place (*sthāna*): *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101). In *latāgram*, when two gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*) meet, the resulting long vowel is also guttural. Regarding meaning (*artha*): *taruṇayuvatiḥ*. Here, the word *taruṇī* is said to behave like a masculine (*puṃvat*) because its meaning is essentially masculine. Regarding quality (*guṇa*): *pākaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*, *rogaḥ*. In these cases, the substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutva*) occurs because both are unaspirated (*alpa-prāṇa*), voiceless (*aghoṣa*), and possess the same quality. Regarding measure (*pramāṇa*): *amuṣmai*, *amūbhyām*. Between a short and a long vowel, the substitute *o* or *ū* must be of the same measure as the original.

The mention of "place" (*sthāna*) is so that proximity of place (*sthānāntarya*) may be stronger than proximity of meaning, quality, or measure. For example: *cetā* (from *citṛ*), *stotā* (from *stu*). Due to proximity of measure, the vowel *a* [of the suffix] should not [be substituted for the radical vowel]. The mention of "the most proximate" (*tamap*) is so that when there are many intervening [factors], the most proximate one may apply. For example: *vāgghasati*, *triṣṭub bhasati*. *uraṇ raparaḥ*: In the place of an *ṛ*-vowel, an *aṇ* vowel occurs followed by a *ra*-sound (*rapara*). For example: *karttā*, *kirati*, *dvaimāturaḥ*, *kārakaḥ*, *kharṭvaśyaḥ*, *tavalkāraḥ*.

*alo'ntyasya*: A substitute should be understood to take the place of the final *al* (vowel or consonant). *id goṇyāḥ*: [The suffix] *id* is added to *goṇī*. Example: *pañcagoṇiḥ* ("worth five ropes"). *hanasta ca*: [The suffix] *ta* is added to the root *han*, and the letter *t* is also substituted for the final *n*. Example: *brahmahatyā* ("the killing of a Brahmin"). *rājñaḥ ka ca*: [The suffix] *ka* is added to *rājan*, and the letter *k* is also substituted for the final *n*. Example: *rājakīyaḥ* ("belonging to the king"). *ruhaḥ paḥ*: [The suffix] *pa* is added to the root *ruh*. Example: *ropayati* ("he causes to grow"). *ṅicca*: And [the substitute] is also marked with the indicator *ṅ*.

A substitute for *ṅit* [elements] shall take the place of the final *al*. In a *dvandva* compound, *ānaṅ* is substituted for the final vowel of a stem ending in short *ṛ*: *mātāpitarau* (mother and father). *Anaṅ* is substituted [for the final vowel] before the nominative singular suffix *su*: *sakhā* (friend), *kartā* (agent). Because of the functional significance (*sāmarthya*) of the *ṅit*-ness of *tātaṅ*, this rule is not considered an "end-substitution" (*antavidhi*): *kurutāt* (imperative). [The rule] "of the first of the following" (*ādeḥ parasya*): When an operation is stated concerning something that follows, it should be understood as applying to the first *al* [of that following element], provided there is a mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). [Example: *īdāsaḥ* (the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of *ās*): *āsīnaḥ* (seated). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "of the final *al*" (*alo'ntyasya*), but it is superseded by the rule "that which has more than one *al* and is marked with *śit*" (*anekālśit*) due to its later occurrence in the sequence. [The rule] "ais for *bhisi* after *at*" (*ato bhisa ais*): *vṛkṣaiḥ* (by trees).
That which consists of more than one phoneme and ends in śit replaces the whole.

A substitute that consists of more than one letter (anekāl), as well as the augment *śit*, shall take the place of the whole original form (*sarvasya*). Examples: *asterbhūḥ* [P. 2.4.52]—*bhavitā*; *liṭastajhayoreśirec* [P. 3.4.81]—*pece*, *pecire*; *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* [P. 7.1.20]—*kuṇḍāni*. The rules concerning the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśāḥ*) have been stated. Now:
"A substitute (*ādeśaḥ*) is like the original (*sthānivat*), except in a rule (*avidhau*) where the cause of substitution (*al*) is itself the object of the operation."

Substitutes (ādeśāḥ) are like the original (sthānivat). [Examples: *brūñ* > *vaktā*, *vaktum*, *vaktavyam*. The suffixes *tavyat* and others are prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). [Example: *āvadhiṣṭa*; here the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ*. Why "not when a rule concerning a phoneme (*analvidhau*)"? It is so that [the substitution] does not take effect in a rule concerning a phoneme (*varṇavidhau*). [Example: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*; here there is no elision of the nominative suffix *su* because of the condition *hal*. A prohibition of the augment *īṭ* must be stated for the roots *ah* and *bhū*: [examples] *āttha* and *abhūt*; this is because of the rules *bruva īṭ* and *astisico 'pṛkte*. [The term *sthānivat* applies] except in the case of a rule concerning what precedes (*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*).

This rule is commenced either for the sake of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) or for the sake of restriction (*niyama*). An *ādeśa* (substitute) whose cause lies subsequent to it shall be treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) when an operation is to be performed on what precedes it. For example: *paṭayati*, *laghayati*, *avadhīt*. Due to the status of the *sthānin* regarding the elision of the *ṭi* suffix and the elision of the vowel *a*, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not take place.

[However, this rule does not apply] in the case of operations concerning: (1) the end of a word (*padānta*), (2) reduplication (*dvirvacana*), (3) the *vara-ēya* suffixes, (4) elision (*lopa*), (5) accent (*svara*), (6) homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), (7) the nasal *anusvāra*, (8) lengthening (*dīrgha*), (9) the *jaś* series of consonants, or (10) the *car* series of consonants.

In these rules, the substitute *aja* (short *a*) is not treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Regarding the rule for the end of a word (*padānte*), the two [substitutes] exist; the substitute *āv* should apply. In the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), as in *dadhy atra* and *madhv atra*, the doubling [of the consonant] by the rule *anaci ca* would not occur. In the case of the *vār* suffix, when *varac* is applied and there is elision (*lopa*), as in *yāyāvaraḥ*, the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* would apply. In a rule concerning homogeneous sounds (*savarṇavidhi*), regarding the elision of *a* in *śnas* (the roots *śo* and *so*), as in *śiṇṭi* and *piṇṭi*, the substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) for the *anusvāra* before a semivowel (*yay*) would not occur. In the case of *anusvāra*, as in *śiṃṣanti* and *piṃṣanti*, the substitution of *anusvāra* by the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali* would not occur. In a rule concerning the *jaś* substitutes...

In the case of an elided *akāra* resulting from a rule of practice (*abhyasta*), [the following applies]: in *dhaddhve* and *dhaddhvam*, the substitution of *jaś* would not occur; in *jakṣatu* and *jakṣuḥ*, the substitution of *car* (as prescribed by the rule *gamahana*)—namely, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*)—would not occur. Therefore, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited.

However, in the cases of vowel-substitution (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), a substitute that consists of an elision (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as a *sthānivat*.

In this context, accent (*svara*) is not illustrated here. Regarding the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*): in *allopo 'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134), as in *pratidīvnā*, the lengthening by *hali ca* (6.4.2) would not otherwise apply. Regarding the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), in *ktici* (3.3.94), as in *kaṇḍūtiḥ*, the elision of *y* before *v* (6.1.66) would not otherwise apply. Why "elision" (*lopa*)? Consider *vāyvoḥ*; here the substitution of *yaṇ* (6.1.77) is indeed treated as the original (*sthānivat*), and thus the elision of *y* before *v* does not occur.

However, in the cases of elision (*luka*), the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the *aṅ* augment, the subsequent shortening (*paranirhrasi*), the substitution of *ku* (*kutva*), and the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*), the substitute is not treated as the original (*na sthānivat*).

From the roots *lāvayati* and *pāvayati*, with the suffix *kvip*, we derive *lauḥ* and *pauḥ*. Because of the rule "that which is elided by *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*," the elision of the causative marker (*ṇi*) is prohibited from being treated as *sthānivadbhūta*; consequently, the substitution of *ūṭh* occurs. Regarding the elision (*luk*): *āmalakaṃ phalam*. [The suffix] *mayaṭ* is applied; then there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix when it refers to the fruit. When the feminine suffix is removed by the rule "elision of the suffix when a *taddhita* suffix is elided" (*luk taddhitaluki*), because that elision is prohibited from being treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, the elision [of the *y*] by the rule "when followed by *ya*" (*yasyeti ca*) does not take place. Regarding the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*): *pārikhīyam*. Since the elision by "when followed by *ya*" (*yasyeti ca*) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* after the suffix *aṇ* belonging to the fourfold group (*cāturarthika*), the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *kha* as a penultimate vowel" (*khopadhācchaḥ*).

Regarding the shortening [of a vowel] in *caṅ*: *avīvadad vīṇāṃ parivādakena* ("he caused the lute-player to play the lute"). Because the first *ṇic* is not treated as *sthānivat*, the shortening occurs by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*. Similarly, from *pāpacyate* comes *pāpakti*; from *pācayate* comes *pākti*; from *yāyajyati* comes *yāyaṣṭi*; and from *yājayati* comes *yāyaṣṭi*. Due to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of *ṇic* (*ṇilopa*), the changes to *k* (*kutva*) and *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) occur by the rule *jhalīti*. [The sūtra] *dvirvacane'ci*...

When a cause for reduplication (dvirvacana) exists, a substitute (ādeśa) is treated as if it were the original (sthānivat); that is, it remains in the form of the original. Where? Only when the reduplication itself is to be performed. Once the reduplication has been performed, it assumes the form of the substitute again, like a person who has vanished. For example: *papatuḥ*, *papuḥ*; *jaghnatuḥ*, *jaghnuḥ*; *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*. Because the elision of the *at* (the penultimate vowel) and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) caused by the rule *gamahana-* are treated as *sthānivat*, the reduplication of the single-vowel roots is established. In *nināya* and *lulāva*, because the *āy* and *āv* substitutes are treated as *sthānivat*, the forms *nai* and *lau* are not reduplicated.
What is the example? *jeghrīyate*. The substitution of *ī* in the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix is not *sthānivadbhūta*. The principle of *sthānivadbhāva* has been explained.
Disappearance is termed *lopa*.

The non-appearance of that which is expected to appear shall be designated as *lopa* (elision). [Examples: *rājā*, *bhavān*, *paceyuḥ*. The suffixes are marked by the technical terms *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup*.

There would be three designations for that which has become manifest through the non-perception of a suffix: *atti* (he eats) from the roots beginning with *ad-* due to the elision of *śap*; *juhoti* (he offers) from the roots beginning with *hu-* due to *ślu*; and *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ* (the people of Aṅga and Vaṅga) where there is *lup* of the suffix after words denoting a country; [and] *dvyaṅgamagadhetyaṇ* (the suffix *aṇ* after *dvyaṅga* and *magadha*). [And finally: when a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by the suffix still take place (*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*).

Even when the affix is elided, the effect caused by it should still occur. For example: *gomān* (possessing cows), where *num* is applied because of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [affix]; *ahan* (day), *agnicit* (one who has piled the fire-altar), *adhok* (he milked); and *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (that which ends in a nominal suffix or a verbal suffix is a *pada*). In *atṛṇeṭ*, the substitution of *im* for *tṛṇaha* occurs before an affix beginning with a *hal*. Here, although the word *pratyayasya* ("of the affix") is already understood from the previous context, its repetition is made so that the operation applies when the entire affix is elided, and not when only a portion of the affix is elided.

In the case of *āghnīya*, because the *s* of *sīyuṭ* and the *ṭ* have been elided, there is an absence of "as if the affix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); consequently, since it does not begin with a *jhal* sound, the elision of the nasal [of the root *han*] would not occur. Although it could have been stated simply as "that characterized by it" (*tallakṣaṇam*), the word "affix" (*pratyaya*) is mentioned again in order to exclude cases where the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). Thus, in *gave hitam* → *go-hitam* and *rāyaḥ kulam* → *rai-kulam*, because there is an absence of "as if the affix were present" due to the condition "before a vowel" (*aci*), operations such as *avādi* that depend on a phoneme do not take place.
[This is governed by the rule: *na lumatāṅgasya* ("When an affix is elided by the marker *lu*, the operation of the *aṅga* [stem] does not apply").

When an operation is prescribed by means of the suffixes *luk*, *ślu*, or *lup*, that operation shall not apply to the *aṅga* (the stem). For example: *mṛṣṭaḥ*, *juhutaḥ*, *gargāḥ*. In these cases, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur before the *śap* and *yañ* suffixes respectively. In *rājapuruṣaḥ*, the status of being a *bha* does not apply to the element ending in *ṅas*. In *ahardadāti* and *aharbhuṅkte*, the prohibition [of *ru*] stated in the rule *ro'supi* does not take effect. Why specify "of the *aṅga*"? Consider *pañca*, *sāma*, and *payaḥ*; here, the status of being a *pada* applies to the entire aggregate.

Furthermore, when a word is the latter member (*uttarapada*) and a rule applies to what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādau*), the designation *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (as if it were still a suffix) does not apply. Thus, in the cases of *paramavācau*, *paramaśvalihau*, *paramagoduhau*, and *paramadaṇḍinau*, the rules for *kutva* (the change of *v* to *ū*), *ḍhatva* (the change of *l* to *ḍh*), *ghatva* (the change of *d* to *gh*), and the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)—which would have applied by relying on the status of being a "word" (*pada*) based on the internal case-ending within the compound—would not take effect. Why say "when a rule applies to what is not the beginning of a word"? Consider *dadhisecau* and *madhusecau*. In these cases, the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*) by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* still correctly applies. [Derivation: From the root *sic*, we derive *sek* (the agent who sprinkles); here, the portion beginning with the final vowel of the verbal root is called *ṭi*.

Among these vowels (ac) that are situated together, that which is the last vowel (antya), beginning with it, shall be designated as *ṭi*. [Examples: *ātām*, *āthām*, the word *ām*; *paṭat*, *damat*, the word *ac*. In forms such as *pacete* (they two cook), the status of being "end" and "beginning" (*antādivattva*) applies by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvāt*).

The letter preceding the final (last) letter is called the *upadhā*. A penultimate phoneme is termed the *upadhā*. [Examples: *pācakaḥ* (cook), *śiṣṭaḥ* (taught/instructed), *bhettā* (breaker), *nartakaḥ* (dancer).

In the rule "tasmin" (in that), it refers to what precedes; when [an element] is indicated by the locative case, the grammatical operation applies to what precedes it. For example: *dadhyudakam* (curd-water), *madhvidam* (this honey). In the rule "tasmāt" (from that), it refers to what follows.

When [an operation] is indicated by the fifth case (ablative), it should apply to what follows. [This applies] from one word to another word. *grāmo vaḥ* ("the village is yours"); *putro naḥ* ("the son is ours"). It does not apply to what precedes. *yuṣmākaṃ grāmaḥ* ("the village of you all"); *asmākaṃ putraḥ* ("the son of us all"). A word's own form [is to be understood], except when it is a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*).

In this treatise (śāstra), the own form (svarūpa) of a word is to be understood [as the referent], not its meaning (artha). For example, by the rule *agner ḍhak*, [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after the word *agni*, resulting in *āgneyam*; it does not apply to synonyms such as *pāvaka*. By the rule *rājñaḥ ka ca*, [the suffixes] *ka* and *ḍhak* are applied after *rājan*, resulting in *rājakīya*; it does not apply to synonyms such as *nṛpa*. Why is it said "not when it is a technical term" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*)? [Consider] *ṭi-ghu-ghaḥ*; here, only the meaning is grasped. However, in cases such as the optional rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga-* (P. 2.4.12), where one says *plakṣanyagrodham* or *rurupṛṣatam*, or in *sve puṣaḥ* (P. 3.4.40) where one says *svapoṣam*, *raipoṣam*, *gopoṣam*, and so on, an effort must be made to distinguish whether a specific term or a synonym is being grasped. Furthermore, by the rule *aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (P. 1.1.69), [an indicatory letter] *aṇ* or one marked with an *u*-diacritic denotes its homogeneous phonemes, provided it is not itself a suffix (*apratyaya*).

An *aṇ* vowel, when followed by an *uc* (an *u* with an indicatory *c*), should be the indicator (*grāhaka*) of its own homogeneous class (*savarṇa*) and of its own form (*svarūpa*). [This is taught by] *asya cvau*: *khaṭvī syāt*. [And by] *yasyeti ca* and *cauṅiḥ*. [It indicates] its own form as well: *śuklīkaroti*. *dākṣiḥ*. [The rule applies to] *u*, *it*, *ku*, *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, and *pu*. Why "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*)? [Consider] *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ*. [The term *pratyaya* is used] in the sense of "that which is understood here," "that which is prescribed," or "that which is brought about. Because of that prohibition, they say the meaning is this: an *aṇ* vowel being brought about does not include its homogeneous sounds. Therefore, there is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds in cases such as *idama iś* and *am saṃbuddhau valādeḥ*.

A phoneme followed by *tapara* (a short vowel marker) causes its own duration to be understood. Therefore, *ais* is substituted for *bhis*: *vṛkṣaiḥ*. But not here—*khaṭvābhiḥ*. [The substitution of] *it* occurs for the final vowel of a verbal root (*dhātu*): *kirati*, *girati*.
[In a group of phonemes], the first one, together with the last one, denotes the whole.

An initial phoneme (ādi-varṇa), when joined with a final phoneme (antya) bearing the technical designation *it*, shall include those phonemes falling between them as well as its own form (*svarūpa*). [Examples of such markers: *aṇ*, *ak*, *hal*, *ac*, *sup*, *tiṅ*, *suṭ*, *āp*, *tṛn*, *kṛñ*. *Yena vidhistadantasya*:

By whatever [phoneme] a rule (*vidhi*) is stated, that [rule] shall apply to that which ends in it. In the rule *erac*, since the suffix *ac* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the vowel *i* (the *ikāra*), the letter *i* causes the inclusion of everything ending in it. [Examples: *cayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*.

When a rule is stated with reference to a specific grammatical element, that element is understood at the beginning of the rule. In the case of *aci*, it means "in a vowel beginning with *a*"; thus, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions occur [before such vowels]. Examples: *śriyau*, *bhruvaḥ*.
Thus has been explained the science of technical designations (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*).
That [stem] whose first vowel among its vowels is a *vṛddhi* [vowel] is called *vṛddha*.

Among these vowels, that whose first vowel is a *vṛddhi* [vowel] shall have the designation *vṛddha*. From a *vṛddha* [stem], the suffix *cha* [is applied]. [Examples: *pāṇinīyam*, *śaivīyam*, *vauddhīyaṃ matam*.
It should be stated that the name of a person may optionally have the designation *vṛddha*. [Examples: *devadattīyāś chātrāḥ* or *daivadattāḥ*.
From a word ending in a *gotra* [suffix], it should be stated that the suffix is applied as if it were not part of a compound. [Examples: *vṛddhabhāradvājīyāḥ*, *vṛddhakāśyapīyāḥ*, *ajātaulvalīyāḥ*.

And *tyad* and so forth [are also designated as *vṛddha*]. The words beginning with *tyad* shall be designated as *vṛddha*. For example: *tadīya*, *idamīya*, *adasīya*, *yuṣmadīya*, *madīya*, *asmadīya*, and *kimīya*. [Also:
*eṅ* [is designated as *vṛddha*] when denoting a region of the easterners.

That vowel which has *eṅ* (e, o, ai, au) as its initial among the vowels (*acām*) shall be designated as *vṛddha*, provided it refers to a place in the East (*prāgdeśe*). Examples: *eṇīpacanīyaḥ* village; *bhojakaṭīyaḥ* region. Why "in a place"? [Consider: *gaumatāḥ* fish found in the *gomatī* river. Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Teacher Śrī Puruṣottamadeva. 1.1.1.
And the first quarter is completed.
The Second Quarter of the First Chapter.

*Gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ-añ-ṇit-ṅit*: After these [roots], affixes other than those marked with *ṇ* (añ-ṇit) are treated as if they were marked with *ṅ* (*ṅit*). *Gāṅ* is the substitute for *iṅ*. Examples: *adhyagīṣṭa*, *adhyagīṣṭhāḥ*. [As in: "Surely you have studied the Smṛtis" (*nādhyagīḍhvaṃ dhruvaṃ smṛtīḥ*). From the *kuṭādi* group: *kuṭitā*, *puṭitā*; *kuṭitum*, *puṭitum*; *saṃkuṭitavyam*. Why "other than *ṇ*" (*añ-ṇit*)? [Consider] *ṇic*: *koṭayati*; *ghañ*: *koṭaḥ*. It should be stated that *vyac* belongs to the *kuṭādi* group except when followed by the suffix *asun*. Examples: *vicitā*, *vicitum*. Why "except when followed by *asun*" (*anasi*)? [Consider] *asun*: *uruvyacāḥ*.
The root *vij* (to tremble) takes the augment *iṭ*.

A suffix beginning with *ṛ* or *i* that follows the root *vij* shall be marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter (*ṅit*). Examples: *udvijitā* (one who has trembled), *udvijitum* (to tremble). "This is not the time to tremble. *udvijitavyam* (it should be trembled). "We have become such as to tremble before a man. "How is it that they take refuge [only] after being made to tremble by rains? [This applies] when the root is followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
[Regarding the root *ūrṇu*: there is] an option (*vibhāṣā*) for the root *ūrṇu*.

After the root *ūrṇu*, an affix beginning with *iṭ* may optionally be treated as having the marker *ṅ*. Thus: *prorṇavitā* or *prorṇuvitā*; *prorṇavitum* or *prorṇuvitum*. [This applies to] a sārvadhātuka affix that is not marked with *p*.

Furthermore, the *sārvadhātuka* [affix] would be *ṅit*. [Examples: *kurutaḥ*, *kurvanti*; *cinutaḥ*, *cinvanti*. Why "furthermore" (*api*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to: *karoti*, *karoṣi*; *cinoti*. Here, they say that by dividing the rule (*yoga-vibhāga*) with the preceding "furthermore" (*api*), the meaning is that [an affix] which is *ṅit* is not *pit*. Consequently, in the case of *stuyāt*, because the *yāsuṭ* [augment] is *ṅit*, its status as *pit* is prohibited; thus, unlike in *stauti*, there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] by the rule "there is *vṛddhi* for *u* and *o* when a *pit* [affix] follows, provided the root ends in a consonant. In *brūtād bhavān*, the *iṇ* [augment] does not occur after the root *brū*. [The rule] "the *liṭ* [affixes] are *kit* after a root ending in a non-conjunct consonant" [applies].

The *liṭ* suffix shall be *kit* after a verbal root that does not end in a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyoga*). Examples: *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*; *bibhidatuḥ*, *bibhiduḥ*; *dudruvatuḥ*, *dudruvuḥ*; *juhuvatuḥ*, *juhuvuḥ*; *ūcatuḥ*, *ūcuḥ*. Why "not ending in a conjunct"? Witness: *valir babandhe*, *jaladhir mamanthe*. [The rule applies] even when preceded by *api*—as in *vibheda*. And also after the roots *indh* and *bhavati*.

The *liṭ* [affix] shall be *kit* after these two [roots]. *samīdhe*, *babhūva*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Since *indh* pertains to the Vedic domain (*chandas*) and the *vuk* augment for *bhū* is obligatory, the rule prescribing the *kit* status for these two is purposeless. However, in the secular language (*bhāṣā*), the *ām* [augment] occurs after *indh* in the *liṭ*. *samindhāñcakre*. Regarding this, Jayāditya maintains that there is an exception (*iṣṭi*) based on the rule "of *granth*, *śranth*, *dambh*, and *svañj*" (*granthi-śranthi-dambhi-svañjīnām*). [Examples: *grethatuḥ*, *grethuḥ*; *śrethatuḥ*, *śrethuḥ*; *debhatur*, *debhuḥ*; *pariṣasvaje*. [The suffix] *ktvā* follows *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas*.

After these [roots], even when followed by a suffix marked with *ṣ* (seṭ), the *ktvā* suffix shall be *kit*. Examples: *mṛḍitvā*, *mṛditvā*, *gudhitvā*, *kuṣitvā*, *kliśitvā*, *uditvā*, *uṣitvā*. *Rud-vid-muṣ-grahi-svap-pracchaḥ saṃś-ca*: After these roots, even when followed by a suffix marked with *ṣ* (seṭ), the *ktvā* suffix shall be *kit*, and so too the suffix *saṃ*. Examples: *rutitvā* (after which) *rurudiṣati*; *viditvā* (after which) *vividiṣati*; *muṣitvā* (after which) *mumuṣiṣati*; *gṛhītvā* (after which) *jighṛkṣati*. The mention of *svap* and *pracch* is for the sake of the desiderative (*san*) suffix: *suṣupsati*; *pipṛcchiṣati*.
*iko jhal*:

After a verbal root ending in an *ik* vowel (*i*, *u*, or *ṛ*), an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant (any consonant except *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*, and nasals) shall be treated as *kit*. Examples: *cikīrṣati* ("he desires to do"), *cicīṣati* ("he desires to gather"). Why say "beginning with a *jhal*"? Observe *śiśayiṣate* ("he desires to lie down"). Why say "after an *ik* vowel"? Observe *pipāsati* ("he desires to drink"). This rule regarding affixes beginning with a *jhal* occurs in the ninth sūtra. And [the following applies]: *halantācca* ("and after a root ending in a consonant").

A *san* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant shall be *kit* after a root ending in a *hal* consonant and having a penultimate (*upadhā*) *it*. Thus: *bibhitsati*, *bubhutsate*. The inclusion of *hal* in the rule is established by its denoting the entire class [of consonants]. Hence: *dhīpsati*, *dhīpsati*.
[The suffixes] *liṅ* and *sic* are *kit* when used in the *ātmanepada*.

The affixes *liṅ* (optative) and *sic* (aorist augment) are *kit* when they follow a root ending in a consonant (*hal*) or having a penultimate *u*, provided they are the domain of the *ātmanepada*. Examples: *bhitsīṣṭa* (may he split), *bhotsīṣṭa* (may he know). *abhitta* (he split), *abuddha* (he knew).
The reference to the *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* markers) continues through the next six sūtras. [Sūtra 1.2.12: *uś ca*.

The suffixes *ta* and *iṭ* are optionally *kit* after roots ending in the vowel *ṛ*. *kṛṣīṣṭa*, *hṛṣīṣṭa*; *akṛta*, *ahṛta*. *tīrṣīṣṭa nadī*; *atīrṣṭa nadī svayameva*. *Vā gamaḥ*: After the root *gam*, the suffixes *ta* and *iṭ* are optionally *kit*. Due to the *kit* designation, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). *saṃgasīṣṭa* or *saṃgaṃsīṣṭa*. "May you be united with victory in battle," *saṅgasīṣṭhāḥ* or *saṅgaṃsīṣṭhāḥ*. "The bee was united with the lotus," *samagata* or *samagaṃsta*.
The suffix *sic* is added after the root *han*. When the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affixes follow, *sic* is treated as having the *kit* designation after the root *han*. [Examples: *āhata*, *āhasātām*.
After the root *yam*, [the suffix *sic* is added] when it means "obstructing."

The suffix *sic* shall be *kit* after the root *yam* when followed by the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings. For example: *udāyata*, meaning "he indicated. In the sense of "seeking out" (*gandhana*), as in: "Do not seek out Sītā with fear" (*nopāyadhvaṃ bhayaṃ sītām*). Why [is it] "seeking out"? [Consider: *āyaṃsta pādam* ("he stretched out his foot"). Optionally, when the sense is "accepting" (*svīkāra*), the suffix *sic* after *yam* followed by *taṅ* may optionally be *kit*. Examples: *upāyata kanyām* ("he accepted the girl"); *upāyaṃsta mahāstrāṇi* ("he accepted the great weapons"); *saumitre mām upāyaṃsthāḥ* ("O son of Sumitrā, you have accepted me").

*sthādhvoricca*: After the roots *sthā* and *dhū*, when followed by the affix *taṅ* (the ātmanepada suffixes), the augment *sic* shall be *kit*, and the letter *i* shall be the substitute for the final phoneme. *sthā*: *upāsthita kareṇuḥ* (the female elephant approached); *prāsthitānekaḥ* (many set out). *ghu*: *adita* (he ate); *adithāḥ* (you ate); *adhita* (he ate); *adhithāḥ* (you ate). *adhiṣātāṃ gāvau vatsena* (may the two cows eat with the calf). *na ktvā seṭ*: [The augment *iṭ* is not applied] to the affix *ktvā* when it is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*).

Why should the *ktvā* suffix not be *kit*? [In forms such as] *devitvā*, *varttitvā*, and *mṛḍitvā*, its *kit*-status has been stated. The recurrence of the term "having an *iṭ*" (*seṭ*) occurs in the nine subsequent sūtras:
"The *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] following *śīṅ*, *svidi*, *midi*, *kṣvidi*, and *dhṛṣ* [are *kit*]."

Why would the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix *kta*) not be *kit* after these [roots]? *śayitaḥ*, *śayitavān*; *prasveditaḥ*, *prasveditavān*; *prakṣveditaḥ*, *prakṣveditavān*; *prameditaḥ*, *prameditavān*; *pradharṣitaḥ*, *pradharṣitavān*. According to the rule *svidādeḥ vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoriṭ*, the augment *iṭ* is optional after roots beginning with *svid* when used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object of the action (*ādikarman*). However, in the *Dhātupārāyaṇa*, it is stated that even for the root *ḍīṅ* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class, the *niṣṭhā* suffix is *akittva* (not *kit*): *uḍḍayitaḥ*, *uḍḍayitavān*. Regarding *mṛṣastitikṣāyām*: the *niṣṭhā* suffix after the root *mṛṣ* in the sense of endurance (*titikṣā*) should not be *kit*.
Examples: *marṣitaḥ*, *marṣitavān*. What is meant by "in the sense of endurance"? Example: *apamṛṣitaṃ vākyam āha* ("he spoke an unendurable statement").

*Udupadhād bhāvādikarmaṇor anyatarasyām*: After a verbal root having *u* as its penultimate letter, the suffix *kta* (niṣṭhā) may optionally be replaced by *kin* when expressing an abstract action (*bhāva*) or a beginning action (*ādikarman*). For example: *dyotitam* or *dyutitam* anena ("it has been illuminated by him"). As in: "The sun was indeed illuminated by the spreading moonbeams, but it was not yet fully illuminated. This applies likewise to roots such as *mud*. However, this substitution is not desired for roots belonging to the *aś* conjugation class (*aś-bikaraṇa*), as in *nigudhitam*.
Regarding the rule *pūṅaḥ ktvā ca*:

Should not the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* also be *kit* after the root *pūṅ*? [Examples would be] *pavitaḥ*, *pavitavān*, and *pavitvā*. [In these cases,] the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *pūṅaśca*. The mention of *ktvā* is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
[The next rule is: *nopadhāt thaphāntādvā*.

The suffix *ktvā* may optionally be treated as having the *kittva* marker after a verbal root ending in *tha*, provided it has *na* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*), and also after roots ending in *pha*. Examples: *śrathitvā* / *śranthitvā*; *grathitvā* / *granthitvā*; *guphitvā* / *gumphitvā*. Why "having *na* as its penultimate letter"? Consider *rephitvā*. Why "ending in *tha* or *pha*"? Consider *sraṃsitvā*.
[Also, the suffix *ktvā* is optionally *kit*] after the roots *vañci*, *luñci*, and those ending in *ṛ*.

The suffix *ktvā* may optionally be *kit* after these [roots]: *vacitvā* or *vañcitvā*, *lucitvā* or *luñcitvā*, *ṛtitvā* or *arttitvā*. According to Kāśyapa, *ktvā* may optionally be *kit* after the roots *tṛṣ*, *mṛṣ*, and *kṛś*: *tṛṣitvā* or *tarṣitvā*, *mṛṣitvā* or *marṣitvā*, *kṛśitvā* or *karśitvā*.

*ralo vyupadhād dhalādeḥ saṃśca*: After a root beginning with a consonant (*hal*), having *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter (*upadha*), and ending in *r* or *l*, both the suffix *ktvā* and the suffix *san* may optionally be *kit*. Examples: *likhitvā* / *lekhitvā*; *lilikhiṣati* / *lilekhiṣati*. The same applies to roots beginning with *dyut* and others: *dyutitvā* / *dyotitvā*; *didyutiṣate* / *didyotiṣate*. Why "ending in *r* or *l*"? Consider *devitvā*, *dideviṣati*. Why "beginning with a consonant"? Consider *eṣitvā*, *eṣiṣiṣati*. [The rule applies] only when [the root] takes the augment *iṭ*: *bhuktvā*, *bubhukṣate*. The *kit*-status has been explained. *ūkālo’j jhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ*: A vowel (*ac*) whose duration is that of the short *u*, long *ū*, or protracted *ū* is respectively termed *hrasva* (short), *dīrgha* (long), or *pluta* (protracted).

*Ukāla:* A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *u*, *ū*, or *ū3*—that is, one *mātrā*, two *mātrās*, or three *mātrās*—is respectively designated as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), or protracted (*pluta*). Examples: *agnicit* (short), *hrīcchati* (long). A protracted example is not cited here, as such usage is not observed in common speech (*bhāṣā*).

*Ac-cha ca:* It should be understood that the short vowels and others resulting from those [designations] are themselves the substitutes for the original vowels (*ac*). Short: *atiri*, *atikhaṭvam*. Long: *stūyate*, *paṭūbhavati*.

Here, there are twelve rules concerning *chandah* (Vedic meter). In this [work], however, the rules for accents (*svara*) that are applicable to spoken language (*bhāṣā*) are not composed, because accentuation is not in common use in spoken language and because people have no need for it; the application of accent is necessary only in the Veda, due to the fear of undesirable consequences arising from a wrong accent. An *apṛkta* suffix is a suffix consisting of a single phoneme (*ekāl*). That which is a suffix consisting of one phoneme is called *apṛkta*. Example: *āsīt* (he was). The augment *iṭ* is applied after an *apṛkta* suffix. Example: *ardhabhāk* (sharing half). [Derivation: From the root *bhaj*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied. There is elision (*lopa*) of an *apṛkta* suffix ending in *v*. Example: *ardhabhāk*.

A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common referent is called *karmadhāraya*. A *tatpuruṣa* whose constituent words denote the same object shall be designated as *karmadhāraya*. Example: *pācakavṛndārikā*. In a *karmadhāraya*, [the first member] is treated like the masculine (*puṃvat*). That which is established by the first case ending is the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in a compound.

In a compound-forming rule (*samāsasūtra*), that which is designated by the nominative case shall bear the technical name *upasarjana* (subordinate member). For example: [the rule] "the fifth case with *bhaya*" [yields] *vṛkabhayam* ("fear of a wolf"). [The rule] "the seventh case with *śauṇḍa*" [yields] *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* ("skilled at dice"). And [the word] having a single case-ending shall bear the name *upasarjana*, except when it is placed first in the compound; that is, in a sentence, a word with a fixed case-ending shall be called *upasarjana* provided it is not the first member. For example: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has gone out from Kauśāmbī"), as in "he has gone out from Kauśāmbī" (*nirgataḥ kauśāmbyāḥ*) or "see his departure from Kauśāmbī" (*niṣkauśāmbiṃ paśya*). And so forth.

Kātyāyana states that when there is a single case-ending, the word must not end in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Example: *ardhapippalī* (half a pippalī fruit). Here, the shortening of the *upasarjana* does not take place.
A meaningful form that is neither a root (*dhātu*) nor an affix (*pratyaya*) is called a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

A meaningful verbal form is termed a nominal stem: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *śuklaḥ*, *ḍitthaḥ*, *kuṇḍam*, *vipraḥ*, *sarvaḥ*, *uccaiḥ*. Why "meaningful" (*arthavat*)? [To exclude] *vanam*, *dhanam* [which are considered mere collections of sounds]. [This is to ensure] it does not apply to those ending in *-n* as a limit. Why "not a root" (*adhātu*)? [Consider] *ahan* from the root *han* in the *laṅ* tense; otherwise, the elision of *n* would occur. Why "not an affix" (*apratyaya*)? [Consider] *kāṇḍe*, *kuṇḍe*, *trapuṇī*; otherwise, by the rule "short vowel in the neuter," a short vowel would occur.

The designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) should be stated for a meaningless particle (*nipāta*). Examples: *adhyāgacchati*, *pralambate*. And [the categories of] *kṛt*-derived, *taddhita*-derived, and compound words should also have the designation of *prātipadika*. Examples: *kartā*, *śrīḥ*, *dākṣiḥ*, *varaṇāḥ*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *kumbhakāraḥ*. Because of the restrictive rule that "only compounds among meaningful aggregates [are *prātipadikas*]," a sentence lacks the status of a *prātipadika*. Example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*.

*Hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*: In the neuter gender, the final vowel of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) shall be short. Examples: *atiri*, *atinu*, *grāmaṇi-kulam*. Not here: *ramate kulam*; *kāṇḍībhūtaṃ kulam*—because verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and indeclinables (*avyaya*) lack gender. Also not here: *vanāgram*, *vanāya*—because the long vowel [of the compound] is external (*bahir-aṅga*). *Gostriyor upasarjanasya*.

The final vowel of a word ending in *go* or of a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) that functions as an *upasarjana* (secondary member) shall be shortened. Examples: *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows), *strī* (a woman). Examples: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī), *atikhaṭvaḥ* (one who has surpassed a bed). Why "of the *upasarjana*"? [Consider: *rājakumārī* (the king’s daughter). Regarding the term *strī*: because it refers to a feminine suffix prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*stryadhikāra*), this shortening does not apply here: *atitantrīḥ* (one who has surpassed a lute-string), *atiśrīḥ* (one who has surpassed glory), *atilakṣmīḥ* (one who has surpassed fortune). There is a prohibition of this shortening for a word ending in *ī* or *yas* when it is an *upasarjana* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound: *bahupreyasī rājā* (a king who has many beloveds) or *kulaṃ* (a family with many beloveds). By the rule *iryasaśca*, the suffix *kap* is prohibited. [In the case of the suffix *kap*,] there is elision (*luk*) when a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is elided.

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. For example: *pañcaśaṣkulih*. [In this case], there is elision of the suffix *ṭhak* by the rule "adhyardha" (Pāṇini 5.1.28), as it denotes the sense of "purchased. [Example: *āmalakam phalam*. Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule "nityaṃ vṛddha" (Pāṇini 4.3.143), and there is elision of the suffix by the rule "phale luk" (Pāṇini 4.3.163). [The rule] "id goṇyāḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.50) states: when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix, the substitution of *it* shall take place for the word *goṇī*. For example: *pañcagoṇiḥ paṭaḥ*. By means of a division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*), we also have *pañcasūciḥ*.

*Lupi yuktavad vyaktivacane*: When *lup* occurs, the gender and number [of the derivative] should be like those of the base (*prakṛti*)—that is, like the gender and number of the meaning of the base—when the sense of *lup* is present. The many descendants of Vaṅga are called *vaṅgāḥ*. In the sense of "their residence," the suffix *aṇ* is elided by the rule for country names (*janapade lup*). Thus, *vaṅgāḥ* refers to the country. Similarly, *pañcālāḥ*, *kuravaḥ*, and *puṇḍrāḥ*. Why "when *lup* occurs"? Consider *lavaṇālluk*: the elision of the suffix after *lavaṇa*. In *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* ("salted soup") and *lavaṇā yavāgūḥ* ("salted gruel"), the gender and number belong only to what is expressed [by the base]. In the case of *harītakyādi* (the group beginning with *harītakī*), there is [agreement in] gender, but not in number. The fruits which are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *harītakī* tree are called *harītakyaḥ phalāni*. This is because of the suffix *aṇ* [denoting a modification].

The suffix *lup* is applied after [the group beginning with] *harītakī* and so forth. Regarding the mention of *khalatikādi* [in the rule], it refers to the location (*sthāna*) and not to the individual entity (*vyakti*). Thus, "forests near the mountain Khalatika" is expressed as *khalatikaṃ vanāni*. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *adūrabhavaḥ*, and then *lup* is applied by the rule *varaṇādibhyaśca*. According to the *Bhāṣya*: "In a compound, the quality of being treated like the singular (*yuktavadbhāva*) applies only to the final member when it denotes a plural object. For example: *mathurā ca pañcālāśca* = *mathurāpañcālāḥ*. Why specify "only the final member"? Consider: *pañcālamathure*. (In this case, the dual form is used because both members are plural.)
And [the elision applies] to qualifiers of that which is not a genus (*ajāti*).
The same would apply to qualifiers of the meaning of the *lup* elision: "The Aṅgas are prosperous, with much milk and ghee. Why "not a genus"? [Consider: "The country of Vaṅga is beautiful.

There is a prohibition regarding the *lup* elision after the word *manuṣya*: "Cañcā is a handsome man. It should not result in the form "Cañcā is handsome. [The suffix] *kan* occurs after the word *iva* when there is a comparison; its *lup* elision occurs by the rule "after *manuṣya*."
In that case, it need not be taught as a rule because the name itself is the authority.

That is to say, the characteristic of expressing individual instances (*vyaktivacana*) need not be formulated. This is because the name is the authority; these words such as *aṅga*, *vaṅga*, and *varaṇā* are names. Their very gender and number are the authority, just as in the cases of *āpaḥ* (waters), *dārāḥ* (wife/wives), *gṛhāḥ* (house/houses), and *varṣāḥ* (rainy season/plural rains).
[Furthermore,] there is elision (*lub*) because the connection [of the suffix] is not perceived.

In the rule *janapade laṭ* and *varaṇādibhyaśca*, the elision (*lub*) is also unnecessary to be taught, because no connection (*yoga*) or relation is perceived. For the country is not called "Pañcāla" because it is the domain of the Pañcālas; nor is the village called "Varaṇā" because of its connection with trees. Furthermore, if the connection were the basis for the designation, then in the absence of that [connection], the term would not be used.

For if the connection with trees and so forth were the authority [for the name], then in the absence of those trees, the terms "Varaṇā" and "Pañcāla" would cease to be employed, just as the term "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) ceases when there is no connection with a staff. Therefore, this is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*).
The statement that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together with the primary meaning [of the base]"—because the meaning is established by other means—is unnecessary.

The rule that "the primary and the subordinate express the primary meaning together," as well as the definitions provided by former teachers such as "a verb has action as its primary meaning, a *kṛt*-derived word has the instrument as its primary meaning, and a *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its primary meaning," and the principle that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," need not be stated. Why? Because the world is other than the treatise; the meaning is established by that [worldly] authority.

Even one who has not studied grammar, when told "Bring the king's man" (*rājapuruṣam*) and "Bring Upagu’s descendant" (*aupagavam*), brings a man qualified by the king and a descendant qualified by Upagu. This is the same regarding time and secondary members (*upasarjana*). Time and secondary members do not require a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), because they are the same as what was stated previously; this is the rejection [of a separate rule] on the grounds that it is understood from common usage itself. However, in the *Māthurī-vṛtti*, the mention of "the pupil" (*aśiṣya*) continues until the end of the chapter.
When a genus is denoted, the plural may optionally be used for a single entity.

When the meaning is that of a genus, a single thing may optionally take a plural form. For example: *sampanno yavaḥ* (the barley has ripened) or *sampannā yavāḥ* (the barley has ripened). Why "for a single entity"? Consider: *sampanno vrīhiyavau* (rice and barley have ripened). There is a prohibition when a numeral is employed: *eko vrīhiḥ sampannaḥ subhikṣakaraḥ* (a single grain of rice, when ripened, brings about plenty). [The plural is also used] for the word *asmad* ("we") when two [persons] are intended.

In the case of *asmad* (the word for "I/we"), the plural number may optionally be used when expressing singularity or duality. For example: *ahaṃ karomi* ("I do") or *vayaṃ kurmaḥ* ("we do"); *āvāṃ kurvaḥ* ("we two do") or *vayaṃ kurmaḥ* ("we do"). By the rule of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality), this substitution is prohibited when the pronoun is accompanied by a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Examples: *ahaṃ paṭur bravīmi* ("I, being clever, say") and *āvāṃ paṭutarau chātrau brūvaḥ* ("we two, being very clever students, say"). Regarding *yuṣmad* (the word for "you"), Jayāditya maintains that according to some authorities, the singular may be used when addressing a superior: *tvaṃ guruḥ* ("you, the teacher") or *yūyaṃ guravaḥ* ("you, the teachers"). Furthermore, the singular is used for the asterisms *Phalgunī* and *Proṣṭhapada*.

In the case of the two *phalgunī*s and the two *proṣṭhapada*s, the plural may optionally be used when referring to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). For example: *pūrve phalgunyau* or *pūrvāḥ phalgunyaḥ*; *pūrve proṣṭhapade* or *pūrvāḥ proṣṭhapadāḥ*. Why "when referring to the lunar mansions"? [Because] in the case of *phalgunyau māṇavike*, it refers to two girls named Phalgunī. Furthermore, in Vedic usage (*chandas*), the singular is used for the two *punarvasu*s.
And also for the two Viśākhās.
There are two sūtras concerning *chandas*.
In the dual compound of the lunar mansions Tiṣya and Punarvasu, the dual number necessarily replaces the plural number.

Tiṣya is one, and Punarvasū are two. When a dual number would otherwise result from these two pairs of constellations, the dual is prescribed. "The Tiṣya and Punarvasū have risen. Because of the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning), we have "Siddhya and Punarvasū" [as a single entity]. What is the purpose of the plural [in the rule]? [To show: "This is Tiṣya and Punarvasu" [where it remains singular]. This very point is an indicator that every *dvandva* compound may optionally be singular. The transfer of number has been explained. *Ekaśeṣa* (single remainder) occurs for those of identical form when they are in the same case-ending (*ekavibhakti*).
Of those with identical forms, only one remains. Tree and tree = two trees (*vṛkṣau*). Tree and tree and tree = three trees (*vṛkṣāḥ*).

For when a case-ending is prescribed after a collection [of sounds] that possesses a specific form, it is established therein that one [element] alone is the expressive unit of that collection and possesses meaning. (1)

The elision of one [term] occurs even when there is a difference in meaning due to the perception of different forms: *vrīhiś ca māṣaḥ* (rice and beans), *mānaṃ ca māṣaḥ* (a measure and a bean), *mūrkhaś ca māṣaḥ* (a fool and a bean), and *māṣāḥ*. "Pāda" means ray, foot, or a quarter. Why [is it said] "when in the same case-ending"? [Consider: *viprābhyāṃ kṛtam* (done by two Brahmins) and *viprābhyāṃ dehi* (give to two Brahmins). Furthermore, it should be stated that for words having the same meaning but different forms, there is sometimes elision of all but one (*ekaśeṣa*): *vakradaṇḍaś ca kuṭiladaṇḍaś ca* results in *vakradaṇḍau* or *kuṭiladaṇḍau*. When an elder is mentioned with a youth, [the elder alone remains] provided that the distinction between them consists solely of that characteristic.

When a feminine [term] is mentioned together with a masculine [term], the feminine term in its elder (vṛddha) form remains, and the younger (yuvan) form is excluded—provided that the distinction between them is based solely on the technical markers (pratyaya-lakṣaṇa) of "elder" and "younger. For example: *gārgyaśca gārgyāyaṇaśca gārgyau* ("Gārgya and Gārgyāyaṇa are both Gārgyas"). But not here: *gārgyavātsyāyanau* ("Gārgya and Vātsyāyana"). An intermediate descendant is called "elder" (*vṛddha*). And [the rule applies] when a feminine [term] is used like a masculine (*puṃvat*): when a feminine term in its elder form is mentioned together with a masculine [term], the feminine term in its elder form remains, and the meaning of the feminine term should be expressed like the masculine. For example: *gārgī ca gārgyāyaṇaśca gārgyau* ("Gārgī and Gārgyāyaṇa are both Gārgyas"); *dākṣī ca dākṣāyaṇaśca dākṣī* ("Dākṣī and Dākṣāyaṇa are both Dākṣīs"); *vātsī ca vātsyāyanaśca vātsyau* ("Vātsī and Vātsyāyana are both Vātsyas"). But not here: *gārgīvātsyāyanau* ("Gārgī and Vātsyāyana") or *dākṣīvātsyāyanau* ("Dākṣī and Vātsyāyana").

The masculine [remains] when co-uttered with a feminine. When a masculine and a feminine are mentioned together, the masculine alone remains. *devaśca devī ca* (the god and the goddess) becomes *devau* (the two gods). *asurau*, *brāhmaṇau*, *kukkuṭau*, *mayūrau*. *gaurayaṃ gauriyametau* (this bull and this cow—these two) becomes *gāvau* (the two cattle). *śivaśca śivā ca* (Śiva and Śivā) becomes *śivau* (the two Śivas). As in: "He describes the union of the bodies of the two Śivas. This applies only if they possess the same characteristics; thus, *kukkuṭamayūryau* (the cock and the peahen). [Also,] *bhrātṛputrau* (brother and son) [is used] with *svasṛduhitṛbhyām* (sister and daughter).

When a brother is mentioned together with a sister, the sister remains; when a son is mentioned together with a daughter, the son remains. When a neuter noun is mentioned together with a non-neuter noun, the neuter noun remains, and it may optionally take the singular number, provided that the distinction between them lies solely in their gender. For example: *śuklaḥ prāvāraḥ* (a white cloak), *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth)—[when combined] this results in *tad idaṃ śuklam* (this is white) or *tānīmāni śuklāni* (these are white). Why "with a non-neuter"? [Consider: *śuklaṃ ca śuklaṃ ca śuklaṃ ca* (white and white and white); here, the plural form *śuklāni* is used, and the singular does not apply.

The father [is compounded] with the mother; the father-in-law with the mother-in-law. When mentioned together with both the mother and the mother-in-law, either the father or the father-in-law may remain as the residue: "I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world. And [the term] *mātāpitarau* (mother and father) is also used.
*Śvaśrū* and *śvaśura* form the dual compound *śvaśurau*.
Regarding the rule *tyadādīni sarvair nityam*:

"with all" (*sarvaiḥ*) means that when there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*) with *tyadādi* pronouns and others, the *tyadādi* pronouns remain [as the sole survivors]. For example: *sa ca devadattaśca tau* ("he and Devadatta—those two"); *yaśca vipraśca yau* ("who and the Brahmin—those two").

According to some, among the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (i.e., *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, etc.), whichever occurs later remains; for example: *sa ca yaśca* = *yau*; *yaśca kaśca* = *kau*; *sa ca tvañca* = *yuvām*; *sa ca tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca* = *vayam*. In the case of a group of domestic animals that are not young, the feminine form remains when there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*). In groups of domestic animals that are not young, when they are mentioned together, the feminine is retained. Examples: *imā gāvaḥ* (these cows); *imā ajāḥ* (these goats). Why "in groups"? Witness: *etau gāvau* (these two oxen). Why "not young"? Witness: *ime vatsāḥ* (these calves). This does not apply here because of the specific designation [of "domestic"] regarding animals with non-divided hooves: *ime aśvāḥ* (these horses); *ime gardabhāḥ* (these donkeys).
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the Bhāṣāvṛtti composed by the Great Preceptor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva. || 1.2 ||
And the section on the *kuṭādi* group is completed.
First Chapter. Third Pāda.
*Bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*. The roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā* shall have the technical designation *dhātu* (verbal root). *Bhū*: *bhavati*; *edh*: *edhate*.
"An *aj* [vowel] that is nasalized (*anunāsika*) in its instruction (*upadeśa*) is designated as *it*.

"Instruction" means that which is taught; thus, the root-initial and so forth. Among those, an *aj* distinguished by nasality shall be termed *it*. For example: *edham̐*, *sparddhaṃ*. The followers of Pāṇini maintain that nasality is inherent (by convention). Therefore, this [designation] would apply here as well: *ragem̐*, *lagem̐*. An addition must be made for the case of *ir*: *bhidir*, *abhidat*. Here, *aṅ* replaces *cli* according to the rule "or *haritaḥ*."
*Halantyam*:
In an *upadeśa*, the final consonant (*hal*) shall bear the technical designation *it*. *Ai-u-ṇ*; *ḍu-kṛñ*; *nadaṭ*; *san*; *puk*; *anaṅ*.
*Na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*: In a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the letters *t*, *u*, and *m* are not designated as *it*.
In a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the letters *tavarga* (the dental stops), *s*, and *m* shall not be designated as *it*. [Examples: *vṛkṣān*, *paceyuḥ*, *yasmin*, *pacataḥ*, *apacam*.

The rule "the first" (*ādiḥ*) applies to *ñ*, *ṭu*, *ḍu*, and *u*. That is to say: the letters *ñ*, *ṭu*, *ḍu*, and *u* occurring at the beginning [of a root] shall be designated as *it*. [Examples: from the root *ñimidā* comes *minnaḥ*; from *ṭunadi* comes *nandathuḥ*; from *ḍupacaṣ* comes *paktrimam*.

*ṣaḥ pratyayasya*: The *ṣ* at the beginning of an affix shall be designated as an *it*. [Examples: *ṣvun*—*nartakī*, *khanakī*, *rajakī*. *cuṭū*: [The *c* and *ṭ* at the beginning of an affix are also designated as *it*.]

The *c*-class (*cavarga*) and the *ṭ*-class (*ṭavarga*), when occurring as the initial elements of an affix (*pratyaya*), shall be designated by the term *it*. *phañ*: *kauñjāyanyaḥ* (descendant of Kuñja). *jus*: *brāhmaṇāḥ*, *vṛkṣāḥ* (the nominative plural ending). *ñya*: *śāṇḍikyaḥ* (descendant of Śāṇḍika). *ṭa*: *kurucarī* (a woman who wanders among the Kurus). *ḍa*: *upasarajaḥ* (born from a secondary wife). *annāṇṇaḥ*: *ānnaḥ* (descendant of Anna). How is it that *keśacuñcuḥ* and *keśacaṇaḥ* (one who fancies his hair) are formed? Because there is no grammatical operation (*kārya*) dependent on the *cit* designation [of the suffix]. The *Bhāṣya* states: "In the case of suffixes beginning with *ya*, the suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* are taught with their *y* elided. [This is governed by the rule: *laśakvataddhite* ("*l*, *ś*, and *k* are *it* in a *taddhita* suffix").

The letters *l*, *ś*, and the *ka*-group (k, kh, g, gh, ṅ), when occurring at the beginning of an affix excluding *taddhita* affixes, shall bear the designation *it*. Examples: *lyap*: *vijitya* (having conquered). *lyuṭ*: *cayanam* (the act of piling). *śap*: *bhavati* (he becomes). *kta*: *bhūtam* (become/past). *khac*: *priyaṃvadaḥ* (one who speaks kindly). *ghurac*: *bhāsuram* (shining); *bhaṅguram* (fragile/bending). *ṅe*: *paṭave* (to the clever one). Why "excluding *taddhita*"? Consider: *aveḥ kaḥ* → *avikaḥ* (a sheep). *Tasya lopaḥ* (There is elision of that):
There shall be elision of that which has been assigned the designation *it*. This has already been illustrated accordingly.
The subsequent mention of equal [elements] follows their respective order.

For equal elements—that is, those mentioned in the original rule (*uddeśin*) and those mentioned subsequently (*anudeśin*)—the subsequent mention shall occur in sequential order. [Examples: from roots such as *nandi*, *grahi*, and *pac* [the suffixes] *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* [are added]: *nandanaḥ*, *grāhī*, *pacaḥ*.
An adhikāra (governing heading) is indicated by an accented vowel.

The term *svarita* refers to a certain property of a phoneme (*varṇadharma*). By means of that mark, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is to be understood, as in the case of *ātmanepada*, *pratyaya*, and *aṅgasya*. [For example:
"The *ātmanepada* [suffixes] follow a root marked with an *anudātta* vowel or the letter *ṭ*."

The *ātmanepada* suffixes shall occur after a root that has an anudātta vowel as its final phoneme, and after a root marked with the *ṅit* indicator. Examples: *āste* (he sits), *vardhate* (he grows). Regarding the *ṅit* indicator: *plavate* (he floats), *śete* (he lies down), *haṃsāyate* (he acts like a swan), *plavamānaḥ* (floating), *pavamānaḥ* (purifying), *śayānaḥ* (lying down). The rule applies specifically to the root as taught [in the Dhātupāṭha]. This is so that it does not apply when the *ṅit* status is merely extended by analogy, as in *uccukuṭiṣati* (he desires to frown repeatedly). Regarding the "state" (*bhāva*) and the "object" (*karman*): the *ātmanepada* shall occur after all roots in the sense of the state and in the sense of the object. In the sense of the state: *sthīyate tvayā* (you are standing), *vismīyate mayā* (I am being amazed). In the sense of the object: *kriyate kaṭaḥ* (the mat is being made).

When there is reciprocal action, the ātmanepada occurs in the sense of the agent when there is an exchange of actions. For example: *vyatibhavate śrīḥ padmānām* (fortune reciprocally manifests among the lotuses); *vyatibhavamānāḥ puruṣāḥ* (men are mutually overcoming one another); *vyatilunante vīrāḥ* (heroes cut each other down).
This does not apply to roots meaning motion or injury.
