In these cases, when there is an exchange of action (*kriyāvinimaya*), that [suffix] does not occur after the verbal root. For example: *vyatigacchanti* (they go against one another), *vyatihiṃsanti* (they injure one another). And also after roots such as *has* (to laugh) and others: *vyatihasanti* (they laugh at one another), *vyatijalpeyuḥ* (they would chatter with one another). [The rule applies] only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed: *vyatigamyante grāmāḥ* (the villages are being traversed by one another). There is no prohibition for the root *hṛ* (to take): *saṃpraharante yodhāḥ* (the warriors strike at one another).
And also when the words *itaretara*, *anyonya*, and [the word formed with] *upapada* are used:

there is no such [substitution] for a verbal root joined with these two. For example: *itaretarasya vyatilunanti* ("they cut one another's [crops]"), *anyonyasya vyatipibanti jalam* ("they drink water from one another"). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), [the substitution is also absent] when *paraspara* is used: *parasparasya vyatilunanti*.
[The substitution occurs] after the prefix *ni-* when followed by the root *viś-*.

The ātmanepada suffix shall occur after the root *viś* when preceded by the prefix *ni*. Example: *niviśate*. How is it that [the expression] "bees enter into honey" (*madhuni viśanti bhramarāḥ*) is possible? It is because it is based on figurative usage (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*).
After the prefixes *pari*, *vi*, and *ava*, the suffix *kriyaḥ* (i.e., the root *krī*) shall take that [ātmanepada suffix]. Examples: *parikrīṇīte*, *vikrīṇīte*, *avakrīṇīte*.
After the prefixes *vi* and *parā*, the suffix *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *ji*. Thus: *vijayate* (he conquers), *parājayate* (he is defeated).
After the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *dā*, except in the sense of opening the mouth.

The suffix *sta* shall be applied after the root *dāñ* (to give) when preceded by the prefix *ā*. Example: *ādatte dhanam* (he takes the wealth). Why is it said "not when meaning the opening of the mouth"? Consider: *vyādadāti mukham* (he opens his mouth). How then is [the form] "kiṃ vyādatse vihaga vadanam" (O bird, why do you open your beak? explained? It will occur in the sense of the agent's own intention (*kartrabhiprāya*). The suffix *sta* shall also be applied after the root *krīḍ* (to play) when preceded by *anu*, *sam*, *pari*, and *ā*. Examples: *anukrīḍate*, *saṃkrīḍate*, *parikrīḍate*, *ākrīḍate*.

Because of the mention [of the root] *kuji* in the sense of "not making a sound," [the rule does not apply] here: "The chariots are racing. With the root *ā-gam*, the Ātmanepada occurs in the sense of "endurance": "Wait for a while, O boy"; the meaning is "do not hasten.

With the root *śikṣ*, [the Ātmanepada occurs] in the sense of "desire to learn": "He learns the arts"; "he learns the sciences. This is a form derived from the root *śak* with the desiderative suffix (*san*).

The root *nāth* is used with the sense of "blessing" (*āśis*): *sarpiṣo nāthate gṛdhnuḥ* ("the greedy man prays for clarified butter"). Regarding the root *hṛ*, [it is used] in the sense of "having gone" (*gata*) when it denotes habitual action (*tācchīlya*). Bhartṛhari states that the words *vidha*, *prakāra*, and *tulya* have the same meaning; thus, the suffix *sta* (forming *hṛt*) occurs after *hṛ* in the sense of habitual practice of similarity (*sādṛśya-śīlana*). Examples: *jaladhimanuharate saraḥ* ("the lake imitates the ocean"), *paitṛkamaśvā anuharante* ("the horses imitate their father"). However, the *Nyāsa* commentary maintains that it is used when the habitual action is a movement (*gati-tācchīlya*). Regarding the root *kṛ* (in the form *kirati*), it is used in the senses of joy (*harṣa*), livelihood (*jīvikā*), and making a lair (*kulāya-karaṇa*). Examples: *apaskirate vṛṣabho hṛṣṭaḥ* ("the bull wallows in joy"); *apaskirate kukkuṭo bhakṣyārthī* ("the cock wallows seeking food"); *apaskirate śvāśrayārthī* ("the dog wallows seeking shelter").

[The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied] after the roots *nu* and *praccha* when preceded by the prefix *ā*. *Ānute śivā*: it means she curses. *Āpṛcchate*: "Farewell to that dear friend; embrace this lofty mountain. After the root *śap*, [the *ātmanepada* is used] in the sense of making a formal declaration (*upalambhana*). "A lover makes a declaration (*śapate*) to his beloved.
[The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied] after the root *sthā* when preceded by *sam*, *ava*, *pra*, and *vi*.
From these [roots], there occurs *tiṣṭhate*: *santiṣṭhate*, *avatiṣṭhate*, *pratiṣṭhate*, and *vitiṣṭhamānaḥ*.
After the prefix *āṅ*, the root *sthā* is used in the sense of "promising": the Buddhists maintain (*ātiṣṭhante*) that an entity is momentary.
Also [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after [the root *sthā*] in the senses of "manifesting" and "presiding."

In this context, the suffix *sthāt* (the present participle suffix *śatṛ*) would apply. A courtesan stands by wealthy men (*dhanibhyaḥ tiṣṭhate vaiśyā*); the meaning is that she reveals her own [desire]. People stand before the king (*nṛpatau tiṣṭhate janaḥ*); the meaning is that they act as if he were a pillar (*stheyaṃ*). With the prefix *ud*, it applies except when the action is upward; *udasthāt* would apply when there is no upward movement. He stands for his own sake (*svārtheṣu uttiṣṭhate*). People stand up for pearls (*muktāsu uttiṣṭhate janaḥ*); the meaning is that they exert themselves toward them.
Why is the mention of *anūrdhva* (not upward) made? [Consider: "The Imperishable One rose quickly from his seat.
[This applies] when the prefix *upa-* is used with the verb *sthā* (to stand) and a mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*). A Brāhmaṇa worships the sun with the Gāyatrī.

It should be stated that [the suffix *upāt*] is used in the sense of "worship," "association," "making friends," and "a path. A Brahmin worships the sun (*vipra upatiṣṭhate 'rkam*). The Gaṅgā flows toward the ocean (*gaṅgā samudram upatiṣṭhate*). A king pays homage to a king (*rājā rājānam upatiṣṭhate*). This path leads to the wood-apple tree (*ayaṃ panthāḥ kapitthīm upatiṣṭhate*).
Or, it is used when there is a desire for gain (*lipsāyām*): A seeker approaches a donor (*arthī dātāram upatiṣṭhate* or *upatiṣṭhati*).
And [it is also used] after an intransitive verb (*akarmakāt*).

The root *sthā* (to stand) takes the *ātmanepada* when preceded by *upa*. As long as it stands near for the purpose of eating, it is so used. In the group of four sūtras beginning with this, the rule applies to intransitive roots.

The root *tap* (to heat) takes the *ātmanepada* after the prefixes *ud* and *vi*. Thus: *uttapate* (shines forth) and *vitapate* (shines forth) the sun. Only when intransitive: *uttapati suvarṇaṃ suvarṇakāraḥ* (the goldsmith heats the gold).

[The affix *śyan* is applied] also after [the roots *vitap* and *vyāyām*] when their object is one's own limb (*svāṅga*). [Examples: *vitapate svaṃ śṛṣṭham* ("he fans his own hair"). After the roots *yam* and *han* preceded by the prefix *ā*, [the same applies].

[Examples: *āyacchate* ("he stretches out"); *vyāyacchamānaḥ* ("striving"); *āhate* ("he strikes"). [The affix *śyan* is applied] also after [the root *han*] when its object is one's own limb. [Example: *āhate svaṃ vakṣaḥ* ("he strikes his own chest").

The suffix *sa* (the *liṭ* affix *kvasu*) is applied after the roots *gam*, *ṛcchi*, *pracchi*, *svarati*, *ṛ*, *śru*, and *vid*, when preceded by the prefix *sam*. From *gam*: *saṅgacchate*; *sañjagme*. From *ṛcchi*: *samṛcchate*; *samṛcchiṣyate*. From *pracchi*: *sampṛcchate*. From *svarati*: *saṃsvarate*. From *ṛ*: *samṛcchate*; *samiyṛte*. From *śru*: *saṃśṛṇute*. From *vid* in the sense of "knowing": *saṃvitte*. [This rule applies] only when [the roots] are intransitive (*akarmaka*). [Example of a transitive usage: *vādaṃ saṅgacchati* ("he joins the conversation"). It should be stated that [the suffix *sa* is also applied] after *dṛś*: *sampaśyate*.

The affix *hva* is applied after these [prefixes]: *ni*, *sam*, *upa*, and *vi*. Thus, from the root *hve* (to call), that [affix] occurs after them: *nihvayate tvām* (he calls you); *saṃhvayate sakhīm* (he calls his friend together); *upahvayate*; *vihvayate*.
There is an optional statement regarding the prefix before the roots *as* (to throw) and *ūh* (to push): *nirasyati* or *nirasyate*; *samūhan* or *samūhamānaḥ*.

Regarding the prefix *āṅ* [with the root *hveñ*]: the suffix *tat* (the *ātmanepada* endings) shall occur after the root *hveñ* when it means "to challenge" (*spardhā*). For example: *mallo mallam āhvayate* ("one wrestler challenges another wrestler").

[The suffix *tat* occurs] after the root *kṛñ* when it signifies: threatening (*gandhana*), casting down (*avakṣepaṇa*), serving (*sevana*), violence (*sāhasikya*), preparation (*pratiyatna*), narration (*prakathana*), and employment (*upayoga*).

The suffix *ta* (the *kṛt* suffix *kvip*) occurs after the root *kṛ* (*kṛñ*) in the following senses: 1. **Hinting at injury** (*hiṃsāsūcanam*, i.e., *gandhana*): *udākurute*. 2. **Threatening or reviling** (*bhartsanam*, i.e., *avakṣepaṇam*): *utkurute śatrūn* ("he threatens his enemies"). 3. **Service** (*sevanam*): *nṛpaṃ prakurute* ("he serves the king"). 4. **Violence** (*sāhasam*): *parastrīṃ prakurute* ("he commits violence against another's wife"). 5. **Appropriation for religious purposes, etc.** (*dharmādyupayoga*): *śataṃ prakurute* ("he appropriates a hundred [coins] for dharma, etc."). 6. **Refinement or improvement** (*pratiyatna*): In this sense, the genitive case is used and the augment *suṭ* is added. *guṇānām upaskurute* ("he refines the qualities"). 7. **Proclamation** (*prakathanam*): *saddharmaṃ prakurute* ("he proclaims the true Dharma"). 8. **Overpowering** (*adheḥ prasahanam*):

*Prasahana* means overcoming (*abhibhava*) or neglect (*upekṣā*). In these cases, the suffix *ta* occurs after *adhi-kṛ*. *tam adhicakre* ("he overcame him"); *bhavādṛśāś ced adhikurvate ratim* ("if those like you were to take pleasure [in it]").
[The suffix *yaṅ* is applied] after the root *vi* when it has sound as its object;
that [suffix] occurs after the root *kṛ* when it has sound as its object. For example: *kroṣṭā vikurute svarān* ("the jackal modulates his cries").
It also occurs after [roots] that are intransitive (*akarmaka*).

After the root *kṛ*, when it is intransitive, that [ātmanepada] shall occur. "The students transform themselves" (*vikurvate chātrāḥ*); the meaning is that they act according to their own will. [The root] *ni* [takes the ātmanepada] in the senses of honoring, piling up, acting as a teacher, knowing, hiring, counting, and spending.

In these senses, when accompanied by these qualifiers, the root *nī* (to lead) takes the suffix *ṇic*. He leads the meaning of the scripture; he establishes it through logical arguments. He initiates a child [into learning]; he raises him up. He initiates a disciple; he treats him as his own self, making him an instructor. The wise man leads matters; he brings them within the scope of knowledge. He employs laborers; he brings servants near. *Vigaṇana* means the clearing of debts and so forth. The Madras pay a tax; they remit it. Regarding expenditure: he spends a hundred [coins] on dharma and other such ends. And [the suffix *ṇic* is used] when the object resides in the agent and is not corporeal.

When the object (*karman*) is not the body (*aśarīra*), the prefix *vi-* [is used with the root *ṇī*]. One subdues anger (*krodhaṃ vinayate*). One subdues resentment (*manyuṃ vinayate*). Why say "when the object resides in the agent" (*kartṛsthe*)? [Because in: "He subdues the teacher’s wrath" (*guroḥ kopaṃ vinayati*). Why say "not the body"? [Because in: "He removes a goiter" (*gaḍuṃ vinayati*). By the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) principle, it is understood that this applies only after the prefix *vi-*. [Examples of other prefixes: "He raises up anger" (*krodhaṃ samunnayati*). "O proud woman, cast away your pride" (*apanaya mānini mānam*). The root *kram* is used in the senses of movement (*vṛtti*), beginning (*sarga*), and extension (*tāyana*). It is also used for non-obstruction (*apratighāta*), exertion (*utsāha*), and expansion (*sphītatva*). [Examples: "His intellect moves toward the mantra" (*mantre 'sya kramate buddhiḥ*). "The soldier advances for battle" (*yuddhāya kramate bhaṭaḥ*). "The scriptures penetrate the wise man" (*prājñe śāstrāṇi kramante*).

[The suffix] *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *kram* when preceded by these two [prefixes], *upa* and *parā*, according to the immediately preceding rule. For example: "In this mantra, his intellect exerts itself" (*asyopakramate buddhiḥ*), or "the warrior exerts himself for battle" (*yuddhāya parākramate bhaṭaḥ*), and so forth.
[The suffix *ātmanepada* occurs] after the root *kram* when preceded by *āṅ* in the sense of rising up (*udgamana*).

The suffix *ātmanepada* shall occur after the root *kram* following the prefix *ā*. Example: *ākramate bhānuḥ* (the sun ascends). This does not apply when the meaning is "the rising of light": *ākrāmati dhūmo harmyatalam* (the smoke spreads over the roof-terrace). Why specify "rising"? [Consider: *ākrāmati giriṃ raviḥ* (the sun traverses the mountain); here the meaning is "he takes hold of" (*avaṣṭabhnāti*). After the root *kram* following the prefix *vi*, the suffix *ātmanepada* occurs when it means "stepping with the feet. Example: *vikramate suṣṭhu aśvaḥ* (the horse strides well).

[The suffix *kṛt*] occurs after the roots *kram* preceded by the prefixes *pra* and *upa*, when these two are semantically connected [to the action], in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). For example: *prakramate bhoktum* (he begins to eat) and *upakramate śrotum* (he begins to listen).
Alternatively, it occurs even when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*).

After the prefix *apa*, the suffix *krama* may optionally take the suffix *śyan*. Thus: *kramate* or *krāmati*. After the root *jñā*, when used in the sense of concealment (*apahnava*), that same suffix is applied. Thus: *śatam apajānīte* ("he denies a hundred [having received it]").
And [the affix *śānac*] follows an intransitive verb.
That [affix] occurs after the root *jñā* when it is intransitive: *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he is aware of the ghee"). Here, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the instrument.
[The suffix *śānac* also occurs after roots preceded by the prefixes *sam-* and *prati-*,] except when the sense is that of "thinking about" (*anādhyāne*).

From these two [roots], the [action] would be known (*jña*). He recognizes the cow (*sañjānīte*). He promises to give the girl (*pratijānīte*). Why "except for recollection" (*anādhyāne*)? It is so that it does not apply to memory (*smṛti*). He remembers his mother (*mātuḥ saṃjānāti*); the meaning is "he recalls.
[The root] *vad* [is used] in the senses of appearing, addressing, knowing, effort, disagreement, and consultation.

When used with these meanings as qualifiers, it would be [conjugated] as follows: *bhāsana* (shining) is *śobhā* (beauty). He speaks beautifully in the Lokāyata system; he is speaking. *Upasambhāṣā* (addressing) is *upasāntvana* (consoling). He speaks kindly to the child. Regarding knowledge: this one speaks alone. Regarding effort: he speaks in the house. Regarding diverse opinion: the farmers dispute over the field. *Upamantraṇa* (persuading) is secret inquiry. He speaks to another's wife. In the utterance of distinct speech:

The [affix *śatṛ*] shall be used when expressing the simultaneous speech (*sahokti*) of humans. Example: *sampravadante viprāḥ* ("the Brahmins speak together"). Why specify "of those with distinct speech" (*vyaktavācām*)? Consider: *varatanu saṃpravadanti kukkuṭāḥ* ("O fair-limbed one, the cocks are crowing"). Why specify "in simultaneous speech"? Consider: *krameṇa vadanti chātrāḥ* ("the students speak in succession"). [The affix *śatṛ* is used] after the root *vad* preceded by *anu*, provided it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Example: *anuvadate kaṭhaḥ kalāpasya* ("Kaṭha repeats after Kalāpa"). The meaning is that he speaks in the same manner as him. Why specify "intransitive"? Consider: *pūrvoktamanuvadati* ("he repeats what was previously said").

The term *vibhāṣā* applies when there is idle chatter (*vipralāpa*). When there is simultaneous utterance consisting of idle chatter, the suffix *vat* may optionally be used after the root *vad*. For example: *vibravante gaṇakāḥ* or *vibravanti gaṇakāḥ* ("the accountants chatter"). Why "in simultaneous utterance"? [Observe: *krameṇa vadanti chātrāḥ* ("the students speak in succession").
After the root *vad*, the suffix *ghra* [is applied].
The suffix *niṣṭhā* (kta) may occur after the root *gṛ* [meaning "to swallow"] when preceded by *ava*. One swallows meat (*avagīrṇaṃ māṃsam*). They swallow beans (*avagīrṇā māṣāḥ*).
After the root *gṛ* meaning "to promise" when preceded by *sam*, that same suffix occurs. One promises a duty or a word (*kāryaṃ śabdaṃ saṅgirate*).

The suffix *ghan* occurs after the root *car-* when it is preceded by the prefix *ut-* and is transitive (*sakarmaka*). [Example: *raja udacarat* (dust rose up). The meaning is "it goes having ascended. Why "when it is transitive"? [Counter-example: *śaṅkhadhvanir udacarat* (the sound of the conch rose up); *nāda uccarati* (a sound issues forth). [The suffix *ghan* also occurs] after [the root *car-*] when it is joined with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and the prefix *sam-*.

When used in conjunction with a word ending in the third case, [the suffix *saN*] would apply to the root *sam-car*. A *vidyādhara* moves about by means of a chariot (*rathena sañcarate vidyādharaḥ*). And regarding the root *dāṇ* (to give), if it is used in the sense of the fourth case, the third case should be prescribed for the sense of the fourth case when referring to the conduct of the unrefined (*aśiṣṭa-vyavahāra*). The [suffix *saN*] would apply to that which is connected with such [a word in the third case], signifying the recipient (*sampradāna*). "The lover bestows a garland upon the maidservant" (*dāsyā mālāṃ samprayacchate kāmukaḥ*). The meaning is: "He gives a garland to the maidservant" (*dāsyai mālāṃ dadāti*).

The suffix *san* is applied after the roots *jñā*, *śru*, *smṛ*, and *dṛś* when preceded by *upa*. The root *yam* with the prefix *upa* takes this suffix in the sense of "accepting" (*svīkāra*). For example: *kanyām upayacchate* ("he marries the girl"). Also: *upāyaṃsta mahāstrāṇi* ("he acquired the great weapons") and *upāyaṃsata nāsavam* ("they accepted the wine"); the meaning here is that they did not accept it. The suffix *san* is also applied after these four roots when preceded by *upa*.

This [suffix] occurs after these [roots] ending in *san* (desiderative): he desires to know dharma (*dharmam jijñāsate*); he desires to serve the teacher (*gurum śuśrūṣate*); he desires to remember (*susmūrṣate*); he desires to see (*didṛkṣate*).
[However,] not after *jñā* following *anu*: that [suffix] does not occur after *jñā* when preceded by *anu*. He desires to know [it] after [hearing it from] his son (*putram anujijñāsati*).

[The suffix *liṭ* is replaced by *kvasu*] after the root *śru* when preceded by *prati* or *āṅ*. This does not apply to the root *śru* followed by the causative marker (*san*) when preceded by those two prefixes. [Examples: *pratiśuśrūṣati*, *āśuśrūṣati*.
[The substitution of *śn* for the root vowel occurs] for the root *śad* when followed by a suffix marked with *ś* or *it*.
The ātmanepada ending shall occur after the root *śad* when it is caused by a suffix marked with *ś* (śit). Examples: *śīyate*, *śītaḥ*. Why "caused by a śit suffix"? [Counter-example: *śatsyati*.

[The ātmanepada ending] shall occur after the root *mṛ* in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses, and also when caused by a śit suffix. Examples: *amṛta*, *mṛṣīṣṭa*, *mriyate*. Why is this a restrictive rule (*niyama*)? [Counter-examples: *mariṣyati*, *mamāra*.
By the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the agent (*kartṛ*): "The heroes died like moths.

As before, [the rule] concerning *san*: the *ātmanepada* ending shall occur after a root with *san* just as it would after a root without *san*. *āste*, *āsisiṣate*; *vijayate*, *vijigīṣate*; *pacati*, *pacate*, *pipakṣati*, *pipakṣate*.

Regarding the employment of *kṛ* following a root ending in the *ām* affix: the same [rules] that apply to a root ending in the *ām* affix also apply to the *kṛ* employed after it. For example: *ihate*, *ihāñcakre*.
[Also, the *ātmanepada* endings are used] with *yuj* preceded by *pra* or *upa*, except when referring to sacrificial vessels.

The suffix *ta* (the ātmanepada) shall occur after the root *yuj* when preceded by the prefixes *pra* and *upa*. He employs (*prayuṅkte*). He employs (*upayuṅkte*). Not here: "The wise man employs the sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātrāṇi prayunakti*).

It should be stated that [the suffix occurs] after *yuj* when it is preceded by a vowel or by a prefix ending in a vowel. He exerts himself (*udyuṅkte*). He appoints (*niyuṅkte*). He employs (*upayuṅkte*). How is it that [the form] "he employed (*ayayuṅkta*) to know the conduct among his subjects" occurs from the root alone? It will occur in the sense of the agent's own interest (*kartrabhiprāya*). [The suffix *ta* occurs] after the root *kṣṇu* when preceded by *sam*.
That [suffix] should occur after the root *śvi* (to sharpen). As in: *saṃkṣṇute śastram* ("he sharpens the weapon").
[The suffix] occurs after the root *bhuj* when not meaning "to protect.

As in: *bhuṅkte*, *bhuñjāte*. Why say "not meaning to protect"? Consider: *bhunakti rājā pṛthvīm* ("the king enjoys the earth"), which means "he protects. It was not stated that [the suffix occurs] after *bhuj* only in the sense of "eating," so that it may also occur in the sense of "experiencing": *sukhamanubhuṅkte* ("he experiences happiness").

In the case of a root ending in *ṇic*, that which was the object (*karman*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇic* form, provided it is not a case of remembering (*anādhyāne*). This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding cases where the action is intended to benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). The *ātmanepada* suffix shall occur after a root ending in *ṇic* if that which was the object in the *ṇic* form becomes the agent in the *ṇic* form. Example: *ārohati kareṇuṃ niṣādī* (The female elephant rider mounts the elephant). *ārohayate kareṇur niṣādinam* (The elephant causes the rider to mount itself). Example: *paśyanti bhṛtyā nṛpam* (The servants see the king). *darśayate bhṛtyān nṛpaḥ* (The king shows himself to the servants). Why "not in the case of remembering" (*anādhyāne*)? So that it does not apply to the act of remembering. *smarati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ* (The cuckoo remembers the forest thicket). *smarayaty enaṃ vanagulmaḥ svayam eva* (The forest thicket itself causes him to remember). [The *ātmanepada* occurs] after the roots *bhī* (to fear) and *smi* (to smile) when the cause of fear is the agent.

The suffix *ṇic* (ṇi) shall be applied after the roots *bhī* and *smi* when they are in the causative form (*ṇyanta*). *muṇḍo bhīṣayate* ("the shaven-headed one causes fear"). *jaṭilo vismāpayate* ("the matted-haired ascetic causes amazement"). What is the purpose of the condition "when there is fear caused by an agent" (*hetubhaye*)? *Kāṣṭhikayā bhāyayati* ("he causes fear by means of a piece of wood"). In this case, the fear arises from an instrument (*karaṇa*). The suffix *ṇic* is applied after the roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* in the causative form when meaning "deceiving" (*pralambhana*). *śiśuṃ gardhayate* ("he deceives the child"). *śiśuṃ vañcayate* ("he deceives the child"). What is the purpose of the condition "when meaning deceiving"? *Ahiṃ vañcayati bālaḥ* ("the boy avoids the snake"). Here, it simply means avoiding.

The suffix *ṇic* is applied after the root *lī* in the senses of honoring (*sammānana*) and making submissive (*śālīnīkaraṇa*). Likewise, it is applied after the causative (*ṇyantāt*) of *lī* in the senses of worship (*pūjā*), humiliation (*paribhava*), and deception (*pralambhana*). Examples: *jaṭābhir ālāpayate* (he honors [the guest] with matted locks); *śyeno varttikām ullāpayate* (the hawk deceives the quail); *śiśum ullāpayate* (he deceives the child). In other cases, it is used as *kanyām ullāpayati* (he deceives the girl).
Furthermore, the suffix *ṇic* is applied after the root *kṛñ* when preceded by a false word (*mithyā*) in the sense of repetition (*abhyāsa*).

After a root ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*, that [suffix] occurs when there is repetition (*abhyāsa*), meaning repeated occurrence. For example: *mithyā kārayate padam* ("he causes the word to be pronounced incorrectly again and again").

The *ātmanepada* endings occur after a root marked with a svarita accent or one marked with the suffix *ñi*, provided the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*). If the agent intends the result of the action for himself, the *ātmanepada* shall be used after a root having a svarita accent or the suffix *ñi*. Examples: *pacate* ("he cooks for himself"), *yajate* ("he sacrifices for himself"). Regarding roots marked with *ñi*: *kurute* ("he does for himself"), *kaṇḍūyate* ("he scratches for himself"). Why "provided the fruit accrues to the agent"? To prevent it from applying when the purpose is for another. Examples: *pacati* ("he cooks for another"), *karoti* ("he does for another"), *yajati* ("he sacrifices for another"). How is it that forms such as *vikrīṇīte* ("he sells for another") and *prayuṅkte* ("he employs for another") occur even when the purpose is for another? This is because of specific rules (*viśeṣavidhāna*) regarding the roots *krī* (to buy), *dā* (to give), *hu* (to sacrifice), *kṛ* (to do), *hṛ* (to take), *nī* (to lead), and *yuj* (to join).
The suffix *ap* is used after the root *vad* [when compounded with a word denoting the object of censure].
That would be so: one who desires grain censures justice; one who desires wealth censures justice. [The suffix *ap* is also used] after a causative (*ṇic*) verb.

The same [ātmanepada] would apply after a causative (*ṇijanta*) verb: *kārayate* (he causes to do), *pācayate* (he causes to cook). However, when it is for the sake of another, one says *kārayati* (he causes to do) or *pācayati* (he causes to cook).

After the root *yam-* preceded by *sam*, *ud*, or *ā*, the [ātmanepada] occurs except in the sense of a book (*agranthe*): *saṃyacchate indriyāṇi* (he restrains his senses), *udyacchate bhāram* (he lifts a burden), *āyacchate vastram* (he stretches out a garment), *āyaṃsta pādam* (he stretched out his foot). Why "except in the sense of a book"? [Because] a physician exerts himself toward medical treatment (*cikitsām udyacchati vaidyaḥ*).
The suffix *niṣṭhā* (past participle) is applied after the root *jñā* when it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*).

It should be understood in the same way: *gāṃ jānīte* ("he recognizes the cow [as his own]"); *parārthe gāṃ jānāti* ("he recognizes the cow for the sake of another"). How is it that one says *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he recognizes the clarified butter")? Because the rule "also after an intransitive verb" (*akarmakācca*) prescribes its application even in the sense of acting for another.
Furthermore, the suffix is optional (*vibhāṣā*) when the object is already understood through an accompanying word (*upapada*).

When the intention of the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya*) is understood from the context of the proximate word, that [ātmanepada] may occur; for example: *svaṃ kaṭaṃ kurute* or *karoti* ("he makes a mat for himself"). In this manner, it should be inferred through the five sūtras. Thus, the [use of] ātmanepada when the intention of the agent is expressed has been stated. Now, the parasmaipada [is taught] by means of eleven sūtras.
*Śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam* ("From the remainder, parasmaipada occurs in the sense of the agent"):

Parasmaipada shall occur in the sense of the agent after a verbal root (*dhātu*) that is devoid of ātmanepada endings. Examples: *yāti*, *vāti*, *praviśati*. Why "from the remainder" (*śeṣāt*)? [Consider: *rocate* ("it pleases").
After the prefixes *anu* and *parā*, the root *kṛ* takes the *parasmaipada* even when used in its own sense (*svārtha*). Thus: *anukaroti*, *parākaroti*.
After *abhi*, *prati*, and *ati*, the root *kṣip* [takes the *parasmaipada*].
From these [roots], *kṣip* would be used as follows: *abhikṣipati*, *pratikṣipati*, *atikṣipati*.
Likewise, from *vah* preceded by *pra*, it would be used as follows: *pravahati*.
*pari-mṛśaḥ*. That would be [the case]. *pari-mṛśati*.
[The suffix *khaś* is applied] after the root *ram*, when preceded by *vi*, *āṅ*, or *pari*.

The suffix *iṣṇu* shall be applied after these [verbs] when preceded by *vi*: *viramati*, *vyaraṃsīt*. It shall also be applied after these when preceded by *ā* or *pari*: *āramati*, *pariramati*. Why [mention] "after these"? [Consider: *abhiramate*. It shall also be applied after [the verb *ram*] when preceded by *upa*:
*upādrameṣṇu* shall be applied. Example: *devadattam uparamati*. Here, the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*) is understood.

[The rule] *vibhāṣā 'karmakāt* [states that] after an intransitive verb, there may optionally be [the substitution of *ta* for *ti*]. For example: *bhojanād uparamati* or *uparamate*. Now, since [the rule] *ṇicaś ca* would otherwise apply, he states three exceptions:
*budha-yudha-naśa-jana-iṅ-pru-dru-srubhyaḥ ṇeḥ*.

The *parasmaipada* suffix shall occur after roots such as *budh* when followed by the causative marker *ṇic*. He causes the lotus to bloom (*bodhayati padmam*). He causes the wood to fight (*yodhayati kāṣṭham*). He causes sin to perish (*nāśayati pāpam*). He causes happiness to arise (*janayati sukham*). He causes the pupil to study (*adhyāpayati śiṣyam*). The wise man causes wealth to flow forth (*prāvayaty arthān dhīraḥ*). He causes the metal to melt (*drāvayati lauham*). He causes the small pot to drip (*srāvayati kuṇḍīm*). And [the *parasmaipada* occurs] after roots meaning "swallowing" and "moving. It shall occur after those ending in *ṇic* which mean "eating" and "shaking. He causes to eat (*āśayati*). He causes to feed (*bhojayati*). He causes to move (*calayati*). The wind causes the branch to shake (*kampayati śākhāṃ vātaḥ*).
There is a prohibition regarding the root *ad* (to eat). Example: *ādayate 'nnaṃ putreṇa pitā* (The father causes the son to eat food). [Rule:

After a causative (*ṇi*) verb derived from a non-causative (*aṇ*) root that is intransitive and has a sentient agent (*cittavat-kartṛka*), the Parasmaipada endings shall be used. Examples: *āste vipraḥ* (The Brahmin sits); *āsayati vipram* (He causes the Brahmin to sit). *śāyayati mitram* (He causes the friend to lie down). Why "having a sentient agent"? [Counter-example: *śoṣayate vrīhīn ātapaḥ* (The sun dries the rice). [Note: Only when used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Counter-example: *śāyate vipro bhavatā* (The Brahmin is made to lie down by you).

The roots *pā* (to drink), *dam* (to tame), *āṅ-ya* (to stretch), *āṅ-ya* (to exert), *pari-muh* (to be bewildered), *ruc* (to please), *nṛt* (to dance), *vad* (to speak), and *vas* (to dwell) do not take the *parasmaipada* endings by virtue of the two preceding rules. Consequently, they shall take only the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (the affix *śānac*) endings. Examples: *pāyayate ghṛtam* (he causes himself to drink ghee). *damayate śatrūn* (he tames his enemies). *āyāmayate* (he stretches himself). *āyāsayate* (he exerts himself). *āyāsayamānaḥ* (exerting himself). *parimohayate* (he deludes himself). *rocayate* (he finds pleasure). *narttayate* (he causes himself to dance). *vādayate* (he causes himself to be played [an instrument]). *vāsayate* (he causes himself to dwell). However, when the action does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*), the *parasmaipada* is used: *damayati gajam* (he tames the elephant). *narttayati bhujam* (he makes the arm dance). *bhikṣāṃ vāsayati* (he causes alms to be dwelt upon—i.e., he begs for alms). An addition must be made for the root *dhēṭ* (to suckle): *dhāpayate śiśum* (she causes the infant to suckle). Or, the *kyap* affix may optionally be applied.
The ātmanepada suffix may optionally follow a root ending in *kyap*. For example: *lohitāyati* or *lohitāyate*.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, after roots beginning with *dyut*, the ātmanepada suffix may optionally occur. For example: *vyadyutat* or *vyadyotiṣṭa*. There are twenty-two such roots beginning with *dyut*.

After the roots *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *śṛdh*, and *syand*, [the augment *iṭ*] may optionally be applied before the suffixes *sya* (the future marker) and *san* (the desiderative marker). Thus: *vartsyati* or *vartiṣyate*; *avartsyat* or *avartiṣyata*; *vivṛtsati* or *vivarttiṣate*. Furthermore, [the augment *iṭ* is optional] after the root *klṛp* when followed by the suffix *luṭ* (the periphrastic future).

In the case of the root *klṛp*, the [suffixes] *luṭ*, *syasana* (the future and periphrastic future suffixes), and the [desiderative suffix] *sa* may optionally take that [same form]. Thus: *kalptāsi* or *kalpitāse*; *kalpsyati* or *kalpiṣyate*; *akalpsyat* or *akalpiṣyata*; *ciklṛpsati* or *cikalpiṣate*. Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Preceptor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.
The section on *bhūpāda* is completed.
This is the fourth quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*adhyāya*). From here up to the word *kaḍāra*, there shall be only one technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

Up to the rule *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye*, only one designation (*saṃjñā*) is to be understood [for each item]. That [designation] is sometimes without scope (*anavakāśā*), as for instance the designation *bh* [which applies to the final consonant of a root], which subverts the designation *pada*—which otherwise has scope—in forms such as *rājabhyām*; [whereas in other cases, like] *rājñā* or *rājñe*, the *bh*-designation prevails over the *pada*-designation. Sometimes [the designation] is subsequent (*parā*), as for instance the designation *bahuvrīhi*, which subverts the designation *tatpuruṣa* in the form *vīrapuruṣako grāmaḥ*. In this case, however, it must be stated that there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *aṅga*, *bha*, and *pada*. By virtue of that, in *bābhravyaḥ*, because of the status of being an *aṅga*, there is initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), and because of the status of being a *bha*, there is *guṇa* of the *i* [in *babhru*]. In *dhānuṣkaḥ*, because of the status of being an *aṅga*, there is initial *vṛddhi*, and because of the status of being a *pada*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *iṇ* [sound].

In the case of a conflict, the subsequent rule takes effect. When two rules of equal strength are in opposition, that which comes later shall be the operative rule. [Thus, by *supi ca*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs: *vṛkṣābhyām*. [By *bahuvacane jhalyet*, the substitution of *e* occurs: *vṛkṣeṣu*. In a conflict, the subsequent rule prevails: *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*. However, between an obligatory (*nitya*) and a non-obligatory (*anitya*) rule, the obligatory is stronger. Between an internal (*antaraṅga*) and an external (*bahiraṅga*) operation, the internal is stronger. And between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), the exception prevails. Feminine stems ending in *ī* and *ū* are termed *nadī*.

In this context, the word "stry-ākhyah" (called feminine) refers to the technical term *saṃjñī* [the thing to be named], while "ī, ū, yū" are its qualifiers; thus, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in those sounds (*tadantavidhiḥ*). That which ends in *ī* or *ū* and is feminine shall bear the technical name *nadī*. According to the *Bhāgavṛtti*, this designation applies only to those ending in *ī* and *ū*. Examples: *kumāryai*, *lakṣmyai*, *dhībandhvai*, *yavāgvai*. Why is the word "ākhyā" (called/named) included? It is so that the designation does not apply when femininity is expressed by another word, as in *senānye striyai* (to a female army commander). How then is the form *atilakṣmyai viprāya* (to a Brahmin who surpasses Lakṣmī) explained? And how about *bahupreyasyām rājani* (in a king who has many beloveds)? The *Bhāṣya* states that these are established because the designation applies to the feminine nature of the constituent parts (*avayava-strī-viṣayatvāt*).
[The following is the next rule: *neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī* (Those that do not stand in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are not [designated *nadī*], except for the word *strī*).

The vowels *i* and *u*, when they are the bases of feminine nouns (*vaṅādhārau*), do not receive the designation "nadī" (feminine stem). For example: *he śrīḥ*, *he dhīḥ*, *he bhrūḥ*. Why does the rule specify "not feminine" (*astrī*)? [To exclude cases like] *he stri*. Regarding the rule *vā''mi*: this prohibition may optionally apply before the suffix *ām*. Thus, one may have either *śriyām* or *śrīṇām*; *bhruvām* or *bhrūṇām*.

*ṅiti hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.6): When a *ṅit* [suffix] follows, there may be either this [prohibition of the *nadī* designation] or the designation *hrasva*. Thus: *śriyai* or *śriye*; *bhruvai* or *bhruve*; *bhuvi śete* (he lies on the earth). And regarding *hrasva*: when *ṅit* suffixes follow, the short *yū* (the vowels *i* and *u*) may optionally be designated as *nadī*. Thus: *matyai* or *mataye*; *dhenvai* or *dhenave*. Only those expressing feminine gender (*stryākhyau*) are so designated. Thus: *agraye*, *vāyave*. Here, the optional *nadī* designation applies to the *ami* case-ending and to *ṅit* suffixes, as well as to the *yū* that occupy the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. This is desired only for words denoting feminine; it is not based on the constituent parts [of a compound], according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*).
Thus, for *sumati*, *atiśrī*, *sudhī*, and *vipra*—that is, for the wise (*sudhī*) and the learned (*vipra*)—it becomes *mañjuśriyi sudhiyi vipre*.

The rule *śeṣo ghyasakhi* states: "The remainder, ending in a short *i* or *u*, excluding a river name, is designated as *ghi*. By the rule *gher ṅiti*, there is *guṇa* [substitution]. Thus: *agnaye*, *viṣṇave*, *vāyave*, *mataye*, *dhenave*. Why "excluding a friend" (*asakhi*)? [Because] *sakhyā*, *sakhye*, *sakhyuḥ*, *sakhyau*. Here, only that which ends in a short *i* or *u* is designated as *ghi*. Accordingly, in the rule *dvandve ghi*, it is stated that a word ending in *ghi* is placed first.

Therefore, because the vowel *i* in the word *sakhi* is prohibited from being designated as a *ghi* when it occurs in the form *asakhi*, they say that even though it is a constituent part of the word *sakhi*, in cases such as *bahusakhyā kṛtam* (done by one who has many female friends) and *bahusakhyuḥ svam* (the property of one who has many female friends), the designation does not apply. However, the *Nyāsa* commentary states *susakher āgacchati* (he comes from a good female friend).

*Patiḥ samāsa eva*: The word *pati* is designated as a *ghi* only in a compound (*samāsa*). Thus, *śrīpatinā*, *śrīpataye*, *śrīpateḥ*, and *śrīpatau* are formed. Not otherwise: *patyā*, *patye*, *patyuḥ*, and *patyau*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [a word] joined with a genitive case ending may optionally [be elided].
*Chandas* refers to the Vedic scriptures.
A short vowel is light (*laghu*).
A short vowel is called *laghu* (light). [Examples: *bhedanam*, *gardhanam*, *vardhanam*. In a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), it is heavy (*guru*).
When followed by a conjunct consonant, a short vowel is called *guru*. [Examples: *śikṣā*, *bhikṣā*.
And long [vowels]. A long syllable is called "heavy" (guru). For example: *ūhāñcakre*, *īhāñcakre*.
That which is the beginning of an element from which a suffix is prescribed is the "base" (*aṅga*) with respect to that suffix.

That which begins with the element after which an affix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed shall be designated as a *aṅga* (base). Examples: *kartṛ*, *kāraka*; *lavitr̥*, *lāvaka*. Why "that which begins with it" (*tadādi*)? [Consider: *kariṣyamāṇaḥ*, *pacāmaḥ*. If that which ends in a *syat* suffix were also treated as a *aṅga*, then the *muk* augment and vowel lengthening would apply. Why is there a repeated mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*)? So that [the designation] does not apply when the affix has been elided, even if another element follows. [Example: *śryartham*—here, *iyaṅ* substitution would otherwise have applied. *Suptiṅantaṃ padam*:
That which ends in a *sup* (nominal) suffix or a *tiṅ* (verbal) suffix shall be designated as a *pada* (word). Example: *chātrāḥ paṭhanti me*.

Before the particle *kye*, a word ending in *n* remains as such when followed by *kye*. Examples: *rājīyati*, *rājāyate*. Why is this a restrictive rule? [To show that it does not apply] in cases like *vācyati* or *tapasyati*. When the suffix *s* is present, the changes of *k* to *g* (*kutva*) and *r* to *ḍ* (*rutva*) do not occur. And [this applies] before the suffix *sit*.
The preceding element shall be a *pada*. [Examples: *chas* → *bhavadīyam*; *yus* → *ūrṇāyuḥ*. This subverts the designation *bha*.

In the domain of suffixes beginning with *sva-* (i.e., case endings) that are not *sarvanāmasthāna*, the preceding element shall be a *pada* up to the end of the suffix *kap*. [Examples: *rājabhyām*, *rājasu*; *rājatvam*, *rājatamaḥ*. Why specify "not a *sarvanāmasthāna*" (*asarvanāmasthāne*)? [Consider: *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*. How about in the nominative singular (*sau*)? Is it not the case that *rājā* is a *pada* there? No; because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*.

*Yaci bham*: Before suffixes beginning with *y* or *ac*, and those belonging to the *svādi* group (i.e., case endings), the preceding element shall be designated as *bha*. *Yi*: *gārgyaḥ*. *Aci*: *rājñaḥ paśya*. The restriction "not being a *sarvanāmasthāna*" applies here as well. Thus: *rājānau*, *sāmāni*.

There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* [to receive the *bha* designation] when followed by *vat*. The *bha* designation shall apply: *nabhasvat*, *aṅgirasvat*, *manusvat*. The substitution of *r* (dependent on the word boundary) does not occur. The *bha* designation must be stated for *vṛṣan* when followed by *vasu* and *aśva*. Thus: *vṛṣaṇvasuḥ*, *vṛṣaṇaśvaḥ*. The elision of the nasal *n* does not take place.
*tasau matvarthe*: When a suffix expressing possession (*matvartha*) follows, that which ends in *t* or *s* is designated as *bha*. Examples: *vidyutvān*, *marutvān*, *payasvī*, *tapasvī*, *yaśasvī*.
*ayasmayādīni chandasi*: Words such as *ayasmaya* (made of iron) and others are so designated in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
This is one *chandas* (Vedic) rule:

the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is used for many [objects]. Since the rules for case-endings (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are prescribed without distinction [between singular, dual, and plural], and because we observe such usage in common worldly parlance—as in "your eyes are red" (*akṣīṇi te rakte*)—this restriction is established: the plural number shall be used only when there are many referents. For example: "The monks recite the True Dharma" (*bhikṣavaḥ saddharmān paṭhanti*); "The Brahmins sing the *Sāman* hymns" (*vipraiḥ sāmāni gīyante*).

The dual and singular endings occur for two and one [respectively]. The dual and singular endings shall occur only when there is duality and singularity of meaning; for example: *mātāpitarau janayataḥ* (the mother and father produce) and *dharma rakṣati rakṣitaḥ* (Dharma protects when protected). [This applies] in the context of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*).
This is a governing heading (adhikāra). Henceforth, whatever will be stated should be understood as applying among the *kārakas*. For example:
"That which is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to departure (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*."

In the case of separation (*viśleṣa*), that which is the constant factor (*dhruva*) shall be the *apādāna* (ablative). And that [is] "of some [type] where the object is explicitly stated" (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*): "The leaf falls from the tree. "He has risen from the water. "Likewise, that where the object is implied" (*upāttaviṣaya*): "Lightning flashes from the cloud. [Here] the word "having emerged" (*niḥsṛtya*) is to be supplied. "He desists from unrighteousness" (*adharmād viramati*). "He feels aversion toward unrighteousness" (*adharmāj jugupsate*). The meaning is that, while desisting and feeling aversion, he turns away from that. "And that where the action is expected" (*apekṣitakriya*); thus the *apādāna* is held to be threefold: "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Srughna."

By rule, the action of excellence (*utkarṣa*) is understood; thus, [the term] "agent" (*kāraka*) alone [is used]. In the example "a leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), [the word *parṇa*] is not [an agent] because it is other than many [agents]. From the word "agent," the suffix *śas* is not applied.
For verbs meaning "fear" or "protection," the cause of fear [is the locus].

When a verbal root is used in the sense of protection from fear (*bhaya-trāṇa*), the cause of that fear shall be the *apādāna* [ablative case]. Examples: *caurād bhītaḥ* (frightened by a thief); *vyāghrād apatrastaḥ* (terrified by a tiger); *dasyubhyo rakṣitaḥ* (protected from bandits). In the case of the root *parā-ji* (to be defeated), that which is "unbearable" (*asoḍha*) shall be the *apādāna*. When the root *parā-ji* is employed, that which cannot be endured shall be the *apādāna*. Examples: *adhyayanāt parājayate mandabuddhiḥ* (the dull-witted one fails in his studies); *bhojanāt parājayate* (he gives up eating).

Regarding verbs meaning "to ward off" (*vāraṇārtha*), that which is desired (*īpsita*) [becomes the *apādāna*]. In the usage of these [verbs], the desired object shall be the *apādāna*. For example: *yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the cow away from the barley"). How is it that one says *kūpād andhaṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the blind man away from the well")? The meaning is that, having mentally reached [the well], he turns him back from there. [Also]: "In the sense of concealment (*antardhi*), [it is the person] by whom one desires to be unseen."

When, for whatever reason, one desires to become invisible—that is, to remain unseen—the [person from whom this is sought] shall be the *apādāna*. *Upādhyāyād antardhatte chātraḥ* (The student hides from the teacher). *Upādhyāyān nilīyate śiṣyaḥ* (The disciple conceals himself from the teacher). Regarding verbal instruction (*ākhyāta-upayoga*): when there is the formal acquisition of a statement according to a rule, the instructor (*pratipādayitṛ*) shall be the *apādāna*. *Paṇḍitāt purāṇaṃ śṛṇoti* (He hears the Purāṇa from the scholar). *Rāmād adhīta-sandeśaḥ* (Having received the message from Rāma).

The source (prakṛti) of that which acts as the agent of birth is the apādāna [kāraka]. The cause (kāraṇa), which is the source of that which is being born, shall be the apādāna. A fruit arises from a collection of causes (sāmagrī).
The origin (prabhava) of "to be" (bhū) [is the apādāna].

The source (*prabhava*) of an agent who produces something shall be the *apādāna*. For example: "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat" (*himavato gaṅgā prabhavati*). Also: "A fragment of Indra’s bow originates from the top of an anthill" (*valmīkāgrāt prabhavati dhanuṣkhaṇḍam ākhaṇḍalasya*).
That person whom one intends [to benefit] by means of an object is the *sampradāna*.

That [person] whom one connects with an action (*karman*) functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*) shall be the *kāraka* termed "recipient" (*sampradāna*). For example: "The righteous man gives a cow to the Brāhmaṇa"; "An angry man pays wealth to the teacher"; "The schoolmaster gave a slap on the ear to the pupil"; "He gives fear to the enemy. [One might ask: "Give terrors to Sītā. How is it that in the expressions "he gives cloth to the washerman" and "he gives a blow to the back of the striker," [the recipient is not so designated]? It is because the sense of "intending for" (*abhipraitṛ*) is not intended to be expressed, just as in the expression "giving is equal toward a non-Brāhmaṇa."

In this context, because it is the most desired object of the agent through actions such as praying or resolving, the action itself also becomes an *karman* (object). That which is connected with that action is the *sampradāna* (recipient), according to the very rule [Pāṇini 1.4.32]. Examples: *yuddhāya saṃnahyate* (he prepares for battle); *patye śete* (she lies down for her husband); *nivedyatāṃ sugrīvāya* (let it be announced to Sugrīva); *praṇamya śāstre sugatāya tāyine* (having bowed to the Teacher, the Sugata, the Protector). And here, in the case of *paśunā rudraṃ yajate* (he sacrifices a beast to Rudra), he pleases Rudra by means of the beast to be given; the actual meaning is "he gives the beast to Rudra. [The recipient is also the one being pleased] in the case of verbs meaning "to please" (*rucy-arthānām*).

When used with roots having the sense of "to please" (*ruc*), that which is being pleased shall be the *sampradāna*. Example: *nāradāya rocate kalahaḥ* ("The quarrel pleases Nārada"). This means the quarrel becomes an object of Nārada's liking.

In the case of the roots *ślāgh* (to praise), *hnuṅ* (to deny/steal), *sthā* (to stand), and *śap* (to swear), that which is intended to be made aware [of the action] shall be the *sampradāna*. Example: *nṛpāya ślāghate bandī* ("The bard praises the king"). *ślāghamānaḥ parastrībhyaḥ* ("Praising himself before the wives of others"). *putrāyāpahanute vaṇik* ("The merchant denies [the debt] to his son"). *chātrāya tiṣṭhate kanyā* ("The maiden stands [as a prize] for the student"). *priyāyai śapate kāmukaḥ* ("The lover swears by his beloved").
In the case of the root *dhāri* ("to owe"), the creditor is [the recipient].

When *dhāri* is employed, the moneylender shall be the recipient (*sampradāna*). Example: *viprāya śataṃ dhārayati* ("He owes a hundred to the Brahmin"). In the case of the root *spṛh* ("to desire"), the object of longing is [the recipient].
In construction with the verb *spṛh* ("to desire"), that toward which one desires becomes the *sampradāna*. Example: *dhanāya spṛhayati* ("he desires wealth").

In construction with verbs having the meaning of *krudh* ("to be angry"), *druh* ("to bear malice"), *īrṣyā* ("to envy"), or *asūyā* ("to find fault"), that person toward whom the anger is directed becomes the *sampradāna*. Example: *putrāya krudhyati* ("he is angry with his son"); *śatrave druhyati* ("he bears malice toward the enemy"); *ekasmai īrṣyati* ("he envies one person"); *anyasmai asūyati* ("he finds fault with another"). This does not apply here: *striyam īrṣyati kāmukaḥ* ("the lustful man envies a woman").
The object of the roots *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice) when preceded by prepositions is [the *karman*].

When *krudh* and *druh* are accompanied by prepositions, that toward whom the anger is directed shall be designated as the *karman*. For example: *putram abhikrudhyati* (he is angry with his son); *śatrum anudruhyati* (he bears malice toward his enemy).
[The object] of the roots *rādh* and *īkṣ* when there is an inquiry is [the *karman*].

In the employment of the roots *rādh* and *īkṣ*, that which one asks about in various ways shall be the *sampradāna*. *Putrāya rādhyati*: "He consults regarding his son"—that is, "Does he do this, or does he not? *Strībhya īkṣate*: "He looks at the women"—that is, "Who are they, and what are they like? Regarding the necessity of looking at the wives of others, Bhaṭṭi says: "This is the duty of protectors. With the prefixes *prati* and *āṅ* used with the root *śru* ("to hear"), the agent of the preceding action is the *sampradāna*. In the employment of the root *śru* preceded by *prati* and *āṅ*, the agent of the preceding action—such as a request—shall be the *sampradāna*. *Tubhyaṃ gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti*: "He promises a cow to you. *Mahyaṃ gām āśṛṇoti*: "He promises a cow to me. The meaning is that he accepts it.
And [the same applies] to one who responds in recitation.

And in the usage of this [verb], the agent of the preceding action shall be the recipient (*sampradāna*). For example: *hotre 'nugṛṇāti* (he responds to the Hotṛ-priest); *potrē pratigṛṇāti* (he responds to the Potṛ-priest). The meaning is that he follows with sound the one who is reciting, i.e., he encourages him. The most effective instrument is called the instrument (*karaṇa*). That which provides the most excellent assistance in the accomplishment of an action is termed the instrument. For example: *paraśunā vṛkṣaṃ chinatti* (he cuts the tree with an axe); *buddhyā jānāti* (he knows by means of the intellect). Due to the speaker's intention, it is said: "the axe cuts."
And [the word] *div* (to play/dice) has the object as its [kāraka].

That which is most effective in accomplishing the action of *div* may be either the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). For example: *durakṣān dīvyati rājñā* or *durakṣaiḥ* ("He plays with bad dice by means of the king").
In the sense of "bargaining for hire" (*parikrayaṇa*), [the word denoting the price] is optionally the recipient (*sampradāna*).

In the case of accepting wages and the like, the instrument (*karaṇa*) may optionally become the recipient (*sampradāna*). For example: *śatāya parikrītaḥ* or *śatena parikrītaḥ* ("bought for a hundred").

The locus (*ādhāra*) is the locus-case (*adhikaraṇa*). That which serves as a substratum is called the locus. For example: *gṛhe tiṣṭhati* ("he stands in the house") and *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("he cooks in a pot").
The object of the roots *adhi-śī*, *adhi-sthā*, and *adhi-ās* is [the *karma*].
For these, the locus (*ādhāra*) shall be the *karma*. He lies upon the bed; he stands upon the mountain; he sits in the village; he lies upon the dry land.
And also for *abhi-ni-viś*.
The locus (ādhāra) of this [verb] should also be the object (karman). [Examples: *grāmam abhiniviśate* (he enters the village).

Regarding the rule *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ*: the locus of this [verb] should also be the object. [Examples: *grāmam upavasati* (he dwells near the village); *nadīm anuvasati* (he dwells along the river); *girim adhivasati* (he dwells on the mountain); *pallīm āvasati* (he dwells in the hamlet). As for the example *iha grāme upavasati* (he fasts here in the village), its meaning is of the nature: "dwelling in the village, he fasts for three nights. As it has been said:
"Even when not explicitly employed [in the verbal form], the location is considered the locus (*adhikaraṇa*);
and even when not explicitly employed, the ritual act such as the three-night period is recorded as 'you shall fast' (*upavaseḥ*).
Thus: "The object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent."

The object (*karman*) is that which the agent most desires to be reached by the action. [For example: "He produces conjunction"; "He cooks rice-grains into porridge"; "He studies the Veda. And likewise, there is that which is not desired (*anīpsita*), though it is connected with the agent's action like the desired object; such is the other type of object. [Examples: "One desiring to eat porridge eats poison"; "While looking at his son, he looks at the sun."

And that which is unspoken (*akathita*) [is also *karman*]. That which is not designated by other technical terms such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth shall be considered the object (*karman*). Examples: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (He milks milk from the cow). By the rule of *kāraka* alone: *gavāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (He milks milk from the cows). By the force of intended expression (*vivakṣā*): *gobhyo dogdhi payaḥ* (He milks milk from the cows). Likewise: *yācamānaḥ śivaṃ surān* (Begging for Śiva from the gods). *so'pṛcchallakṣmaṇaṃ sītām* (He asked Lakṣmaṇa about Sītā). *śiṣyaṃ dharmaṃ brūte* (He tells the student the Dharma). *viprāñ śataṃ jayati* (He wins a hundred from the Brahmins). *gargāñ śataṃ daṇḍayati* (He fines the Gargas a hundred). *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* (He leads the goat to the village). *bhāraṃ grāmaṃ harati* (He carries the load to the village). And here also: [the following examples follow].

"For roots that govern two objects (*dvikarman*), they say that the *l*-affixes and so forth are used when the primary object is to be expressed. The goat is led to the village (*nīyate 'jā grāmam*). The load is to be carried to the village (*voḍhavyo bhāro grāmam*). The wood is carried to the house (*hriyate kāṣṭhaṃ gṛham*). The branch is dragged to the village (*ākṛṣyate śākhā grāmam*). "For roots such as *duh* (to milk) and others, [the *l*-affixes are used] when the non-primary object is to be expressed. The cow is milked for milk (*duhyate gauḥ kṣīram*). The pupil is told the Dharma (*ucyate śiṣyo dharmam*). Let the Gargas be fined a hundred [*daṇḍyantām*]. The Brahmin is made to pay a hundred [*jīyate vipraḥ śatam*].

"In the case of a causative (*ṇyanta*), [the suffixes] *la* and so forth denote both the agent and the object. This means that the suffixes beginning with *la* denote either the agent who has attained the status of an object in the causative (*ṇic*) or the object itself. The Brahmin is reached at the village. The son is to be made to go to the village by the father. The disciple is made to understand the Dharma. The Brahmin is fed rice. The son is made to recite the Sūtra. The Brahmin is seated for a month.

"For those verbs whose meanings involve motion, cognition, eating, or which have sound as their object, or which are intransitive, the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative (*aṇic*) becomes the object (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇau*).

For these verbs, that which is the agent in the non-causative shall be the object in the causative. The Brahmin goes to the village. He causes the Brahmin to go to the village. "Make Rāvaṇa attain joy."

The roots *nī* and *vah*, however, denote "causing to reach" with the sense of motion as a subordinate factor; they do not have the meaning of mere motion. Examples include: *nayati vāhayati bhāraṃ dāsena* ("he causes the servant to carry the load"). Regarding the sense of "awakening": *bodhayati śiṣyaṃ śāstram* ("the scripture awakens the student"); *jñāpayati nṛpaṃ hitāhitam* ("he makes the king know what is beneficial and harmful"); *upalambhayati vipraṃ gandham* ("he causes the Brahmin to perceive the fragrance"). Regarding "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*, i.e., eating): *āśayati bhojayati vipram odanam* ("he causes the Brahmin to eat the rice"). Regarding "sound as an object" (*śabdakarma*): *adhyāpayati vaṭuṃ vedam* ("he causes the boy to study the Veda"); *pāṭhayati putraṃ sūtram* ("he causes his son to recite the Sūtra"); *śrāvayati śiṣyaṃ śabdam* ("he causes the student to hear the sound"). From intransitive roots (*akarmakāt*): *āsayati putram* ("he causes the son to sit"); *śāyayati mitram* ("he causes the friend to lie down").

[This rule applies] elsewhere than in the case of roots meaning "motion" (*gati*) and so forth. In the example *pācayaty odanaṃ sahāyena* ("He causes the companion to cook the rice"), it is said that the one who is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *aṇ* [causative base] becomes the object (*karman*) in the *ṇi*-causative; yet, because he is independent through his own activity, he also possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*). Thus, since both designations would be established, this restriction is formulated: for roots meaning "motion" and so forth, that which is the agent in the *aṇ* [base] becomes only the object in the *ṇi*-causative, and not the agent.

Consequently, some who maintain that for roots other than those meaning "motion" (*gati*) and the like, both agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) occur in the atom (*aṇu*) when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, assert that such forms as *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattaṃ devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to cook the rice by means of Devadatta") are also valid. And thus, the rule *hṛkror vā* ("Optionally after *hṛ* and *kṛ*") should be understood as being for the sake of elaboration (*prapañcārtha*).

There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the rule to roots such as *jalpati* ("he whispers"), because they do not have sound as their object (*aśabdakarman*). [Examples: *jalpayati mitraṃ putram* ("He makes the friend speak to the son"); *ālāpayati putraṃ mitram* ("He makes the son converse with the friend"); *sambhāṣayati devadattaṃ bhāryām* ("He makes Devadatta speak to his wife").
A prohibition must be stated for the roots *ād* and *khād*: *ādayate* and *khādayati odanaṃ vipreṇa* ("He causes the Brahmin to eat the rice"), because these have the sense of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*).

[However,] for the root *bhakṣ*, it applies when there is no violence (*ahiṃsā*): *bhakṣayati piṇḍīṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to eat the cake"). But in the case of violence, one says *bhakṣayati yavaṃ vṛṣabhān* ("He causes the bulls to eat the barley").

According to Kātyāyana, [the rule applies] to the root *vah* when the agent is not the controller (*aniyantṛkartṛka*): *vāhayati bhāraṃ manuṣyaiḥ* ("He causes the men to carry the load"). But when the agent is the controller (*saniyantṛkartṛka*), one says *vāhayati vṛṣabhān bhāram* ("He causes the bulls to carry the load").

*hṛkroranyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.53): When the causative suffix *ṇic* is added to the roots *hṛ* (to take) and *kṛ* (to do), the agent of these roots may optionally become the object (*karman*) of the causative verb. He causes the servant to carry the load: *hārayati bhāraṃ dāsaṃ* or *dāsena*. He causes the son to make the mat: *kārayati kaṭaṃ putraṃ* or *putreṇa*. *abhivādidṛśorātmanepade vā* (Pāṇini 1.4.54): When used with the roots *abhivad* (to salute) and *dṛś* (to see) in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the agent of these roots may optionally become the object of the causative verb. He causes the son to salute the teacher: *gurumabhivādayate putraṃ* or *putreṇa*. He causes the servants to see the king: *darśayate nṛpaṃ bhṛtyān* or *bhṛtyaiḥ*.

The agent (*kartṛ*) is independent. That which is intended to be expressed as being non-subordinate (*aguṇatva*) with respect to the accomplishment of an action shall be the agent. For example: *vipreṇa pacyate* ("it is cooked by the Brahmin"), *kriyā jāyate* ("the action arises"), or *odanaḥ sidhyati* ("the rice is prepared").
Furthermore, that which prompts the agent is called the cause (*hetu*).

The instigator of one who is independent is called both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the cause (*hetu*). For example: "Devadatta causes [someone] who is acting to act" (*kārayati devadattaḥ*). The case-factors (*kārakas*) have been explained.
From here until the rule *adhir īśvare* (Pāṇini 1.4.97), the items are to be understood as particles (*nipāta*).

"Particles such as *ca* and others, when not denoting a substance (*asattve*), are called *nipātas* (indeclinables). This refers to those particles whose function does not consist in denoting a substance. Examples include: *yāti ca vāti ca* ("he goes and he blows"); *ghaṭaṃ vā paṭaṃ vā paśya* ("look at the pot or the cloth"); *ca*, *vā*, *vai*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *om*, *ām*, *paśu*, *tu*, *manye*, *asti*, *brūhi*, *vibhāṣā*, *anyatarasyām*, *nañ*, *no*, *na*, and so forth. Furthermore, particles (*nipātas*) are also those that resemble prepositions (*upasarga*), case endings (*vibhakti*), or accents (*svara*). Why "when not denoting a substance"? [Consider: *svāhā agnāyī* ("Svāhā is Agnāyī"). [Also included are] *pra* and other such prefixes (*prādayaḥ*).

*pra*, *parā*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *nir*, *dur*, *nis*, *abhi*, *vi*, *adhi*, *su*, *ud*, *ati*, *ni*, *prati*, *pari*, *api*, *upa*, and *āṅ*—these are *nipātas*. *Pratanu*, *pravirala*, *abhinava*, and *abhilīna* are examples; when joined with a verbal action (*kriyā*), they are called *upasargas*.

The particles beginning with *pra* (and others) are called *upasargas* when they are joined with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*). Examples: *praṇamati* ("he bows"), *pariṣiñcati* ("he sprinkles"). Why specify "when joined with a verbal action"? [Consider: *praṇāyako deśaḥ* ("a region with a leader"). Here, in cases such as *durnītam* ("ill-conducted") or *avadattam* ("not given"), because these are particles that resemble *upasargas*, the rules for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) and *tattva* (the retention of *t*) do not apply. As it is said: "O friend, the wise poet has declared this list of more than twenty *upasarga*-rules to consist of: *pra*, *para*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *ni*, *dur*, *abhi*, *vi*, *adhi*, *su*, *ud*, *ati*, *ni*, *pra*, *ti*, *pari*, *upa*, and *āṅ*. And [these particles are also] *gatis*.
The words beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ) are designated as *upasargas* and also as *gatis*. For example: *praṇamya*, *abhiṣicya*.

And the items beginning with *ūry-ādi*, as well as those ending in the suffixes *cv-i* and *ḍāc*, are also designated as *gatis*. For example: *ūrīkṛtya*, *urarīkṛtya*; *cv-i*: *śuklīkṛtya*, *śuklībhūya*; *ḍāc*: *paṭapaṭākṛtya*, *damadamākṛtya*.
An imitation [of sound] that does not end in *iti* is a *gati*.

An imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) shall be a *gati*. Example: *khaṭatkṛtya bhagnaḥ* ("Having made the sound 'khaṭat,' he broke [it]"). Why "not ending in *iti*"? Example: *khaṭaditi kṛtvā bhagnaḥ* ("Having said 'khaṭat,' he broke [it]").
The words *sat* and *asat* are [gatis] in the senses of respect and disrespect, respectively.
In these two cases, the following would be the usage: "He went after having honored his elders"; "He went after having dishonored the wicked.
Regarding the sense of "sufficiency" (*bhūṣaṇa*), this would be the usage here: "He went after having adorned the maiden."

In the case of *antar* when it does not mean "appropriating" (*aparigrahe*), the word *antaḥ* should be treated as a verbal prefix (*gati*). Example: *antarhatya sthitaḥ khalaḥ* ("the villain stands having struck [him] within"). The meaning is "having struck him in the middle. Why say "when not meaning appropriating"? Consider: *antarhatvā mūṣikāṃ gataḥ śyenaḥ* ("the hawk has gone away after having seized the mouse within"). The meaning here is "having appropriated. It should be stated that the designation "prefix" (*upasarga*) applies to the word *antaḥ* in the rules concerning the suffix *aṅ*, the suffix *ki*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. Examples: *antardhā* (the act of hiding), *antardhiḥ* (concealment), *antarṇayati* (he leads inside).
*kaṇe* and *manas* signify the absence of faith and resentment, respectively.
The words *kaṇe* and *manas* may also denote the cessation of thirst (*tṛṣṇā-vigama*). For example: *kaṇehatya manohatya payaḥ pibati*, meaning "he drinks water until his thirst is gone.
*Puras* is an indeclinable.

It would be a *gati* [particle]. In the case of *puraskṛtya śikhaṇḍinam*, there is the substitution of *s* by *Pāṇini 8.3.40*: *namaspurasorgatyoḥ*. And *astaṃ*: *astaṃ* is an indeclinable that is a *gati*. In *astaṅgatya ka āgataḥ*, the meaning is "having died."
*Accha* is used in the sense of motion (*gaty-artha*) and in the sense of speaking (*vadati*).

The indeclinable *accha*, when functioning in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), is a *gati* with respect to the verb *vada*. Examples: *acchagatya* (having gone toward), *acchodya* (having spoken toward). *Adaḥ* [is a *gati*] except when used as an instruction (*anupadeśe*).

The word *adas* (that), when beginning with *tyad* [i.e., as part of the *tyadādi* group], shall be a *gati*. Example: *adaḥkṛtya sthitaḥ* (having done that, he remained). Why "when not used as an instruction" (*anupadeśe*)? Example: *adaḥ kṛtvā gaccha* (go, having done that). *tiras*, in the sense of disappearance (*antardhi*), shall be a *gati*. Example: *tirobhūya sthitaścauraḥ* (the thief remained hidden). Why "in the sense of disappearance"? Example: *tiro bhūtvā sthitaṃ kāṇḍam* (the arrow remained having passed through).

The *vibhāṣā* (option) applies when the root *kṛñ* is used. When the sense is "disappearance," the word *tiras* may optionally be treated as a *gati* when used with the root *kṛñ*. Examples: *tiraskṛtya*, *tiraḥ kṛtvā*. [The rule also applies] in the cases of *upāja* and *anvāja*.
These two particles (*upāje* and *anvāje*) are optionally termed *gati* when used with the root *kṛ*. Thus: *upājekṛtya* or *upāje kṛtvā*; *anvājekṛtya* or *anvāje kṛtvā*.

And the words beginning with *sākṣāt* [are also optionally termed *gati* when used with the root *kṛ*]. The words starting with *sākṣāt* may optionally be designated as *gati* when used with *kṛ*. Thus: *sākṣātkṛtya* or *sākṣāt kṛtvā*. [The following are included: *mithyā*, *lavaṇam*, *vaśe*, *prādus*, *āvis*, *namas*.

The words *uras* (chest) and *manas* (mind) [are used as locatives] when not placed upon something else. These two may optionally be treated as *gati*s when used with the root *kṛ* (*kṛñ*) in the sense of "placing near" or "fixing. For example: *urasikṛtya* or *urasi kṛtvā*—one should mutter the mantra; *manasikṛtya* or *manasi kṛtvā*. But not here: *urasi kṛtvā hastaṃ śete* ("having placed his hand on his chest, he lies down").
Also [the word *madhye* is a *gati*] when used with *pada* and *nirvacana*.

These [words] may optionally be *gati*s with the root *kṛ* (to do/make). For example: *madhyekṛtya*, or *madhye kṛtvā*; *padekṛtya*, or *pade kṛtvā*; *nivacanekṛtya*, or *nivacane kṛtvā*. The meaning is "having become silent. Only when not referring to placing [something]—as in: "having placed his head on the foot of the elephant, he sleeps. However, in the sense of "taking as one's own," these two are always *gati*s with *kṛ*: *haste* and *pāṇau*. Examples: *tāṃ haste kṛtya mā śvasīḥ* ("Having taken her by the hand, do not sigh"); *pāṇau kṛtya bhuṅkte* ("He eats after taking [it] in his hand").

*Prādhvam* is used in the sense of binding. When combined with the root *kṛ*, *prādhvam* is invariably a *gati* [particle] in the senses of binding and going: *prādhvaṃkṛtya kuṭumbaṃ sthitaḥ* ("having bound his family, he remained"). *Jīvikā* and *upaniṣad* are [used as *gatis*] in the sense of comparison.

These two [terms, *jīvikā* and *upaniṣad*,] may be used with the root *kṛ* in the sense of similarity. For example: *jīvikāṃ kṛtvā vyācaṣṭe* (having made it his livelihood, he explains); *upaniṣadaṃ kṛtvā kathayati* (having made it a secret doctrine, he tells). These [prepositions] must be placed before the verbal root; those designated as *gati* and *upasarga* are to be employed prior to the root. This has been illustrated accordingly.
In the Vedic language (chandas), [the augment] occurs even when [a word] follows; and [the augment occurs] even when [words] are separated [by others]. These are two Vedic rules (sūtra).
The *karmapravacanīyas*. This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). [Now follows:
"The term *anu* [is a *karmapravacanīya*] when it denotes a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*)."

The particle *anu* shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya* when it signifies a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), an agent (*kāraka*), or a cause (*hetu*). Example: *homamanu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It rained after the oblation").

It shall also bear that designation in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) and in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). Example: *gaṅgāmanvavasitā purī* ("The city is situated along the Ganges"); the meaning is "built together with it."

In the sense of inferiority (*hīna*), when that [inferiority] is to be expressed, the word *anu* becomes a name for that [inferior object]. For example: *anvarjunam yoddhāraḥ*. The meaning is: "the warriors are inferior to Arjuna. Also, *upa* [is used] in the sense of superiority (*adhika*) and [inferiority].

When [the sense of] "near" (*upa*) is applied to something superior (*adhika*) or inferior (*hīna*), it takes that same name [as a preposition]. For example: *upakhāryāṃ droṇaḥ* ("A *droṇa* measure is near a *khārī*") and *upagovardhanaṃ śābdikāḥ* ("The grammarians are near Govardhana").

*Apa* and *pari* [are prepositions] when used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). These two function as such when denoting exclusion: *apa trigarttebhyaḥ* ("excluding the Trigarttas") and *pari srughnād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it has rained around Srughna").

The particle *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). When denoting a boundary (*sīmā*), *āṅ* takes that [following] name as its designation. For example: "The god has rained as far as the ocean" (*ā samudrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ*). Because of the inclusion of the word "mentioning" (*vacana*), it is also used in the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*): "Your fame extends even to children" (*ākumāraṃ yaśastava*).

The particles *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* are used in the senses of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), a description of a state (*itthambhūtākhyāna*), a portion (*bhāga*), and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

The particles *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* are termed *karmapravacanīya* when they signify a mark (*cihna*) and so forth. Examples: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut* (the lightning flashes toward the tree); *vṛkṣam pari*; *vṛkṣamanu*. Similarly: *mātaraṃ prati sādhuḥ* (he is kind toward his mother); *yad atra māṃ prati syāt* (whatever may be for my benefit here). *Vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* (he waters tree after tree). The particle *abhi* is termed *karmapravacanīya* when it signifies a mark and so forth, excluding the sense of "share" (*abhāga*). Examples: *vṛkṣam abhi vidyotate vidyut* (the lightning flashes toward the tree); *mātaram abhi sādhuḥ* (he is kind toward his mother); *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam abhi siñcati* (he waters tree after tree).

What is the purpose of [specifying] *abhāge*? [Consider: *yad atra mamābhiṣyāt* ("whatever may accrue to me here"). [In this case,] the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) [sibilant] is based on the prefix (*upasarga*).
*Prati* [is used] in the sense of a representative (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*).

Likewise, *prati* occurs in the senses of similarity (*sadṛśa*) and returning (*pratyarpaṇa*). [Examples: *yo nārāyaṇataḥ prati* ("one who is a counterpart to Nārāyaṇa"); *māṣān asmai tilebhyaḥ pratiyacchati* ("he exchanges beans for these sesame seeds").

The prefixes *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless (*anarthaka*). *Adhi* and *pari* may likewise be meaningless. [Examples: *kuto’dhyāgacchati* (from where does he come?), *kutaḥ paryānayati* (from where does he bring?). The result is the sublation of their designations as "verbs" (*gati*) and "prepositions" (*upasarga*). Why specify "meaningless"? [Counter-examples: *adhigamya* (having approached), *pariṇīya* (having led around).

*su-* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). In the sense of worship, *su-* becomes a name for that [action]. For example: *susiktaṃ tvayā* ("well-sprinkled by you"). The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] does not occur when it is dependent on a prefix (*upasarga*).
*ati-* is also used in the sense of exceeding (*atikramaṇa*).

*Atipravṛttiḥ* means excessive engagement; *atikramaḥ* means transgression. In the context of worship (*pūjā*), it may take that [same] name [of "excessive"]. For example: *atisiktam tvayā* (you have sprinkled too much); in the sense of worship: *atistutam*, *atistutiḥ*.
The particle *api* is used in the senses of the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), possibility (*sambhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), censure (*garhā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

One interpretation of the sūtra is that the word *api*, when occurring in these [contexts], should be a *karmapravacanīya*. For example: *sarpiṣo 'pi syāt* ("there might be even a drop of clarified butter"). Here, the word *api* occurs in the sense of a "drop" (*bindu*). According to the second interpretation of the sūtra, the word *api* should be a *karmapravacanīya* with respect to whatever word occurs in these [contexts]. For example: *sarpiṣo 'pi syāt*. Here, the word *syāt* occurs in the sense of a "drop. With respect to that, the word *api* is a *karmapravacanīya*. Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* (based on the rule for verbal prefixes) does not take place. However, since *api* is not a *karmapravacanīya* with respect to the word *sarpiḥ*, the accusative case ending would not occur [if it were].

*Sambhāvanā* (possibility) and *yogyatā* (fitness): "Rāma might even conquer a pillar. *Anvavasarga* (permission or indulgence): "Pour if you wish; praise if you wish. *Garhā* (censure or reproach): "He might even praise a low-caste man (*vṛṣala*). In the sense of *samuccaya* (conjunction): "Pour and praise; do both. *Adhi* [is used] in the sense of a lord (*īśvara*). When sovereignty (*aiśvarye*) is to be understood, *adhi* takes that [name of the lord] as its technical designation (*tannāmā*). Example: "Brahmadatta is over the Pañcālas" (*adhi pañcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ*).

*Vibhāṣā kṛñi*: The particle *adhi* may optionally be a *karmapravacanīya* when used with the root *kṛ*. For example: *yan māmadhikariṣyati* or *yan māmadhi kariṣyati*; likewise, *adhikṛtya* or *adhi kṛtvā*. The particles (*nipāta*) have now been explained.
*laḥ parasmaipadam*:
The substitutes for *la* are called *parasmaipada*. [They are: *ti, tas, jhi, si, thas, tha, mi, vas, mas, ta, ātām, jha, thās, āthām, dhvam, iḍ, vahi, mahiṅ*.
*taṅānāvātmanepadam*: The *taṅ* suffixes and *āna* are called *ātmanepada*.

The *taṅ* and *āna* substitutes are called *ātmanepada*. *Taṅ* refers to *ta*, *ātām*, *jha*, *thās*, *āthām*, *dhvam*, *iṭ*, *vah*, and *mahin*; *āna* refers to the *śānac* and *kānac* suffixes. Regarding *tiṅ*: "Of the *tiṅ*s, three by three are designated as first, middle, and last. Of the *tiṅ* endings, the three sets of three shall respectively be known as the first, middle, and last persons. *Ti*, *tas*, *jhi*, *tā*, *ātām*, *jha* constitute the first person; following that is the middle person; and following that is the last person.

Those [suffixes] are, respectively, singular, dual, and plural. Each of those three sets of three words shall individually be designated as singular, dual, and plural. *ti* is the singular; *tas* is the dual; *jhi* is the plural. The same applies elsewhere. [This concludes the section on] *sup*.
And *sup* shall be likewise: *su* is the singular, *au* is the dual, and *jas* is the plural; thus it is everywhere.
And *vibhakti*: *sup* and *tiṅ* are called *vibhakti*.

When *yuṣmad* is present as an upapada (governing word) and is coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*), even when [the verb] is in its original form (*sthānin*), the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) is used. When the verb is coreferential with *yuṣmad* as an upapada, the second person should be employed. For example: *tvaṃ pacasi* (you cook); *yuvāṃ pacathaḥ* (you two cook); *yūyaṃ pacatha* (you all cook). *Tvaṃ dṛśyase* (you are seen); *yuvāṃ dṛśyethe* (you two are seen); *yūyaṃ dṛśyadhve* (you all are seen). The phrase "even when in its original form" applies even when *yuṣmad* is merely implied. For example: *odanaṃ pacasi* (you are cooking rice); *mayā dṛśyase* (you are seen by me). This is not desired when *bhavat* is employed: *bhavān karoti* (you, sir, do it). Why specify "coreferential"? [Consider: *tvayā dṛśyate* (it is seen by you).
