And when *prahāsa* (jesting) is intended and *manya* is the attendant word, the *uttama* (first person) is used for the root *man*, and it is treated as singular.

When the root following the attendant word *manya* would otherwise take the *madhyama* (second person) because it refers to jesting, the *uttama* person shall be used; and for the root *man*, although the *madhyama* would be expected, the *uttama* is used. And that [first person] is singular, even if the agent is plural. "Come, I think you will drink milk? You will not drink it; it has been drunk by the guests. Why "in jesting"? "Come, you think I shall eat curd-rice? You think well; you all think so too. The *uttama* person is used when *asmat* (the first person pronoun) is the agent.

In our speech, the *uttama-puruṣa* (first person) should be used. *I cook*: *ahaṃ pacāmi*. *We two cook*: *āvāṃ pacāvaḥ*. *We cook*: *vayaṃ pacāmaḥ*. *I am seen*: *ahaṃ dṛśye*. *We two are seen*: *āvāṃ dṛśyāvahe*. *We are seen*: *vayaṃ dṛśyāmahe*. This applies even when the action is being experienced (*gamyamāne*). *I cook*: *pacāmi*. *I am seen*: *dṛśye*. *The first person is used for the remainder* (*śeṣe prathamaḥ*).

When [the referent] is other than *yuṣmad* (you) and *asmad* (I/we), the *prathama-puruṣa* (third person) should be used. *He shines*: *sa bhāti*. *They two shine*: *tau bhātaḥ*. *They shine*: *te bhānti*.
*Paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ saṃhitā*: "Extreme proximity" is called *saṃhitā*. For example: *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*. *Virāmaḥ avasānam*: "Cessation" is called *avasāna*.

The absence of a following vowel is called *avasāna* (pause). Examples: *vṛddhaḥ*, *siddhiḥ*. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Teacher Śrī Puruṣottamadeva. 1.4.105.

An indeclinable (*avyaya*) is compounded with a case-inflected word (*sup*) when it expresses the meanings of case endings, proximity, prosperity, adversity, absence, passing away, inappropriateness, manifestation, sequence, simultaneity, similarity, perfection, totality, or limit. Regarding the meaning of case endings and so forth: an indeclinable is compounded with a case-inflected word. In the sense of a case ending: "A discourse proceeds concerning women" is *adhistri*; likewise, *adhipāṇi*.

*Kapola* means "nearby" (in *upakumbha*, "near the jar"). *Sumadra* means "prosperous. *Vyṛddhi* is the absence of prosperity (*ṛddhi*). *Duryavana* means "famine. [The prefix *dur*] expresses the absence of a thing, as in *nirmakṣika* ("free from flies").

*Atyaya* means the state of having occurred (*bhūtatva*) or transgression (*atikrama*). *Niḥśīta* means "not cold. Regarding the sense of non-immediacy (*asamprati*): "This is not the time for the use of this blanket" is *atikambala*. *Prakāśatā* (manifestation) is the appearance of a word; thus says Pāṇini. *Udvikramādityam* [is used] in the sense of "afterwards. *Anu* has four meanings: fitness (*yogyatā*), distribution (*vīpsā*), non-transgression of the object (*padārthānativṛtti*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*). In the sense of fitness: "A gift suitable to him" (*anurūpam asya dānam*). In the sense of distribution: "He gives every day" (*pratidinam dadāti*). In the sense of non-transgression of the object: [He follows the chariot] (*anuratham*).

One studies the recitation according to one's ability (*yathābalaṃ*). In the sense of similarity (*sādṛśye*): it sounds like a lute (*vīṇāvat*), thus *savīṇaṃ dhvanati*; he goes together with a swan (*sahaṃsaṃ gacchati*). In the sense of succession (*ānupūrvye*): let them enter according to seniority (*anujyeṣṭhaṃ praviśantu*). In the sense of simultaneity (*yaugapadye*): place [it] together with the wheel (*sacakraṃ nidhehi*). And in an *avyayībhāva* compound, when not referring to time (*cākāle*), the substitute *sa-* is used for *saha-* [as in *sacakraṃ*]. In the sense of similarity even when applied figuratively (*gauṇe'pi sādṛśye*): similar to a partridge (*kikhyā*), thus *sakikhi*; with women who are like Lakṣmī, thus *salakṣmi strībhiḥ*. In the sense of excellence (*sampattau*): accompanied by the kṣatriyas (*sakṣatram*). In the expression of totality (*sākalyavacane*): he eats everything down to the grass (*satṛṇam abhyavaharati*); the meaning is that he does not leave out even a blade of grass. In the expression of inclusion of the end (*antavacane*): he studies including the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) (*sataddhitam adhīte*).

The word *yathā* is compounded when it does not signify resemblance (*asādṛśye*). For example: *yathāvṛddham*, meaning "those who are elders, according to their seniority. It is not compounded when it signifies resemblance (*sādṛśye*); for example: *yathā śakraḥ tathā tvam* ("just as Śakra, so are you").
The word *yāvat* is compounded when it signifies limitation (*avadhāraṇe*).

The word *yāvat* is compounded when it expresses a measure (*iyattā*). Example: *yāvallayanaṃ bhikṣūn vāsaya* ("Accommodate as many monks as there is space for"). With *prati* in the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*), a *sup*-ending word is compounded. Example: *na sukhaprati saṃsāre* ("There is no trace of happiness in saṃsāra"); *na doṣaprati bauddhadarśane* ("There is no trace of fault in the Buddhist philosophy").

The words *akṣa*, *śalākā*, and numerals are *pariṇ*. These *pariṇ* are compounded. This is a designation used in the context of gambling (*dyūta-vyavahāra*). Examples: *akṣapari*, *śalākāpari*, *saṃkhyā*, *ekapari*, *dvipari*.
[This formation occurs] optionally (*vibhāṣā*).

Henceforth, the optional compound (*vibhāṣā-samāsa*) should be stated. [The rule: *apari-bahi-rañcavaḥ pañcamyā*. These—*apa*, *pari*, *bahiḥ*, and words ending in *añcu*—are compounded with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Examples: *apatrigartam* (outside the Trigartas), *paritrigartam* (around the Trigartas), *bahirgrāmam* (outside the village), *prāggrāmam* (east of the village). Because of the governing heading *vibhāṣā*, the analytical sentence (*vākya*) is also permitted: *apa trigartebhyaḥ*, *pari trigartebhyaḥ*, *bahir grāmāt*, *prāk grāmāt*.

The particle *āṅ* is used in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*). In these two senses, *āṅ* is compounded with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Examples: *āsamudraṃ gataḥ* (he has gone as far as the ocean); *ākumāraṃ yaśas tava* (your fame extends even to children).
When expressing direction toward something, *abhi* and *prati* are compounded with a word denoting a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

The words *abhi* and *prati*, when used in the sense of "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), are compounded with a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix that expresses a "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*). Examples: *abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* (moths fly toward the fire); *pratidīpaṃ śalabhāḥ patanti* (moths fly toward the lamp).
Why "with a mark"? [Counter-example: *diṅmohāt srughnaṃ prati gataḥ* (due to disorientation, he went toward Srughna).
[Now for the rule: *anu* is compounded with that which is *samayā*.

The word *anu* is compounded with that which expresses proximity (*samīpa*) and that which expresses length (*dairghya*). Examples: *anuvanam caurāḥ* ("thieves near the forest"), meaning they are in its vicinity; *anugaṅgam vārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī along the Gaṅgā"), meaning it is as long as the Gaṅgā. And there are also compounds beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*.

These words should be considered correct according to their recited forms: *tiṣṭhadgu* (the time when cows stand), *vahadgu* (the time when they move), *āyatīgavam* (when the cows return). Also: *khaleyavam*, *prāhṇam*, *pradakṣiṇam*, *pratyakṣam*, *samakṣam*, *apasavyam*. The suffix *ic* is added in the sense of mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatīhāra*). Examples: *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (stick-for-stick fighting). Regarding *pāra* and *madhya*: "Or with the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyā vā*).

These two may optionally be compounded with a word in the genitive case. Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the final vowel becomes *e*. Examples: *pāreśmaśānam sarit* (the river on the far side of the cemetery); *madhyegaṅgam* (in the middle of the Gaṅgā). In the alternative, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*): *śmaśānapāram*, *gaṅgāmadhyam*.

A numeral is compounded with a word denoting lineage (*vaṃśya*). A numeral is compounded with a word meaning "born in the lineage" (*vaṃśabhava*); for example, *dvimuni* (the two sages who are the authorities on grammar) or *trimuni* (the three sages who are the authorities on grammar). It is also compounded with words denoting rivers (*nadī*).
A numeral is compounded with river names. This denotes a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*): *dvigaṅgam* ("two Gaṅgās") and *pañcanadam* ("five rivers").
Furthermore, when denoting another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*), provided it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*):
a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix is compounded with river names to denote another word-meaning when it is a name. For example: *unmattagaṅgam*, the name of a region.
The Tatpuruṣa compound.
Now, therefore, the Tatpuruṣa is to be explained before the Bahuvrīhi;
and the Dvigu as well.

A *dvigu* compound shall be designated as a *tatpuruṣa*. Examples: *pañcarājī* (five kings), *pañcagavam* (five cows). Because it is a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied. [The rule: "A word ending in the second case is compounded with [the words] *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, *gata*, *atyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna*. A word ending in the second case is compounded with these. Examples: *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* → *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship); *lokātītaḥ* (beyond the world); *bhūmipatitaḥ* (fallen to the ground); *vipadgataḥ* (gone into calamity); *taraṅgātyastaḥ* (cast down by a wave); *sukhaprāptaḥ* (attained happiness); *sukhāpannaḥ* (entered into happiness). By means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) regarding the term "second case," we have examples such as: *viśeṣaviduṣaḥ śāstram* (the scripture of one who knows the particulars) and *viprāya vedaviduṣe* (to the Brahmin who knows the Veda).

And [the suffix] *gami* and *gāmi*, etc.: *grāmagamī* (one who goes to the village), *grāmagāmī* (one who goes to the village). *odanabubhukṣuḥ* (desiring to eat rice); "one who seeks to overcome the strength of the enemy" (*dviṣadvīryanirākariṣṇuḥ*). With *svayam* and a *kta*-suffix: it is compounded with a word ending in a *kta*-suffix. *svayaṃvilīnam* (melted by itself), *svayaṃkṛtam* (done by itself). With *tasyedaṃ* (belonging to that): *svāyaṃkṛtam* (done by oneself).

Regarding the *khaṭvā* in the sense of reproach (*kṣepe*): a word ending in the accusative case, *khaṭvā*, is compounded with a word ending in a *kta*-suffix if it expresses censure. For example: *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ pramādavān* ("one who has climbed onto the bed," i.e., one who is negligent).
[Also, the word] *sāmi*.

This [compound] is formed with a word ending in the *kta* suffix. Examples: *sāmivilokitam* ("half-seen"), *sāmikṛtam* ("half-done"). The remainder of that is *sāmikṛtaśeṣaḥ*. Because the term *sāmi* is taken as denoting the meaning [of "half"], some say that *nemabhinna* ("half-split") and *ardhakṛta* ("half-done") are not included. [The category of] *kāla*: words expressing time ending in the accusative case are compounded with a word ending in the *kta* suffix. Examples: *aharatisṛtāḥ* ("those who have passed three days"), *rātryārūḍhāḥ* ("those who have ascended for a night").
And [the rule] regarding continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

In this case, words denoting time ending in the second case are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*). Examples: *muhūrtasukham* (happiness lasting for a moment), *cirauṣitaḥ* (dwelt for a long time), *varṣabhogyaḥ* (to be enjoyed for a year). [The rule] "the third case [ending] is compounded with a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) when that [quality] is produced by it": *atyantasaṃyoge ca* | *atra ca dvitīyāntāḥ kālaśabdāḥ supā saha samasyante* | *muhūrtasukham* | *cirauṣitaḥ* | *varṣabhogyaḥ* | *tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena* |

A word ending in the third case is compounded with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) that denotes something produced by that [instrument]. A "quality-word" is one that expresses a quality. Examples: *śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* (broken by a wedge) becomes *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*; *śalākākāṇaḥ* (blind in one eye from a splinter). It is also compounded with the word *artha* (purpose/wealth): *dhānyenārthaḥ* (wealth consisting of grain) becomes *dhānyārthaḥ*. Why say "produced by that"? Consider: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* (blind in one eye because of the eye). Why include the term "word" (*vacana*)? Consider: *ghṛtena pāṭavam* (cleverness through ghee). [Also compounded] with *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, *sama*, words having the sense of *unmāna* (measure), *kalaha*, *nipuṇa*, *miśra*, and *ślakṣṇa*.

A word ending in the third case (instrumental) is compounded with these [words]. *masena pūrvaḥ* → *māsapūrvaḥ* (one who is a month early). *pitṛsadṛśaḥ* (like a father). *gurusamaḥ* (equal to a teacher). *ekonaḥ* (one less). *vākkalahaḥ* (a quarrel by words). *vāṅnipuṇaḥ* (skilled in speech). *guḍamiśraḥ* (mixed with molasses). *ācāraślakṣṇaḥ* (gentle in conduct). How is it that *gurutulyaḥ* (equal to a teacher) and *dvyaṅgavikalaḥ* (deficient in two limbs) are not included? Because of the rule stating "the majority of cases" (*bahulavacana*). *Kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*:

A word ending in the third case, when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), is frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. *caureṇa hataḥ* → *caurahataḥ* (killed by a thief). *vyāghreṇa hataḥ* → *vyāghrahataḥ* (killed by a tiger). In the sense of the instrument: *śareṇa bhinnaḥ* → *śarabhinnaḥ* (pierced by an arrow). *loṣṭena hataḥ* → *loṣṭahataḥ* (struck by a clod of earth).

What is the purpose of including the term *bahulam* (diversely)? As in: *dātreṇa lūnavān* ("he has reaped with a sickle"). The preceding and following rules constitute the detailed exposition of *bahulam*.

[The rule] *kṛtyair adhikārthavacane*: a word ending in the third case is compounded with *kṛtya* suffixes when there is an expression of excess. Examples: *kākapeyā nadī* ("a river so shallow it can be drunk from by crows") and *bāṣpacchedyāni tṛṇāni* ("grass so tender it can be cut by dew-drops").

The word *vyañjana* (condiment) is compounded with *anna* (food). For example: *dadhnopasikta odano dadhyodanaḥ* (rice sprinkled with curd = curd-rice). [Also,] *miśrīkaraṇa* (the act of mixing) is compounded with *bhakṣya* (edible food).

It is compounded. *Guḍadhānāḥ* (sugar-coated grains) means grains mixed with sugar; *guḍapiṣṭakāḥ* (sugar-cakes); *tilataṇḍulāḥ* (sesame and rice). The rule *caturthī tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ*: A word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*) is compounded with these [words]: *tadartha* (for that purpose), *artha* (meaning/purpose), *bali* (offering), *hita* (beneficial), *sukha* (pleasant/happiness), and *rakṣita* (protected). This applies when there is the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthye*). For example: *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post) becomes *yūpadāru*. This does not apply here because it is not expressed as a relationship between material cause and modification (*prakṛtivikārabhāva*): *randhanāya sthālī* (a pot for cooking); *avahananāyolūkhalam* (a mortar for threshing); *yakṣabaliḥ* (an offering for a Yakṣa); *go hitam* (beneficial for a cow); *gosukham* (pleasure for a cow); *gorakṣitam* (protected by a cow). In this case, however, compounds such as *vāsagṛha* (dwelling-house) and *aśvaghasa* (horse-eating) occur due to a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the fourth case, or they may be explained as genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

The word *artha* forms a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) and takes all genders. Examples: *viprārthaḥ sūpaḥ* (soup for a Brahmin), *viprārthā śāṭī* (a garment for a Brahmin), *viprārthaṃ payaḥ* (milk for a Brahmin).

[The rule] *pañcamī bhayena*: A word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is compounded with a word expressing fear (*bhaya*). Examples: *caurād bhayaṃ* → *caurabhayam* (fear of a thief), *vyāghrabhītiḥ* (fear of a tiger). How [is it explained] that *sitetaraḥ* means "one who has departed from the village" or "one who loathes unrighteousness"? It is due to a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) from the term *pañcamī*.

The fifth case is only rarely compounded with these words: *apeta*, *apoḍha*, *mukta*, *patita*, and *apatrasta*. Examples: *duḥkhāpetaḥ* (free from suffering), *sukhāpetaḥ* (free from happiness), *kalpanāpoḍhaḥ* (free from conceptual construction), *rogamuktaḥ* (freed from disease), *svargapatitaḥ* (fallen from heaven), *caurāpatrastaḥ* (terrified by a thief). Why say "rarely"? [Because it is not compounded in cases such as: *prāsādāt patitaḥ* (fallen from the palace).

Words meaning "a little" (*stoka*), "near" (*antika*), "far" (*dūra*), and "with difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) are compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Words having the sense of "a little" and so forth, as well as "with difficulty," are compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Examples: *stokānmuktaḥ* ("freed with little effort"), *alpānmuktaḥ* ("freed with little effort"), *antikādāgataḥ* ("come from nearby"), *abhyāśādāgataḥ* ("come from close by"), *dūrādāgataḥ* ("come from afar"), *kṛchrādavāptaḥ* ("attained with difficulty"). [In these cases], there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) after words such as *stoka*, according to the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*. [The following rule applies: A word in the seventh case (*saptamī*) is compounded with words belonging to the *śauṇḍa* group.

A word ending in the seventh case is compounded with words beginning with *śauṇḍa*. Examples: *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* (skilled at dice), *akṣadhūrtaḥ* (a cheat at dice). With *adhi*: *parādhīnaḥ* (dependent on another), *svādhīnaḥ* (dependent on oneself). *raṇapaṇḍitaḥ* (skilled in battle), *kāryanipuṇaḥ* (expert in business). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

Also, with *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, and *bandha*, the seventh case is compounded. Examples: *kāmpilyasiddhaḥ* (perfected in Kāmpilya), *ātapaśuṣkaḥ* (dried in the sun), *chāyāśuṣkaḥ* (dried in the shade), *śākhāgrapakvaṃ phalam* (fruit ripened on the tip of a branch), *sthālīpakvaḥ* (cooked in a pot), *cārakabandhaḥ* (bound in prison).

In the sense of reproach (*kṣepa*). A word denoting a crow (*dhvāṅkṣa*) is compounded with a word ending in the locative case, provided that reproach is intended. For example: *tīrthadhvāṅkṣaḥ* (a "crow at a sacred bathing place") or *tīrthakākaḥ* (a "crow at a sacred bathing place"). This means one who is similarly unstable or fickle. [Also, a word ending in the locative is compounded] with words ending in kṛtya suffixes when debt (*ṛṇa*) is intended.

The term *kṛtyaiḥ* is a Pāṇinian technical designation (*sautra-nirdeśaḥ*). A word ending in the locative case is compounded with a *kṛtya* suffix. Examples: *māsadeyam* (to be paid in a month), *varṣadeyam* (to be paid in a year).

Because the word *ṛṇa* (debt) serves as an indicator for the sense of "obligation," we have *pūrvāhṇageyaṃ sāma* (the Sāman to be sung in the forenoon). [This also applies] when it is a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*).
A word ending in the locative case is compounded with a noun. Examples: *vane kiṃśukāḥ* ("kiṃśuka trees in the forest"). [The elision of the locative suffix occurs] by the rule *haladantāt*.

Words denoting parts of days and nights are compounded with a past passive participle (*kta*). These words ending in the locative are compounded with a *kta*-suffix. Examples: *pūrvāhṇakṛtam* ("done in the forenoon"), *apararātrakṛtam* ("done in the latter part of the night"). Why is the mention of "parts" (*avayava*) necessary? [Consider: *ahni kṛtam* ("done during the day").

In this regard: this [word] is compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. Examples: *tatrabhuktam* (eaten there), *tatrakṛtam* (done there). [Also when meaning] "belonging to that": *tātrakṛtam* (done for that). [This occurs] in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*).

In the sense of censure (*kṣepa*), a word ending in the locative case is compounded with a *kta*-formed word. Examples: *pravāhemūtritam* ("one who urinates while walking"), *bhasmanihutam* ("one who offers oblations into ashes"). In these *tatpuruṣa* compounds, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative suffix by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*. The following are also irregularly formed (*nipātana*) in the sense of censure: *pātresamitāḥ* ("those who meet only at the dining table"), *kūpamaṇḍūkāḥ* ("frogs in a well"), *udumbarakṛmiḥ* ("a worm in an udumbara fruit"), *piṇḍīśūraḥ* ("a hero at a feast"), *mātaripuruṣaḥ* ("a man [only] toward his mother"), *mātariśūraḥ* ("a hero toward his mother"), *goṣṭhepravīraḥ* ("a hero in the cow-pen"), *gehenardī* ("one who roars at home"), *gehepaṭuḥ* ("clever at home"), *gehemehī* ("one who wets the bed at home"), *gehapaṇḍitaḥ* ("wise at home").

Words expressing prior time, as well as *eka*, *sarva*, *jara*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala*, are compounded with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Words denoting prior time and words beginning with *eka* are compounded with a case-inflected word (*sup*) that stands in apposition to them. Examples: *dagdhaprarūḍhaḥ* (one who has grown back after being burnt). *snātānuliptaḥ* (one who has bathed and anointed himself). Examples of [words] beginning with *eka*: *ekapaṇḍitaḥ* (the one scholar). *ekapatnī* (a wife having only one husband). *sarvadevāḥ* (all the gods). *jaradgavaḥ* (an old ox). *purāṇataruḥ* (an ancient tree). *navodakam* (fresh water). *kevalānnam* (exclusive food). Why "with a word in apposition"? *ekasyāḥ śauklyam* (the whiteness of one [person]). [Also: *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Direction and number are compounded when they form a proper name).

These two [words] are compounded when they form a name (*nāman*). The phrase "with a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) also continues to apply from the previous rule. Examples: *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*, *Pañcāmrāḥ*, *Saptarṣayaḥ*. How is it that the rule for *caturvarṇāḥ* and *dvipadāśritaḥ* applies even when not a name, while the rule for *dvīndriyaḥ* does not? Effort must be made here [to resolve this]. Also [the compound occurs] in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), in the case of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), and in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*).

When a *taddhita* derivative meaning is intended, when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and when a collective (*samāhāra*) is to be expressed, direction (*dik*) and number (*saṃkhyā*) are compounded with that appositional member. Regarding the *taddhita* meaning: *paurvaśālaḥ* ("one belonging to the eastern hall"), *pāñcanāpitiḥ* ("one belonging to five Nāpitas"). Regarding the subsequent member: *pañcagavapriyaḥ* ("one who loves five cows"), *pañcagavadhanaḥ* ("one whose wealth consists of five cows"). Regarding the collective: a direction cannot form such a compound [with a numeral]. Thus, *pañcakumāri* ("five girls") is a collective. A compound preceded by a numeral is called a *dvigu*.

In the immediately preceding sūtra, a compound whose first member is a numeral is called a *dvigu*. For example: *pañcakapālaḥ sūpaḥ* ("a soup made from five pots"). [Here,] by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*. *Pañcanāvapriyaḥ* ("one who loves five ships"): [here,] by the rule *nāvo dvigoḥ*, the suffix *ṭac* is added. *Pañcapūlī* ("five bundles"): [here,] by the rule *dvigoḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. *Pañcakumāri* ("five girls").
*kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* ("things denoting contempt are compounded with words expressing contempt").

Items signifying that which is contemptible are compounded with words that cause the contempt. Example: *vaiyākaraṇakhasūciḥ* ("a grammarian who is a bad needle," i.e., one who fails to pierce through difficult points).

With words denoting contempt (*kutsita*), [the first member] is compounded with these [words]. For example: *pāpapuruṣaḥ* (a contemptible man), *aṇakabhāryā* (a contemptible wife). [As in: "What have I to do with a contemptible wife?
Words expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) are compounded with words expressing a common quality (*sāmānyavacana*).

Words expressing the object of comparison (upamāna) are compounded with words expressing the common attribute (sāmānyadharma). Examples: *śaṅkha iva pāṇḍaraḥ* = *śaṅkhapāṇḍaraḥ* ("white as a conch"); *kanakagauraḥ* ("fair-skinned like gold"); *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark-complexioned like a knife"). When the feminine form is treated as masculine (*puṃvat*), we have *mṛgacapalā* ("fickle as a deer") and *kākavandhyā* ("barren as a crow").
[Also, a word] compared [to another] is compounded with words such as *vyāghra*, provided that the common attribute is not expressed.

The object of comparison (*upameya*) is compounded with words such as *vyāghra* (tiger) and the like. For example: "This man is like a tiger" becomes *puruṣavyāghraḥ* (a tiger-like man); *mukhacandraḥ* (a moon-like face); *karapadmam* (a lotus-like hand). Why is it said "when the common property (*sāmānya*) is not employed"? Consider: "This man is a tiger-like hero. One might object: "In this case, because of the mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), the compound will not occur. [The author replies: Then this very rule indicates that there is a compound even for a principal member (*pradhāna*) that is dependent. Therefore, we have examples such as *rājapuruṣo'bhirūpakaḥ* (the king’s man is handsome) and *rājapuruṣo darśanīyaḥ* (the king’s man is beautiful). An adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*) is frequently (*bahulam*) compounded with the noun it qualifies (*viśeṣya*).

A *subanta* (inflected word) expressing a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is compounded with a *subanta* expressing the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Examples: *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus), *kṛṣṇatilāḥ* (black sesame seeds), *lasadutpalam* (shining lotus), *idaṃstrī* (this woman), *idampuruṣaḥ* (this man). Because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely), it does not occur here: *bodhisattvo mahāsattvaḥ* (the Bodhisattva, the Great Being), *rāmo jāmadagnyaḥ* (Rāma, the son of Jamadagni). And in this case, it is obligatory: *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ* (black snake). What is the purpose of the word "qualifier"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaḥ śiṃśapā* (the tree is a *śiṃśapā*), *asuro'ndhakaḥ* (the Asura is Andhaka). And they say that the rule for the *tatpuruṣa* compound here is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very rule; for these too are indeed qualifiers: *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship), *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man).

The words *pūrva*, *apara*, *prathama*, *carama*, *jaghanya*, *samāna*, *madhya*, *madhyama*, and *vīra* are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) that is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Examples: *pūrvapaṇḍitaḥ* (an earlier scholar), *aparabhāryā* (a later wife), *prathamapuruṣaḥ* (the first person), *caramaparvataḥ* (the last mountain), *jaghanyadharmaḥ* (the lowest dharma), *samānabalaḥ* (equal strength), *madhyadeśaḥ* (the middle country), *madhyamanaraḥ* (a middling man), *vīrapuruṣaḥ* (a brave man).
The words *śreṇi* and others are compounded with *kṛta* and others.

These [words] are compounded with these [others]. This is an expression used in the sense of the suffix *cv*. "Rows that were not rows" having been made [into rows] are called *śreṇikṛtāḥ*. Likewise, "become soft" (*mṛdubhūtāḥ*). The words beginning with *śreṇi*, *pūga*, *kūṭa*, *paṭu*, *deva*, *mṛdu*, *śravaṇa*, *paṇḍita*, and so forth, are the *śreṇyādayaḥ* (the group beginning with *śreṇi*). The words beginning with *kṛta*, *bhūta*, and *samākhyāta* are the *kṛtādayaḥ* (the group beginning with *kṛta*). A word ending in a *kta* suffix that is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ* is compounded with another word ending in a *kta* suffix that is qualified by *nañ* and which does not itself contain *nañ*. For example: something done and something not done is *kṛtākṛtam* work; *bhuktābhuktam* (eaten and not eaten); *aśitānaśitam* (consumed and not consumed).
An addition [to the rule] should be made for *kṛtāpakṛta* and so forth: *kṛtāpakṛtam* (done and undone), *gatapratyāgatam* (gone and returned).

In the case of compounds such as *śākapārthiva*, there is elision of the middle member (*madhyapadalopa*). For example: *śākapradhānaḥ pārthivaḥ* (a king for whom vegetables are the main thing) becomes *śākapārthivaḥ*; *ajātaulvaliḥ* (one who is not born of the Taulvali lineage); *vindhyagiriḥ* (the Vindhya mountain); *candanadrumaḥ* (a sandalwood tree); *śrīharṣanṛpatiḥ* (King Śrīharṣa); *sugrīvakapiḥ* (the monkey Sugrīva); *karaṇakārakam* (the instrument as a factor of action); *tarkavidyā* (the science of logic); *vyākaraṇaśāstram* (the treatise on grammar). [Also, the words] *san*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* form a tatpuruṣa compound when joined with those things that are objects of respect.

These are compounded with words meaning "being honored. Examples: *satpuruṣaḥ* (a good man), *mahāpuruṣaḥ* (a great man). With what [words] meaning "being honored"? As in *utkṛṣṭā gauḥ paṅkāt* ("the cow has been pulled out from the mud"); the meaning is "extracted.

[The compound is formed] with *vṛndāraka*, *nāga*, and *kuñjara* when they mean "being honored. When being honored by these, [the word] is compounded: *govṛndārakaḥ* (a bull among cows), *yoṣidvṛndārikā* (an excellent woman), *puruṣanāgaḥ* (an elephant-like man), *munikuñjaraḥ* (an elephant among sages). With what [words] meaning "being honored"? As in *devadatto nāgo yatī mūrkhaḥ* ("Devadatta is an elephant among fools").

The two suffixes *katara* and *katama* are used when there is an inquiry regarding a class (*jāti*). These two, which function in inquiries concerning a class, are compounded: *katarakaṭhaḥ* (which one is a Kaṭha?), *katamakālāpaḥ* (which one is a Kālāpa?). Why "when there is an inquiry regarding a class"? [Consider: *katamo bhavatāṃ paṭuḥ* (who among you is clever?).
For this very reason, even when not referring to a class, the suffix *ḍatama* is understood [to apply] as in *katamau caitramaitrau* (which two are Caitra and Maitra?).
What [is] in the sense of censure?

The word *kiṃ* is compounded when it expresses censure: *kiṃgauḥ* (a useless ox), because he does not carry or draw; *kiṃputraḥ* (a bad son), because of his wicked character; *kiṃrājā* (what a king!), one who does not protect. A genus (*jāti*) is compounded with *poṭā*, *yuvati*, *stoka*, *katipaya*, *gṛṣṭi*, *dhenu*, *vaśā*, *vehat*, *baṣkayaṇī*, *pravaktṛ*, *śrotriya*, *adhyāpaka*, and *dhūrta*.

The genus (*jāti*) is compounded with these [words]. Examples: *gopoṭā* (a young female cow), *goyuvatiḥ* (a young female cow), *agnistokaḥ* (a small fire), *ghṛtakatipayam* (a little clarified butter), *gogṛṣṭiḥ* (a cow that has calved once), *godhenuḥ* (a milch cow), *govaśā* (a cow that miscarries), *govehat* (a cow that does not conceive), *gobaṣkayāṇī* (a cow with a calf at foot). Also, the genus is compounded with words such as *kaṭhapravaktā* (a teacher of the Kaṭhas), *kaṭhaśrotriyaḥ* (a learned Kaṭha), *viprādhyāpakaḥ* (a Brahmin teacher), and *bakadhūrtaḥ* (a rogue crane). Why "the genus"? [Observe: *yajñadatto dhūrtaḥ* (Yajñadatta the rogue). And [the genus is compounded] with words expressing praise (*praśaṃsāvacana*). The genus is compounded with these: *gomatallikā* (an excellent cow), *aśvaprakāṇḍam* (an excellent horse).

A young man [is compounded] with women who are bald, gray-haired, or wrinkled. A young man who is bald is *yuvakhalati*; a young gray-haired man is *yuvapalita*; a young wrinkled man is *yuvavalinaḥ*. Here, because of the inclusion of gender-distinct forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇa*), or by the force of the governing rule concerning coreferential terms (*sāmānādhikaraṇādhikāra*), a young woman who is old is *yuvajaratī*.
[Also included are] those called participles (*kṛtya*) and words expressing similarity (*tulyākhyā*), when not denoting a genus (*ajāti*).

Words denoting actions (*kṛtya*) and words having the same meaning (*tulyākhyā*) are compounded with words that do not denote a genus (*ajāti*). Examples: *uṣṇaṃ bhojyam* (hot food), *bhojyoṣṇam* (food that is hot); *pānīyoṣṇam* (hot drink); *bhojyalavaṇam* (salty food). Regarding words having the same meaning: *tulyaśvetaścandreṇa* (as white as the moon); *sadṛśamahān giriṇā* (as large as a mountain). Why "not denoting a genus"? Example: *bhojya odanaḥ* (edible rice)—here it is not compounded because *odana* denotes a genus. The *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound) is also superseded [in these cases]. A word denoting color (*varṇa*) is compounded with another word denoting color:
*kṛṣṇalohitaḥ* (blackish-red); *kṛṣṇaśabalaḥ* (black-spotted); *śvetaraktaḥ* (white-reddish).

The word *kumāra* (boy) is compounded with *śramaṇā* (female ascetic) and others: by these it is formed as a compound. *Kumārī śramaṇā* becomes *kumāra-śramaṇā* (a young female ascetic). Likewise: *kumāra-kulaṭā* (an unchaste young woman), *kumāra-paṇḍitaḥ* (a learned young man), and similarly *tāpasī* (a female ascetic), *garbhiṇī* (pregnant), *adhyāpaka* (teacher), *paṭu* (clever), *nipuṇā* (skilled), and so forth.
A four-footed animal [is compounded] with *garbhiṇī*.

Words denoting quadrupeds are compounded with the word *garbhiṇī* (pregnant). Examples: *gogarbhiṇī* (a pregnant cow), *aśvagarbhiṇī* (a pregnant mare). This does not apply here because [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*): *kālākṣī garbhiṇī* (a black-eyed pregnant woman). The group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* is also included. These are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) as *tatpuruṣa* compounds. *Vyaṃsaka* means a rogue. Examples: *mayūravyaṃsakaḥ* (a rogue of a peacock), *chātravyaṃsakaḥ* (a rogue of a student). *Kāmbojamuṇḍaḥ* (one who shaves like a Kamboja), *yavanamuṇḍaḥ* (one who shaves like a Yavana). Their inclusion in this list is for the purpose of ensuring the final member of the compound is placed last. Examples: *uccāvacam* (high and low), *paramakṛtvā* (having done the utmost), *pītvāsthirakaḥ* (one who becomes steady after drinking), "rāghavaḥ proṣyapāpīyān" (Rāghava became more wicked after going abroad). [The rule applies to] *yā*... [etc.]
*icchā-yadṛcchā*:
it should be stated that this is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*). *prātardohaḥ*. *avaśyaṅkārī*.
*ehīḍādayo’nyapadārthe*: in cases where "come and praise" (*ehi īḍa*) is expressed, that is *ehīḍam*; in cases where "come here" (*ihi iha*) is expressed, that is the action *ehīham*.

*Jahi-karmanā bahulam ābhīkṣṇye kartāraṃ cābhidadhāti*: The word *jahī* (imperative of *hā*, "to abandon") is compounded with its object when there is frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), and the compound denotes the agent. It is compounded with the object that follows it; the compound also expresses the agent. For example, one who repeatedly says "Go away, fool! is called *jahijoḍaḥ*. Similarly, *jahistambaḥ*. *Ākhyātam ākhyātena kriyāsātatye*: A verb may be compounded with another verb when there is continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*). Where it is said, "Eat and drink," that act of engaging [someone] is expressed as *aśnītapibatā*. Likewise, *pacatabhṛjjatā*, *khādatamodatā*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Thus ends the section from the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Preceptor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.
The first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter (adhyāya).
The *Samarthapāda* is concluded.
The Second Chapter (*Adhyāya*). The Second Quarter (*Pāda*).

[A word denoting] a part—whether "prior" (*pūrva*), "posterior" (*apara*), "lower" (*adhara*), or "upper" (*uttara*)—is compounded with a word denoting the whole (*ekādhikaraṇa*) when they stand in apposition.

Terms such as *pūrva* ("front") and others, when denoting parts of a single substance (*ekadravya*), are compounded. For example: *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* (the front part of the body) becomes *pūrvakāyaḥ*; likewise, *aparakāyaḥ*, *uttarakāyaḥ*, and *adharakāyaḥ*. How is it that *madhyāhnaḥ* ("midday"), *sāyāhnaḥ* ("evening"), and *paścimarātraḥ* ("latter part of the night") are formed? Let them be treated as descriptive compounds (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). If this were so, the form would be established simply by saying "it is both *pūrva* and *kāya*"; what then is the purpose of the rule? It is not so, because the rule serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For the form *kāyapūrvaḥ* does not occur. [The rule continues: *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* ("the word *ardha* [is compounded] when it is neuter").

A word meaning "half" (*ardha*) having a neuter gender is compounded with a part-possessor (*ekadeśin*) when the two parts are equal. Examples: *ardhapippalī* (half a long pepper), *ardhanakharañjanī* (half a nail-painter). Why "neuter"? [Counter-example: *grāmārdhaḥ* (half a village), *nagarārdhaḥ* (half a city). The words *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* are optionally compounded with a part-possessor when they refer to a single substance. Examples: *dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyāḥ* → *dvitīyabhikṣā* (the second alms); *tṛtīyavāpī* (the third well); *caturthanadī* (the fourth river); *turyakathā* (the fourth story). In the alternative case: *bhikṣādvitīyam*, *vāpītṛtīyam*, *nadīcaturtham*, *kathāturyam*.

*Prāpta* and *āpanna* are compounded with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*). These two are compounded with a word ending in the second case. Regarding the word *ca* ("and"): when the inclusion of the feminine gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇa*) applies, the compound is formed with words ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and in that case, the letter *a* is substituted for the final [of the first member]. This *a* is included by *praśleṣa* (elision and re-insertion) because it is a Vedic rule (*sautratvāt*). Examples: *prāptajīvikaḥ* (one who has obtained a livelihood), *āpannasukhaḥ* (one who has attained happiness). Feminine forms: *prāptajīvikā* (a woman who has obtained a livelihood), *āpannasukhā* (a woman who has attained happiness). How is it that *jīvikāprāptaḥ* and *sukhāpannaḥ* are formed? It is by the force of the rule stating "the second case [is compounded] with *āśrita* and so forth. [The next rule: Time-words are compounded with a word denoting the thing measured (*parimāṇin*).

Words denoting time are compounded with that which is delimited by them: *māso jātasya* becomes *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month"), *varṣajātaḥ* ("born after a year"), *dvyahajātaḥ* ("born after two days"). The negative particle *nañ*:

*nañ* is compounded with a *sup*-ending word with which it is semantically connected: *abrāhmaṇaḥ* ("non-Brahmin"), *aśuklaḥ* ("not white"), *anekaḥ* ("not one"), *asarvaḥ* ("not all"), *asarvasmai* ("not to everyone"), *akṛtvā* ("without having done"), *akartum* ("not to do").

*irṣadakṛtā*. The term *akṛt* is an indication for "that which has not undergone a grammatical modification" (*guṇa*). [The word] *irṣat* is compounded with that which has not undergone a modification. *iṣadraktaḥ* (slightly red). *aiṣadraktiḥ putraḥ* (a son who is slightly red). [This is an example of] the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

A word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is compounded with a *sup*-ending word. For example: *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *rājapuruṣadhanam* (the king’s man’s wealth). It should be stated that the sixth case [ending] used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is also compounded: for example, *idhmapravraścanaḥ* (one who cuts fuel) and *uṣṭrāsikā* (an elephant-like sitting posture).

And [the compound is formed] with qualities residing in that [substance], but not with its qualifiers. Those qualities which exist in the substance itself (guṇātmaka) are compounded with it by means of the sixth case, as in the case of "white" and so forth, through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), such as "this is that. He will state a prohibition regarding the word *guṇena* ("with a quality"); this is an exception (*apakarṣa*) to that. Examples: *brāhmaṇavarṇaḥ* (the color of a Brahmin), *candanagandhaḥ* (the scent of sandalwood), *kapittharasaḥ* (the juice of the wood-apple), *paṭahadhvaniḥ* (the sound of a drum), *aṅgasparśaḥ* (the touch of the body). But not with its qualifiers: *ghṛtasya tīvraḥ* (the sharpness of the ghee), *candanasya mṛduḥ* (the softness of the sandalwood). And [the compound is formed] with words such as *yājaka* ("sacrificer") and others.
Since this rule regarding the agent (*kartari*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition [of compounding], it must be explained as being for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*).
*Na nirdhāraṇe*:

A genitive case used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is not compounded. Examples: *narāṇāṃ kṣatriyaḥ śūratamaḥ* (Among men, the Kṣatriya is the most brave); *gavāṃ kṛṣṇā sampannakṣīratamā* (Among cows, the black one yields the most milk); *adhvagānāṃ rathinaḥ śīghratamāḥ* (Among travelers, those on chariots are the swiftest).

The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) prescribed by way of specific rules is not compounded. Examples: *sarpiṣo jñātam* (the knowledge of ghee), *mātuḥ smṛtam* (remembered from the mother), *caurasya rugṇam* (the illness of the thief).
[This rule applies] with words expressing ordinal numbers, qualities, satisfaction, the sense of "existent," indeclinables, gerundives, and words in apposition.

The genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not compounded with words such as *pūraṇa* (ordinal numbers). For example: *chātrāṇāṃ pañcamaḥ* ("the fifth among students") and *bhikṣūṇām aṣṭādaśaḥ* ("the eighteenth among mendicants"). Regarding the term *guṇa* (quality): examples include *balākāyāḥ śauklyam* ("the whiteness of the crane"), *paṭasya lauhityam* ("the redness of the cloth"), and *paṭasya śuklaḥ* ("the white [cloth]"). Here, however, the qualities recognized by the Vaiśeṣika school—such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth—are not intended, because of the rule stating "from *niṣka* up to *śatasahasra*" (*niṣkād iti vacanāt*). Nor is *guṇa* taken here to mean a mere property (*dharmamātra*), because of the specific instruction: "*vartamāne sāmīpye vartamānavat*" ("when referring to proximity to the present time, it is treated as if it were present").

By that [rule], the following would be correct: *gośatam* (a hundred cows), *gocatuḥ* (four cows), *buddhivaiguṇyam* (deficiency of intellect), *vacanasāmarthyam* (capacity for speech), *padmāsanakauśalam* (skill in the lotus posture), *municāpalyam* (the fickleness of a sage), *vastrapītimā* (the yellowness of a garment), *dravyakāṭhinyam* (the hardness of a substance), *pakṣālīpiṅgalimnaḥ* (the tawny color of the armpits), *udaragauravam* (heaviness of the belly), and so forth. The words *suhita*, *tṛpta*, and *āśita* have the meaning of satisfaction. Examples: *phalānāṃ tṛptaḥ* (satisfied with fruits), *phalānāṃ suhitaḥ* (well-satisfied with fruits), *phalānām āśitaḥ* (eaten his fill of fruits). This is the genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), because the prohibition [of the genitive] for words joined with a *kṛt*-suffix (by Pāṇini 2.3.69) does not apply here. Examples: *caurasya dviṣan* (hating the thief), *mitrasya kurvan* (doing for a friend).

While performing a favor for a friend (*mitrasya kurvāṇaḥ*); [the word] *avyaya*; having done something for a learned brahmin (*viprasya kṛtvā*); [the suffix] *-tavya-*; that which is to be done for a brahmin (*brāhmaṇasya karttavyam*). When there is a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇe*): [the genitive of] Sraughna, the king (*rājñaḥ sraugghnasya*); [the genitive of] Pāṇini, the author of the *Sūtras* (*pāṇineḥ sūtrakārasya*). And with a past passive participle (*ktena*) when expressing honor (*pūjāyām*): when honor is expressed, the genitive case is not compounded with a past passive participle. For example: "the opinion of the kings" (*rājñāṃ matam*).

And [the genitive is used] with a word expressing the locus (adhikaraṇa). For example: "This is their place of sitting" (idameṣām āsitam). And [the genitive is used] in the sense of the object (karman).
The genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) is not compounded. Example: *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopālakena* ("It is a marvel that the milking of cows was done by one who is not a cowherd").

With respect to the suffixes *tṛc* and *aka*, when used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), the genitive case is not compounded. Examples: *bhavata āsikā* ("the sitting of you"), *bhavato 'gragāmikā* ("the going ahead of you"). The inclusion of the term *tṛc* is for the sake of subsequent rules.
And when the agent [is expressed].

When the suffixes *tṛc* and *ak* are prescribed in the sense of the agent, a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expressing the object (*karman*) is not compounded with them. Examples: *apāṃ sraṣṭā* (the creator of waters), *purāṃ bhettā* (the breaker of cities), *odanasya bhojakaḥ* (the eater of rice).

This group of five prohibitive sūtras is intended for the sake of accentuation (*svarārtha*), because the genitive compound with a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) has not been prohibited. Therefore, compounds such as *rājasammataḥ*, *rāmamahitaḥ*, *bhavadāsitaṃ*, *bhavadāsikā*, and *godohaḥ* are indeed formed. As Bhartṛhari says: "Since the agent of that [action] partakes in the fruit. Thus, compounds with a genitive [expressing] qualifiers of action (*kriyā-viśeṣaka*), those denoting a genus (*jāti-vācaka*), or those expressing the prompter (*tat-prayojaka*), and so forth, certainly do occur as genitive compounds. Consequently, when there is a genitive compound with a mere kāraka, by the rule "after a preverb (*gati*), a kāraka, or an upapada, the suffix *kṛt* [is treated as having its own accent]," the natural accent (*prakṛti-svara*) of the final member applies, as in *odana-pāka*.

Let not words such as *bhojaka* have the middle syllable as udātta; rather, so that they may have the final syllable as udātta when forming a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), this prohibition is commenced. Furthermore, because of the rule "with *yājaka* and others" (*yājakādibhiś ca*), which provides a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the agentive-genitive compound (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), in cases such as *brāhmaṇayājaka*, the original accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*) prevails. [The suffix *kvin* is applied] invariably in the sense of play (*krīḍā*) and livelihood (*jīvikā*).

Of these two, the sixth case (genitive) is compounded with one [of the others]. The word *nityam* ("always") is for the purpose of excluding the formation of a sentence (*vākya*). *Damanakabhañjikā* is the name of a game; [the suffix] *ṇvul* is used here in the sense of a "name" (*saṃjñā*). In the sense of "livelihood" (*jīvikā*): *dantalekhakaḥ*, *nakhalekhakaḥ*. [The suffixes] *ṇvul* and *tṛc* [are applied]. [The rule] *kugatiprādayaḥ* [applies].

These are always compounded: *kunṛpaḥ* (bad king), *kusṛṣṭiḥ* (bad creation), *koṣṇam* (slightly warm), *gatiḥ* (motion), *ūrīkṛtya* (having accepted), *prakṛtya* (having made manifest), *prādiḥ* (the group beginning with *pra*), *duṣkulam* (low-born family), *sumānuṣī* (a beautiful woman), *āpiṅgalaḥ* (somewhat tawny). *Pragata ācāryaḥ* becomes *prācāryaḥ* (one who has gone beyond the teacher); *atikhaṭvaḥ* (beyond the bed); *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī). Regarding the rule for *prādi* (prefixes), there is sometimes a prohibition of *karmapravacanīya* particles due to non-mention (*anabhidhānāt*). For example: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut* (the lightning flashes toward the tree). In some cases, it does indeed occur: *atistutam*. Because *ati* is a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of "transcending" (*atiratikramaṇe*), there is an absence of the *ṣatva* substitution [of *s* to *ṣ*]. *Upapada* (co-occurring word) that is not a finite verb (*atiṅ*) [is compounded].

A constant (nitya) upapada is always compounded. Examples: *kumbhakāraḥ* (pot-maker), *grāmaṇīḥ* (village-leader), *agnicit* (fire-piler). Why "not ending in a verbal suffix" (*atiṅ*)? [Because in these cases it does not apply: *kartuṃ vrajati* (he goes to do), *kārako vrajati* (the agent goes). [The rule] "only with an indeclinable" (*amaivāvyayena*): If an upapada is compounded with an indeclinable, it must be an accusative case (*am*). Example: *svāduṅkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it sweet). Not with anything else: *kālo bhoktum* (it is time to eat).
From the third case on, [the following] optionally [form a compound]:

in rules such as *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām*, the governing words (*upapada*) beginning with the third case are optionally compounded. For example: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* or *mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*. Also, [compounding occurs] after [a word ending in] the suffix *ktvā*: *uccaiḥkāram*.

These [words] may optionally be compounded with a word ending in the suffix *ktvā*. For example: *uccaiḥkṛtya* or *uccaiḥ kṛtvā* "having raised [the voice]," he speaks. This applies only when [the preceding word] begins with the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth; for instance: *alaṃ kṛtvā* "having done enough," *khalu kṛtvā* "having indeed done.
The *tatpuruṣa* compound has been explained. Now, the *bahuvrīhi* follows as the remainder.
A compound called *bahuvrīhi* must be stated as distinct from the *tatpuruṣa* and *avyayībhāva*. [Pāṇini 2.2.24 states: "Many [words] in the sense of another word.

Several inflected words (*subanta*) occurring in the sense of another word are compounded. Examples: *prāptodako grāmaḥ* (a village reached by water), *ūḍharatho’śvaḥ* (a horse that has carried a chariot), *dattabalirdānavaḥ* (a demon to whom an offering was given), *cyutaphalastaruḥ* (a tree from which fruit has fallen), *susūkṣmajaṭakeśo vratī* (an ascetic with very fine matted hair), *bahuśasyo deśaḥ* (a region with abundant crops). And here, the application is determined according to what is actually expressed; therefore, a *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), as in *citragur devadattaḥ* (Devadatta who possesses brindled cows), but not in the sense of mere relation. Likewise, it does not occur in the sense of the nominative (*prathamā*), as in *vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ* (he went when it had rained).

In some cases, even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the compound does not occur—as in *pañca bhuktavanto'sya* ("five have eaten of this"). Conversely, it occurs even with non-coreferential terms—as in *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one with a dark throat"), *urasilomā* ("hairy-chested"), and *uccairmukhaḥ* ("high-mouthed"). In some instances, the second member is included within the formation of the compound, as in *dadhyodanaḥ* ("rice mixed with curd"), following the pattern of *dadhnopasikta odanaḥ*. Similarly, *uṣṭramukhaḥ* ("one whose face is like a camel's face") and *suvarṇālaṅkāraḥ* ("one whose ornament is made of gold," i.e., *suvarṇavikāro'laṅkāro'sya*). In certain cases, even a word whose meaning is already expressed may optionally be employed, as in *praparṇaḥ* ("fallen-leaved") for *prapatitaparṇaḥ*.

"One whose son does not exist" is *aputra*. Here, "a Brāhmaṇī who has milk" is *astikṣīrā*, and "one who has wealth" is *astidhanā*. In the cases of "a scribe who has no fault" (*nāstidoṣaka*) and so forth, there is a compound with the indeclinables (*avyaya*) *asti* and *nāsti*.
[Furthermore,] numbers (*saṃkhyā*), indeclinables, words meaning "near," "not far," and "exceeding," are compounded with a word denoting the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).

Indeclinables and the like are compounded with a numeral expressing that which is to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*). Examples: *upadaśāḥ* (near ten), *āsannaviṃśāḥ* (approaching twenty), *adūradaśāḥ* (not far from ten), *adhikadaśāḥ* (exceeding ten). Regarding numerals: *dvitrāḥ* (two or three), *tricaturāḥ* (three or four), *pañcaṣāḥ* (five or six), *catuṣpañcāḥ* (four or five), *lakṣakoṭāḥ* (a hundred thousand or ten million). [Examples: "Stay for one or two days" (*ekadvān divasāṃstiṣṭha*); "You will depart after seven or eight days" (*saptāṣṭairdivasairyāsyasi*). Names of directions are compounded when expressing an intermediate direction. Names of the cardinal points are compounded when an intermediate direction is to be expressed. Examples: *dakṣiṇapūrvā dik* (the south-eastern direction), *pūrvottarā* (the north-eastern), *uttarapaścimā* (the north-western).
In all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), there is the substitution of the masculine form for a pronoun.

Regarding the rule *tatra tenedamiti sarūpe*: when two words of identical form—one ending in the locative case and the other in the instrumental case—are used in the sense of "this" (*idam*), they are compounded. The word *iti* is intended to indicate a worldly (conventional) usage. [Example: *keśeṣu...*

Having seized each other by the hair, this battle occurred; thus it is a *keśākeśi* (hair-to-hair) battle. Having struck each other with staffs, this battle occurred; thus it is a *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (staff-to-staff) battle. The lengthening [of the final vowel] is seen in other cases as well. By the rule *ic karmavyatihāre*, the suffix *ic* is added as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*). Due to its inclusion in the *tiṣṭhadgu*-class, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). With the word *saha* in the sense of equal connection (*tulyayoga*): the word *saha* is compounded with a word ending in the third case if there is equal connection. *Saputra āgataḥ* (he came with his son); *sacchātraḥ* (with his student). Because equal connection is generally implied, we have *sadarpaḥ* (with pride), *sadhanaḥ* (with wealth), *sapakṣaḥ* (with wings/sides). The *bahuvrīhi* has been explained.

The term *ca* (and) [indicates] the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*). It is understood as "more than one" (*aneka*) alone. When more than one inflected word (*subanta*) occurs in the sense of conjunction, it is compounded; this compound is called *dvandva*. In the sense of mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*): *plakṣāśokau* (the *plakṣa* and the *aśoka*), *plakṣāśokavaṭāḥ* (the *plakṣa*, the *aśoka*, and the *vaṭa*). In the sense of collective totality (*samāhāra*): *vāktvacam* (speech and skin), *dhavakhadirapalāśam* (the *dhava*, the *khadira*, and the *palāśa*).
The subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first.

In compound words (*samāsa*), that which bears the designation of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) should be placed first. Examples: *adhistri* (with respect to a woman), *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man). In the group beginning with *rājadanta*, the subordinate member is placed last. In these cases, the subordinate member—even if it ends in a long vowel (*dīrgha*)—is placed after [the other member]. Examples: *rājadantaḥ* (the king of teeth); *rājajambuḥ* (the king of rose-apples); *sapatnīmātā* (the co-wife of the mother); *agrevaṇam* (at the front of the forest)—here the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending is by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Example: *liptavāsitam* (first scented, then smeared); *siktasammṛṣṭam* (sprinkled and wiped clean); *nagnamuṣitam* (robbed while naked). In a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the order is as follows: *putrapaśū* (son and cattle).

In the case of *dharma* and so forth, both [orders] are used: *dharmārthau* and *arthadharmau*; *candrārkau* and *arkacandrau*; *antādī* and *ādyantau*; *sarpirmadhunī* and *madhusarpiṣī*. For the word *jāyā*, there is the substitution of *jam* and *dam*: *jāyāpatī*, *jampatī*, and *dampatī*. In a *dvandva* compound, a stem ending in a *ghi* vowel [is placed first].

In a *dvandva* compound, that which ends in a feminine suffix (*ghī*) is placed first. For example: *kamaṇḍalu-kṛṣṇājina*. When there are many [feminine] members in one [compound], a restriction [is applied]: *paṭu-śukla-mṛdavaḥ*. That which begins with a vowel other than *a* (*ajādya*) and ends in *a* (*adanta*) is placed first in a *dvandva*. For example: *uṣṭra-śaśam*; *indra-vāyū*. This is desired because it is subsequent [in the sequence of rules]. How is it that "the object and the sense organ" (*viṣaya-indriyayoḥ*) is accepted? Because it is subsequent, it will be governed by the rule "that which has fewer syllables" (*laghvakṣara*). When there are many [members] in one [compound], a restriction [is applied]: *aśva-ratha-indrāḥ*.

*Alpāctaram*: In a *dvandva* compound, that which has fewer syllables should be placed first. For example: *plakṣanyagrodham*, *dhavāśvakarṇam*. Why is it not so in cases such as *vāgagnī* or *vāgindrāviti*? Because this [rule] is intended to apply when followed by a word ending in *ghī* (long *ī*), a word beginning with a vowel (*ajādya*), or a word ending in a short *a* (*adanta*), since it takes precedence over other rules. When there are many items, the restriction applies to one specific case: *śaṅkhadundubhivīṇāḥ* or *vīṇāśaṅkhadundubhayaḥ*.
It should be stated that that which is more venerable (*abhyarhitam*) comes first: *mātāpitarau*.
Of an elder brother; Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna;
and short syllables: *kuśakāśam*, *śaraśīrṣam*; according to the sequence of the castes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.

In the case of seasons and constellations, as well as words with identical vowels, they are compounded in their natural order: *hemanta-śiśira-vasantāḥ* (winter, cool season, spring); *bharaṇī-kṛttikā-rohiṇyaḥ* (the constellations Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and Rohiṇī).
A numeral is placed first when it is the smaller in value: *ekādaśa* (eleven), *dvādaśa* (twelve), *dvitrāḥ* (two or three), *navatiśatam* (one hundred and ninety).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a word ending in the seventh case or a qualifier is placed first.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, an adjective ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and a qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇa*) are placed first. Examples: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one who has Kāla on his neck"), *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"). There is an extension [of this rule] to include pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and numerals (*saṃkhyā*). Examples: *sarvaśvetaḥ* ("entirely white"), *dvikṛṣṇaḥ* ("two black ones"), *saptakṛtaḥ* ("seven times done"), *bahuśrutaḥ* ("one who has heard much"), *saptonnataḥ* ("seven prominent ones"). Optionally, the word *priya* may be placed first. Examples: *guḍapriyaḥ* ("one who likes molasses") or *priyaguḍaḥ*.
The mention of the locative case [in the rule] is for the sake of those beginning with *gaḍu*. Examples: *gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ* (one with a goitre on the neck), *aruḥśirāḥ* (one with sores on the head).
**Niṣṭhā**:

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix (a past passive participle) is placed first. Examples: *kṛtakṛtyaḥ* (one who has accomplished his duty), *gataratiḥ* (one whose pleasure has departed), *jitaśatruḥ* (one who has conquered his enemies).

The suffix *para* (forming a bahuvrīhi) occurs after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), happiness (*sukha*), and so forth, when they precede a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). After a word denoting genus: *māṃsabhakṣitī* (one who has eaten meat), *surāpītī* (one who has drunk liquor), *nṛjagdhaḥ* (one who has devoured a man), *kaṭakṛtaḥ* (one who has made a mat). After a word denoting time: *māsajātaḥ* (born a month ago), *varṣajātaḥ* (born a year ago). After words such as "happiness" (*sukha*): *sukhajātāḥ* (born in happiness), *kṛcchrajātaḥ* (born in hardship).

Furthermore, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case (*saptamī*) occur after words meaning weapons (*praharaṇa*) when they follow [another word]. Examples: *śastrodyataḥ* (one with a raised weapon), *asyodyataḥ* (one with a raised sword), *śūlapāṇiḥ* (one with a spear in hand), *daṇḍapāṇiḥ* (one with a staff in hand). All of this is merely illustrative (*prāyika*). Therefore, one may also form *kṛtakaṭaḥ* (one who has made a mat) and *udgūrṇabāṇaḥ* (one who has raised an arrow). Or, it occurs in the case of the group beginning with *āhitāgni*.

In compounds such as *āhitāgni* ("one who has established the sacred fires"), the word ending in the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) should be placed first, or optionally at the end. Examples: *āhitāgniḥ* (or *agnyāhitaḥ*), likewise *jātaputraḥ*, *jātaśmaśruḥ*, *ghṛtapītaḥ*, *ūḍhabhāryaḥ*, *gatārthaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). **Kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye**: Words beginning with *kaḍāra* ("tawny") that denote qualities may optionally be placed first in a *karmadhāraya* compound. Examples: *kaḍārajaiminiḥ* or *jaiminikaḍāraḥ*. The words are: *kaḍāra*, *gaḍula*, *kāṇa*, *khañja*, *kubja*, *vāmana*, *khalati*, *gaura*, *vṛddha*, *piṅgala*, *khala*. The section on the rule for a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāraḥ*) is complete.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* of the great preceptor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva. || 2.2 ||
The second chapter, the second quarter, is completed. The third quarter:
[The rule applies] when not already expressed.

When [the meanings of] object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as singularity and so forth, have not been expressed by means of primary suffixes (*lakāra*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), or compounds (*samāsa*), the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and others should be employed. The second case ending occurs when there is an object (*karmani*). The second case ending should be used for the object. Examples: *kāśān kaṭaṃ karoti* (He makes a mat from *kāśa* grass); *odanaṃ bubhukṣur vrīhīn prokṣati* (Desiring to eat rice, he sprinkles water on the grains); *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* (He leads the goat to the village).

The rule applies only when [the case] is not already expressed [by another word]. Examples: *ajā grāmaṃ ninye* (the goat was led to the village), *ajā grāmaṃ nayanīyā* (the goat is to be led to the village), *aśvaḥ śatikaḥ* (a horse worth a hundred), *grāmaḥ prāptātithiḥ* (the village has received a guest).
Regarding the words *ubha*, *sarvatas*, and the three beginning with *dhik* and *upari*:
when followed by a doubled word (*āmreḍita*), the second case ending must be used; however, it is also observed in other instances besides these.

On both sides of the village (*ubhayato grāmam*); on all sides of the village (*sarvato grāmam*). Fie upon the wicked person (*dhig durjanam*)! Over the village (*uparyupari grāmam*); above the village (*adhyadhi grāmam*); below the village (*adho'dho grāmam*).

It is also seen elsewhere than these—e.g., "nothing appears to one who is hungry" (*bubhukṣitaṃ na pratibhāti kiñcit*), meaning "to one who is hungry. Likewise in cases such as *caitraṃ yāvacchītam* ("as far as Caitra is cold"). It is also seen in connection with *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, and *nikaṣā*: e.g., *abhito grāmam* ("on both sides of the village"), *parito grāmam* ("all around the village"), *samayā grāmam* ("near the village"), *nikaṣā grāmam* ("close to the village"), and *hā devadattam* ("alas for Devadatta!").
"And the third [vibhakti] is used in the Veda. This is one *chandas* (Vedic) rule. [The word] "antarā" and "antareṇa," when joined with [another word], [take the fifth case].

When these two [words] are used, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall occur. "Enraged *antarā* Vaidehīm" (enraged between Vaidehī). The meaning is: "in the midst of Vaidehī. "A water-pot *antarā* you and me" (a water-pot between you and me). The meaning is: "between you and me. The case-ending of the *kāraka* (the agent or object) is stronger than the case-ending of the *upapada* (an accompanying word). Therefore, the second case does not apply to the water-pot. For all *upapada* case-endings are exceptions to the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). "Not without qualities (*antarā guṇān*) is there happiness. The meaning is: "without qualities. [The second case is used after words denoting] time and distance when there is continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

If there is absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall be used for time (*kāla*) and distance (*adhvan*). Examples: *sarvarātraṃ kalyāṇī* (she is auspicious throughout the night); *māsaṃ ramaṇīyāḥ* (the [days] are pleasant for a month); *kṣaṇam ūce* (he spoke for a moment); *divasaṃ paṭhati* (he studies all day). For distance: *krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī* (the river is winding for a *krośa*); *yojanaṃ dhāvati* (he runs for a *yojana*). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, it is established that in the case of *yojanaṃ dhāvati*, the absolute connection is with the action (*kriyā*). This is for that purpose. In examples such as *māsam āste* (he sits for a month) and *krośaṃ svapiti* (he sleeps for a *krośa*), these are indeed objects (*karman*) in the primary sense. As it is said: "Time, state (*bhāva*), distance, and place [are called objects] because they contain within themselves other actions."
"When all [factors] are non-actions, action-ness (*karmatva*) arises through connection" (P. 1.4.51).

Thus, in the expression *māsa āsyate* ("he sits for a month"), the designation of the object (*karman*) by means of the verbal suffix (*lākāra*) is justified. What is the purpose of the term "absolute contact" (*atyantasaṃyoga*)? Consider: *māsasyaikarātraṃ ramyā* ("the river is pleasant for one night out of the month") and *krośasyaikadeśaṃ kuṭilā nadī* ("the river is winding for one part of a *krośa*"). [In these cases, the third case ending is used. When there is completion (*apavarga*), the third case ending is employed.

Upon the attainment of the result, there is the abandonment of the action; this is liberation (*apavarga*). In that context, when [the time or distance] is yet to be traversed (*gamye*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used for both time and distance. *The book was studied in a month.* *The meaning was understood in an instant.* *He studied for the distance of a *krośa*.* *The meaning was understood for the distance of a *krośa*.* The seventh and fifth case endings are used when [time or distance] lies between two factors of action (*kāraka*). When time or distance lies between two factors of action, these two endings shall be used for them. *Having eaten today, he will eat in two days, or after two days.* In this case, the time lies between the agent and the power [of the action]. "Standing here, this archer hits the target at a *krośa*, or from a *krośa*. (This indicates the distance between the agent and the object.)
The second case ending is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*.
When there is a connection with *karmapravacanīyas*, the second case should be employed. For example: *yajñamanu prāvarṣat* ("It rained after the sacrifice").
The seventh case ending is used in the sense of "that which is superior to" (*yasmād adhikam*) and in the sense of expressing "lordship over" (*yasya īśvaravacanam*).

The locative case shall be used when there is a connection with that which is superior (*adhika*) and with that which expresses sovereignty (*īśvara*). For example: *upa śate viṃśatiḥ* ("twenty [is] over a hundred") and *upa khāryāṃ droṇaḥ* ("a *droṇa* measure [is] in a *khārī* measure"). Also, when expressing sovereignty: *adhi pañcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ* ("Brahmadatta [is] over the Pañcālas"). With the particles *apa*, *ā*, and *pari* used as *karmapravacanīyas*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) shall be used. For example: *apa trigarttebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("the god has rained away from the Trigarttas") and *ā trigarttebhyaḥ*. Regarding *pari*: *pari paryudadheḥ* ("around the ocean"); here *pari* signifies exclusion (*varjanārtha*). Example: *ā pāṭaliputrāt* ("as far as Pāṭaliputra").
And [the fifth case is used] in the sense of a substitute and an exchange;

because a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*) occur there, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) shall be used in connection with them. For example: *sa rājā śakrāt prati* (that king is a substitute for Śakra); *tilebhyaḥ prati māṣān prayacchati* (he gives beans in exchange for sesame seeds).
Regarding the object of a verb meaning "to go," the second and fourth cases are used when there is physical movement, provided it is not a road.

These two [the accusative and dative] may be used for the object of verbs meaning "to go. For example: *grāmaṃ gacchati* or *grāmāya gacchati*; *nagaraṃ gacchati* or *nagarāya gacchati*; *grāmaṃ yāti* or *grāmāya yāti*; *vanaṃ* or *vanāya prasthitaḥ*. Why [is it said] "where are you going? It is because there is an intention to express the locus (*ādhāra*). The meaning is: "Where are you going in order to stay? Why [is it said] "in the case of movement" (*ceṣṭā*)? [Because] *mohaṃ gacchati* ("he falls into delusion") does not involve physical motion. Why [is it said] "not on a path" (*anadhvani*)? [Because] *mārgaṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the road") involves a path.
The dative case (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*).

The fourth case ending shall be used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*). He gives a cow to the Brahmin (*viprāya gāṃ dadāti*). "Give fears to Sītā" (*sītāyai bhayāni datta*). He gave him a cry of approval (*sa tasmai sādhukāram adāt*). He desires flowers (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*). And [the fourth case is used] in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). Wood for a sacrificial post (*yūpāya dāru*). And also when something is being prepared (*klṛpi sampadyamāne*). A bean serves as excrement (*uccārāya kalpate māṣaḥ*).
When an omen is being indicated: lightning that is tawny indicates wind; lightning facing upward indicates rain;
and so too in the case of a beneficial application: for one suffering from loss of appetite, *sauvīra* and fresh ginger are beneficial.
Also, [the sixth case ending is used] after a verb whose object is implied, when it has another word as its adjunct that expresses the purpose of the action.

The fourth case ending shall be used for the object of a verbal root that ends in *tum* or *am*, provided that another word expressing the purpose of the action (*kriyārthopapada*) is present as a substitute (*sthānin*). Examples: *edhebhyo vrajati* (he goes for fuel), *phalebhyas tiṣṭhati* (he stands waiting for fruits).
Why "provided there is a substitute"? [Consider: *edhān āhartuṃ vrajati* (he goes to fetch fuel). [Also: after words expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*) that have the sense of *tum*.

The fourth case ending shall be used after a word that has the same meaning as *tumun* (the infinitive suffix). *Pākāya vrajati* (He goes for the sake of cooking). *Bhūtaye dhāvati* (He runs for the sake of prosperity). Why is it said "after a word expressing a state" (*bhāvavacanāt*)? [Consider: *Odanaṃ pācako vrajati* (The cook goes for the rice); *odanaṃ bhojako vrajati* (The eater goes for the rice). [The rule] "also after connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*" means that the fourth case ending shall be used after words joined with *namas* and so forth. *Namo viṣṇave* (Salutation to Viṣṇu). *Svasti prajābhyaḥ* (Prosperity to the subjects). *Alaṃ pradoṣaḥ priyasaṅgamāya* (Enough, O evening, for the meeting with my beloved). *Swāhā agnaye* (Svāhā to Agni). *Swadhā pitṛbhyaḥ* (Svadhā to the ancestors). *Namaḥ śivāya* (Salutation to Śiva).

*Manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣā'prāṇiṣu*: When the verb *man* (to think) is used in the sense of disregard regarding its object, the fourth case (*caturthī*) may optionally be employed. For example: *na tvā tṛṇaṃ manye* or *tṛṇāya*. "I consider my own sovereignty as mere grass" (*manye tṛṇāya svarājyam*). "They even considered Hari as mere grass" (*harimapyamaṃsata tṛṇāya*). Here, the fourth case does not apply to words such as *tvām* when they are in apposition with *tṛṇam*, due to the rule of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). It should be stated that the term *aprāṇiṣu* ("not living beings") means "not things like boats," etc. For example: *na tvā nāvaṃ manye* ("I do not consider you a boat"); *na tvā kālaṃ manye* ("I do not consider you time").

The third case ending is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). The third case shall be applied to these two: *vipreṇa pacyate* (it is cooked by the Brahmin); *agninā dahyate* (it is burned by fire); *paraśunā vṛkṣaṃ chinatti vardhakiḥ* (the carpenter cuts the tree with an axe). There is an extension [of this rule] to words such as *prakṛti*: *prakṛtyā subhagaḥ* (naturally handsome); *gotreṇa gārgyaḥ* (a Gārgya by lineage); *samena dhāvati* (he runs on level ground); *viṣameṇa dhāvati* (he runs on uneven ground). "In that house, ours is to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth."

When joined with the sense of "accompanied by" (*saha*), the third case ending shall be used for the subordinate (*apradhāna*) element. [Examples: The teacher has come together with the student (*śiṣyeṇa saha*); the owner of cows is accompanied by his son (*putreṇa sārdham*).
[Also applied] when there is a deformity of a limb (*yenāṅgavikāraḥ*).

Diminution and increase constitute *vikāra* (modification). The third case ending shall be used for that limb by which, being modified, the modification of the whole (*aṅgin*) is indicated: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye"), *pādena khañjaḥ* ("lame in the foot"), *mukhena trilocanaḥ* ("three-eyed in the face"). This is in the sense of indicating a particular state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*). The third case shall be used to indicate a specific characteristic of one who has already attained a general status: *śikhayā parivrājakaḥ* ("a wandering mendicant by virtue of his topknot").

In the case of the root *sañj* (to recognize), when used in the sense of an object, the third case may optionally be employed. Thus, one recognizes his mother either as *mātrā sañjanīte* or *mātaraṃ sañjanīte*.
It should be stated that when *sañjñaḥ* is joined with a *kṛt* suffix, the sixth case takes precedence by way of prohibition [of the third case]: *mātuḥ saṃjñātā* (the recognizer of the mother).

In the sense of cause (*hetu*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) should be used. For example: *dhanena kulam* (the family [is distinguished] by wealth); *vidyayā yaśaḥ* (fame [is attained] by learning).
There is a distinction between cause and instrument: the agent is dependent upon the cause, while the instrument is dependent upon the agent.

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used for a cause that is not the agent (*akartṛ*). When the cause is a debt (*ṛṇa*), the fifth case should be employed. For example: *ṛṇād baddhaḥ* ("bound because of a debt") or *śatād abhibhūtaḥ* ("overpowered because of a hundred"). Why "not the agent"? [Consider: *śatena prayojakakartrā bandhitaḥ* ("caused to be bound by a creditor who is the instrumental agent").
Optionally so when the cause is a quality (*guṇa*), provided it is not feminine.

A quality (*guṇa*) is that which depends on something else. When a quality functions as the cause (*hetu*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) may optionally be used. *Jāḍyād gṛhītaḥ* (seized because of dullness) or *jāḍye na vā* (or not [seized] because of dullness). *Dhūmād agniḥ* (fire [inferred] from smoke) or *dhūmena vā*. *Kṛtakatvād anityaḥ śabdaḥ* (sound is impermanent because of its being produced) or *kṛtakatvena vā*. Why "not feminine" (*astriyām*)? *Prajñayā dhīraḥ* (wise because of his wisdom).

When the word *hetu* (cause/reason) is employed, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used to express the cause. *Arthasya hetor vasati* (he dwells for the sake of wealth). *Icchan bahu hātum alpasya hetoḥ* (desiring to give much for the sake of little). Where there is a compound with the word *hetu*, the sixth case is applied to the whole compound. *Vyācaṣṭe bālabodhahetoḥ* (he explains for the sake of the understanding of children).
"And the third case [is used] after a pronoun.

When the word *hetu* ("cause") is employed, both the third and sixth cases may occur after a pronoun. For example: "O friend, for what reason (*kasya hetoḥ*) have you not come? By what cause (*kena hetunā*) have you arrived after so long?

When words expressing the sense of "cause" are employed, the observation of all case endings is generally seen. For instance: *kiṃnimittam āgataḥ* ("for what purpose have you come?"), *kena nimittena*, *kasmai hetave*, *kasmāt kāraṇāt*, *kasya prayojanasya*, *kasmin nimitte*.
The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used for the ablative (*apādāna*).
For example: *grāmād āgacchati* (he comes from the village); *vṛkād bibheti* (he fears the wolf).
When a suffix beginning with *lyap* is elided, it is used for the object (*karman*): *prāsādāt prekṣate* (he looks out from the palace); the meaning is "having ascended the palace."

And [the ablative case is used] in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). One looks from the seat (*āsanāt*); one ascertains from the mat (*kaṭakāt*). And [it is used] in the sense of questioning and narration: "From where do you come? "From the city.

Furthermore, the fifth case is used for that by which the measurement of distance or time is determined. For distance, the first and seventh cases are used; for time, it should be stated that the seventh case is used: "Five *yojanas* from Campā to Somatīrtha," or "in five *yojanas*"; regarding time: "from the month of Phālguna, the month of Caitra [is three months away]."

When joined with words meaning "other than" (*anya*), "different from" (*itarat*), words denoting "direction" (*dik-śabda*), or words ending in the suffix *añc* as the final member of a compound, as well as with *āc* and *āhi*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) shall be used. The fifth case occurs when these are joined [with another word]: *dravyād anyaḥ guṇaḥ* ("A quality is other than a substance"). *"paraistvad anyaḥ ka ivāpahārayet"* ("Who else but those superior to you could possibly take it away?"). Because of the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning), [the rule applies to] *bhinnaḥ bhrātṛbhyaḥ* ("different from his brothers"). *ārād grāmāt* ("far from the village"). *śuklād itaraḥ* ("other than white"). *"aṃśād ṛte niṣiktasya nīlalohitaretasaḥ"* ("Except for a portion of him whose seed is blue and red [Śiva]"). A word denoting direction: *pūrvaḥ grāmāt* ("east of the village"). [Words] having *añc* as the final member: *prāk grāmāt* ("to the east of the village"), *āc dakṣiṇā grāmāt* ("south of the village"). And [words ending in] *āhi*: *uttarāhi grāmāt* ("north of the village"), *uttarāhi samudrāt* ("north of the ocean"). The sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used with a suffix having the sense of *atas*.

The sixth case ending shall be used in connection with words expressing direction (*atasuc*) and suffixes having the sense of *artha*. For example: *dakṣiṇato grāmasya vṛkṣaḥ* ("a tree to the south of the village"). Similarly: *uttarataḥ*, *puraḥ*, *purastāt*, *upari*, *upariṣṭāt* [with *grāmasya*]. How is it that [the sixth case] does not occur in *prāg grāmāt* ("east of the village")? Because of the inclusion of the term "having *añc* as the final member" [in the rule]; or because the general rule sometimes applies even in the domain of an exception, since there is an intention to express separation (*apāya*). Examples: *mātuḥ purastāt* ("in front of the mother"), *tata upariṣṭāt* ("above that"), and *kaphoṇiḥ kūrparādadhaḥ* ("the elbow is below the shoulder-joint"). In the case of *napāt*, the second case is used.

When used in conjunction with a word ending in the suffix *enap* (denoting direction), the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall be employed. For example: *dakṣiṇena gayāṃ mahābodhiḥ* ("The Great Bodhi tree is to the south of Gayā"). Some authorities maintain that the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may also be used: *dakṣiṇena gayāyāḥ*.
