In connection with the words *pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally used. When these are joined [with another word], either the third or the fifth case may occur. Examples: *pṛthak candreṇa* or "the bodiless god of love torments even more than the moon" (*dunoti candrāt pṛthag apy anaṅgaḥ*). *vinā kāryeṇa* or *vinā kāryād vā* ("without purpose"). *nānā vṛkṣeṇa* or *nānā vṛkṣād vā* ("different from the tree"). Furthermore, the second case is also seen: *vinā vātam*, *vinā varṣam*, and so forth.

And when expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*), the fifth case may optionally be used after *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya*, provided they denote non-substances (*asattvavacana*). That is, when expressing the instrument, the fifth case may optionally occur after *stoka* and the others, provided they denote non-substances—that is, do not denote a substance (*adravyavacana*). Examples: "Stokena ruṣṭā dayitāya nārī stokādupetā punareva toṣam" (The beloved woman was angered by a little [stokena], but she returned to her joy after a little [stokāt]). "Kṛcchrād avāptaḥ" or "kṛccheṇa" (Obtained with difficulty). "Kṛcchrāt muktaḥ" or "kṛccheṇa" (Released from difficulty). Why "denoting non-substances"? (Counter-example: "Stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ" (Killed by a small amount of poison). With words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the sixth case may optionally be used.

When used in conjunction with words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and fifth (*pañcamī*) case endings may occur. *Dūraṃ grāmasya* or *grāmāt* (Far from the village). *Viprakṛṣṭaṃ śailasya* or *śailāt* (Remote from the mountain). *Antikaṃ gṛhasya* or *gṛhāt* (Near the house). The second (*dvitīyā*) case ending also occurs after these [words meaning far or near]. After these, the second, fifth, and third (*tṛtīyā*) case endings may occur. *Dūraṃ*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa* grāmasya nadī (The river is far from the village). *Antikam*, *antikāt*, or *antikena* mūrkhāṇāṃ paśutvam (The beast-nature of fools is near [to their true state]). This applies only when [the word] does not denote a sentient being (*asattvavacana*). *Dūraḥ paśuḥ* (A distant animal). *Āsannā munayaḥ* (The sages are near).

The seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The seventh case should be employed when expressing the locus. For example: *kaṭe āste* ("he sits on a mat"). Because of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], it is also used after words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*). For example: *dūre grāmasya* ("far from the village") and *antike nadyāḥ* ("near the river"). The seventh case is used for the object (*karman*) of a word ending in a *kta* suffix that has *in* as its scope. For example: *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("one who has studied grammar") and *nipaṭhitī tantreṣu* ("one who has mastered the treatises").
[The suffix *lyap* is applied] after [a word denoting] a cause (*nimitta*) when there is a connection with an action (*karmasaṃyoga*).
"One kills the leopard for its skin; one kills the elephant for its two tusks;
one kills the yak for its hair; the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland. (1)

The locative case shall be used when the state of one thing characterizes the state of another, or when the action of one thing characterizes the action of another. For example: *goṣu duhyamānāsu gato devadatto dugdhāsv āgataḥ* ("While the cows were being milked, Devadatta went; he returned when they had been milked"). Or: *asmin sati idaṃ bhavati* ("When this exists, that comes to be"). Or: *ṛddheṣv āsīneṣu daridrā bhuñjate* ("While the wealthy sit, the poor eat"). It is not used here: *śayānena bhuktam* ("He ate while lying down"), because such usage is not sanctioned by the rules.
Furthermore, the locative is also used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*), along with the genitive.

When there is an excess of disregard (*anādara*) as a characteristic of an action (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*), both the sixth and seventh case endings may be used. For example: *rudataḥ* or *rudati pravrajitavān* ("he went forth [into homelessness] while [they] were weeping"). The meaning is: "disregarding those who were weeping. Similarly: *paśyatoharaḥ* ("one who steals while [others] are looking on").

With the words *svāmī*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sākṣin*, *pratibhū*, and *prasūta*, both the sixth and seventh case endings may be used when they are employed in conjunction [with another word]. For example: *gavāṃ svāmī* or *goṣu svāmī* ("the owner of cows"); *prāṇānām īśvaraḥ* or *prāṇeṣu īśvaraḥ* ("the lord of life-breaths").
And with the two [terms] *āyukta* and *kuśala*, there is [the suffix *kha*] in the sense of practice (*āsevanā*).

When these two are used in the sense of application (*yoga*) or intent (*tātparya*), those two [suffixes] may occur: *āyukta* in the sense of making a dwelling (*vihārakaraṇa*) or in a dwelling; *kuśala* in the sense of practice (*sevā*) or in practice. And because [the rule] is restricted (*nirdhāraṇa*) by this.

Since [a group] is distinguished by birth and so forth, therefrom those two [the genitive and locative] would occur: "Among men, the Kṣatriya is the most heroic," or "among men"; "Among cows, the black one yields the most milk," or "among cows"; "Among travelers, the chariot-warriors are the swiftest," or "among travelers. The fifth case (ablative) occurs when there is a division based on selection (*nirdhāraṇa*): therefrom the fifth case would occur; for example, "The Mathurans are wealthier than the Srughnas."

When used with *sādhu* or *nipuṇa* in the sense of "worship" (*arcā*), the seventh case ending occurs after these two words provided they are not preceded by *prati*. When joined with these two, the seventh case is employed when the meaning is "reverence" (*pūjā*) or "proficiency" (*gata*). Examples: *pitari sādhuḥ* (devoted to the father); *mātari sādhuḥ* (devoted to the mother); *mātari nipuṇaḥ* (skilled toward the mother); *bodhe nipuṇaḥ* (skilled in understanding). Why "not preceded by *prati*"? Example: *mātaraṃ prati sādhuḥ* (devoted toward the mother). Here, *prati* is an illustration; it includes others such as *mātaram anu*. In this context, they split the rule *aprater* and connect it with other rules as appropriate to prohibit specific case endings. Thus, in the sentence *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati puṣpāṇi santi*, the seventh case of the locative (*adhāra-saptamī*) does not apply.

In the expression *tvāṃ prati svāmī* ("the master with respect to you"), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and locative (*saptamī*) case endings are not used. In *keśān pratyutsukaḥ* ("eager for his hair"), the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) and locative (*saptamī*) are not used. In *devadattaṃ prati kupyati* ("he is angry with Devadatta"), the dative (*caturthī*) of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is not used. Regarding the rule *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca*: when these two [words] are joined [with another word], both the instrumental and the locative cases may be employed. For example: *keśaiḥ prasitaḥ* or *keśeṣu prasitaḥ* ("addicted to his hair"); *keśair utsukaḥ* or *keśeṣu utsukaḥ* ("eager for his hair"). As in: *bhavatyām utsuko rāmaḥ* ("Rāma is eager for your ladyship").

And when the elision (*lup*) occurs after a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the third and seventh case endings may occur after that word which has undergone elision. For example: *puṣyeṇa pāyasamaśnīyāt* (one should eat milk-rice under the asterism Puṣya) or *puṣye* (under Puṣya). This applies only when [the asterism] is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Otherwise: *adya puṣyaḥ* (today is the asterism Puṣya).
The first case ending occurs only in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), gender (*liṅga*), measure (*parimāṇa*), and number (*vacana*).

If only this much were stated—that is, even when the object (*karman*) and so forth have been expressed—the nominative case (*prathamā*) would still apply. That which constitutes the primary function of a word is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). For example: *vṛkṣo dṛśyatām* ("Let the tree be seen"), *śveto dhāvati* ("The white one runs"), *pācakaḥ* ("the cooker"), *pacanam* ("the act of cooking"), *strī* ("female"), *pumān* ("male"), *napuṃsakam* ("neuter"), *droṇaḥ* ("a droṇa measure"), *khārī* ("a khārī measure"), *āḍhakam* ("an āḍhaka measure"). The primary function of words such as "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) pertains to their initial form (*ādyākṛti*). Through metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), it also applies to the substance (*dravya*) and so forth, as well as to gender (*puṃstva*) and the rest. Because the "tree" and other such terms always involve a correlative relation (*anvaya*), they denote only their own inherent meaning (*svārtha*) and nothing more. Nevertheless, this [inherent meaning] includes gender and the like.

If it is accomplished even by means of a case-ending (*vāra*), then an innumerable number of examples of the non-case-terminations (*aliṅga*) may be cited: *uccaiḥ* (highly), *tvam* (you), *aham* (I). Because of the mention of "mere" (*mātra*), [the suffix does not occur] when something additional is not expressed: *vṛkṣaṃ paśyati* (he sees the tree); *aśvena gamyate* (it is traveled by horse). In the case of mere gender (*liṅga*) being additional: *kumārī* (a young girl); *śṛṅkhalā* (a chain). Measure (*parimāṇa*) refers to a conventional unit (*upacāra*). In the case of mere measure being additional: *prasthena parimito vrīhiḥ* (rice measured by a *prastha*); *prasthaḥ*, *droṇaḥ*, *khārī*, *āḍhakam* [are used for] rice. Number (*vacana*) refers to quantity (*saṃkhyā*). In the case of that alone: so that it occurs even when [the number] has already been stated: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*. And also in the case of address (*sambodhana*).

The first case ending occurs when there is an addition of address. *He vipra* (O Brahmin), *he viprau* (O two Brahmins), *he viprāḥ* (O Brahmins). That [first case] is called *āmantrita* (vocative). *He vipra, tava svam* (O Brahmin, your own); *he vatsa, tavāśvaḥ* (O child, your horse).
The singular number is called *sambuddhi*.

The singular number of that which is addressed (*āmantrita*) is termed *sambuddhi*. Examples: *he vṛkṣa*, *he pate*, *he nadi*, *he paṭo*. "The genitive case is used for the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*).

The non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), which is a relationship (*sambandha*). In that case, when [the relationship] is to be understood, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used. Examples: *rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam* (the wealth of the king's man); *sukhasya jānāti* (he knows of happiness); *māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* (one should eat of the beans). "Fire is not satiated by wood, nor is the great ocean by rivers. The rule for the "remainder" applies up until the connection with verbal roots (*ākṛd-yoga*). [Also]: *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* (the sixth case is used for the instrument of the verb *jñā* when it does not mean "knowing").

The genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) shall be used for the instrument (*karaṇa*) when the root *jñā* (to know) is employed. Example: *madhuno jānīte*. The meaning is: "He engages with honey" (*madhunā pravartate*). Example: *tailasya ghṛtasya jānīte*. Why [is it said] "not having the sense of 'ignorance' (*avidartha*)"? Example: *svareṇa putraṃ jānāti* ("He recognizes the son by his voice"). Since this would be established by the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), this section is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): namely, that only the instrument, object, and so forth of roots such as *jñā*, *dhī*, and *artha* should be intended as the residual relation (*śeṣatva*). [Furthermore: For roots having the sense of *adhī* (to study), *day* (to pity), and *īś* (to rule), [the genitive is used] for the object (*karman*).

When the object (*karman*) of these [verbs] is intended to be expressed as a *śeṣa* (remaining relation), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used. Example: *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"). This is because the object is intended to be expressed as a *śeṣa*. Even from intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*), the suffixes *la* etc. occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Examples: *mātuḥ smaryate* ("the mother is remembered") and *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("the mother was remembered"). Similarly: *mamaivādhyeti nṛpatiḥ* ("the king studies only my [work]") and *rāmasya dayamāno'sau* ("he is feeling pity for Rāma"). Example: *sarpiṣo jñāsyati* ("he will know the ghee"). Only when it is a *śeṣa* [is this rule applied]. Otherwise: *mātaraṃ smarati* ("he remembers his mother") and *mātā smaryate* ("the mother is remembered"). With the root *kṛñ* ("to do/make"), when there is an improvement (*pratiyatna*), the sixth case shall be used for the object. Example: *alaṅkārasyopaskurute kāmukaḥ* ("the lover improves the ornament").

For verbal roots meaning "to cause pain" (*ruj-artha*) that express a state (*bhāva-vacana*) and have a state as their agent (*bhāva-kartṛka*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the object (*karman*), provided the root does not mean "to fever" (*ajvareḥ*). Example: *caurasya rujati rogaḥ* ("the disease afflicts the thief"). Why "not *jvari*" (*ajvareḥ*)? Example: *cauraṃ jvarayati jvaraḥ* ("the fever causes the thief to suffer from fever"). [Note: *Jvari* is an illustrative term (*upalakṣaṇa*). Example: *cauraṃ santāpayati santāpaḥ* ("the torment torments the thief"). [The rule applies] only when the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is intended. Example: *rujanti cetaḥ prasabhaṃ mamādhayaḥ* ("my anxieties violently afflict my mind").

In the sense of "blessing" (*āśis*), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall apply to the object of the verb *nāth*. For example: *sarpiṣo nāthate gṛdhnuḥ* ("the greedy man prays for clarified butter"). [Also, the sixth case applies] to the objects of the verbs *jas*, *ni-pra-han*, *naṭ*, *krāth*, and *piṣ* when used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*).

The sixth case ending shall be used for the object (*karman*) when these [roots] signify injury (*hiṃsā*). *caurasya ujjāsayati* (he causes the thief to be terrified). *caurasya prahanti* (they strike the thief). *caurasya nihanti* (he strikes down the thief). *caurasya praṇihanti* (he strikes forward at the thief). *caurasya niprahanti* (they strike down the thief). The root *krathi* belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group; its vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *dhairyasyotkrāthayati śokaḥ* (grief causes him to lose his fortitude). *vivekasya pinaṣṭi kāmaḥ* (lust grinds away his discrimination). In the case of the roots *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ*, when they have the same meaning—namely, in gambling or buying and selling—the sixth case ending shall be used for their object. *śatasya vyavaharati* (he deals with a hundred). *śatasya paṇate vaṇik* (the merchant bets a hundred). *"prāṇānāmapaṇiṣṭāsau"* (he staked his very life).
[The rule applies] to the root *div* in the sense of gambling.

When *div* has the sense of gambling, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the object (*karman*). Example: *śatasya dīvyati* ("He gambles with a hundred"). [As in: *adevīt bandhabhogānām* ("He gambled away his bonds and enjoyments").
[This is] optional (*vibhāṣā*) when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present.

The same [option] applies when the root *div* is accompanied by a prefix: one plays for a hundred (*śatasya pratidīvyati*) or (*śataṃ* pratidīvyati). Since the accusative case is already established by the intention to express the entirety [of the stake], the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) is for the sake of clarity. Here, the accusative occurs in the rule:
"In the case of *preṣya* and *brūhi*, when the oblation is the recipient for a deity."
In the Vedic language, the dative sense is frequently expressed by the genitive case;
likewise, the genitive is used for the instrument of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
These four sūtras constitute the meaning of the Veda.
When used in connection with words having the sense of *kṛtvas* (times), the sixth case ending is employed for the time that serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

When there is usage with words having the sense of *kṛtvas*, the sixth case shall be used for that which is the time acting as the substratum. Examples: *pañcakṛtvo divasasya bhuṅkte* (he eats five times a day); *śatakṛtvo rātreḥ smarati priyām* (he remembers his beloved a hundred times at night); *dvirahno'dhīte* (he studies twice a day). [The rule applies] only when it is "the remainder" (*śeṣa*); thus, in *dvirahnyadhīte*, the second case is used. [Furthermore, the sixth case is used] for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix is present.

When a *kṛt* suffix is employed, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). Because the term "remainder" (*śeṣe*) has ceased to apply here, this is a case-ending based on grammatical function (*kāraka-vibhakti*). It supersedes the second and third cases. Examples: *bhavata āsikā* (the sitting of you), *odanasya bhojakaḥ* (the eater of rice). Here, by the mention of the word *tadarham*, its non-obligatory nature (*anityatva*) is indicated. Therefore, Bhaṭṭi uses: *dhātryai rāmodamuttamam*. Alternatively, this form arises from the avyayībhāva compound *ā modāt sammada-paryantam*; thus, because it is a *kṛt* formation, the sixth case is not applied. The rule must simply be stated as *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"). Regarding the phrase *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*: [this refers to the rule governing the sixth case when both agent and object are possible].

When both [the agent and the object] are applicable in one instance, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall apply only to the object, not to the agent. For example: *adbhutaḥ samudrasya bandho vānaraiḥ* (The binding of the ocean by the monkeys was wonderful); *āścaryaṃ subhagāroṣasya dūtībhiḥ parimārjanam* (It is a marvel that the anger of the beloved woman was wiped away by her messengers). However, there is a restrictive prohibition regarding the feminine gender when the suffixes *ka* and *aka* are absent. For example: *bhedikā candrasya tamasām* (The dispeller of the darkness of the moon); *cikīrṣā raveḥ ālokānām* (The desire to produce the light of the sun). Regarding the "remainder" (*śeṣe*), it is optional (*vibhāṣā*). That is, other than when the suffixes *ka* and *aka* are absent, it is optional. For example: *vicitrā sūtrasya kṛtiḥ pāṇineḥ* (The composition of the Sūtras by Pāṇini) or *pāṇininā* (by Pāṇini).

And [the genitive is used] with a *kta*-suffix when it denotes the present. When a *kta*-suffix is employed in the sense of the present, the genitive case shall be used. This is an exception to the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām*. Examples: *rājñāṃ matam* (approved by kings), *satāṃ mataḥ* (approved by the virtuous), *satāmarcitaḥ* (honored by the virtuous), *prajānāṃ kāntaḥ* (beloved by the subjects). How is it that [in the examples] *tvayā śīlitaḥ* (practiced by you) and *mayā rakṣitaḥ* (protected by me), the genitive is not used? Effort must be made here [to explain]. In these cases, such as *iha chātrasya hasitam* (the laughing of the student here) and *mayūrasya nṛttam* (the dancing of the peacock), this is the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), because the prohibition in *na loka...* applies to [genitives] connected with a *kṛt*-suffix. However, when the agency (*kāraka*) is intended to be expressed, the traditional usage is *chātreṇa hasitam* (laughed by the student). And [the genitive is used] after a word expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

When a *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the locus (*ādhāra*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be employed for the agent and the object. Examples: *idameṣām āsitam* (this is where they sat); *idamasya śayitam* (this is where he lay). *bhuktamidam odanasya* (this much of rice was eaten). The sixth case is not applied when there is the usage of *la*-affixes, indeclinables (*avyaya*), past participles (*niṣṭhā*), *khalartha* suffixes, or *tṛn* suffixes. Examples: *la*: *odanaṃ pacan* (cooking rice); *odanaṃ pacamānaḥ* (cooking rice). *upasedivān pāṇinim* (one who has approached Pāṇini). *u*: *kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ* (desirous of making a mat); *dhanaṃ gṛdhnuḥ* (greedy for wealth). *kṣipṇuḥ rakṣogaṇam* (swiftly destroying the host of Rākṣasas). *kāryaṃ kāruḥ* (a maker of what is to be done). *uka*: *gaṅgāṃ gāmukaḥ* (one prone to going to the Gaṅgā).

In the prohibition [of the genitive] mentioned above, there is no prohibition for the verb *kam* (to desire) in common usage (*bhāṣā*). Examples: *dāsyāḥ kāmukaḥ* ("one who desires a maidservant"). [The prohibition applies to: 1. An indeclinable (*avyaya*): *kaṭaṃ kṛtvā* ("having made a mat"), *kaṭaṃ kartuṃ* ("in order to make a mat"). 2. A past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*): *tena kṛtam* ("done by him"), *so 'nnaṃ bhuktavān* ("he has eaten food"). 3. Words having the sense of the suffix *-khal* (*khalartha*): *īṣatkaraḥ*, *sukaraḥ kaṭo bhavatā* ("the mat is easy to be made by you"). 4. The suffix *-tṛn*: *kartā kaṭān* ("one who makes mats"). The mention of *-tṛn* here is intended as a *pratyāhāra* (a collective term); therefore, it also includes the prohibition for suffixes such as *-śānan*. Example: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* ("purifying the Soma"), *naḍam āghnānaḥ* ("striking the reed"). 5. Regarding the suffix *-śatṛ* after the root *dviṣ* (to hate), there is an option: *caurasya dviṣan* or *cauraṃ dviṣan* ("hating the thief"). [The prohibition does not apply] to the suffix *-aka* when used with a future meaning or with a non-ethical obligation (*abhaviṣyad-adharmaṇya*). Example: *akārakaḥ kaṭasya* ("one who will make a mat").

The sixth case (genitive) shall not be used for the object of a future passive participle (*akenoḥ*), nor when it denotes a debt (*ṛṇe*). Examples: *odanaṃ pācako vrajati* ("the cooker goes to cook rice"), *vārtām ākhyāyakaḥ* ("the narrator of news"), *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"), *śataṃ dāyī* ("one who will give a hundred"). For the agent of a gerundive (*kṛtyānām*), the sixth case is optional.

In these cases, the genitive case may optionally be used for the agent. For example: *tvayā kaṭaḥ kartavyas tava vā* ("The mat is to be made by you" or "of you"); *mayā kaṭaḥ kartavyo mama vā* ("The mat is to be made by me" or "of me"). *Tava gamyo grāmas tvayā vā* ("The village is accessible to you" or "by you"). [As in: *"Gantavyā te vasatir alakā nāma yakṣeśvarāṇām"* ("Your dwelling, named Alakā, the city of the lords of the Yakṣas, is to be gone to by you"). Why specify "for the agent"? [Consider: *upasthānīyaḥ śiṣyo guroḥ* ("The disciple is to be attended upon by the teacher"). When both [agent and object] are possible, there is a prohibition of the genitive in the case of *kṛtya* suffixes: *kraṣṭavyā śākhā grāmaṃ vānareṇa* ("The branch is to be pulled toward the village by the monkey"); *neyā grāmam ajā gopālakena* ("The goat is to be led to the village by the cowherd"). With words having the sense of "equal," except for *atula* and *upama*, the third case is optionally used.

When joined with words having the sense of *tulya* ("equal"), the third case may optionally be used. For example: *tulyaḥ śakreṇa* (equal to Śakra), or, alternatively, because it is treated as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the sixth case is used: *tulyaḥ śakrasya*. Similarly: *samaḥ sūryeṇa* or *sūryasya* (equal to the Sun). Why [is this rule] not applied to *atula* and *upama*? As in: "The moon is the equal (*upamā*) of the woman's face; the woman's face is the equal (*tulā*) of the moon. Here, the words *tulā* and *upamā* have the meaning of "similar.
Furthermore, the fourth case is used with words expressing a blessing (*āśis*) when combined with *āyuṣya*, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita*.

When used in conjunction with words meaning "long life" (*āyuṣya*) and so forth, as well as with the word *hita* ("beneficial"), the fourth case (*caturthī*) or the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may be employed. For example: *āyuṣyaṃ rājñe astu* or *rājñaḥ* ("May there be long life for the king"). Likewise: *cirañjīvitam*, *kuśalam*, *madram*, *bhadram*, *sauhityam*, *śivam*, *sukham*, *hitam* [may these be] for the cows (*gobhyaḥ* or *gavām*), or for the subjects (*prajābhyaḥ* or *prajānām*). Why specify "in a benediction" (*āśiṣi*)? [Because in a non-benedictory sense: *āyuṣyaṃ te tapaḥ* ("Your asceticism is conducive to long life").
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.
The section on the "unexpressed" (anabhihita) is completed.
In the second chapter, the fourth quarter: "A *dvigu* compound takes the singular number."

In a collective compound (samāhāra), a *dvigu* functions as a singular. For example: *pañcapūlī śobhanā* (five beautiful bundles); *daśaśatī ramyā* (ten beautiful hundreds). And a *dvandva* consisting of parts of living beings (*prāṇin*), musical instruments (*tūrya*), or military units (*senāṅga*) is also singular. A *dvandva* beginning with parts of living beings and so forth shall be singular. For example: *hastapādam* (hand and foot); *karṇanāsikam* (ear and nose); *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (drummers and pan-pipers); *rathikapādātam* (charioteers and infantry). How is it that *hastyaśvau* (elephant and horse) is not singular? Because of the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 2.4.12], which provides an option for *dvandvas* of animals (*paśu*).
Regarding the mention of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*):

when Vedic schools are mentioned, their *dvandva* compound shall be singular. This applies to the mention of Vedic schools in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense after the roots *sthā* and *i*. For example: *udagāt kaṭhakālāpam* ("The Kaṭha and Kālāpa [schools] emerged") and *pratyaṣṭhāt kaṭhakauthumam* ("The Kaṭha and Kauthuma [schools] were established").
Furthermore, a *dvandva* compound denoting a sacrificial ritual (*kratu*) performed by an *adhvaryu* priest is neuter.

In the *Adhvaryu* branch of the *Yajurveda*, the names of sacrifices such as the *Soma-yāga* and others form a *dvandva* compound that is treated as singular. Example: *arka-aśvamedham*. Why "not neuter"? [Counter-example: *rājasūya-vājapeye*.
[This applies] to those whose names are not separated by their order of study.

In a *dvandva* compound consisting of words that are closely related in their recitation (*pāṭha*), the compound shall be singular. This is the *Kramaka-vārttika*. For example: *chātropādhyāyam* (the student and the teacher).

A *jāti* (genus) term, when not referring to living beings, forms a singular *dvandva*. For example: *ārāśastri* (the awl and the knife); *drumaśailam* (the tree and the mountain). Why "a genus"? [Consider: *vindhyahimālayau* (the Vindhya and the Himalaya mountains). In this case, "badarāmalakāni santi" (there are jujubes and myrobalans in the bowl)—why is this not a singular *dvandva*? Because it refers to individual fruits, not a genus. Why "a *dvandva*"? [Consider: *ārāśastrīyam*, which means "an awl accompanied by a knife."
Rivers and regions that do not include villages, when distinguished by different genders, form a dvandva compound in the singular.
A dvandva consisting of rivers and regions of different genders shall be treated as a singular. Examples: *gaṅgāśoṇam*, *śoṇanarmadam*, *varendrīmagadham*, *magadhaśrāvastī*.
Why "of different genders"? [Answer: *gaṅgāyamune*. Why "not including villages"? [Answer: *jāmbavaśālūkiṇyau*.
In the prohibition concerning villages, there is no prohibition concerning cities: *mathurāpāṭaliputram* (Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra).
"Small creatures" (*kṣudrajantavaḥ*): a *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting small creatures shall be singular. *daṃśamaśakam* (gnats and mosquitoes); *yūkālikṣam* (lice and nits).

And for those whose enmity is perpetual, a *dvandva* compound of things that are eternally opposed shall be treated as a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*). Examples: *ahinakulam* (snake and mongoose), *kākolūkam* (crow and owl), *śvaśṛgālam* (dog and jackal), *mārjāramūṣikam* (cat and mouse). By the inclusion of "and" (*ca*), the optionality regarding animals and birds is also set aside. [Examples of this would be: *iha devāsurāṇām* (here, the gods and the demons) and *kauravapāṇḍavānām* (the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas); in these cases, the enmity is occasional (*naimittika*). Also: *śūdrāṇām aniravasitānām* (Śūdras who have not been cast out).

For Śūdras, a copulative compound (dvandva) shall be treated as a singular. Examples: *rajakatantuvāyam* ("the washerman and the weaver"). There is an exception for those who have been cast out (*niravasita*): *cāṇḍālamṛtapāḥ* ("the Cāṇḍāla and the Mṛtapa"). And the group beginning with *gavāśva*: these shall be correct according to their recited order. Examples: *gavāśvam* ("a cow and a horse"), *kubjavāmanam* ("the hunchback and the dwarf"), *putrapautram* ("son and grandson"), *dāsīdāsam* ("female slave and male slave").

The *Vibhāṣā* (optional rule) applies to compounds consisting of: trees, wild animals, grasses, grains, condiments, domestic animals, birds, horses and mares, and the terms "prior" (*pūrva*), "posterior" (*apara*), "lower" (*adhara*), and "upper" (*uttara*). For these, a *dvandva* compound may optionally be singular. Examples: *plakṣavaṭam* (the *plakṣa* and *vaṭa* trees); *rurupṛṣatam* (the *ruru* and *pṛṣata* deer); *kuśakāśam* (the *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses); *vrīhiyavam* (rice and barley); *dadhikṣīram* (curd and milk); *gomahiṣam* (cows and buffaloes); *haṃsacakravākam* (swans and ruddy geese); *aśvavaḍavam* (horses and mares); *pūrvāparam* (the prior and the posterior); *adharottaram* (the lower and the upper). In the alternative case [of non-singular form], one has: *plakṣavaṭau*, *rurupṛṣatau*, and so forth.

A *dvandva* compound consisting of many constituents—namely fruits, armies, trees, wild animals, birds, small creatures, grains, and grasses—shall be treated as a singular (*ekavat*), provided they do not consist of only two constituents. Examples include: *badarāmalake* (jujube and myrobalan), *rathikapādāte* (charioteers and infantry), *plakṣavaṭau* (the *plakṣa* and *vaṭa* trees), and *yūkālikṣe* (lice and nits), and so forth. Furthermore, a *dvandva* of contradictory terms that do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*) may optionally be treated as a singular. Examples include: *śītoṣṇam* or *śītoṣṇe* (cold and heat), *himātapam* or *himātapau* (snow and sun). However, this does not apply here: *sukhaduḥkhau* (pleasure and pain) or *svarganarakau* (heaven and hell).
Not so for curds, milk, and the like;

these do not form a singular compound. Examples: *dadhi-payasī* (curds and milk), *dadhi-sarpiṣī* (curds and ghee), *sarpiḥ-madhunī* (ghee and honey), *śukla-kṛṣṇe* (white and black), *ṛk-sāme* (Ṛc and Sāman), *vāk-manase* (speech and mind).
Also [the singular is used] when the sense is that of a "container" (*adhikaraṇa*) or a specific measure (*etāvat-tva*).

When the total number of items denoted by a compound is fixed, a *dvandva* (copulative compound) shall not be singular. For example: *daśa dantauṣṭhāḥ* ("ten teeth and lips") and *sapta mārdaṅgikapāṇavikāḥ* ("seven drummers and players of the *pāṇava*").

The rule *vibhāṣā samīpe* ("optionally when near"): When the proximity of the total number of items in a locative context is indicated, a *dvandva* may optionally be singular. For example: *upadaśaṃ dantauṣṭham* ("nearly ten teeth and lips") or *upadaśā dantauṣṭhāḥ* ("almost ten teeth and lips").
That is neuter.
That for which singularity has been stated shall be neuter: *pañcagavam* (a collection of five oxen), *pāṇipādam* (hands and feet).
A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the vowel *a* is said to be feminine: *pañcapūlī* (a collection of five bundles).
Or [the suffix] *āp* is applied. For example: *pañcakhaṭvam*, *pañcakhaṭvī*.

It should be stated that for words ending in *an*, there is optionally the elision of *n* when used in the feminine: *pañcatakṣam*, *pañcatakṣī*. There is a prohibition [of the application of *āp*] after words such as *pātra*: *dvipātram*, *tribhuvanam*, *caturyugam*, *pañcagavam*. Also from the word *diś*, [the compound] *caturdiśam*.

And the *avyayībhāva* [compound] is neuter. This [compound] shall be neuter. Examples: *adhistri*, *adhilakṣmi*, *unmattagaṅgam*. By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the sūtra], [the neuter gender applies] also to *ahar* when preceded by *paṇya* and *sudina*: *puṇyāham*, *sudināham*. [The neuter gender applies] to *pathin* when preceded by a numeral or an indeclinable: *dvipatham*, *catuṣpatham*, *vipatham*, *utpatham*.

Adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) possess the status of an object (*karman*) and are neuter. *Tatpuruṣo’nañkarmadhārayaḥ*: With the exception of those containing the negative particle *nañ* or those being *karmadhāraya* compounds, a *tatpuruṣa* compound shall be neuter; this is the governing rule. For example, by the rule *vibhāṣā senā*, one may say either *śatrusenam* or *śatrusenā*. Why specify "*tatpuruṣaḥ*" [in the rule]? Consider *dṛḍhaseno rājā* ("the king with a firm army"), which is not neuter because it is a *bahuvrīhi*. Why specify "*anañkarmadhārayaḥ*" [in the rule]? Consider *asenā* ("not an army") and *paramasenā* ("supreme army"), which are not neuter because they are respectively *nañ-tatpuruṣas* and *karmadhārayas*.
Regarding the term *kantha* when it denotes a proper name (*saṃjñā*) among the Uśīnaras:

a Tatpuruṣa compound ending in *kantha* is neuter when it refers to a name. For example, *sauśamikantham*, meaning "the region named Sauśamikantha. Why "when it denotes a proper name"? [Consider] *vīraṇakanthā*.
Why "among the Uśīnaras"? [Consider] *dākṣikanthā*.

The compound *upajñā-upakrama* becomes neuter when there is a desire to express that [person] as the originator (*ādi*) thereof; *upajñā* and *upakrama* are both derived from the object (*karman*). A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in these two shall be neuter if there is a wish to designate them as the beginning of those two. Examples: *āgamopajñaṃ dharmādharmau* (dharma and adharma originated by Āgama); *manūpajñaṃ lokavṛttam* (the conduct of the world originated by Manu); *āḍhyopakramaṃ dānam* (a gift initiated by a wealthy person); *brāhmaṇopakramaṃ pratigrahaḥ* (acceptance of a gift initiated by a Brāhmaṇa). [The word] *chāyā* [becomes neuter] when it denotes abundance.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *chāyā* (shadow) is neuter when it means "within" (*antah*). Examples: *khaḍgacchāyam* (the interior of a sword), *śalabhacchāyam* (the interior of a locust). Why [is it not neuter] in the case of multiplicity? Example: *vṛkṣacchāyā* (the shadow of trees). The word *sabhā* (assembly/hall), when preceded by a synonym of *rājan* (king) or by a word other than *manuṣya* (human), is neuter. *Sabhā* means a hall. Examples: *inasabham*, *īśvarasabham*. [Also: *nṛpatisabhā*.

However, when a specific distinction is intended, as in "trembling on the path," it is like the term *gajapati* (lord of elephants). Since the word *rājan* here serves merely as an indicator for any synonym of king, one does not say "the assembly of the king" (*rājasabhā*) when referring to the assembly of Candragupta;

rather, one says "the assembly of Rākṣasa. Because the word *amanuṣya* (non-human) is conventionally restricted to beings such as *rakṣas* and *piśāca*, one does not say "the assembly of gods" (*devasabhā*). Furthermore, it does not denote a non-hall.
A *sabhā* (assembly) that does not mean a "hall" is neuter: *strīsabham*, *dāsīsabham*; the meaning is "an assembly of women" or "an assembly of female slaves.

The rule *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyāśālāniśānām* states that a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *senā*, *surā*, *chāyā*, *śālā*, or *niśā* may optionally be neuter. Examples: *śatrusenam* (army of enemies), *yavasuram* (liquor made from barley), *vṛkṣacchāyam* (shade of trees), *gośālam* (cow-pen), *śvaniśam* (night for dogs). In the alternative case, they are feminine: *śatrusenā*, *yavasuret*, and so forth.

In the case of *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, the gender of the final member alone shall prevail. For example: *kukkuṭamayūryāv ime* (these two are a cock and a peahen); *mayūrīkukkuṭāvimau* (these two are a peahen and a cock). In the case of *tatpuruṣa*: *rājastrī* (the king’s wife), *ardhapippalī* (half a long pepper), *mukhacandraḥ* (moon-like face). There is an exception (*pratiṣedha*) for *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam-pūrva*, and *gati* compounds: *pañcakapālaḥ sūpaḥ* (soup prepared in five pots), *prāptajīvikaḥ* (one who has obtained a livelihood), *āpannasukhaḥ* (one who has attained happiness), *alaṅkumāriḥ* (one who is sufficient for a maiden), *pratigato’kṣam pratyakṣaḥ paṭaḥ* (a cloth that has come before the eye—*pratyakṣa*), and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī). In these cases, the compound takes the very gender of the word it qualifies (*vācyaliṅgatā*).
The terms *aśva* (horse) and *vaḍabā* (mare) are as previously stated.

Except when they form a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*), the gender of *aśva* and *vaḍabā* shall be as before: *aśvavaḍavau*, *aśvavaḍavān*, *aśvavaḍavaiḥ*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the terms *hemanta* (winter) and *śiśira* (cool season), as well as *ahorātra* (day and night), follow the same rule.
*Chandas* is a neuter noun.
*Rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine. These [words] are used in the masculine: "These two, day and night (*ahorātrau*), are meritorious"; *pūrvāhṇaḥ*; *dvyahaḥ*; *tryahaḥ*; *ekāhaḥ*.

The word *apatha* is neuter. It may be [neuter]; for example, "this is an *apatha*" (an improper path). Because of the continued application of the rule for *tatpuruṣa* compounds, it can also be masculine: "this region is an *apatha*" (a place without a path). Furthermore, the words beginning with *ardharca* are both masculine and [neuter].

Words beginning with *ardharca* may be used in both the masculine and neuter genders: *ardharcam* or *ardharcaḥ*; *yūtham* or *yūthaḥ*; *madhu* or *madhuḥ*. [As it is said: "It destroys inauspicious karma and accumulates auspicious karma. Similarly, there are *gomaya*, *sara*, *kaṣāya*, *varṇa*, *padma*, *śaṅkha*, *kuliśa*, *divasa*, *kārpāsa*, *karpūra*, *dharma*, *vrata*, and so forth. The rules for gender have been stated. Regarding the pronoun *idam*: when it is used as a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the form *aś-* is substituted, and it is unaccented (*anudātta*) before the third case endings and those that follow. When *idam* is preceded by the suffix *ka* (i.e., *imakā*) and is being referred back to what was previously mentioned, the forms beginning with *aś-* are prescribed when the third case ending or any subsequent case ending follows. For example: *imābhyāṃ rātrir adhītā* ("By these two, the night was studied"); *atho ābhyām ahar apy adhītam* ("Moreover, by these two, the day was also studied").

The forms *etad-a* and *etad-au* are also [treated as such], provided they are unaccented (*anudātta*). The term *etadaḥ* is understood here as a governing heading (*adhikāra*). Regarding the suffixes *-tra-* and *-tas-*, since the substitution of *aś* for *etad* is already established by the rule *etado'ś*, this present rule is stated for the purpose of ensuring the unaccented nature (*anudātta*) of that portion; and that portion consists of the vowel. Examples: *etasmin vasāmaḥ* ("we dwell in this"), *atho atrādhīmahe* ("and so we study here"), and *etasmin nirgatā kīrtirathāto bibhyati dviṣaḥ* ("fame has departed from this; therefore the enemies tremble"). [Next: *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* ("the form *enaḥ* is substituted for *etad* when followed by the accusative singular suffix *-am*, or by the dual and plural suffixes beginning with *-au*").

The substitute *enam* shall occur for *etad* when it is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*). "Know him to be equal to Indra; do not think of him otherwise. *Ṭā*-case: *anena rātrir adhītā* ("By him the night was studied"); *atho enenāhar apy adhītam* ("and also by him the day was studied"). *Oṣ*-case: *anayoḥ*; *atho enayoḥ*. In the same way, [the forms] of *etado*: *etam*, *atho enam*; *etena*, *atho enena*; *etayoḥ*, *atho enayoḥ*. Only when there is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*). "This staff—take it with this. This does not apply here because it is not in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*): "Feed this student, and this Brahmin as well."

*enad* is used in the neuter singular. It should be stated that *enad* is substituted for the second case ending when expressing the neuter singular: "Bring this earring" (*idaṃ kuṇḍalam ānaya*), or "Now turn this over" (*atho enat parivarttaya*). "Bring this basin" (*etat kuṇḍam ānaya*), or "Now wash this" (*atho enat prakṣālaya*). *Ārdhadhātuke*:
This is a governing heading (adhikāra) extending as far as the rule concerning *ṇya*-affixes and *kṣatriya*.

*ado jagdhir lyapi tādau ca kiti*: After the root *ad*, *jagdhi* is substituted when followed by the suffix *lyap* and when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *ta*. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. Examples: *prajagdhyā*, *jagdhaḥ*, *jagdhavān*.
How is *anna* [formed]? It is due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) stated as "after *ad*, *anna*" [Pāṇini 6.1.127].
*luṅ-sani-ardha-slaṛ*: In *luṅ* and *san*, *slaṛ* shall be substituted for the initial [of the root] *ad*. [Examples: *adhasat*; *jighatsati*.
There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding *ac*: this is *praghasaḥ*.
"Also after *ghañ* and *ap*:
for these two, *ad* shall be replaced by *ghasṛ*. [Thus] *ghañ* yields *ghāsaḥ*; with *ap*, as in *uparse'daḥ*, it yields *praghasaḥ*.
In the Veda, this substitution occurs diversely."
This is a Vedic (chāndasa) sūtra.

[Pāṇini 2.4.40] *liṭy anyatarasyām*: In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, the root *ghaslṛ* may optionally be substituted for *ad*. Thus: *jaghāsa*, *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*; in the alternative case: *āda*, *ādatuḥ*, *āduḥ*.
The root *veñ* becomes *vayi*.

In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, *veñ* optionally becomes *vayi*. Thus: *uvāya*, *ūyatuḥ*, *ūyuḥ*; or, in the alternative case: *vavau*, *vavatuḥ*, *vavuḥ*. In the *liṅ* [optative], *han* becomes *vadha*.

In the *liṅ* (optative) mood, the substitute *vadha* shall occur [in place of the root *han*]. Thus: *vadhyāt*, *vadhyāstām*, *vadhyāsuḥ*. This applies only when the *liṅ* is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. However, in the case of the *vidhi-liṅ* (prescriptive optative), [the form is]: *hanyāt*, *hanyātām*, *hanyuḥ*.
And in the *luṅ* (aorist) as well, [the substitution is optional] in the *ātmanepada* voices.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the substitute *vadh* shall take the place of the root *han*. [Examples: *avadhīt*. In the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) voice, it is optionally so: *āvadhiṣṭa*, *āvadhiṣātām*; or in the alternative case: *āhata*, *āhasātām*.
In the *luṅ* tense, *gā* is the substitute for *iṇ*.
In the *laṅ* tense, *gā* is the substitute for *iṇ*. [Examples: *agāt*, *agātām*, *aguḥ*. [The village] was gone to: *agāyi grāmaḥ*.
It should be stated that "the root *iṇ* is treated like *ik*" [in the case of the causative]. Thus, *adhyagāt*. Regarding the rule *ṇau gamirabodhane*:

when there is no sense of "understanding," the root *gam* is prescribed in place of *iṇ* in the causative (*ṇic*). Thus, *gamayati*. Why "when there is no sense of understanding"? Consider: *arthān pratyāyayati* (he causes the meanings to be understood). The rule "the root *iṇ* is treated like *ik*" applies here as well: *adhigamayati*.
And before the suffix *san*: after the root *gam*, *san* becomes *iṇ*.

Thus, *jigamiṣati* ("he wishes to go") and *jigamiṣā* ("the desire to go"). Only when not meaning "to understand" (*abodhane*) does this apply; thus, *pratīṣiṣati* ("he intends to understand"). Only when [the rule] *iṇvadikaḥ* applies does this occur; thus, *adhijigamiṣati* ("he wishes to study"). And also after the root *iṅ*.

The root *gam* shall be substituted for *iṅ* when followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*). [Examples: *adhijigāṃsate śāstram* (he desires to study the scripture); *adhijigāṃsamānaḥ* (desiring to study). In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), *gāṅ* is the substitute for *iṅ*. [Examples: *adhijage*, *adhijagāte*, *adhijagire*.
Regarding the *luṅ* and *lṛṅ* [tenses], there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). For the root *iṅ*, *gāṅ* may optionally be substituted. Thus: *adhyagīṣṭa* or *adhyaiṣṭa*; *adhyagīṣyata* or *adhyaiṣyata*.
Also, when followed by *ṇi*, *saṃ*, or *caṅ*, [the substitution does not occur].

When followed by *caṅ* and a *ṇi*-affix, the root *iṅ* may optionally be replaced by *gāṅ*. [Examples: *adhijigāpayiṣati* or *adhyāpipayiṣati* (he wishes to cause the disciple to study). In the case of *caṅ*: *adhyajīgapat*. "The son of Gādhi caused him to study correctly" (*adhyāpipat*).

For the root *as*, there is the substitute *bhū*. [Examples: *bhavitā* (he will be), *bhavitum* (to be), *bhavitavyam* (it must be). Regarding the rule "but when used in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), there is no supersession by *bhū*": here, *ir* is mentioned as a general term for the *ārdhadhātuka* affix. Therefore, because there is no sequence [of specific conditions], this is established as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Consequently, the substitutes for *as*, *añj*, and *cakṣiṅ* occur even before [the *ārdhadhātuka* affix].
When [the substitution] is applied, that which is characterized by having a final vowel (ajanta) is established—as in *bhavyam*, *praveyam*, and *ākhyeyam*.
For the root *brū* (to speak), there is *vac*:
*syāt*, *vaktā*, *vaktum*, *vaktavyam*. This occurs only when an *ārdhadhātuka* affix follows. [In the absence of such an affix, one says] *bravīti*.

For the root *cakṣiṅ*, there is the substitute *khyāñ*. Thus: *ākhyātā* (he will tell), *ākhyāsyati* (he will tell), *ākhyāsyate* (he will tell). Because of the marker *ñ*, it is both parasmaipada and ātmanepada. This substitute also begins with *khś*: *vyākśkhyātā* (one who explains), *vyākśkhyānam* (explanation), *vyākśkhyātum* (to explain). Others say that each [substitute] begins with *kś*: thus *vyākkhyātā* or *vyāśkhyātā*, *vyākkhyānam* or *vyāśkhyānam*. There is a prohibition regarding exclusion (*varjana*): *sañcakṣyā durjanāḥ* (the wicked are to be avoided); the meaning is "they are to be excluded."

In the section on *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, it should be stated that [the application of suffixes] is "diverse" (*bahulam*) in the case of technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic usage (*chandas*). For example: *asun* [suffix] in *nṛcakṣāḥ*; *yuc* [suffix] in *vicakṣaṇaḥ*; *luṭ* [suffix] after the root *aj-* in *vyajanam*; *ṣṭran* [suffix] after the root *iṇ-* in *gātram*. Regarding the rule *vā liṭi*: after the root *cakṣiṅ*, the substitute *khyāñ* may optionally occur in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. Thus, one forms *ācakhyau* or *ācakhye*; in the alternative case, *ācacakṣe*.

*Ajervy-aghāpoh*: For the root *aj*, the substitution *vī* shall occur except when followed by the affixes *ghañ* or *ap*. Examples: *pravāyakaḥ*, *pravayaṇīyaḥ*, *vītvā*, *vītavān*. Why "except when followed by *ghañ* or *ap*"? Consider: *samājaḥ śūrāṇām* (a gathering of heroes), *samajaḥ paśūnām* (a herd of animals). There is also a prohibition when the affix *kyap* follows: *samajyā goṣṭhī* (an assembly or social circle).
In the case of the *vāl* suffix when followed by an *ārdhadhātuka* affix, there is an option. [The forms] *pravetā* and *prājitā* [are derived thus].

Or, when the suffix *yu* follows, there is an option for the substitution of *vī* for the root *aj*. Thus, *prājanaḥ* (a goad) may be called either *daṇḍaḥ* or *pravayaṇaḥ*. This is one interpretation of the sūtra. Alternatively, when the *uṇādi* suffix *yu* follows, there is the optional substitution of *vā* for *aj*. Thus, *vāyuḥ* (wind). This is another interpretation of the sūtra. It has been stated regarding the *ārdhadhātuka* [affixes].

*ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni lugaṇiñoḥ*: After these [bases], there shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* when they have been produced in the sense of a younger descendant (*yuvan*). [From bases] ending in *kurv-ādi* and *iñ*: *kauravyaḥ* (the father) is *kauravyaḥ* (the son). [Here, the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *kṣatriyād vṛṣṇikurubhyaśca*. *śvāphalkaḥ* (the father) is *śvāphalkaḥ* (the son). From an *ārṣa* [base]: *vāsiṣṭhaḥ* (the father) is *vāsiṣṭhaḥ* (the son). [After a base] ending in *ñit* [such as] *vid-ādi* with the suffix *yañ*: *vaidaḥ* (the father) is *vaidaḥ* (the son). In all cases, there is elision of *iñ* after [a base] ending in *at*. There is also elision of *aṇ*. After a base beginning with *tik-ādi* ending in *phiñ*, there is elision of *aṇ*—which belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group—when it has been produced in the sense of a younger descendant.
*taikāyaniḥ* (the father) is *taikāyaniḥ* (the son).

And [the suffix *yuvan*] is elided after Paila and others. After these, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan* suffix. In the case of Pīlāyaḥ, since it ends in the *aṇ* suffix, the *phiñ* suffix is elided by the rule "after a word ending in *daṇ* that has two syllables. Thus, Paila is the father and Paila is the son.
[The suffix *yuvan* is also elided] after an *iñ* suffix when the ancestors were from the East (*prācām*).

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) after a patronymic ending in *iñ* belonging to the Easterners (*prāc*). For example: *pānnāgāriḥ* is the father; *pānnāgāriḥ* is the son. [In this case,] there is elision of the suffix *phaṅ* by the rule *yañiñoś ca*. [Exception: Not so for those beginning with *taulvali*. There is no elision of the suffix *iñ* belonging to the Easterners after words such as *taulvali*. For example: *taulvaliḥ* is the father; *taulvalāyanaḥ* is the son.

The suffix of a *tadrāja* (kṣatriya-tribe name) is elided when it denotes many [descendants], provided it does not refer to females. When denoting many, there is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix. For example: "the many descendants of the Pañcālas" is *pañcālāḥ*. [This is derived from] *kṣatriyādañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.168). Similarly: *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*. [These are derived from] *dvyañmagadha...* (Pāṇini 4.1.170), which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*. Why "provided it does not refer to females"? Consider: *pāñcālyaḥ striyaḥ* ("Pañcāla women"). Why "provided it is by that very same [suffix]"? To prevent the elision when plurality is expressed by another means, as in: *priyavāṅgā viprāḥ* ("Brahmins who are fond of the Aṅgas"). [Furthermore, the suffix is elided] after [names] beginning with *yaska* when they denote a lineage (*gotra*).

From these [names], there shall be elision (*luk*) of the *gotra*-suffix as before. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after [the class beginning with] *śiva*. Examples: *yaskāḥ*, *ayaḥsthūṇāḥ*. [The rule applies] only when not feminine: *yāskyaḥ* (feminine). [The rule applies] only when [the sense is] "by him": *priyayāskā viprāḥ* (Brahmins who are fond of Yaska). And [there is elision] of *yañ* and *añ*. In the *gotra* [sense], there shall be elision of *yañ* and *añ* as before. Examples: *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*. [Examples of] *añ*: *vidāḥ*, *urvāḥ*. As before. Not here: *gārgyaḥ* (feminine); *priyagārgyā viprāḥ* (Brahmins who are fond of Gārgya).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) after words such as *yañ* when followed by a singular or dual ending. For example: *gārgyasya gārgyayor vā kulam* becomes *gargakulam* or *gārgyakulam*; likewise, *vidakulam* or *vaidakulam*. There is also elision (*luk*) of the *gotra* suffix after the following: *atri*, *bhṛgu*, *kutsa*, *vasiṣṭha*, *gotama*, and *aṅgiras*. Thus: *atrayaḥ*, *bhṛgavaḥ*, *kutsāḥ*, *vasiṣṭhāḥ*, *gotamāḥ*, *aṅgirasaḥ*. Regarding *atri*: the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule *atreḥ itaś cāṇiñaḥ*. For the remaining names, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* applies as before. Thus, the women are *ātreyyaḥ* (with the feminine suffix *ṅīp*), and the learned men are *priyātreyāḥ*.

The suffix *iñ* is elided after polysyllabic words denoting ancestors from the eastern regions (*prācya*) and the Bharatas, when the word refers to many individuals. Among the eastern lineages (*gotra*), [the descendants] of Panāgāra are called the Pannāgārās; among the Bharata lineages, those of Yudhiṣṭhira are the Yudhiṣṭhiras, and those of Arjuna are the Arjunas.
This elision does not occur after the group beginning with Gopavana.

The eight groups beginning with Gopavana are sub-divisions of the Vidādi class. For these, there is no elision (luṅ) of the suffix *añ* according to the rule "yañañośca. Examples: *gaupavanāḥ*, *śaigravāḥ*. Regarding the rule "tikakitavādibhyo dvandve":

in a *dvandva* compound formed from words belonging to the *Tika*-group and the *Kitava*-group, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix (*gotrapratyaya*). In a *dvandva*: *taikāyanayaḥ* and *kaitavāyanāḥ* become *tikakitavāḥ*. Here, there is elision of the *phiñ* suffix [from *Tika*]. Examples: *vaṅkharabhaṇḍīrathāḥ*; here, there is elision of the *iñ* suffix [from *Vaṅkhara*].

*Upakādibhyo’nyatarasyāmadvandve*: After these [words beginning with *upaka*], the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*) may optionally occur when there is plurality, whether in a non-dvandva compound or in a dvandva compound. [Examples of non-dvandva: *upakāḥ* / *aupakāyanāḥ*; *lamakāḥ* / *lāmakāyanāḥ*. [The group] *naḍādi* [is as follows]: *upakalamakāḥ* / *āhārakāḥ* / *vihārakāḥ*; *āhārakayaḥ* / *vaihārakayaḥ*; *āhārakavihārakāḥ* / *āhārakivaihārakayaḥ*. [Special rule: For *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, [the suffixes are replaced by] *agasti* and *kuṇḍina* [respectively].

By the suffix *dṛṣyaṇ* after the word *agastya*, and by the suffix *yañ* (from the *gargādi* group) after the word *kuṇḍinī*: there shall be elision (*luk*) of these two when they occur in the plural; furthermore, the substitutes *agasti* and *kuṇḍina* take their place. Thus: *agastayaḥ* (the descendants of Agastya); *kuṇḍināḥ* (the descendants of Kuṇḍinī). *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*:

There shall be elision of the case-ending (*sup*) which is a constituent part of either a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). *sanādyantadhātoḥ*: [Elision applies] to the case-ending of a verbal root that ends in *san* and so forth. Examples: *putrīyati* (he treats as a son); *mālīyati* (he treats as a garland). *samāsaprātipadikasya*: [Elision applies] to the case-ending of a compound nominal stem. Examples: *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship); *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man). Why [is it] for these two? [Consider: *vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree).
*Śap* is elided after roots beginning with *ad*.

The *śap* affix is elided after roots of the *ad*-class. Examples: *atti*, *dveṣṭi*, *śete*. Also, the *carkarīta* [formation]. Example: *bobhavīti*. "Carkarīta" is the designation used by the Eastern grammarians for the elision of *yaṅ*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), this occurs diversely.

Regarding the Vedic (*chāndasa*) [usage]: *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.34). After a *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix, there is elision (*luk*) when an *ac* vowel follows. Examples: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*. Here, by the word "and" (*ca*), the term "diversely" (*bahulam*) is drawn forward, but not the phrase "in the Veda" (*chandasi*). Consequently, in the common language (*bhāṣā*), the elision of *yaṅ* occurs even after vowels other than *ac*. Jayāditya says: "He lolls" (*lālapīti*) and "he speaks repeatedly" (*vāvadīti*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the entire phrase "diversely in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*) is understood to follow. Therefore, due to this diversity, the elision of *yaṅ* occurs in the Veda itself even after vowels other than *ac*. However, in the Mahābhāṣya, by the force of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the mention of *hu* and *snū*, the form *bobhavīti* is considered correct in the common language.
The *Bhāgavṛtti* states that there is no other [meaning]. Furthermore, the usage of learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*) is observed:
"O beloved, if the god rains heavily and the cuckoo cries out repeatedly, and the peacock dances and warbles repeatedly, then [it is so]. (1)
"Bhaṭṭi [says]: 'The splendors made themselves calm' (tejasāṃ śaṃśamāñcakruḥ).
Regarding what you said—'May there be battle for you with Hari'—that is not possible when joined with reason, like that of a lion and an elephant. ||1||
Thus ends Pāṇini’s *Jāmbavatīvijaya-kāvya*. [Pāṇini 2.4.75:
*juhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ*. For the verbal roots beginning with *hu*, there shall be *ślu* (elision) of the *śap* (the present tense marker). [Examples: *juhoti* (he sacrifices), *bibhartti* (he bears).
In the Veda, [the substitution of *i* for *a*] occurs frequently.
This is a Vedic usage.
[The augment *sic* is elided after the roots *gā*, *sthā*, *dhu*, *pā*, and *bhū*, when followed by Parasmaipada endings.]

The elision (*luk*) of *sic* shall occur after these [roots]. For the root *iṇ*, there is *gā*. *agāt*, *agātām*, *aguḥ*. *sthā*: *asthāt*. *ghu* (the roots *dā* and *dhā*): *adhāt*. *pā* in the sense of drinking: *apāt*. *abhūt*. *kai* and *gai* in the sense of sound; *pā* in the sense of protection: for these two, it is not desired. *agāsīt naṭaḥ* (the actor sang); *apāsīt nṛpaḥ* (the king protected). Why "in the parasmaipada endings"? [Observe: *agāsātām grāmau vipreṇa* (the two villages were sung by the Brahmin). *Vibhāṣā ghrādheṭśācchāsaḥ*: After these—*ghrā*, *dheṭ*, *śo*, *cho*, and *so*—there may optionally be the elision of *sic* in the parasmaipada endings. *ghrā*: *aghrāt*. *dheṭ*: *adhāt*. *śo*: *aśāt*. *cho*: *acchāt*. *so*: *asāt*.
In the alternative [pakṣe], there is *aghrāsīt* and so forth.
From the roots beginning with *tan*, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of *sic* when *tathāsu* (the suffixes *tha* and *thās*) follow. Thus: *atata* or *atathāḥ*; *ataniṣṭa* or *ataniṣṭhāḥ*.
In the case of the verbal roots *dhvas*, *hvaraṇa*, *śavṛ*, *dāhṛ*, *vṛc*, *kṛg*, *mi*, and *jan*, the suffix *liṭ* takes the augment *ām*;
this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasam*). The suffix *ām* [is applied].
The *luk* elision shall occur of the *liṭ* suffix of another [verb] when it is in the *āma* form. *ihāñcakre* (he has done here). *avyayādāpsupaḥ*:

After an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there shall be *luk* elision of the feminine suffix *āp* and of case endings (*sup*). *tatra śālāyām* (there, in the hall). [Examples of] case endings (*sup*): *svaḥ* (heaven), *prātaḥ* (morning), *kṛtvā* (having done), *kartum* (to do). Here, [the rule applies to] the indeclinable (*avyaya*)—*iha* (here).
Since the [compound] possesses gender and number, and since there is an absence of the suffixes *āp* (feminine) and *sup* (case endings), the purpose of the elision (*luk*) must be considered.

*Nāvyayībhāvādato 'm tvapañcamyāḥ*: After an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) ending in *a*, there is no elision of the case endings (*sup*), except for the fifth case (*pañcamī*); rather, the substitute *am* is prescribed. Examples: *upakumbhaṃ tiṣṭhati*, *paśya*, or *dehi*. Why "ending in *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider *upāgni*. Why "except for the fifth case" (*apāñcamyāḥ*)? Consider *upakumbhād āgataḥ*.

The substitution [of *am*] occurs diversely (*bahulam*) for the third and seventh case endings. After an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) ending in *a*, the substitution of *am* occurs diversely for these two cases: *upakumbham* or *upakumbhena* kṛtam; *upakumbham* or *upakumbhe* nidhehi. For the seventh case, the substitution of *am* is obligatory after compounds expressing prosperity (*ṛddhi*), river-compounds (*nadīsamāsa*), and those where a number denotes a part (*saṃkhyāvayava*): *sumadram*, *subhikṣam*; in the case of a river-compound: *unmattagaṅgam*; in the case of a number denoting a part: *ekaviṃśatibhāradvājam*. The elision (*luk*) has been explained. [Now follows:
for the first person of the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), the substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* [are applied].

In place of the first person endings of the *luṭ* [future tense], *ḍā*, *auras*, and *ras* shall be substituted. [Examples: *śvaḥ kartā* (he will do tomorrow), *kartārau* (the two will do), *kartāraḥ* (they will do); *śvaḥ adhyetā* (he will study tomorrow), *adhyetārau* (the two will study), *adhyetāraḥ* (they will study). Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Preceptor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva. 2.4.103–109.
And the section on the dvigu compound is completed.
The first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter: A suffix (pratyaya) [is placed] after [the base]. And it is subsequent.
The suffix must be stated; and it should be subsequent. It should be illustrated in the same manner: *yāti*, *kṛtam*.
And [the suffix] is udātta on the first syllable. The case endings (*sup*) and primary suffixes (*pit*) are anudātta.
Two sūtras on verbal roots (*svarasūtra*). *Sūtra*: *gup-ti-j-kid-bhyaḥ san*.

From these [roots], the suffix *san* shall occur. The meaning is understood from common usage (*lokataḥ*). He feels aversion toward unrighteousness (*adharmam jugupsate*). He endures an offense (*aparādham titikṣate*). The physician treats the patient (*cikitsaty āturam bhiṣak*). Likewise: "My mind wavers" (*vicikitsati me manaḥ*). The meaning is "it doubts" (*sandegdhi*).
After the roots *mān*, *vad*, *dāñ*, and *śān*, there is the suffix *san* and the long vowel for the reduplication.

The suffix *san* occurs after *mān* and the others; furthermore, there is a long vowel for the reduplication. For example: *mīmāṃsate śāstram* (he investigates the treatise); *bībhatsate gajam* (he feels disgust toward the elephant); *dīdāṃsate śatrum* (he desires to give to the enemy); *śīśāṃsate śastram* (he desires to sharpen the weapon). Since this is not a desire-suffix (*anicchāsana*), it does not possess the status of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, because [the rule] "after a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is not stated [in that context].
[The rule is: "Optionally, after a root denoting an object, when the agent is the same, the suffix *san* is used to express a desire."

The suffix *san* may optionally be added after a verbal root that has the same agent as the object of the verb *iṣ* ("to desire"), provided it expresses a desire; otherwise, a periphrastic construction (*vākya*) may be used. For example: *kartum icchati* becomes *cikīrṣati*. Similarly, *jugupsiṣate* and *vivartiṣate*. It is not desired [that *san* be added] after a desiderative form already ending in *san*: e.g., *cikīrṣitum icchati*. In such cases, forms like *aśmā luluṭhiṣate* ("the stone wishes to roll") and *nadīkūlaṃ pipatiṣati* ("the riverbank wishes to fall") are used through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).

The suffix *kyac* is added after a nominal stem (*sup*) ending in a case-suffix, when the desire belongs to the agent himself (*ātmanaḥ*). That is, *kyac* may optionally be added after a word ending in a case-suffix which is the object of *iṣ*, expressing the desire of the desirer. For example: *putram icchati ātmanaḥ* becomes *putrīyati*; *putrīyanti*; *putrīyan*. Likewise, *bhāryīyati*, *dadhīyati*, *madhūyati*, *gavyati*, and *rājīyati*.
There is a prohibition [of *kāmyac*] after words ending in *mān* and indeclinables. *kim icchati*, *svar icchati*.
The suffix *kāmyac* occurs in the domain of *kyac*. *putrakāmyati*, *strīkāmyati*.

*Upamānād ācāre*: after the word expressing the object of comparison, *kyac* is added [to form a denominative verb] in the sense of behaving [like that object]. That is to say, *kyac* occurs after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) which is the object of comparison, when the meaning is "behaving like. For example: *putrīyati bhṛtyam* ("he behaves toward his servant as if he were a son"); *mātrīyati parakalatram* ("he behaves toward another's wife as if she were his mother"). *Adhikaraṇācca*: *kyac* is added in the sense of behaving [as if one were located in that place]. For example: *prāsādīyati yaḥ kuṭyām* ("he behaves as if he were in a palace while in a hut"); *paryaṅkīyati mañcake* ("he behaves as if he were on a couch while on a small bed").
*ky-aṅ* is added after the agent [of the action], and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final *s*.

When the sense is that of behaving like the agent who serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), *ky-aṅ* may be added; furthermore, there is the elision of the final *s* of a stem ending in *s*. An old man behaves like a child: *śiśūyate vṛddhaḥ*. "Even a castor-oil plant acts like a tree" (*eraṇḍo'pi drumāyate*). "Even a crow acts like Garuḍa" (*kāko'pi garuḍāyate*). A *gavaya* (wild ox) is treated as a cow: *gavyate gavayaḥ*. A wooden trough is treated as a boat: *nāvyate droṇī*. "For that man of a contented nature, even a hunchback acts like an *apsaras*" (*tasya santoṣaśīlasya kubjikāpyapsarāyate*).

Regarding this elision of *s*: some say that the elision of *s* occurs invariably after *ojas*, *apsaras*, and *payas*; others say that the elision of *s* occurs only after *apsaras* and not after any other word.

The suffix *kvip* is optionally applied after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*). After a nominal stem, *kvip* may optionally occur even when *kyaṅ* would otherwise be applicable. Examples: *aśvati kharaḥ* (the donkey acts like a horse); *prabhavati bhṛtyaḥ* (the servant acts like a master); *ripavanti mitrāṇi* (friends act like enemies); *vidhavati raviḥ* (the sun acts like a widow). [In the case of] *godohati*, some say it is *goduhatī*. Regarding *avagalbha* and others, there is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating that they should be taught as having an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) for the sake of the *ātmanepada* in the application of *kvip*. Therefore: *avagalbhate*, *vihoḍate*, *klībate*. By the rule *kāspratyayād ām*, we have *avagalbhāñcakre*.
From *bhṛśa* and other words, when *bhū* follows, provided there is no *acv-* [prefix], there is elision of the consonant (*hal*).

The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after words such as *bhṛśa* when they signify the sense of "becoming" (*bhū*) in the sense of "to become," provided that the root *bhū* is understood. For example: *abhṛśo bhṛśo bhavati* ("that which was not intense becomes intense") is expressed as *bhṛśāyate* ("it becomes intense"); likewise, *śīghrāyate* ("it becomes swift") and *utsukāyate* ("it becomes eager"). Furthermore, there is elision of the final consonant of a word ending in a consonant: *sumanāyate* ("it becomes well-disposed") and *unmanāyate* ("it becomes dejected"); thus, *unmanāyamānaḥ* ("being dejected"). The suffix *kyaṣ* occurs after the group beginning with *lohita* and after words ending in *ḍāc*, in the sense of "becoming" (*bhū*) in the sense of "to become. After words beginning with *lohita* and those ending in *ḍāc*, the suffix *kyaṣ* occurs in the sense of "becoming": *alohito lohito bhavati* ("that which was not red becomes red") is expressed as *lohitāyati* or *lohitāyate*. Similarly, *mandāyati* or *mandāyate* ("it becomes slow"). In this manner, the following belong to this class: *varma*, *harita*, *nidrā*, *tandrā*, *karuṇā*, *ghṛṇā*, and *kekā*. This is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). However, Kātyāyana [states]: [Note: The text fragment ends here; the commentary on Kātyāyana’s view is not provided in the source.]

He says that while the suffix *kyaṣ* is prescribed after words ending in *lohita* and *ḍāc*, the others [of the *bhṛśādi* group] take [the suffixes] otherwise. *Ḍāc*: *damadamāyati*, *damadamāyate*. In the case of *ḍāc*, there is frequently reduplication (*dve*). *Kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*:

When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) meaning "difficulty" (*kaṣṭa*) is used, the suffix *kyaṅ* shall occur in the sense of "striving toward" (*kramaṇa*). Because the term *kaṣṭāya* is mentioned as a general indication, it applies even to *satra*, *kakṣa*, *kṛcchra*, and *gahana*. Thus, the *Ślokavārttika* states: [The verse follows...]

In this context, the fourth case ending should indeed be used in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that), as in "for the sake of hardship" (*kaṣṭāya*) or "for the sake of action" (*karmaṇe*). For the inclusion of the meaning is obtained through the explanatory statement (*vyākhyāna*), and the desire to commit a sin (*aṃhaścikīrṣā*) is also necessarily implied.

Thus: *kaṣṭāyate*, *satrāyate*, *kṛcchrāyate*, *kakṣāyate*, *gahanāyate*; the meaning is "he desires to do evil. [The rule] *karmaṇo romanthatapobhyāṃ vartticaroḥ* states that the suffix *ky-aṅ* occurs after these two objects when they have the senses of "repeating" (*varti*) and "wandering" (*cara*). For example: *romanthāyate gauḥ* ("the cow chews the cud"). Because the term refers specifically to the movement of the jaw, it does not apply here: *kīṭo romanthaṃ varttayati* ("the insect repeats its digestion").

The suffix *parasmaipada* is also used after the root *tapas*. Thus: *tapasyati*. After the words *vāṣpa*, *ūṣman*, and *phena*, the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs when denoting the act of vomiting forth. Thus: *vāṣpāyate* (the pot emits steam), *ūṣmāyate* (the food emits heat/steam), *phenāyate* (the river foams). Bhartṛhari states that it also occurs after *dhūma*: *dhūmāyate* (the fire smokes). As in: "They were embraced as if they were smoking."

The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after the words *śabda*, *vaira*, *kalaha*, *abhra*, *kaṇva*, and *megha* when they denote the instrument (*karaṇa*). From these, *kyaṅ* is applied in the sense of an action (*kriyā*). One makes sound: *śabdāyate*. One acts with enmity: *vairāyate*; one who is acting with enmity: *vairāyamāṇaḥ*. Likewise, up to *meghāyate*. Also after *sudin*, *durdina*, and *nīhāra*: *sudināyate*, *durdināyate*, *nīhārāyate*. The inclusion of *aṭā*, *aṭṭā*, *śīkā*, *koṭā*, *poṭā*, *soṭā*, *pruṣṭā*, and *pluṣṭā* must be made [to the list]. *aṭāyate*, *aṭṭāyate*, *śīkāyate*, *koṭāyate*, *poṭāyate*, *soṭāyate*, *pruṣṭāyate*, *pluṣṭāyate*. After words beginning with *sukha* when the feeling belongs to the agent (*kartṛvedanā*).

The suffix *ky-aṅ* shall occur after these [roots] when there is the experience of the agent. He experiences happiness for himself: *sukhāyate*. He experiences suffering: *duḥkhāyate*. [The roots] *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *alīka*, *karuṇā*, *kṛcchra*, *pratīpa*, and *ghṛṇā* [are included]. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). The suffix *ky-ac* occurs after the roots *namas*, *varivas*, and *citraṅ*. *ky-ac* shall occur after these [roots], with the expression [of the meanings] "reverence," "service," and "wonder. He reveres the gods: *namasyati devān*. He serves his teachers: *varivasyati gurūn*. He is amazed: *citrīyate*.
*Hemamṛgaḥ*: the meaning is "it causes wonder.

The suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied after the words *puccha*, *bhāṇḍa*, and *cīvara*. The suffix *ṇiṅ* shall occur after these [words] in the senses of throwing up (*udāsana*), gathering together (*samācayana*), and putting on (*paridhāna*). Throwing up (*udāsana*) means lifting up. The tiger raises its tail (*utpucchayate*). The potter gathers his tools (*sambhāṇḍayate*). The monk puts on his robes (*sañcīvarayate*).

The suffix *ṇic* is applied after the words *muṇḍa*, *miśra*, *ślakṣṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *vrata*, *vasra*, *hala*, *kala*, and *tūsta*, provided that they function as instruments (*karaṇe*). That is to say, when these words denote specific actions, the suffix *ṇic* shall be added. Thus: *muṇḍayati*, *miśrayati*, *ślakṣṇayati*, *lavaṇayati*, *vratayati*.

After the root *vas*, [the suffix *ṇic*] is used in the sense of "covering. One causes to cover: *saṃvastrayati*. The non-elision (*atvanipātana*) of the *u* in *hali* and *kali* is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment as *san* (*sanvadbhāva*). One takes hold of a plowshare: *halayati*; one takes hold of strife: *kalayati*. *Ajahalat*; *acakalat*. *Hali* means a large plow. One takes hold of what has been done: *kṛtayati*. The wind drives away the chaff from the path: *vitūstayati*; *tūsta* means dust.
After a monosyllabic verbal root beginning with a consonant, the suffix *yaṅ* is added in the sense of the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after a verbal root (*dhātu*) to express the intensification of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*). For example: *pāpacyate*, meaning "he cooks thoroughly" or "he cooks repeatedly"; *jājvalyate*, meaning "it blazes intensely" or "it blazes repeatedly. [Examples of the participle: *jājvalyamānaḥ*. Why is it specified that the root must have only one vowel (*ekāca*)? Consider: *bhṛśaṃ jāgarti* ("he wakes up intensely")—here *yaṅ* does not apply. Why is it specified that the root must begin with a consonant (*hal-ādi*)? Consider: *bhṛśam īkṣate* ("he looks intently")—here *yaṅ* does not apply. Furthermore, there is no such usage for the roots *śubh* and *ruc*, nor for the root *gṛ*.

An addition [to the rule] is made for the roots *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭ*, *ṛ*, *śūrṇoti*. The suffix *yaṅ* shall apply after these seven. *sosūcyate* (he sews repeatedly), *sosūtryate* (he strings repeatedly), *momūtryate* (he urinates repeatedly), *aṭāṭyate* (he wanders about). "Wandering through the forest" (*aṭāṭyamāno 'raṇyānīm*). *arāryyate* (he goes repeatedly). "Why do you, being fearless, go on and on? (*kim abhīrur arāryyase*). *aśāśyate* (he eats repeatedly), *proṇonūyate* (he covers repeatedly). Regarding the rule "always when there is crookedness in motion": *yaṅ* shall apply only to verbs meaning motion when crookedness is intended. Examples: *jaṅgamyate* (he walks with a limp), *caṅkramyate* (he paces back and forth). The tradition holds that the inclusion of the word "always" (*nityam*) is for the purpose of excluding the case of the intensification of action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*).

After the eight roots *lup*, *sad*, *car*, *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, *daś*, and *gṛ*, the suffix *yaṅ* occurs when there is censure (*bhāvagarhā*) of the verbal meaning. Censure (*garhā*) means blame (*nindā*). When there is censure, *yaṅ* is applied after these eight roots. *Lolupyate* (he repeatedly cuts in a censurable manner). *Sāsadyate*. "Of her as she was being repeatedly seated. *Cañcūryate*. *Jañjapyate*. *Jañjabhyate*. *Dandahyate*. *Dandaśyate*. *Nijegilyate*.
The causative suffix *ṇic* is added after the words *satyāpa*, *pāśa*, *rūpa*, *vīṇā*, *tūla*, *śloka*, *senā*, *loman*, *tvaca*, *varman*, *varṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and after the roots beginning with *cur*.

The suffix *ṇic* shall be added after these [roots]. The understanding of their meaning is derived from common usage (*loka*). Examples: *satyāpayati*, *arthāpayati*, *vedāpayati*. The rule "there is the augment *āpuk* after *artha*, *veda*, and *satya*" is an illustration of the previous traditional authority (*smṛti*). Examples: *vipāśayati*, *nirūpayati*, *upavīṇayati*, *anutūlayati*, *upaślokayati*, *abhiṣeṇayati*, *anulomayati*. The word *tvac* ends in a short vowel (*adanta*); it takes *tvacayati* when meaning "he takes the skin. Examples: *saṃvarmayati*, *varṇayati*, *avacūrṇayati*. After roots beginning with *cura* (the *curādi* group), the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *corayati*, *cintayati*.
In the *curādi* group, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) may optionally take *ṇic* in the sense of a verbal root (*dhātvarthe*), and it is treated like the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* in many instances.

"The [verbal root] *karoti* (he does) and *ācaṣṭe* (he tells)" is a *gaṇasūtra*. From this, one forms: *sūtraṃ karoti* → *sūtrayati*; *mūtrayati*; *sūcayati*; *kumārīm ācaṣṭe* → *kumārayati*; *mālām* → *mālayati*; *mātaram* → *mātayati*. This is due to the rule of "frequentative usage" (*bahulavacanāt*).

From a nominal stem ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "he causes that to be told" (*tad-ācaṣṭe*). There is the elision of the *kṛt* suffix and so forth, the restoration of the original form of the base, and the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) remains as it was in the original base. For example: *kaṃsasya vadham ācaṣṭe* becomes *dhātayati kaṃsam* ("he tells the story of Kaṃsa’s killing"); *baliṃ bandhayati naṭaḥ* or *kathakaḥ* ("the actor or storyteller makes Bali captive"). Similarly: *rājānam āgamayati* ("he causes the king to come"); *mṛgān ramayati* ("he amuses the deer"); *udgamayati sūryam* ("he makes the sun rise"). The rule regarding *pāśa* and others is merely an elaboration of this very same *ṇic*. [The rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26) also applies here.]

In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), that is to say: the activity of the cause (*hetu*)—the instigator—which consists of impelling toward actions or rendering them favorable, is "possessing a cause" (*hetumān*). In that case, the suffix *ṇic* shall be applied to the verbal root. For example: *kārayati* ("he causes to do") means he employs one who is doing; *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"); *āsayati* ("he causes to sit"); *śāyayati* ("he causes to lie down"). In the expression *bhikṣā vāsayati* ("alms cause one to dwell"), it is used figuratively for the fire of cow-dung (*kārīṣo 'gniḥ*). In *pañcabhir halaiḥ karṣati* ("he plows with five ploughs"), the term *kṛṣi* (plowing) serves the purpose of indicating the means. In *yājakā yajanti* ("the sacrificers sacrifice"), the root *yaj* has the meaning of casting the oblation. From roots such as *kaṇḍū* and others, the suffix *yak* is applied.

The suffix *yak* shall be applied after these [roots]. *kaṇḍūñ*: *kaṇḍūyati*, *kaṇḍūyate*. "Seeing you moving gracefully (*valgūyantīm*), what woman here would not feel remorse (*na mantūyati*)? *mahīṅ*: "Being excessively honored (*mahīyyamānā*) by you. *hṛṇīṅ*: "The earth, though possessing heroes, does not feel shame (*hṛṇīyate*). *mṛga*: "Searching for the track (*mṛgyantaḥ*). For even a wise man, though suffering (*kliśyan*): [the suffix *yak* is added]. *sukha*: "The subjects might find happiness (*sukhyeyuḥ*) in the king.
After the roots *gup*, *dhūp*, *vicch*, *paṇi*, and *pani*, the suffix *āya* is applied.

From these [roots], the suffix *āya* occurs: *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*, *vicchāyati*, *paṇāyati*, *panāyati*. After the root *ṛti*, the suffix *īyaṅ* occurs; that is, after the root *ṛti* mentioned in the Sūtra, *īyaṅ* shall occur: *ṛtīyate*.
The suffix *kāmiṅ* [is applied after a verbal root to form a denominative verb]. Thus: *kāmayate*.
[According to Pāṇini 3.1.31: "Before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, the affixes *āya*, etc., are optionally [applied]."

In the domain of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, the [suffixes] beginning with *āya* may optionally occur. For example: *goptā* or *gopāyitā*; *guptiḥ* or *gopāyā*. *Arttitā* or *ṛtīyitā*; *kāmayitā* or *kamitā*. The roots ending in *san* and so forth are called verbal roots (*dhātu*). These twelve, beginning with *san*, are as follows: *sankyackāmyackyaṣaḥ*, then *āy*, *ārak*, *kvip*, *ṇic*, and *yaṅ*; likewise *yac*, *āya*, *iryaṅ*, and *ṇiṅ*. Those ending in *san* and so forth shall have the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñaka*). They are illustrated in the same manner as above.

The affix *sya* occurs before the affixes *lṛ* (the marker of the future tense) and *luṭ* (the marker of the periphrastic future). Thus, in the *laṭ* and *lṛṅ* tenses, *sya* is applied: *kariṣyati* ("he will do") and *akariṣyat* ("he would have done"). In the *luṭ* tense, *tāsi* is applied: *kartāsi* ("you will do") and *kartāse* ("you will do for yourself").
