Furthermore, after the root *kāsu* ("to shine") and before an affix beginning with a consonant other than *m*, the augment *ām* is inserted before the *liṭ* tense.

The suffix *ām* is applied after the root *kās-* and after any root ending in a suffix (*pratyayānta*) when the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) follows. Examples: *kāsāñcakre*, *purī saudhaiḥ*, *cikīrṣāmbabhūva*, *pātayāmāsa*, *santāsayāñcakāra*, *bhūyastaṃ bebhidāñcakre*. According to traditional grammatical authority (*smṛti*), the mention of "a suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) here is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "having more than one vowel" (*anekāj*). By this rule, we have: *daridrāñcakāra*, *culumpāñcakāra*.
Furthermore, the suffix *ām* is applied after a root beginning with *ij* (i, u, ṛ, lṛ) that contains a heavy syllable (*gurumat*), provided it is not the root *ṛcch*.

The suffix *ām* shall occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) beginning with the letter *i*, provided that it contains a heavy vowel (*gurumān*), when the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) follows. Examples: *irhāñcakre*, *irkṣāñcakre*, *ḥḍhadyahāñcakre*. Why is it said "not beginning with *ṛ*"? [Observe: *ārnaccha*. It should be stated that for the root *ṛ*, there is a substitution of *nu* [before the suffix *ām*]. Example: *prorṇunāva*. And after the roots *day*, *āy*, and *ās*, the suffix *ām* shall occur in the *liṭ*. Examples: *dayāñcakre na rākṣasaḥ*, *palāyāñcakre*, *āsāñcakre*, *āsāmbabhūva*, *āsāmāsa*.

After the roots *uṣ* (to burn), *vid* (to know), and *jāgṛ* (to wake), the suffix *ām* optionally occurs in the *liṭ* tense. Thus, there is an option: *oṣāñcakāra* (he burned) or *uvoṣa*; *vidāñcakāra*, *vidāmbabhūva*, *vidāmāsa*, or *viveda* (he knew); *jāgarāmāsa*, *jāgarāñcakāra*, *jāgarāmbabhūva*, or *jajāgara* (he woke). Furthermore, after the roots *bhī*, *hrī*, *bhṛ*, and *hu*, the suffix *ślu* (indicating reduplication without *guṇa*) also applies.

For these [roots], there may optionally be the suffix *ām* in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). When *ām* is present, there is reduplication and the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel. Examples: *bibhayāñcakāra*, *jihrayāmbabhūva*, *bibharāmāsa*, *juhavāñcakāra*. The root *kṛ* is added after [the root ending in] *ām* when the periphrastic perfect follows. By "the root *kṛ*," the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are meant. It has been illustrated in exactly that manner.
The form *vidāṅkurvantu* is optionally prescribed as a Vedic substitute for the imperative (*loṭ*). Thus, one may say either *vidāṅkurvantu* or *vidantu*; *vidāṅkuru* or *viddhi*.
Furthermore, the forms *abhyutsādayāṃ*, *prajanayāṃ*, *cikayāṃ*, *ramayāmakaḥ*, *pāvayāṃkriyāt*, and *vidāmakran* are [optionally] prescribed in the Veda.
The Vedic form;
*cli* [is replaced] by *luṅ*;
*sic* [is the substitute] for *cli*.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, *cli* shall occur; its substitutes, beginning with *sij*, are prescribed. *Akārṣīt*, *ahārṣīt*, *apākṣīt*. It should be stated that *sij* is optionally applied after the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*. After these, *sij* may optionally occur: *asprākṣīt* / *aspārkṣīt*; *amrākṣīt* / *amārkṣīt*; *akrākṣīt* / *ākarkṣīt*; *atrāpsīt* / *atārpsīt*; *adrāpsīt* / *adārpsīt*. In the alternative case, *ksa* occurs: *aspṛkṣat*, *amṛkṣat*, *akṛkṣat*. After the roots beginning with *puṣ*, the suffix *aṅ* occurs: *atṛpat*, *adṛpat*. After a root ending in a consonant (*śal*), having a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* (*igupadha*), and being devoid of the augment *iṭ*, the suffix *ksa* occurs.

The suffix *ksa* shall be substituted for *cli* after a root ending in *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, or *h*, provided that the penultimate letter (*upadha*) is a guttural (*ku*). For example: from *spṛś*, *aspṛkṣat*; from *guh*, *aghukṣat*. [As in: "Do not hide yourself from your husband! Why specify "of a root lacking *iṭ*"? [Observe: *amoṣīt*.
[Also,] *śliṣ* is used in the sense of embracing.

The suffix *ksa* occurs after the root *śliṣ* only when it means "embracing a living being. Examples: *aślikṣat kanyām* (he embraced the girl); *aślikṣad bhāryām* (he embraced his wife). In other cases—*samāśliṣaj jatu kāṣṭham* (the lac resin adhered to the wood).
[This rule] does not apply to the root *dṛś*:
*ksa* shall not occur after *dṛś*. Examples: *adrākṣīt* (he saw); *adarśat*. Alternatively, by the rule *irito vā*, the suffix *aṅ* may optionally occur.

*ṇi-śri-dru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ*: After these roots and after *cal*, the suffix *caṅ* shall be applied when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Examples: *acīkarat*, *alīlavat*, *anīnaśat*. [He said: "O Tapas, accomplish it; do not let it perish! *acikliśat*, *aśiśriyat*, *adudruvat*, *asusruvad dhanaṃ jalam*. The term "when the agent is expressed" (*kartari*) continues in force from before the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*. There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the root *kam*: *acakamata sapallavāṃ dharitrīm*. In the case of the *ṇiṅ* suffix, the previous rule applies: *acīkamata*. Here: "He goes to heaven, which is full of desired pleasures, in well-yoked chariots drawn by horses."
"Then those who speak what is not desired go on foot. This verse from the *Bhāṣya* is intended to praise the use of specific grammatical forms. Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ*:

after the roots *dheṭ* (to suck) and *śvi* (to swell), as well as *cal*, the suffix *caṅ* may optionally be applied. Thus, one may say either *adadhat* or *adhāsīt*. According to the rule *vibhāṣā ghrādheṭ*, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix is mentioned in the alternative case—thus *adhāt*. For *śvi*, one may say either *aśiśviyat* or *aśvayīt*; with the *aṅ* suffix, it is *aśvat*. The restriction "in the sense of the agent" (*karttari*) applies here; thus, *adhiṣātāṃ gāvo vatsena* ("the cows were sucked by the calf").
The suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *gup* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
[The suffixes] do not occur after the roots *nī*, *han*, *il*, or *ard*.
These two rules are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
After the roots *as* (to throw), *vac* (to speak), and *khyā* (to tell), the suffix *aṅ* is substituted for *cli*.
Thus: *āsthat*, *avocat*, *ākhyat*. In the case of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings—*paryāsthata*, *avocata*, *vyākhyata*.
Also after *lipi*, *sic*, and *hve*.

In the *ātmanepada* [voices], optionally [the substitution of] *aṅ* for *cli* occurs after the roots beginning with *lip*. Here she anointed herself with perfumes (*sā vyalipat gandhaiḥ*), and here, while bathing, she sprinkled herself with waters (*abhyaṣicat jalaiḥ*). "Here I called upon her to see me" (*ihāhaṃ draṣṭum āhvam*); thinking thus, as it were, he fainted (*smarann evaṃ mumoha saḥ*). [The substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs] optionally when the *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* endings) follow: The fire of grief anointed her (*tasyā alipata śokāgniḥ*); the cool wind seemed to anoint her (*alipatevānilaḥ śītaḥ*); that [fire] sprinkled water for her bath (*srānam abhyaṣicata ambhaḥ asau*); likewise, the waters were sprinkled over her (*tathā abhyaṣicata vārīṇi*). He repeatedly called upon the gods (*āhvasta sa muhuḥ surān*) and repeatedly called upon the Rākṣasas (*muhuḥ āhvata rākṣasān*). [The substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs] necessarily after the roots beginning with *puṣ*, those beginning with *dyut*, and those ending in *ṛt*, when the *parasmaipada* endings follow.

After roots beginning with *puṣ* (from the sixth class), those beginning with *dyut* (from the first class), and those marked with the indicatory letter *ḷ*, the suffix *aṅ* shall replace *cli*. Examples: *apuṣat*, *aśuṣat*, *adyutat*, *aśvitat*; from *śaklṛ*: *aśakat*; from *gamlṛ*: *agamat*. Why "in the Parasmaipada"? [Consider: *vyadyotiṣṭa*. And after the roots *sṛ*, *śās*, and *ṛt*, *aṅ* shall replace *cli*. Examples: *asarat*, *aśiṣat*, *ārat*, *āratām*. How is it that [the form] *samāranta mamābhasīṣṭāḥ* occurs? The Teachers maintain that [the substitution of *aṅ*] is desired even when the *taṅ* (Atmanepada) endings follow.

Or after a root ending in *ṛ*: after a root ending in *ṛ*, *aṅ* may optionally replace *cli*. [Examples: *acyotīt* or *acyutat*; *abhidat* or *abhaitsīt*; *arudhat* or *arītsīt*. Only when the *parasmaipada* endings are used—[as in] *aruddha*.
Also after the roots *jṝ*, *stambhū*, *mruć*, *mluć*, *gluć*, *ñcū*, and *śvi*.

After these roots, *cleri* may optionally take the suffix *aṅ*. Examples: *ajarat*, *astabhat*, *abhrucat*, *aglucat*. Regarding *gluñc*, some say *agluñcat*. *aśvat*. In the alternative case, with *sic*: *ajārīt*, *aśvayīt*.
[The suffix *aṅ* is applied] after *kṛ*, *mṛ*, *dṛ*, and *ruh* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
This is a Vedic usage.

The affix *ciṇ* is substituted for *ta* after the root *pad* when used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and followed by the suffix *ta*. For example: *samapādi śasyam* ("the grain ripened"). Why "when followed by *ta*"? [Observe: *udapatsātām*.
[The affix *ciṇ* is also applied] optionally after the roots *dīp*, *jan*, *budh*, *pūr*, *tāy*, and *pyāy*.

When the *takāra* (the suffix *ta*) follows a root such as *dīp* etc. in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), the *ciṇ* substitute shall take the place of *clī*. The tiger among the Raghus was enraged: *adīpi* or *adīpiṣṭa*. He was born: *ajani* or *ajaniṣṭa*. He awoke: *abodhi* or *abuddha*. He was filled: *apūri* or *apūriṣṭa*. He was stretched: *atāyi*, *atāyiṣṭa*; or he was swollen: *apyāyi*, *apyāyiṣṭa*. *acaḥ karmakarttari*: When the *takāra* follows a root ending in a vowel (*ac*) in the sense of the agent who is also the object (*karmakarttari*), *ciṇ* shall optionally take the place of *clī*. The forest grew by itself: *upācāyi* or *upācāyiṣṭa*. The mat was made by itself: *akāri* or *akṛta*.
And [the rule] regarding *duh*: in that context, the *ciṇ* substitute may optionally occur for *duh*. Thus: *adohi* or *adugdha* "the cow milked by itself.
But not for *rudh*.

The affix *ciṇ* shall not occur after the root *rudh* in that case: *aruddha gauḥ svayameva* ("the cow restrained itself"). [The rule] "after *tap*, and in the sense of repentance" means that *ciṇ* shall not occur after *tap* in that case: *atapta tapastāpasaḥ* ("the ascetic performed penance"). And in the sense of repentance, *ciṇ* does not occur even when the action is intransitive or has a reflexive object: *anvavātapta pāpena karmaṇā* ("he was tormented by his sinful deed").

*ciṇ* is substituted for *cl* when *ta* or *kṛ* follows, provided that these [suffixes] denote the passive (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Examples: *aśāyi tvayā* ("it was slept by you"), *akāri kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"). When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, *yak* is added [to the root].

The affix *yak* shall occur before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix when expressing either the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). In the sense of the action: *āsyate tvayā* ("you sit"). After the root *kṛ*, there is also the affix *śa*: *kriyā* ("action"), *paricaryā* ("service"). In the sense of the object: *kriyate kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is being made"), *kriyete kaṭau* ("two mats are being made"). *Śap* occurs when expressing the agent (*kartṛ*).
The affix *śap* shall occur before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix when denoting the agent. Examples: *bhavati*, *edhate*, *dhāvati*, *dhāvate*, *corayati*, *cikīrṣati*, *mālyadhārayaḥ*.
*Śyan* is added after [roots] beginning with *div*. After these, *śyan* shall occur: *dīvyati*, *sīvyati*, *śūrammanyaḥ*.
Or [the suffix *śyan* is optional] after *bhrāś*, *bhlāś*, *bhram*, *kram*, *klam*, *tras*, *truṭ*, and *laṣ*.

Or, the affix *śyan* may optionally occur after these roots: *bhrāśyate*, *bhrāśyate*, or *bhrāśate*; *bhlāśyate* or *bhlāśate*; *bhramyati* or *bhramati*. However, in the *divādi* class, it is obligatory: *bhrāmyati*. [Similarly,] *abhilaṣyati* or *abhilaṣati*; *trasyati* or *trasati*; *truṭyati* or *truṭati*. After the root *yas*, when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the affix *śyan* is optional: *yasyati* or *yasati*. But with a prefix, it is obligatory: *prayasyati*.

Or there may be *śyan*. [The forms] *saṃyasyati* or *saṃyasati* [are derived from the root *yas*]. After roots beginning with *su*, there is *śnu*. After these [roots], *śnu* shall occur. [Examples: *sunoti*, *cinoti*.
*Śru* becomes *śṛ*. The suffix *śnu* is substituted for [the root] *śru*, and there is also the change to *śṛ*. [Thus: *śṛṇoti*, *śṛṇutaḥ*. [The substitution of] *akṣa* is optional.
Or *akṣu* may take the suffix *śnu*: it carves or it pierces wood. In the sense of making thin, there is the root *takṣ*.
After *takṣ*, in the sense of making thin, *śnu* may optionally occur: it carves or it pares wood.
*Śa* is added after the roots beginning with *tud*.
After these, the suffix *śa* shall occur: *tudati*, *upadiśati*. *Śnam* is added after the roots beginning with *rudh*.
The affix *śnam* shall occur after these [roots]: *ruṇaddhi*, *bhinatti*, *pinaṣṭi*, *hinasti*. After roots beginning with *tan* and the root *kṛñ*, the affix *u* [is applied].
The suffix *u* shall be applied after these [roots]: *tan* (as in *tanoti*), *kṛ* (as in *karoti*), and after *dhinv* and *kṛṣv*, with the replacement of the final vowel by *a*.
The suffix *u* shall be applied after the roots *dhivi* and *kṛvi*, with *a* substituted for their final vowels; furthermore, there is elision (*lopa*) of that *a*. [Thus one forms:
*dhinoti* (he delights) the Fire-god with an oblation; *kṛṇoti* (he makes). After the group of roots beginning with *krī*, the suffix *śnā* is applied.

The suffix *śnā* shall be applied after these [roots]: *krīṇāti*, *krīṇīte*; *prīṇāti*; *gṛhṇāti*, *gṛhṇan*, *gṛhṇīte*, *gṛhṇāṇaḥ*. After the roots *stambhu*, *stumbhu*, *skambhu*, *skumbhu*, and *skuñ*, there shall be both *śnu* and *śnā*: *uttabhnāti* or *uttabhnoti*; *stubhnāti* or *stubhnoti*; *skabhnāti* or *skabhnoti*.

*Halaḥ śnaḥ śānaj jhau*: After a consonant (*hal*), the suffix *śnā* is replaced by *śānac* when followed by the suffix *jh*. Examples: *puṣāṇa*, *badhāna*, *gṛhāṇa*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), *śāy* may also be substituted.
The Vedic forms have been stated.
There is extensive irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
By the term "extensively" (*bahulam*), the rules for verbal roots and suffixes are governed. Whatever remains is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The suffix *liṅ* is used for benediction (*āśis*).
This is a Vedic usage.
[A reflexive verb] whose action is identical to that of the object is treated like the object (*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*).

"Only when [the agent] is the agent. An agent whose action is similar to that of the object shall be treated like the object (*karmavat*); this is an extended application (*atideśa*) regarding actions residing in the object. The purpose [of this rule] is [to trigger] the *yaṅ* suffix, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and the *ciṇvadbhāva* substitution. The rice cooks by itself (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*). The sixty-day rice ripens in sixty nights (*ṣaṣṭikāḥ ṣaṣṭirātreṇa pacyante*). The wood split by itself (*abhedi kāṣṭhaṃ svayameva*). The mat will be made by itself (*kariṣyate kaṭaḥ svayameva*). How is it that [in the cases of] "they embrace each other" (*anyonyam āśliṣyataḥ*) or "they seize each other" (*anyonyaṃ gṛhṇītaḥ*), [the rule does not apply]? Because the action is distinct due to the distinction between the instruments [of the action].

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In the case of the transitive roots *duh* (to milk) and *pac* (to cook), [the agent] is frequently treated like the object (*karmavat*). The cow milks the milk by herself (*dugdhe gauḥ kṣīraṃ svayameva*). The cow yields the milk by herself (*adugdha gauḥ kṣīraṃ svayameva*). The *udumbara* tree ripens its red fruit (*udumbaraḥ lohitaṃ phalaṃ pacyate*).

Likewise, when the action of the instrument is identical to that of the agent, the agent is frequently treated like the object. For example: "He surrounds the tree with thorns" (*parivārayati kaṇṭakair vṛkṣam*); "The thorns surround themselves around the tree" (*parivāryante kaṇṭakāḥ svayameva vṛkṣam*).
[Furthermore,] the root *tap* (to heat/afflict) is [treated like the object] only when it has "heat" (*tapas*) as its object.

The agent of the root *tap* (to heat/perform penance) shall be treated like the object. For example: *tapyate tapas tāpasaḥ* ("the ascetic performs penance"). The meaning is "he acquires [merit]. Why specify "only when *tapas* is the object"? [Consider: *uttapati suvarṇaṃ suvarṇakāraḥ* ("the goldsmith heats the gold").

For the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*, the passive suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur when they have a reflexive agent (karmakartṛ). Thus: *dugdhe gauḥ kṣīraṃ svayameva* ("the cow milks milk by herself"), *adugdha gauḥ kṣīraṃ svayameva* ("the cow milked milk by herself"); *prasnute gauḥ*, *prāsroṣṭa gauḥ svayameva* ("the cow yields milk," "the cow yielded milk by herself"); *namate daṇḍaḥ*, *anaṃsta daṇḍaḥ svayameva* ("the staff bends," "the staff bent by itself").

"According to the followers of Bhāradvāja, for the roots *ṇi*, *śranth*, *granth*, *brū*, and those that are ātmanepada and intransitive, the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur when the object becomes the agent (*karmakartṛ*). *ṇi*: The girl adorns herself (*bhūṣayate kanyā*). The mat causes itself to be made (*kārayate kaṭaḥ*), [or] the mat caused itself to be made (*acīkarata kaṭaḥ*). *Granth*: The girdle strings itself (*granthate mekhalā*), [or] the garland was strung by itself (*agranthiṣṭa mālā*). *Śranth*: The girdle strings itself (*śranthate*), [or] the girdle was strung by itself (*aśranthiṣṭa mekhalā*). *Brū*: She tells the story (*brūte kathā*). The milk transforms itself (*vikurute payaḥ svayameva*). For roots beginning with *kṝ* and for those ending in the desiderative suffix (*san*), the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur when the object becomes the agent."

The elephant scatters [itself]. The mat desires to be made. The mat desired to be made by itself. According to the Eastern grammarians, the suffix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings are used for the roots *kuṣ* (to tear) and *rañj* (to color) when they function as agent-reflexives (*karmakartṛ*). By these two roots, according to the opinion of the Easterners, *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings shall occur. He tears his foot with his foot. The foot tears itself. By the rule "after *śya* and *śyan*, *num* is always added," there is the nasal augment: the shank tears itself. The cloth colors itself. The dewdrop colored itself spontaneously.
"From a root. This is a governing rule (adhikāra) extending up to the end of the third chapter. Kṛt and tiṅ suffixes are to be prescribed after a verbal root.
In that context, an "upapada" is that which stands in the locative case.

In this section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), that which is designated by the locative case shall be termed an *upapada*. As he will state: "The suffix *aṇ* after an object," "the root *sthā* after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*"), and "kṛt suffixes other than *tiṅ*.
In that context, within the section on verbal roots, those other than *tiṅ* suffixes shall be termed *kṛt*, such as *ṇvul*, *śatṛ*, and so forth.

*Vā'sarūpo'striyām*: Among *kṛt* suffixes, a dissimilar form (*asarūpa*) exception may optionally supersede [its regular rule], except in the feminine gender. Examples: *kartavyam* or *kāryam*; *viboddhā* or *vibudhaḥ*; *hasitam* or *hasanam*. Why "except in the feminine"? [Consider: *cikīrṣā* (here the feminine suffix *ktin* does not supersede the regular rule). Why "dissimilar form"? [Consider: *godah* (where the suffix is similar) and *śarmadah*.
Kṛtyas before the suffix *ṇvul*.
The seven suffixes preceding *ṇvul* shall be designated as *kṛtya*. Tavyat, tavya, anīyar, kelimar, as well as yat, ṇyat, and kyap—these seven are declared to be the *kṛtyas*.

The suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Examples: *bhātavyam*, *bhānīyam*; *bhavitavyam*, *bhavanīyam*; *vaktavyam*, *vacanīyam*. Here, *vāstavyaḥ* ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, this is a *taddhita*: that which exists in a dwelling (*vāstu*) is *vāstavya*. An addition should be made regarding the suffix *kelimara*: it denotes the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*). Examples: *pacelimā māṣāḥ* (the beans are ready to be cooked); *chidelimā rajjuḥ* (the rope is ready to be cut).

The suffixes *kha*, *mī*, *tavyat*, and others apply when there is no specification of time (*kālasāmānye*). Likewise, they apply even in the past tense—as in "those who have declared the object [of action] are called *karmapravacanīya*s. In the present tense: from the root *bhū*, we have *bhavya* (meaning "he becomes"). By the rule *aco yat* ("*yat* shall be added after a vowel"), *yat* is added after a word ending in a vowel. Thus: *lavyam*, *bhavyam*, *pavyam*, *peyam*, *geyam*, *deyam*, *ditsyam*, *putrīyyam*, *dedīpyam*, *putrakāmyam*, and *gardabhyam*. [Question: How is it that [the form] *bhāvyam* occurs in the sense of "it must be brought about by this"? [Answer: Let it be so in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). The meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *orāvaśyake* ("*ṇyat* after a vowel in the sense of necessity").
The suffix *yat* is applied after the roots *taka*, *praśaṃs*, *cat*, *yat*, and *jan*. [Examples: *takyam*, *praśasyam*, *catyam*, *yatyam*, *janyam*.

After the root *han*, there is optionally the substitution of *vadh* for the root, and the suffix *yat* is applied. Thus, it may be *vadhyaḥ*, with *vadh* as the substitute; alternatively, when the suffix *ṇyat* is used—[the form is] *ghātyaḥ*.
After a root ending in *p* that has a light penultimate vowel, [the suffix *yat* is applied].

The suffix *yat* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a letter of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) that has *a* as its penultimate vowel (*adupadha*). This serves to set aside the suffix *ṇyat*. Examples: *śapyam*, *japyam*, *labhyam*. Why "having *a* as its penultimate vowel"? Consider *gopyam*. Why "followed by *t*" (*tapara*)? Consider *āpyam*.
[The suffix *yat*] also occurs after the roots *śaki* and *sahi*. The suffix *yat* shall occur after these two: *śakyam*, *sahyam*.

After the roots *gad*, *mad*, *car*, and *yam*, when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *yat* shall be applied. Thus: *gadyam*; that by which one becomes intoxicated is *madyam*; *caryam*; *yamyam*. How is it that *niyamyam* and *yatnāparyam* are formed? They are like *duṣprāpya* and others, being formed subsequently through composition (*samāsa*). After the root *car*, when preceded by *āṅ*, the suffix *yat* shall be applied provided it does not mean "teacher" (*aguru*). Thus: *ācaryo dharmaḥ* (the practice of dharma). Why "not meaning teacher"? Because *ācāryaḥ* (teacher) is formed with the suffix *ṇyat*.

The words *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) in the senses of "blameless," "to be sold," and "unrestricted," respectively. In these cases, they are thus established: *avadya* means "not to be censured" (*anindya*); *paṇya* means "to be sold" (*vikreya*); *varya* means "one whose activity is unrestricted" (*aniruddhapravṛtti*). For example: *śatena varyaḥ* ("one who chooses from among a hundred [suitors]"); *sugrīvo nāma varyo 'sau paṇyabhrātṛvadhaḥ kapiḥ* ("that monkey named Sugrīva is one who chose [his wife] after the killing of his brother as a commodity"). Some say that *varyā* means "a woman chosen by a husband. *Vahyam* means "the means of conveyance" (*karaṇa*).
The suffix *yat* occurs after the root *vah* when it denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*). That by which they carry is a "vehicle" (*vahnyaṃ*), such as a cart (*śakaṭam*).
The suffix *yat* occurs after the root *ṛ* when meaning either a master (*svāmin*) or a Vaiśya (*vaiśya*). Thus, *aryaḥ*. In other cases, *āryaḥ* refers to a region that is to be traversed.
*Upasaryā* means fit for breeding;
that is, a cow who has reached the time for conception at her first pregnancy is called *upasaryā*. *Ajarya* means a union [that is not subject to decay].
This is what is prescribed here: "One should quickly perform that which is agreeable to the noble one with whom you have met. The rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* states:

after the root *vad*, the suffix *kyap* occurs when a noun (*sup*) is present as an upapada, and the suffix *yac* also occurs. Thus: "There is no speaking of untruth there; I tell you the speaking of truth (*satyavadyam*). When the possessive suffix *ac* is added in the sense of "possessing," we get: "The best of the Raghus is truthful (*satyavadyaḥ*). Why "when a noun is present" (*supi*)? [Otherwise, we would have] *vādyam*. Why "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*)? [Otherwise, we would have] *pravādyam* and *suvādyam*. How then is *anūdyam* formed? It is formed with the prefix *anu*.
*bhuvo bhāve*:
After the root *bhū*, when expressing a state (*bhāva*) and followed by a *su*-ending [nominal suffix], the suffix *kyap* shall occur. Examples: *brahmabhūyam*, *brahmatvam*.
*hanasta ca*: [The suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *han* to express a state,] and there is also the substitution of *t* for the final consonant.

After the root *han*, the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and this [suffix] is also substituted for the final letter [of the root]. Thus: *brahmahatyā* (the killing of a Brahmin). "When he has become a friend, you shall commit the murder of his enemy.

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *i*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*. From these, *kyap* shall occur: *ityaḥ* (to be gone to), *stutyaḥ* (to be praised), *śiṣyaḥ* (to be taught), *vṛtyaḥ* (to be chosen), *ādṛtyaḥ* (to be respected), *juṣyaḥ* (to be enjoyed). How is *upeya* [formed]? It is from the root *ir* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*).
The suffix *kyap* is optionally applied after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*. [Examples: *śasyam* / *śaṃsyam*; *duhyam* / *dohyam*; *guhyam* / *gohyam*.

The suffix *kyap* is also applied after the root *añj* when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). [Example: *ājyam* (clarified butter). The suffix *kyap* is also applied after a root having *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel, except for the roots *kḷp* and *cṛt*.

The suffix *kyap* shall occur after a verbal root having a light vowel (*ṛt*) as its penultimate letter. Examples: *vṛtyam*, *nṛtyam*, *gṛdhyam*. An exception: it does not occur after the roots *klṛp* and *cṛt*. Examples: *kalpyam*, *cartyam*. Furthermore, the suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *khan*, and the final vowel of the root is replaced by long *ī*. The application of *guṇa* (P. 6.1.87) results in *kheyam*.

After the root *bhṛ* (to support), the suffix *kyap* occurs when it does not denote a name (*saṃjñā*). Example: *bhṛtyaḥ* (a servant). However, when it denotes a name, [the suffix *kyap* is applied after *bhṛ* with the prefix *sam*]: *bhāryā* (a wife). Furthermore, after the root *bhṛ* with the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kyap* is applied diversely (*bahulam*). Examples: *sambhṛtyāḥ* (those who are to be supported) or *sambhāryāḥ*. After the root *mṛj* (to cleanse), the suffix *kyap* is optionally applied.
The suffix *kyap* may optionally be applied after the root *mṛj*. Thus, one says either *mṛjyaḥ* or *mārgyaḥ*.

The words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kuṣya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *avyathya* are formed as *kyap*-derivatives by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Rājasūya*: a sacrifice (*kratu*). It is so called because the king (*rājā*) causes it to proceed (*sūyate*). *Sūrya*: the sun; it shines (*suvati*), that is, it blazes. *Mṛṣodya*: one who speaks falsely (*mṛṣā udyate asau*). *Rucya*: that which is pleasing (*rocate asau*). In the case of the root *gup*, there is also the addition of the prefix *ā*: *kuṣyam* (base metal); anything else is *gopyam* (to be protected). *Kṛṣṭapacyāḥ śālayaḥ*: rice crops that ripen in cultivated soil. *Avyathyā durjanāḥ*: wicked people who do not falter (or are unshakable).

*Bhidya* and *ujjhya* are [nouns] denoting rivers; these two are irregularly formed (nipātita) as specific types of rivers. *Bhidyaḥ* is that which breaks the banks; *ujjhyaḥ* is that which releases water.
*Puṣya* and *siddhya* are [names of] lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
These two [suffixes] may occur following the word *nakṣatra* when it denotes a specific division [of time].

The forms *vipūya*, *vinīya*, and *jitya* are derived through the application of these suffixes when they refer respectively to *muñja*, *kalka*, and *halin*. Thus: *vipūya* refers to the *muñja* grass; *vinīya* refers to a medicinal paste (*kalka*); and *jitya* refers to a large plow (*bṛhaddhala*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *prati* and *apa* when combined with *grah*,
according to the Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
It is also applied [after *grah*] in the senses of "foot," "independent," "external," and "hostile faction" (*bāhyāpakṣya*).

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *grah* (to seize) in the following senses: 1. *pragṛhyaṃ padaṃ*: a word that is not subject to sandhi changes. 2. *gṛhyakā asvairiṇaḥ*: those who are dependent or lack independence. 3. *grāmagṛhyā senā*: an army stationed outside the village; that is, one located beyond the village. 4. *grāmagṛhyā vacane vipaścitaḥ*: scholars who are partial to a particular doctrine; that is, those who favor a specific school of thought.

[The suffix *kyap*] is optionally applied after the roots *kṛ* (to do) and *vṛṣ* (to rain). In these cases, *kyap* may optionally occur: - From *kṛ*, either *kṛtyam* or *kāryam*. - From *vṛṣ*, either *vṛṣyam* or *varṣyam*. In the alternative case (*pakṣe*), the suffix *ṇyat* is used.
The word *yugya* is used in the sense of "leaf" (*patra*) or "vehicle" (*vāhana*); otherwise, it means "suitable" (*yogya*). The suffix *amāvasyad* is optionally applied [to form *amāvāsya*].

After the word *amā* preceding the root *vas*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, and the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) is optionally prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Thus, one has either *amāvāsyā* or *amāvasyā*.

In the Vedic language (*Chandas*), the following words are formed with the suffix *kyap*: *nirṣṭakya*, *devahūya*, *praṇīya*, *unnīya*, *ucchiṣya*, *marya*, *starya*, *adhvaryu*, *khanya*, *khānya*, *devayajya*, *āpṛcchya*, *pratiṣīvya*, *brahmavādya*, *bhāvya*, *stāvya*, *upacāyya*, and *pṛḍā*.

This is Vedic usage. [The rule] *ṛ-halor ṇyat* [states that] the suffix *ṇyat* occurs after roots ending in the vowel *ṛ* or after those ending in a consonant (*hal*). Examples: *kāryam*, *hāryam*, *āhāryam*, *pākyam*, *vādyam*, *pādyam*, *vāhyam*, *vākyam*, *pāṭhyam*. From the root *kavṛ*: *kāvyam*. [From roots ending in *ās*: *vāsyam*. How is it that *samasyam* and *abhyasyam* are formed? In that case, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* because the rule is conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*); for "a rule conditioned by a technical name is not obligatory" (*anitya*). [The rule] *pāṇau sṛjeḥ* [states that] the suffix *ṇyat* occurs after the root *sṛj* when preceded by *pāṇi*. Example: *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ* (a rope released from the hand). Also [after the root *sṛj*] preceded by *samava*: *samavasarjyaḥ*. And after the root *dabh*: [the suffix *ṇyat* occurs].

The suffix *ṇyat* shall be an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "after a root ending in a consonant preceded by *ra*. For example: *avadābhya*. The root *dabh* is a Vedic (*sautra*) root. After a root ending in *u*, when necessity (*āvaśyakatva*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. For example: *lāvya*, *pāvya*. Through the inclusion in the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*, a compound is formed: *avaśyalāvyam*.
The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after the roots √ās, √yu, √vap, √rapi, √lap, √trap, and √cam. [Examples: *āsāvyam*, *yāvyam*, *vāpyam*, *rāpyam*, *lāpyam*, *avatrāpyam*, *ācāmyam*.
The suffix *ānāyya* is used when the object is not permanent.
*Ānāyya* refers to that which is to be brought [into the fire]; it would be used for the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
*Praṇāyya* means one who is not approved of.
"Not approved of" (*asammati*) refers to an undesirable person, such as a thief; in that case, *praṇāyya* would apply.
*pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* [are derived from] *māna*, *havis*, *nivāsa*, and *sāmidhenī*.

The forms *pāyya* and so forth are established as irregular (*nipātana*) derivatives of the roots *mā* (to measure), *ṇī* (to lead), *ñci* (to collect), *dhā* (to place), and *ñi* (to suck) in the senses of measuring, sacrificial oblation, dwelling, and *sāmidhenī* verses respectively. *Pāyya* means a measure; *sānnāyya* means a sacrificial oblation; *nikāyya* means a dwelling; *dyāyyā* refers to a *sāmidhenī* verse.
In the context of a sacrifice, the terms *kuṇḍapāyya* and *sañcāyya* [are used].
These two are irregularly derived (nipātyete) in the sense of *kratu*.
*Paricāyya*, *upacāyya*, and *samūhya* are irregularly derived in the sense of *agni*. From the root *vah*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and lengthening; thus, *samūhya*.

The words *citya* and *agnicitya* are also irregularly formed (*nipātyete*). *Citya* refers to the fire-altar (*agni*). In the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), it becomes *agnicityā*. The *kṛtya* suffixes have been explained.
Now, the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* [are treated].

The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur after a verbal root in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: *dāyakaḥ*, *dātā*; *adhiṣṭhāyakaḥ*, *adhiṣṭhātā*; *vācakaḥ*, *vaktā*; *pācakaḥ*, *paktā*; *kārakaḥ*, *kartā*.
[Furthermore,] the suffixes *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* occur after roots such as *nandi*, *grahi*, and *paci*.

The suffix *lyu* (ana) occurs after roots such as *nandi*: *nandanaḥ*, *madanaḥ*, *damanaḥ*, *śobhanaḥ*, *tapanaḥ*, *darpaṇaḥ*, *pavanaḥ*, *ramaṇaḥ*, *janārdanaḥ*, *vibhīṣaṇaḥ*, *lavaṇaḥ*. The change to *ṇ* [in *lavaṇa*] is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The suffix *ṇini* occurs after roots such as *grah*: *grāhī*, *paripanthī*, *sthāyī*. The suffix *ac* occurs after roots such as *pac*: *pacaḥ*, *śvapacaḥ*, *vadaḥ*, *kadvadaḥ*, *meṣaḥ*, *devaḥ*, *śvetaḥ*, *yodhaḥ*, *krodhaḥ*, *sarpaḥ*, *sparśaḥ*, *narttaḥ*. [Examples with *ac*: *nartta*, *haladharaḥ*, *gadādharaḥ*, *payodharaḥ*.
*Yaśodhara*, *Śaktidhara*, *Gaṅgādhara*, *Jātismara*, *Loluba*, *Popuva*, *Cañcura*. [The suffix *ka* is applied] to the *pacādi* group, which is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).

[By the rule] *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*: the suffix *ka* shall be added after these: *budha*, *kuṣa*, *irśa*, *vipula*, *kṛṣa*, *mṛḍa*, *jña*, *priya*, and *utkira*. Thus: *budha-ka* > *budha*, *kuṣa-ka* > *kuṣa*, *irśa-ka* > *irśa*, *vipula-ka* > *vipula*, *kṛṣa-ka* > *kṛṣa*, *mṛḍa-ka* > *mṛḍa*, *jña-ka* > *jña*, *priya-ka* > *priya*, *utkira-ka* > *utkira*.
And after a prefix, [the suffix *ka*] follows a root ending in long *ā*. After a prefix, *ka* shall be added to roots ending in long *ā*: *prasthaḥ*, *susthaḥ*, *prasraḥ*, *samlaḥ*, *suglaḥ*.
After the roots *pā*, *ghrā*, *dhmā*, *dheṭ*, and *dṛś*, the suffix *śa* [is applied].

The suffix *śa* shall be applied after these [roots]: *ut-pibaḥ*, *uj-jighriḥ*, *ā-jighraiḥ* (of flower-fragrances), *ud-dhamaḥ*, *ud-dhayaḥ*, *ut-paśyaḥ*. According to some, *paśyaḥ* is also included by the rule *aprapadeś ca*. [Examples of] *jighraḥ*. The sense is that the term *upasarge* does not carry over [from previous rules]. [The suffix *śa* is not applied] when it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*): *vyāghraḥ* (tiger). Or rather, it is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

And [the suffix *śa* is applied] after the roots *limpa*, *vinda*, *dhāri*, *pāri*, *vedi*, *udeji*, *ceti*, *sāti*, and *sāhi* when they are not preceded by an *upasarga*: *anupasargāl limpavindadhāripārivedyudejicetisātisāhibhyaś ca*.

After these roots, when not preceded by *ap*, the suffix *śa* shall occur. Examples: *limpaḥ*, *vindaḥ*, *mālyadhārayaḥ*. The root *sāti* is Vedic (sautra)—examples: *sātayaḥ*, *sāhayaḥ*. After the root *vid*, when preceded by *go* and others, [the suffix *śa* occurs] in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *govindaḥ*, *aravindam*. After the root *lip*, when preceded by *nau* (boat), [the suffix *śa* occurs]: *nilimpā devāḥ* (the gods are "the unsmearing ones"). After the roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place), there is an option (*vibhāṣā*): when not preceded by *ap*, the suffix *śa* may optionally occur after *dā* and *dhā*. Examples: *dadaḥ* or *dāyaḥ*; *dadhaḥ* or *dhāyaḥ*.

The suffix *ṇa* is applied after roots beginning with *jval* and ending with *kas*. After roots beginning with *jval* and ending with *kas*, the suffix *ṇa* may be applied. Examples: *jvālaḥ*, *jvalaḥ*; *cālaḥ*, *calaḥ*; *rāmaḥ*, *ramaḥ*. Only when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasargāt*)—as in *prajvalaḥ*. The suffix *ac* is applied invariably after roots beginning with *pac*. And also after the root *tan*: *avatānaḥ*, *avatanah*. [The suffix *ac* is also applied] after the roots *śyai*, *vyadh*, *asru*, *saṃsru*, *tṛ*, *ṇu*, *sā*, *vah*, *hṛ*, *liś*, *śliṣ*, and *śvas*.

The suffix *ṇa* shall be applied after these roots. From *śyaiṅ*: *avaśyāyaḥ* (dew), *pratiśyāyaḥ* (catarrh). From roots ending in long *ā*: *dāyaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*. From *vyadh* and others: *vyādhaḥ* (hunter), *āsrāvaḥ* (flowing out), *saṃsrāvaḥ* (flowing together), *atyāyaḥ* (passing beyond). *Avasāyaḥ* means "one who brings to an end"; *avahāraḥ* (withdrawal); *lehaḥ* (licking). "I am burned by the lickings of honey" (*dahye 'haṃ madhuno lehaiḥ*). *Śleṣaḥ* (adhesion). *Śvāsaḥ* (breathing) from the root *śvas* with the sense of "he breathes. The inclusion of *śyaiṅ* is for the purpose of precluding *ka* when a prefix is present.

*Du* and *nī* without a prefix: the suffix *ṇa* shall be applied after the roots *du* and *nīñ*. *Dāvaḥ* (forest fire); *nāyaḥ* (leader). Because this is also considered a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) due to the subsequent optional rule, they say that with a vowel suffix (*ac*), one has *davaḥ* and *nayaḥ*. Why "not beginning with *pra*" (*apra-ādau*)? [Counter-example: *praṇayaḥ* (affection).

The term *vibhāṣā* indicates an option. Thus, the suffix *ṇa* may optionally be applied after the root *grah*. Hence, we have both *grāhaḥ* and *grahaḥ*. It should be stated that this also applies to the root *bhū*: thus, from *bhavati*, we have both *bhāvaḥ* and *bhavaḥ*.
After the root [ending in] *guh*, the suffix *ka* is applied when it means "house."
The suffix *ka* occurs after the root *grah* when "house" (*geha*) is the agent. [Examples: *gṛham*, *gṛhāḥ*.
The suffix *ṣvun* occurs when the agent is a craftsman (*śilpin*). It applies only after the roots *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj*. [Examples: *nartakī*, *khanakī*, *rajakī*.
The suffix *sthakan* occurs after the root *gai*. [Thus] *gāthakaḥ*.
And the suffix *ṇyuṭ* also [occurs].
The suffix *ṇyuṭ* occurs after the root *gā*. [Thus: *gāyanaḥ* (a singer). Due to the inclusion of the letter *ca*, [the suffix also occurs after the root *kṛ*: *kāraṇam* (a cause).
And after the root *hā*, when referring to rice or time, [the suffix *ṇyuṭ* occurs]. The suffix *ṇyuṭ* occurs after the root *hā*. [Thus: *hāyanaḥ* (a type of rice); *hāyanaḥ* (a year).

The suffix *vun* is applied after the roots *pra*, *sṛ*, and *lū* when there is repetition of action (*samabhihāra*). After the roots *pra*, *sṛ*, and *lū*, the suffix *vun* shall occur when there is repetition of action: *pravakaḥ*, *sarakaḥ*, *lavakaḥ*.
[The suffix *vun* is also applied] in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*).

The suffix *vun* shall occur after a verbal root in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). Examples: *nandatāt* [he may rejoice] → *nandakaḥ*; *jīvatāt* [may he live] → *jīvakaḥ*; *bhūyāt* [may he be] → *bhavakaḥ*. Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* of the Great Professor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.

*karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1): The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after a verbal root when a word denoting an object (*karman*) alone is used as an upapada. Examples: *kumbhakāraḥ* (pot-maker), *nagarakāraḥ* (city-builder), *śatrulāvaḥ* (slayer of enemies), *vedādhyāyaḥ* (Veda-student). [The following examples illustrate] when the action is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*): *chatradhāraḥ* (umbrella-bearer), *hārapālaḥ* (guardian of the necklace), *vipraghātaḥ* (slayer of Brahmins), *aśvavāraḥ* (horse-keeper), *kamaṇḍalugrāhaḥ* (holder of the water-pot), *ripudhātaḥ* (slayer of foes).

*śīlikāmibhakṣyācaribhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1): After these—namely, roots meaning "having a habit" (*śīlin*), "desiring" (*kāmin*), "eating" (*bhakṣin*), and "practicing" (*ācarin*)—the suffix *ṇa* shall be applied. Examples: *māṃsaśīlaḥ* (flesh-eating by habit); in the feminine, with the suffix *ṭāp*: *māṃsaśīlā*. *māṃsakāmaḥ* (desirous of meat); in the feminine: *māṃsakāmā*. *dharmakāmaḥ* (desirous of dharma); in the feminine: *dharmakāmā*. *māṃsabhakṣaḥ* (meat-eater); in the feminine: *māṃsabhakṣā*. *sādhvācāraḥ* (of virtuous conduct); *kalyāṇācārā kanyā* (a girl of auspicious conduct).

And after the roots *īkṣi* and *kṣami*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs. From these two, the suffix *ṇa* shall be applied: *sukhapratīkṣā* (waiting for happiness), *bahukṣamā* (great forbearance). After the roots *hveñ*, *veñ*, and *māṅ*, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied as an exception to *kā*. *svargahvāyaḥ* (one who calls out to heaven), *tantuvāyaḥ* (a weaver). "It rose up like the sky-maker (*vyomamāya*)."

*Āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*: After a verbal root ending in long *ā*, when no prefix (*upapada*) precedes it, the suffix *ka* is applied. Examples: *godah* (cattle-giver), *śarmadah* (giver of happiness), *kambaladah* (woolen-cloth giver), *sukhadah* (giver of pleasure), *dharmadah* (giver of dharma), *sarvajñaḥ* (all-knowing), *nṛpaḥ* (king), *aṅgulitraḥ* (finger-guard), *pārṣṇitraḥ* (heel-guard). Why "when no prefix precedes"? [Counter-examples: *gosandāyaḥ* (one who gives a cow), *vaḍavāsandāyaḥ* (one who gives a mare). *Supi sthaḥ*: [The suffix *ka* is applied after the root *sthā*] when a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) precedes it.

Regarding *supi*: by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), when a word ending in *su* (a case-ending) is present as an upapada, the suffix *ka* may be applied. Examples: *dvipaḥ* (an elephant), *pādapaḥ* (a tree), *kacchapaḥ* (a tortoise); *susthaḥ* (well-situated), *duḥsthaḥ* (ill-situated), *prasthaḥ* (a plateau), *viṣamasthaḥ* (standing on uneven ground), *madhyasthaḥ* (standing in the middle). Then, from *stha*: after the root *sthā*, *ka* may be applied when a word ending in *su* is present. This is stated with reference to the abstract state (*bhāva*). Example: *ākhūtthaṃ vartate* (there is an occurrence of rats). From this point forward, the rule "when a word ending in *su* is present" (*supi*) continues to apply as far as possible, specifically in the sense of the object (*karman*). *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ*: after these two roots (*parimṛj* and *apanud*), *ka* may be applied when *tunda* and *śoka* are respectively the objects. Example: *tundaparimṛjaḥ* refers only to one who is lazy; *śokāpanudaḥ* refers only to one who is beloved.

In the section on *ka*, there is an addition [to the rule] for words such as *mūlavibhuja*. The suffix *ka* should be applied. Examples: *mūlavibhujaḥ* (a chariot with wide-spreading roots), *nakhamucam* (a bow that releases [arrows] like claws), *priyākhyo brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin who speaks kindly). *Abhram* (a cloud) from *apo bibharti* (it carries water); *mahīdhraḥ* (a mountain, earth-bearer); *kṛtaghno naraḥ* (an ungrateful man); *śatrughnaḥ* (a slayer of enemies); *pralambanaḥ* (one who hangs down); *kumudam* (a white lotus); *saroruham* (a lotus growing in water). *Tridivaḥ* (heaven) means "that in which three [gods] play. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class of words defined by its formative pattern). *Pra* [is added] after *dā* and *jñā*; *sam* after *khā*.

An exception to the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed after words ending in] *prada*, *prajña*, and *saṃkhyā* is that the suffix *ka* should be applied. Examples: *viśvāsapradaḥ* (one who inspires confidence), *pathiprajñaḥ* (one who knows the way), *gosaṃkhyaḥ* (one who counts cattle).

Regarding the rule *gāpo ṣṭak*: the suffix *ṭak* should be applied as an exception to the suffix *ka* after the roots *gā* (to sing) and *pā* (to drink). Examples: *sāmagaḥ* (a singer of Sāman hymns), *sāmagī* (a female singer of Sāman hymns). This applies only when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). Example with a prefix: *sāmapragāyaḥ* (one who sings the Sāman in a loud voice). It should be stated that the suffix *ṭak* is applied after the root *pā* (to drink) when preceded by the words *surā* (liquor) or *śīdhu* (spirituous liquor). Examples: *surāpaḥ* (a drinker of liquor), *śīdhupaḥ* (a drinker of spirits); *surāpī* (a female drinker of liquor), *śīdhupī* (a female drinker of spirits).

The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *hṛ* (to take) when preceded by *anu*, provided it does not mean "lifting up. Thus: *aṃśaharaḥ* (an heir), *manoharaḥ* (charming), *pittaharaṃ kṣīram* (bile-removing milk), and *vākyaharā dūtī* (a messenger who conveys words). However, in the sense of "lifting up," one has *bhārahāraḥ* (a porter).
Furthermore, the suffix *ac* is applied after *hṛ* when preceded by *vayas*.

When the root *hṛ* (to take) occurs with the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ac* shall be applied in the sense of habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*). Thus: *puṣyāharaḥ*, *phalāharaḥ*, *sukhāharaḥ*; the meaning is "one who is habitually inclined toward taking flowers," "one who is habitually inclined toward taking fruit," and "one who is habitually inclined toward bringing happiness. [In the case of] the root *hṛ* (to carry), when combined with the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ac* shall be applied [in the sense of habitual tendency]. [Examples: *puṣyāharaḥ*, *phalāharaḥ*, *sukhāharaḥ*. The meaning is "one who is habitually inclined toward that. When the age (*vayas*) is being traversed, the suffix *ac* shall be applied after the root *hṛ*. [Examples: *asthiharaḥ śvā* ("a dog that carries bones"); *varmmaharaḥ kumāraḥ* ("a youth who carries armor"). When the prefix *āṅ* is present, the suffix *ac* shall be applied after the root *hṛ* [in the sense of habitual tendency]. [Examples: *puṣyāharaḥ*, *phalāharaḥ*, *sukhāharaḥ*. The meaning is "one who is habitually inclined toward that."

*Arhaḥ*: After the root *arh*, there shall be the suffix *ac* as an exception to *aṇ*. For example: *pūjārhaḥ paṇḍitaḥ* (a scholar worthy of honor), *pūjārhā brāhmaṇī* (a Brahmin woman worthy of honor), *kāryārhā brāhmaṇī* (a Brahmin woman worthy of work). *Śakti-lāṅgūla-aṅkuśa-yaṣṭi-tomara-ghaṭa-ghaṭī-dhanuḥṣu graheḥ*: After the root *grah*, there shall be the suffix *ac* when these [words] follow: *śakti*, *lāṅgūla*, *aṅkuśa*, *yaṣṭi*, *tomara*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus*. Examples: *śaktigrahaḥ* (seizing a spear), *lāṅgūlagrahaḥ* (seizing a tail), *dhanurgrahaḥ* (taking up a bow).

And in the case of *sūtra*, when the sense is "to ascertain," there shall be the suffix *ac* after the root *grah*. One who ascertains the meaning of a *sūtra* is a *sūtragrahaḥ*, a wise person. But elsewhere, it is *sūtragrāhaḥ*.
[Also, the suffix *ac* occurs] after the roots *ram* and *jap* when combined with *stamba* and *karṇa* respectively.

The suffix *ac* is applied after the roots *rami* and *japi* when preceded by the upapadas *stamba* and *karṇa* respectively; this denotes an elephant and a slanderer. Thus: *stamberamaḥ* (an elephant) and *karṇejapaḥ* (a wicked person). When the word *śam* is an upapada, the suffix *ac* is applied to the root in general to form a name (*saṃjñā*). Thus: *śaṃkaraḥ* (Śiva), *śaṃvaraḥ* (a Daitya), and *śaṃvadaḥ* (a certain person).
[The suffix] *ac* is applied after the root *śī* (to lie) when preceded by a word denoting a location (*ādhāra*). Thus, from *kheśayaḥ* ("lying in the sky") and *guhāśayaḥ* ("lying in a cave").
There is an extension [of this rule] to words such as *pārśva*. In these cases, *ac* is applied after *śī*: one who lies on his sides is *pārśvaśayaḥ*; one who lies on his chest is *uraḥśayaḥ*.

In the case of agents such as *uttāna* and others: *uttānaḥ śete* (he lies on his back) results in *uttānaśayaḥ*; likewise, *avamūrdhaśayaḥ*. [The suffix *kha* is applied] after words preceded by *digdha* and *saha*: *digdhasahaśayaḥ*. However, the word *giriśa*—ending in the suffix *śa* according to the rule for *loman* and others—is correct in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
[The suffix] *ṭa* is applied after the root *car*.

The suffix *ṭa* (forming *cara*) is prescribed after the verb *car* when preceded by a support (*ādhāra*) or a subordinate word (*upapada*). Examples: *kurucaraḥ* (one who moves among the Kurus), *vanecaraḥ* (one who moves in the forest), *rātricaraḥ* / *rātriñcaraḥ* (one who moves at night), *khecaraḥ* (one who moves in the sky), *khecarī* (female sky-walker), *naktañcarī* (female night-walker). How is *sahacarī* (companion) explained? This must be considered [as an irregularity].

And [the suffix *ṭa* is applied] after *car* when followed by *bhikṣā*, *senā*, or *ādāya*. In these cases, *ṭa* is applied: *bhikṣācaraḥ* (one who lives on alms), *senācaraḥ* (one who moves with an army), *ādāyacaraḥ* (one who takes up and moves; meaning one who seizes for himself).

The suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *sṛ* when preceded by *puras*, *agrataḥ*, or *agre*. Thus: *puraḥsaraḥ* (one who goes before), *agrataḥsaraḥ* (one who goes in front). From *agre sarati* (he goes at the head), one forms *agresaraḥ* (a leader); likewise, *agresarī* (a female leader). How then is the form *puraḥsarāḥ* used for "words"? It is derived through a different etymological analysis: using the suffix *ac* from the *pacādi* group, with *pur-* as the agent (*kartṛ*).
The suffix *ṭa* (a) shall be applied after the root *sṛ* when preceded by *pūrva*. Thus, *pūrvasaraḥ* ("one who goes ahead").

After the root *ruj*, the suffix *ṭa* shall be applied when a cause (*hetu*), habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*), or compliance (*ānulomya*) is to be understood, provided it is not within the scope of the suffix *kañ*. Examples: *dāridryaṃ puruṣasya viklavakaram* ("poverty causes dejection in a man"); *puṣṭikaraṃ māṃsam* ("flesh is nourishing"). In the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*): *vyasanakaraḥ* ("addicted"), *dayākaraḥ* ("compassionate"), *āśākaraḥ* ("hopeful"), *tāpakaraḥ* ("causing pain"). In the sense of compliance (*ānulomya*): *prītikaraḥ* ("pleasing"). Example: *pitur vāk-karaṃ rāmam* ("Rāma who carries out his father's word"). Why say "when a cause and so forth are to be understood"? Consider: *bhāṣyakāraḥ* ("the author of the Bhāṣya"). Here, the suffix *kṛt* is applied with the suffix *aṇ*.

When the words *divā*, *vibhā*, *niśā*, *prabhā*, *bhāskara*, *anta*, *ananta*, *ādi*, *bahu*, *nāndī*, *kilibi*, *bili*, *bhakti*, *kartṛ*, *citra*, *kṣetra*, *saṃkhyānaka*, *abāhu*, *ahaḥ*, *yatta*, *dhanus*, and *arus*—that is, in these twenty-six words beginning with *divā*—occur as upapadas (governing words) in the locative case (*sup*) or as objects (*karman*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *kṛ* (*√kṛ*) according to their respective requirements. Examples: *divākaraḥ* (maker of the day/sun) *vibhākaraḥ* (maker of light) *prabhākaraḥ* (maker of radiance) *bhāskaraḥ* (maker of light) "May that one who is the first maker of the state of divinity [grant us] safety. (*devāpadām ādikaraḥ*) *kiṃkaraḥ* (servant) *kārakaraḥ* (doer of deeds) *saṃkhyākaraḥ* (enumerator) Some authorities maintain that the inclusion of *saṃsthā* is for the sake of its meaning (i.e., it refers to numbers). Examples: *ekakaraḥ* (maker of one) *hikaraḥ* (maker of two) *catuṣkaraḥ* (maker of four) *ahaskaraḥ* (maker of the day) *aruṣkaraḥ* (maker of the dawn)

Kātyāyana maintains that the suffix *ṭa* has the same meaning as the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Thus: *kiṃkarā*, *yatkarā*, *tatkarā*, *bahukarā*. However, in the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, because these words are included in the list beginning with *ajādi*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
The rule *karmaṇi bhṛtau* means:

when the word *karman* is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṭa* occurs after the root *kṛ* in the sense of "wages" (*bhṛti*). Thus: *karmakaraḥ* (a servant) and *karmakarī*. Why "in the sense of wages"? [To exclude: *karmakāraḥ* (a craftsman).

The suffix *ka* does not occur after the words *śabda*, *śloka*, *kalaha*, *gāthā*, *vāc*, *caṭu*, *sūtra*, *mantra*, and *pada*; nor does it occur after the nine words beginning with *hela*. Examples: *śabdakāraḥ papāta kham* ("the author of the sound fell into the sky"), *ślokakāraḥ*, and likewise up to *padakāraḥ*.
[The suffix] *in* occurs after *stamba* and *śakṛt*.

The suffix *in* shall be applied to these two [roots] with the augment *kvac*. Examples: *stambakariḥ*, *śakatkariḥ*. The terms refer to rice and a calf respectively. With the words *harati* and *nātha*, when referring to an animal: when *paśu* (animal) is the agent and *dṛti* (leather bag) or *nātha* (lord/master) is the upapada, the suffix *in* shall be applied to the root *hṛ*. Examples: *dṛtihariḥ* refers to a dog; *nāthahariḥ* refers to a lion.

The suffixes *phal* and *igahira* are introduced after [the root] *ātmambhṛ*, and they are both treated as *nipātana* (irregularly formed) words. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), *kukṣimbhari* is also included. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffixes *van*, *san*, *rakṣi*, and *math* [are applied].
This is Vedic grammar.
[The rule] *ejeḥ khaś* [means]:

after the root *ej*, the suffix *khaś* occurs when followed by a form ending in *syant* (the future participle marker), provided it does not fall under the scope of *aṇ*. Examples: *aṅgamejayaḥ*, *janamejayaḥ*, *śatrumaijayaḥ*, *cāṭamejayaḥ*.

The suffix *khaś* is applied after the words *vāta*, *śunī*, *tila*, *śada*, *iva*, *jaṭ*, *tuda*, and *jaha*, when these are followed by *aja* and others respectively. Thus: *vātamajaḥ* (a deer that does not flee from the wind), *śunindhayaḥ* (a wicked person who sucks at a bitch), *tilantudaḥ* (a crow that pecks at sesame seeds), and *śaījahāḥ* (deer that abandon their young).
[The suffix *khaś* is also applied] after the root *dhā* (*dheṭ*) following *nāsikā* and *stana*;
and also after *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi*.

And in the case of *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and *vāta*: when these are used as upapadas, the suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *prādhi* and *dheṭ*. *nāsikandhamaḥ* (one who breathes through the nose), *nāsikandhayaḥ* (one who drinks through the nose). [In the case of the suffix *khit*, there is shortening of the vowel according to the rule *khityanavyayasya*. It is traditionally taught that *dheṭ* alone is used with *stana*. *stanandhayaḥ* (an infant). *nāḍindhamān mārgān* (pipes blowing through the channels), *nāḍindhayaḥ* (one who drinks through a tube). *muṇindhamaḥ* (one who blows through a fist), *muṣṭindhayaḥ* (an infant who sucks from a fist). *ghaṭindhamaḥ* (one who blows into a jar), *ghaṭindhayaḥ* (one who drinks from a jar). *khārindhamaḥ* (one who blows into a measure of grain), *khārindhayaḥ* (one who drinks from a measure of grain). *vātandhamaḥ* (one who blows wind), *vātandhayaḥ* (one who drinks wind).

When *ut* is the upapada, it is so for the roots *hruj* and *vah* with *kūla*: here, *khaś* is applied to these two. *kūlamudrujaḥ* (an elephant breaking the bank), *kūlamuddhā* (a river overflowing its banks).

After the root *lih* (to lick), the suffix *khaś* is applied when preceded by *vaha*, *abhra*, or *vah*. Examples: *vahaliha* (a bull that licks the yoke), *analih* (a tree that licks fire). After the root *pac* (to cook), the suffix *khaś* is applied when a measure (*parimāṇa*) is the preceding word.

The suffix *khaś* shall occur [after the root *pac*]. Examples: *prakhampacā sthālī* ("a pot that cooks thoroughly"); *pāntāvalpampacān munīn* ("protecting the sages who cook little"); *tāpo'mbhaḥ pramṛtampacaḥ* ("the heat that cooks away the water"). Also after *mitanakhau*: the suffix *khaś* occurs after *pac* in connection with these two. *Mitampacaḥ* means a miser; *nakhampacā yavāgūḥ* means gruel that burns the nails.
The suffix *khaś* occurs after the roots *tud* when preceded by *vidhu*, *aruṣ*, or *anu*. *Vidhuntuda* is Rāhu; *aruntuda* is one who causes pain.
[The suffix *khaś* also occurs] after the roots *bhī* and *tṛ* when preceded by *asūrya* and *lalāṭa* respectively.

The word *asūryampaśya* (not seeing the sun) occurs with reference to the forehead (*lalāṭa*) and asceticism (*tapas*). The wives of kings (*rājadārāḥ*) are *asūryampaśyāḥ*. The words *sūrya*, *ugrampaśya*, *irammada*, and *pāṇindhama* are also [included].

These are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). "By that brother Ugrampaśya, Sugrīva was driven out. *Meghajyotirirammadaḥ*: [This refers to] one who gladdens with the lightning of clouds. *Pāṇindhamāḥ*: those who blow with their hands (cooks).

The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *vad* when preceded by *priya* or *vaśa*. The suffix *khac* shall occur after these two [words] following *vad*. Thus: *priyaṃvadaḥ* (one who speaks kindly); *vaśaṃvadaḥ* means compliant or submissive.
The suffix [is applied] after the root *tap* when preceded by *hiṣat* or *para*.

The suffix *khac* occurs after these two [roots] when followed by the word *tapa*. Examples: *viṣantapaḥ* (one who torments enemies), *parantapaḥ* (one who torments foes). In the case of *khac*, there is the substitution of *h* for the penultimate vowel. This is not desired when the feminine gender marker is present: *dviṣatītāpaḥ*. The suffix *khac* occurs after the root *yam* when preceded by *vāc* in the sense of a religious vow (*vrata*). Example: *vācaṃyamaḥ* (a sage who restrains his speech). Why "in the sense of a vow"? [Counter-example: *vāgyāmaḥ* (the restraint of speech).

The suffix *khac* occurs after the roots *dṛ*, *sah*, and *kaṣ* when preceded by *puri*, *sarva*, and *kūla*, respectively. After the root *dṛ* (to split), *khac* is applied when preceded by *puri*: *puramdaraḥ* (the destroyer of cities). When preceded by *sarva*, it forms *sarvasahaḥ* (all-enduring); *sarvasahā bhūmiḥ* (the all-bearing earth). When preceded by *bhaga*, it is applied to *dṛ*: *bhagandaraḥ* (a fistula disease). After the root *kaṣ* (to rub/scratch), *khac* is applied when preceded by *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*. When preceded by *kara*, *khac* is applied: *sarvaṅkaṣaḥ khalaḥ* (a villain who scrapes everything away). *kūlaṅkaṣā nadī* (a river that erodes its banks). *abhraṅkaṣo giriḥ* (a mountain scraping the clouds). *karīṣaṅkaṣā vātyā* (a whirlwind that scatters dried cow-dung).

After the words *megha*, *ṛti*, and *bhaya*, the suffix *khac* occurs after the root *kṛ*. Thus, there shall be *khac* after *kṛ* in these cases: *meghara* (cloud-causing), *ṛtikara* (causing distress), and *bhayaṅkara* (causing fear).
Also [the suffix *khac* occurs] after the word *kṣema* when combined with *priya* and *madra*.

In these cases, the suffix *khac* shall be applied after the root *kṛ*, and *aṇ* as well. Thus: *kṣemakaraḥ* or *kṣemakārī*; *priyaṅkaraḥ* or *priyakāraḥ*; *madraṅkaraḥ* or *madrakāraḥ*. How is it that [the form] *kṣemarī* occurs? This must be considered. [The rule: After the root *bhū* following the prefix *āśita*, when expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the state (*bhāva*). When the word *āśita*—which is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) ending derived from the root *aś* with the prefix *ā*—is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *khac* shall be applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). [Example for the instrument: "That by which one becomes satiated while being hungry" is *āśitambhava odanaḥ* (rice that satisfies the hungry). [Example for the state: "In those [places] where there is satisfaction through fruits. [The rule: After the roots *bhṛ*, *vaj*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam*, when a Name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed.

The suffix *khac* occurs after these eight roots when used with an object (*karman*) or a word ending in the locative case (*sup*), provided that the resulting form is a proper name (*nāmni*). *viśvambharaḥ* (the sustainer of the universe) = Viṣṇu; *rathantaram* (that which is within the chariot) = a *sāman*; *paritvarā* (one who chooses for herself) = a maiden; *śatruñjayaḥ* (conqueror of enemies) = a king; *dhanañjayaḥ* (winner of wealth) = Arjuna; *vasundharā* (bearer of riches) = the earth; *sarvasahā* (enduring all) = the earth; *uṣṇatapaḥ* (heating intensely) = the sun; *balindamaḥ* (subduer of Bali) = Kṛṣṇa. And [the suffix *khac* occurs] after the root *gam*. After the root *gam*, *khac* shall occur with a word ending in the locative case, whether it is a proper name or not. *Bhaṭṭi* says: "I tell you this which goes to the heart" (*hṛdayaṅgamam etat tvāṃ bravīmi*). *mātāpitṛpūrvaṅgamaḥ* (one who goes before his mother and father); *plavaṅgamaḥ* (monkey); *sutaṅgamaḥ* (name of a sage); *bhujaṅgamaḥ* (snake).

The suffix *viha* is used for the sense of "in the sky" (*vihāyasī*). Thus, *vihaṅgamaḥ* means "a bird. Words such as *vihaga* and *vihaṅga*, however, are established as correct by virtue of their inclusion in the *Trikāṇḍa* lexicon. Regarding the rule "after *sura-* [and the following], the suffix *ḍa* is applied before *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhvan*, *dūra*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta*": the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *gam* when these words follow. Thus: *antagaḥ* ("reaching the end"), *atyantagaḥ* ("going beyond"), *adhvagaḥ* ("a traveler").

It is also seen in other cases: when *su* is used as an upapada, the suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *gam*. Thus: *sarvatragaḥ* (going everywhere), *svāgāragaḥ* (going to one's own house). From *khe gacchati* (he goes in the sky) comes *khagaḥ* (bird); from *plavane gacchati* (he goes by leaping) comes *plavagaḥ* (monkey). There is also elision (*lopa*) of the vowel in *uras* [when combined with *gam*]: from *urasā gacchati* (he goes on his chest) comes *uragaḥ* (serpent). When *su* or *dur* are used as locative (*adhikaraṇa*) upapadas, [the suffix *ḍa* is applied]: *sugaḥ* (easy to go), *durgaḥ* (difficult to go).

The suffix *ghan* is applied after the root *diś* when preceded by *ni*. Thus, *nirdeśaḥ* (an instruction) and *nirdeśaḥ* (a place). [The suffix *ghan* is also applied] after the root *gam* when preceded by *pad*. One who does not move with his feet is a *pattragaḥ* (a snake); this belongs to the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*.
The suffix *ghan* is applied after the root *han* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

In the sense of a benediction, *ghan* may be used after *han*. For example: *śatruhaḥ* (may he slay the enemy) and *dasyuhaḥ* (may he slay the robber). Why "in the sense of a benediction"? [Consider: *śatrughātaḥ* (the slaying of an enemy). In this context, regarding the forms *dāghāṭaḥ* and *cārvādhāṭaḥ*, where there is a collection of phonemes, they are simply elaborations of the *pṛṣodarādi* class under the rule for the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The suffix *ḍaḥ* occurs after the roots *apa* and *hṛ* when combined with the words *kleśa* and *tamas*. Thus, *leśāpahaḥ* (one who removes affliction) refers to a son; *tamopahaḥ* (one who removes darkness) refers to the sun, Kumāra, or Śauri.

The suffix *ṇini* shall be applied after the root *han* (to kill) in these two cases: *kumāraghātī* (one who kills a child) and *śīrṣaghātī* (one who strikes the head). The change of *śiras* to *śīrṣa* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The suffix *ṭak* is applied after the roots *jan* (to be born) and *han* (to kill) when followed by the words *jāyā* (wife) and *pati* (husband), provided they do not denote a physical mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, *jāyāghnī* refers to a mole (*tilakālaka*) on the body, and *patighnī* refers to a line on the hand. As it is said: "I consider the fortune of Bālin to be possessed of the marks of one who destroys her husband."
And [the suffix *khañ*] is used when the agent is not a human being.
In these cases, the suffix *iṣṭhak* occurs when the agent is not a human being: *śleṣmannaṃ madhu* ("honey that destroys phlegm"), *pittaghnaṃ kṣīram* ("milk that destroys bile").
The suffix *śakti* is used in the sense of "capable" with respect to an elephant and a door-panel.

The suffix *iṣṭhan* occurs after the word *anaya*. For example: *yudhi-hastin* ("one who kills elephants in battle") and *kapāṭana-caura* ("a thief who breaks through doors"). What about after *śakti*? [Answer: *hastighāta-viṣaprada* ("one who administers poison to elephant-killers").
The two words *pāṇigha* and *tāḍagha* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when referring to an artisan (*śilpin*).

And because of an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), [the suffix *khyun*] is applied after the root *kṛ* when combined with *rājagha*, *stīkṣṇa*, *āḍhya*, *subhaga*, *sthūla*, *palita*, *nagna*, *andha*, and *priya*, provided that these words have the sense of "becoming" (*cyartha*) and the suffix *ac* does not follow; furthermore, it is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

In the sense of making something "not rich" (*āḍhya*) and so forth, the suffix *khyun* occurs after the root *kṛ* when it has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). For example: *āḍhyaṅkaraṇo mantraḥ* (a mantra that makes one wealthy), *subhagakaraṇaṃ dānam* (a gift that makes one fortunate), *sthūlaṅkaraṇaṃ vṛtam* (an action that makes one stout). *Palitaṅkaraṇī jarā* (aging that makes one grey), *nagnaṅkaraṇaṃ dyūtam* (gambling that makes one naked), *andhaṅkaraṇo mūtranirodhaḥ* (suppression of urine that makes one blind). The condition "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*) is stated for the sake of subsequent rules; here, however, since *khyun* is excluded, *lyuṭ* should apply: *āḍhīkaraṇo rasavidhiḥ* (a preparation of juice that makes one rich), *sthūlīkaraṇam auṣadham* (medicine that makes one stout). This is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The prohibition of *sthūni* is purposeless, because there is no difference between *lyuṭ* and *khyun*."

The suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukan* are added after the root *bhū* when used in the active sense (*kartari*). After roots such as *āḍhya*, the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukan* may optionally be added in the active sense. For example: "one who becomes wealthy" (*āḍhyo bhavati*) is expressed as *āḍhyambhaviṣṇuḥ* or *āḍhyambhāvukaḥ*—as in "the prince is becoming illustrious through fame. Similarly, *priyambhaviṣṇuḥ* or *priyambhāvukaḥ*. This applies only when the suffix *ac* follows (i.e., not in the future tense). Thus, *āḍhyobhavitā* (he will become wealthy). Hereafter, the rule applies even after words ending in *sakambha* when a nominal suffix (*sup*) follows; it does not apply only to the object (*karman*). The suffix *kvin* is added to the root *spṛś* when it is not followed by the word *udaka*.

The suffix *kvin* occurs after the root *spṛś* when followed by a word ending in the locative case (*sup*). Examples: *vyomasmṛk* (one who touches the sky), *marmaspṛk* (one who touches the vital spots). [Also] *mantrasmṛk* (one who touches with a mantra), *akhasmṛk*, *tasmṛk*, *amnismṛk*, *hādasmṛk*. By the rule *kinpratyayasya kuḥ*, the final consonant of a suffix ending in *kin* is replaced by *k*. [Question: What about when it does not mean "water" (*anudaka*)? [Example: *udakaspargaḥ* (one who touches water) is a Brahmin.

The suffix *kvip* also occurs after the roots *ṛt* (to sacrifice), *añj* (to anoint), *sraj* (to string), *adi* (to eat), *uṣṇih* (to heat), *añcu* (to bend), *yuj* (to yoke), and *kruñc* (to walk crookedly).

Words such as *ṛtvij* and others are derived by adding the suffix *kin* and are treated as irregular (*nipātana*). 1. One who sacrifices at the proper time (*ṛtu*) is an *ṛtvij*. [The suffix *kin* is added, and there is also the substitution of *dhṛṣad* for *ṛtu*]. 2. *Dadhaka* means "one who has been asked. 3. After the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*, the suffix *kin* is added when it denotes the object (*karman*). - That which they create (*srjanti*) is a *srak* (garland). - That which they point out (*diśanti*) is a *dik* (direction). 4. After the root *uṇ*, the suffix *kin* is added, with the elision of *ha* and *ta*, and the substitution of *ṣ* for *t*. Thus, *uṇik*. 5. After the root *pañc*, the suffix *kvin* is added when *sup* (a nominal suffix) follows. - *Prāṅ*, *prāñcau*. - *Nyaṅ*, *nyañcau*. - *Adhyaṅ*. - *Sadhrāṅ*. - *Devadāṅ*. - Words such as *prāk* and *pratyak* end in the suffix *astāti*. 6. After the root *yuj* alone, the suffix *kvin* is added. - *Yuṅ*, *yuñjau*. 7. Also after the root *kruñc*. - *Kruṅ*, *kruñcau*. - Because it has a *ja*-stop as its penultimate letter (*jopadha*), there is no elision [of the nasal].

After the words *tyad* and others, the suffix *kañ* is applied to the root *dṛś* when it does not mean "seeing" (perception). When *tyad* and others are used as upapadas, the suffix *kañ* is applied to *dṛś*; by the force of the word *ca*, the suffix *ki* is also applied. The word *tyad* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [Examples: He is seen like that: *tādṛśaḥ*, *tādṛk*, *tādṛśī*. He is seen like this: *yādṛśaḥ*, *yādṛk*, *yādṛśī*. What kind? *kīdṛśaḥ*. Like you: *tvādṛk*, *tvādṛśaḥ*. Like your honor: *bhavādṛk*, *bhāvādṛśaḥ*. Why "when it does not mean seeing"? [Example: He sees him = *taddarśaḥ*.

It should be stated that [the suffix *ka*] is applied after the words *samāna* and *anya*. One who sees himself as equal (*samāna*) is called *sadṛśaḥ*, *sadṛśī*, or *saṭṭak*. One who sees himself as different (*anya*) is called *anyādṛśaḥ*, *anyādṛk*, or *anyāśī*. However, the form *sadṛkṣaḥ* is Vedic (*cchāndasa*). After the roots *sad*, *sū*, *hiṣ*, *ṣṭhā*, *han*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *jin*, and *rāj*, the suffix *kvip* is applied even when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present.

The suffix *vip* occurs after verbal roots beginning with *sad-* when followed by a *sup*-ending beginning with *pra-*, as well as in other cases. Examples: *girisat* (dwelling on a mountain), *prasat* (procreating), *prasūḥ* (mother). [As in: "To strike the enemy again. *prahita* (sent forth), *mitrahita* (beneficial to a friend), *mitradhruk* (betraying a friend), *godhuk* (milking a cow), *aśvayuk* (yoking a horse), *śabdavit* (knowing words), *pravīt* (well-known), *kāṣṭhabhit* (splitting wood), *śatrucchit* (cutting enemies), *śatrujit* (conquering enemies), *praṇīḥ* (leader), *senānīḥ* (army leader), *sanmārganīḥ* (leading the right path). [As in: "The evening twilight is the guest of the lunar day. *rājan* becomes *samrāṭ* (emperor), *khārāṭ* (sovereign), *kururāṭ* (king of the Kurus). [As in: "The sun fell upon the row of mountains. The suffix *khi* occurs after the root *bhaj*.
After the roots *sup* and *prā*, as well as after *bhaj*, the suffix *vi* shall occur. Examples: *aibhāk*, *prabhāk*. Here follows the *Chandaḥpañcasūtrī*: [the suffix] *viṭ*.
After the root *ad*, when not meaning food (*anna*), the suffix *viṭ* shall occur.

Examples: *śasyāt*, *matsyāt*. [As in: "He threw the arrow at the life-devourer. Why "not meaning food"? Example: *anādaḥ*. How is *kaṇādaḥ* [formed]? By means of the rule for optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*).
And with *kravya*:

when the word *kravya* is used as an upapada, the suffix *viṭ* is applied after the root *ad* (to eat). Thus, one who eats raw flesh is called *kravyād*. Although the formation would have been established by the rule *ado 'nane* alone, the explicit mention of *kravya* in the sūtra is for the purpose of preventing the application of other suffixes according to the principle of *vāsarūpa*. After the root *duh* (to milk), the suffix *kvan* is applied, and the letter *gh* is substituted for the final consonant.

After the root *duh*, the suffix *kap* occurs, and there is the substitution of *gha* for the final letter [of the root]. Thus: *kāmadudhaḥ* (the wish-granting tree). Here, the four sūtras concerning the Vedic language [are as follows]: *āto maninkvanipvanipaśca*: After verbal roots ending in long *ā*, the suffixes *manin*, *kvanip*, and *vanip* occur. Thus: *śubha-yāḥ* (one who goes beautifully) and *kolāla-pāḥ* (one who drinks the dregs). *Manin*: *sūtrāmā* (the protector of the thread/world) and *aśvatthāmā* (the son of Aśvatthāman). [The latter is formed] by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. *sudāmā* (one who gives well).

They are also seen after other [roots]: *suśarmā*, *devaśarmā*. The suffix *kvanip* [is applied]. According to some, it is also used in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) as in *dhauvā* and *povā*. Thus, there is the Cāndra sūtra: "The suffixes *vivic*, *manin*, *kanin*, and *vanip*. Others say no. When *vanip* is applied, then [the forms are] *dhāvā*, *pāvā*, and *avāvā*.
There is also the suffix *vip*.

The suffix *kvi* shall be applied to a verbal root according to its specific rule. Examples: *ukhāsat*, *parṇadhvat*, *prayuk*, *jeścakradhaka*. After the root *sthā*, the suffix *ka* is also applied.

After the root *sthā* (tiṣṭhati), when followed by a nominal stem (*sup*), the suffix *ka* shall be applied, as well as *kvi*. Examples: *śaṃsthaḥ*, *śaṃsthāḥ*. This statement is made in order to override the suffix *ac* prescribed after the root *śam*.

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*). After a verbal root (*dhātu*), *ṇini* shall occur when a case-suffix follows. Examples: *uṣṇabhojī* (one who habitually eats hot food), *śīghrabhojī* (one who eats quickly), *mṛdubhāṣī* (one who speaks softly), *vṛhasevī* (one who serves extensively), *nityajāgarī* (one who always stays awake). [The form] *āvī* is derived from the sense "he does not cause himself to hear" (*ātmānaṃ na śrāvayati*), using a suffix such as *kvip*. Why "not when denoting a genus" (*ajātau*)? [Counter-example: *netā narāṇām* (a leader of men). And [the suffix *ṇini* occurs] when denoting one who performs an action well (*sādhukārin*). When the agent performs an action well, *ṇini* shall occur after a verbal root, even in the absence of a habitual disposition. Examples: *sādhukārī* (one who acts well), *sādhudāyī* (one who gives well), *turaṅgagāmī* (one who goes swiftly like a horse), *turayāyī* (one who moves swiftly).

Regarding *brahman* with the sense of "speaking": the suffix *ṇini* should be applied. Thus, *brahmavādī* ("one who speaks of Brahman"). However, *brahmavāda* does not occur, because it is not so designated [by the grammatical tradition].
Regarding *karta* when used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*):
here the suffix *ṇini* should be applied to the verbal root. Thus, *haṃsagāmī* ("one who walks like a swan") and *siṃhagāmī* ("one who walks like a lion").

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a word denoting a religious vow (*vrata*). For example: *sthaṇḍilagāyaḥ* ("one who practices the vow of sleeping on the bare ground"). The suffix *ṇini* occurs diversely (*bahulam*) after a word denoting repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*). When repetition is intended, *ṇini* is used; for example: *madhupāyinaḥ* ("those who drink honey repeatedly") refers to bees; *kaṣāyapāyiṇaḥ* ("those who repeatedly drink astringent decoctions").

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the root *man* when used with the object *manaḥ*. For example: *darśanīyamānī bhāryāyāḥ* ("one who considers his wife to be beautiful") and *ripumānī bhrātuḥ* ("one who considers his brother to be an enemy").
When used in the sense of self-conceit (*ātmamāna*), the suffix *khaś* also occurs.

The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *man* when it conveys the sense of "regarding oneself as"; the suffix *ṇini* is also applied. One who regards himself as a hero is called *śūramanyaḥ*, *śūramānī*, *sādhummanyaḥ*, or *sādhumānī*.
[The rule] "in the past" (*bhūte*) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) extending forward until the section on the present tense (*vartamāna*).
*Yajaḥ* [is used] in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *yaj* when it has an instrumental word as its upapada. Examples: *haviryājī*, *agniṣṭomayājī*, *rājasūyayājī*. [The suffix *ṇini* is also applied] after the root *han* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the root *han* when preceded by an object (*karma*) or an upapada. Examples: *piṭavyaghātī* (one who kills his uncle), *anyāsaktaghātī* (one who kills one attached to another). This designation applies when there is censure (*nindā*). In other cases, as in *cauraṃ hatavān* (he killed a thief), it does not apply. In the case of *brahma*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra*, the suffix *kvip* is used. After these words, *kvip* is applied to the root *han*. Regarding the rule *anyeṣvapi dṛśyate* ("it is seen after others as well"), the *Mahābhāṣya* states that the mention of *kvip* for the root *han* even when these specific words are present serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning it applies only to *brahman* and so forth. Due to this restriction, it also applies to the past tense (*bhūte*). When there is a desire to express time in general, examples include: *himahā* (destroyer of snow), *vīrahā* (slayer of a hero), *tamohā* (dispeller of darkness), and *tamopahā* (remover of darkness).
"Bahulam chandasi": this is one metrical rule. "Kṛñaḥ" [is used] in the sense of performing good deeds, evil deeds, mantras, or meritorious acts.

In these cases, the suffix *kvip* shall be applied after the root *kañ*. Thus: *sukṛt*, *karmakṛt*, *pāpakṛt*, *puṇyavān*, *mantrakṛt*. After the root *suñ* (to press), when preceded by *soma*, the suffix *kvip* shall be applied: *somasut*.
After the root *ci* (to pile), when *agni* is the object, the suffix *kvip* shall be applied to form the name of a fire-pile: *agnicit*. This applies when the term refers to a fire-altar (*agni*).

The suffix *kvip* is applied after a verbal root preceded by an object (*karman*) when it denotes the name of a fire-altar (*agni-ākhyā*). For example: *śyena iva cīyate citā ceṣyate vā* = "built like a hawk" or "is intended to be built like a hawk" = *śyenacit*; *rathacakracit*. The inclusion of the term "name" (*ākhyā-grahaṇam*) is for the purpose of establishing conventional usage (*rūḍhi-prasiddhy-artham*).

The suffix *ini* is applied after a verbal root preceded by an object when the sense is "selling. The repetition of the word "object" (*karma-grahaṇam*) is for the purpose of indicating contempt (*kutsā-artham*). Examples: *tailavikrayī*, *māṃsavikrayī* (a Brahmin who sells oil or meat).
The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the root *dṛś* (to see).

The suffix *kvanip* occurs after *dṛś* when it denotes the object of the action. Examples: *meradṛkhā* (one who has seen Meru), *paralokaṭṭakhā* (one who has seen the next world), *bahudṛśkhā* (one who has seen much), *pārakhā* (one who has seen the other side).
After the root *yudh* (to fight), the suffix *kvanip* occurs when *rājan* is the object.

And after *saha*: the suffix *kan* shall be applied after the roots *yudh* and *kṛ* when followed by *saha*. One who has fought with a king is called *rājayudhvā*. [As in: "Your father was not one who fought with a king. [The form] *sahayudhvānam* [is used] with another [object]. [The form] *sahakatvā*. After a locative case ending, the suffix *ḍa* is applied.

The suffix *ī* occurs after the word *jana-* when it follows a locative case-ending (*saptamī*) as an *upapada*. For example: *upasarajaḥ* ("born from dust").
