[As stated in the verse: "Those which were produced by the twice-born. [Another example: *mandurajaḥ* ("born in a stable"). When following a word in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the suffix *ī* occurs after *jana-* provided it does not refer to a genus (*ajāti*). For example: *buddhijaḥ* ("born of the intellect") and *kauśalyājaḥ rāmaḥ* ("Rāma, born of Kauśalyā"). Why "not a genus"? [Counter-example: *avāj jātaḥ* ("born from a sheep").
And when there is a prefix, if it is a name, the suffix *ḍaṅ* is applied after the root *jan* (to be born) provided it occurs at the beginning [of a compound]. *Prajā* means all people.
After the prefix *anu*, it is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The suffix *ī* occurs after the word *anuja* when it follows a word denoting an object of action (*karma*). Examples: *pumanujaḥ*, *rāmānujaḥ*, *ātmānujaḥ*. It is also seen after other words.

The suffix *ī* shall be applied after the root *jan* (*to be born*) when other [words] are used as upapadas (governing words). Examples: *ajaḥ* ("unborn"), *dvijaḥ* ("twice-born"). With *kena jātaḥ* ("by whom born? we have *kiñjaḥ*. *Sahajaḥ* ("co-born"). And in the sense of "birth": *brāhmaṇajo dharmaḥ* ("the duty born of Brahminhood"). Also after *pra-* and so forth, provided it is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*): *abhijāḥ keśāḥ* ("hair growing upwards"), *adhijaḥ*. "Born first" is *prathamajaḥ*. Also in the sense of "not the primary action" (*anāvakarmaṇi*): *anujaḥ* ("younger brother"). Because of the word *api* ("also"), the suffix *ḍa* occurs after other roots as well: *ākhā* ("hole"), *parikhā* ("moat"). He who seizes excellent things (*varān ādatte*) is *varāhaḥ* ("boar"). *Svarāpahaḥ* ("one who takes away sound"), *kaṭāhaḥ* ("frying pan"), *dūrāpahaḥ* ("one who drives away from afar"), *prahaḥ* ("one who strikes"), *kahaḥ*. *Giriśaḥ* ("dweller on the mountain"). Thus, what was stated regarding the rule for *ī* after *gam*—namely, "also after others"—is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point.

The *niṣṭhā* suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* occur after a verbal root when it has reached its completion (*niṣṭhā*). For example: *tataḥ* (he stretched) and *kṛtavān* (he did). It should be stated that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of the inception of an action (*ādikarman*). Example: *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ caitraḥ* (Caitra has begun making a mat).
After the root *suyaj*, the suffix *ṅanip* occurs.

The suffix *in* shall be applied after the roots *su* (to press) and *yaj* (to sacrifice). [Examples: *sutvā*, *sutvānau*; *yajvā*, *yajvānau*. [As in the verse: "The oblation is prepared by the *yajvans*.
[Root *jṛ*: *jarat*, *sthāt*, *jaran*, *jarantau*, *jarantaḥ*.
In the Vedic language, the *liṭ* [perfect] tense occurs.
For the *liṭ*, there is optionally the substitution of *jakṣ* [for *ad*].
And [the suffixes] *vasu* and [others] also occur.

The three rules beginning with *liṭaḥ kasuśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.107) are now governed. The term *śeṣaḥ* (the remainder) is Vedic. However, the author of the Nyāsa, because of the *kit* designation of *kānac* and *kasu*, desires their usage even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Examples: from *ciñ*, *cikyānaḥ*; from *pṛ*, *papurāṇaḥ*; from *sthā*, *tasthivān*—as in "by you who have taken your stand on the path" (*padamātasthuṣā tvayā*); from *pā*, *papivān*; from *tṛ*, *titīrvān*. In the common language, after the roots *sad*, *vas*, and *śru*, the suffix *kasu* optionally occurs in place of the *liṭ* (perfect). Thus, after these roots, *kasu* may optionally be used in the common language. Examples: *upasedivān* (with the instrumental *upaseduṣā*); *aṣivān*. As in "those who have approached the wives of others" (*jaṣuṣāṃ paradāraiśca*); *śuśruvān*. In the alternative case, the *luṅ* (aorist) and *laṅ* (imperfect) are to be understood.

*upeyivān*, *anāśvān*, and *anūcāna*: these are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the suffix *liṭ*. From the root *iṇ* comes [the form] with the suffix *kvasu* and the augment *iṭ*: *upeyivān*. From *aś* comes *anāśvān*. [The Vedic rule states: "From *ji* and *dhū*, [the suffix *kvasu* occurs] after *anāśuṣ-*. From *anu-vac* in the sense of the agent, [comes] *kānac*: "one who has studied the scriptures is called *anūcāna*. In the grammatical rule (*sūtra*), gender and number are not restrictive. [As in the verse: "Even for those who have enjoyed heaven... By the recurrence of the word *vā* ("or"), the *luṅ* (aorist) and *laṅ* (imperfect) are to be understood as alternatives. [Example of] *luṅ*: *...upeyivān...* *...anāśvān...* *...anūcānaḥ...* *...upayuṣām api divam...* *...luṅ...*
The *luṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) to express a past event that has actually occurred. For example: *akārṣīt* (he did), *aneṣīt* (he led).
The *laṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root to express a past time other than the recent past (*anadyatana*). For example: *akarot* (he did), *apacat* (he cooked).
And the *laṅ* suffix should be prescribed for an action that is not witnessed by the speaker, yet is known to the world and within the range of the speaker's vision.

The elaboration beginning with "Aruṇa [went] to Sāketa" and so forth does not constitute a new definition [of the *parokṣa* past]. This is because the rule is established even for cases that are beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*) when there is merely the intention to express the non-recent (*anadyatana*) past. If it is argued: "Even in the case of what is not within the range of observation, would there not be the usage 'Viṣṇu indeed slew Kaṃsa'?"—Certainly! Let it be so. What loss is there for you? For instance, even regarding what is real (*vāstavika*), there are various verbal usages based on differences in intention (*vivakṣā-bheda*) concerning the non-recent, past, and beyond-perception: "The king was," "They threw down Aṅgada," "He spoke to Sugrīva having come to his true state," and so forth. [Furthermore,] the *luṭ* (future) occurs after a statement of recognition (*abhijñāvacana*). [And finally: "Not when *yadi* [is used]."

When a word expressing remembrance (*smṛti*) is used as an upapada, the present tense (*laṭ*) shall be employed for the past time not belonging to the current day. Examples: *smarasi puṇḍravardhanaṃ vatsyāvaḥ* ("Do you remember that we two lived in Puṇḍravardhana?"); *sambhaviṣyāva ekasyām abhijānāsi mātari* ("Do you recognize us two as having been born of the same mother?"). However, when joined with the word *yat*, this present tense (*laṭ*) does not apply; rather, only the imperfect (*laṅ*) is used. Examples: *abhijānāsi yad yavāgvāṃ vayam atiṣṭhāma* ("Do you remember that we stood in the barley-gruel?"); *avasāma nagendreṣu yat* ("That we dwelt among the lords of mountains"). *Vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe*: When there is an expectation (*sākāṅkṣa*), this present tense (*laṭ*) may optionally be used before the speaker of that expectation. Example: *tat smarasi yatrānaikasatraṃ gamiṣyāmas tatra vrīhibhir odanaṃ bhokṣyāmahe* ("Do you remember that place where we shall go for the many-day sacrifice, where we shall eat rice with grain?"). In the alternative case, one uses the aorist: *agacchāma* or *abhujāmahe*. For the remote past, the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used.

The *liṭ* (perfect) suffix shall be used for an action that occurred in the past, not in the current day, and which was not witnessed by the speaker. Examples: *jagāma* (he went), *cakāra* (he did), *papāca* (he cooked).
It is also used for absolute negation (*atyantāpahnava*). In such cases, the *liṭ* is used for the mere past tense: "I saw you in the Kapittha grove; I did not go to the Kapittha grove.
After the particles *ha* and *śaśvat*, the *laṅ* (imperfect) suffix is also used.

In these two cases, the *laṭ* (present) and *liṭ* (perfect) may optionally be used. *Itihākarot* (Thus he did); *śaśvadakarot* (He did so repeatedly). In the alternative: *itihacakāra*. Also, in the case of a question regarding a time not present (*asanakāle*), the *laṭ* and *liṭ* may be used in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative). For example: *pṛcchāmi tvāmagacchajjagāma vā caitraḥ* (I ask you: did Caitra go?). Why "not present"? [Example: *jahāra sītāṃ paulastyaḥ* (The descendant of Pulastya carried off Sītā). A period within five years is considered "not present."
*Laṭ* [is used] with *sma*.
And also in the non-witnessed (*aparokṣa*).

When joined with *sma*, the suffix *laṭ* shall occur after the root *ah* (to say) in the sense of the past not of today, whether it be witnessed (*parokṣa*) or non-witnessed (*aparokṣa*). Example: *adhīte sma* (he studied); *viharati sma* (he wandered).

The particle *nanu* is used in response to a question; [the suffix *laṭ*] is optionally [used after a root] following *na* and *nu*. After a root preceded by *na* or *nu*, when not joined with another question, the present tense (*laṭ*) shall be used to express mere past action, provided it is an answer to a question. "Did you make the mat, Devadatta? "Indeed, I am making it, sir. [The suffix *laṭ* is] optional when in conjunction with *na* or *nu*: "I am not making it," or "I did not make it. [The suffix *laṭ* is also used] after *nu* when expressing something that was not done: "Am I making it? or "Was it not made?"

*Purā luṅ, cāsme*: When *purā* is used [with a word expressing] the past not of today (*bhūtānadyatane*), there shall optionally be either *luṅ* or *laṭ* after the verbal root. Examples: *avātsuriha purā vṛkṣāḥ* (In the past, trees used to dwell here); *vasantīha purā mṛgāḥ* (In the past, deer used to dwell here). [Also]: *purādhirūḍhaḥ śayanaṃ mahādhanaṃ vibodhyase yaḥ stutigītimaṅgalaiḥ* (Having ascended to a costly couch in the past, you are awakened by hymns, songs, and auspicious rites). The optionality (*vibhāṣā*) applies only here. Examples: *avasan purā* (They dwelt in the past); *aṣuḥ purā* (They went in the past). Why say *asme*? [To exclude cases where it is not "not of today"]: *purā vasanti sma* (In the past, they used to dwell). It has been stated regarding the past; for the present, there is *laṭ*.

The present time (*vartamānakāla*) is the state of having begun but not yet completed. In that case, the suffix *laṭ* shall be applied after a verbal root. Examples: *bhavati*, *atti*, *asti*, *juhoti*, *tanute*, *ruṇaddhi*, *corayati*, *cikīrṣati*. Here too, there is indeed the state of having begun but not yet completed: "the mountains stand," "the rivers flow," "Upendra conquers. The section governing the present tense extends prior to the future tense.
After *laṭ*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are applied when they do not share the same coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with the first case (the nominative).

These two [suffixes] shall occur in place of *laṭ*. The term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) continues from the previous rule (Pāṇini 3.2.124), and according to the established position of the *Bhāṣya*, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus: *pacan vipraḥ* or *pacati vipraḥ*; *san asti*; *adhīyānaḥ* or *adhīte*. Because it is a restricted option, it is sometimes obligatory: *kurvataḥ*, *pācataḥ* (with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the base itself); *kurvadbhaktiḥ*, *pacamānabhaktiḥ*—it is called "devotion" (*bhakti*) because it is being partaken of; *pacamānataraḥ*; *gacchadrūpaḥ*, *kurvadrūpaḥ*.

The *pacatkalpa* (one who cooks somewhat). *Lasaddiśacchedaḥ* (the cutting of the directions while shimmering). *Ghūrṇamānapradīpaḥ* (a flickering lamp)—in some cases, not so. *Pacatitarām* (he cooks exceedingly). *Jalpatirūpam* (the form of one who prattles). Why [is it said] "not having the same coreferentiality as a non-nominative" (*apathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*)? [Because] here they would always occur: *atra nityaṃ tau syātām*. *Pacantaṃ pacamānaṃ paśya* (see him cooking). *Pacatā pacamānena kṛtam* (done by the one cooking).
Also in the vocative: here they would always occur: *he kurvan*, *he kurvāṇa*.

The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are used after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when it denotes either a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*) of an action (*kriyā*). Regarding the action: *tiṣṭhan mūtrayati gauḥ* (The cow urinates while standing). *śayāno bhuṅkte* (He eats while lying down). Regarding the cause: *arjayan āste* (He sits while earning money). *mevyamāno vilasati* (He sports while being praised). *yācamānaḥ prasīdati* (He is pleased while begging). Why "of an action"? [Consider: *yaḥ kampate so 'svasthaḥ* (He who trembles is unwell). Regarding the prohibition (*māṅ*) in the sense of reviling (*ākrośe*): The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are used after a verbal root following the prohibitive particle *māṅ*. *mā jīvan* (May he not live!). *mā pacamānaḥ* (May he not cook!). "May he not live, even though he lives consumed by the pain of others' contempt! (*mā jīvan yaḥ parāvajñāduḥkhadagdho 'pi jīvati*)

The two suffixes *sat* and *śānac* are called *sat*. The grammatical operation [prescribed] for *sat* applies to the *luṭ* [suffix], and so forth. After the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj*, the suffix *śānan* occurs.
The term *laṭ* is discontinued. After these two [roots], the suffix *śānac* shall occur. Examples: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* (purifying the Soma), *yajamānaḥ* (the sacrificer).
Furthermore, the suffix *cānaś* occurs in the senses of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), age (*vayaḥ*), and ability (*śakti*).

In these cases where the action is to be understood (*gamye*), the suffix *ānaś* shall occur after a verbal root. Examples: *vanaṃ paryaṭamānaḥ* (wandering through the forest); *ātmānaṃ varṇayamānaḥ* (describing himself); *bhūṣayamāṇaḥ* (adorning himself); *jīvamānaḥ* (living); *lasamānaḥ* (shining); *sphuramāṇaḥ* (throbbing). “*dīvyamānaṃ śitān vāṇān*” (discharging sharpened arrows); *jvalamānaḥ* (blazing); *vadhūṃ maṇḍayamānaḥ* (adorned with a bride). In the sense of age (*vayasi*): *striyaṃ gacchamānaḥ* (approaching a woman [in youth]); *śikhaṇḍaṃ vahamānaḥ* (bearing a crest [in youth]). In the sense of capability (*śaktau*): *hastinaṃ nighnānaḥ* (capable of killing an elephant). 130. After the roots *dhṛ* and *dhyai*, the suffix *śatṛ* occurs when there is difficulty (*kṛcchriṇi*).

The suffix *śatṛ* occurs after the roots *adhi-i* and *dhṛ* when used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Examples: *adhīyan sakalaṃ śāstram* ("studying the entire scripture") and *dhārayan maskarivratam* ("observing the vow of a mendicant"). However, in some cases where the suffix *śnu* occurs in the sense of the agent, it is used with difficulty: *kaṣṭena adhīte*.

The suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed after the root *dviṣ* in the sense of "enemy" (*amitra*), and optionally after the root *duṣ* in the sense of "hating. Examples: *dviṣan* and *dviṣatī* (the latter being feminine). The suffix *śatṛ* is also used after the root *yaj* when it is connected with a sacrifice (*yajñasaṃyoga*). Examples: *yajamānaḥ*.

In this context, *śaṭ* shall be the suffix for *su* when it means "pressing. Thus, *sunvantaḥ* refers specifically to the sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*). The suffix *śaṭ* is used after the root *arh* in the sense of praise;
that is, *śaṭ* occurs after *arh* when expressing eulogy. For example: *arhan pūjāṃ muniḥ* ("the sage deserving honor"). It is not used here: *vadham arhati* ("he deserves death").
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*), "having that as one's duty" (*taddharma*), or "one who performs that well" (*tatsādhukārī*).
Alternatively, a suffix may be applied in the sense of "having that as one's habit" and so forth, provided it denotes the agent;
such as the suffix *tṛn*.

The suffix *tṛn* shall be applied after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when denoting habitual action (*śīla*). Examples: *virudaṃ vaditā* (one who habitually speaks praises), *āhāraṃ kartā* (one who habitually performs eating), *āsanaṃ dātā* (one who habitually gives a seat), *vadhūṃ muṇḍayitāraḥ* (those who habitually shave the bride). When denoting excellence (*sādhu*), the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after twelve roots: *hṛ*, *gam*, *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *pra-jan*, *ut-pad*, *ut-pat*, *ut-pad*, *un-mad*, *ruc*, *apa-nat*, *tud*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, and *car*. Examples: *manaḥ hartā* (one who is excellent at taking the mind), *kheṭaṃ gantā* (one who is excellent at going to a village), *hotṛpotṛ-ādayaḥ* (the Hotṛ, Potṛ, and others—these are formed by *tṛn* in the sense of office, etc.). Examples with *iṣṇuc*: *kanyām alaṃkariṣṇuḥ* (one who is skilled in adorning a maiden), *śatrūn nirākariṣṇuḥ* (one who is skilled in repelling enemies), and so on up to *bhaviṣṇuḥ* (one who is skilled in becoming). Regarding the rule "and after *bhū*," because of the word "and" (*ca*), some say that *bhajiṣṇuḥ* (one who is skilled in serving) is also included.
ṇa is used in the Veda;
this is a Vedic usage;
and [the suffix ṇa is applied] after the root bhū.
The suffix *iṣṇuc* shall occur [after roots ending in long vowels]. *bhaviṣṇuḥ*. After the roots *mlai*, *ji*, and *sthā*, the suffix *kasnu* occurs.

After these [roots], the suffix *kmuc* shall occur: *glāsnuḥ*, *jiṣṇuḥ*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], *bhṛṣṇuḥ* is also included. For the root *sthā*, the substitution of *ī* for the vowel is not desired; thus, *sthāṇuḥ*.
The suffix *u* occurs after the roots *vas*, *grabh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*.

The suffix *kta* occurs after a root that has been strengthened (*jītaḥ*) in the sense of the present tense. Examples: *bhinnah* (split), *kṣviṇṇaḥ* (sweated).

[The suffix *kta* is used] after roots meaning "to think," "to understand," or "to worship. After roots meaning "desire," "knowledge," or "worship," these [suffixes] occur in the present tense. For example: *janānāṃ mataḥ* (respected by people). The meaning is "he is esteemed by kings. By the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*), the present tense (*laṭ*) also occurs. Regarding the statement that "there is no rule of non-identity of form in the case of *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and *khalartha* suffixes," the absence of the rule of non-identity of form applies here because of the association with *lyuṭ* as a neuter noun. As in: "O dear one, his sequence of prior and posterior was not understood by you. Likewise: *satāṃ viditaḥ* (known/understood by the virtuous) or *avagataḥ*.

In this system, the suppression of the past tense by the present tense is intended. Therefore, in cases such as "tvayā jñātaḥ" (known by you) or "mayā arcitaḥ" (worshipped by me), the *bhāga-vṛtti* (the rule regarding parts) is inapplicable. From the root meaning "to worship," we have *satām arcitaḥ* (worshipped by the virtuous), *surāṇām pūjitaḥ* (honored by the gods), and *satām pūjitaḥ* (honored by the virtuous). Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated, there is the establishment of forms such as *śīlitah*, *rakṣitah*, *kāntaḥ*, *vyāhṛtaḥ*, *dayitaḥ*, *snigdhaḥ*, *tuṣṭaḥ*, and *kṣāntaḥ*.

Oṃ. In the third chapter, the third quarter:
"The *uṇādi* suffixes are applied diversely."

When there is a desire to express the present tense, the *uṇ*-class suffixes and others are generally correct. Examples: *uṇ*—*kāruḥ* (artisan), *vāyuḥ* (wind); *enuḥ*—*kareṇuḥ* (elephant); *ālañ*—*pātālam* (netherworld); *alac*—*maṅgalam* (auspiciousness).
They are also seen used in the sense of the past.
The *uṇādi* suffixes are also valid when expressing an actual state of being (*bhūtārtha*). For example: *vṛttaṃ* means "path" (*vartma*), and *bhasitaṃ* means "ashes" (*bhasma*).
The present tense has been explained.
The section on the future suffix *kṛt*: in the sense of the future, there are *gamī* and others.

The six suffixes beginning with *gam-i* (Pāṇini 3.3.3–8) are correct when used in the sense of the future. Examples: *grāmaṃ gamī* (one who will go to the village), *agāmī* (one who will not go), *grāmagāmī* (one who goes to the village), *pratiyogī* (an opponent), *prasthāyī* (one who sets out), *pratibodhī* (one who awakens), *bhāvī* (one who will come to be).
The section concerning the future extends prior to the suffix *ghañ*.
[Next: The present tense (*laṭ*) is used after the particles *yāvat* and *purā*.

When used in conjunction with the particles *yāvat* and *purā*, the present tense (*laṭ*) shall be employed to denote the future. For example: *yāvad bhuṅkte* ("as long as he eats") and *na gacchāmi purā laṅkām* ("I will not go to Laṅkā [until now]"). Why mention "the two particles"? [Because the rule would otherwise apply to finite verbs]. Example: *yāvad bhokṣyase tāvad dāsyati* ("He will give as much as you will eat"). [In the case of the particles] *kadā* and *karhicit*, it is optional (*vibhāṣā*).
When used with *kadā* or *karhi* in reference to a future sense, the present tense (*laṭ*) may optionally be employed. [Examples: "When will there be joy for me? "Then will there be wealth for me?
In the alternative case, the aorist (*luṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) are used.
[The present tense is also used] after interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*) when expressing a desire (*lipsā*).

When used in conjunction with an interrogative pronoun (*kiṃvṛtta*) to express a desire (*lipsā*), the *laṅ* (imperfect) may optionally be employed. For example: *kaḥ te bhikṣāṃ dadāti?* ("Who gives you alms?"), *kas tvāṃ bhojayati?* ("Who feeds you?"). The inclusion of the term *vṛtta* is for the sake of [including] the suffixes *-tara* and *-tama*: *kataraḥ bhikṣāṃ dadāti?* ("Which one gives alms?"), *katamaḥ bhojayati?* ("Which one feeds [you]?"). In the alternative case, the *luṅ* (aorist) and *lṛṭ* (future) are also used. This also applies when there is the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained (*lipsyamānasiddhi*).

When the accomplishment of a desired object is understood to be occurring, the *laṅ* (imperfect) may optionally be used; for example: "He who gives curd-rice goes to heaven. In this alternative case, the *luṅ* (aorist) and *lṛṭ* (future) are also used.
And [the *laṅ* is also used] when there is an indication of the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*).

The *laṭ* (present tense suffix) may optionally be used after a verbal root whose meaning is characterized by an injunction (*praiṣa*) and so forth. For example: "If the teacher comes (*āgacchati*), will come (*āgamiṣyati*), or is to come (*āgantā*), then you should study the Veda. Furthermore, the *liṅ* (optative suffix) is also used when the time is more than a moment (*ūrdhvamauhūrttike*).

In the sense of "after a short while" (ūrdhvamauhūrtika), the suffixes *liṅ* and *laṭ* may optionally occur after a verbal root, because they indicate the meaning of the *loṭ* (imperative) mood. For example: *yadi guruḥ muhūrtasyopari āgacchet*, *āgacchet*, or *āgamiṣyati*.
[Furthermore,] the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when one action is for the sake of another action (*kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*).

The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* shall be applied after a verbal root when another action is the *upapada* (governing word) for the sake of that action. For example: *odanaṃ bhoktuṃ vrajati* ("He goes in order to eat rice") and *odanaṃ bhojako vrajati* ("He goes as one who eats rice"). Here, the action of "going" (*vrajati-kriyā*) has the purpose of eating (*bhojana*) as its *upapada*.
Furthermore, [the suffix *tumun* is applied] after roots expressing a state of being (*bhāva*).

And verbal roots ending in *ghañ* and similar suffixes, when they denote the meaning of the action itself (*bhāvārtha*), may optionally take the fourth case (*caturthī*) in the same sense as the suffix *tumun*; for example: *lābhāya sthitaḥ* ("he stands for the sake of gain") and *bhūtaye dhāvati* ("he runs for the sake of prosperity").
Furthermore, the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after a verbal root when *tumun*, *nañ*, or *artha* are used as subsequent members (*upapada*). Examples: *śatrulāvaḥ vrajati* (he goes for the purpose of killing the enemy), *godāyaḥ vrajati* (he goes for the purpose of milking the cow).
Furthermore, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied [after a root] when another suffix follows, and also in the remaining cases.
The suffix *lṛṭ* shall be used in the sense of "intention" (*tumun-arthe*). For example: "He goes [thinking], 'I will see the play'.
In other cases, it is used for the mere future tense—as in "he will do" (*kariṣyati*) or "he will read" (*paṭhiṣyati*). There is also an option for *lṛṭ* to take the suffix *saddhā*.

In place of *lṛṭ*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* may optionally occur. [Examples: *kariṣyati*, *kariṣyate*; *kariṣyan*, *kariṣyamāṇaḥ*. [The suffix] *luṭ* is used for the future not of today (*anadyatana*).

The *luṭ* suffix shall be used for future time that is not of today. For example: "He will do it tomorrow" (*śvaḥ karttā*), "He will eat the day after tomorrow" (*paraśvo bhoktā*). However, regarding the question, "When indeed will he go, who thus sets his feet down?"—even though this refers to the present day, because of the temporal distance, the status of "not being of today" (*anadyatana*) is superimposed by way of comparison, and thus the *luṭ* suffix is employed; such is the established position in the *Bhāṣya*.
It will be explained [later].
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the verbal roots *pad*, *ruj*, *viś*, and *spṛś*.

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after these roots. *Padyate gacchati* ("he goes") thus forms *pādaḥ* ("foot"). *Rogaḥ* ("disease"), *veśaḥ* ("entrance"). Regarding the root *spṛś*, when it denotes "affliction," [the suffix *ghañ* is applied]: *sparśaḥ*. But in other cases, by the addition of *ac* (under the rule *pacādyac*), we have *kambalasparśaḥ* ("the touch of a woolen blanket"); there is a difference in accent. [The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] to *sṛ* when meaning "firmness."

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *sṛ* when it denotes a stable agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: *sāraḥ* (essence), *candanasāraḥ* (the heartwood of sandalwood), *kāryasāraḥ* (the essence of the task). It should be stated that this applies in the sense of disease, fish, and strength. Example: *atīsāraḥ* (a type of diarrhea/disease), *visāraḥ* (a kind of fish), *sāraḥ* (strength).
[The suffix *ghañ* also occurs] in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after a verbal root in the sense of an action (*bhāva*). Examples: *pākaḥ* (cooking), *rogaḥ* (disease).
It also occurs in the sense of an agent other than the subject (*akartṛ-kāraka*) when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after a verbal root when it denotes an action and a non-agentive *kāraka*, provided the resulting word is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *prāsaḥ* (a dart), from *pra-as* ("to throw"); *prasevaḥ* (a sack); *āhāraḥ* (food), from *ā-hṛ* ("to bring"). The mention of "technical name" is used in a general sense; therefore, it may also apply here: *dāyaḥ* (inheritance) from *dattaḥ* (given), and *lābhaḥ* (gain) from *labdhaḥ* (obtained). Why "non-agentive"? Consider *meṣaḥ* (ram), derived from *miṣ* ("to blink") with the suffix *ac* (the *pacādi* group); there is a difference in accent between the two cases.

In this context, it need not be stated that *dāra* and *jāra* are formed with the suffix *kṛt*; for the traditional rule (*smṛti*) states that they are established in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in: "by them the wife is split apart" (*dīryante tair dārāḥ*) and "by him he is worn out" (*jīryate tena jāraḥ*).

Hereafter follows the prescription [of suffixes] in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and in senses other than the agent (*akartṛ-kāraka*). Among these, first, the suffix *ghañ*, which supersedes both *er-ac* and *ṛdor-ap*, is stated. For example: [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after all roots when expressing a measure (*parimāṇa*).

The suffix *ghañ* shall occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) alone when there is a designation of measure (*parimāṇa*). Examples: *ekaḥ taṇḍulaniścāyaḥ* (one handful of rice), *dvau śūrpaniṣpāvau* (two winnowings with a basket). How [do you explain] "the eighteen suffixes of the *tiṅ* [verbs]," "five calamities," or "not even one of your certainties"? [These will be explained] under the view that word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) occurs first. And [the rule applies] after the root *iṅ*.

The suffix *ghañ* shall apply after the root *iṅ*. Thus: *adhyāyaḥ*, *upādhyāyaḥ*. In the feminine gender, there is an option for the suffix *ṅīṣ*: *upādhyāyī* or *upādhyāyā*. It should be stated that the suffix *ghañ* applies to the root *śṛ* (to tear) when meaning wind, variegated color, or a covering. Thus: *śāraḥ* as wind; *śāraḥ* as variegated; *nīśāraḥ* as a cloak.
The root *ru* [takes the suffix *ap*] when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*).
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *ru* (to cry out) when preceded by the prefixes *upa*, *sam*, or *vi*. Examples: *uparāvaḥ*, *saṃrāvaḥ*, *virāvaḥ*.
[The suffix *ghañ* also occurs] after the roots *yud*, *rud*, and *du* when preceded by *sam*.
The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after these [roots] when preceded by *sam*: *saṃyāvaḥ*, *sandrāvaḥ*, *sandāvaḥ*.
In other cases than with *sam*: *yavaḥ*, *prayavaḥ*, *upayavaḥ*, *nidravaḥ*.
[The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] after the roots *śri*, *ni*, and *bhū* when no prefix (*anupasarga*) precedes them.

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after these [roots] when preceded by *pra* and others. *Śrāyaḥ*, *nāyaḥ* (from *nī*), and *bhāvaḥ*. How is *prabhāvaḥ* formed? It is through a compound (*samāsa*) formed subsequently.
[The suffix *ghañ* occurs] after *kṣu* and *śru* when preceded by *vi*.
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *kṣu* and *śru* when preceded by *vi*. Examples: *vikṣāvaḥ*, *viśrāvaḥ*.
[The suffix *ni* occurs after the root *yā*] when preceded by *ava* or *ud*.
The suffix *ghañ* shall also occur after the roots *ava*, *ud*, and *ni*. Examples: *avanāyaḥ*, *unnāyaḥ*.
How are *avanayaḥ* and *unnayaḥ* formed? By virtue of general usage, as in the cases of *rāva*, *prabhāva*, and *garbhasrāva*.
[The suffix *ghañ* occurs] after *pra* following the roots *dru*, *stu*, and *sru*.

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after these prefixes [pra, parā, apa, sam, anu, ava, nis, dus, dur, vi, ā, ni, adhi, api, ati, su, ud, abhi, prati, upa] when they precede the roots *dru*, *stṛ*, and *sru*. Examples: *pradrāvaḥ*, *prastāvaḥ*, *prasrāvaḥ*.
[Furthermore, *ghañ* is applied after *nis* and *abhi* when they precede the roots *pū* and *lū* respectively.]
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots √lū preceded by *nis* and *abhi*. Thus: *niṣpāvaḥ* (winnowing) and *abhilāvaḥ* (reaping).
After the root √grah preceded by *ud*, [the suffix *ghañ* occurs].

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the root *gṛ* (to swallow) when preceded by *ud* and *ni*. Thus: *udgāraḥ* (belching), *nigāraḥ* (swallowing). [The root] *kṝ* [is used] in the sense of grain.

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *kṛ* (kirati) when preceded by the prefix *ut* in the sense of grain. Examples: *utkāraḥ* (a heap of grain), *nikāraḥ* (a heap). Why "in the sense of grain"? [Consider] *puṣpanikaraḥ* (a cluster of flowers).
[The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *stu* (stauti) preceded by *sam* in the sense of a sacrifice.]
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *stu* when it means "sacrifice. For example: *saṃstāvaḥ* (a place for chanting) of the *Chandoga* singers.
Why "in the context of sacrifice"? [Answer: When qualities are intended as objects of praise, it is called *saṃstava*, not *saṃstāva*.
[The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] after *stu* preceded by *pra*, except in the context of sacrifice.
The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the root *pra-stṛ* (to spread) when used outside of a sacrificial context. Examples: *puṣpaprastāraḥ* (a spreading of flowers).

Why "outside of a sacrifice"? [Counter-examples: *barhiṣprastaraḥ* (a sacrificial grass-spreading), *vrīhiprastaraḥ* (a rice-spreading). [The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] after the root *prath* (to spread) when not preceded by the word *ava*.

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *stṛ* (to spread) in the sense of spreading (*prathana*). Spreading means extension (*vistīrṇatā*). Example: *vārivistāraḥ* (the expanse of water). Why "not meaning sound" (*aśabde*)? [Counter-example: *vāgvistaraḥ* (an elaborate speech). And [the suffix *ghañ* occurs] when it is the name of a meter (*chandonāmni*).

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the root *tan* when preceded by *vi-*, provided it forms the name of a meter (*vṛtta*). Thus, the name of the meter is *viṣṭārapaṅkti*. By the rule *chandonāmni ca*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs.
[Furthermore, the suffix *ap* is applied after the root *grah* when preceded by *ud-*.]

The suffix *ghañ* shall occur after the root *grah* when preceded by the prefix *ud*; thus, *udgāhaḥ*. [The suffix *ghañ* occurs] after the root *muṣ* when preceded by *sam*, provided it refers to a fist.

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the root *grah* when preceded by *sam* in the sense of "fist"; for example, *aho mallasya saṃgrāhaḥ*, meaning the firmness of the wrestler's fist. In other cases, it is *saṃgrahaḥ*.
[The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] after the roots *nī* and *ṇī* preceded by *pari* and *ni* respectively, in the senses of gambling and non-deviation.

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *nī* when preceded by *pari* in the sense of gambling (*dyūta*) and when it means non-deviation (*abhreṣa*). Thus, *pariṇāya* refers to the movement of dice; *nyāya* means not overstepping established order; and *abhreṣa* means the absence of deviation.
Furthermore, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *iṇ* when preceded by *pari* in the sense of non-transgression (*anupātyaya*).

*Anupātyaya* means the non-passing over of that which has reached its turn. From the root *iṇ* preceded by *pari*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of "succession" (*paripāṭī*). For example: *tava paryāyaḥ* ("It is your turn") and *mama paryāyaḥ* ("It is my turn").
Why "in the sense of non-passing over"? [Consider: *kālaviparyayaḥ* ("reversal of time").
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *śī* (to lie down) when preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-*, provided it denotes a turn of action (*paryāya*).

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the root *śī* when preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-*. For example: *tava adya viśāyaḥ* (your resting today), *mama upaśāyaḥ* (my resting). This means "alternating sleep.
[Furthermore, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *ci* when preceded by *hastāt* in the sense of taking with the hand, provided it is not theft.]

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after the root *ci* (to gather) when it conveys the sense of proximity. Examples: *puṣpapracāyaḥ* (the gathering of flowers), *phaloccāyaḥ* (the gathering of fruits), *phalopacāyaḥ* (the gathering of fruits). [The rule applies] when the gathering is by means of the hand? Example: *laguḍena puṣpapracayaḥ* (the gathering of flowers with a stick). Why "when not involving theft"? Example: *vṛkṣāgre cauryeṇa puṣpoccayaḥ* (the gathering of flowers from the top of a tree by stealth). [Furthermore, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after *ci* in the senses of dwelling, piling up, and preparing the body, and the initial *c-* is replaced by *k-*. Example: *nikāyaḥ* (a collection/dwelling), *saṃkāyaḥ* (a pile), *śarīrasaṃkāyaḥ* (the preparation of the body).

In these meanings, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *ci*, and the initial *ā* is replaced by *ka*. *Nikāya* means a house; *nikāya* means fire; that is, "accumulated. *Kāya* means the body. It also means piling up or making into a heap, as in *gomayanikāyaḥ* (a heap of cow dung) and *kāṣṭhanikāyaḥ* (a pile of wood).
Furthermore, when referring to a community (*saṃgha*) provided there is no vertical superposition [of parts], the suffix *ghañ* is applied.

The collection (*samudāya*) of living beings is a *saṅgha*. In the sense of a *saṅgha*, the suffixes *ciñ* and *ghañ* are applied, and the initial vowel is replaced by *ka*. Examples: *bhikṣunikāyaḥ* (the community of nuns), *mṛgyāḥ śatrunikāyānām* (of the enemy-hordes of the deer).

Why [is it specified] "not in the sense of vertical stacking" (*anauttarādharye*)? [Consider: *śūkaranicayaḥ* (a heap of boars). When there is a mutual exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*), the suffix *ṇac* is applied, and it is feminine.

The suffix *ṇac* occurs after a verbal root in the feminine gender to denote the abstract action (*bhāva*) when the action is performed reciprocally. Examples: *vyākrośīṃ vidadhate* (they engage in mutual abuse); *vyāvahāsīmanāśritaiḥ* (a mutual joking not resorted to by others). After the suffix *ṇac*, the suffix *añ* is added in the feminine; this is due to its general applicability, sometimes occurring even in cases where it would otherwise be barred—e.g., *vyāvacorī*. Example: *vyātyukṣīm abhisaraṇaglahāmadīvyan* (they played at the game of splashing water while pursuing one another).
The suffix *inuṇ* denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*) in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*).

The suffix *inuṇ* is applied after a verbal root in the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*) or "pervasion" (*abhivyāpti*). Examples: *sāṃrāviṇam* (the act of making a general sound), *sāṅkūṭinam* (the act of plotting). By the rule *aṇ-inuṇ-aḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the same sense [to form a noun denoting the action].
The verb *grah* is used with the prefixes *ava* and *ni* in the sense of reviling (*ākrośa*).

The suffix ghañ shall be applied after the root *grah* when preceded by *ava*, provided it denotes an insult: *avagrāhaḥ*. [It shall also be applied] after *ni* when it means "may it happen to you, O low-born one": *nigrāhas te vṛṣala bhūyāt*. [And it shall be applied] after *pra* when it denotes the desire to obtain: *pre lipsāyām*.
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *grah* when preceded by *pra* in the sense of desire; for example, "the mendicant wanders with a bowl as his *pragrāha* (desire) for alms.
[The suffix *ghañ* also occurs] after *pari* when used in the context of a sacrifice.

The suffix *ghañ* shall be used after the root *grah* when preceded by the prefix *pari* in the sense of a sacrifice; for example, *uttaraparigrahaḥ*, which refers to a specific type of sacrifice. [The suffix *ghañ* is also used] after the root *vṛ* with the prefix *ni* in the sense of grain.
The suffix *ghañ* shall occur after the verbal root *vṛdh* when preceded by the prefix *ni*. Examples include *nīvārāḥ* (wild rice) and *vrīhayaḥ* (cultivated rice).
[The suffix *ghañ* also occurs] after the roots *śri*, *yu*, *pū*, and *dru* when preceded by the prefix *ud*.
The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after these [roots] following the prefix *ud*. Examples: *ucchrāyaḥ*, *udyāvaḥ*, *utpāvaḥ*, *uddrāvaḥ*.
[However], the application of *ghañ* after the roots *rup* and *plu* following the prefix *āṅ* is optional.

The suffix *ghañ* is optionally used after the roots *rūp* and *lup* when preceded by the prefix *ā*. Thus, one may say either *ārāvaḥ* or *āravaḥ*. Rāma spoke to Hanumān, who had leaped from afar, saying "gajāplavaḥ" (an elephant-leaper).
The root *grah* with the prefix *ava* is used in the sense of obstructing rain.

The word *avagraha* may optionally take the suffix *ghañ* to mean "cessation of rain"; thus, there are the forms *avagrāhaḥ* or *avagrahaḥ* for "the stopping of a cloud. [In the sense of] "obstruction," it is used for merchants.
When referring to the string of a merchant’s scale, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *grah* with the prefix *pra*; thus, one says either *pragrāhaḥ* or *pragrahaḥ*.
It also occurs in the sense of a rein.

*Raśmi* is a rope for restraining horses and the like; in this context, the suffix *ghañ* may optionally be applied to the root *pra-grah*, resulting in either *pragrāhaḥ* or *pragrahaḥ*. [The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] to the root *vṛ* in the sense of covering.

The suffix *ghañ* may optionally occur after the root *vṛ* when preceded by *pra-* in the sense of "covering. Examples: *prāvāraḥ* (an outer garment) and *vastraṃ* (a cloth). [Also: *vindhyasya pravaraḥ* (the most excellent wealth of the Vindhya mountains).
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *bhū* preceded by *pari-* in the sense of "disregard."
The suffix *ghañ* may optionally occur after the root *bhū* with the prefix *pari-* in the sense of "contempt" (*tiraskāra*). Thus, *paribhāvaḥ*;
in the alternative case, with *ap*, *paribhavaḥ*. The suffix *ghañ* has been explained.
Thus it is said.
After verbal roots ending in vowels, *ac* shall be substituted as an exception to *ghañ* and *na*. Examples: *cayaḥ*, *śiloccayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*, *vyayaḥ*, *praṇayaḥ*, *praśayaḥ*.

There is an addition [to the rule] for *bhaya* and others after the prefix *a-* when not forming a compound (*avigrahe*), in order to prevent the application of suffixes such as *kta* in the neuter gender. Examples:
*bhayam*, *varṣam*.

By the rule *vāsarūpa*, the suffixes *kta* and others also occur—as in *bhītaṃ śiśunā* ("frightened by the child"), *vṛṣṭaṃ devena* ("rained by the god"), and *varṣaṇaṃ meghasya* ("the raining of the cloud"—according to the Bhāgavṛtti).
[This concludes] the section on the *ap* suffixes.
The suffix *ap* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*.

The suffix *ap* occurs after roots ending in the vowel *ṛ* and after the roots *varṇ*. *kṛ*—*karaḥ*; *tṛ*—*taraḥ*; *bhṛ*—*bharaḥ*; *gṛ*—*garaḥ*; *śṛ*—*śaraḥ*; *pra-tṛ*—*prataraḥ*; *pra-dṛ*—*pradaraḥ*; *sam-gṛ*—*saṅgaraḥ*; *su-nu*—*snuvaḥ*; *stu*—*stavaḥ*; *bhū*—*bhavaḥ*; *sam-bhū*—*sambhavaḥ*; *lū*—*lavaḥ*; *pū*—*pavaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *ṝditaḥ*, the *dakāra* (the letter *d*) is for the sake of pronunciation; it is not the letter *takāra* (*t*), according to the Bhāṣya.
[The suffix *ap* occurs] also after the roots *grah*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, *niści*, and *gam*.

And after the roots *vaś*, *raṇ*, and those ending in *niś-cigrahaṇa*, the suffix *ap* occurs. From these [roots], the form *ap* is applied: *grahaḥ*, *varaḥ*, *daraḥ*. The inclusion of *niś-cigrahaṇa* is for the sake of a specific accent: *niścayaḥ*. Also from *gam*, *vaś*, *raṇ*: *gamaḥ*, *vaśaḥ*, *raṇaḥ*. Due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*), there is *svayaṃgrāhaḥ*. After the roots *sthā*, *snā*, *pā*, *vyadh*, *han*, and *yudh*, the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the suffix *ghañ*. Examples: *prasthaḥ*, *prasnaḥ*, *prapādyaḥ* (where they drink in it), *āvidhaḥ*, *vidhnaḥ*, *āyudham*. After the root *ad* when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), the suffix *ka* is used.
The suffix *ghan* is applied after the root *ad* (to eat) when preceded by a prefix; the resulting form is *ap*. Examples: *vighasaḥ*, *praghasaḥ*, *saṃghasaḥ*.
Why "when preceded by a prefix"? Consider *ghāsaḥ*.
[When preceded by] *nau* (the prefix *ni*), there is also the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*.

The suffix *ap* shall be applied after the roots *nau*, *vṛt*, and *ṇaś*; [the resulting forms are] *nighasaḥ* and *nyādaḥ*. After the roots *vyadh* and *jap*, [the suffix *ap* is applied] when no prefix (*anupasarga*) precedes them.

The suffix *ap* occurs after these two when preceded by *pra*. For example: *vyadhaḥ* (piercing) and *japaḥ* (muttering). However, when preceded by *upa*, it is as follows: *upāvyādhaḥ* (a near-piercing) and *upajāpaḥ* (instigation).
After the roots *svan* and *has*, the suffix is optional.
Before these [prefixes], there may optionally be *v* (guṇa) substitution. Thus: *svanaḥ* or *svānaḥ*; *hasaḥ* or *hāsaḥ*.
Also before *sam*, *upa*, *ni*, and *vi*, [the same applies to] *yama*.
And in the case of roots beginning with *pra*, there may optionally be *yama* or *yāma*. Thus: *saṃyamaḥ* or *saṃyāmaḥ*; *upayamaḥ* or *upayāmaḥ*; *niyamaḥ* or *niyāmaḥ*; *viyamaḥ* or *viyāmaḥ*.
[The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the roots *gad*, *nad*, *paṭh*, and *svan* when preceded by *ni*.
The suffix *ap* may optionally follow these [roots]: *ni-gad*, *ni-gād*; *ni-nad*, *ni-nād*; *ni-paṭh*, *ni-pāṭh*; *ni-svan*, *ni-svān*.
[The suffix *ap* is also used] after the root *kvaṇ* when it refers to a lute (*vīṇā*).
The suffix *ap* may optionally be applied after the root *kvaṇ*. Thus: *kvaṇaḥ* or *kvāṇaḥ*.
It is also used with the prefix *ni*: *nikvaṇaḥ* or *nikvāṇaḥ*.
And in the context of the lute (*vīṇā*), it is used as *prakvāṇaḥ* or *prakvaṇaḥ* for the sound of a lute.
The word *nityam* [is used] in the sense of measure (*parimāṇe*).

In this context, the word *paṇa* always takes the suffix *ap*. For example: *śākapaṇaḥ* (a handful of vegetables); *narāḥ kṣīṇapaṇā iva* (men like those whose money has been spent). [The suffix *ap* is also applied] to *mada* when it does not have a prefix (*anupasarga*).
In the beginning, *mada* (intoxication/arrogance) would be [formed] with *pra*. Thus: *vidyāmadaḥ* (arrogance of learning), *dhanamadaḥ* (arrogance of wealth).
Due to its abundance, there is *mādaḥ*. *Pramada* and *sammada* denote joy.
In this context, these two [prefixes] are treated as nipātanas (irregular forms): *pramadaḥ* and *sammadaḥ*.
Also, when combined with *sam* and *ud*, the root *rañj* takes the suffix *ap* in the sense of "animals."
The suffix *ap* shall be applied after the root *aj* preceded by the prefix *sam-*. An assembly (*saṃgha*) of elephants is a *samaja*; the rising (*udgamana*) of horses is an *udaja*.
Why "among animals"? [Because] a gathering of Brahmins is a *viprasamāja*.
Among dice, it is a *glaha*.
In the case of dice, the term *glaha* is used;
elsewhere, it is *graha*.
[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *sṛ* when preceded by *pra* in the sense of procreation.

The suffix *sarter ap* occurs after [the root] *sṛt* in the sense of "first conception" (*prajanana*). [The suffix] *upasaraḥ* occurs [after the same root]. After the root *hve*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) when preceded by *ni*, *abhi*, *upa*, or *vi*.

In these cases, the suffix *ap* is added to the root *hve*, and there is also vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). [The forms are: *nihavaḥ*, *abhihavaḥ*, *upahavaḥ*, and *vihavaḥ*. When preceded by *āṅ*, it means "battle."
After the root *hvayati* (to call), when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ap* is applied and there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). *Āhavaḥ* means battle;
*āhāvaḥ* means a watering place.
The word *āhāva-* is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) when it means a watering place (*nipāna*);
[the suffix -ghañ is applied] in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), provided no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it.

The suffix *ap* occurs after the root *hve* (to call) when it does not begin with *pra* and when it denotes an action (*bhāva*). [Examples: *kurvantaḥ* (those performing the invocation), *āptānām havaḥ* (the invocation of the trustworthy ones). And after the root *han*, the form *vadha* is used.
In the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), the suffix *ap* is added after the root *han*, and there is the substitution of *vadh* for it; thus, *vadhaḥ*.
Because of the inclusion of the letter *ca*, the suffix *ghañ* is also desired; thus, *ghātaḥ*.
When denoting a solid mass (*mūrti*), the form is *ghanaḥ*.
After the root *han*, when meaning "hardness," the suffix *ap* is added and *dhan* is substituted for the root. Examples: *lauhadhanaḥ* (an iron hammer), *amradhanaḥ* (a soft hammer).
How is it that [the word] *ghanaṃ dadhi* ("thick curd") is used? It is by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*).
When meaning "a place," [the suffix *ap* with *dhan* substitution occurs after *han*]: *antarghaṇaḥ* (an inner courtyard or enclosed space).

This [term] occurs in the sense of an inner chamber, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is desired there; thus, Bhaṭṭi says "paśyan tasminnantarghaṇe" (seeing in that inner chamber). In the sense of a portion of a house, the words *praghaṇa* and *praghāṇa* are used.
These two should be located in one part of the house;
the *udghana* is the *atyādhāna*.
That piece of wood upon which another piece of wood is placed for carving is called *udghana*;
*apaghana* refers to a limb of the body.
This [suffix] may occur in the sense of a limb; [it forms words for] mangled limbs with indistinct gurgling sounds from wounds;
and it occurs in the sense of an instrument [as in] iron and gems.

In these cases, the suffix *ap* is applied after the root *han*, and there is the substitution of *ghan* for the root. Examples: *ayoghanaḥ* (iron club), *vighanaḥ* (cleansing), *dughanaḥ* (a type of mallet). [The word] *kuṭhāraḥ* (axe) [is formed similarly].
Regarding the change of *h* to *gh*, some say it is *drughaṇaḥ*.
In the feminine gender, the suffixes *khal* and *ana* apply by way of overriding [the previous rule]: *ayohanani* (iron-smashing), *druhanani* (smashing with force), *vihanani* (striking apart).
And [the suffix] *ka* is applied after the word *stamba*.
What [suffix] would there be after *stamba*? That [suffix] is *gha*, as in *stambaghna* (a post-digger). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also *apa*: *stambaghna*.
After the prefix *pari*, the suffix is *gha*.

When used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the suffix *ap* is added after the root *han*, and there is the substitution of *ghā* for it; thus, *parighaḥ*. When meaning a support (*āśraya*), [the suffix *ap* is added] after *upa*; thus, *upaghnaḥ*.
In this context,
the suffix *ya* is elided when *saṅgha* and *udgha* denote a group and praise, respectively.
In the sense of a group, there is *saṅgha*; in the sense of praise, there is *udgha*;
and *nigha* means a cause.
That which is measured should be called *nigha*. Trees are *nighas*. The suffix *ap* has been explained.
The suffix *ktri* occurs after a root ending in *ḍu*.
The suffix *ktri* occurs after a verbal root that has *ḍu* as its indicatory letter (*anubandha*). After *ktri*, the suffix *mam* is applied invariably.
Examples: *kṛtrimam*, *krītrimam*, *labdhrimam*, *bhṛtrimam*, *paktrimam*.
The suffix *athuc* occurs after a root ending in a vowel (other than *ṛ*) or a consonant with an indicatory *ṭi*.
The suffix *athuc* occurs after verbal roots having *ṭu* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Examples: *nandathuḥ*, *vamathuḥ*, *bhrājathuḥ*, *vepathuḥ*.
The suffix *naṅ* occurs after the roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *yat*, *vicch*, *pracch*, and *rakṣ*.

The suffix *naṅ* occurs after these [roots] when expressing a state (*bhāva*) or an agent other than the subject (*akartṛ-kāraka*). Examples: *yajñaḥ*, *yācññā*, *yatnaḥ*, *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*. Regarding *praśnaḥ*, there is an absence of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule): "and in the case of *praśna* when referring to immediate time. Examples: *rakṣṇaḥ*. After the root *svap*, the suffix is *nan*.
From this [root], *nan* would not occur; rather, *svapnaḥ* [is formed].
[The rule] "after a prefix, *kiḥ* is substituted for *ghu*" [applies here].
The suffix *ki* occurs after the roots *dā* and *dhā* when preceded by certain prefixes: *ādi*, *ādhi*, *nidhi*, *pradhi*, *antarddhi*, and *praṇidhi*.
Due to the abundance of usage, this rule is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*).
The sixth case-affix is used after a word denoting the object of an action (karman) and after a word denoting the locus (adhikaraṇa).

After the verbal root *ghu* (meaning "to sound"), when preceded by a direct object (*karman*) or a secondary member (*upapada*), the suffix *ki* occurs in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*). Examples: *jaladhiḥ*, *vāridhiḥ*, *oṣadhiḥ*, *bāladhiḥ*.
In the feminine, the suffix *ktin* is used.

The suffix *ktin* occurs after a verbal root to denote the feminine gender, the abstract state (*bhāva*), or a factor other than the agent (*akartṛ-kāraka*). Examples: *śritiḥ*, *citiḥ*, *siddhiḥ*, *nītiḥ*. *Śrutiḥ* (that by which something is heard); *bhūtiḥ*, *sūtiḥ*, *kṛtiḥ*, *ṛddhiḥ*, *sṛṣṭiḥ*. After roots containing the vowel *ṛ* or those beginning with *lū* etc., the suffix *ktin* is treated like the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (i.e., it causes *guṇa*): *kīrṇiḥ*, *gīrṇiḥ*, *lūniḥ*, *dhūniḥ*. The suffix *ktin* occurs after roots beginning with *āp* and after roots ending in a heavy vowel (*guru*) or a consonant (*hal*), as an exception to the rule for the suffix *ap*: *āptiḥ*, *dīptiḥ*, *rāddhiḥ*, *sāddhiḥ*, *praśastiḥ*.
Because of its predominance, the substitution of *i* for *śās* does not occur—thus, *śāstiḥ*.
From the roots *glai*, *mlai*, *jyā*, and *hā*, the suffix *ni* is applied. After these, *ni* shall occur: *glāniḥ*, *mlāniḥ*, *jyāniḥ*, *hāniḥ*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the words *sampad* and others. Thus: *sampat*, *pratipat*, *vipat*, *saṃvit*. It is understood that the suffix *ktin* is also desired: *sampattiḥ*, *pratipattiḥ*, *vipattiḥ*.
[The suffix *kvip* is also applied] after the roots *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *pā*, and *pac* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
In place of these [suffixes], there shall be the suffix *ktin* as an exception (*apavāda*). Examples: *prasthitiḥ*, *saṅgītiḥ*, *pragītiḥ*, *āpītiḥ*, *paktiḥ*.

How is it that *āsthā* and *vyavasthā* are formed? It is due to the authority of usage (*abhidhāna-prāmāṇyāt*). Furthermore, their formation is established by the mention of the word "establishment" (*vyavasthāyām*) in the rule *pūrvāparād ekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.4.12).
In a mantra, the vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *i*, *u*, *e*, *o*, and *ai* are acute (*udātta*).
This is Vedic usage:
and [the suffixes] -ūti, -yūti, -jūti, -sāti, -heti, and -kīrti [are also used].
These six suffixes are prescribed after verbal roots beginning with *veñ* and others.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *vraj* and *yaj* in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*).
The suffix *kyap* occurs after these two roots (*vraj* and *yaj*) when expressing the abstract action (*bhāva*). Thus: *vrajyā*, *pravrajyā*, *ijyā*.
Due to the abundance [of usage], the form *iṣṭiḥ* is also seen.
When forming a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *samaja*, *niṣad*, *nipata*, *mana*, *vida*, *suñ*, *śīṅ*, *bhṛñ*, and *iṇ*.

The suffix *kyap* is applied after these nine roots when a feminine noun (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed; this indicates that the meanings are the abstract state (*bhāva*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), or the instrument (*karaṇa*). [Examples: *samajyā*, *niṣadyā*, *nipatyā*, *manyā*, *vidyā*, *sutyā*, *śayyā*, *bhṛtyā*, *ityā*.
Because of the general rule of abundance (*bāhulyāt*), some say [the suffix applies] even to *samasyā*.
How is it that *bhṛtiḥ*, *matiḥ*, and *āsūtiḥ* are formed? The author of the Nyāsa says: "By means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*)."
And *śa* is also [the suffix] after the root *kṛñ*.

After the root *kṛ*, there shall be the suffix *śa* and also *kyap*. [Examples: *kriyā* (action), *kṛtyā* (magical power). By means of a word-split (*yogavibhāga*), [we also have] *kṛtiḥ* (creation) and *icchā* (desire).
The word *iṣṭi* is an irregular formation (nipātana) in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). In the sense of an object (*karman*), it is formed with the suffix *ktin*.

Regarding the forms *paricaryā*, *parisaryā*, *mṛgayā*, *aṭāṭyā*, *jāgaryā*, and *jāgarā*: these six must be treated as irregular formations when the suffix *śa* is applied, because [otherwise] they would have taken the suffix *ap*.

The suffix *a* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a suffix; from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Examples: *cikīrṣā* (desire to do), *tiṣṭhāsā* (desire to stand), *putrīyā* (desire for a son), *putrakāmyā* (desire for a son), *lolūyā* (repeated cutting), *caṅkramā* (wandering), *sesicā* (desire to sprinkle), *kaṇḍūyā* (itching).
[This applies] also after a heavy vowel (*guru*) followed by a consonant (*hal*).
The suffix *a* occurs after verbal roots ending in *ha* that belong to the *gurumat* (heavy-vowel) class. Examples: *śikṣā*, *bhikṣā*, *irkṣā*, *pratīkṣā*, *vyatīhā*, *ūhā*.
Due to the abundance [of usage]—there is the form *rūḍhiḥ*. Because of the mention of the letter *ca*—there is *śobhā*.
After roots beginning with *ṣid* and *bhad*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied.

The suffix *aṅ* is applied after roots beginning with *bhid*, provided they end in *ṣ*. Examples: *pacā* (cooking), *trapā* (shame). In the case of the roots *ṛ* and *dṛś*, there is *guṇa* substitution when *aṅ* follows: *jarā* (old age), *ghaṭā* (a group), *vyathā* (pain), *jaṭā* (matted hair). Due to the abundance of usage—such as in *upalabdhiḥ* (perception)—the grammarians record the application of *aṅ* specifically for the group beginning with *bhid*. Thus: *bhidā* (splitting); whereas *bhittiḥ* is something else. When *aṅ* is applied to the root *ṛt*, there is *guṇa*, but by irregularity (*nipātana*) there is lengthening: *ārā* (an awl); whereas *ṛtiḥ* is something else. Similarly: *kārā* (a prison); *tārā* (a star); *dhārā* (a stream); whereas *dhṛtiḥ* is something else.
Due to their abundance—*asidhārā*; in the sense of "writing" (*likha*), there is the substitution of *r* for *l* and the suffix *aṅ*: *lekhā*, *rekhā*;

from *kṛp* there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and [the suffix *aṅ*]: *kṛpā*; *guhā*, *pṛcchā*, *mṛjā*, *rujā*, *vidā*; *bhidā* and so forth constitute a class of words defined by their form (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
And he was one who meditated, worshipped, spoke, and performed ritual service.
The suffix *aṅ* shall occur after these roots ending in *ṇic*; it is an exception to the suffix *yuc*. [Examples: *cintā*, *pūjā*, *kathā*, *kumbā*, *carcā*.
[Also: *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106).
The suffix *aṅ* shall be applied after roots beginning with *pra* when preceded by a prefix ending in a vowel. Examples: *pramā*, *pratimā*, *pradhā*, *upadhā*, *prabhā*, *pratibhā*.
The function of the prefixes *śrat* and *antar* is like that of verbal prefixes (*upasarga*). Examples: *śraddhā*, *antardhā*.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *ktin* is also applied: *pramitiḥ*.
The suffix *yuc* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṇi* (causative) and after the root *śranth*.

The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots ending in the causative marker *ṇi*, as well as after the roots *ās* (to sit) and *śranth* (to loosen). Examples: *dāpanā* (causing to give), *dīpanā* (causing to shine), *kāraṇā* (causing to do), *bhūṣaṇā* (adorning), *kāmanā* (desiring), *codanā* (impelling), *upāsanā* (worshiping), *śranthanā* (loosening).
Due to the rule's broad application (*bāhulyāt*), it also occurs after *pācayati*: *pāktiḥ* (cooking).
The suffix *yuc* is added after the roots *ghaṭ*, *ṭuvi*, and *vid*. [Examples: *ghaṭṭanā*, *vandanā*, *vedanā*.
[The suffix *yuc* is added] after the root *iṣ* when it does not mean "desire. [Example: *anveṣaṇā*.
[The suffix *yuc* is added] optionally after *pari*. [Examples: *paryeṣaṇā*, *parīṣṭiḥ*.
The suffix *ṇvul* is applied diversely to form names of diseases.
The suffix *ṇvul* is frequently used when a disease is to be expressed. Examples: *pracchardikā*, *pravāhikā*, *vicarcikā*, *praskandikā*.
And it does not occur [in these cases]: *śiro'rtiḥ*, where *ktin* is used after the root *ard*.
The suffix *ṇvul* should be stated [as applicable] when the meaning of a verbal root is indicated: *āsikā*, *āśikā*, *śāyikā*.
The suffixes *ik* and *tiP* are used when indicating verbal roots (*dhātu*). For example: *paciḥ*, *yāciḥ*, *karotiḥ*, *yajeḥ*, *vapeḥ*. The vowel *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
After a phoneme (*varṇa*), the suffix *kāra* is applied. Examples: *akāraḥ*, *ākāraḥ*, *aukāraḥ*, *kakāraḥ*, *oṃkāraḥ*, *huṃkāraḥ*, *evakāraḥ*, *phaṭkāraḥ*, *śītkāraḥ*, *phutkāraḥ*, *thutkāraḥ*.
According to others, in cases such as *evakāra* and so forth, there is a compound with a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*.

*rādiphaḥ* || *rephaḥ* | [The suffix] *cha* is applied after a word having the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*). [Thus] *matvarthīyaḥ*. Due to its frequency, even though it is not a *bha*-stem, there is elision by the rule *yasyeti ca*. [The suffixes] *iñ*, *añ*, and others are applied after [words ending in] *āji*, etc. [Examples: *ājiḥ*, *ātiḥ*, *āṭiḥ*.
The suffix *ika* is applied after words such as *kṛṣi*. Examples: *kṛṣiḥ*, *giriḥ*. This entire extensive elaboration [of suffixes] applies when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *ṇvul* shall be applied after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting a name. [Examples: *puṣpabhañjikā*, *śālabhañjikā*—these are names for games.
Furthermore, the suffix *iñ* is also applied after a verbal root when it denotes a descriptive statement (*vibhāṣā*) or an inquiry (*ākhyāna*).

In the case of questions and narratives, the suffixes *iñ* and *ṇvul* may optionally occur. [Examples: "What deed (*kāri*) did you do?"—[the possible forms are] *kārikām*, *kriyām*, *kṛtyām*, *kṛtyām*, or *kṛtim*. "I did every deed"—[the possible forms are] *kārikām*, *kriyām*, *kṛtyām*, *kṛtyām*, or *kṛtim*. Similarly: *sthāyim*, *sthitim*, or *sthāyikām*.
The suffix *ṇvuc* occurs in the senses of turn, worthiness, and origin.

The suffix *ṇvuc* occurs after a verbal root in these senses: "Your lying down. "I perform a fast unto death (*prāyopaveśikā*) that has reached its turn. "You ought to perform a meal of sugarcane (*ikṣubhakṣikā*). "You maintain for me a habit of eating sesame-sweets (*tilamodakakhādikā*). "A drinking of milk (*payaḥpāyikā*) has arisen for me.
The suffixes *nañ*, *ñya*, and *ni* occur [after a root] in the sense of reproach.

In the sense of a curse (śāpe), the suffix *ani* shall be applied after a root preceded by the negative particle *nañ* and the word *upapada*. Let there be the non-birth (*ajanani*) of that one who causes distress to his mother; let there be the non-existence (*abhavani*) of the Mind-born (Kāma) at that time. [The rule] "in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), in the sense of an agent other than the karty, and in the feminine" is no longer operative here.
[The governing rule is: "the kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely (*bahulam*)."

The suffix *lyuṭ* and the *kṛtya* suffixes occur frequently after verbal roots (*dhātu*) with meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. In the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*): *locanalobhanīyā śasyapaṅktiḥ* (a row of grain that captivates the eyes). In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*): *snānīyaṃ cūrṇam* (bath-powder). In the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*): *dānīyo bhikṣuḥ* (a monk worthy of gifts). In the sense of the locus (*ādhāra*): *śayanīyaṃ kaṭitram* (a mattress for lying down); *ramaṇīyā vāpī* (a beautiful pond); *ramyam udyānam* (a delightful garden). In the sense of the locus (*ādhāra*): *tiṣṭhanty asmin stheyaḥ* (that in which they stand is the "place to stand"). The suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*): *guṇam uktavān guṇavacanaḥ* (one who has spoken of qualities is a "quality-expresser"). In the sense of the object (*karman*): *avasecano vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree to be watered); *rājabhojanāḥ śālayaḥ* (rice fit for the king's meal).
In the sense of the source (*apādāna*): *prapatanaṃ* (falling away), and so forth. The suffix *kta* is used in the neuter gender in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*).
The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root to express a neuter state (*bhāva*). For example: *hasitam* (the laughing) of the mendicant; *gatam* (the going) of the Brahmin.
The suffix *lyuṭ* also occurs [in this sense].
The suffix *lyuṭ* occurs after a verbal root in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) when it is neuter: *karaṇam*, *gamanam*, *haraṇam*.
It also occurs in the sense of an object (*karman*) when, through contact with it, pleasure is produced in the body of the agent.

From this very rule regarding the application of the suffix *lyuṭ*, it occurs in the neuter gender when expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*). For example: *payaḥpānaṃ bhujaṅgānāṃ sukham* (the drinking of milk is a pleasure for serpents); *guḍabhojanaṃ bhikṣoḥ sukham* (the eating of molasses is a pleasure for a mendicant). This compound with an upapada is obligatory. Why [is the word] "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) mentioned? [Consider: *kaṇṭakānāṃ mardanaṃ kaṇṭakamardanaṃ duḥkham* (the crushing of thorns; the crushing by thorns is pain).
[The suffix *lyuṭ* is also applied] after verbal roots when expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The suffix *lyuṭ* shall apply after these two [roots]. A sword that cuts the body (*dehavraścanaḥ khaḍgaḥ*). The moon is the comparison for the face (*upamānaṃ mukhasyenduḥ*). In the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*): a royal capital (*rājadhānī*), a vessel for the best portion (*varārdhānī*), a pot for milking cows (*godohanī sthālī*), a cauldron for cooking rice (*odanapacanaḥ kaṭāhaḥ*), a granary for holding rice (*vrīhibharaṇaḥ kusūlaḥ*). The rule for the suffixes *khal* and *ghañ* applies to both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The suffix *gha* generally occurs in the masculine when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *gha* generally occurs after verbal roots ending in a consonant (*nāmni*) to form masculine nouns. In the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*): *dantacchadaḥ* (lip); *karaḥ* (hand), as in "that by which one acts"; *śaraḥ* (arrow). In the sense of a locus (*ādhāre*): *ākaraḥ* (mine); *ālayaḥ* (abode). *Parisara*, *avasara*, and the following—*gocara*, *sañcara*, *vaha*, *vraja*, *vyaja*, *āpaṇa*, and *nigama*—belong to this very category.
These seven [roots] ending in *gh* are treated as exceptions (*nipātana*). From the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], [the following is understood]: that by which one is called is "āhvayaḥ";
[this is formed] by the suffix *ghañ* after the roots *ā-hve* and *tṛ*.
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after these two [roots] (*ava* and *stṛ*). Examples: *avatāraḥ*, *avastāraḥ*. [Also, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after a root ending in a consonant. *Halaśca*.

The suffix *ghañ* shall be applied after a root ending in a consonant (*hal*) when it occurs in the domain of the suffix *gha*. Examples: *lekhaḥ*, *vedaḥ*, *bandhaḥ*, *apāmārgaḥ*, *bhargaḥ* (that by which one is purified). Only "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*)—for example, *nikaṣaḥ*.
Furthermore, the forms *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *udyāva*, *saṃhāra*, *ādhāra*, and *āvāya* are also [formed with *ghañ*].

These six words ending in the suffix *ghañ* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of "in this" (*asmin viṣaye*). *Adhyāya*: that in which one studies (*adhīyate atra*). From the root *i-* preceded by *ni-*, *nyāya*: that by which one is led (*nīyate anena*). *Udaṅka*: [this is formed] when it does not mean water (*anudake*).
In this case, [the suffix] *udañc* is substituted [for *udak*]. As in: *ghṛtodañcaḥ*. But not here: *jalodanvan*.
[The suffix] *ānāya* [is used] for a net.
If it means "net," [the suffix] *ānāya* is used after the root *khan*; and the suffix *gha* is also applied.

The suffixes *ghañ* and *gha* may be applied after the root *khan*. That by which something is dug is called *ākhānaḥ* or *ākhanaḥ*. In this context, words such as *ākhā* and *ākhānikā* are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes. The rule "in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*)" has ceased to apply here.
The suffix *khal* is applied after the particles *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su* when they signify difficulty (*kṛcchra*) or ease (*akṛcchra*).
The suffix *khal* shall be applied after a verbal root in these [meanings]. That which is performed with difficulty is *duṣkara* ("difficult to do"), *durlabha* ("hard to obtain").

That which is performed without difficulty is *sukara* ("easy to do"), *īṣatkara* ("slightly easy"), *subhoja* ("easy to eat"), *subodha* ("easy to understand"), *subheda* ("easy to split"), *sulabha* ("easy to obtain").
[The suffix *khal* is also applied] after the roots *bhū* and *kṛ* when the agent or the object is expressed.

The suffix *khal* shall occur after the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and likewise after the root *kṛ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). It is also prescribed in the sense of the *cvy-artha* (the state of becoming something else). Examples:

*durāḍhyambhavaṃ tena* ("he became difficult to enrich by him"), *surājambhavam amunā* ("he became a good king by means of this"). *īṣadāḍhyaṅkaraḥ putraḥ tvayā* ("your son was made somewhat wealthy by you"), *supaṇḍitaṅkaraḥ śiṣyaḥ* ("the pupil was made very learned"). Although *su* and *dur* function as *gatis*, they do not precede the verbal root here; this is because the suffix *khal* is marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*).
The suffix *yuc* is applied after a verbal root ending in long *ā*.

The suffix *yuc* indeed occurs after a verbal root ending in a short vowel when [the following] object is present. Examples: *supānaṃ payaḥ* (easy-to-drink milk), *durupasthāno guruḥ* (a teacher difficult to attend upon), *durdānā gauḥ* (a cow difficult to give away), *durjñānā gauḥ* (a cow difficult to recognize).
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), it occurs after roots meaning "to go."
It is also seen after other [roots].
In the Chāndasa Sūtra:

"In the spoken language (bhāṣā), [the suffix] *yuc* is added after the roots *śās*, *yudh*, *dṛś*, *dhṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ*. From these, *yuc* shall be applied: *duḥśāsanaḥ*, *duryodhanaḥ*, *durdarśanaḥ*, *durdharṣaṇaḥ*, *durmarṣaṇaḥ*, *suyodhanaḥ*, *sudarśanaḥ*, *sumarṣaṇaḥ*.
When there is proximity to the present time, it may optionally be treated as the present tense.
When the past or future is in proximity to the present, the suffix may optionally be like that of the present tense. For example: *gacchāmi* (I go), which means "know me as one who is going.
In the alternative case, the suffixes are used according to their regular application.
Furthermore, when expressing a wish (*āśaṃsā*), the suffixes are treated as if they were those of the past tense.

When there is an expectation [of something yet to happen], the suffixes may be used as if it were present or as if it were past. For example: "If the teacher comes" (āgacchati), "has come" (āgataḥ), "will come" (āgamiṣyati), "is to come" (āgantā), "might come" (āgacchet), or "did come" (āgamat)—in these cases we study the Veda; or alternatively: "we have studied" (adhyagīṣmahi). Optionally, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) may also be used, as in:
"O Saumitri, you would have approached me" (mām upāyaṃsthāḥ) or "you approached me" (mām upāyaṃsta), O Rāma.
Now he states two exceptions to this rule:
The suffix *lṛṭ* is used to express quickness of action.
The *lṛṭ* (future) suffix shall be used when there is a connection with a word expressing hope (*śiprā*). For example: "If he will come quickly, I shall study swiftly.
[Additionally,] the *liṅ* (optative) suffix is used in a statement of hope (*āśaṃsā*).

The optative (liṅ) shall be used in connection with a desired object. For example: "If he were to come, I would wish that I might study with diligence. Or: "I hope that we shall not perish; we shall live under the Ten-headed One. However, [the optative] is not used in the sense of the immediate future, nor when there is continuity or proximity of action.

The *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes have been prescribed for the past and future non-current times; however, these two are prohibited when there is continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*) or proximity (*sāmīpya*). For example: "He ate food constantly throughout his life," and "He will give [it] constantly. Regarding proximity: "On the immediately preceding full moon, he taught the Dharma of the Guru," and "He will teach it on the coming [full moon].
[Furthermore, the *luṭ* is used] in the future when expressing a limit that is posterior (*avarasmin*).

When a limit is stated, in the lower portion [of that limit], the future tense shall not be used as if it were the immediate past (*anadyatana*). For example: "On this path which is to be traveled as far as the mountain, we shall eat rice with sesame at that point which is lower than the river.
And this also applies when there is a division of time, provided it does not involve periods of day and night (*ahorātra*).

And in the division of time, as before, it shall not be as if it were not of the current day. For example: "Whatever portion of the coming year remains after the full moon of Vaiśākha, we will go to Gayā during that.
However, in the case of a division of time connected with a specific day and night: "In the coming month, on the fifteenth night from now, we will go to Mahābodhi.
In other divisions of time, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*).

In reference to a future division of time other than the immediate present, the *lṛṭ* (future) shall optionally take the place of the *anadyatana-lṛṭ*. For example: "I will hear the Dharma after the Āgrahāyaṇī of the coming year," or "I shall hear it.
When there is a cause for the application of the conditional (*liṅ*), the *lṛṅ* (conditional) is used to express the non-occurrence of the action.

In cases involving cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*) and so forth, when there is a scope for a conditional marker (*liṅ*) and the action is not completed (*kriyātipatti*), the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* shall be used for the future tense. For example: "If I had lived for a thousand years, then I would have fathered a hundred sons.
And [it is also used] for the past tense.

And in the case of the past (*bhūte*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) should occur as before. For example: *yadi śilāḥ komalā abhaviṣyan, tadā kroṣṭubhir evābhakṣayiṣyanta* ("If the stones had been soft, they would have been eaten by jackals").
[This applies] in the presence of *vā* or *āpi*.

Furthermore, by virtue of the word *uta* (and), it is established that the conditional (*lṛṅ*) may optionally occur when referring to the past; [this applies] when there is censure (*garhā*) in the presence of the particles *api* and *jātu*.
*Laṭ* [is used] with *api* and *jātu* when expressing censure.

When the word *jātu* is used in reference to a general time (*kālasāmānya*), the suffix *laṭ* (present tense) shall be employed after a verbal root if censure (*nindā*) is intended. For example: "Does your honor ever officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra? Or: "The ignorant ones sometimes utter mantras; do you even approve of them? [In the sense of inquiry,] when the word *katham* is used, the suffixes *liṅ* (optative) and *laṭ* (present) are optionally employed. [That is, one may say either: "How could your honor [possibly] officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra? or "Does your honor officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra? (in a sense of inquiry).

How is it that when expressing censure (*garhā*), the potential (*liṅ*) and the present (*laṭ*) may optionally occur after the root *kathaṃ-yuj*? For example: "How could he officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra? (*sa kathaṃ śūdraṃ yājayet* or *yājayati*). In the alternative case: *yājayitā*, *yājayiṣyati*, *ayīyajat*, or *yājayāñcakāra*. When there is the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) in the past, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used—*ayājayiṣyat*. "O Kākutstha, how could you have suspected your virtuous beloved?

In this context, however, whenever the conditional (*liṅ*) would otherwise be required due to the non-occurrence of the action, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) must always be understood to apply throughout this section.
The optative (*liṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) are used in the sense of "what" (*kiṃvṛtta*).

When used in conjunction with interrogative pronouns (*kiṃvṛtta*) to express censure (*garhā*), the optative (*liṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) shall be employed. This supersedes all other verbal suffixes. For example: "Who indeed—what sort of person indeed—would officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra, or will so officiate?
[The same applies] even when not joined with interrogative pronouns, to express impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) or intolerance (*amarṣa*).

The optative (*liṅ*) and the future (*lṛṭ*) suffixes may be used after the roots *aśraddhā* (not to trust) and *akṣamā* (not to tolerate), even when combined with an interrogative particle (*akiṃvṛtta*). For example: "I do not believe that your honor would accept an elephant-chariot, nor that you will accept it" (*nāvakalpayāmi bhavān hastirathaṃ pratigṛhṇīyāt, pratigrahīṣyati vā*). "I do not trust it, nor do I tolerate it—that a wicked person should obtain a position, or that he will obtain it" (*na śraddadhe, na kṣame durjanaḥ pratiṣṭhāṃ labheta, lapsyate vā*). The future suffix (*lṛṭ*) is used after the particles *kiṃkila* and those expressing existence (*astyartha*).

The *lṛṭ* (future) suffix shall be used in connection with the words *kiṃkila* and *asti*. For example: "Will your honor indeed drink liquor? (*kiṃkila bhavān surāṃ pāsyati!*); "Will this dwarf indeed take a step? (*kiṃ kramiṣyati kila eṣa vāmanaḥ!*); "It is said that a Śūdra will explain the Veda"—[in such cases] one does not believe it, nor can one tolerate it. [Furthermore, the *liṅ* (optative) suffix is used after the particles *jātu* and *yadā*.]
The suffix *yat* is used after both *yad* and *tad*.
And when *yadā*, *yadā-yadā*, *jātu*, *yad*, *yadā*, *yadi*, *yaccit*, and *yatra* are used as subordinate particles (*upapada*), the potential mood (*liṅ*) alone shall be employed. For example:

"A wise person would never be deluded like an ordinary person" (*na jātu pramuhyet paṇḍito janaḥ*); "It is not conceivable that even you should falter in times of distress" (*nāvakalpyam idaṃ glāyed yat kṛcchreṣu bhavān api*); and "When one such as you would officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra," and so forth. [The potential mood is also used] in the sense of censure (*garhā*).

When *yacca* and *yatra* are used in conjunction with a sense of censure, the potential suffix (*liṅ*) alone should be employed: "That you should sit there, O Great Lord—that is indeed censurable. And [the suffix is used] in the sense of wonder (*citrīkaraṇa*).

And in the sense of "wonder," as before, there shall be only the *liṅ* (optative) suffix; and where we say "we shall tell you what is wonderful," the *lṛṭ* (periphrastic future) and others [are used].
In the remaining cases, the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix is used when it does not begin with *ya*.

The *śeṣa* (remainder) refers to anything other than *yat* and *yatra*. Therefore, after such a *upapada*, only the *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) shall be used to express wonder (*āścarya*). For example: "It is a marvel that a blind man will climb a mountain! or "It is a marvel that a deaf man will study grammar! Why say "other than *yat* and *yatra*"? [Consider: "It would be strange indeed if he were to eat.
When *uta* and *api* are used with the same meaning [of expressing wonder], the *liṅ* (optative suffix) is used.

When used in conjunction with *vāḍham* (yes), *artham* (for the sake of), or *uta* and *api*, the optative (*liṅ*) alone shall be employed. For example: *uta kuryāt* (perhaps he would do it) and *api kuryāt* (even he might do it).
[Furthermore, the optative is used] in the expression of a wish, except when *akaccit* is present.

In the expression of desire (*icchāprakāśana*), there would be an exception to all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) such that only the optative (*liṅ*) would apply: *kāmo me śṛṇuyād bhavān* ("It is my wish that you should hear"). Why is it said "when not preceded by *kaccit*"? [Consider: *kaccij jīvati te pitā?* ("I hope your father is alive?"). This rule does not depend on a governing word (*upapada*); for it is accepted that the communication of a wish is understood through implication.
The rule *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* (Pāṇini 3.3.157), however, depends upon an *upapada* [i.e., a governing word]; thus, these two rules have different scopes.
Furthermore, as for the usage *kāmo me* in this very sūtra, it should be understood as intended for clarity, since the meaning is already implied.
