[The rule] *sambhāvane 'lamiti cet siddhāprayoge* (Pāṇini 3.3.154) [is explained as follows].

If *alam* is understood as "sufficient" (*samabhāvyate*) and yet it is not employed [as a separate word], then the suffix *liṅ* would apply after the verbal root; for example: *api śirasā giriṃ bhindyāt* ("He might even split a mountain with his head"). Why say "*alam*" [in the rule]? [Consider: *videśasthaḥ prāyeṇāyāsyati* ("One staying abroad will likely return").
But in the case of connection with *alam* [meaning "enough"], as in *alaṃ hastinaṃ haniṣyati* ("Enough, he will kill the elephant"), [the suffix *liṅ* does not apply].
In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is stated that when expressing possibility (*sambhāvana*) within the verbal root (*dhātu*), the particle *yad* is not used.

The suffix *liṅ* may optionally occur when a verbal root expressing probability (*sambhāvanā*) follows immediately after [the particle *yadi*], provided that *yadi* is not present. For example: *sambhāvayāmi sa bhuñjīta* (I think it probable that he will eat) or *sa bhokṣyate vā* (or he might eat). Why say "provided that *yadi* is not present"? [Observe: *śraddadhe yat sa bhuñjīta* (I believe that he will eat). [Furthermore, the suffix *liṅ* is used] for the cause (*hetu*) and its effect (*hetumat*).

The *liṅ* (optative) may optionally be used after a verbal root in the sense of cause and its effect. For example: "If he should go by the right [path], the cart would not overturn. In the alternative case, the *lṛṭ* (future) is used; "overturning" here means breaking both [axles]. After verbs expressing desire, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* (imperative) are used.

In connection with verbs having the sense of "desire" (icchā), the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* shall apply as exceptions to all other verbal suffixes. For example: *kāmaye tvaṃ bhuñjīthāḥ* ("I desire that you eat") and *icchāmi sa gacchatu* ("I wish that he go"). When the agents are the same, the suffix *tumun* is used.
And [the suffix] *liṅ* [is used].

When a verb meaning "to desire" (icchārtha) is used with another verb having the same agent (ekakartṛka), the suffixes *tumun* and *liṅ* may be employed. For example: *icchati bhoktum* ("he desires to eat") or *vāñchati gaccheyam* ("he wishes that he might go").
Regarding verbs meaning "to desire," there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) for the present tense as well.

The optative (*liṅ*) may optionally be used in the present tense after a root meaning "to desire. For example: *icchati* or *icchet* ("he desires"); *iccheḥ* ("may you desire") or *kāmayituṃ tvāṃ mām* ("to desire you, me"). Also: *vaṣṭi* or *uśyāt* ("he wishes").
The optative is used in the senses of injunction, invitation, entreaty, request, inquiry, and prayer.

In these meanings, the optative (liṅ) shall be used as an exception to all other verbal suffixes. In the sense of injunction (*vidhi*): "One should give a gift" (*dānaṃ dadyāt*). In the sense of invitation (*nimantraṇa*), which is performing an act out of duty (*niyogataḥ*): "You should eat here" (*iha bhuñjīthāḥ*). In the sense of permission (*kāmacāra*), meaning according to one's own desire: "One may eat as one pleases" (*yathāruci bhuñjīta*). In the sense of entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇa*): "One should teach" (*adhyāpayet*). In the sense of inquiry (*sampraśna*): "What indeed should I study? (*kiṃ nu tam adhīyīya?*). In the sense of begging (*yācñā*): "May I obtain alms? (*labheya bhikṣām*). And the imperative (*loṭ*) is also used in these senses.
In the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) shall also occur. For example: *karotu* (let him do), *vinotu* (let him remove), *adhītām* (let them two study).
Furthermore, the kṛtya suffixes occur in the senses of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*).

Here, *upadeśa* (instruction) is the making known of what was previously unknown; this is said to be a *vidhi* (an injunction). A *praiṣa* (command), however, is merely an urging (*upreṣaṇa*). An *atisarga* (permission) is the authorization for acting according to one's own desire. *Prāptakālatā* (the arrival of the proper time) is the attainment of the time that serves as the cause for an action. When these meanings—command and so forth—are to be understood, the *kṛtya* suffixes may be used, as well as the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix. For example: *tvayā kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ* ("The mat must be made by you") and *tvaṃ kaṭaṃ kuru* ("You, make the mat").

The mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes here is for the purpose of allowing them to coexist with the *loṭ*, thereby indicating through the rule of non-identity (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) that the subsequent rules under the heading of "Feminine" (*stryadhikāra*) are generally applicable. Furthermore, the *liṅ* (optative) suffix is used when the time is within a short duration (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*).

The suffixes *liṅ*, *loṭ*, and *kṛtya* occur after a verbal root when the sense of "more than a moment" (*ūrdhvamauhūrttika*) is to be understood in the sense of an injunction (*preṣa*) and so forth. For example: *muhūrtasyopari kaṭaṃ kuryāḥ* ("After a moment, you should make a mat"), *kaṭaṃ kuru* ("Make a mat"), and *kaṭas tvayā kartavyaḥ* ("A mat is to be made by you"). [Furthermore,] the suffix *loṭ* occurs after a root when followed by the particle *sma*.

In the sense of "immediate sequence" (*anantara-viṣaya*) used with *sma*, only the imperative (*loṭ*) shall be employed. For example: *muhūrtasyopari kaṭaṃ kuru sma* ("Do the mat immediately after a moment").
And [the imperative is also used] in the sense of a request (*adhīṣṭa*).

In this case, when used with *sma*, only the imperative (*loṭ*) shall be employed: "May you teach me, indeed. [Furthermore,] the suffix *tumun* is used after verbs in connection with words expressing time such as *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*.
The optative suffix (liṅ) is used when [the condition] is hypothetical (yadi).

The suffix *tumun* occurs in connection with words such as *kāla*, when an injunction (*praiṣa*) or similar sense is to be understood: *kālo bhoktum* (it is time to eat), *samayo bhoktum* (it is the occasion to eat), *velā bhoktum* (it is the hour to eat).
However, when the word *yat* is used, the suffix *liṅ* is employed: *kālo 'yaṃ yad bhuñjīthāḥ* (this is the time that you should eat).
Furthermore, the *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* occur in the sense of fitness (*arha*).

The suffixes *kṛtya*, *tṛc*, and *liṅ* occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when it is fit (*arha*). A maiden is to be married by a youth; [he is] the one who shall marry the maiden with a youth; a youth should marry a maiden. The suffix *ṇini* occurs in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) and duty (*adharmarṇya*).
And [the suffixes] kṛtya.
The suffix *ṇini* occurs after these two [roots *kṛ* and *dā*]. Examples: *avaśyaṃkārī kaṭasya* ("one who must make a mat"); *śataṃ dāyī ṛṇasya* ("one who must pay a hundred of debt").
And [the suffixes] *kṛtya*: *tvayāvaśyaṃ kaṭaḥ kāryaḥ* ("a mat must be made by you"); *dātavyaṃ śatam* ("a hundred must be paid").
The mention of *kṛtya* is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *ṇini* with them, according to the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*).
The suffixes *śaki* and *liṅ* [are used after a verb when it expresses capability].

The potential mood (liṅ) and the kṛtya suffixes are used in the sense of capability: "He may carry the burden"; "the burden is to be carried by him. In the sense of benediction, the potential mood (liṅ) and the imperative (loṭ) are used.

The suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* occur in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). For example: "May you perform auspicious deeds" (*kalyāṇaṃ vaḥ kriyāsuḥ*); "May the Buddha, the Victor, protect you" (*bauddho jinaḥ pātu vaḥ*); "May Śiva protect [you]" (*śivaḥ pātu*). [In the case of misfortune—this is an alternative reading (pāṭha)—the same applies.
Furthermore, the suffixes *ktic* and *kta* occur when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed.

The suffix *ktic* is applied after a verbal root in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), and *kta* as well, provided that the resulting word is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *tanutāt* (may he extend) → *tantiḥ*; *bhavatāt* (may he be) → *bhūtiḥ*; *vīro bhūyāt* (may he become a hero) → *vīrabhūtiḥ*; *agnir asya bhūyāt* (may fire be his portion) → *agnibhūtiḥ*; *brahmabhūtiḥ*; *vṛddhiḥ*; *buddhiḥ*. *devair asau dāsīṣṭa* (may he be served by the gods) → *devadattaḥ*; *brahmadattaḥ*; *buddhaḥ*. [When the prohibitive particle] *māṅ* [is used], the *luṅ* tense is employed.

When the particle *māṅ* is used with a verbal root, the *luṅ* (aorist) tense shall apply as an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*s). For example: *mā tvaṃ pāpaṃ kārṣīḥ* ("May you not commit sin") and *mā ujjihīrṣīḥ sva-pauruṣam* ("Do not abandon your own manliness"). Furthermore, when followed by *smā*, the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense may also be applied.

The *laṅ* [aorist] suffix shall be used in connection with *mā sma*. Examples: *mā sma karot* ("let him not do") and *mā sma drākṣīr mṛṣā doṣam* ("let him not see a false fault"). Thus, in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* by the Great Professor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.
The third quarter of the third chapter is concluded;
and the *bahula* section is finished.

Regarding the connection between verbal roots (*dhātusambandhe*): when there is a connection between two meanings of a root, suffixes (*pratyaya*) are grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*) even if they belong to different tenses. Examples include: "A son who will kill his paternal uncle is being born" (*pitṛvyaghātī putro janitā*); "Rāma went to the forest and will be [there] tomorrow" (*gato vanaṃ śvo bhavitā rāmaḥ*); "The doorkeeper will become [one]" (*dauvārikaḥ sampatsyate*); "This man was a cow-owner" (*gomānayamabhāsīt*); "While dwelling, he saw" (*vasan dadarśa*); "I have eaten" (*bhuktavānasmi*); "He went while intending to fight" (*yotsyamāno jagāma*). The rule for the application [of suffixes] in the context of a connection between roots applies to the agent (*kartari*).
The imperative suffix (loṭ) is used to express the repetition of an action; after the imperative, the substitutes hi and svu may optionally take the place of ta and dhvam respectively.

When the repetition of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*) is to be understood, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) shall be used for the verbal root even across the three times (past, present, and future). And for that [imperative], the suffixes *hi* and *sva* must be applied. In the case of the second person plural ending *tadhvam*, *hi* and *sva* may optionally be used. For example: *lunīhi lunīhi* (cut, cut!)—he has been cutting repeatedly, he will cut repeatedly, or he cuts repeatedly. *Lunīhi lunīhīty eva* (just "cut, cut!")—they have been cutting repeatedly, they will cut repeatedly, or they cut repeatedly. *Adhīṣvadhīṣva* (study, study!)—he has studied repeatedly, he will study repeatedly, or he studies repeatedly.

In the domain of *tad* (the third person), *hi* and *sva* are optionally used: *lunīta lunīta* or *lunīhi lunīhi*—thus you [plural] cut; or *lunītha*, *laviṣyatha*, or *alāviṣṭa*. Or likewise: *adhīdhvam adhīdhvam* or *adhīṣva adhīṣva*—thus you [plural] study; or *adhyeṣyadhve*, *adhyagīḍhvam*.

And in all cases within this section, there is a relationship between the meaning of the suffix and the meaning of the root employed after it, by way of the relation between the general and the particular.
[This applies] optionally in the case of a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

In the case of a combination of actions (*kriyāsamuccaya*), the imperative (*loṭ*) and other such suffixes may be used. For example: *khamaṭa*, *dyāmaṭa*, *kṣmāmaṭa*—meaning "he wanders thus"; *imāvaṭataḥ* or *ime'ṭanti*—"these two wander" or "these [many] wander. Or: *odanaṃ bhuṅkṣva*, *saktūn piba*, *dhānāḥ khāda*—"eat rice," "drink barley-meal," "chew parched grains"—meaning "he consumes these things. In this manner, it should be inferred for all tenses and numbers. Regarding the rule: "The subsequent verb is used according to the form of the preceding one" (*yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ pūrvasmin*).

In the first case, regarding the prescription of the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, that very root after which the *loṭ* was prescribed must be employed as the auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*). For example: "He cuts" is expressed as *lunīhi lunīhi evāyaṃ lunāti* ("Cut! Cut!—thus he cuts"), and not *chinatti*.
This applies when there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of actions, provided the root used is one expressing a general sense.

In the case of a conjunction [of actions], the augment *luṅ* (the aorist) and *vivadha* (the periphrastic future) must be employed after a verb expressing a general action. For example: *bhuṅkṣva piba khādetyevāyam abhyavaharati* ("He eats, drinks, and chews; thus he consumes"). Here, there are twelve rules concerning Vedic meter (*chandas*). And these are as follows: *chandasi luṅ-laṅ-liṭaḥ* ("In the Veda, the aorist, imperfect, and perfect [suffixes are used]").
The *leṭ* [suffix] occurs in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*).
And [the same applies] in cases of doubt regarding a conversation.
For you: śe, se, sa, e, sen, adhyai, adhye, ka, dhyai, ññ, śadhyai, śadhya, iṣṭave, iṣṭaveṅ, iṣṭavenaḥ.
I go forth for Rohiṣī, the unswerving one.
And for the purpose of seeing and for the purpose of looking about.
The suffixes *ṇamul* and *kamul* are used after a verbal root when capability (*śaki*) is expressed.
The suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* are used after a verbal root when *īśvara* (the agent) is the object.
The suffixes *tavya*, *anīya*, *ya*, *enya*, and *kṛtya* are used in the sense of what ought to be done (*kṛtyārtha*).
And he spoke.
The suffix *tosun* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *kṛ*, *vadi*, *car*, *hū*, *mi*, and *jan* when expressing a characteristic of an action (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*).
The suffix *kasun* occurs after the roots *sṛp*, *tṛd*, and *dṛ*.
In the opinion of the Eastern grammarians, the suffix *ktvā* is used after a verb when it follows the prohibitive particles *alam* and *khalu*.

The term *tum-artha* (the sense of the infinitive suffix *tumun*) continues to apply as far as the rules for indeclinable formations (*avyaya-kṛt*). It has been stated that the sense of *tumun* is "action" (*bhāva*). The suffix *ktvā* shall occur after a verbal root when it is accompanied by the particles *alam* or *khalu*, which express prohibition. Examples: *alaṃ kṛtvā* (having done enough), *khalu kṛtvā* (having indeed done). The meaning is "it should not be done.

However, when there is a connection with an external object (*bāhya-karma*), as in *alam ālambya vyavasāya-bandhyatām* (enough of resorting to a state devoid of resolve) or *khalu uktvā khalu vācikam* (having indeed spoken the verbal message), the accusative case is used because the prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the object—as prescribed by the rule *na loka-*—applies here.

For even when the suffix is in the sense of a state (*bhāva*), the connection with an object still occurs after a transitive root, as stated in the *Bhāgavṛtti*: "The cooking of rice," "having made a mat, he lies down," and "I am going to the village.
The mention of the Easterners (*prāñcaḥ*) is for the sake of honor.
[Now follows: "According to the Northerners (*udīcām*), [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after the root *māṅ* in the sense of reciprocity (*vyatīhāra*)."

The term *māṅ* is a mention of *meṅ*, which has undergone the substitution of *atva*; this is because only that [root] occurs in the sense of exchange (*vyatihāra*). Therefore, according to the opinion of the Northern grammarians, the suffix *ktvā* would be an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for prior time. For example: *pūrvaṃ yācate tato'pamayate* (he first begs and then exchanges), which means *apamitya yācate* (he begs after having exchanged).
This is also the case in connection with "the further and the nearer" (*parāvarayoga*).

When these two [actions] are to be understood as being in conjunction, the suffix *ktvā* shall be used. For example: *bālyamatikramya yauvanam* ("having passed beyond childhood, [one reaches] youth");
the meaning is "after that. *aprāpya nadīṃ giriḥ* ("the mountain, having not reached the river"); the meaning is "on the side of the river" (*avara*).
[This applies] when there are two actions with the same agent, and [the suffix is used for] the earlier time.

The suffix *ktvā* is applied after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting an action occurring at a prior time (*pūrvakāla*), provided that the agent (*kartṛ*) is the same for both actions. Examples: *nītvā hasati* (having led [someone], he laughs). *snātvā bhuktvā pītvā vrajati* (having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he departs). *snātvā bhuktvā śrutvā vrajati* (having bathed, eaten, and heard, he departs). Why "prior time"? *bhuṅkte jalpati ca* (he eats and chatters [simultaneously]). Why "same agent"? *brāhmaṇe bhuktavati sevako vrajati* (when the Brahmin has eaten, the servant departs).
Expressions such as *jhanatkṛtya patati* (falling with a *jhanat* sound) and *akṣiṇī sammīlya hasati* (closing his eyes and laughing) should also be included as supplementary examples.
But here, in such cases as "Having bathed here, one becomes happy" or "Having committed a sin, there would be remorse," the word *sthitasya* ("of one who stands") is to be supplied [as an ellipsis].
Furthermore, the suffix *ṇamul* is used in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇye*).

The suffixes *ṇamul* and *ktvā* may be used after a verbal root to express repetition. Examples: *bhojaṃ bhojaṃ*, *bhuktvā bhuktvā vā vrajati* (he goes along eating repeatedly). *Sthāyaṃ sthāyaṃ kvacid yāntaṃ krāntvā krāntvā sthitaṃ kvacit | na yadyanākāṅkṣe* (if it is not required by the context, one does not go on walking here and stopping there).

If the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* were not permitted after a verbal root when followed by a subordinate word (*upapada*), then [the following would be impossible]: "Since he eats, therefore he studies"; "Since he studies, therefore he sleeps. However, in a sentence that is still expectant of further connection—such as "Since he goes after eating, he will surely study"—[the suffixes are indeed used].
[The rule] *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu* [provides for this optionality].

The sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) has ceased. When these words are used as upapadas, the suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap* may optionally be applied to the verbal root. For example: *agre bhojam* or *agre bhuktvā vrajati* ("having first eaten, he goes"). The same applies to *prathamam* and *pūrvam*.
When a direct object (*karman*) is involved in the sense of reviling, the suffix *khamuñ* is added to the root *kṛ*.

The suffix *khamuñ* is applied after the root *kṛ* when it denotes an object, provided that the sense is one of reviling. For example: *cauraṅkāram ākṣipati* (he reviles him, calling him a thief). Having reviled him with the words *bhītaṅkāram*, Rāvaṇa replied.
[The suffix] *ṇamul* is applied when the sense is "well-tasting" (*svādumi*).

The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *kṛñ* when preceded by words meaning "sweet" (*svādu*) as an upapada. For example: *svāduṅkāram bhuṅkte* ("he eats making it sweet"). The anusvāra is introduced here by means of a formal rule (*nipātana*). Similarly: *miṣṭaṅkāram bhuṅkte*.
[The suffix *ṇamul* is also applied] after the words *anyathā*, *evam*, *katham*, and *ittham*, provided that the action is already established and not being performed for the first time.

In these cases, the suffix *ṇamul* shall be applied after the root *kṛ*, provided that the verb *karoti* is not actually employed because its meaning is already understood. For example: *anyathā bhuṅkte* (he eats otherwise), *anyathākāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats in another manner); *evam vakti* (he speaks thus), *evaṅkāraṃ vakti* (he speaks in this way); *kathaṃkatham āgacchati* (how does he come?); *itthaṃ śete* (he lies down thus), *itthaṅkāraṃ śete* (he lies down in this manner). Why specify "provided that the verb is not employed"? Consider: *anyathā kṛtvā śiro bhuṅkte* (having placed his head otherwise, he eats).
[The suffix *ṇamul* is also used] after the words *yathā* and *tathā* when expressing envy or a retort.

When *yathā* and *tathā* are joined with a verb meaning "to speak" (*vac*) preceded by *asūyā* (disparagement), the suffix *kṛtya* (specifically *ktvā*, i.e., *lyap*) is applied after the root *kṛ*. For example: *yathākāraṃ tathākāraṃ bhuṅkte kiṃ tavātra?* ("He eats according to his own way; what is that to you?").
The mention of *yathātathayoḥ* is a Vedic (sautra) usage. Furthermore, when used in the sense of totality (*sākalya*), the suffix is applied after the roots *dṛś* and *vid* when they take an object.

That [suffix *kha*] occurs after the roots *dṛś* and *vid* when the object is denoted in its entirety. Examples: *brāhmaṇadarśam praṇamati* (he bows down so as to see all the Brahmins); *bhikṣuvedam bhojayati* (he feeds all the monks).
This rule regarding the object applies before the rule concerning the instrument (*karaṇe*) for the root *han*.
It also applies when the extent of the object is indicated for the roots *vid* and *jīv*.
In this case, that [suffix] would apply to these two: *yāvajjīvam adhīte* ("he studies as long as he lives") and *yāvadvedam bhuṅkte* ("he eats as much as the Veda [requires]").
[The suffix applies] after the root *pṛ* when combined with *carman* and *udara*.
The suffix *pūra* (fullness) occurs after these two [words]. He gives sesame seeds filling a skin (*carmapūraṃ tilān dadāti*). He eats filling his belly (*udarapūraṃ bhuṅkte*).
When it denotes the measure of a year, there is optionally the elision of the final syllable.

In the sense of measuring the amount of rain, there is the elision of the vowel *ū* after the root *pṛ* (to fill), or it may remain; thus, "it has rained as much as a cow's footprint" is expressed as either *goṣpadapram* or *goṣpadapūram*. After the root *knūyī* (to moisten), [the suffix *kha* is applied] when referring to a garment (*cela*).

The suffix *sa* (forming a *kṛt* affix) is applied after the root *kup* when *celārtha* ("meaning clothing") is the upapada, provided that the measure of rain is intended; for example: *vastrakropaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("the god rained so much as to wet a garment").
[The suffix *sa* is also applied] after the root *kaṣ* when the upapadas are *nimūla* or *samūla*.

In these two cases, the suffix *sa* (lyap) occurs after the root *kaṣ*. For example: *nimūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati* ("he scrapes away down to the roots") and *samūlakāṣaṃ cakaṣū rudantaḥ* ("they, weeping, scraped them up with their very roots"). After the root *piṣ*, the suffix *sa* occurs when used with the words *śuṣka*, *cūrṇa*, and *rukṣa*.

In these cases, the suffix *sa* (lyap) shall be used after the root *piṣ*. For example: *śuṣkapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi* ("he grinds dryly"), *cūrṇapeṣam*, *rukṣapeṣam*. [The suffix *sa* is also used] after the roots *han*, *kṛñ*, and *grah* when combined with the words *samūla*, *akṛta*, and *jīva* respectively.

In the case of *samūla* and similar words, the suffix *ṇamul* shall be applied after the root *han* and others. For example: *samūlaghātaṃ nyavadhīdarīn ca* ("He struck down the enemies, destroying them along with their very roots"). The meaning is "he struck them down together with their roots.

Indeed, roots such as *kaṣ* and others have their meanings already expressed [by the preceding word], yet they are employed in all cases [with this suffix]. For example: *akṛtakāraṃ kurute* ("He makes what was not made") and *jīvagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* ("He seizes [him] alive"). It has been stated that [this suffix is used] when the object is expressed.
The root *han* [takes the suffix *kvip*] when used in the sense of an instrument.

The suffix *sa* (forming a *saṃjñā*) occurs after the root *han* when it is preceded by a *karaṇa* (instrument) that is not a *pada*. For example: *pāṇighātam hanti*, meaning "he strikes with the hand. Similarly: *śaraghātam arīn hanti*, meaning "he strikes the enemies with arrows.
[The suffix *sa* also occurs] after the root *piṣ* when preceded by a word denoting an unctuous substance (*snehana*).

The suffix *sa* (ṇamul) occurs after the root *piṣ* when "with oil" (*sneha*) is the instrument. For example: *ghṛtapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*, meaning "he grinds with ghee. Similarly: *tailapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*. [The suffix *sa* occurs] after the roots *vṛt* and *grah* when "in the hand" (*haste*) is the locus.

The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *vṛt* and *grah* when preceded by *hasta* and *kara*, provided that they signify the act of taking; likewise, it is applied after the root *puṣ* when preceded by *sva*. Examples: *hastavarttaṃ vartayati* (he turns it with his hand), *karavarttaṃ vartayati* (he turns it with his hand); *hastagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* (he takes her by the hand), *pāṇigrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* (he takes her by the hand).
*Sve puṣaḥ*: [The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *puṣ* when preceded by *sva*].

When words expressing "self" (ātman), "one's own" (ātmīya), "dense" (ghana), or "kinsman" (jñāti) are used as upapadas, the suffix *sa* is applied to the root *puṣ* when it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Examples: *svenāpuṣat*, *svapoṣam apuṣat*. He nourishes his own nourishment (*ātmīyapoṣam*), the nourishment of wealth (*raipoṣam*), the nourishment of the self (*ātmapoṣam*), the nourishment of cattle (*gopoṣam*), the nourishment of wealth (*dhanapoṣam*), or the nourishment of kinsmen (*bandhupoṣam*).
When the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is expressed, the suffix *bandh* is applied.
In the case of *saṃjñā*.

The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after the root *bandh* when preceded by a word that serves as its support (*ādhāra*). Thus, in the sense of "protecting," one says *guptiṃ badhnāti* ("he binds for protection") or *guptibandhaṃ badhnāti* ("he performs the act of binding for protection"). Similarly, *cakraṃ badhnāti* ("he binds in a circle") or *cakrabandhaṃ badhnāti* ("he performs the act of circular binding").

However, in cases such as *mayūrikābandhaṃ baddhaḥ*, *cāṇḍālikābandhaṃ baddhaḥ*, and *aṭṭālikābandhaṃ baddhaḥ*, the *Mahābhāṣya* states that the suffix *ṇamul* is applied because these are instances where the object (*karman*) is used both as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and as the actual object (*karman*).
There is no destruction for the two agents, the individual soul (jīva) and the person (puruṣa), who are not Śiva.

When *jīva* or *puruṣa* ending in the agentive case (*kartari*) is the upapada, the suffix *kha* (forming *khac*) is applied after the roots *naś* and *vah*. For example: *jīvanneva naṣṭaḥ* becomes *jīvanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ* ("perished while still living"); *puruṣaḥ san vahati* becomes *puruṣavāhaṃ vahati* ("carried by a man"). [The suffix *kha* is also applied] after the roots *śuṣi* and *pūr* when preceded by *ūrdhva*.

The suffix *sa* (kṛt) occurs after the roots *śuṣ* and *pṝ* when used with the word *ūrdhva* as the agent; [thus] *ūrdhvaśoṣam* means "he dries while standing upright," and *ūrdhvapūram* means "it is filled while standing upright. It also occurs when the object is a word expressing a comparison (*upamāna*).

That suffix (kyaṅ) shall occur after a verbal root when the word in comparison is used as the object or the agent. Regarding the object: *ratnanidhāyaṃ nihitaḥ* ("placed like a treasure of jewels"), *ghṛtavilāyaṃ vilīnaḥ* ("melted like clarified butter"). Regarding the agent: *mṛganāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ* ("perished like a deer"), *ajakanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ* ("perished like a goat").
In the case of roots such as *kaṣ*, there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) according to the specific rule.

In rules such as *nimūla-samūlayoḥ kaṣaḥ*, the verb root itself must be employed in the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*) following the suffix *ṇamul*; this has been illustrated accordingly. And that [subsequent usage] occurs even when there is an intervention, just like the subsequent usage in the case of *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition); for example, as stated in the Bhāgavṛtti: *ghṛtanidhāyam udakaṃ nidadhāti* ("he places the water down, repeatedly depositing it with ghee").
In the third [case], there is the use of the word *upadaṃśa*.

The term *upadaṃśa* (eating with a side-dish) occurs when it has a word ending in the third case as its attendant (*upapada*). For example: *mūlakenopadaṃśya* or *mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats with a radish as a side-dish"). From this point onward, the formation of an *upapada-samāsa* is optional. Thus, one may also say: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*.
[This also applies] to verbs meaning "injury" provided they share the same object.

When a word ending in the third case is used as an upapada, that [suffix *ṇamul*] shall occur after a root meaning "to strike" (*hiṃsā*). For example: *daṇḍopaghātaṃ gāḥ kālayati* (he drives the cows while striking them with a staff), or *daṇḍenopaghātam*. Why is it said "when they have the same object" (*samānakarmakāṇām*)? [Consider: *daṇḍenāhatya vyāghraṃ gāḥ kālayati* (having struck the tiger with a staff, he drives the cows).
Also, [the suffix occurs] when *upapīḍ*, *rudh*, and *karṣ* are used with a word in the seventh case.

When words ending in the seventh (locative) or third (instrumental) case are used as *upapadas*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *pīḍ* preceded by *upa*, as well as after *rudh* and *kṛṣ*. Examples: *pārśvopapīḍaṃ śete* (he lies down pressing against his sides), or *pārśvayor upapīḍam* (pressing against the two sides). *Stanopapīḍam āśliṣyati* (she embraces while pressing against her breasts), or *stanābhyām upapīḍam* (pressing with the two breasts). Similarly, Bhaṭṭi [uses] *hastarodhaṃ dadhad dhanuḥ* (holding the bow while obstructing with his hand). *Pāṇikarṣaṃ vaṭakān atti* (he eats the dumplings while pulling them with his hand), or *pāṇinā karṣam* (pulling with the hand). Since no specific distinction is made, *pāṇyupakarṣam* is also valid.
In the case of proximity.

That [suffix] shall occur after a verbal root when the words ending in the third or seventh case are used as *upapadas* in the sense of "proximity" (*sannidhāna*) or "attainment" (*gati*). For example: *keśagrāhaṃ yudhyante* ("they fight seizing by the hair"), or *keśair grāham*, or *keśeṣu grāham*.
And [the suffix occurs] in the sense of "measure" (*pramāṇa*).

In the sense of "extent" (*āyāma*), that [suffix *ghañ*] occurs after the aforementioned prepositions (*upapada*). One cuts the staff with an increase of two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgulotkarṣam*). Cutting the limbs of enemies in battle with an increase of two finger-breadths.
[The suffix *ghañ* is used] in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) when there is a desire for haste (*parīpsā*).

That suffix shall occur after a verbal root that has an ablative (apādāna) as its upapada when there is haste; for example, *śayyotthāyaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats immediately upon rising from bed"). It also occurs after [a root] having a second case (dvitīyā) as its upapada.

The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after a verbal root that has an object as its upapada when there is haste. For example: *loṣṭagrāhaṃ yudhyante* ("they fight seizing clods of earth"). Here, they say that the word "haste" (*tvarā*) does not carry over [from the previous rule]. By this, the formation of *ṇamul* in the sense of "excluding one" (*ekavarjam*) is established. The point is that the word "haste" (*parīpsā*) from the rule *apādāne parīpsāyām* does not carry over here; "haste" (*parīpsā*) means "speed" (*utvarā*).
[The suffix *ṇamul* is also applied] after a verbal root whose object is a non-permanent part of one's own body (*svāṅge'dhruve*).

That [suffix *am*] shall occur after a verbal root when the object is one's own limb (*svāṅga*). Examples: *akṣinikocam hasati* (he laughs with a contraction of the eyes); *bhrūkṣepam vakti* (he speaks with a raising of the eyebrows). Why "when not fixed" (*adhruve*)? [Consider: *utkṣipya śiraḥ kathayati* (having raised his head, he speaks). That [limb] upon whose being severed the living being dies is considered "fixed" (*dhruva*).
And while being afflicted.

In the case of *kleśi*, it [the suffix *ṇini*] occurs when the action refers to one's own limb; for example, *uraḥpratiṣpaśo yudhyante* ("they fight with their chests bared"). This *yoga* (rule) has a fixed meaning (*dhruvārtha*).
[The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after the roots *viś*, *pat*, *diś*, and *skand* in the senses of "being pervaded" and "being served."

When a word denoting an object (*karman*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *kha* (forming a feminine noun) occurs after roots such as *viś* and others, provided there is pervasion of a substance (*dravyavyāpti*) and the action is constant (*kriyānityatā*). Examples: *gehapraveśam āste* ("he sits [repeatedly] entering the house"); *latānupātaṃ kusumāny agṛhṇāt* ("he gathered flowers, following along the creepers"); *maṇḍapānuprapādam āste* ("he sits, stepping into the pavilions one after another"); *nadyavaskandaṃ ācāmati* ("he sips water, leaping down into the river"). However, in the absence of compounding, there is reduplication according to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*—such as *gehaṃ gehaṃ praveśam* or *gehaṃ praveśaṃ praveśam*, and so forth.
The suffix *kha* also occurs after the roots *as* (to throw) and *tṛṣ* (to thirst) when time is the intervening factor between actions.

The suffix *sa* (kṛt) is applied after the roots *as* ("to throw") and *tṛṣ* ("to thirst") when followed by a word denoting time that functions as an interval for an action. Examples: *dvyahātyāsam* "he causes the cows to drink [after] an interval of two days"; *dvyahatarṣam*. The meaning is "having passed two days.
[Also, the suffix *sa* is applied after the root *diś* ("to point out") when followed by a name (*nāman*) or the word *ādiśi* ("instructing").]

The suffix *ñ* (forming the feminine noun) occurs after the words *nāman*, *ādeśa*, and *grahaṇa* when used as the object of the verb *kṛ*. One says: *nāmādeśam ācaṣṭe* ("he pronounces the name") or *nāmagrāham stauti* ("he praises by mentioning the name"). When an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is used to express something contrary to what was intended, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are added to the root *kṛ*.

The suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* may follow the root *kṛ* when preceded by an indeclinable (*avyaya*) as an upapada, provided that the context is the reporting of something undesirable. Example: "A son has been born to you, O Brāhmaṇa! [To which he replies: "What then? A low-caste man (*vṛṣala*) reports it by saying *nīcaiḥkṛtya* or *nīcaiḥkāram*. Indeed, it is appropriate to report pleasant news loudly. Example: "Announcing the death of the king due to the grief of separation from Rāma, they cried out *uccaiḥkāram*," or *uccaiḥkṛtya*. However, in this case, it is appropriate to report unpleasant news in a low voice.
[The suffix *ṇamul* is used] after the word *tiryak* when the action is completed.

After the word *tiryak*, when used in the sense of completion, the suffixes *kṛn* and *kvip* may occur before the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*. For example: *tiryakkṛtya gataḥ* or *tiryakkāram gataḥ*; the meaning is "having completed [the action] sideways.
[The suffix] *tas* occurs after a word denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*) when followed by the suffix *t* and the roots *kṛ* or *bhū*.

When a word ending in a suffix having that as its cause (tas-pratyaya) is used as an upapada, the suffixes *ktvā* and *am* (denoted by *tau*) shall be applied after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*. For example: *mukhataḥkṛtya gataḥ* ("having gone after making [it] in front"), or *mukhataḥkāram*; likewise, *pṛṣṭhatobhūya*, or *pṛṣṭhatobhāvam*.
[This does not apply] when a suffix expressing the sense of *nañ* or *ā* is present, nor in the sense of the *cvī* suffix.

When words having the sense of *nañ* (negation), *dhā* (division), or *cvī* (change of state) are used as upapadas, the suffixes *ktvā* and *am* are applied after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*. Examples: *nānākṛtya gataḥ*, or *nānākāram* (having become different); *nānābhūya*, or *nānābhāvam* (having become separate). In the sense of *dhā*: *dvidhākṛtya*, or *dvidhākāram* (having made twofold); *dvaidham bhāvam*, or *dvaidham bhūya* (having become twofold). Why is there a mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*)? [To exclude cases where the word is not a suffix: *pṛthak kṛtvā* (having made separate). [The rule continues: After the root *bhū*, when preceded by *tūṣṇīm*, the suffix *am* is applied.

When the word *tūṣṇīm* is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffixes *kvi* and *a* shall be applied after the root *bhū*. Thus: *tūṣṇīmbhūya āste* (he remains silent) or *tūṣṇīmbhāvam* (the state of being silent). [The suffix] *anvac* is used in the sense of conformity (*ānulomya*).
The suffixes *ktvā* and *am* may follow the root *bhū* when preceded by the prefix *anvaga*, provided there is conformity (*ānukūlya*). Thus: *anvagbhūyāste* or *anvagbhāvam āste*.
Those compounds beginning with the third case (instrumental) which have been mentioned are optionally compounded with the suffix *ktvā*.
The suffix *tumun* is used after the roots *śak*, *dhṛṣ*, *ājñā*, *glā*, *ghaṭ*, *rabh*, *labh*, *kram*, *sah*, and *arh* when they have the sense of "to be able" (*asti-artha*).

The suffix *tumun* is applied after a verbal root when it has as its attendant word (*upapada*) a term such as *śak* (to be able), etc. Examples: *śaknoti bhoktuṃ bālakaḥ* (the child is able to eat); *arhati dātum* (he deserves to give); *asti bhoktum* (there is [an opportunity] to eat); *vidyate bhoktum* (it is found that there is to eat).
This rule applies when the attendant word does not denote an action;
it applies to words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*) in the sense of "being capable of" (*alam*).

*Paryāpti* means sufficiency or fullness. After a verbal root (*dhātu*) used with words expressing that [sufficiency], the suffix *tumun* shall be employed when the sense is one of capability regarding a specific object. Examples: *alaṃ bhoktum* (capable of eating), *pārayati dātum* (is able to give).
Why "after words expressing sufficiency"? Consider: *alaṃ bhuktvā* (enough after having eaten), *alaṃ kṛtvā* (enough after having done).
This concludes the section on the connection of roots with the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
The section on *kṛt* suffixes used in the sense of the agent:
"A *kṛt* suffix [is applied] when the agent is to be expressed."

Verbal roots whose meaning has not already been expressed [by another suffix] form their derivatives in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: *odanasya pācakaḥ* (the cooker of rice), *pakvavān* (one who has cooked), *nandanaḥ* (one who delights), *grāhī* (one who seizes), *pacaḥ* (one who cooks).
It has been stated that indeclinable *kṛt*-suffixes occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*).
Alternatively, the following may optionally occur in the sense of the agent: *bhavya*, *geya*, *pravacanīya*, *upasthānīya*, *janya*, *āplāvya*, and *āpātya*.

These seven [suffixes] may optionally occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). For example: *bhavyo 'yam* ("this one is capable") or *bhavyam anena* ("he is capable by means of this"); *geyo 'yaṃ sāmnām* ("this one is a singer of Sāmans") or *geyāny anena sāmāni* ("the Sāmans are to be sung by him"). [Now follows: "The letter *l* [denotes] the object (*karman*) as well as the state (*bhāva*) after intransitive verbs."

The *lakāra*s (verbal suffixes) occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and also in the sense of the object (*karman*). [Examples: *annaṃ pacati* (he cooks the food); *pacyate 'nnam* (the food is cooked).

From intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*), they occur in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*): *śete vipraḥ* (the Brahmin lies down); *śayate vipreṇa* (it is slept by the Brahmin). The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes occur only in those two senses (agent and object).
These [suffixes] occur only in the sense of the state of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*): *kaṭo 'nena kartavyaḥ* ("a mat is to be made by him"), *kāryaḥ*, *kṛtaḥ*.
In the sense of the suffix *khal*: *īṣatkaraḥ* ("easy to do").

From an intransitive verb in the sense of the state of being: *bhavitavyam anena* ("he must be"), *bhūtam*, *durāḍhyambhavam* ("it is difficult for one to become wealthy"), *īṣadāḍhyambhavam* ("it is easy for one to become wealthy").
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action, and it may also denote the agent.

The affix *kta* occurs after a verbal root when it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) in connection with an action that has begun, and also when it denotes the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). For example: *prabhukto odanaṃ vipraḥ* (the Brahmin has eaten the rice) [agent]; *prabhukta odano vipreṇa* (the rice was eaten by the Brahmin) [object].
Furthermore, the affix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "to go," after intransitive roots, and after the roots *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*.

The suffix *kta* shall occur after these [roots] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: "the traveler has gone to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ pānthaḥ*), "set out" (*prasthitaḥ*), "gone" (*yātaḥ*). After intransitive roots (*akarmaka*): "he sat" (*āsitaḥ*), "he stood" (*sthitaḥ*). After roots such as *śliṣ* preceded by the prefix *ā*: "he embraced the maiden" (*āśliṣṭaḥ kanyām*), "he surpassed the teacher" (*atiśayito gurum*), "he waited upon him" (*upāsthitastam*), "he served him" (*upāsitastam*), "he dwelt with him" (*anuṣitastam*), "he was born after him" (*anujātastam*), "he climbed the tree" (*āruḍhastarum*), "he grew old after him" (*anujīrṇastam*). By the force of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, it also occurs according to what is otherwise prescribed: "the village was gone to by him" (*gato grāmo 'nena*), "it was gone by him" (*gatamanena*).
The particle *ca* (and) is understood here; therefore, by the prescription of additional [suffixes], the forms *vyavasita*, *pratipanna*, and so forth are established.
The suffixes *dāś* and *goghra* occur when the recipient (*sampradāna*) is expressed.
These two [suffixes] are substituted here: a *brāhmaṇa* who possesses good qualities is a *dāśa*; a guest who harms cows is a *goghra*.
[The suffix *ka* is applied] after words such as *bhīma* when they denote the point of departure (*apādāna*).
These would be *sādhavaḥ* (grammatically correct) here: *bhīmaḥ*, *bhīṣmaḥ*, *bhayānakaḥ*, *rahaḥ*, *khalatiḥ*, *rakṣa*, *prapatanaḥ*, *samudraḥ*.
Other than these two [categories], there are the *uṇādi* derivatives.

The *uṇādi* suffixes are to be understood as occurring elsewhere than in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*) or the point of departure (*apādāna*). For example: *vṛttaṃ* (a path) from the root *vṛt*, and *bhasitaṃ* (ashes) from the root *bhas*.
Furthermore, the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after roots whose meanings involve stability (*dhrauvya*), motion (*gati*), or consumption (*pratyavasāna*).

The suffix *kta* shall be used after these [roots] in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also used as prescribed by general rules. Roots meaning stability are intransitive (*akarmaka*). Examples: *idameṣām āsitam* (this is the place where they sat), *ihānenāsitam* (here he sat), *ayamatrāsitaḥ* (he has sat here). *idamahēḥ sṛptam* (this is the place where the serpent crawled), *idamahinā sṛptam* (the serpent crawled here), *ayamahinā sṛpto deśaḥ* (this region was crawled over by the serpent), *ihāhiḥ sṛptaḥ* (the serpent crawled here). From a root meaning eating: *idamasya bhuktam sthānam* (this is the place where he ate), *ihānena bhuktam* (he ate here), *bhukto'nenaudanaḥ* (rice was eaten by him).

And here, in the expressions "the brothers have been divided," "the Brahmins have been fed," and "the cows have been drunk [from]," the suffix *a* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) to words ending in the past passive participle (*bhāvaktānta*).
Thus, [the forms] *uktāḥ* and *kṛtāḥ* are explained.
Of Lasya.
This is a governing rule (adhikāra):
*ti*, *tas*, *jhi*, *si*, *thas*, *tha*, *mi*, *vas*, *mas*; *tā*, *ātām*, *jha*, *thās*, *āthām*, *dhvam*, *iṭ*, *vahi*, *mahin*.

In place of *la*, these suffixes beginning with *ti* shall occur: *bhavati*, *bhavataḥ*, *bhavanti*; *pacate*, *pacete*, *pacante*. [The forms] *bhūyate* occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*); *pacyate* occurs in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). In this manner, it should be inferred for the *liṅ* and other moods as well. [Furthermore, by the rule] *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*: [The final *e* of those *ātmanepada* suffixes that have a *ṭ* marker is replaced by *i*.]

In the *ātmanepada*, the substitution of *e* for the portion beginning with *ṭi* [i.e., the last vowel and following consonant] shall occur after a root ending in *ṭu*. Thus: *pacate*, *pacante*, *pecāte*, *paktāsāthe*, *pakṣyate*.
How is it that *pacamānaḥ* [is formed]? Because of the mention of *taṅ* [the *ātmanepada* suffixes] as the subject under discussion.
[And] *se* is substituted for *thās*.
For the *thās* of the *ṭi*-class [roots], *se* shall be substituted. [Examples: *pacase*, *kriyase*. For the *liṭ* [affixes] *jhi* and *as*, *eś* and *irec* [shall be substituted].
In place of *ta* and *jha*, which are the substitutes for *liṭ*, there shall be *eś* and *irec*, respectively. Thus: *pece*, *pecire*.

For the *parasmaipada* [terminations] of *liṭ*, there shall be *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*, *thal*, *atha*, *us*, *ṇal*, and *vam*. The determination of the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is based on semantic proximity (*arthāntaratamya*), as there is no identity of form (*śabdasāmya*). Thus: *cakāra*, *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*; *cakartha*, *cakrathuḥ*. Since there is no purpose for a partial substitution (*antādeśa*) of *tha*, the letter *a* is a full substitution (*sarvādeśa*)—thus: *cakra*. [And finally: *cakāra*, *cakara*, *cakṛva*, *cakṛma*.
The suffix *laṭ* is optionally replaced by *vid*.

In the *laṭ* [present tense], the *parasmaipada* endings may optionally be replaced by *ṇal* and the others. Thus: *veda*, *vidatuḥ*, *viduḥ*; *vettha*, *vidathuḥ*, *veda*; *veda*, *vidvaḥ*, *vidmaḥ*. In the alternative [when the original endings remain]: *vetti*, *vittaḥ*, *vidanti*, and so forth.
Of the five [verbal suffixes] beginning with the first, [the augment] āḍ is applied to those beginning with āha and bruvaḥ.

For the five [suffixes] beginning with *parasmaipada* of the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *brū*, the five [suffixes] beginning with *ṇal* may optionally be substituted; and for the root *bru*, the substitute *āh* is applied. Thus: *āha*, *āhatuḥ*, *āhuḥ*; *āttha*, *āhathuḥ*. In the alternative [case]: *bravīti*, *brūtaḥ*, *bruvanti*; *bravīṣi*, *brūthaḥ*.
The imperative (*loṭ*) follows the pattern of the aorist (*laṅ*).

The *loṭ* [imperative] should undergo the same operations as the *laṅ* [imperfect]. There is the elision of the suffixes *tām*, *tam*, *ta*, and *si*. [Examples: *pacatām*, *pacatam*, *pacata*, *pacāva*, *pacāma*.
[In the case of the root *pā* "to drink,"] *e* [is replaced by] *uḥ*.

The *u* should be substituted for the *loṭ* affix *kāra*. [Examples: *pacatu*, *pacantu*. It must be stated that the substitution of *u* is prohibited after the affixes *hi* and *ni*. [Examples: *lunīhi*, *karavāṇi*, *pacāni*.
[The rule] *ser hy apicca* [applies].

The *sip* of the imperative (*loṭ*) shall be replaced by *hi*, and that [replacement] is also considered as not being marked with *p* (i.e., it is treated as having the *apṛkta* designation). Examples: *lunīhi*; *rādhnuhi*.
Or, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is an option.
Vedic;
the peak of Mount Meru.
For the *loṭ* [imperative] endings, *mip* is replaced by *ni*. Thus: *bhavāni*, *pacāni*. For the ending *ta*, *ām* is substituted.
The substitution of *am* shall occur for the *loṭ* affix *kār*. [Examples: *kurutām*, *kurvātām*.
[And] *vām* is optionally substituted for *sva* and *bhyām*.
In place of the single *e* of the imperative (*loṭ*), *am* and *au* may optionally occur after *sa* and *vas* respectively. [Examples: *śrāddhaṃ kuruṣva*, *kurudhvam*.
Furthermore, for the first person (*uttama*) ending, *āṭ* is added and it is also treated as having the marker *p*.
The augment *aṭ* shall be added to the first person of the imperative (*loṭ*), and that *aṭ* is followed by *pit*. [Examples: *karavāṇi*, *tanavāni*; *karavāva*, *tanavāva*.
[In this context,] *e* becomes *ai*.

In place of the final vowel of the first person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*), there shall be the substitution of *e* for the long *ā*. This is an exception to [the rule regarding] *ām*. Examples: *tanavai*, *tanavāvahai*.
Here, the group of five sūtras concerning the subjunctive (*leṭ*) constitutes a portion of the Vedic section. And this is that group of five sūtras:
*leṭo’ḍāṭau*.
From here, indeed!
Except elsewhere.
And for this reason as well,
there is elision [of the *śap*] before the *parasmaipada* endings.
That belongs to the highest.
The two rules "there is elision [of the augment] in the *parasmaipada* endings" and "that [elision] applies to the last [person]" are hereby governed.
[This applies] always to that which has the marker *ṅ*.

There shall be elision of the *sakāra* of the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) following a *lakāra* that has an *ik* vowel [as its penultimate]. The inclusion of the term "nitya" (invariably) is meaningful in the case of a single substitute. Examples: *apacāva*, *apacāma*; *paceva*, *pacema*; *apākṣva*, *apākṣma*; *apakṣyāva*, *apakṣyāma*.
Also, [there is elision] after an *ik* vowel.
There shall be elision of the letter *i* following the letter *ṅ*. Examples: *apacat*, *pacet*, *apacaḥ*. This applies only when *parasmaipada* endings are used—as in *apacāvahi*—but not otherwise.
[Furthermore,] for the suffixes *ta*, *tha*, *tha*, and *mi*, there shall be substituted *tā*, *ta*, *n ta*, and *āma* respectively.
For the *liṅ* [optative] ending beginning with *ta*, there shall be *tām* and so forth. [Examples: *apacatām*, *apacatam*, *apacata*, *apacam*.
For the *liṅ*, there is the augment *sīyuṭ*.
The augment *sīyuṭ* shall be added to the optative (*liṅ*). [Examples: *kurvīta*, *kurvīyātām*, *kṛṣīṣṭa*, *kṛṣīyāstām*.
The suffix *yāsuṭ* is added to the active endings (*parasmaipada*) and is both udātta-accented and marked with the *ṅit* indicator.

The augment *yāsuṭ* shall be added to the optative (*liṅ*) in the *parasmaipada* endings; and it functions like a *ṅit* suffix. [Examples: *kuryāt*, *kuryātām*, *kuryuḥ*; *kriyāt*, *kriyāstām*, *kriyāsuḥ*.
[Furthermore,] *yāsuṭ* is *kit* in the benedictive (*āśīḥ*).
In the *āśīr* (benedictive) mood, the *liṅ* suffix shall have *yāsuṭ*, which is *kit*. Examples: *ijyāt*, *jāgaryāt*.
Why "in the *āśīr*"? [To exclude] the injunctive (*vidhi*) and other moods—e.g., *yajet*, *jāgṛyāt*. [In the *liṅ* of the *āśīr*,] *ran* replaces *jha*.
In place of *jha* following a *liṅ* (optative), *ran* shall be substituted. Thus: *paceran*, *kurvīran*, *kṛṣīran*.
[And] after an *iṭ* augment, there is *at*.
In the optative (liṅ), *iṭ* shall be replaced by *at*. [Examples: *kurvīya*, *kṛṣīya*.
[The augment] *suṭ* [is applied] before *ti* and *tha*.
The augment *suṭ* shall be applied after the *liṅ* suffixes *ta* and *tha*. [Examples: *kṛṣīṣṭa*, *kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ*. [Furthermore,] *jus* is substituted for *jhi*.
The *jus* should replace the *jhi* of the optative (*liṅ*). [Examples: *paceyuḥ*, *pacyāsuḥ*.
[This applies] after the *sic*, after reduplicated stems (*abhyasta*), and after the root *vid*.

For these [roots], the *jhi* of the following *ṅit* and *l*-marked [suffixes] becomes *jus*: *sic*—*akārṣuḥ*; the reduplicated (*abhyasta*)—*ajāgaruḥ*; *vid*—*aviduḥ*. [Also after a root ending in] *ā*.

After a root ending in a vowel that ends in *sij* and lacks the *luK* elision, *jus* shall be substituted for *jhi*. Examples: *aduḥ*, *adhuḥ*. Not here: *abhūvan*. According to Śākaṭāyana, this applies only to the *laṅ* [aorist].
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a verbal root denoting enmity (*dviṣ*).

According to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana, the suffix *jhi* of the *laṅ* [aorist] following a verbal root ending in a vowel, as well as the root *dviṣ*, shall be replaced by *jus*. Thus: *ayuḥ*, *avuḥ*, *adviṣuḥ*.
According to others: *ayān*, *avān*, *adviṣan*. The *tiṅ* suffixes have been explained.
The thirty [suffixes] beginning with *ti* are termed *sārvadhātuka*.
A suffix (pratyaya) that has a *tiṅ* as its marker shall be designated by the name *sārvadhātuka*. Examples: *nayati*, *roditi*, *pacyate*, *utpibaḥ*, *śūrammanyaḥ*, *kurvāṇaḥ*, *kurvan*.
The remainder [of suffixes] shall be designated by the name *ārdhadhātuka*.

That which is ordained after a verbal root (*dhātu*) by means of *taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) and *śit* (suffixes beginning with *ś*), other than these, shall be called *ārdhadhātuka*. [Examples: *bhavitā*, *bhaviṣyati*, *bhavitavyam*, *bhavitum*.
And [the suffix] *liṭ* is also [an *ārdhadhātuka*].
The word *eva* (only) is understood [from the previous rule]. A substitute for *liṭ* shall have the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka* only. Examples: *pecitha*, *śekitha*, *jagle*.
[Regarding] *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*):
a substitute for *liṅ* in the sense of benediction shall have the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka* only. Example: *paviṣīṣṭa*.
Why [is it] "in the benedictive" (āśiṣi)? [Consider: *punīyāt*.
[The rule] "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasy ubhayathā*) [applies].
[This is] Vedic.
It has been stated [that the suffixes apply] after a verbal root.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva, as well as the "Quarter on the Connection with Verbal Roots" (*dhātusaṃbandhapāda*).
The Fourth Chapter. The First Pāda. [Sūtra 1:
From a feminine suffix (ṅī), a neuter suffix (āp), or a nominal stem (prātipadika).
The base (prakṛti) of taddhita suffixes such as *svādiṭa* and others is now governed [as the subject].
*Kha*, *au*, *jas*, *am*, *auṭ*, *cha*, *ṣa*, *ṭā*, *bhyām*, *bhis*, *ṅe*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*, *ṅasi*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*, *ṅas*, *os*, *ām*, *ṅi*, *os*, *sup*:
these *sup* suffixes shall follow nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in vowels or consonants. [Examples: *nadī*, *nadyau*, *nadyaḥ*; *rāmā*, *rāme*, *rāmāḥ*; *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣau*, *vṛkṣāḥ*.
In the feminine.

This is a governing rule (adhikāra), extending as far as "from a word standing in the nominative case among those that are semantically connected" (samarthānāṃ prathamād vā). [The suffix] *ṭāp* is applied after words beginning with *ajā* and ending in short *a*.

The suffix *ṭāp* shall be applied in the feminine after a class of words beginning with *ajā* and after those ending in short *a*. Examples: *ajā*, *akhā*, *kokilā* (as a genus). [The suffix is applied] after *pūrvahāyanī* because it ends in a *ṭi*-letter: *jyeṣṭhā*, *kaniṣṭhā*, *madhyamā*. After a word in compound with *paṅkti*: *daṃṣṭrā*. After *phala* when preceded by *sam*, *bha*, *sva*, *ajina*, *śaṇa*, or *piṇḍa*: *samphalā*, and so forth. After *puṣpa* when preceded by *sat*, *prāk*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, or *eka*: *satapuṣpā*, *ekapuṣpā*.

The word *śūdrā* is a genus (*jāti*) that does not have the prefix *mahat*. However, for one preceded by *mahat*, it is *mahāśūdrī*. [The suffix] *ṅīp* follows words ending in *mūla*. *amūlā*. This inclusion in the list beginning with *aja* is an exception (*bādhaka*) to the *ṅīṣ* suffix and others prescribed for genus and other categories. [The suffix *ṅīp* follows] words ending in short *a*. *khaṭvā*. *devadattā*. Why "with a following *t*" (*tapara*)? [Consider: *śaṃsthāḥ* (the woman who is well-established).
*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*: After bases ending in *ṛ* or *n*, the suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied in the feminine. Examples: *kannī*, *daṇḍinī*. Also after bases marked with the *ugit* designation.

The affix *ḍīp* shall occur after a stem ending in *uk*. Examples: *gomatī*, *śreyasī*, *pacantī*, *atibhavatī*. There is a prohibition [of this rule] when the *uk* belongs to a verbal root (*dhātu*). Examples: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*. An addition should be made for the root *añc*: *prācī*, *pratīcī*.
The suffix *ḍīp* occurs after the roots *vṛ* and *vṛñ*, and the letter *r* is substituted for the final letter [of the root]. Examples:

*dhīvarī*, *pīvarī*, *paralokadṛśvarī*, *svarlokadṛśvarī*, *sahakṛtvarī*, *sutvarī*. How is it that *atiśunī* and *niḥśunī* are formed? Because the rule applies only to words that possess meaning (*arthavadgrahaṇāt*).

It should be stated that [the suffixes] do not apply after *haś*. The feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* do not occur after a word ending in *vaṃ* (m) which is followed by *haś*. For example: *rājayudhvā* as a feminine. However, the word *śarvarī* ends in the *uṇādi* suffix *varaṭ*. *pādo 'nyatarasyām*:
The suffix *ṅīp* may optionally occur after a word ending in *pād*. Examples: *vipadī* or *dvipadā*.
*ṭābṛci*:
After a word ending in *pāda*, when it signifies a verse (*ṛc*), the suffix *ṭāp* shall be applied. [Examples: *dvipadā*, *tripadā* (verse).
[Exception: Not after words such as *ṣaṣ* or *khaśra*.

The feminine suffix shall not occur after words denoting the number six, nor after *svasṛ* and the like. For example: *pañca striyaḥ* ("five women"), likewise *sapta*, *nava*, and *kati*. This prohibition applies even when these numbers are at the end of a compound, as in *priyapañcāno veśyāḥ* ("courtesans whose favorite number is five"). Regarding *svasṛ* and the like: *svasā*, *tisraḥ*, *catasraḥ*, *nanāndā*, *duhitā*, *yātā*, *mātā*, and according to Bhāguri, *naptā*. Regarding *man*: the suffix *ṅīp* shall not occur after words ending in *man*. For example: *pāmā*, *pāmānau*; *sīmā*, *sīmānau*. This prohibition applies even when the word ends in such a form, as in *atipaṭimā*, *atipaṭimānau*.
The *ano-bahuvrīhi* rule:
the suffix *ṅīp* shall not occur after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *an*. For example: *suparvā*, *suparvāṇau*. Why "after a *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīheḥ*)? [Consider: *surājñī*.
[The suffix] *ḍāp* may optionally occur after both [the aforementioned types of compounds].

The suffix *ḍāp* may optionally occur after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *mann* or *an*. Thus: *sīmāḥ* or *sīmānaḥ*; *suparvāḥ* or *suparvāṇaḥ*. This is because in the rules concerning the suffixes *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man*, there is no mention of meaningful (*arthavat*) elements [but rather of the suffixes themselves]. Examples include: *supaṭimāḥ* or *supaṭimānaḥ striyaḥ*; *nirgarimāḥ* or *nigarimāṇaḥ*. According to the *Bhāṣya*, because of the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), when the suffixes *ḍāp* and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) are excluded, the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* apply. Example: *bahusutvarī nagarī*. [The rule applies] "provided it is not a secondary member" (*anupasarjanāt*).
The feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) to be mentioned hereafter shall not occur after a secondary member (*upasarjana*). Examples: *bahukurucarā nagarī*; *bahukukkuṭā aṭavī*.
Of words ending in *ṭi*, *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, *ṅīn*, *aṇ*, *añ*, *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, *mātraC*, *tayaP*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhañ*, *akaÑ*, *kv*arap, and *khyuN*.

The suffix *ṅīp* shall occur after these [bases] ending in the aforementioned affixes when denoting a feminine. [Examples of bases] marked with the indicator *ṭ*: *kurucarī*, *gāyanī*, *sāyantanī*. By virtue of the force of the indicator *ṭ*, [we have] *nadaṭ* → *nadī*; *dheṭ* → *stanandhayī*. [Bases] marked with the indicator *ḍh*: *vainateyī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *aṇ*: *kumbhakārī*, *bhaṅgakārī senā*, *aupagavī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *añ*: *autsī*, *baidī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *dvayasac*: *jānudvayasī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *daghnac*: *jānudaghnī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *mātrac*: *jānumātrī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *tayap*: *dvitayī*, *dvayī*, *ubhayī*, *pañcatayī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *ṭhak*: *ākṣikī*. [Bases] marked with the suffix *ṭhañ*: *lāvaṇikī*.

The suffix *kañ* [is applied after a word ending in *taddhita* suffixes *ivarṇa*, *uvarṇa*, *ṛvarṇa*, or *śas*]: *yādṛśī*, *tādṛśī*. The suffix *kvarap* [is applied after a verbal root ending in *i* or *u*]: *naśvarī*, *jitvarī*, *gatvarī*. The suffix *khyun* [is applied after a verbal root ending in *i* or *u*]: *subhagaṅkaraṇī*. The suffixes *nañ-srañ-īkak* [are applied after a word ending in *ī*]: *streṇī*, *pauṃsrī*, *śāktīkī*, *tārtīyikī*, *haitīyīkī*. The suffix *īkak* [is applied] after a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix *tīya*: *tīyādīkak*. [The suffix *īkak* is also applied] after a word ending in the *taddhita* suffix *yañ*.
The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after [patronymic] stems ending in *yañ*. Examples: *gārgī*, *vātsī*.

The suffix *ṣpha*, which is designated as a *taddhita*, shall be applied after stems ending in *yañ*. Because it contains the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Examples: *gārgyāyaṇī*, *vātsyāyanī*. Why specify "of the Easterners" (*prācām*)? [To show that for others: *gārgī*, *vātsī*.

In all cases, after [patronymic bases] beginning with *lohita* and ending with *kata*, as well as those belonging to the subgroup beginning with *garga*—specifically those ending in *yañ*—the suffix *ṣpha* shall always be applied. Examples are *lauhityāyanī*, *sāṃśityāyanī*, and *kātyāyanī*. Because of the inclusion of the term "in all cases" (*sarvatra*), it applies even where the suffix *āp* would otherwise be expected; thus, according to tradition, we have *āvaṭyāyanī*. Furthermore, this applies after the words *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka*.

The suffix *ṣpha* occurs after the word *kuru* ending in *ṇya*, and after *maṇḍūka* ending in the patronymic suffix *aṇ*. Thus: *kauravyāyaṇī* and *māṇḍūkāyanī*. However, when [the sense] is "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*), from words ending in *iman*, we have *kauravī senā* (an army belonging to the Kurus) and *māṇḍūkī bhāryā* (a wife belonging to the Maṇḍūkas). There is an extension of the rule for words ending in *iñ* such as *āsuri*: *āsurāyaṇī kanyā* (a maiden belonging to Asura). Since *ṣpha* is a *taḍit* (secondary nominal suffix), there is elision according to the rule *yasyeti ca*.
[Now, regarding the suffix *ṅīp*: "In the first age."

The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after words denoting the first stage of life. The mention of "the first" (*prathama*) is intended to indicate "the last" (*acarama*) as well. Examples: *kumārī*, *varkarī*, *taruṇī*, *vadhūṭī*, *ciraṇṭī*. How is *kanyā* [formed]? By means of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). [The suffix *ṅīp* applies] after a *dvigu* compound. The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after a *dvigu*. Examples: *pañcapūlī*, *trilokī*, *ṣaḍakṣarī*. However, *triphalā* is established by conventional usage in medical science (*vaidyaka-rūḍhi*).

The suffix *ṅīp* does not occur after words ending in *apari-māṇa*, *vi-stā*, *ā-ci-ta*, or *kam-bala* when the *taddhita* suffix is elided (*luk*). That is to say, *ṅīp* shall not be applied after a word ending in these [elements] when the *taddhita* suffix is dropped. [Examples of] ending in *apari-māṇa*: *pañcāśvā* ("bought for five horses"), *triśatā* ("three hundred"), *dvivarṣā* ("two years old"). Time and number are not considered "measure" (*parimāṇa*). [Examples of] ending in *vi-stā* and so on: *dvivistā* ("two spans wide"), *dvyācitā* ("measured by two *ācita*s"), *trikambalyā* ("worth three *kambalyas*"). Why "when the *taddhita* suffix is elided"? Consider: *daśaśatī* ("a collection of ten hundred") [where the *taddhita* suffix is not elided]. [Furthermore, the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied] after a word ending in *kāṇḍa* when it refers to a field (*kṣetra*).

The suffix *ṅīp* shall not occur after a *dvigu* compound ending in *kāṇḍa* when a *taddhita* suffix is elided (*luk*). Example: *dve kāṇḍe pramāṇam asyāḥ* ("its measure is two *kāṇḍas*") → *dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ* ("a field-division measuring two *kāṇḍas*"). Here, the suffix *mātrac* is elided by the rule *pramāṇe lo dvigoḥ*. Why "in the case of a field" (*kṣetre*)? [Counter-example: *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ* ("a rope two *kāṇḍas* long"). [From here on, the rule applies] optionally after *puruṣa* when it denotes a measure. Question: After *puruṣa* used in the sense of a measure, when it is part of a *dvigu* compound and a *taddhita* suffix is elided, the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally occur. Examples: *dvipuruṣī* or *dvipuruṣā parikhā* ("a moat two *puruṣas* wide").

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas*. The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *ūdhas*. This serves as a prohibition against *ḍāp* and a sublation of *ṅīp*. Examples: *kuṇḍodhnī*, *ghaṭodhnī*.
After a *bahuvrīhi* beginning with a numeral or an indeclinable, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with these [words] when they end in *ūdhna*. For example: *caturūdhnī*, *nirūdhnī*. There is a difference in accent. [The suffix *ṅīp* is also applied] after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *dāman* and *hāyana*. It is understood that this applies only when the compound begins with a numeral. The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *dāman* and *hāyana*. For example: *dvidāmnī*, *tridāmnī*. Regarding compounds ending in *hāyana*, there is a specific designation for age (*vayas*). Furthermore, there is the substitution of *ṇa* for the final consonant after the numerals *tri* and *catur*. For example: *dvihāyanī*, *trihāyaṇī*, *caturhāyaṇī*.

*Ana upadhālopino'nyatarasyām*: After a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *a* or *ā* that is eligible for the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopin*), the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally be applied. Examples: *surājñī*, *bahutakṣṇī*, *sudāmnī*, *bhūridhāmnī vidyā*. When *ṅīp* is not applied, the suffixes *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] apply: *surājñe*, *surājānau*. Why "eligible for the elision of the penultimate vowel"? Consider *suparvāṇau*, *suparve*.
[In the case of] technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic usage (*chandas*), it is compulsory.

The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied. For example: *surājñī nāma nagarī* (a city named Surājñī). In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), it is not restricted by the rule *nodājñriyate*. From the nine [words] beginning with *kevala*, *māmaka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *apara*, *samāna*, *ārya*, *kṛta*, *sumaṅgala*, and *bheṣaja*, the suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied when they function as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*). Examples: *kevalī nāma jyotiḥ* (a light named Kevalī); *māmakī devatā* (the deity Māmakī); *pāpī*; *aparī*; *samānī kūndaḥ* (a jasmine named Samānī); *sumaṅgalī*. Only when used as a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*) does this apply. Otherwise: *māmikā buddhiḥ* (my own intellect); *sumaṅgalā nārī* (an auspicious woman).
And [the suffix] *ṅīp* occurs after *rātri* when it does not end in *as*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the word *rātri* in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Example: *rātrī*. Why "when it does not end in *as*"? Example: *rātrayaḥ*. It should be stated that this applies to forms beginning with *ajas* (i.e., those ending in *as*). Examples: *rātrim*, *rātribhiḥ*, and so forth. How is it that [the form] *rātrāḥ* appears in the phrase "and nights shrouded by masses of darkness"? [Answer: Here, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārād...*.

The suffix *nuk* is added after the words *antarvat* and *pativat*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to these two, along with the augment *nuk*, and by virtue of this rule, the substitution of *vat* for the final syllable of *mātṛ* is also established through technical prescription (*nipātana*). Thus: *antarvatnī* means "pregnant," and *pativatnī* means "having a husband.
[Furthermore,] the suffix *n* is substituted for the final syllable of *pati* when it is connected with a sacrifice.

The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after the word *pati*, and the letter *n* shall be substituted for its final [letter], provided it is connected with a sacrifice (*yajña*). For example: *brāhmaṇasya patnī* (the wife of a Brāhmaṇa). How is it that there is the form *patnī* for a Śūdra? It is by way of comparison (*upamāna*).

The rule *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya* states that for the word *pati* preceded by another word (*sapūrvapada*), the suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakāra* may optionally be applied. Examples: *vṛddhapatnī* or *vṛddhapatiḥ*. As in: "I have seen the wrathful Rāmapati."

The suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakār* (ṅīn) are applied invariably after these [words]: *sapatnī*, etc. For example: "She whose vow was that of a devoted wife, yet whose character was marked by suffering. *vīrapatnī*, *bhrātṛpatnī*, *putrapatnī*.
Also, for *pūtakratu*, there is the substitution of *ai*.

Therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* shall apply, and the vowel *ai* (āi) shall be the substitute for the final syllable. The wife of *pūtakratu* is *pūtakratāyī*. For the words *vṛṣākapi*, *agni*, *kusita*, and *kusīda*, [the suffix *ṅīp* applies] with an acute accent (*udātta*). For these, the suffix *ṅīp* shall apply, and the vowel *ai* (āi) shall be the substitute for the final syllable. The wife of *vṛṣākapi* is *vṛṣākapāyī*. [The wife of *agni* is] *agnāyī*. The wife of *kusita* is *kusitāyī*. The wife of *kusīda* is *kusidāyī*. The wife of *ambā* is *ambāyī*.
Or rather, *manu* [takes] *ṅīp*, and there are the substitutions of *ai* and *au*. The female of *manu* is *manāyī* or *manāvī*. Some say that *manu* also [forms its feminine]; others say not.
From a base consisting of a single vowel (*varṇa*), which is anudātta and has *t* as its penultimate letter, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied], but with *n* as the augment.

The suffix *ṅīp* may optionally occur after words denoting colors ending in *t*, and the letter *t* is replaced by *n*. Thus: *enī*, *śyenī*, *hariṇī*, *rohiṇī*. According to the alternative view: *etā*, *śyetā*, *haritā*, *rohitā*. Why "after a word with an anudātta vowel"? Consider: *khetā*. [The rule applies] only after a word ending in *at*: *śitiḥ* (as a feminine). There is a prohibition for *asita* and *palita*: *asitā*, *palitā*. Some say there is also a substitution of *k* [for *t*]: "The troop of *asiknikās* has gone quickly. *paliknī*.
An addition [to the rule] is made for the word *piśaṅga*: "In the middle of the ocean, the *kakubha* trees are tawny (*piśaṅgīḥ*).

From other [words], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. After a word ending in a consonant that has *t* as its penultimate letter and which is not a color term, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs provided it is anudātta (unaccented). Examples: *sāraṅgī*, *kalyāṣī*, *śabalī*. Why "anudātta"? Consider *kṛṣṇā* and *kapilā*.

*ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca*: After a word ending in a *ṣit* affix and after the words beginning with *gaura*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied. Examples: *nartakī*, *rajakī*, *khanakī* (the form *daṃṣṭrā* is included because it is read among the words beginning with *aj*). *gaurī*, *matsī*, *manuṣī*, *droṇī*, *āmalakī*, *vadarī*, *dhātakī*, *bimbī*, *revatī*, *pippalī*, *pṛthivī*, *śamī*. *Jānapada-kuṇḍa-goṇa-sthala-bhājana-ānaka-kāla-nīla-kuśa-kāmuka-kabarād vṛtti-amatra-āvapana-akṛtrima-aśrāṇā-sthaulya-varṇa-anācchādana-ājya-vikāra-maithunecchā-keśaveśeṣu*: [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after *jānapada*, *kuṇḍa*, *goṇa*, *sthala*, *bhājana*, *ānaka*, *kāla*, *nīla*, *kuśa*, *kāmuka*, and *kabara*, when they respectively signify: occupation, a vessel, a sowing-basket, being non-artificial, not being warm, thickness, color, not being a garment, a modification of clarified butter (*ājya*), desire for sexual intercourse, and a style of hair-dressing.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after the eleven words beginning with *jānapada*, in their respective order, in the sense of "occupation" (*vṛtti*) and so forth. *jānapadī* = occupation. *kuṇḍī* = a vessel. *goṇī* = a sack for holding grain. *sthalī* = natural (non-artificial) ground. *bhājī* = boiled rice; that is to say, cooked food. *nāgī* = one who possesses stoutness. *kālī* = black-colored.

After the word *nīla*, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] in the sense of a living being or a medicinal herb. *nīlī* = a mare. *nīlī* = a medicinal herb. Some say it is optional when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, *nīlī* or *nīlā*. *kuśī* = a wrought iron object. *kāmukī* = one who has a desire for sexual intercourse. *kavarī* = a style of hair arrangement.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *śoṇa* when it denotes those of the eastern regions.
Examples: *śoṇau*. Why "of the eastern regions"? Example: *śoṇāḥ* (the Śoṇa river).
[The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) ending in *u* or *ī*.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after words denoting qualities that end in the vowel *u*. Examples: *paṭvī* (clever) / *paṭuḥ*; *tanvī* (slender) / *tanuḥ*; *gurvī* (heavy) / *guruḥ*.

There is a prohibition [of this rule] for words ending in *kharu* and for those having a conjunct consonant as a penultimate letter (*upadha*). Examples: *kharuḥ*; *kadruḥ*; *pāṇḍuḥ* (a woman). [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is also applied] after the group of words beginning with *bahu*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally be applied after words beginning with *bahu*. Thus: *bahvyaḥ* (many women) or *bahavaḥ* (many men); *rātriḥ* (night) or *rātrī* (night). As Bhaṭṭi says: "He swallowed [her] as if she were the Night of Doom (*kālarātrī*). Similarly: *śakaṭi*, *śāṭi*, *śakti*, *śāri*, *yaṣṭi*, *pahati*, *yuvati*, *kalyāṇa*, *udāra*, *caṇḍa*, *vikaṭa*, *viśaṅkaṭa*. After this point, when the word refers to a limb of a living being, [the suffix applies]: *kaṭī*, *dhamanī*, *śroṇī*.
After a word ending in the vowel *i* or *u* that has not been formed by the suffix *kin*: *dharaṇī*.

According to some, [the suffix *ṅīp*] is applied after every [stem] except those ending in a verbal root (*aktin*). Examples: *rajanī*, *rājī*, *surabhī*, *bhūmī*. Why "except those ending in a verbal root"? Consider *prakaraṇiḥ*. According to the *Chandaḥsūtra*, there are two [rules]: "Always in Vedic [usage]" (*nityaṃ chandasi*) and "also after *bhuvas*" (*bhuvaśca*).

When a word denoting a male is used for a female due to her connection with that male, the suffix *ḍīṣ* shall be applied after it. For example: *gaṇakī*, *praṣṭhī*. However, there is a prohibition in the case of words such as *gopālikā*; thus, *gopālikā* remains [without the suffix].
The feminine form *sūryā* should be stated for the deity Sūrya; thus, the wife of Sūrya is *sūryā*, while any other woman is *sūrī*.

After the words *indra*, *varuṇa*, *bhava*, *śarva*, *rudra*, *mṛḍa*, *hima*, *araṇya*, *yava*, *yavana*, *mātula*, and *ācārya*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, and the augment *ānuk* is added. Thus, the female of Indra and the others is *indrāṇī*, *varuṇānī*, and *mṛḍānī*.
In the case of *hima* and *araṇya*, when denoting greatness, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* with the augment *ānuk* is applied]: *himānī* and *araṇyānī*.
After *yava*, [the suffix *ānuk* is applied] when it denotes a fault: *yavānī*.

After *yavana*, [it is applied] when it denotes a script: *yavanānī lipiḥ*. After *upādhyāya* and *mātula*, the suffix *ānuk* is optionally applied: *upādhyāyānī* or *upādhyāyī*; *mātulānī* or *mātulī*.
And there is the absence of *aṇ* after the word *ācārya*. [The forms are] *ācāryā* and *ācāryāṇī*.

After the words *ārya* and *kṣatriya*, the suffixes *ṅīṣ* and *ānuk* are optionally applied. [Thus we have] *āryā* and *āryāṇī*; *kṣatriyā* and *kṣatriyāṇī*. But when expressing a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), [the forms are] *āryī* and *kṣatriyī*. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a word ending in *krīta* when preceded by an instrument (*karaṇa*).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied. *dhanakrītī*, *manasākrītī*: for she was purchased by him with wealth, being dearer even than his own life; thus there is a compound with a word ending in *ṭā*. Regarding the rule *ktādalpākhyāyām*: after a word ending in the suffix *kta* that denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied when it expresses a small quantity (*alpākhyā*). Examples: *abhraviliptī dyauḥ* (the sky is slightly covered by clouds), *sūpaviliptī pātrī* (a dish slightly smeared with soup), *akṣaraviliptī jihvā* (a tongue slightly coated with ink).

[The suffix] ṅīṣ is added after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *kta* that has an udātta accent on its final syllable. For example: *urubhinnī* ("one by whom the thighs have been split") and *keśavilūnī* ("one by whom the hair has been shorn"). Here, however, *pāṇigrahītī* ("one who has taken a husband's hand") refers specifically to a wife. On the other hand, forms such as *dantajātā*, *akṛtāmāsajātā*, *akṣaṇajātā*, *asukhajātā*, and *asukṛtā* are derived from the inclusion [of these stems] in the *ajādi* (beginning with *aja*) list.
Furthermore, [the suffix ṅīṣ is added] optionally after a Bahuvrīhi whose prior member is not a word denoting a body part (*asvāṅga*).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally follow a word that does not have a body part (*svāṅga*) as its prior member (*pūrvapada*) when it is immediately preceded [by such a word]. For example: *sāraṅgajagdhī* or *sāraṅgajagdhā*; *murāpītī* or *surāpītā*. [Furthermore,] after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a body part (*svāṅga*) which is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) and does not have a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as its penultimate (*upadhā*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur. For example: *candramukhī* or *candramukhā*; *niṣkeśī* or *niṣkeśā* (a louse that has emerged from the hair). Why "not having a conjunct consonant as its penultimate"? Consider: *sugulphā*, *supārśvā*. Why "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*)? Consider: *dīrghaśikhā*.
Some say it is also [added] after *aṅga*, *gātra*, *netra*, and *kaṇṭha*; for example, *mṛdv-aṅgī* or *mṛdv-aṅgā*, and so forth.
It is also added after *nāsikā*, *udara*, *oṣṭha*, *jaṅghā*, *danta*, *karṇa*, and *śṛṅga*.
The suffix *āp* (which becomes *ī*) is added after words ending in *nāsikā* and the others; for example, *tuṅga-nāsikī* or *tuṅga-nāsikā*, *tanūdarī* or *tanūdarā*, *vimb-oṣṭhī* or *vimb-oṣṭhā*.
And from "tail" (*puccha*). [The suffix *ini* is applied after] "beautiful tail" (*kalyāṇapuccha*) or "excellent tail" (*kalyāṇapucchā*).
After "tawny" (*kavara*), "jewel" (*maṇi*), "poison" (*viṣa*), and "arrow" (*śara*), it is always [applied]. [Examples: *kavarapucchī*, *śarapucchī*.

After a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), after "wing" (*pakṣa*), and after "tail" (*puccha*). [Examples: *ulūkapakṣī śālā* ("a hall with owl-wings"), *kākapucchī senā* ("an army with crow-tails").

The suffix *ḍīṣ* does not apply after words beginning with *kroḍa* or after polysyllabic words ending in a word denoting a body part (*svāṅga*). Thus, there is no *ḍīṣ* in *sukroḍā*, *kalyāṇakhurā*, *sugudā*, *durbhagā*, or *subhagā*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Regarding "polysyllabic": examples include *pṛthujaghanā*.
[The suffix *ḍīṣ* is also absent] after words preceded by *sa-* (*saha-*), *nañ* (*a-*), or *vidyamāna-*.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall not occur after words preceded by *sa-* and so forth: *sakeśā*, *akeśā*, *vidyamānakeśā*. [Also excluded are: *anāsikā*.
After *nakha* and *mukha*, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), there is no *ṅīṣ*: *śūrpaṇakhā*, *kālamukhā*, *dīrghanakhā*.
The word *daurghajihvī* is used in the Vedic language (*chandas*). The rule is "cha daḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.71). For words with a directional term as the first member, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
