In this context, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established by the rule "from its own body parts" (*svāṅgāt*), the rule "from those preceded by a directional word, the suffix *ṅīp*" (*dikpūrvapadān ṅīp*) is for the sake of the accent. Thus we have *prāṅmukhī* and *prāṅmukhā*.
Regarding the term *vāhaḥ*:
the form *vāha* is also Vedic, because the suffix *ṣvi* is prescribed [after the root] *vah* in the Veda.
In common usage (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix *ṅīṣ*] is applied after *sakhi* and *aśiśu*:

*sakhī*, *aśiśvī*. This occurs in common usage, not in the Veda. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is also applied] after a genus term (*jāti*) that does not denote a female, provided its penultimate vowel is not *a* (*ayopadha*).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied to words denoting genus (*jāti*) when used in the feminine. Examples: *kukkuṭī*, *mayūrī*, *yakṣī*, *sarpī*, *vihagī*, *bhūtī*, *pretī*, *amarī*, *purī*, *taṭī*, *dūtī*, *asurī*, *kuṣmāṇḍī*, *naṭī*, *śāṭī*, *nāḍāyanī*, *kaṭhī*. Why does it say "not having a feminine scope" (*astrīviṣayāt*)? So that it does not apply to those that are always feminine: *makṣikā*, *pipīlikā*, *mālā*, *valākā*. Why does it say "not having *y* as a penultimate letter" (*ayopadhāt*)? [So that it does not apply to] *kṣatriyā*. When there is a prohibition regarding a word with *y* as a penultimate letter, the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies to *hayā*, *gavaya*, *mukaya*, *matsya*, and *manuṣya*: *hayī*, *gavayī*, *mukayī*, *matsī*, *manuṣī*. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is also applied] after a word ending in *pāka*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, or *bāla* as its final member.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after a compound whose final member is *pāka* or similar words. This statement is for the purpose of restricting the application to feminine objects. Examples: *odanapākī*, *piṣṭakapākī*, *miṣṭaparṇī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*. The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after a word ending in short *i* that denotes a human species (*manuṣyajāti*). Examples: *dākṣī*, *avantī*, *kuntī*. Because the term "species" (*jāti*) is mentioned again here, the suffix is applied even after a word with *y* as its penultimate letter (*yopadha*). Example: *audameyī*. Why "ending in *i*" (*itaḥ*)? Consider *darat*. Why "human species" (*nṛjāti*)? Consider *tittiri* (which is not a human species). The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall also be applied after a word ending in the suffix *añ* provided it does not denote a *gotra* (patronymic). Example: *sautaṅgamī* (the city).

After a word ending in *aṅ* (the feminine suffix *ā*) or *udantāt* (ending in *u*), the suffix *ūṅ* is applied to denote a human being (*manuṣyajāti*). Examples: *kurūḥ*, *dhībandhūḥ*, *brahmabandhūḥ*, *bhīrūḥ*.

The suffix *ūṅ* is also applied after words denoting non-living beings (*aprāṇijāti*), with the exception of *rajjv-ādi* (the group beginning with *rajjū-*). Examples: *alābuḥ*, *karkandhūḥ*. Why "non-living beings"? [Counter-examples: *ākhuḥ*, *kṛkavākuḥ*. The suffix *ūṅ* does not apply to *rajjv-ādi*. Examples: *rajjūḥ*, *hanūḥ*.

After a word ending in *bāhu*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example, a certain woman is called *Bhadrabāhū*. Why "when it is a proper name"? [Consider: *Bṛhadbāhuḥ* as a woman.
Also after *paṅgu*.
The suffix *uṅ* is applied after [the word] *svādu*. Thus: *paṅguḥ*.
There is also elision of the phonemes *u* and *a* in *śvaśura*. Thus: *śvaśrūḥ*.
[The suffix *uṅ* is applied] after a compound whose final member is *ūru*, when used in a sense of comparison (*aupamye*).
The suffix *ūṅ* occurs after *ūru* when used in comparison; for example, *rambhoruḥ* ("having thighs like plantain stalks") and *karabhorūḥ* ("having thighs like the forearm").
It also occurs after *ūru* when preceded by *saṃhita*, *śapha*, *lakṣaṇa*, or words beginning with *vāma*;

that is, *ūṅ* is applied to *ūru* following these initial elements. For instance, *saṃhitoruḥ* ("having joined thighs"), as in the verse: "O lady with beautiful thighs (*vāmorū*), whose graceful movements have reached the highest excellence."

And [the suffix *aC* is applied] after the words *sahita* and *saha*. Examples: *sahitorūḥ*, *sahorūḥ*. [The suffix *aC* is applied] after *kadru* and *kamaṇḍalu* in the Veda (*chandas*). This refers to the *Chandaḥ-sūtra*.
In the case of a name (*saṃjñā*): after these two [stems], *ūṅ* shall be applied to form a feminine name. *kadrūḥ*; *kamaṇḍalūḥ*.
After the suffix *yañ* following stems such as *śārṅgarava*, *ṅīn* is applied.

"From a genus-name," it is understood. From the class beginning with *śārṅgarava* and from those ending in the suffix *añ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīn* shall be applied. Examples: *śārṅgaravī*, *gautamī*, *putrī*. [The suffix *ṅīn* is applied] to *nṛ* and *nara*, and there is also vṛddhi [of the first vowel]. Example: *nārī*. Furthermore, [the suffix *ṅīn* is applied] after a word ending in *añ*. Examples: *baidī*, *autsī*. After a word ending in *yaṅ*, the suffix *cāp* is applied. Thus, after a word ending in *yaṅ*, *cāp* is applied. Examples: *ñāṅ*: *āmbaṣṭhyā*, *kauśalyā*; *ṣyaṅ*: *kārīṣagandhyā*, *vārāhyā*.
And from *āvaṭya*. The feminine suffix *āp* is applied after words ending in the *yañ* affix belonging to the *garga*-class and after the word *āvaṭya*. Thus: *āvaṭyā*.
[End of] Taddhita [affixes].
From here, the suffixes designated as *taddhita* are to be stated, up to the suffix *kap*. For example:
*yūnastiḥ*. After the word *yuva*, the suffix *ti* occurs; thus, *yuvatiḥ*.

The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed after the *aṇ* and *iñ* [patronymic] affixes when they belong to a *gotra* [lineage], provided that the penultimate syllable is heavy (*guru*) and the [names] are not Vedic seers (*anārṣa*).

Regarding the *gotra*, for those two—*aṇ* and *iñ*—the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is ordained in the feminine. *Example of aṇ*: Kārīṣagandhyā. *Example of iñ*: Vārāhyā. Why "not Vedic seers"? [Counter-example: Vāsiṣṭhī (derived from Vasiṣṭha, a Vedic seer). Why "penultimate syllable is heavy"? [Counter-example: Aupagavī (derived from Upagu, where the penultimate syllable is light). In a word consisting of three or more syllables, the last one is called the "final" (*uttama*), and the one immediately preceding it is the "penultimate" (*upottama*). [The rule applies] when the [name] is a part of a *gotra*.

The *gotra* sub-divisions include the Pauṇikas and others. From these, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* (which becomes *ī*) is prescribed in place of *aṇ* and *iñ*. Thus: *pauṇikyā*, *bhauṇikyā*, *maukharyā*. And from *krauḍi* and others: the suffix *ṣyaṅ* shall apply to these when forming feminine nouns. Thus: *krauḍyā*, *lāḍyā*, *daivadattyā*. From *bhoja*, when denoting the Kṣatriya caste, [the suffix *ṣyaṅ* applies]: *bhojyā*.
*Daivayajñi-śaucivṛkṣi-sātyamugri-kāṇṭheviḍ-vibhyaḥ anyatarasyām*:

after these, the suffix *vyaṅ* may optionally replace *iñ*. [Examples: *daivayajñyā*, *śaucavṛkṣyā*. In the alternative case, by the rule *itaḥ manuṣyajāteḥ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied: *daivayajñī*, *kāṇṭhevidvī*. The section on feminine endings is complete. [Now begins: *samarthānāṃ prathamād vā*.

This governing rule (*adhikāra*) extends prior to the section on primary suffixes (*svārthika*). Among words that are semantically connected (*samartha*), the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) may optionally occur after the word first mentioned in the rule; because of the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*), a full sentence may also be used. It will be stated [later]: "The descendant of that" (*tasyāpatyam*). The descendant of Upagu is *Aupagavaḥ*. Why "among semantically connected words"? Consider: "The blanket belongs to Upagu; the descendant is Devadatta's. *Prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*: Prior to the rule "He plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*), the suffix *aṇ* is governed for those meanings. Examples should be cited accordingly. Also [after] *aśvapati* and so forth.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after these [words]. Examples: *āśvapatam*, *gāṇapatam*, *pāśupatam*. This statement is made because the suffix *ṇya* would otherwise have been applicable. The suffix *ṇya* shall be applied after the words *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, and those whose final member is *patya*; it serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. - From *diti*: since it ends in *ti*, the form is *daityaḥ*. - The offspring of *aditi* is *ādityaḥ*. - From the word *āditya*: "his offspring" is *ādityyaḥ*. - After a word ending in *patya*: *saināpatyam*, *gārhapatyam*, *prājāpatyam*.
And from *yama*: *yāmyam*. From *pṛthivī*: *pārthivaḥ*, *pārthivī*. From *deva*:
*daivyam*, *daivyā*; *devam*, *devī*.
The suffix *bahiṣ* [becomes *bāhya*] with the elision of the sixth case ending. That which is outside is *bāhya*. The suffix *īkak* also [occurs]. *Bāhīka*.
[The suffix *a* occurs after] *sthāman*. *Aśvatthāman*. *Mahāsthāman*.

The suffix *a* is applied after *loman* when forming the plural of a descendant. Thus, *ūrdhvalomāḥ*. Why "in the plural"? [To show: *aurhvalomiḥ*, *aurhvalomī*. [The word *loman*] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group.

In all cases, the suffix *yat* is applied to *go* when there is the possibility of suffixes beginning with vowels other than *a*. Thus, *gavyam*. After words such as *utsa*, the suffix *añ* is applied.
The suffix *añ* shall be applied after these [words]. Examples: *autsaḥ*, *audapānaḥ*. Regarding the rule "after *strī* and *pums*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* [are applied] before *bhavana*":

in the sense of "being" (*bhava*) and its derivatives—such as "collection" (*samūha*), "beneficial" (*hita*), etc.—before the word *bhavana*, the suffix *nañ* is applied after *strī*, and *snañ* is applied after *pum̐s*. In the case of *pum̐s*, there is the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). As in: "May the feminine (*straiṇa*) and the masculine (*pauṃsna*) come together for me. How is it that we have forms such as *strīvat* (like a woman) and *puṃvat* (like a man), as well as *strītva* (femininity) and *puṃstva* (masculinity)? This is because the specific mention of *strī-pum̐vat* (in the rule *striyāḥ pumvad...*) indicates that this application is not universal (*anityatva*).

*dvigor lug anapatye*: There shall be elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) belonging to a *dvigu* compound, provided it belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group. *In that, it is prepared*: *pañcakapālaḥ* (prepared in five pots). *He studies or knows that*: *dvivedaḥ* (one who has studied two Vedas). The elision (*luk*) that has been prescribed for certain [patronymic suffixes] by rules such as *yaskādibhyo gotre* is prohibited when a secondary suffix (*prāgdīvyatīya*) beginning with a vowel (*ac*) is to be applied. [The general sense of these suffixes is: "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*).

The section on *apatya* (offspring) extends up to the end of the *āpād* [Pāṇini 4.1.82].

*Eko gotre*: In the lineage (*gotra*), there shall be only one suffix for the primary base. And it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In the lineage, there is one; the very first word alone produces the suffix. Thus, Garga’s lineage-descendant is *gārgyaḥ*; his grandson also is *gārgyaḥ*.

[The suffix] after a *gotra* [stem] occurs for a young descendant (*yuvan*), provided it is not feminine. For a young descendant, the suffix should be applied from the *gotra* stem itself, and not from any other base. The young descendant of Vātsya is Vātsyāyana. Why "provided it is not feminine"? [Because] Vātsī [is formed] with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. According to tradition, only the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "young descendant" is prohibited.
[The suffix] *dūñ* is added after *ataḥ*.

The suffix *iñ* shall be applied after [patronymic stems] beginning with *adanta*. Examples: *dākṣiḥ*, *dāśarathiḥ*. How is it that [the form] *pradīyatāṃ dāśarathāya maithilī* ("Let Maithilī be given to the son of Daśaratha") occurs? The suffix *iñ* shall be applied after the *ākṛtigaṇa* beginning with *bāhu*. Examples: *bāhaviḥ*, *cauḍiḥ*, *saumitriḥ*, *aurṅghalomiḥ*, *kārṇiḥ*. Here, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for *ṛṣi* names is an exception (*bādhaka*) to this rule.
And [the suffix] akaṅ after *sudhātṛ*.
After *sudhātṛ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied, and there is the substitution of *akaṅ* for the final portion [of the stem]. Thus, *saudhātakiḥ*.
It should be stated that this applies to *vyāsa*, *varuḍa*, *niṣāda*, *caṇḍāla*, and *viṃba*. Thus, *vaiyāsakiḥ*, *vāruḍakiḥ*, *naiṣādakiḥ*, *cāṇḍālakiḥ*, and *vaimbakiḥ*.

*Gotre kuñjādibhyaś-cphañ*: After the words *kuñja* and others, when denoting a descendant in the sense of a *gotra*, the suffix *cphañ* shall be applied. From that, the suffix *ñya* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Thus: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*, *brādhnāyanyaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a *gotra*"? [Consider: *kuñjasyānantarāpatyam kauñjiḥ* (the immediate descendant of Kuñja is Kauñji). The suffix *phak* is applied after [patronymic stems] ending in *vidādi*, *yajanta*, and *harita-ādi* when forming a secondary derivative (*yuvan*) denoting a grandson or later descendant. For example: *Hāritāyanaḥ*, *Kautsāyanaḥ*.
Furthermore, by the rule *yañiñoś ca*:
the suffix *phak* is applied after those [stems] ending in *yañ* or *iñ* which denote a lineage (*gotra*). For example: *Vātsyāyanaḥ*, *Dākṣāyaṇaḥ*.
After *śaradvat*, *śunaka*, and *darbha*, the suffix *phak* is applied when [the patronymic] belongs to the *bhṛgu* group or the *agrāyaṇa* group.

From these—namely, the *bhṛgu* group and so forth—the suffix *phak* occurs in the formation of a gotra name. Examples: *śāradvatāyanaḥ* as a descendant of Bhṛgu; *śaunakāyanaḥ* as a descendant of Vatsa; *dārbhāyaṇaḥ* as this descendant of Agrāyaṇa.
After *droṇa*, *parvata*, and *jīvanta*, the suffix is optionally applied.

The suffix *phak* may optionally be applied after *droṇa* and others to form patronymics (*gotrāpatya*). Thus, one may be called *drauṇāyaṇa* or *drauṇi*; *pārvatāyana* or *pārvati*; *jaivantāyana* or *jaivanti*. After the *bidādi* group, the suffix *añ* is used for non-sage lineages (*anṛṣi*) when there is no immediate descent (*anantarya*). The suffix *añ* is applied to the *bidādi* group to denote a lineage (*gotra*). Examples: *baida*, *aurva*, *hārīta*, *kāśyapa*, *kauśika*, *śaunaka*, *śigru*. However, for those words in the *bidādi* list that are not names of sages, *añ* is applied to denote the immediate offspring (*anantarāpatya*). Examples: *pautra* (son of a daughter), *dauhitra* (daughter's son), *nānāndra* (sister's son).

The words *parastrī* and *paraśu* [form the derivative] *pāraśavaḥ*. [The suffix] *yañ* is applied after [the group of names beginning with] *garga*. After these, the suffix *yañ* shall be used to denote a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*). Examples: *gārgyaḥ* (from *garga*), *vatsa*, *lohita*, *vyāghrapāt*, *kata*, *tṛkṣa*, *śakala*, *kuṇḍinī*, *jamadagni*, *nṛkuṭi*, *śaṇḍila*. 106. [The suffix *yañ* is applied] after *madhu* and *babhru* when [the descendants] are respectively a Brāhmaṇa and a Kauśika.

From these two, when the patronymic *āṅgirasa* follows, the suffix *yañ* shall be applied: *mādhavyaḥ brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin descended from Madhuva), *bābhravyaḥ kauśikaḥ* (a Kauśika descended from Babhru).

From *kapi* and *bodha*, when the patronymic *āṅgirasa* follows, the suffix *yañ* shall be applied: *kāpyaḥ* (descended from Kapi) and *baudhyaḥ* (descended from Bodha). The inclusion of *kapi* in the list beginning with *garga* is for the sake of establishing the substitution of *ṣpha*. [Thus: *kāpyāyanī* (the female descendant of Kāpya).
And from *vataṇḍa*: when this [word] belongs to the *Āṅgirasa* lineage, the suffix *yañ* shall apply. Thus, *vātaṇḍya*. There is elision (*luk*) in the feminine:
for the feminine of *vataṇḍa*, there shall be elision of the suffix *yañ*. Thus, *vataṇḍī*. It belongs to the *śārṅgarava* group.

*Phañ* after *aśva* and others. After [words beginning with] *aśva*, the suffix *phañ* occurs when denoting a lineage (*gotra*). [Examples: *Āśvāyanaḥ*; *Śrāviṣṭhāyanaḥ*. *Śrānaḍuhya* belongs to the *garga*-class; its descendant is *Ānaḍuhyāyanaḥ*. After *bharga*, [the suffix *phañ* is used] when [the lineage is that of] a Trigarta.

After *bharga*, the suffix *phañ* shall be applied. [Thus: *bhārgāyaṇaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a *gotra*"? [Counter-example: *bhārgiḥ*. It has been stated that [the suffixes] after *śiva* and others are used in the sense of offspring in general. After *śiva* and others, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied in the sense of offspring in general. This serves as an exception (*bādhā*) to *iñ* and other suffixes. [Examples: *śaivaḥ*, *bhaumaḥ*, *gāṅgaḥ*, *sāpatnaḥ*. In the analytical statement (*vākya*) "the offspring of Viśravas," the formation occurs through the forms *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa*. [Thus: *vaiśravaṇaḥ*, *rāvaṇaḥ*.

[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after names of rivers and of female human beings that do not begin with a *vṛddhi* vowel, provided they are used as names [of lineages]. This serves as an exception to [the application of] *ḍhak*. Examples: *yāmunaḥ* (descendant of Yamunā), *airāvataḥ* (descendant of Airāvatī). Regarding female human beings: *cāintitaḥ*, *śaikṣitaḥ*, *gautamaḥ*. Why "after those not beginning with a *vṛddhi* vowel"? Consider: *cāndrabhāgeyaḥ* (from Candrabhāgā), *vāsavadatteyaḥ* (from Vāsavadattā).
[The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after the names of *ṛṣis*, *Andhakas*, *Vṛṣṇis*, and *Kurus*.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after these [names], superseding the suffix *iñ*. *Vāsiṣṭhaḥ* (descendant of Vasiṣṭha). *Vaiśvāmitraḥ* (descendant of Viśvāmitra). After *Andhaka*: *Āndhakaḥ* (descendant of Andhaka). *Khāṇḍikaḥ* (descendant of Khaṇḍika). After *Vṛṣṇi*: *Vāsudevaḥ* (descendant of Vāsudeva). *Āniruddhaḥ* (descendant of Aniruddha). After *Kuru*: *Nākulaḥ* (descendant of Nakula). *Sāhadevaḥ* (descendant of Sahadeva). The lineages beginning with Andhaka and others are certain ancient ones. After the word *mātṛ* ("mother"), when preceded by a numeral or the words *saṃ* and *bhadra*, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. There is the substitution of *uc* for the final vowel of the stem. *Dvaimāturaḥ* (having two mothers). *Traimāturaḥ* (having three mothers). *Ṣāṇmāturaḥ* (having six mothers). *Sāmmāturaḥ* (having a good mother). *Bhādramāturaḥ* (having a fortunate mother).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *kanyā*, and there is also the substitution of *kanīna*. Thus, Vyāsa is called *kānīna*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *vikarṇa*, *śuṅga*, and *chagala* when [the offspring] is respectively a Vatsa, a Bharadvāja, or an Atri.

From these very [names], *aṇ* may occur: Vaikarṇa Vātsya; Śauṅga Bhāradvāja; Chāgala Ātreya. By means of [the names] Vatsa and others, that descendant is indicated. Or, from the word *pīlā*, *aṇ* may optionally occur: Paila or Paileya.

And *ḍhak* [is added] after *maṇḍūka*. After *maṇḍūka*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *ḍhak* may occur. [Examples: *maṇḍūkaḥ*, *māṇḍūkeyaḥ*. It is understood that "or" (*vā*) applies here as well: *māṇḍūkiḥ*. After feminine stems, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied].

The suffix *ḍhak* shall be applied after a word ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Examples: *sauparṇeyaḥ*, *saubhadreyaḥ*, *kaumbhakāreyaḥ*. [The suffix] *ḍhak* shall be stated [after the word] *vaḍavā* when referring to a male [offspring]: *vāḍaveyo vṛṣaḥ* (a stallion). It is taught that the suffix *aṇ* is used after *krauñcā* and *kokilā*: *krauñcaḥ*, *kokilaḥ*.

[The suffix] *ḍhak* applies after a word consisting of two syllables. It is an exception to the [suffix] *aṇ* prescribed for words ending in *-stṛ*. For example: *dātteyaḥ*, *gopteyaḥ*. However, *pārthaḥ* is derived from the inclusion [of the word *pṛthu*] in the *śivādi* list.
[The suffix *ḍhak* also applies] after a word ending in *it* (the vowel *i*), provided it does not end in the suffix *ini*.

The suffix *ḍhak* shall occur after a word consisting of two syllables ending in *i*. Examples: *Ātreyaḥ*, *Vaidheyaḥ*. Why "not ending in *in*"? Consider *Dākṣāyaṇaḥ*. It must be "consisting of two syllables" as well; thus, [with the suffix] *aṇ*: *Mārīcaḥ*.

And after words beginning with *śubhra*, the suffix *ḍhak* shall occur. Examples: *Śaubhreyaḥ*, *Lekhābhreyaḥ*, *Kādraveyaḥ*, *Pāṇḍaveyaḥ*, *Gāṅgeyaḥ*. This word *gaṅgā* also belongs to the *tikādi* group; therefore, according to some, [the form] is *Gāṅgāyaniḥ*.

After *vikarṇa* and *kuṣītaka*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of offspring belonging to these two; [the forms are] *vaikarṇeyaḥ* and *kauṣītakeyaḥ*. After *bhru*, the suffix *vuk* is also applied.
After *bhrū*, when *ḍhak* follows, there is the augment *vuk*. Thus: *bhrauveyaḥ*.
For the words beginning with *kalyāṇī*, the suffix *inaṅ* is applied.

After these, *ḍhak* occurs and *inaṅ* is the substitute for the final vowel [and the following consonant]. Thus: *kālyāṇineyaḥ*. Also after *subhagā*, *durbhagā*, *jyeṣṭhā*, *madhyamā*, *kaniṣṭhā*, *rajakī*, *bandhakī*, *parastrī*, and *balīvardī*.

Or [the suffix] *ḍhak* may be applied after *kulaṭā*, or alternatively *inaṅ*; thus [the forms] *kaulaṭineyaḥ* or *kaulaṭeyaḥ*. However, for *kolaṭeraḥ*, there is the intention of expressing the offspring of a woman who is devoid of virtue (*śīlahīnā*). After *caṭakā*, the suffix *airak* is applied.
It may be so. [The suffix] *ai* is applied after *caṭaka*.
It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix when forming the feminine offspring. Thus, *caṭakā*.
After *godhā*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied.
In the eastern regions, [the suffix -eyaka is used].

The offspring of a *godhā* (iguana) is a *gaudhera* or a *gaudhāra*; however, it is also called *gaudheya* because it is listed among the words beginning with *sabhrā*. Or, [the suffix -eyaka is optionally applied] after feminine words denoting small animals.
Those who are deficient in limb or conduct are called *kṣudra*. From these [words], the suffix *ḍhak* may optionally be applied: *kāṇeraḥ* or *kāṇeyaḥ*; *dāseraḥ* or *dāseyaḥ*.
After the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* ("father’s sister"), the suffix *chaṇ* is applied:
*paitṛṣvasrīyaḥ*.
There is elision when the suffix *ḍhak* is applied; furthermore, there is elision of the final [vowel] when *ḍhak* follows. [Examples: *paitṛṣvaseyaḥ*;
and likewise from *mātṛṣvasṛ*.
And for this [suffix], it should be so: *mātṛṣvasrīyaḥ* (son of a maternal aunt) and *mātṛśvaseyaḥ*. From quadrupeds, there is the suffix *ḍhañ*: it should be so.
This is an exception to the suffixes beginning with *aṇ*, etc.: *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ* (descendant of Kamaṇḍalu), *jāmbeyaḥ* (descendant of Jambu).
And after *gṛṣṭi* and the others, the suffix *ḍhañ* shall apply. Thus: *gārṣṭeyaḥ*, *maitreyaḥ*.
After *rājan* and *śvaśura*, the suffix *yat* applies.
From these two [suffixes], *yat* may occur: *rājanyaḥ* means a Kṣatriya; *śvaśuryau* means the husband's brother and the wife's brother. From *kṣatra*, *dhaḥ* occurs:
*kṣatriyaḥ*; this denotes the genus (*jāti*).
The suffix *kha* is applied after the word *kula*. [Examples:
*kulīnaḥ*, *āḍhyakulīnaḥ*. Optionally, when not preceded by another word, the suffixes *yañ* and *ḍhakañ* are applied.
After the word *kula*, when it does not have a preceding member [in a compound], the suffixes *yañ* or *ḍhakañ* may optionally occur. Thus: *kulyaḥ*, *kauleyakaḥ*, or *kulīnaḥ*.
After the word *mahākula*, the suffixes *añ* or *khañ* may occur.
Thus: *māhākulaḥ* or *māhākulīnaḥ*. Or rather, [the suffix *khañ* occurs] after *mahākulīna*: *mahākulīnaḥ*.
From *duṣkula*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs:
*dauṣkuleyaḥ*. Or rather, [the suffix] *inañ*: *duṣkulīnaḥ*. From *sva*, the suffix *uñcha* occurs.
It may be so. *Svasrīyaḥ* (sister's son). From *bhrātṛ*, there is *vya*;
*bhrātṛvyaḥ* would be formed with *vya*. And from *cha* [as a suffix], *bhrātṛvyaḥ*; or else *bhrātrīyaḥ*.

The suffix *vyat* occurs after *sapatna*, as in *sapatnavyat*, meaning "an enemy" or "the offspring of a brother. *Bhrātṛvya* means "an heir" or "a kinsman," derived from the analogy of being a "thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*).
After words such as *revatī*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after the group of words beginning with *revatī*. This serves as an exception to [the application of] *ḍhak* and other such suffixes. For example: *raivatikaḥ*; *dauvārapālikaḥ*. After the name of a woman belonging to a *gotra*, the suffix *ṇa* is also used when expressing contempt. Thus, the suffix *ṇa* is applied, as well as *ṭhak*. For example: the offspring of *Gārgī* (a woman of the Garga *gotra*) who is a scoundrel is called *gārgī* or *gārgikaḥ*. Why "when expressing contempt"? Consider: *gārgeyaḥ* (where there is no contempt). Why "of a *gotra*"? Consider: the offspring of *Kārikā* is *kārikeyaḥ* (which is not a *gotra*). It should be understood that the rules concerning the offspring of a *gotra* apply to the younger generation (*yuvan*).
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied diversely (*bahulam*) after a *vṛddha* [patronymic] name from among the Sauvīras.

After a *vṛddha* name belonging to the Sauvīra lineage, when expressing contempt, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs: *bhāgavittikaḥ*. Optionally, the suffix *phak* occurs: *bhāgavittāyanaḥ*. [Furthermore,] after a name ending in *phe*, the suffix *cha* also occurs.

After a patronymic ending in *phiñ* derived from the Sauvīra lineage, the suffix *cha* shall be used in the sense of contempt; *ṭhak* is also applicable. From *tika* and others, the suffix *phiñ* is applied: *yāmundāyaniḥ*. His descendant (*apatyam*) is *yāmundāyanīyaḥ* or *yāmundāyanikaḥ*.

After *phāṇṭāhṛti* and *mimata*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *phiñ* are applied. After these two, when referring to the Sauvīras, *ṇa* and *phiñ* shall be used: *phāṇṭāhṛtaḥ* and *phāṇṭāhṛtāyaniḥ*; *maimataḥ* and *maimatāyaniḥ*.

*Ṇya* is added after *kuru* and others. After these, *Ṇya* shall be used in the sense of a descendant (*apatya*). Examples: *kauravyaḥ*, *kauravyau*, *kauravyāḥ*. Regarding the phrase "the Kauravyas are cattle," they say that the word *kuru* here refers to a sage. [The list includes: *kuru*, *gardabha*, *śakuni*, *kavi*, *kapiñjala*.

And [the suffix *Ṇya* is added] after words ending in *senā*, as well as after *lakṣaṇa* and *kārin*. After these, *Ṇya* shall be used. After a word ending in *senā*: *hāriṣeṇyaḥ*, *māhāsenyaḥ*. *Lākṣaṇyaḥ*. The word *kārin* denotes an artisan (*śilpin*): *tāntuvāyyaḥ*, *kaumbhakāryyaḥ*.
*udīcām iñ*:
for those [lineages] of the North, *iñ* shall be applied. For example: *māhāseniḥ*, *lākṣaṇiḥ*, *tāntuvāyiḥ*.
From *tikādi* [lineages], *phiñ* is applied.
The suffix *phiñ* shall be applied after these [names] to denote a descendant (*apatya*). Examples: *taikāyaniḥ*, *kauravyāyaṇiḥ*, *kaitavāyaniḥ*.

[And] also after *kauśalya* and *karmārya*. According to another Smṛti: "In the case of *dagu*, *kośala*, *karmāra*, *chāga*, and *vṛṣa*, the augment *yuṭ* is optionally applied before the suffix prescribed. The suffix *phiñ* shall be applied after these to denote a descendant, and *yuṭ* is the augment. Examples: *dāgavyāyaniḥ*, *kauśalyāyaniḥ*, *kārmāryāyaṇiḥ*, *chāgyāyaniḥ*, *vārṣyāyaṇiḥ*.

*phiñ* is added after a *gotra* name ending in two syllables. From such a two-syllable *gotra* name, *phiñ* shall be applied. For example: *kārttryāyaṇiḥ*, *yāskāyaniḥ*. According to the opinion of the Northern grammarians (*udīcām*), *phiñ* is added after a *gotra* name that contains a *vṛddhi* vowel in its first syllable. For example: *āmraguptāyaniḥ*, *śālaguptāyaniḥ*. This applies even when the word is explicitly stated [as a non-*gotra*], because it is a later rule [and thus supersedes the previous one]. For example: *nāpitāyaniḥ*. According to the opinion of others, however, it is *āmraguptiḥ*. Why "after a *vṛddha* [name]"? Consider *yājñadattiḥ*. Why "not a *gotra*"? Consider *aupagaviḥ*.
For *vākin* and others, there is also the augment *kuk*.

According to the opinion of the Northerners (*udīcām*), the suffix *phiñ* is applied after *vākin* and others, and there is also the augment *kuk*. Thus: *vākinakāyaniḥ*, *kārkaṭyakāyaniḥ*. According to others: *vākiniḥ*, *kārkaṭyiḥ*. After a word ending in *putra*, the suffix is optional.

The suffix *phiñ* occurs after a patronymic ending in *putra* that is not *vṛddha*. Optionally, there is also the substitution of *kuk*. Examples: *vātsīputrakāyaṇiḥ*, *vātsīputrāyaṇiḥ*, or *vātsīputriḥ*.
The suffix *phin* occurs diversely (*bahulam*) after an eastern (*prācām*) non-*vṛddha* [patronymic].

After a non-*vṛddha* [patronymic], *phin* occurs. Example: *glucukāyaniḥ*. Why "of the Easterners" (*prācām*)? Example: *glaucukiḥ* (which is not from the East). Because of the word "diversely" (*bāhulyāt*), it does not occur here: *dākṣiḥ*.

The suffixes *añ* and *ya* are applied after the word *manu*, and there is also the augment *ṣuk*, provided that it refers to a genus (*jāti*). Thus, *mānuṣaḥ* and *manuṣyaḥ*. The form *māṇavaḥ* is derived from an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). That which is a descendant starting from the grandson is called a *gotra*.

The offspring beginning with the grandson is called a *gotra*. The offspring of Garga, starting from the grandson onwards, is *Gārgya*. Why "starting from the grandson"? [To show that] the immediate offspring is *Gārgi*. However, when an ancestor of the lineage is living, the descendant is a *yuvan* (younger generation).

When an ancestor such as a father or grandfather is living, the offspring of the grandson and those following shall be a *yuvan*, not a *gotra*. While Garga, Gārga, or Gārgya is living, the *yuvan* offspring of Gārgya is *Gārgyāyaṇa*; but when he is dead, it is simply *Gārgya*. Here, the term "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*) is transformed into the genitive case.
And [the suffix is used] for an elder brother:

when an elder brother is living, a grandson or other descendant may be a youth; while the elder brother is living, the younger brother is called *gārgāyaṇa*. Or [it is used] when another more senior *sapiṇḍa* is living.

Sapiṇḍas are those related through seven generations. In that regard, when a brother or even another sapiṇḍa who is more senior is alive, the offspring of a grandson or similar descendant shall be designated as a *yuvan* (junior) while he is still living. When a paternal uncle or a grandfather is alive, one may be called either *Gārgyāyaṇa* or *Gārgya*. In the absence of a more senior relative, one is simply *Gārgya*. Furthermore, regarding the honorific usage for an elder, the term "gotra" is said by the ancient teachers to signify an elder; in the honorific sense of such a person, the designation *yuvan* may optionally apply. Thus, one may say, "Your Honor, Gārgyāyaṇa," or "Gārgya."
And [the suffix] after *yuvan* is used in the sense of censure;

it may optionally receive the designation *yuvan*. Thus, one may say either *gāāyaṇo jālmaḥ* or *gārgyo jālmaḥ*. He who is independent while his father is still living is a *jālma* (a rogue). The designation *yuvan* has been explained. After a word denoting a country that is the name of a *kṣatriya*, the suffix *añ* is applied.

The suffix *añ* shall be applied after a word denoting a country that signifies a *kṣatriya* lineage to form a patronymic. Examples: *pāñcālaḥ*, *aikṣvākaḥ*, *vaidehaḥ*. Why "after a word denoting a country"? [Consider: *pauravaḥ*.
[The suffix *añ* is also applied] after the words *sālveya* and *gāndhāri*. From these two, *añ* shall be applied: *sālveyaḥ*, *gāndhāraḥ*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [place names] consisting of two syllables, as well as after those beginning with Magadha and others. This supersedes the suffix *añ*. Examples: *Āṅgaḥ*, *Vāṅgaḥ*, *Sauhmaḥ*, *Māgadhaḥ*, *Kāliṅgaḥ*, *Sauramasaḥ*.
After [place names] beginning with Kośala and Jāda that contain a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied.

The suffix *ñyaṅ* shall be applied after [names of] *vṛddha* (first vowel long) ending in *danta*, as well as after *kośala* and *āja*. Examples: *āmbaṣṭhyaḥ*, *āvantyaḥ*, *kauntyaḥ*, *kauśalyaḥ*, *ājādyaḥ*. It should be stated that the suffix *ḍyaṅ* is applied after the name of a country (*janapada*) when it is *pāṇḍu*. Example: *pāṇḍyaḥ*. Why "after a country"? Because in the case of *pāṇḍavaḥ*—referring to Pāṇḍu from the *Mahābhārata*—the suffix is not applied; for his [Pāṇḍu's] country was not named *pāṇḍu*. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after *kuru* and similar names.

The suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *kuru*, when it denotes a *kṣatriya* or a *janapada* (territory), and after words beginning with *nakāra*. Thus: *kauravyaḥ*, *kauravyau*, *kuravaḥ*. [As in: "For a long time the Kurus have flourished there. *Naidhanyaḥ*; *naiṣadhyaḥ*. How is it that in the *Māgha-kāvya* it says, "the women of the Kukuras and Kauravas embraced [him]," and likewise in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, "may the Kauravas be protected"? Some say this is because they do not intend to express them as *janapadas*. Others say that since *viṣaya* means "country," the suffix *aṇ* applies here, and the forms are derived based on their location (*tātsthyāt*). Still others say it is because they intend to express the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*). The suffix *iñ* occurs after *sālva-avayava*, *pratyagratha*, *kalakūṭa*, *aśmaka*, and so forth.

There are six [tribes] belonging to the Sālva group, beginning with Udumbara. From these, as well as from Pratyagratha and others, the suffix *iñ* shall occur. Thus: Audumbari, Yaugandhari, Prātyagrathi, Kālakūṭi, and Āśmaki. 174. *Te tadrājāḥ*: those [suffixes] beginning with *añ* shall bear the technical designation *tadrāja* (denoting a king). For example: the king of the Pañcālas is Pāñcāla; Kauravya; Audumbari.

From a country whose inhabitants share the same designation as the *kṣatriya* class, suffixes are applied to denote its king, just as they are for the offspring of a *rājanya*. These suffixes, which have been explained [in the context of] "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), also apply when denoting the king of that country. For example: the offspring of the Pañcālas, or the kings of the Pañcālas, are called *Pañcālāḥ*; likewise *Vaṅgāḥ*, *Avantayaḥ*, and *Kuravaḥ*. According to the rule *tadrājasya* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), there is elision (*luk*) when the plural is used. There is elision after *Kamboja*: the traditional rule (*smṛti*) states that there is elision of the *tadrāja* suffix after *Kamboja* and others. Thus, the offspring or the king of the Kambojas is simply *Kambojaḥ*; similarly, *Colaḥ*, *Śakaḥ*, and *Keralaḥ*.
After *Avanti*, *Kunti*, and *Kuru*, when used in the feminine, there is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix. Thus: *iyam Avantī*, *Kuntī*, *Kurūḥ*.
And also after [the word] *ataḥ*.

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix *akāra* in the feminine. Examples: Śūrasenī, Madrī, Darad, and Iḍaviḍā. Why "after *ataḥ*" (i.e., when the final vowel is *a*)? [Counter-example: Āmbaṣṭhyā. Also, there is elision after a *yañ* suffix, except for those from the *prācya* group, the *bhargādi* group, and the *yaudheyādi* group.

Consequently, there is no *luṅ* (the feminine suffix) after these: from the Easterners (*prācyāt*), we have *pāñcālī*, *vaidehī*, *māgadhī*, *āṅgī*, and *vāṅgī*. From the group beginning with *bharga* (*bhargādeḥ*), we have *bhārgī* and *kaikeyī*. As for the statement, "Kaikeyī will cause her beloved daughter to depart," how is it that [Bharata] was born from Kekayī? It is because the feminine form is derived through the lineage of the original progenitor (*ādyaprakṛti*) by means of the family name, as in "this person is he. According to the *Bhāgavṛtti*, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied after the group beginning with *śārṅgarava* following the suffix *añ*. He will explain the *tadrāja* suffix *añ* after the group beginning with *yaudheya* in the fifth chapter.
For that [suffix] as well, elision (*luk*) which would otherwise be applicable by this rule is prohibited. *Yaudheyī*, *Śaubhreyī*. Thus ends the section on secondary derivatives (*apatyādhikāra*).
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter of the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Preceptor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva. 4.1.3.3.
Oṃ.
Fourth Chapter, Second Pāda: The Section on the Meanings of "Colored" and Others among Taddhita Affixes.
That which is colored by it arises from passion.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after words denoting color in the sense of "dyed with that. For example: *kaṣāyeṇa raktaṃ kāṣāyaṃ vastram* ("a garment dyed with a decoction is *kāṣāya*"); *kauṅkumam* ("dyed with saffron"); *māñjiṣṭhī patākā* ("a banner dyed with madder"). The word *tena* ("with that") continues to apply up until the rule for *dvaipavaiyāghrādañ*. After the words *lākṣā*, *rocanā*, *śakala*, and *kardama*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after *lākṣā* and others in the sense of "dyed with that. Examples: *lākṣikaṃ vastram* (a cloth dyed with lac), *raucanikī śāṭī* (a garment dyed with yellow orpiment), *śākalikaḥ paṭaḥ* (a cloth dyed with resin). [From *kardama*] *kārdamikam*. Some say that the suffix *aṇ* is also applied after *śakala* and *kardama*: *śākalam*, *kārdamam*. After *nīlī*, the suffix *an* is applied: *nīlaṃ vastram* (a blue cloth).
From *pīta*, [the suffix] *kan* [is applied]: *pītakam*. Time joined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).

In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. A night conjoined with Puṣya is *pauṣī*; [a night conjoined with] Māgha is *māghī*. A day of Puṣya is *pauṣam*; [a day of] Māgha is *māgham*. Why "time"? [Example: The moon conjoined with Puṣya.
[The suffix is elided] when there is no specification (*aviśeṣe*).
The suffix *lup* shall be applied to [names of] lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). For example: "Today is Puṣya," or "Today is Kṛttikā.
Why "without distinction" (*aviśeṣe*)? [Consider: "The night of Pauṣī," or "The day of Pauṣa.
[An exception: The suffix *lup* is also applied after the words *Śravaṇā* and *Aśvattha* when they form a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

From these two [words denoting asterisms], even when there is a specific distinction [of time], the elision (*lup*) may occur: *śravaṇā* (the night of the Śravaṇā asterism); *aśvatthaḥ* (the Muhūrta named Aśvattha). Why "in the sense of a designation" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [Consider: *śrāvaṇī rātriḥ* (the night of the month of Śrāvaṇa). After a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *cha* [is applied].

The suffix *cha* shall be applied after a pair of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). For example: *rādhānurādhīyā rātriḥ* (the night belonging to the [pair] Rohiṇī and Mṛgaśiras). By this rule, the elision (*lup*) is superseded because it is subsequent in the order of rules; for example: *tiṣyapunarvasīyam adya* (today belongs to the [pair] Tiṣya and Punarvasu).
Also: *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* (a Sāman seen [by them]).
In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. A *sāman* seen by Vasiṣṭha is called *vāsiṣṭham*; likewise, *vaiśvāmitram*.
After the word *kali*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied.

It may be so. The *sāman* seen by Kali is called *kāleya*. Regarding the rule *sarvatrāgnikalibhyām*: after these two, the suffix *ḍhak* should be prescribed in all senses belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group—namely, "seen by him," "occurring therein," "come from that," and "this has as its deity. Thus: *āgneyam* (belonging to Agni) and *kāleyam* (belonging to Kali).

Regarding a *sāman* seen [by someone] or a child born [to someone], the suffix *dvyaṇ* is optionally prescribed with the augment *ḍit*. Thus: *auśanasam* or *auśanam* for the *sāman*; *śātabhiṣaḥ* or *śātabhiṣajaḥ* for a child. [The general rule is: *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* ("the suffix *aṇ* applies in all senses prior to *prāgdīvyatīya*").

The meaning is that [the suffix] *sandhivelā* etc., which was previously prohibited by *kālatra*, is prescribed once again. *Tīya* + *īkak*: The suffix *īkak* is applied after a word ending in *tīya* in its own sense. Examples: *dvaitīyīkam*, *dvaitīyīkī*. Not here: *dvitīyā vidyā* (the second science). *Gotra* + *aṅkavat* is prescribed: The suffix *aṅka* is treated like *īkak* after a *gotra* (patronymic) name. Example: *aupagavakam sāma* (the Sāman belonging to the Aupagava clan). [Note: The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after a *gotra* or a *caraṇa* (Vedic school).
After the word *vāmadeva*, the suffixes *ḍyaṅ* and *ḍya* [are applied].
From this, these two [names] would arise: "The Sāman seen by him" and "The Vāmadevya. The *anubandha* (suffix) is for the sake of the accent;
as in "the surrounded chariot."

If it is a chariot (*ratha*), the suffix *aṇ* is used in this sense: a chariot covered with cloth is *vāstra*; a chariot made of leather is *cārmaṇa*. After the word *pāṇḍukambala*, the suffix *ini* is applied.
The suffix *ini* shall occur in the sense of "made from this"; for example, *pāṭukambalī rathaḥ* ("a chariot made of woolen blankets").
After the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra*, the suffix *añ* occurs.

In the sense of "made from these two," there may be another [suffix] after words meaning "two. A chariot covered with a leopard skin is called *dvaipa*; likewise, *vaiyāghra*. The word *tena* (by that) is discontinued [from this point].
In the case of expressing something not previously existing, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *kaumāra*.
The word *kaumāra*, ending in the suffix *aṇ*, is substituted for *apūrva* (meaning "one who has not previously married") when referring to the marriage of an unmarried woman.

A first-married maiden is a *kumārī*, and her husband is a *kaumāra*. Seeing that the *kaumāra* bride was not present, O best of those who fall [from heaven], they took [the offering] from the vessels there.

In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after words denoting vessels. For example: *śārāvaṃ dadhi* (curd taken up in earthen bowls) and *kārpara odanaḥ* (rice taken up in an earthen pot). Here, "taken up" (*uddhṛta*) refers to what has been set aside after being eaten. The word "therein" (*tatra*) continues to apply until the rule for the suffix *ḍhañ* after *kṣīra*.
Furthermore, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *sthaṇḍila* when it denotes one who sleeps there as part of a religious vow (*vrata*).

In this context, the suffix *aṇ* shall be used in the sense of "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*), provided that the items are edible foods. Examples: *bhrāṣṭrā apūpāḥ* (cakes prepared on a frying pan), *paiṭharāḥ* (food prepared in a pot).
[Furthermore,] the suffix *yat* is applied after the words *śūla* and *ukhā*.
From these two [words], in that sense, whatever [suffix] occurs: *śūlya* (meat prepared on a spit) and *ukhya* (prepared in a pot).
[The rule is: *yat* is applied after *śūla* and *ukhā*.

From these two [words], *śūla* and *ukhā*, the suffix *yat* occurs in that sense [of "prepared therein"]. That which is prepared on a spit is *śūlya*; [this refers to] meat. That which is in a pot (*ukhā*) is *ukhya*.
After the word *dadhi*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.
It may be so. *Dādhika* means prepared with curd. [The suffix *ṭhañ*] is optionally applied after *udaśvit*.
Therefore, there may optionally be the suffix *ṭhak*. That which is prepared with whey (*udaśvit*) is called *audaśvitka* or *audaśvita*.
After the word *kṣīra*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied.

It may be so: *kṣaireyī* refers to gruel prepared with milk. In that context, [the word] *tatra* is excluded. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after [a word ending in the seventh case] meaning "the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) occurs in this," when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied if it is a name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *pauṣī* (the full moon day of Puṣya) occurs in this [month], hence *pauṣaḥ*—referring to the month, the half-month, or the year. Similarly: *māghaḥ*, *caitraḥ*, *vaiśākhaḥ*.
[The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after *āgrahāyaṇī* and *aśvattha*.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after these two [stems] in the sense of "belonging to this. For example: *āgrahāyaṇī paurṇamāsī asmin* results in *āgrahāyaṇikaḥ*, meaning a month, a fortnight, or a year in which the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī occurs. Likewise, *āśvatthikaḥ* refers to the month of Śrāvaṇa in which the full moon of Āśvattha (Āśvayuja) occurs.
[This application of the suffix is] optional (*vibhāṣā*) after the stems *phalgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārttikī*, and *caitrī*.

The suffix *ṭhak* may optionally be applied after these [names of months] in the sense of "belonging to" (*pūrvārthe*). For example: *phālgunikaḥ* or *phālgunaḥ* [meaning] a month, a fortnight, or a year; *śrāvaṇikaḥ* or *śrāvaṇaḥ*; *kārttikikaḥ* or *kārttikaḥ*; *caitrikaḥ* or *caitraḥ*.
[The suffix *ṭhak* is also applied] when the meaning is "this has that as its deity" (*sāsya devatā*).
In this case, the suffix shall be applied according to the rule. Indra is its deity; thus, "aindraṃ haviḥ" (an offering for Indra). "Bārhaspatyaḥ mantraḥ" (a mantra for Bṛhaspati).

They say that in a sacrifice, the deity is the recipient of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, as well as the one praised by the mantra. The governing rule "sāsya devatā" (that is its deity) applies up to the word *pitṛvya*.
Of what [is it the deity]?
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after the word *ka*, and the letter *i* shall be the substitute for the final phoneme. [Thus: *kāyam* refers to an oblation whose deity is *Ka*;
the meaning is "Prajāpati.
After the word *śukra*, the suffix *ghan* [is applied].
It may be so. [The word] *śukriya* is a chapter title.
[The suffix] *gha* is applied after the words *aponaptr̥* and *naptṛ*.
The suffix *gha* occurs after these two [words] in the sense of "belonging to" (*pūrvārtha*). Examples: *aponaptriyam*, *apānnaptrimam*. [The suffix *cha* also occurs in this sense. Pāṇini 4.2.27–28.
The suffix *cha* shall occur after these two [words]. *aponaptrīyam* (belonging to Aponaptr). *apānnaptrīyaṃ haviḥ* (the oblation for Aponaptr).
There is an extension [of the rule] to include *paiṅgākṣīputra* and others. *paiṅgākṣīputrīyam*. *tārṇavindavīyam*. *Paiṅgākṣīputrīya* means "the son of Paiṅgākṣī.
After *śatarudra*, the suffixes *gha* and *cha* also occur. After *śatarudra*, the suffixes *ghac* and *cha* shall occur. *śatadrīyam*. *śatarudriyam*.
And from Mahendra, the two nostrils.
From this [word *mahendra*], the suffixes *gha*, *añ*, and *cha* shall apply: *māhendra*, *mahendriya*, and *mahendrīya*.
After *soma*, the suffix *ṭyaṇ* applies.
The suffix *ṭyaṇ* shall occur after [the word] *pūrvā* in the sense of "belonging to. Examples: *saumyaṃ haviḥ* (an oblation belonging to Soma); *saumī ṛk* (a verse belonging to Soma).
After the words *vāyu*, *ṛtu*, *pitṛ*, and *uṣas*, the suffix *yat* occurs.
The suffix *yat* occurs after these [words] in the sense of "belonging to" (*pūrvārthe*). Examples: *vāyavyaḥ mantraḥ* ("a mantra belonging to Vāyu"), *ṛtavyam*, *uṣasyam*, *pitryam*.
Furthermore, the suffix *cha* occurs after *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*.

The suffix *cha* occurs after these six [words] when they denote the sense of "belonging to" (*yat-pūrvārtha*). [Examples: *dyāvāpṛthivīyam*, *dyāvāpṛthivyam*; *śunāsīrīyam*, *śunāsīryam*; *marutvatīyam*, *marutvatyam*; *āgnīṣomīyam*, *āgrasomyam*; *vāstoṣpatīyam*, *vāstoṣpatyam*;
*gṛhamedhīyam*, *gṛhamedhyam*. [The suffix] *ḍhak* occurs after the word *agni*.
It may be so: "The *caru* offering belongs to Agni," according to the rule for words derived from time-periods, like *bhava*.

After words denoting time, suffixes applicable in the sense of "this is its deity" (sāsya devatā) shall also apply in the sense of "occurring therein" (bhava). Examples: *māsikam* (monthly), *prāvṛṣeṇyam* (occurring in the rainy season), *haimanam* (occurring in winter), *vāsantam* (occurring in spring).
After the words *mahārāja* and *proṣṭhapada*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied.

The suffix *ṭhañ* shall be applied after these two in the sense of "belonging to this. For example: *māhārājikam* (belonging to the Great King) and *prauṣṭhapadikam* (belonging to Proṣṭhapada), meaning "related to Indra. The suffix *ṭhañ* shall be applied after words such as *navayajña* (new sacrifice) in the sense of "that which occurs on this [day/time]. For example: *nāvayajñikaḥ kālaḥ* (a time when the new sacrifice occurs); *svādhyāyikaḥ* (a time for Vedic study); *autpātikaḥ* (a time of portents). The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *pūrṇamāsa*. For example: *paurṇamāsī tithiḥ* (the full-moon lunar day), meaning "that on which the full moon occurs."
The governing rule "that is its deity" is completed.
Paternal uncles, maternal uncles, maternal grandfathers, and paternal grandfathers.
These are irregularly formed (nipātita). With the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* applied according to the *gaura*-group: *pitāmahī*, *mātāmahī*.

The suffixes *soḍha*, *dūsa*, and *marīsa* are added to the word *avi* when it means "the milk of a sheep": *avisoḍham*, *avidūsam*, *avimarīsam*. The suffixes *piñja* and *peja* occur after *tila* when it means "barren" (*niṣphala*): *tilapiñjaḥ*, *tilapejaḥ*.
Its collection.

In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall apply. A collection (*samūha*) of crows is *kāka*; a collection of cranes is *vāka*; a collection of parrots is *śauka*. The governing rule for "collection" extends up to the section on *kaṭac*.
[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the group beginning with *bhikṣā*.
An affix denoted by the marker *ṇa* shall supersede these [affixes] that cause obstruction. A collection of beggars is *bhaikṣam*. *Gārbhiṇam*, *cārbhiṇam*, *dhārmiṇam*, *sāhasram*, *pādātam*.

Regarding the word *yuvati*, Jayāditya says it becomes *yauvatam*; however, according to the *Bhāgavṛtti*, when the word belongs to the neuter class (*bha*) and a non-*āḍha* secondary suffix follows, there is a substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), resulting in *yauvanam*.
[The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after words ending in *otra*, *ukṣan*, *uṣṭra*, *urabhra*, *rājan*, *rājanya*, *rājaputra*, *vatsa*, *manuṣya*, and *aja*.

The suffix *vuñ* shall be applied after words denoting lineages (*gotra*) and after *ukṣan* and so forth, in the sense of a collection. Examples: *dākṣakam*, *gārgakam*, *aukṣakam*, *auṣṭrakam*, *aurabhrakam*, *rājakam*, *rājanyakam*, *rājaputrakam*, *vātsakam*, *ajakam*. [The suffix *vuñ* is also applied] after a word ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel: *vārddhakam*.
And [the suffix] *yaÑ* after *kedāra*.

The suffix *yañ* occurs after *kedāra*, as in *kaidārya* and *kedāraka*. The suffix *ṭhak* is set aside when it does not refer to a non-sentient being. The suffix *yañ* also occurs after *gaṇikā*, as in *gāṇikya*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after *kavacin*.
The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñ* shall be applied after the words *kavacin* and *kedāra*. [Examples: *kāvacikam*, *kaidārikam*.
After the words *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, and *vāḍava*, the suffix *yan* is applied.
[The suffix *yañ*] may occur [after these]: *brāhmaṇyam*, *māṇavyam*, *vāḍavyam*.
Also after *pṛṣṭha*: *pṛṣṭhyam*. After *ahan*, the suffix *kha* occurs when referring to a sacrifice (*kratu*): when a collection of days refers to a sacrifice, *kha* is used; e.g., *ahīnaḥ*.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after *parśu* [to form a word for] a collection. *Pārśvam*: the meaning is "a collection of ribs" (*parśūṇām samūhaḥ*).
The suffix *tal* is applied after the words *grāma*, *jana*, *bandhu*, and *sahāya*.

The suffix *tal* occurs after these [words] when they denote a collection (*samūha*): *grāmatā*, *bandhūtā*, *janatā*, *sahāyatā*. As for the usage *suratā* in the *purāṇas*, it is indeed based on the authority of the sages (*ārṣa*). [The suffix *tal* also occurs] after the word *gaja*: *gajatā*.
The suffix *añ* is applied [to form a patronymic] after a word whose first syllable is unaccented (*anudātta*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *khaṇḍika* and others.

The suffix *añ* occurs after these [words] to form a collective sense: *kāpotam*, *māyūram*, *khāṇḍikam*. After words denoting female animals, the suffix *aṇ* is used: *vāḍavaṃ* for a multitude of mares (*vaḍavānām*).
This is similar to the formation of religious duties (*dharma*) from names of schools (*caraṇa*).

The suffixes [denoting the author] should also apply to denote a collection of those [works] whose purpose is the practice [of the Veda], just as they do for the Veda itself: *kāṭhakam*, *chāndogyam*, *ātharvaṇam*.
[Furthermore, the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after words that are not names of sentient beings, and after *hasti* and *dhenu*: [e.g., *hāstikam*, *dhainukam*].

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after words denoting things that have no consciousness, as well as after the words *hastin* (elephant) and *dhenu* (cow), when forming a collective sense: *āpūpikam*, *śāṣkulikam*, *hāstikam*, *dhainukam*.
After *dhenu*, the suffix *añ* may also be applied: *dhainavam*. After the words *keśa* (hair) and *aśva* (horse), the suffixes *yañ* and *cha* are optionally applied respectively.

These two suffixes should apply according to their respective order. Or, after the word *keśa*, the suffix *yañ* may be applied: *kaiśyam*. By the preceding rule, the suffix *ṭhak* [is also applied]: *kaiśikam*.
After the word *aśva*, the suffix *cha* is optionally applied: *aśvīyam*; or *āśvam*. In the alternative case, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
The suffix *ya* is applied after words such as *pāśa*.
The suffix *ya* occurs after *pāśa* and others when they denote a collection (*vṛnda*): *pāśyā*, *tṛṇyā*, *vanyā*, *vātyā*, *dhūmyā*. [The suffix *ya* also occurs] after *khala*, *go*, and *ratha*.
The suffixes *ya*, *khal*, *ya*, *ini*, *tra*, *kaṭya*, and *ac* are applied after these [words]. For example: *khalyā*, *gavyā*, *rathyā*.
And [the suffix] *ini*, *tra*, *kaṭya*, and *ac*.
These suffixes occur in sequence after the words *khala* and so forth: *khalinī*, *gotrā*. [In the verse: "The fish joined with the *gotrā* woman. *Rathakaṭyā*.
It should be stated that the suffix *ini* occurs after *khala* and so forth: *khalinī*, *ulukinī*, *padimanī*. The formation of collective nouns has been explained.
The word "of that" (tasya) continues to apply [from the preceding rule]. "Region" (viṣaya) refers to a place.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case when it denotes the domain (*viṣaya*) of that [group], provided that the domain is a country (*deśa*). For example: the domain of the Śivīs is *śaiva*; likewise, *āṅga* and *paurava*. After words such as *rājanya*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied.
The suffix *vuñ* shall occur after these [names] in the sense of "belonging to them" (*pūrvārtha*). Examples: *rājanyakaḥ* (a country belonging to the Rājanyas), *mālavakaḥ*.
After the group beginning with *bhauriki* and the group beginning with *aiṣukāri*, the suffixes *vidhal* and *bhaktal* [respectively] are applied.
The suffixes *vidhal* and *bhaktal* occur after these two classes [of words] in the sense of "originating from that. Examples: *bhaurikividhaḥ*, *aiṣukāribhaktaḥ*.
Furthermore, the suffix *cha* (forming *chandas*) occurs after [words denoting] meters in the sense of "that is the beginning of," when referring to *pragāthas*.

In the case of *pragāthas*, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied to denote the meter (*chandas*), provided that the *pragātha* is a specific type of mantra. For example: the *pragātha* whose [constituent verses] begin with *paṅkti* is called *pāṅkta*; likewise, *ānuṣṭubha* and *jāgata*. There is an extension of the rule for the neuter gender of *chandas* to express its own meaning: *triṣṭubh* itself is *traiṣṭubham*; likewise, *jāgatam* and *ānuṣṭubham*. [The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after words denoting the battle, the purpose, and the warriors.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after these [words] in the sense of "this is for its purpose" (*tadartha*), provided that it refers to a battle (*saṃgrāma*). For example: *subhadrā* is the purpose of this, thus *saubhadraḥ* is a battle; likewise *draupadaḥ*, *saitaḥ*, *straiṇaḥ*, and *pauṃsnaḥ*. When the Bharatas are the combatants of this, it is *bhārataḥ* a battle; likewise *pādātaḥ* (infantry) and *āśvaḥ* (cavalry). Furthermore, the suffix *ṇa* is applied after these [same words] in the sense of "this is the weapon used in this," when referring to a game (*krīḍā*).

In this sense, the suffix *ṇa* occurs if it is a game (*krīḍā*). For example: "A stick (*daṇḍa*) is the weapon used in this [game]" → *dāṇḍā* (stick-game); *mauṣṭā* (fist-game); *pāllavā* (leaf-game). The suffix *ñya* occurs when the meaning is "this is the activity (*kriyā*) performed in this [place]."

The suffix *ñya* occurs after a word ending in *ghañ* in this sense [of "that which belongs to it"]. For example: *śyainampātā mṛgayā* ("a hunt characterized by the swoop of a hawk") and *mausalapātā bhūmiḥ* ("ground characterized by the fall of clubs"). [The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] in the senses of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that."

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied in these two senses. One who studies or knows grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is a *vaiyākaraṇa*. A *chāndasaḥ* (one who studies the Vedic phonology). A *jyautiṣaḥ* (one who studies astronomy). One who studies or knows the omens (*nimitta*) is a *naimittaḥ*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, etc., and those ending in *sūtra*.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall apply after both [categories] when the sense is "one who studies" (*pūrvārtha*). Examples: *kratūḥ*—*āgniṣṭomikaḥ*; *ukthādiḥ*—*aukthikaḥ*, *yājñikaḥ*. [The *ukthādi* group consists of:

*uktha*, *yajña*, *lokāyata*, *nyāya*, *nyāsa*, *tarka*. [There is also the following] *gaṇasūtra*: "After words ending in *vidyā*, *lakṣaṇa*, or *kalpasūtra*, provided they do not begin with *kalpa*. Examples: *vāyasavidyikaḥ*, *dhānurvidyikaḥ*.

In the case of *cātuvaidya*, however, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "skill" (*kuśala*), according to the rule *kṛta-labdha-krīta-kuśalāḥ*. From words ending in *lakṣaṇa* and others: *gaulakṣaṇikaḥ*, *prāthamakalpikaḥ*, *vārttikasūtrikaḥ*. But not here: *kālpasūtraḥ*. The suffix *ṭhak* is not applied after the word *vidyā* when preceded by *aṅga*, *kṣatra*, *ṛddhi*, or *tri*. Thus: *āṅgavidyaḥ*, *traividyaḥ*.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall also be applied after the names of *ākhyāna*, *ākhyāyikā*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*. For *ākhyāna* and *ākhyāyikā*, there is the inclusion of their meaning; for *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*, however, there is the inclusion of their own form. Examples: *yāvakrītikaḥ*, *vāsavadattikaḥ*, *aitihāsikaḥ*, *paurāṇikaḥ*. The suffix *la* (which causes elision) is applied after these when preceded by *sarva*, *sa*, or a *dvigu* compound. After those beginning with *sarva*: *sarvavedaḥ*. After those beginning with *sa*: *savārttikaḥ*. After a *dvigu*: *pañcakalpaḥ*, *dvivedaḥ*, *dvitantraḥ*. The suffix *ikan* is applied after a word ending in *pada* as its final member. Example: *padottarapadikaḥ*.
The suffix *ṣikan* is added to *śatapaṣṭi* and *pathin*. [Examples: *śatapathikaḥ*, *ṣaṣṭipathikī*. The suffix *vun* is added to *krama* and other such words.
There may be one who studies or knows the *krama* [recitation], being called a *kramaka*; likewise a *padaka* [one who knows the word-by-word recitation].
From *śikṣā*, *mīmāṃsā*, *upaniṣad*, *anubrāhmaṇa*, and so forth, the suffix *-in-* is applied.
The suffix *ini* occurs after words meaning "similar to" (*pūrvārtha*). A text similar to the *Brāhmaṇa* is called *anubrāhmaṇa*; one who studies or knows that is *anubrāhmaṇī*.
After words such as *vasanta*, the suffix *ṭak* is applied.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied in the sense of "belonging to the preceding [time]. Examples: *vāsantikaḥ* (pertaining to spring), *vārṣikaḥ* (pertaining to the rainy season). Likewise, a treatise associated with spring and so forth is designated in this way.
[Furthermore,] there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix when [a work] has been "proclaimed" (*prokta*).

The suffix produced after a word ending in the suffixes prescribed for one who teaches or knows shall be elided (*luk*). A book taught by Pāṇini is *pāṇinīyaḥ* (by *vṛddhācchaḥ*), and a student who studies or knows that [book] is a *pāṇinīyaś chātraḥ*. That which was taught by Āpiśali is *āpiśalam* (by *iññaśca*), and a Brāhmaṇī woman who studies or knows the *āpiśalam* is an *āpiśalā brāhmaṇī*.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a root ending in a vowel and having *k* as its penultimate letter, according to the Sūtra.

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffix produced after a word denoting a follower of a *sūtra* that has a *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), provided it refers to one who studies or knows [that work]. For example: those who study or know the *Aṣṭaka-sūtra* of Pāṇini are called *Aṣṭakāḥ* or *Pāṇinīyāḥ*; the *Daśakāḥ* are the followers of Vyāghrapada; the *Dvādaśakāḥ* are the Mīmāṃsakas. This designation applies only when the base is a numeral. Here it does not apply: one who studies the *Mahāvārttika-sūtra* is a *Māhāvārttikaḥ*. Why "having *ka* as its penultimate letter"? Consider: one who studies the *Catuṣṭaya* is a *Cātuṣṭayaḥ*.
And the *chandobrāhmaṇas* (the Vedic hymns and ritual manuals) have those [meters] as their subject matter.

It is stated [in the rule] by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). The Vedic meters (*chandas*) and Brāhmaṇas that end with the suffix *prokta* (P. 4.3.101), as well as—by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*)—certain Kalpas and Sūtras spoken by ancient authorities, should have [the suffixes] whose objects are the students and knowers of those subjects; they do not [themselves] end with the *prokta* suffix. Examples: *kaṭhāḥ* (the Kaṭhas)—those who study the Vedic meter (*chandas*) taught by Kaṭha. *Maudāḥ* (the Maudas). *Tāṇḍinaḥ* (the Tāṇḍins)—those who study the Brāhmaṇa taught by Tāṇḍya. Regarding the Kalpa: *Kāśyapinaḥ* (the Kāśyapins). Regarding the Sūtra: *Pārāśariṇaḥ* (the Pārāśarins).
[The suffix *ini* is applied] in the sense of "this exists in this," when referring to a country bearing that name.

In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied when the name of a place is [derived from its inhabitants]. For example: since *udumbaras* exist in this region, it is called *audumbara*; likewise, *pārvata*. In the sense of "established by that," the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. For example: the city established by Kuśāmba is *kauśāmbī*; the moat is *sāhasrī*.
His dwelling place.
In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. For example: "The residence of the Śivīs" is *śaivaḥ*;
and it also applies to that which is situated nearby.

In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. For example: *vaidiśam* (Vaidiśa) is a city not far from Vidiśā; *pāmpāni* (Pāmpa) refers to forests. These four meanings continue to apply throughout the section on the remainder (*śeṣādhikāra*).
or forest-dweller.

The secondary suffix *añ* (with the augment *ṇya*) shall be applied after a word ending in the vowel *u* to express the four meanings [of place, product, inhabitant, and origin]. For example: *kārkaṭavam*.
The governing rule for *añ* extends from here until before the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after *suvāstu* and others.
Furthermore, it applies after a word ending in the suffix *matup* that has more than two syllables.

The suffix *añ* shall be applied after a word ending in the possessive suffix *matup*, provided that the word contains many long syllables (*bahu-ajaṅga*). For example, there is a region named Aikaṭāvata. [The suffix *añ* is also applied] after words with many vowels when referring to wells.

The suffix *añ* shall be used after a word with many vowels if it refers to a well (*kūpa*). For example: *dairghavaratraḥ kūpaḥ*, meaning "a well made with a long rope. Also, [the suffix *añ* is applied] to denote what is not far from the root of a tree, as in *vārkṣamūlaḥ*.
Furthermore, the suffix *udak* is applied after the word *vipāś*.
In the case of wells on the northern bank of the Vipāśā river, the suffix *añ* should be used. For example: *dātta-kūpaḥ*, meaning "a well established by Datta"; *gaupta-kūpaḥ*.
This also applies after words beginning with *saṅkala*.

The suffix *añ* is added to these [names of countries] in the four senses [of the fourth case]. *Sāṅkalaḥ* and *pauṣkalaḥ* refer to specific regions. [The suffix is applied] to feminine names in the sense of women belonging to Sauvīra, Sālva, and Prācya.

The suffix *añ* shall be applied in the feminine gender for place-names beginning with *sauvīra*. For example: *dāttāmitrī*, a city established by Dattāmitra; *vaidhūbhāgrī*, [a city] among the Śālvas; *mākandī*, a city in the East. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after [place-names] beginning with *suvāstu*.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after these [words]. For example: *sauvāstavaṃ nagaram* (the city of Sauvāstava), *sauvāstavī nagarī* (the city of Sauvāstava), *sauvāstavī nadī* (the river of Sauvāstava); *vārṇavam*, *vārṇavī*, *roṇī*.
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after [the word] *roṇī*. For example: *ājakarṇaḥ*.
It is also applied after a single [word ending in] *roṇī*: a well constructed from *roṇī* grass is called *rauṇaḥ*.
It is also applied after [a word] having *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*).
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied [to form patronymics and derivatives]. [Examples: *kārṇacitrakaḥ*, *kārṇacchidrakaḥ*. [The suffix] *traiaśaṅkavam* [is formed with *aṇ*].

The suffixes *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, *kaṭhac*, *ilac*, *seniRa*, *aḍhañ*, *ñyaṅ*, *ya*, *phak*, *phiñ*, *ñiñ*, *ñyaṅ*, *kak*, *ṭhak*, and *aṇ* are applied after the following groups of bases: *arīhaṇa*, *kṛśāśva*, *śvāśya*, *kumuda*, *kāśa*, *tṛṇa*, *prekṣā*, *aśman*, *sakhi*, *saṅkāśa*, *bala*, *pakṣa*, *kaṇera*, *sutaṅgama*, *pragadin*, *varāha*, and *kumuda*, etc.

From these seventeen groups, the suffixes *vuñ* and others shall apply as appropriate to four types of meanings. 1. From the group beginning with *arīhaṇa*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied: *ārīhaṇaka*. 2. From the group beginning with *kṛśāśva*, the suffix *chaṇ* is applied: *kārśaśvīya*. 3. From the group beginning with *ṛśya*, the suffix *ka* is applied: *ṛśyaka*. 4. From the group beginning with *kumuda*, the suffix *ṭhac* is applied: *kumudika*. 5. From the group beginning with *kāśa*, the suffix *ila* is applied: *kāśila*. 6. From the group beginning with *tṛṇa*, the suffix *sa* is applied: *tṛṇasa*, *naḍasa*, *vīraṇasa*. 7. From the group beginning with *prekṣā*, the suffix *ini* is applied: *prekṣī*, *phalakī*. 8. From the group beginning with *aśman*, the suffix *ra* is applied: *aśmara*. 9. From the group beginning with *sakhi*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied: *sākheya*.

The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [the group beginning with] *saṅkāśa*: *sāṅkāśyam*, *kāmpilyam*. The suffix *ya* is applied after [the group beginning with] *bala*: *balyam*. The suffix *phak* is applied after [the group beginning with] *pakṣa*: *pākṣāyaṇaḥ*. The suffix *phiñ* is applied after [the group beginning with] *karṇa*: *kārṇāyaniḥ*. The suffix *iñ* is applied after [the group beginning with] *sutaṅgama*: *sautaṅgamiḥ*. The suffix *ñya* is applied after [the group beginning with] *pragadin*: *prāgadyam*. The suffix *kak* is applied after [the group beginning with] *varāha*: *vārāhakam*, *pālāśakam*, *śārkarakam*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [the group beginning with] *kumuda*: *kaumudikam*, *gaumathikam*. [When the name refers to] a country (*janapada*), there is elision (*lup*).

The suffix of the fourth case (cāturarthika) shall be elided when referring to a country (janapada), that is, a region bearing that name. For example, the country which is the residence of the Pañcālas is called "Pañcāla"; likewise, "Kuru" and "Vaṅga.
A janapada is a specific division of a country.
[The suffix is also elided] after words such as "varaṇa" and others.

The suffix *cāturarthika* (the fourth set of meanings) shall be elided after these [words]: *varaṇā* as a village; *godau* as a village; *khalatikaṃ* as forests; likewise *śirīṣāḥ*, *śṛṅgī*, *gayā*, and *ujjayinī*. After *śarkarā*, it is optional.
The suffix *lup* may optionally occur after this [term]. [Thus,] "produced from gravel" (*śarkarābhinirvṛttam*) can be expressed as either *śarkarāḥ* or *śārkaram*.
Furthermore, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha* [may also occur].
For this [suffix], there shall be two [substitutes]: *śārkarika* and *śarkarīya*.
[The suffix] *matup* is applied after the word "nadī" (river).

The suffix *matup* occurs after the word *nadī* in four senses. [Examples: *udumbarāvatī nadī* ("a river possessing udumbara trees"), *ikṣumatī*. [The suffix] *ñ* also occurs after words beginning with *madhu*.
The suffix *matup* shall occur after these four types of words [to express the aforementioned meanings]: *madhumān*, *visavān deśaḥ*.
After the words *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa*, the suffix *ḍmatup* is applied.

The suffix *ḍmatup* is applied after these [words]. By the rule *ḍiti ṭilopaḥ*, there is elision of the final syllable. Thus: *kumudvān*, *naḍvān*, *vetasvān*; and *vetasvatī* as a river. [The suffix *ḍmatup* is also applied] after *mahiṣa*: *mahiṣmān* is the name of a country.
After *naḍa* and *śāda*, the suffix *ḍvalac* is applied.
The suffix *ḍvalac* is applied after these two: *naḍvalaḥ* (a place abounding in reeds), *śādvalaḥ* (a place abounding in young grass). *Śādvalam* is a bed, a seat, or a pure stone slab.
The suffix *valac* is also applied after *śikhā*.
It may be so. The city is Śikhāvala.
[The suffix] *cha* is applied after [words beginning with] *utkara*, etc.
The suffix *cha* is applied [after the word *utkara*] to form *autkariya*.
After words beginning with *naḍa*, the suffix *cha* is applied and the final syllable is replaced by *kuk*.
For these [words], *cha* shall be the suffix, and there shall be the addition of *kuk*. *naḍakīya* (belonging to the Naḍas). [The base words are: *naḍa*, *veṇu*, *plakṣa*, *bilva*.
In the case of *kruñcā*, there is also shortening [of the vowel]. *kruñcakīya* (belonging to the Kruñcas).
In the case of *takṣan*, there is also the elision of *n*. *takṣakīya* (belonging to the Takṣans).
The suffixes with four meanings have been explained.
In the remainder.

In the remaining cases, suffixes should be expressed for meanings such as "born there" and so forth. For example: born in the kingdom, come from the kingdom, or existing in the kingdom—*rāṣṭriyaḥ*; *śālīyaḥ*. Here, that which is perceived by the eye is *cākṣuṣaṃ rūpam* (visible form); sound is *śrāvaṇaḥ śabdaḥ* (audible sound); a chariot carried by horses is *āśvo rathaḥ* (horse-drawn chariot); a cart for four [horses] is *cāturaṃ śakaṭam*; beans ground on a stone are *dārṣadā māṣāḥ* (stone-ground beans); flour from a mortar is *audūkhalāḥ saktavaḥ* (mortar-flour); a demon seen on the fourteenth day is *cāturdaśaṃ rakṣaḥ* (fourteenth-day demon). Thus, according to the *Bhāgavṛtti*, these are used generally when one intends to express the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*).

Jayāditya states that "the remainder" (śeṣa) refers both to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) and to the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). [The suffixes] *gha* and *kha* are applied after the words *rāṣṭra* and *avārapāra*.

The suffixes *gha* and *kha* shall occur after these two [words]. Thus: *rāṣṭriyaḥ* (belonging to the kingdom) and *avārapārīṇaḥ* (going from this shore to the other). [The suffix *kha*] also occurs after [the words] when they are separated [by a vowel]: *avārīṇaḥ* (going toward this shore) and *pārīṇaḥ* (going toward the other shore).
[The suffix *kha*] also occurs after [the word] when it is reversed: *pārāvārīṇaḥ* (going from the other shore to this shore) is thus desired.
The suffixes *ya* and *khañ* are added after the word *grāma*.
[The suffixes] syātām [are applied]: grāmyaḥ, grāmīṇaḥ.
After words such as katri, the suffix ḍhakañ is applied.
The suffix *ḍhakañ* shall be applied after words such as *kattrī* and others. For example: from *kattrī*, *kāttreyaka*; from *umbhī*, *aumbheyaka*; *grāmeyaka*; *nāgareyaka*.
After *kuḍyā*, there is also the elision of the *y*. Thus: *kauḍeyaka*.
[The suffix *ḍhakañ* is applied] after *kula*, *kukṣi*, and *grīvā* when referring respectively to a dog, a mouth, and an ornament.

The suffix *ḍhakañ* shall be used when expressing a dog and so forth as originating from a family (*kula*) and the like. For example: *kauleyakaḥ śvā* (a dog of noble breed); *kaukṣeyakaḥ asiḥ* (a sword made in the Kukṣi region);
*graiveyakaḥ kaṇṭhālaṅkāraḥ* (an ornament for the neck).
The suffix *ḍhak* is used after words such as *nādi*.
There may be water that is not to be drunk; a person from Vārāṇasī; one from Śrāvastī;
and one from the southwestern city.

The suffix *tyak* is applied after these [words] when the sense is "remaining" (*śeṣe*). The word *dakṣiṇā*, ending in the suffix *āc*, is not feminine; therefore, in the case of a compound formation (*vṛtti*), the substitution of the masculine form for a pronoun does not apply. Examples: *dākṣiṇātyaḥ*, *pāścāttyaḥ*, *paurastyaḥ*.
After the word *kāpiśī*, the suffix *ṣphak* is applied.
The suffix *ṣphak* shall be applied to this [word *kāpiśa*]. *Kāpiśāyanaṃ madhu* (honey from Kāpiśa); *kāpiśāyanī drākṣā* (grapes from Kāpiśa).
The suffix *ṣphak* shall be applied after words ending in *bāhu*, *ūru*, and *pardi*. *Bāhṇāyanī*; *aurdāyanī*; *pārdāyanī*.
After the word *raṅku*, when not referring to a human being, the suffix *aṇ* is also applied.
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied in the sense of "produced therefrom" (*tatra-bhava*) after the word *raṅku*; furthermore, the suffix *ṣphak* is also applied. Thus: *rāṅkavaḥ* and *rāṅkavāyaṇaḥ*.
After the words *dyu*, *prāc*, *apāc*, *udac*, and *pratīc*, the suffix *yat* is applied.

From these [words], there shall be [the suffixes]: *divyam*, *prācyam*, *apācyam*, *udīcyam*, *pratīcyam*. From an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are added with the augment *tuṭ*: *prāktanam*.
After the word *kanthā*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.
The suffix *kānthika* is applied [to form a word meaning "belonging to the same region"];
the suffixes *varṇa* and *vuk* are also applied [in this sense].
The suffix *vuk* occurs after the word *kaṇṭhā* when it denotes a region (*deśa*). [Thus: *kānthakam*.
After an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffix *tyap* occurs.

The suffix *tya* is applied after the words *ama*, *iha*, *kva*, *tasi*, and *tre* to form designations. *Amātyaḥ* (a minister). *Kvatyeyam durmatistava* (Whence comes this evil-mindedness of yours?). *Tatastyaḥ* (one from there). *Yatastyaḥ* (one from where). *Kutastyaḥ* (from where?). *Yatratyaḥ* (one from where). *Atratyaḥ* (one from here). *Tatratyaḥ* (one from there). By the rule *tyab ner dhruve*: *Nityam* (eternal/permanent). By the rule *niso gate tyap*: *Niṣṭyaḥ* (one who has gone out from a country), such as a Cāṇḍāla or similar outcaste.
From *araṇya* comes *-ña*: *āraṇyāḥ sumanasaḥ* ("wild flowers"). From *dūra* comes *-etya*: *dūretyaḥ pathikaḥ* ("a traveler from afar"). From *uttara* comes *-āhañ*: *auttarāhaḥ*.
The suffixes for "this year" (aiṣamas), "next year" (hyas), and "the day after tomorrow" (śvas) are optionally applied [to the word *para*].
The suffix *tyap* may optionally be applied after these [words]: *aiṣamastyam*, *hyastyam*, *śvastyam*.
In the alternative (*pakṣe*), there are: *aiṣamastanam*, *hyastanam*, *śvastanam*.
The suffixes *añ* and *ññ* are applied when *tīra* or *rūpya* are the final members of the compound.
The suffix *ñya* shall be applied after a word ending in *tīra* or *rūpya*. [Examples: *vārkatīram*, *vārkarūpyam*.
When preceded by a word denoting direction (*dik*), the suffix *ñya* is applied provided it is not a proper name (*asaṃjñāyām*).

After a word denoting a cardinal direction as the first member, the suffixes *ñya* and *ñ* shall be applied when the final member is not *amra*. For example: *paurvaśālaḥ* (dwelling in the eastern hall), *auttaraśālaḥ* (dwelling in the northern hall).
After the word *madra*, the suffix *añ* is applied.
The suffix *añ* shall be applied after the name of a village of the Madra people when preceded by a word denoting direction; for example, *paurvamadraḥ*.
It shall also be applied after the name of a northern village that consists of more than two syllables and is oxytone.
The suffix *añ* shall be applied to names of villages located in the northern region. Examples: Śaivapura, Māhānagara. Why "having many syllables"? [Counter-example: Dhvāja.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied to words ending in *prastha*, to those having *paladi* as their initial member, and to those having *ka* as their penultimate element (*kopadha*).

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after these: after a word ending in *prastha*—e.g., *mādrīprastha* (the village of Mādrīprastha); after words beginning with *paladi*—e.g., *pālada*, *pāriṣada*; after a word having *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*)—e.g., *vaighātaka*. This is an exception to the suffix *añ* for villages of the Northern regions.
[The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after the *gotra* names beginning with *kaṇva*.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after [names] beginning with *kaṇva* when they end in a *gotra*-suffix; this serves as an exception (*bādhā*) to the suffix *cha*. Since [the names] beginning with *kaṇva* belong to the *garga*-class, the suffix *yañ* applies: *kāṇvyaḥ*; the students (*chātra*) of that [teacher] are *kāṇvāḥ*. Similarly, *gaukakṣāḥ*. And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after [names ending in] *iñ*.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after a word ending in the suffix *iñ* when it denotes a lineage (*gotra*); this is an exception to the rule for feminine forms (*chāp*). Examples: *dākṣer amī* (these are the descendants of Dakṣa) become *dākṣāḥ*; likewise, *plākṣāḥ*.
However, this does not apply to two-syllable names among the Easterners (*prācya*) or the Bharatas.
The suffix *iñ* ending in a word with two syllables belonging to the *gotra* (lineage) of the Easterners and the Bharatas shall not take the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *vaiṅkīyāḥ*, *kāśīyāḥ*.
[In other cases,] the suffix *cha* is applied after a *vṛddha* (first vowel long) stem.

The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) occurs after words designated as "vṛddha" when they are used as secondary (*śaiṣika*) derivatives. Examples: *śālīyaḥ*, *ācāryīyaḥ*, *bauddhīyaṃ matam*, *tvadīyaḥ*, *madīyaḥ*.
After the word *bhavat*, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *chas* occur.
From this [base *bhavat*], these two suffixes [ṭhak and cha] may occur. They supersede the suffix *cha*. Thus: *bhāvatkaḥ* and *bhavadīyaḥ*.
[The suffixes] *ṭhañ*, *ñ*, and *ñiṭh* are applied after words beginning with *kāśi*.

From these [provinces], the following two [suffixes] may occur: *kāśikī* and *kāśikā*; *baidikī* and *baidikā*; *caidikī* and *caidikā*. And [the suffixes *cha* and *aṇ* occur] after names of villages of the Vāhīkas.
The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ññiṭh* shall be applied after these [names] when they denote an elder (*vṛddha*). Examples: *śākalikī*, *śākalikā*.
[This application is] optional (*vibhāṣā*) among the Uśīnaras.

Or rather, these two [suffixes] may optionally apply after the names of villages belonging to the Vāhīkas: *āhvajālikī*, *āhvajālikā*, or *āhvajālīyā*. In the region of Ordeśa, the suffix *ṭhañ* is used.
The suffix *ṭhañ* (which becomes *-ika*) is applied after a word ending in *u*, when denoting a region, provided it is not one of the exceptions; for example, *śābarajambuka*.
After a word containing a *vṛddhi* vowel, this suffix is used when denoting a region of the easterners (*prāc*).
In the eastern region, the suffix *ṭhañ* (which becomes *īya*) shall be applied after a word ending in a vowel that contains a *vṛddhi* vowel in its first syllable. For example: *āḍhakajambukaḥ*.
Why "after a *vṛddhi* vowel"? Consider: *mallavāstu*—the derivative is *māllavāstavaḥ*.
