For these [words], *puru*, *adhas*, and *avas* shall be substituted by *pur-*, *adh-*, and *av-*, respectively, when followed by the suffix *astāti*, provided they signify "dwelling," "having come," or "delightful.
And [the same applies] when followed by *astāti*.

In place of *asta* and *ati*, the forms *pura* and so forth shall be substituted for *pūrva* and the others [in the sense of "before" and "below"]. Examples: *purastāt*, *adhastāt*, *avastāt*. How then is *puratas* formed? This must be considered. [The substitution is] optional (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of *avara*.
The substitution of *ava* for *avara* may optionally occur before the suffix *astāti*. Thus, one says either *avarastāt* or *avastāt*, meaning "dwelling" or "pleasant" [in that direction].

The meanings of the suffixes beginning with *atasuc* have been stated; when used in conjunction with these, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs. With words ending in *ena*, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used. However, with words having *añc* as the final member, and with *adhi* and *abhi*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs.
The suffix *dhā* is used after a numeral in the sense of "dividing" (*vidhā*).

The suffix *dhā* shall be applied after a numeral when it denotes a manner of action; this is an exception to [the rule for] *jātīyar*. Examples: *pañcadhā bhuṅkte* (he eats five times), *saptadhā*, *viṃśatidhā*, *ekadhā*, *dvidhā*, *ṣoḍhā*.
[Question: How is *ekajātīyaḥ* (of one kind) explained? [Answer: It will apply to a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*) that possesses a variety of modes.
And [it is also used] when there is a change of location (*adhikaraṇavicāla*).

The suffix *dhā* is used after a numeral when there is a division of a substance. For example: "divide one into two ways" (*ekaṃ dvidhā kuru*), "into five ways" (*pañcadhā*), or "into six ways" (*ṣoḍhā*). Also, "make many into one way" (*anekamekadhā kuru*).
After the word *eka*, the suffixes *dha*, *dhyam*, or *uñ* may optionally be used.
The suffix *dhyamuñ* may optionally occur in place of *dhā* when it follows *eka*. Thus, one eats either "ekadhā" or "aikadhyam.
Furthermore, the suffix *dhamuñ* occurs after the words *dvi* and *tri*.
And may he prosper.

After the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffixes *dha*, *dhamuñ*, and *ñ* may optionally occur, and [the final vowel] becomes *edhā*. Thus: *dvidhā*, *dvaidham*, or *dvedhā*; *tridhā*, *traigham*, or *tredhā*. After a word ending in *dhamuñ*, the suffix *ṅa* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *dvaidhāni* (various dualities) or *traidhāni* (various triads), used when one hesitates due to doubt. Words beginning with *tasil* and ending in *edhā* are indeclinables (*avyaya*).
The suffix *pāśap* is used in the sense of "deserving" (*yāpye*).

The suffix *pāśa* may optionally be used after a word signifying "inferior" (*hīna*). Thus, one who is inferior in ritual science is called *yājñikapāśaḥ*, and one who is inferior in grammar is called *śābdikapāśaḥ*.
After a ordinal number ending in *-tīya*, the suffix *an* is added to denote a portion (*bhāga*).
Before eleven [stems], [the suffix *aC* is applied] except in the Vedic language (*acchandasi*).
In the Chāndasa Sūtra: [the suffix] *an* is added after [the word] *bhāga*; and after *ṣaṣṭha* and *aṣṭama*, [the suffixes] *ñ* and *ña* are also added.

The suffix *an* shall be applied after these two [words] when meaning "a part. After the word *ñña*, there is also [the suffix *an*]. For example: *ṣaṣṭho bhāgaḥ* or *ṣāṣṭho bhāgaḥ*; *aṣṭamo bhāgaḥ* or *āṣṭamo bhāgaḥ*.

The mention of the term *an* as having an indicatory letter *n* (*nit*) is recorded here incidentally for the purpose of its accentuation. Furthermore, when the meanings are "measure" (*māna*) or "limb of an animal" (*paśvaṅga*), the suffixes *kan* and *luk* (elision) also apply.

The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *ṣaṣṭha* when it denotes a portion of a whole; thus, *ṣaṣṭhakaḥ*. When denoting a portion of an animal limb, the suffix *anaṅ* is applied after *aṣṭama*, and there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ña*; thus, *aṣṭamaḥ*. Due to the word "and" (*ca*), the suffixes *ññān* and *ññānau* should also be understood; thus, *ṣaṣṭhaḥ*, *ṣāṣṭhaḥ*; *aṣṭamaḥ*, *āṣṭamaḥ*. After the word *eka*, the suffix *ākinic* is applied in the sense of "not being accompanied by another."
The suffix *ākin* may optionally be added to *eka* in the sense of "without a companion"; there is also the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *kan*. Thus: *ekākī*, *ekaḥ*, and *ekakaḥ*.
The suffix *caraṭ* is added in the sense of "having occurred previously."

It may be so: one who was formerly wealthy is called *āḍhyabhūta* (formerly wealthy); an old woman who acted like a maiden is called *kumāracarī*; and [the suffix] *rūpya* is used after a word in the genitive case.

The suffix *rūpya* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). By the force of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *caraṭ* also occurs. For example: *brāhmaṇarūpyaḥ* (formerly belonging to a Brāhmaṇa) or *brāhmaṇacaraḥ* (frequented by Brāhmaṇas) village.
[Now, for the expression of excellence: the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used.

The suffix *atiśāyana* denotes that which makes a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) possess an exceeding degree (*atiprakarṣa*); thus, it refers to the excellence of a quality. From a word endowed with such [excellence], the suffixes *tamaP* and *iṣṭhan* may occur in the sense of the base itself. For example: "Among these, this conch is the whitest" (*ayameṣāṃ śuklaḥ śuklatamaḥ śaṅkhaḥ*). "Among these, this one is the most clever" (*ayameṣāṃ paṭuḥ paṭutamaḥ*), or *paṭiṣṭhaḥ*; "the lightest" (*laghiṣṭhaḥ*).
When a dual number or a word signifying a comparison (*vibhajya*) is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are used.

The term *dvivacanam* means "the expression of two. In that context, when there is a correlative word (*upapada*), the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are applied after a comparative sense (*sātiśāyana*) and after a verbal form (*tiṅ*). Examples: *ayamanayorāḍhyataraḥ* (this one is wealthier of the two), *āḍhyīyān*; *paṭutaraḥ*, *paṭīyān*; *pacatitarām*. [The suffixes are also applied] after a word that is to be divided (*vibhajya* / *vibhaktavya*): *tadupapadācca*—for example, *pāścāttyā gauḍebhya āḍhyatarāḥ* (the people of the West are wealthier than the Gaudas), *paṭutarāḥ*, *paṭīyāṃsaḥ*.
The suffixes *añ* and others are applied only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).

The suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* should occur only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). Examples: *paṭiṣṭhaḥ* (most clever), *paṭīyān* (cleverer). Why "after a word expressing a quality"? [Counter-examples: *pācakattaraḥ* (a better cook), *pācakatamaḥ* (the best cook); *pacatitarām* (he cooks more), *pacatitamām* (he cooks most). [An exception: In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), however, [these suffixes may occur] even after [words not expressing a quality].
The *chandas* (Vedic) rule:
for a praiseworthy [word], *śra-* [is substituted].
And [the word] *jyā*.

The substitutes *śra-* and *jya-* shall take the place of the word *praśasya* when followed by the suffixes beginning with vowels (the first case-ending) or the comparative suffixes (*iyasun* and *īyasun*). Thus: *śreṣṭhaḥ*, *śreyān*; *jyeṣṭhaḥ*, *jyāyān*. [In the latter case,] the substitution of *ā* for *jya-* occurs before the suffix *īyasun* according to the rule *jyādādīyasaḥ*. Regarding this, some maintain that in the common language (*bhāṣā*), a second degree of excellence is not desired; therefore, forms such as *śreṣṭhataraḥ* and *jyeṣṭhatamaḥ* do not occur. Jayāditya, however, maintains that they do occur; hence, one may say: "Yudhiṣṭhira is the most excellent among the Kurus."
And [the same applies] to one who is aged.

For the words *aja* and others, as well as for *vṛddha*, the substitute *jya* shall occur [in the superlative and comparative degrees]. Thus: *ayam eṣām jyeṣṭhaḥ* (this one is the eldest among these); *ayam anayor jyāyān* (this one is the elder of these two). By virtue of the rule "priya-sthira-etc.," there is also the substitution of *varṣa*: *varṣiṣṭhaḥ* (eldest) and *varṣīyān* (older).
For the words *antika* and *bāḍha*, the substitutes are *nedas* and *sādhu* respectively.

These two [suffixes] may occur after these two [words], *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*: *nediṣṭham* (nearest), *antikamam* (most near); *nedīyaḥ* (nearer), *antikatarām* (nearer). "Among these, he studies most thoroughly" (*sādhiṣṭham adhīte*). "The teacher became more excellent than the young woman of the earth" (*sādhīyo gurur abhavad bhuvastaruṇyāḥ*). Since *bāḍham*, *bhṛśam*, and *nityam* are adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), even when ending in a suffix, they would likewise [be treated as such].
[The rule] *yuvālpayoḥ kann anyatarasyām* [is now introduced].

The substitution of *kan* for these two [the superlative suffix *iṣṭha* and the comparative suffix *īyas*] may optionally occur when *iṣṭha* and *īyas* follow. Examples: *ayameṣāṃ kaniṣṭhaḥ* (he is the youngest among these);
*ayamanayoḥ kanīyān* (he is the younger of these two). Or, when preceded by *ati*: *atiyuvā*, *aty-alpaḥ*. In the alternative case: *yaviṣṭhaḥ*, *yavīyān*; *alpiṣṭhaḥ*, *alpīyān*.
The *luk* elision of the suffixes *matup* and *vin*.

The suffix *vin* and *matup* are elided (*luk*) when followed by the superlative suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyasun*. Examples: "these are garlanded" (*ime sragviṇaḥ*); "among these, this one is most garlanded" (*ayameṣāṃ srajiṣṭhaḥ*); "between these two, this one is more garlanded" (*ayamanayoḥ srajīyān*). Similarly: "most powerful" (*ojiṣṭhaḥ*), "more powerful" (*ojīyān*); "these are possessed of skin" (*ime tvagvantaḥ*); "among these, this one has the best skin" (*ayameṣāṃ tvaciṣṭhaḥ*); "more skinned" (*tvacīyān*). Likewise: "most righteous" (*dharmiṣṭhaḥ*), "more righteous" (*dharmīyān*); "most wicked" (*pāpiṣṭhaḥ*), "more wicked" (*pāpīyān*).
In all cases, the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* are added after words that do not denote a quality (*aguṇavācin*), as well as after the word *bhūman*, according to this rule.
The suffix *rūpap* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).

It may be so. A praiseworthy student is "chāttrarūpaḥ" (one who is a student in form). [Likewise] "yājñikarūpaḥ" (one who is a sacrificer in form). By the rule "tiṅśca" (also after a verbal suffix)—[we have] "pacatirūpam" (the act of cooking in form), "pacantirūpam" (the act of cooking in form). The neuter gender is due to following worldly usage.
[The suffixes] *kalp*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are used in the sense of being slightly incomplete.

The suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* occur after a word meaning "almost incomplete" (*īṣadasamāpta*). For example: *bhikṣukalpaḥ* (a monk who is almost, but not quite, complete); *paṇḍitadeśyaḥ* (one who is almost a scholar); *bodhisattvadeśīyaḥ* (one who is almost a Bodhisattva); *indradeśīyo rājā* (a king who is almost Indra); *aṣṭādaśavarṣadeśīyā kanyā* (a girl who is almost eighteen years old). They also occur after verbal roots (*tiṅ*): *pacatikalpam* (he cooks almost completely), *dīyatekalpam* (it is given almost completely), *pacatideśyam*, *pacatideśīyam*.

Since suffixes added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) may deviate from the gender and number of the original base, we have: *guḍakalpā drākṣā* (grapes that are almost like molasses), *payaskalpā yavāgūḥ* (rice-gruel that is almost like milk), *ayaskalpaṃ ghṛtam* (clarified butter that is almost like iron), *abdeśīyaṃ ghṛtam* (clarified butter that is almost like water).
Optionally, the suffix *bahuc* is added to a nominal stem (*sup*), and it is placed before the word.

The suffix *bahuc* is added after a nominal stem (*subanta*) meaning "slightly incomplete" (*īṣadasamāpti*), either before or after [the word]; for example, *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grapes that are slightly less than full of molasses") or *guḍakalpā* ("almost like molasses"). Also, *laghur bahutṛṇaṃ naraḥ* ("a man who is slightly less than a blade of grass") or *tṛṇadeśyaḥ* ("almost a blade of grass"). Why "after a nominal stem" (*supaḥ*)? To prevent it from occurring after a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
When expressing a manner or kind (*prakāra*), the suffix *jātīyar* is used.
It may be so. [The suffix] *prakāra* means "of a sharp kind" (*paṭuprakāraḥ*) or "belonging to that kind" (*tajjātīyaḥ*), or "of such a kind" (*tathājātīyaḥ*).
The suffix *thāl* is used for the mere abstract quality (*prakāramātre*), whereas *jātīyar* is used for the possessor of that quality (*prakāravati*); this is the distinction between these two.
These belong to the *prāgivīya* section among the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
The suffix *ka* is applied after words ending in *prāgīva*.

The suffix *kap* should be stated [as an alternative] before the rule *ive pratikṛtau*. This is not desired after forms ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*); rather, *akac* alone is intended. The suffix *akac* is applied to indeclinables and pronouns before the final vowel (*ṭi*).
And for whom is there giving?

The augment *akac* is optionally prescribed before the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of indeclinables and pronouns when used in the sense of "like" (*prāgivārtha*), according to the rule *yathāsambhavamalo'ntyasya*; furthermore, in this case, the final *k* is replaced by *d*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states that *akac* is added before the final phoneme of a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), provided it does not begin with *u*, *s*, or *bh*. Examples: *uccakaiḥ* (highly) *nīcakaiḥ* (lowly) *dhik* / *dhakit* (fie! *hiruka* / *hirakut* (separately) *pṛthak* (separately) *sarvake* (all-like) *viśvake* (all-like) *tvayakā* / *tvayaki* (you-like) *mayakā* / *mayaki* (I-like)

Regarding the rule "after [stems] beginning with *an*, *oka*, *ra*, *sa*, and *bha*": here, the suffix *akac* is applied before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus we have: *yuvakayoḥ*, *āvakayoḥ*, *yuṣmakāsu*, *asmakāsu*, *yuṣmakābhiḥ*, and *asmakābhiḥ*.
In this context, the rule *tiṅśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56) is also remembered: *jalpataki* ("he speaks badly") and *pacataki* ("he cooks badly").

However, here in the case of the root *vac* in the *laṅ* tense, we have *avak* and *avakak*; likewise, *aneḥ* and *anenek*. The rule *kasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.104) does not apply here, because the letter *k* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of that rule.

The suffix *ka* is added after *tūṣṇīm* to express desire (*kāma*). The letter *m* is for the purpose of indicating the scope of the rule. Thus, "the wise sit silently" (*tūṣṇīkā āsate vijñāḥ*). After *tūṣṇīm*, the suffix *ka* is added when expressing habit (*śīla*), and there is also the elision of the letter *m*. Thus, "one whose habit is silence" (*tūṣṇīṃśīlas tūṣṇīkaḥ*). [The suffix *ka* is added] when something is unknown (*ajñāta*).

The suffixes *kāku* and *cau* occur after an unknown qualifier (*ajñātaviśeṣaṇāt*). It is not known whose horse this is, or what its nature is—[it is called] *aśvakaḥ*. [It is called] *navakaḥ*. When unknown, it is *uccakaiḥ*, meaning "high" in such or such a manner. That woman is *asakau*, meaning "whose" or "of what kind. She who drinks and protects you in secret is *asakau*. The same applies to *sarvake*, *viśvake*, and *pacataki*. And the rule *kasya ca daḥ* is applied separately for the sense of contempt (*kutsite*).

In this sense, the suffixes *kā* and *ka* may be used. For example: *aśvakaḥ* (a contemptible horse); *uccakaiḥ* (loudly); *sarvake* (in every case); *pacataki* (you cook poorly); *hirakut* (a poor horse).
When forming a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *kan* is applied.
The suffix *kan* occurs after a name that possesses a contemptible attribute. Examples: *śūdrakaḥ*, *dhārakaḥ*, *cūrṇakaḥ*, *vyādhakaḥ*.
[It also occurs] in the sense of compassion.
In this context, the suffixes *kāka* and *cau* may occur: *putrakaḥ*, *durbalakaḥ*, *pātaki*, *svapitaki*, *pacataki*, *yātaki*.
And [the suffix *cau* occurs] after a word joined with that [action], when it refers to conduct (*nīti*).

In the sense of policy (*nīti*) and compassion (*anukampā*), the suffixes *kāka* and *cau* may be applied [to a word denoting a person]. For example: *hanta te vastrakam* ("Alas, this garment for you! and *hanta te'śvakaḥ* ("Alas, this horse for you!").
When the name of a person consists of more than two syllables, the suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally used.
And [the suffixes] ghañ and ilac.
In the speech of the easterners, the affix *aṭ* is added after the prefix *upa*, and the suffixes *ac* and *vuñ* are also applied.

In the sense of "pitying" (*anukampā*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied after a human name, or optionally the suffix *iṣṭhan*. Thus, one who is pitied by Devadatta is called *devikaḥ* or *devadattikaḥ*. Optionally, the suffix *ka* may also be used: *devadattakaḥ*. Furthermore, the suffixes *ghan* and *ilac* are also applied: *deviyaḥ* and *devilaḥ*. [Similarly,] *yajñikaḥ*. However, according to the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*), the suffixes *aḍac* and *vuñ* are also applied after a human name in this sense. Thus, one who is pitied by Upendradatta is called *upaḍaḥ* or *upakaḥ*.
Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, the suffixes obtained by default are also applied: *upiyaḥ*, *upilaḥ*, *upikaḥ*, and *upendradattakaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the rule "bahuvacaḥ"? [Examples: *dattakaḥ*, *guptakaḥ*.
[The suffix] *kan* is applied after a name of a genus (*jātināman*).

The suffix *kan* may be used in the sense of "compassion" (*anukampā*). For example: *vyāghrakaḥ* ("a little tiger") or *siṃhakaḥ* ("a little lion," i.e., someone). Furthermore, there is the elision of the final member of the compound *ajinānta*.

The suffix *kan* may be added to words ending in *ajina* (skin) when expressing compassion for a person, and there is the elision of the final member [of the compound]. For example, one who is piteously called by the name "Tiger-skin" is *vyāghrakaḥ*; one who is piteously called "Black" is *kṛṣṇakaḥ*. [In this formation], the suffix is applied after the second vowel.

"Elision (lopa)"—this much alone [is the rule]. When a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or a vowel follows, there shall be elision of the portion following the second vowel. The mention of *ṭha* is for the sake of ensuring that when the suffix is in the state of *ṭha*, elision occurs before the substitution of *kā* after a stem ending in *u*. Examples: *vāyudattakaḥ*, *vāyukaḥ*; *pitṛkaḥ*; *devikaḥ*, *deviyaḥ*, *devilaḥ*. Here, words such as *devika* and others are derived through the process of elision as distinct words themselves; this is merely an illustration. The phrase "from the second vowel onwards" applies even from the fourth vowel: *bṛhaspatidattakaḥ*, *bṛhaspatikaḥ*.

And [the suffix] *ka* is optionally applied after [a word ending in] *u*, provided it is not followed by a vowel or *j* etc.—as in *devadattakaḥ* or *devakaḥ*. There is also the elision of the first member [of the compound]—as in *dattikaḥ*, *dattakaḥ*, or *dattiyaḥ*. Even when there is no suffix, the elision of both the preceding and following members should be stated—as in *devadattaḥ* becomes *dattaḥ* or *devaḥ*. After a word ending in *u*, the suffix *ilaC* is applied, and *la* is substituted for *l*—as in *vāyudattakaḥ* becomes *vāyulaḥ*; *bhānudattakaḥ* becomes *bhānulaḥ*. As it has been said:
"From the fourth [case-ending], and when [a suffix] beginning with a non-vowel (*anajādau*) follows, there is elision of the first member;
likewise, when there is no suffix (*apratyaye*), this is desired. And from a word ending in *u*, *la* is substituted for *ila*."

Regarding the second vowel of a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), there is a rule for the elision of that [vowel] and the following syllable: *upendradattaka* becomes *upaḍaḥ*, and *upakaḥ*. Furthermore, for words preceded by *ekāpacc-* as the first member, there is elision of the subsequent member: *vāgāśīḥ* becomes *vācikaḥ*; *tvagāśīḥ* becomes *tvacikaḥ*. For if there were elision of everything after the second vowel, then because of the rule *yasyeti ca*, the elided portion would be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). Consequently, since the status of being a nominal stem (*bhatva*) would be absent, yet the status of being a word (*padatva*) would exist due to the intervening case-ending, the change of *c* to *k* (by *coḥ kuḥ*) would occur. Regarding the elision of the sixth vowel when it is followed by a vowel beginning with *ā*: however, by the rule *ṭhājādi*, the elision of the sixth vowel is taught only when it is the second vowel; thereafter, because of the status of being a word, the change to a voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) occurs: *ṣaḍaṅgulidattaḥ* becomes *ṣaḍikaḥ*.
The *śevala* [measure] is for Varuṇa, Aryaman, and the others who are broad above; it is three finger-breadths [from the bottom].

In these [words], there shall be the elision of the portion following the third vowel of the second member. Thus, *anukampitaḥ śevaladattaḥ* becomes *śevalilaḥ*, *śevaliyaḥ*, or *śevalikaḥ*. Similarly, *śevalendradattaḥ* becomes *śevalilaḥ*, *śevaliyaḥ*, or *śevalikaḥ*.
[This applies when the suffix denotes] "smallness" (*alpe*).
The suffixes *kāk* and *cak* occur in the sense of "a little. Examples: *alpaṃ dhṛtaṃ ghṛtakam* ("a little ghee"), *uccakaiḥ*, *viśvake*, *pacataki*. [They also occur] in the sense of "short."
In this sense, the suffixes *ka* and *kañ* may be applied. For example: *hrasvo daṇḍaḥ* (a short staff) becomes *daṇḍakaḥ*; *stambhakaḥ*.
The suffix *kan* is used when forming a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *kan* shall be applied after a short feminine noun. Examples: *veṇukaḥ*, *vaṃśakaḥ*.
After the words *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*, the suffix *ra* is applied.

The suffix *ra* is applied after these [words]. From *kuṭī* (a small hut), with a short vowel, we have *kuṭīraḥ*; from *śamī*, *śamīraḥ*; from *śuṇḍā*, *śuṇḍāraḥ*, which is a name for a young elephant (*karabha*). Some say it refers to a small body or a corpse. After *kutū*, the suffix *ḍupac* is applied.
*Kutū* becomes *kutupa* when short;
after *kāsū* and *goṇī*, the suffix *ṣṭarac* is applied.

The word *kāsū* (a type of spear) takes the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* because it ends in the *ṣit* marker; thus, *hrasvā kāsūḥ* means "a short spear" and *kāsūtari* means "one who possesses a short spear. Similarly, *goṇītari* means "one who possesses a small load-carrying bag. [The rule] *vatsokṣāśvarṣabhebhyaśca tanutve* states that the suffix *taraP* is added after the words *vatse*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*, and *ṛṣabha* when their smallness (*tanutva*) is expressed.

The suffix *ṣṭarac* is applied here after these [words]. *Vatsataraḥ*: a calf that is not fully developed in its state as a calf; it is in the second stage of age. *Ukṣataraḥ*: a bull in the third stage of age. "A *ukṣatara* does not accept fodder at every moment. *Aśvatarī*: a female mule born from a donkey. *Ṛṣabhataro mandaḥ*: a dull ox. Here, the attenuation (*tanutva*) of the cause for the application of the word is intended. However, the suffix is not applied when one is thin merely due to emaciation (*kṛśatva*). As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "There is a prohibition regarding attenuation (*kārśya*) after words such as *vatsa*.
[The suffix] *ḍatarac* is applied after *kim*, *yat*, and *tat* when there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of one out of two.

When selecting one out of two based on quality, action, or name, the suffix *ḍatarac* shall be applied after the words *kim*, *yat*, and *tad*. For example: "Which of you two is clever? (*kataraḥ bhavatoḥ paṭuḥ*); "Whichever is clever, let that one come" (*yataraḥ paṭus tatara āyātu*); likewise, "Which Caitra? (*kataraś caitraḥ*) or "Which agent? (*kataraḥ kārakaḥ*).
Alternatively, when inquiring about one among many based on a genus, the suffix *ḍatamac* is used.

When selecting one from among many, the suffix *ḍatamach* (forming *katama*) should be used after *kim* and other such words: *katamo bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ* ("Which among you is Kaṭha?"). The suffix *yatama* may also be used: *yatamaḥ*. The mention of the option (*vāvacana*) is for the sake of the *akac* suffix: *yakaḥ*, *sakaḥ*.
Furthermore, by the rule of "great option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*), the analytical sentence (*vākya*) is also permitted: *ko bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ*.
In the case of an inquiry regarding caste, what [is the usage]? "Who among you is Devadatta?
[This applies] after a singular [word], according to the Eastern grammarians.

The two [suffixes] *eka* and *ekata* shall occur [after the word *anya*]. [Examples: *ekataro bhavatoḥ yātu* ("let one of you two go"); *ekatamo bhavatāṃ śṛṇotu* ("let one among you listen"). The mention of "the Easterners" (*prācām*) is for the sake of honor, since the optionality of this formation is already established by the *mahāvibhāṣā*.
[The suffix] *kan* occurs in the sense of disparagement (*avakṣepaṇa*).

In this context, the suffix *kan* may occur. For example: *vyākaraṇakena ayaṃ garvitaḥ* ("He is proud because of his grammar"). According to tradition, pride (*garva*) is here being censured. [The suffix] *iva* is used in the sense of "a likeness" (*pratikṛti*).

The meaning of *iva* is similarity (*sādṛśya*). A "likeness" (*pratikṛti*) is its qualifier. The suffix *kan* occurs after a word [ending in *a*] when the sense of *iva* is that of a likeness. An image of a horse is *aśvakaḥ*; [an image of] a donkey is *gardabhakaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a likeness"? [Consider: "A *gavaya* is like a cow.
This rule for the sense of *iva* applies prior to the suffix *ññya* (P. 5.3.112), which begins with *pūga*.
The suffix *ḍhañ* (which becomes *īya*) occurs after the word *vasti* in the sense of "a substitute for" (*pratikṛti*), provided it does not denote a name;
furthermore, the suffix *ñ* (which becomes *ya*) also occurs in this sense when the word is a proper name.
In the human realm.
And [it is not a sale] when it is for the sake of a livelihood and [the item] is not for sale.

The suffix *kan* occurs after a noun in the sense of "like" (*iva*). For example: *aśvakaḥ* ("a small horse"). When referring to a human being, there is optionally elision (*lup*) of *kan*. For example: *cañcā* (meaning "one who is like a wooden doll") and *vardhrikā* (meaning "one who is like a wooden doll"). When the meaning is "one who makes a living by means of [something]," there is elision of *kan*. One who wanders about carrying an image of Āditya or another deity for the sake of a livelihood is called *ādityaḥ*, *skandaḥ*, or *vāsudevaḥ*. Why say "not when it is merchandise"? Because one might say: *vāsudevakān vikrīṇīte* ("he sells Vāsudeva-merchandise").
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words such as *devapatha*.

The suffix *lup* may optionally apply [to a compound ending in a word denoting a path]. Examples: *devapathaḥ*, *haṃsapathaḥ*. [When the suffix *kan* is applied to denote a likeness: *kāśyapapratikṛtiḥ* becomes *kāśyapaḥ*.
This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). The suffix has been explained in the sense of "likeness" (*pratikṛti*).
The suffix *ḍhañ* follows [the word] *vasta*.

The suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the word *vasti* in the sense of "like" (*ivārthe*). For example: *vāsteyaḥ* (meaning "like a bladder"). *Vāsteyī* refers to a woman separated from her husband. After the word *śilā*, the suffix *ḍha* is applied.
It may be so. *Śaileyam* means "that whose body is like a stone (*śilā*).
According to some, the suffix *ḍhañ* is also applied—thus *śaileyaṃ dadhi* ("curd from a mountain").
[The suffix] *yat* is applied after [the group beginning with] *śākha*.
The suffix *ya* is applied after the word *śākhā* to denote "belonging to it," as in *śākhya*. It is also applied after *mukha* and *jaghana*, as in *mukhya* and *jaghanya*.
Furthermore, the suffix *ya* is applied to a noun (*dravya*) when it denotes something that is capable of becoming that thing (*bhavya*).
If *bhavya* is to be declined as a substance (*dravya*) because it possesses all qualities like a tree, then indeed a substance alone is beloved by all.
[The suffix] *cha* is applied after *kuśāgra*.
The intellect that is as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass is called *kuśāgrīyā*;
this [term] is derived from the compound [of its constituent parts] referring to that object.

The suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) occurs after a compound whose meaning is similar to the sense of the word *iva* (*ivārtha*), provided that it does not end in *samāsa*. Examples: *kākatālīyam* ("like the crow and the palm fruit"), *ajākṛpāṇīyam* ("like the goat and the sword"). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "There are these two meanings of *iva*: 'Just as the arrival of the crow and just as the falling of the palm fruit, so was Devadatta's encounter with the robbers'—this is *kākatāla*. The compound is formed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Thereafter, 'just as the killing of the crow by the palm fruit, so was Devadatta's killing by the robbers'—this is *kākatālīyam*.
[The suffix] *aṇ* occurs after words such as *śarkara* and others.
As in *śārkara* from *śarkarā*, and *kāpāla*;
[the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after words such as *aṅguli*.

The suffix *kan* is applied after *aṅguli* to form *aṅgulika*; after *bhāruji*, it forms *bhārujika*; and after *bharuja*, it forms *bharujaka*. After *ekaśālā*, the suffix *ṭhan* is optionally applied.
The suffix *aṣṭhañ* may optionally be applied to this [word *ekaśāla*]. Thus, *ekaśāleva* becomes *ekaśālikaḥ*.

In the alternative, the suffix *kan* is used: *ekaśālakaḥ*. Others say the suffix *ṭhak* is used: *aikaśālikaḥ*. Like a white horse (*karka*), a cow is *kārkīkaḥ*; like a red [stone], a crystal is *lohitīkaḥ*.
The suffix *ādikak* is applied after the words *karka*, *lohitaka*, and so forth.
*Kārkīka* means "like a white goat"; *lohitīkaḥ* means "crystal-like. In the Vedic language, the suffix *thāl* is added after the words *pratna*, *pūrva*, and *viśva*.
The *Chandas-sūtra*:
the suffixes have been stated for the sense of "as it were" (*iva*).
From [a word denoting] a *pūga* other than one preceded by *agramaṇī*.

*Pūga* refers to a specific kind of association (*saṅghaviśeṣa*). The suffix *ñya* occurs after words denoting such associations, in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *lauhadhvajyaḥ*, *lauhadhvajyau*, *lohadhvajāḥ*; *śaivyaḥ*, *śaivyau*, *śivayaḥ*. Why [is it said] "not preceded by *grāmaṇī*"? [Consider: *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīr devadattakāḥ* ("Devadatta is their leader").
[The suffixes] *vrāta* and *cphañ* occur in the same sense, except in the feminine.

The suffix *ñya* shall be applied in the sense of the original meaning (*svārthe*) after words denoting a class (*vrāta*) and after those ending in *cphañ*. Examples: *vrīhimatyaḥ*, *kauñjāyanyaḥ*. Why "not in the feminine"? (Answer: *vrīhimatī*, *kauñjāyanī*; [here] *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *jāteḥ*.
[Furthermore, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied] after a guild (*saṃgha*) of weapon-bearers (*āyudhajīvinaḥ*) in the Vāhīka region, provided it does not denote a non-Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya (*rājanya*).

The suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after words denoting groups of weapon-bearers among the Vāhīkas. Examples: *kauṇḍīvṛsyaḥ*, *kṣaudrakyaḥ*; [the feminine form is] *kṣudrakī*. Why "among the Vāhīkas"? [Counter-example: *śavaraḥ*. Why "after a word other than a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya"? [Counter-examples: *gopālavāḥ* (Brāhmaṇas), *śālaṅkāyanāḥ* (Rājanyas). After the word *vṛka*, the suffix *ṭeṇyaṇ* is applied.

Similarly, the suffix *ṭeṇyaṅ* shall be applied after *vṛka*: *vārkeṇyaḥ* (masculine) and *vārkeṇī* (feminine). After the group beginning with *dāmanī* and including *trigarta* as the sixth, the suffix *cha* is applied.

The suffix *cha* shall be applied after these: *dāmanīyaḥ*, *aulapīyaḥ*. Regarding those weapon-bearers who belong to the sixth group, the Trigarta-group—after them [the suffix *cha* is applied]: *kauṇḍoparathīyaḥ*.
After words beginning with *parśu* and after words beginning with *yaudheya*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are respectively applied.
The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the group of words beginning with *parśu* when denoting a community of weapon-bearers (*śastrajīvin*). Examples: *pārśavaḥ*, *āsuraḥ*.
After words beginning with *yauveya*, the suffix *añ* is used—e.g., *yaudheyaḥ*, *śaubhreyaḥ*.
The word *parśu* ends in a long vowel (*dīrghānta*) and consists of two syllables (*dvyañ*); it is an augment (*āgama*).
The suffix *yañ* is applied after *abhijit*, *vidabhṛt*, *śālāvat*, *śikhāvat*, *śamīvat*, *ūrṇāvat*, and *śrumat*.

The phrase "from the group of those who live by arms" is excluded. From [names] beginning with Abhijit and ending in the suffix -gotra, the suffix *yañ* occurs in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). For example: the male descendant of Abhijit is *Ābhijitaḥ*; from that, with the suffix *yañ*, we get *Ābhijityaḥ*. Similarly: *Vaidabhṛtyaḥ*, *Śālīvatyaḥ*, *Śāmīvatyaḥ*, *Aurṇāvatyaḥ*, *Śrīmatyaḥ*.
It does not apply here: *ābhijitaḥ sthālīpākaḥ* (a pot-offering belonging to Abhijit).
The suffixes *ñya* and so forth are called *tadrāja* (kingship/designation of a royal lineage).

The suffixes beginning with *ñ* and *ñya* have been stated; now those called *tadrāja* (denoting a king) are discussed. Following that, when many [descendants] are denoted, there is elision (*luk*). Examples: *lohadhvajāḥ*, *kauñjāyanāḥ*, *kṣudrakāḥ*, *dāmanayaḥ*, *parśavaḥ*, *ābhijitāḥ*, *vṛkāḥ*.
After the word *pādaśata* (one hundred feet), when it begins with a numeral and expresses repetition (*vīpsā*), the suffix *vun* is added and its elision (*lopa*) occurs.

The suffix *vun* occurs after a numeral beginning with *pāda* ending in *śata*, when expressing repetition (*vīpsā*), and there is elision of the final phoneme. [Examples: "He gives two feet each" (*dvau dvau pādau dadāti*). When a compound is formed for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning, one says: "He gives a pair of feet" (*dvipādikāṃ dadāti*), "He gives two hundred" (*dviśatikāṃ dadāti*), or "He has been fined three hundred" (*triśatikāṃ daṇḍitaḥ*).
It is also desired after other words: "He gives two sweets" (*dvimodakikāṃ dadāti*).
And [the suffix *vun* is used] in the sense of punishment (*daṇḍa*) and relinquishment (*vyavasarga*).

And for these two, it should be so. This statement is for the purpose of excluding the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). "He has been fined two pādas" or "he releases [the fine] as a *dvipadikā*"; "he has been fined three hundred" or "he releases [the fine] as a *triśatikā*. *Vyavasarga* means giving.
After words such as *sthūla*, the suffix *kan* is used in the sense of expressing a manner or kind.

The suffix *kan* occurs after words such as *sthūla* when expressing a manner; it serves as an exception to the suffix *jātīyar*. Examples: *sthūlaprakāraḥ* (of a thick kind) becomes *sthūlakaḥ*; likewise, *yavakaḥ* and *aṇukaḥ*. [The suffix *kan* also follows] *cañcat* and *bṛhat*: *cañcatprakāraḥ* (of a flickering kind) becomes *cañcatkaḥ*, which is similar to something moving (*gatvara*). *Bṛhatkaḥ* refers to a large gem.
[The suffix *kan* occurs] after a word ending in the suffix *kta* when it does not mean "complete attainment."

In this sense, the suffix *kan* may be added after a word ending in the *kta* suffix; for example, *bhinnakam* (not excessively broken) and *chinnakam* (not excessively cut). However, it is not used when expressing "half" (*sāmi*).

The suffix *kan* shall not occur after a word ending in the past passive participle suffix *kta* when a word expressing "half" (*ardha*) is used as an upapada. Examples: *sāmikṛtam*, *sāmibhuktam*; *ardhapītam*, *ardhabhuktam*; *nemakṛtam*, *khaṇḍakṛtam*; *nemabhinnam*. This prohibition applies to the *svārthika* (inherently reflexive) *kan*. And this very [rule] is the evidence for its existence. Therefore, according to Jayāditya, forms such as *bahutarakam* are established. [Also, the suffix *kan* occurs] after *bṛhatī* in the sense of "covering."

In this context, the suffix *kan* would apply [to form the word *bṛhatikā*]. A garment is called *bṛhatikā*. [The rule] "the suffix *kha* occurs after compounds whose final members are *aṣaḍakṣa*, *āśitaṅga*, *valaṅkama*, *alam-puruṣa*, or *adhi-uttara*" [is relevant here].

The suffix *kha* occurs after these [words] in their own sense (*svārthe*), and this is obligatory (*nitya*). Other such obligatory suffixes are also enumerated in the Bhāṣya. As it has been said: "The obligatory suffixes are those beginning with *tamap* up to *kan*, those beginning with *ñya* up to *vuñ*, those beginning with *ām* up to *mayaṭ*, as well as *bṛhatī*, those ending in a genus-name (*jātyanta*), and compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*). *Aṣaḍakṣīṇa*: that which is prepared by two people. *Āśitaṅgavīnam araṇyam*: a forest where cows have been fed; the letter *m* is introduced here by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Alaṅkarmīṇaḥ pāṇiḥ*: a hand capable of performing work. *Alampuruṣīṇaḥ*: sufficient for a man. It means "capable for that person."

The suffix *kha* (i.e., *īna*) is applied after a word ending in *adhi* when it follows a word that is its superior (*guru*), provided the resulting sense is one of dependence. Examples include *gurva-dhīnaḥ* ("dependent on the teacher"), *daivā-dhīnaḥ* ("dependent on fate"), and *rājā-dhīnaḥ* ("dependent on the king"). The term *adhīna* is also a synonym for *āyatta* ("subordinate" or "under the control of"), as seen in this usage from the *Ślokavārttika*: "For a sentence is dependent (*adhīna*) upon the speaker.
Furthermore, the suffix *kha* is optionally applied after the prefix *añci-* when it does not denote a cardinal direction or a feminine noun.
After a word ending in *añc*, either *vā* (the suffix *vati*) or [the suffixes mentioned previously] may occur. For example: *prāk* or *prācīnam*; *tiryak* or *tiraścīnam*; *pratyak* or *pratīcīnam*.

Why is it specified "when referring to a direction" (*dikstriyām*)? [Consider: *prācī dik* ("the eastern direction"). Why is the mention of "direction" (*diggrahaṇam*) necessary? [Consider: *prācīnā brāhmaṇī* ("an eastern Brahmin woman").
After a word ending in *jāti*, the suffix *cha* occurs when expressing a relationship of kinship (*bandhuni*).

The suffix *cha* (iya) occurs after a word ending in *jāti* when it denotes a relative (*bandhu*) with respect to a substance (*dravya*). Examples: *brāhmaṇajātīyaḥ* ("one who is of the Brāhmaṇa class") and *tajjātīyaḥ* ("of that same class"). Why "when denoting a relative"? [Consider: *brāhmaṇajātir aduṣṭā* ("the Brāhmaṇa class is not defective"). [Vārttika:
Optionally, the suffix *cha* occurs after a word ending in *sthāna* when the sense is "having the same position" (*sasthāna*).

The suffix *śas* may optionally occur after a word ending in *sthāna*, provided that the meaning of "standing in the place of" (*sthānānta*) is understood. Thus, *sasthānaḥ* means "having the same position as," i.e., equal; for example, *pitṛsthānaḥ* or *pitṛsthānīyaḥ* ("standing in the father's place"). Similarly, *rājasthānaḥ* or *rājasthānīyaḥ*. The meaning is "equal to that.
[Furthermore, the suffix] *ām* occurs after words ending in *kim*, *etad*, *tiṅ*, and indeclinables (*avyaya*), when there is an excellence of substance (*dravyaprakarṣe*).

The suffix *ām* is added after a word ending in *kim*, a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), or an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that bears the designation *gha*. Examples: *kintarām*, *kintamām*. The suffix *gha* is applied to express the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of either an action or a quality. Examples: *pūrvāhṇetarām*, *pūrvāhṇetamām* (here, the excellence belongs to the power of the substratum). *yātitarām*, *vaktitarām*, *patatitarām*, *patatitamām*, *gacchatitamām*. *prātastarām*, *natarām*, *nitarām*, *sutarām*, *uccaistarām*.
The prohibition applies when there is excellence of substance—such as "somebody very tall.
And [the suffix] *amu* occurs in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
The *chandas* [section] is one *sūtra*;
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [words denoting] followers (*anugādin*).
The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after this [word]. Thus, from *anugādi*, we have *ānugādika*.
After a word ending in the suffix *ṇac*, the suffix *añ* is used in the feminine.

The suffix *añ* shall be applied after a word ending in *ṇac* in the feminine gender when the sense is reflexive (i.e., denoting the same agent as the action). Examples: *vyākrośī*, *vyāvahāsī*, *vyāvalekhī*. The suffix *añ* should be stated [after the words] *agnīdhra* and *sādhāraṇa*; and there is optionally the application of the suffix *ṅīp*. Thus: *āgnīdhrī* or *āgnīdhrā*; *sādhāraṇī* or *sādhāraṇā* (referring to a ground).
[The suffix *ṅīp* is also applied] after words ending in *aṇ*, *ini*, or *uṇ*.
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after a word ending in *inu*. Examples: *sāṃkūṭinam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*.
[Additionally, the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *visārin* when it means "fish."
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after the word *visārin*. Thus, *vaisāriṇaḥ* means "a fish.
Other than when referring to a fish, it is *visārī*.
After a numeral, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used to denote the counting of the repetition of an action.

The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is added after a numeral denoting a count of actions when there is repetition of those actions. For example: *pañca vārān pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte* ("he eats five times"); *śatakṛtvaḥ proktavān divam asya* ("he has spoken of heaven a hundred times"); *sahasrakṛtvaḥ*.
The suffix *suc* is added after the numerals *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*.

In these cases, there would likewise be the suffix *suc*: *dvir adhīte* (he studies twice), *tris pradakṣiṇīkṛtya* (having circumambulated three times clockwise), *tris pradakṣiṇaṃ kurute* (he performs circumambulation three times clockwise), *catur bhuṅkte* (he eats four times), and *ekasya sakṛt ca* (and once of one).

There would be substitution for a single [element] at once; there is the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), as in *sakṛd dadāti*. Optionally, the suffix *dhā* is applied to *bahu* when referring to time that is not remote (*aviprakṛṣṭakāla*).
In the domain of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, the word *dhā* may optionally be used for *bahu*. Thus, one eats many times a day (*bahudhāhno bhuṅkte*). In the alternative case: *bahukṛtvaḥ*.
Why [is it said] "when the time is not distant"? [Consider: he eats many times during the month (*bahukṛtvo māsasya bhuṅkte*).
The suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of "consisting of that" (*tat-prakṛta-vacana*).

"That which is both this [suffix] and the subject under discussion (prakṛta)"—this is "tatprakṛta. The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs when expressing that. For example: "food is the subject under discussion, commenced here; thus it is *annamaya*" (consisting of food); "here it is *ghṛtamaya*" (consisting of ghee). Another says: "Food is the material cause (*prakṛti*) in this; thus it is *annamaya* sacrifice"; "the festival is *apūpamaya*" (consisting of cakes). And like the word for a collection, it is used when there are many.
When many base forms (*prakṛti*) are mentioned, suffixes should apply as if they were a collective whole. When *apūpa* (cakes) are the base forms, [the derivative is] *āpūpikam*.

And here—*āpūpikaṃ parva* (a festival of cakes). By the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is also included: *apūpamayam* (made of cakes), *apūpamayī pātrī* (a bowl made of cakes), *vaṭakamayī* (made of dumplings).
The suffixes *ana*, *anta*, *avasatha*, *it*, *iha*, *bha*, *iṣa*, and *jña* are applied after a word ending in *añ*.
After these [words], the suffixes *ñ* and *ñya* occur in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*). Examples: *ānantyam*, *āvasathyam*, *aitihyam*, *bhaiṣajyam*.

Here, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* is connected [to this rule], according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "the suffixes beginning with *ām* and ending before *mayaṭ* [apply here]. After a word ending in *devatā*, the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of being for the sake of that deity (*tadarthya*).

It may be so. "Tadarthya" means that which is for the sake of that; it refers to things such as the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), as well as that which has Agni as its deity (*agnidevatya*) and that which has the ancestors (*pitṛ*) as its deity. [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after the words *pāda* and *argha*.

From these two [suffixes], the following forms are derived: *tādarthya* (that which is for the sake of that), *pādya* (water for washing the feet), *arghya* (an offering of flowers, etc.), and *atithiñya* (a guest).

The term *ātithya* [is formed] from *atithi* with the suffix *yat* in the sense of "for the sake of a guest," as in *nīvārādi* (wild rice, etc.). From *navyas*, *sūrya*, *martya*, and *yaviṣṭha*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), resulting in *navyam*, *sūryaḥ*, *martyaḥ*, and *yaviṣṭhyaḥ*. From *kṣema*, the suffix *ya* is applied, resulting in *kṣemyam*.

In place of the word *nava*, the substitute *nū* is applied, and the suffixes *tnap*, *tanap*, and *khā* are also added. Thus: *nūtnam*, *nūtanam*, *navīnam*. Furthermore, after the word *prāc* when it has the sense of "ancient," the suffix *na* is added. Thus: *praṇam*. And with the suffixes *tnap* and so forth: *pratnam*, *pratanam*, *prīṇam*.
The suffix *dheya* is applied after the words *bhāga*, *rūpa*, and *nāman*. The suffix *dheya* occurs after these: *rūpadheyam*, *bhāgadheyam*, *nāmadheyam*.
After the word *deva*, the suffix *tal* is applied.
It may occur in its own sense: *deva* itself is *devatā*. [The suffix] *ka* occurs after the root *av*.
It may be so: [the suffix] *kan* is applied after [words beginning with] *yāva* and others.

The suffix *kan* may be added to these words in their own sense (*svārthe*). Examples: *yāvakaḥ*, *maṇikaḥ*, *nāntarīyakaḥ*, *śreyaskaḥ*, *kandukaḥ*. After the word *putra*, it is used in the sense of "artificial" (*kṛtrima*): *putrakaḥ*. After the word *snāta*, it is used in the sense of "one who has completed the study of the Vedas": *snātakaḥ*.
Red [objects] [are used] for a gem.
The suffix *kan* shall be applied after the word *lohita* when it denotes a gem (*maṇi*). Examples: *lohitakaḥ maṇiḥ* (a red gem); *lohitakanirmitā bhūḥ* (ground made of red gems).
Why "when it denotes a gem"? [Observe: *lohitaḥ parvataḥ* (a red mountain); *lohitā gauḥ* (a red cow).
Furthermore, the suffix is applied when the color is not permanent.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *lohita* when it denotes an unstable color. For example: *lohitakaḥ* (red with anger).

Why "when not permanent"? Consider: *lohitā gauḥ* (a red cow). It should be stated that there is optionally a sublation of the gender [of the base] after *lohita*: *lohitikā* or *lohinikā* (red with passion).
In the case of blood.
The suffix *kan* occurs after the word *lohita* when it means "dyed with lac and so forth": *lohitakaḥ kambalaḥ* ("a blanket dyed red").
[The suffix *kan* also occurs] after *kāla*.

The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *kāla* when it means "dark" (*asita*) or "red" (*rakta*). For example: *kālakaṃ mukham* ("a dark face" due to embarrassment); *kālakaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a dark cloth"). After words such as *vinaya*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after these: *vinaya* becomes *vaina*yika*; *samaya* becomes *sāmayika*; *upacāra* becomes *aupacārika*; *atyaya* becomes *ātyayika*. "He did not approach him with what was urgent" (*nātyayikaṃ tametya*). *Akasmāt* ends in *d*; [from it] *ākasmikaṃ*. *Muktā* becomes *mauktikaṃ*.
Likewise for *vyavahāra*, *samūha*, and *viśeṣa*. After *upāya*, there is also shortening: *śivamaupayikaṃ garīyasām*.
When the meaning of a speech-utterance [is to be expressed].

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the word *vāc* when it expresses the aforementioned meaning. Thus, *vācikaṃ* refers to a message. The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word denoting an action connected with that [message].
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after the word *karma* when it follows a word expressing "that which conveys the stated meaning. An action conveyed by a message is called *kārmaṇa*.
[The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after *oṣadhi*, except when denoting a genus.

The suffix *aṇ* shall occur after the word *oṣadhi*. One drinks *auṣadham* (medicine). Why [is it said] "not when denoting a genus"? [Answer: Where herbs (*oṣadhayaḥ*) exist at night. [Example: One kindles with fire produced from herbs (*oṣadhijena kṛśānunā*). And [the suffix occurs] after *prajñā* and other such words.

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. For example: *prājña* becomes *prājñaḥ*; *prājñī* (feminine); *vaṇij* becomes *vāṇijaḥ*; *marut* becomes *mārutaḥ*; *cora* becomes *cauraḥ*; *caurī* (feminine); *rakṣas* becomes *rākṣasaḥ*; *devatā* becomes *daivatam*; *manas* becomes *mānasam*; *śatru* becomes *śātravaḥ*; *piśāca* becomes *paiśācam*; *vayas* becomes *vāyasaḥ*; *bandhu* becomes *bāndhavaḥ*; *vikṛta* becomes *vaikṛtam*; *dvitā* becomes *dvaitam*; *pratibhā* becomes *prātibham*; *caṇḍāla* becomes *cāṇḍālaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). [The suffix] *takan* is added after *mṛd*.
It may be *mṛttikā*; [it may also be] *mṛd* alone. The suffix *sasnu* is used in the sense of praise.
The suffixes *sasnau* occur after the word *mṛd* when excellence is expressed; they supersede *rūpap*. Thus: *mṛtsā*, *mṛtsnā*.
Furthermore, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffixes *til* and *tātil* occur after the words *vṛka* and *jyeṣṭha*.
This is the Chandas-sūtra:
"The suffix *śas* is optionally [used] after a word denoting a small quantity, provided it functions as a *kāraka*."

The suffix *śas* may optionally occur after words meaning "many" (*bahu*) or "few" (*alpa*). He gives many times: *bahuśaḥ*, *bhūriśaḥ*; he gives few times: *alpaśaḥ*, *stokaśaḥ*. According to tradition (*smṛti*), this designation applies when the action is auspicious; it should not occur in contexts such as funeral rites (*śrāddha*). Why [is it said] "after a kāraka"? (Consider: "the owner of many."

The inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* is for the sake of clarity, since the optionality of the *vṛtti* (compound formation) is already established by the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Furthermore, [the suffix *śas*] occurs after a numeral and a singular term when expressing distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

The suffix *śas* may optionally be used after these two [words] in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). After a numeral: *dviśaḥ* (two by two), as in "he gives two by two"; *pañcaśaḥ* (five by five), as in "he gives five by five. After a word denoting a single object that expresses a measure (*parimāṇa*): *paṇaśaḥ*, as in "he gives a *paṇa* at a time"; *prasthaśaḥ*; *pādaśaḥ*.
Only when [the word] is a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is it so; for example, "the owner of two by two" (where the numeral is not a *kāraka*).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "from a numeral and a singular word"? [Examples: *ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ dadāti* (he gives pot after pot); *kuṇḍaṃ kuṇḍaṃ pibati* (he drinks from one vessel after another). [The suffix] *tasi* occurs after the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) when used with *prati*.

When used in conjunction with the *karmapravacanīya* particle *prati*, the suffix *tasi* may optionally occur after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: *yo nārāyaṇataḥ prati* or *nārāyaṇāt prati* ("who [stands] opposite Nārāyaṇa"); *vāṇijaścaurataḥ prati* or *caurāt prati* ("the merchant [stands] opposite the thief"). And [the suffix *tasi* occurs] after words beginning with *ādi*. *Ādi* means "first"; after words beginning with that, or after those ending in the case-affixes beginning with that, the suffix *tasi* may optionally occur according to usage. In the sense of "an action or quality" (*karmaguṇa*), we have *karmaguṇataḥ*. Likewise: *smaraṇāt* (from remembrance) becomes *smaraṇataḥ*; *ādau* (in the beginning) becomes *āditaḥ*. Examples include: *śarīreṇa* (by the body) becomes *śarīrataḥ kṛśaḥ* ("thin by reason of the body"); *pṛṣṭhataḥ* ("behind"); *śabdataḥ* ("by way of sound"). A corrupt word is [corrupt] *svarato* (by accent) or *varṇato* (by phoneme).
And [the sixth case ending is used] for the ablative (apādāna), except in the case of the roots √hā "to abandon" and √ruh "to ascend."

The suffix *tas* may optionally occur after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) that denotes an ablative (*apādāna*). Examples: *grāmata āyāti* (he comes from the village); *caurataḥ bibheti* (he fears the thief).

There is a prohibition [of this suffix] for the roots *hā* ("to leave") and *ruh* ("to ascend"). Examples: *svārthād dhīyate* (he departs for his own sake); *parvatād avarohati* (he descends from the mountain).
Because the term *hīya* is specified [in the rule], there is no prohibition for the root *jihāti*. Example: *udayācalata ujjihīte* (he rises from the mountain of sunrise).

How is it "deficient in mantra"? The suffix *tasi* is used after a word ending in the third case. [This is according to] Pāṇini 5.4.46: "The third case-ending is used in the senses of surpassing, not being distressed, and reproach, when the agent is not expressed."

The suffix *tas* may optionally be added after a word ending in the third case when it signifies "surpassing," "not wavering," or "being censured. He is surpassed by his conduct (*vṛttenātigṛhyate*), or "he is surpassed on account of his conduct" (*vṛttato'tigṛhyate*). He does not waver from his character (*caritrato na calati*). He is censured because of his behavior (*vyavahārato ninditaḥ*).
Why say "when not denoting the agent"? [Observe: "It was thrown by the Brahmin" (*vipreṇa kṣiptam*). [The suffix is also applied] after words joined with the sense of "declining" or "sinful."

The suffix *tas* may optionally occur after a word ending in the third case, provided it denotes that by which one is surpassed (*hīyamāna*) or is evil (*pāpa*), when the agent is not expressed. For example: *vṛttena hīyate*, *vṛttato hīyate* (he is surpassed in conduct); *vyavahārato hīyate* (he is surpassed in legal proceedings); *vṛttataḥ pāpaḥ* (evil in conduct).
[The suffix *tas*] is also used with the genitive case when there is a mutual relation (*vyāśraya*).

The suffix *tas* may optionally occur after a word ending in the sixth case when there is recourse to various sides (*pakṣa*). For example: *devā arjunato 'bhavan*, meaning "the gods were on Arjuna's side" (*arjunasya pakṣe*). *ādityāḥ karṇataḥ*, meaning "the Ādityas were on Karṇa's side" (*karṇasya pakṣe*). Why "when there is recourse to various sides"? [Observe: *vṛkṣasya śākhā* ("the branch of the tree").
And in the removal of disease.

The suffix *tas* may optionally occur after a word denoting a disease ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), when it signifies "removing" [that disease]. For example: *hikkātaḥ kuru cikitsām* ("Perform treatment for hiccup") or *pravāhikātaḥ* ("for dysentery"). Why "when signifying removing"? [Consider: *hikkāyāḥ prakopaḥ* ("the aggravation of hiccup").

When there is a transition from not being something to becoming that thing (*abhūtatadbhāva*), the suffix *cvi* is added after a word in construction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, provided the agent is the one who becomes [the state] (*sampadyakartṛ*).

The suffix *cvi* occurs after the verb *sampad* when it denotes the agent in the sense of "becoming that which one was not before," provided it is in conjunction with the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*. For example: "That which was not white becomes white" (*aśuklaḥ śuklaḥ sampadyate*). To make it so, one says *śuklīkaroti*. By the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, one may also say *śuklaṃ karoti*. Likewise: *śuklībhavati*, *śuklīsyāt*; *mṛdūsyāt*; *paṭūbhavati*.
Furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final syllables of the words *arus*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas*. (When followed by *cvi* and the aforementioned verbs).

The suffix *cvi* occurs after these [words], and there is elision of the final phoneme. Examples: *arūkaroti* (he makes formless), *sumanīkaroti* (he makes well-disposed). *uccakṣū syāt* (may he have eyes raised up), *sucetīkṛtaḥ* (made well-minded). *raṇhībhūtaṃ daśānanam* (the ten-faced Rāvaṇa became swift), *nīrajīkāritakṣmām* (the earth was made free from dust).
The suffix *sāti* is optionally used when expressing completeness.

In the sense of "complete attainment" (*kārtsnyagati*) regarding an object, there may be the suffix *āti* (forming *sāt*). For example: *kāṣṭhaṃ bhasmasāt karoti* or *bhasmīkaroti* ("he reduces the wood to ashes"). When that [wood] has become ashes through fire, [the suffix is used]. And [the suffix *sāt* is also used] with the word *sampad* in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*).

The suffix *sāti* may optionally be used in the sense of *cvī* (denoting a complete transformation) when expressing pervasion; furthermore, the verb *sampad* is used as an auxiliary. For example: *udakasāt sampadyate lavaṇam* ("salt becomes completely transformed into water"), or *udakasād bhavati*, or *udakībhavati*.
[This rule applies] when expressing that something has come under the control of another.

When the word *tadāyatta* (dependent on that) is used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, as well as with *sampad*, the suffix *sāti* may optionally be employed. For example: *rājādhīnaṃ karoti* (he makes [it] dependent on the king), or *rājasāt karoti*; *strīsāt sampadyate yuvā* (the youth becomes dependent on a woman).
When the sense is "to be given," the suffix *trā* is also used.

When that which is to be given is dependent [on another], the suffixes *tra* and *sāti* may be used. For example: *devatra karoti* (he gives to the gods), *devasāt karoti* (he gives away to the gods). *viprasād akṛta bhūyasīrbhuvaḥ* (he has made many worlds for the sake of the Brahmins); *vipratrā karoti* (he gives to the Brahmins), *vipratrā saṃpadyate* (it becomes for the Brahmins). [The suffixes *tra* and *sāti* are] frequently used after the words *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puru*, and *martya* when they are in either the second or the seventh case.

After these [words], when used in the sense of the second case (accusative), as well as in connection with *kṛñ* and other verbs, the suffix *trā* occurs. For example: *sātiḥ nivṛttaḥ* ("the gain has ceased");

*devān karoti* becomes *devatrā karoti* ("he treats them as gods"); *devatrā gacchati* ("he goes among the gods"); *deve vasati* becomes *devatrā vasati* ("he dwells among the gods"). Due to the abundance [of usage]—*bahutrā jīva bālaka* ("live long, O child, in many places").
The suffix *ḍāc* is added after an imitative sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) consisting of two or more syllables, provided it does not end in *it*, when expressing the manner of an action.

When reduplication has occurred, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied after an unexpressed sound that imitates a word consisting of two or more syllables, provided it is used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*. Examples: *paṭapaṭākaroti* (he makes a "paṭ-paṭ" sound), *damadamāsyāt* (he would make a "dama-dama" sound). The mention of "two syllables" (*dvyaj*) is illustrative of one, two, or more syllables—as in *kharaṭakharaṭākaroti* (he makes a "kharaṭa-kharaṭa" sound). Why say "provided it is not *iti*"? Because in *paṭiti karoti* (he does it with a "paṭ" sound), the suffix is not applied.
The roots *kṛñ* (to do/make) and *kṛṣ* (to plow) take the affix *ṇamul* after the second, third, and *śamba* as upapadas, provided that the action refers to agriculture.

The suffix *ḍāc* is applied after these [words] when used in conjunction with the root *kṛ* (to do/make), provided the meaning is "ploughing. For example: *dvitīyākaroti* ("he ploughs for a second time"), *tṛtīyākṛtam* ("ploughed for a third time"). Also, *śambākṛtya* ("having ploughed in rows") and *bījākṛtavān* ("having sown seeds"). This rule is prescribed in the context of the root *kṛ* within ten sūtras.
Furthermore, it applies after a numeral ending in the word *guṇa*.

The suffix *ḍāc* shall be applied after a number ending in a vowel or the word *guṇa*, when used in connection with the root *kṛ* (to do) in the sense of agriculture; as in *triguṇākaroti kṣetram* ("he prepares the field three times"). It is also applied after the word *samaya* in the sense of passing time.

The suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the words *yāpanā* and *samaya*. *Samayākaroti* means "he passes the time" or "he delays. [In this sense] it means "he makes a delay. *Samayākuruta mā vāgbhiḥ* ("Do not mock me with your words").
After the words *sapatra* and *niṣpatra*, [the suffix *ḍāc* is used] in the sense of causing extreme pain.

The suffix *ḍāc* is applied after these two [words] when expressing extreme affliction. For example: *sapatrākaroti mṛgaṃ vyādhaḥ* (the hunter pierces the deer through with an arrow); *niṣpatrākaroti*. [As it is said: "Even the sky was made *sapattrākṛta* (pierced through) by the flight of the bow-wielder.
The suffix *ḍāc* is applied after *niṣkula* when expressing the act of eviscerating.

In this context, the suffix *ḍāc* shall be applied after these words: "He makes the pomegranate seedless" (*niṣkulākurute dāḍimam*). [The suffix *ḍāc* is also applied] after *sukha* and *priya* when expressing compliance.

The suffix *ḍāc* shall be applied after these two [words] when expressing favorability (*ānukūlya*). Examples: *mukhākaroti*, *priyākaroti*. The meaning is "he acts favorably. As in: "He said to Sītā, 'Be pleasant' (*sukhābhava*)," and "She was sweet-spoken (*priyaṃvadā*) in order to make him pleased (*priyākartum*). [The suffix *ḍāc* is also applied] after *duḥkha* when expressing opposition (*prātilomya*).

The suffix *ḍāc* shall be used [after a word denoting an instrument] when it expresses the sense of "making difficult. For example: *duḥkhākaroti kuputraḥ* ("a bad son makes one suffer"); *adaḥ duḥkhākaroti mām* ("that makes me suffer"). [The suffix *ḍāc* is also used] after the word *śūla* when the sense is "cooking."
The suffix *ḍāc* occurs after this [root] *kṛñ* when it is in conjunction with an object. For example: *śūlākṛtam māṃsam* (meat roasted on a spit); *śūlākaroti māṃsam* (he roasts meat on a spit).
[The suffix *ḍāc* also occurs] after *satya* when not referring to an oath.

The suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the word *satya*. [Examples: *satyākaroti bhāṇḍaṃ vaṇik*—"The merchant makes the merchandise true"; he gives a "true-mark" (*satyaṅkāra*), meaning: "This has been received by me. Why [is it] not [used] when there is no oath? *satyaṃ karoti vipraḥ*—"The Brahmin makes it true"; the meaning is that he swears.
[The suffix *ḍāc* occurs] after *madrā* in the sense of shaving.

The suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the word *madrā* in the sense of performing a propitiatory tonsure (*māṅgalika-muṇḍana*). Examples: *madrākṛto bālaḥ* ("the boy has had the propitiatory tonsure performed by the Madras"), *madrākaroti bālam* ("he performs the propitiatory tonsure on the boy"). It should be stated that this also applies after the word *bhadrā*. Example: *bhadrākaroti nāpitaḥ* ("the barber performs the auspicious shaving"). The rule regarding *mahāvibhāṣā* is fully established. The suffixes having the sense of *kṛtvasuc* [and others] are also included. Furthermore, those beginning with *śas* are indeclinables (*avyaya*).
The suffixes forming the end of compounds.

Henceforth, the suffixes that form the members of a compound or the compound itself must be explained. *Adhirājam* and *uparājam* [are examples]. [The rule] "not from an indeclinable" [is stated]; thus, *dvidhurī* and *tridhurī*—the suffix *ṅīp* is applied because it is a *dvigu* compound. *Vāktvacinī*—the suffix *ini* is applied because it is a *dvandva* compound denoting a disease or something censurable. *Ardhadhurā* (half of the yoke)—because it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it takes the gender of the final member. [The rule] "not after a word used for praise" [is stated].

The suffix *samāsānta* (compound-final suffix) should not be applied after another word following a term used in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*). Examples: *surājā*, *atirājā*; *sugauḥ*, *atigauḥ*. Here, the inclusion of the term *su-* and *ati-* must be made; it should not apply here: *paramagavaḥ*.
And the inclusion of the term *bahuvrīhi* [must be made] prior [to this rule]: *susaktham*, *atisakthaḥ*.
The word *kim* [is used] in the sense of censure.

In the sense of censure (*kṣepa*), there shall be no compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) after the word *kim* that follows [another word]. For example: *kiṃrājā* ("what a king!"), one who does not protect; *kiṃsakhā* ("what a friend!"), because of practicing treachery; *kiṃgauḥ* ("what a cow!"), because of not yielding milk or being unable to carry a load. Why "in the sense of censure"? Consider: *kasya rājā* ("the king of whom? = *kiṃrājaḥ*. [Also, the suffix is not applied] after a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound.

The suffix [ṭac] prescribed for this compound shall not occur. Examples: *arājā* (non-king), *asakhā* (non-friend), *agauḥ* (non-cow). Why "from a *tatpuruṣa*"? Consider: *adhuraṃ śakaṭam* (a cart without a pole).
Regarding the word *pathin*, it is optional.
This [suffix] may optionally be applied after the word *pathin* when it means "not a path," as in *apatha* or *apanthāḥ*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound where a numeral is the object of specification, the suffix *ḍac* is added after words other than *bahu* and *gaṇa*.

The suffix *ḍac* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose final member is a numeral. Examples: *upadaśāḥ* (nearly ten), *āsannaviṃśāḥ* (nearly twenty), *dvitrāḥ* (two or three), *pañcaṣāḥ* (five or six), *ekadvāḥ* (one or two), *lakṣakoṭāḥ* (a hundred thousand or ten million). Why "not after *bahu* or *gaṇa*"? Example: *upabahavaḥ* (nearly many), *upagaṇāḥ* (nearly a group). After a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a numeral, provided it begins with an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffix *ḍac* shall be applied. Example: *nistriṃśāni varṣāṇi* (years that have passed beyond thirty), *niścatvāriṃśāni* (years that have passed beyond forty).

*varṣāṇi* (years). *Nistriṃśaḥ* means a sword, [so called because it has] gone out from thirty fingers (*triṃśat-aṅguli*). Why [is the rule] stated as "after indeclinables and so forth" (*avyayādeḥ*)? [Observe: *gotriṃśat*, *goviṃśatiḥ*. [The rule] *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ pathām ānakṣe* [applies here].

In a compound, the vowel *a* is substituted for the initial vowel of *ṛc* and so forth. *Ardharcaḥ* (half-verse); *anṛcaḥ māṇavakaḥ* (a boy who has not learned the *ṛc*s); *bahvṛcaḥ* (a specific Vedic school). *Pur*: *nāndīpuram*. Because gender is based on worldly usage (*lokāśrayatva*), it is neuter: *dvipurī*, *tripurī*. *Ap*: *dvīpam*, *bahvāpāni taḍāgāni*. How is *bahvṛvāmpi* [formed]? They say it is because the rule for compound suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
*Dhur*: *rājadhurā*, *mahādhuraḥ*. *Pathin*: *rājapathaḥ*, *mahāpathaḥ*. Why [is the suffix not applied] when it does not mean "a chariot"? (i.e., why is it *akṣapathaḥ* rather than *akṣapathaḥ*)?

The word *akṣadhūḥ* means "the pole of chariots. The word *dṛḍhadhūḥ* means "a strong axle. [The suffix *khañ* is applied] after the words *sāman* and *loman* when preceded by *a*, *prati*, *anu*, or *ava*.

The suffix *ac* shall be applied after the words *sāman* and *loman* when preceded by *prati* or *anu*. Examples: *pratisāmam*, *anusāmam*, *pratilomam*, *anulomam*. In this context—it is traditionally taught that the suffix *ac* is added to the word *bhūmi* (earth) when it is preceded by *kṛṣṇa*, *udaka*, or *pāṇḍu*, provided that [the word] follows the name of the river Godāvarī or a numeral.

Thus says Jayāditya: *kṛṣṇabhūmam*, *udakabhūmam*, *pāṇḍubhūmam*, *pañcagodāvaram*, *dvinadam*. [The rule] "and after *bhūmi* when preceded by a numeral" [is applied]: *daśabhūmaṃ sūtram* (the ten-grounded sutra), *dvibhūmaḥ prāsādaḥ* (a two-storied palace). Due to the division of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*) [allowing for] *ajit*, there are: *padmanābhaḥ*, *ūrṇanābhaḥ*, *dīrgharātram*, *gaṇarātram*, *varṣārātram*, and so forth.
Because of the non-perception of the eye.
The suffix *ac* is applied after the word *akṣi* when it does not mean "the eye. Examples: *puṣkarākṣa* ("lotus-eyed"), *gavākṣa* ("bull's eye" = window).

The following are *ac*-compounds: *acatura*, *avicatura*, *sucatura*, *asra*, *strīpumsa*, *dhenu*, *anaḍuh*, *rk-sāma*, *vāṅmanasa*, *akṣibhruva*, *dāragava*, *urvaṣṭhīva*, *padaṣṭhīva*, *naktaṃdiva*, *rātriṃdiva*, *ahardiva*, *sarajas*, *niḥśreyasa*, *puruṣāyuṣa*, *dvyāyuṣa*, *tryāyuṣa*, *ṛgyajuṣa*, *jātokṣa*, *mahokṣa*, *vṛddhokṣa*, *upaśuna*, *goṣṭhaśva*.
These twenty-five [words] ending in the suffix *ac* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*). Among them, the first three are *bahuvrīhi* compounds.

Then there are eleven *dvandva* compounds: *ahardivam*, meaning day after day; *sarajasam*, meaning with all its pollen (properly so used in an *avyayībhāva*, but incorrect in a *bahuvrīhi* such as *sarajasaṃ padmam*). Then two *tatpuruṣa* compounds: *niḥśreyasam*, meaning certain welfare; and *puruṣāyuṣam*, meaning the lifespan of a man. Then two *dvigu* compounds. Then a *dvandva*. Then three *karmadhāraya* compounds: *upaśunam*, meaning near a dog; *goṣṭhaśvaḥ*, meaning a dog in a cow-pen (like a stray);

and *tricaturāḥ* and *upacaturāḥ*, which require the addition of the rule regarding *catur* preceded by *tri* or *upa*. (Note: The term *sarajasam* is cited here as an example of correct usage in an *avyayībhāva*; its use in a *bahuvrīhi* is considered incorrect according to the grammatical tradition followed here.)
The suffix *varcas* is added after the words *brahman* and *hastin*.

The suffix *ac* is applied after these two [words] to form a compound meaning "splendor" (*varcasa*). Examples: *brahmavarcasam*, *hastivarcasam*. However, it is not applied when preceded by *hetu*: *hetubrahmavarcasam*. It is also applied after *palya* and *rājan*: *palyavarcasam*, *rājavarcasam*.
The suffix *ac* is applied after *tamas* when preceded by *ava*, *sa*, and *andha*: [e.g., *avatasam*, *satasam*, *andhatamasam*].
The suffix *ac* shall be applied after these words [to form adverbs of comparison]: *avatamasam*, *santamasam*, and *andhatamasam*.
[The suffix *ac* shall also be applied] after *śvas* when followed by *vasīyas* and *śreyas*: *śvovasīyam* and *śvaḥśreyasam*.
After the word *śvas* (tomorrow), the suffix *ac* may be added to the words *vasīyas* (better) and *śreyas* (more excellent). [Examples: *śvovasīyasam*, *śvaḥśreyasaṃ*—may it be yours!
After the word *rahas* (secret), [the suffix *ac* is added] when preceded by *anu* or *ava*.
The suffix *ac* shall be applied after these [words] when they mean "secret. Examples: *anurahasam anāyi nāyakena* ("he was led by the lover secretly"), *avarahasam*, *taptarahasam*.
[The suffix *ac* is also applied] after *uras-* when it occurs in the locative case and is preceded by *prati*.

The suffix *ac* is applied after the word *uras*, when it occurs in the sense of the seventh case (locative) following the prefix *prati*. For example: *urasi kṣatāḥ* becomes *pratyurasaṃ kṣatāḥ* ("wounds on the chest"); *nyapatan pratyurasaṃ priyāḥ priyāṇām* ("the beloveds fell upon the chests of their lovers"). These are indeclinable compounds (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of a case ending.
Furthermore, the compound *anugavam* is formed in the sense of length.
This is what is elided here: *anugavo rathaḥ* (a chariot following the oxen). This is a compound formed by the rule *yasya cāyāmaḥ*.
Likewise, *dvistāvā* and *tristāvā vedīḥ* (altars twice or thrice as large).
If it is an altar (vedi), it should be twice as large or three times as large; otherwise, the cord (rajju) should be twice as long or three times as long.
[The suffix -tva is added] after a word for a road following a prefix.

The suffix *ac* shall be applied after words beginning with *pra* when they denote a distance. For example: *prādhvo rathaḥ* (a carriage that has traversed a distance), *niradhvaḥ* (one who has left the path). [Furthermore, the suffix *ac* is applied] to a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *aṅguli*, provided it begins with a numeral or an indeclinable.

The suffix *ac* shall occur after the word *aṅguli* when it follows a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*). For example, in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is a compound meaning "that whose measure is two fingers": *dve aṅgulī pramāṇam asya*. By the rule *pramāṇe la dvigoḥ*, the suffix *mātrac* is elided. Thus: *dvyaṅgulam*, *tryaṅgulam*. Regarding "after an indeclinable, etc.": *nirgatam aṅgulibhyaḥ* (gone out from the fingers) = *niraṅgulam*; *atyaṅgulam*. Why "of a *tatpuruṣa*"? [Counter-example: *pañcāṅgulir hastaḥ* ("a hand with five fingers"). This rule applies to *tatpuruṣa* compounds up to the *dvandva* class.

[The suffix -tva- is applied] after the words *ahar* (day), *sarva* (all), a word expressing a part [of a whole], *saṃkhya* (number), and *puṇya* (meritorious), as well as after the word *rātri* (night).

The suffix *ac* shall be applied after numerals, indeclinables (*avyaya*), and words beginning with *ahar*, when followed by *rātri*. The aggregate of five nights is *pañcarātram*. *Trirātram* (three nights). *Dvirātram* (two nights). That which has passed beyond the night is *atirātraḥ*. *Nīrātraḥ* (without night). The mention of *ahar* is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound: *ahorātraḥ* (day and night). *Sarvarātraḥ* (the whole night). *Saṃkhyātarātraḥ* (a counted night). *Puṇyarātraḥ priyāgame* (an auspicious night at the arrival of a beloved)—these are *karmadhāraya* compounds. From [words denoting] a part: *pūrvaṃ rātreḥ* (the front part of the night) becomes *pūrvarātraḥ*. *Apararātraḥ* (the latter part of the night). *Ardharātraḥ* (midnight).
The word *ahna* is substituted for *aha-* before these [suffixes].

The word *ahar* (day) undergoes the substitution of *ahn* when followed by a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) after these [words]: numerals, indeclinables, and the group beginning with *ahar*. In the case of the suffix *ṭac*: *dvyahnaḥ* (occurring in two days), *tryahnaḥ* (occurring in three days). [Here,] the suffix *ṭhañ* prescribed after words denoting time is elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* ("there is elision of the suffix after a *dvigu* compound, except when forming a patronymic"). Examples: *atyahnaḥ*, *nirahnaḥ*—these are *prādi* compounds. *Sarvāhnaḥ*, *saṃkhyātāhnaḥ*—these are *karmadhāraya* compounds. *Pūrvāhṇaḥ*, *aparāhṇaḥ*—these are compounds formed by the rule for *pūrva-apara*. In all these cases, the suffix *ṭac* is applied. However, it is not applied when a numeral begins the compound and it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*).

In a compound denoting a collective sum, the substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* (day) would not occur after a numeral and so forth. For example: two days collectively = *dvyahaḥ*; three days = *tryahaḥ*; seven days = *saptāhaḥ*; ten days = *daśāhaḥ*.
[This substitution also occurs] after the words *uttama* and *eka*.

In these two cases, there is no substitution of *ahna* for *ahan*. The meaning is that the word *puṇya* is the final [member] of a compound beginning with *ahan*, and it is the last member. Examples: *puṇyāham* (an auspicious day), *ekāhaḥ* (a single day).
[The suffix] *ṭac* is applied after words ending in *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*.

The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after these [words] when they form a *tatpuruṣa* compound: *mahārājaḥ*, *devarājaḥ*, *dvyahaḥ*, *uttamāhaḥ*, *rājasakhaḥ*. "There are jackals as companions, not elephants.
Because the inclusion of the specific gender [is intended]: *mahārājñī*. [Also applied after *go-*] except when a *taddhita* suffix is elided (*ataddhitaluki*): *gorataddhitaluki*.

The word *go* [retains its final vowel length] in the following cases: *goṣṭha* (cow-pen), *puṅgavaḥ* (bull), *uttamagavaḥ* (excellent bull), *pañcagavī* (five cows), *strīgavī* (female cow), *rājagavī* (royal cow), *pañcagavadhanam* (wealth consisting of five cows), and *daśagavadhanam* (wealth consisting of ten cows). Why is it said "except when there is elision of a taddhita suffix"? Consider *pañcaguḥ paṭaḥ* (a cloth worth five cows); here, the suffix *ṭhak* [denoting "purchased for"] is elided by the rule *adhyardha-* [Pāṇini 5.1.28].
[The word *go* retains its vowel length] after *uras* when it is designated as *agra* (forepart).

The suffix *u* (forming *ura*) shall be applied after the word *śreṣṭha* when it denotes excellence; for example, *hastyurasaṃ* ("excellent among elephants") and *aśvorasaṃ* ("excellent among horses").
It also occurs after *anaḥ*, *aśman*, *ayas*, and *saras* when they denote a genus (*jāti*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied to these: in the sense of a genus—*upānasa*, *amṛtāśma*, *kālāyasa*, *maṇḍūkasarasa*;
in the sense of a name—*mahānasa*, *piṇḍāśma*, *lohitāyasa*, *kālasarasa*.
And [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] to *takṣan* after the words *grāma* and *kauṭa*.
The suffix *ṭac* is applied after these two [words] when followed by *takṣan*. [Examples: *grāmatakṣaḥ* (village carpenter), *kauṭatakṣaḥ* (house-carpenter).
[The suffix *ṭac* is also applied] after *śvan* when preceded by *ati*.

The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied [after a word ending in *a* when preceded by *ati*]. For example: *atiśvaḥ sevakaḥ* (a servant who surpasses a dog); *atiśvī mṛgī* (a female deer that surpasses a dog).
[This rule applies] after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), except when the object compared is not a living being (*aprāṇi*).

The suffix *śvan* (replacing *śvan*) may optionally occur after [a word ending in] *a* when used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). For example: *phalakaśvaḥ*, meaning "a plank-like horse" (*phalakaḥ iva śvaḥ*).
Why "not among non-living things"? Consider: *vānaraśvā*, meaning "a monkey-like horse" (*vānaraḥ iva śvā*), which is a compound by virtue of belonging to the *vyāghrādi* group.
Furthermore, the suffix *śvan* is applied after the word *sakthi* when it follows *uttara* or *mṛga*.

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after these [words ending in *sakthi*]: *uttarasaktham*, *mṛgasaktham*, *pūrvasaktham*. By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also applied after words denoting a comparison—e.g., *phalakasaktham*.
[The suffix *ṭac* is also applied] after the word *nau* when it forms a *dvigu* compound.
The suffix *ṭac* shall not occur after a *dvigu* compound ending in *nau*. Examples: *dvināva*, *pañcanāva*, *daśanāvapriyaḥ*.

This applies only when there is no elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix; for instance, when the suffix *ṭhan* (denoting "purchased") is elided: *pañcanaurgajaḥ*. [The suffix *ṭac* is also applied] after *ardha*.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the first member is *nau* (boat) and the second is *ardha* (half), the suffix *ṭac* shall be applied. Thus, *ardha-nau* becomes *ardhanāvam*.
However, in the form *ardhanāvī*, there is no application of the gender of the subsequent member because gender is dependent upon worldly usage.
According to the Eastern grammarians, this applies when the word is derived from *khārī*.

The same applies as after a *dvigu* compound. According to the opinion of the Easterners (*prācām*), the suffix *aṣṭac* is added after *khārī*. It is also added after *ardha*. Examples: *dvikhāra*, *ardhakhāra*. According to others—*dvikhārī*, *ardhakhārī*.
[The suffix *aṣṭac* is added] after *añjali* when preceded by *dvi* or *tri*.
