The suffix *iṣ* (forming a feminine noun) may optionally occur after these two [words ending in *añjali*]. The collection of two *añjali*s is *dvyañjalam* or *tryañjalam* water.
This applies only by virtue of the rule regarding *dvigu* compounds—[as in] *dvyañjaliḥ*, meaning "two *añjali*s" [of grain].
[Furthermore, the suffix *iṣ* occurs] after words ending in *anna* and after neuter nouns in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
The *chandas* [suffix] is applied after the word *brahman* when it denotes a person from a country.

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *brahman* when it follows a term denoting a region (*janapada*) or a part thereof, provided that the name [of the Brahmin] is identical to that [region]. For example: *surāṣṭrabrahmaḥ* (a Brahmin from Surāṣṭra) and *kāśibrahmaḥ* (a Brahmin from Kāśi). In other cases—such as *devabrahmā nāradaḥ* (the divine Brahmin Nārada)—it does not apply.
Furthermore, the suffix is optionally applied after the words *ku-* and *mahat-*.

After these two words, the suffix *ṭac* may optionally be applied to *brahman*. Thus, one obtains *kubrahmaḥ* or *kubrahmā*. [The suffix *ṭac* is also applied] after *pariṣad* and *balāt* when followed by *mahābrahmaiḥ*.
The compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) for the *tatpuruṣa* have been explained.
A Tatpuruṣa compound ending in the letters c, ṭ, t, p, h, or s, when it denotes a collective (samāhāra), takes the feminine suffix ṅīp.

The suffix *ṭac* shall be added after a *dvandva* compound ending in a letter of the *ca*-class (*c, ch, j, jh, ñ*), *da*, *ṣa*, or *ha*. Examples: *vāktvacam* (speech and skin), *upādhyāyaśabdaprāccham* (the teacher and the questioner), *śrīsrajam* (fortune and a garland). After one ending in *d*: *sampadvipadam* (prosperity and adversity). After one ending in *ṣ*: *vāktviṣam* (speech and luster), *grīṣmaprāvṛṣam* (summer and the rainy season). After one ending in *h*: *chatropānaham* (umbrella and sandals), *pikamadhuliham* (the cuckoo and the honey-bee). Why "in the sense of a collective" (*samāhāre*)? [Answer: *prāvṛṭśaradau* (the rainy season and autumn). Why "after a *dvandva*" (*dvandvāt*)? [Answer: The collection of five speeches is *pañcavāk*. In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, [the suffix is applied] after those beginning with *śarat*.

The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied here after these [words]: *upaśaradam*; then, for example, *upaśaradam apaśyat*. Likewise [after] *diś*, *vipāś*, *div*, *dṛś*, and *catur*. [Also] *jarā* becomes *jaras*: *upajarasam*.

[The suffix *aC* is applied] after the words *prati*, *para*, *sama*, and *anu* when [the word] *akṣi* follows. Thus, *pratyakṣam* ("before the eyes") and *parokṣam* ("out of sight")—the latter being a compound by virtue of a formal rule (*nipātana*) and featuring the substitution of *u* for *o*. [Similarly,] *samakṣam* ("in the presence of") and *anvakṣam* ("following after"). This prescription applies up to the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds; furthermore, [the suffix *aC* is applied] after the word *anas*.
After a neuter [stem], [the suffix *ṅi*] optionally [becomes *nā*].
The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after [a word ending in] the feminine suffix *ān*. Examples: *uparājam*, *pratirājam*; *upadaśam*, *adhyātmam*, *pratyātmam*.
After a neuter noun, it is optional: *upacarmam* or *upacarma*; *upabhasmam* or *upabhasma*; *pratyahaḥ* or *pratyaham*. An *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe*).
[The suffix *ṭac* is also applied] after words denoting a river, the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), or the month of *āgrahāyaṇī*.
Or there may be *ṣṭac*: *upanadam* or *upanadi*; *upapaurṇamāsam* or *upapaurṇamāsi*. He saw the moon at the time of the full moon (*upapaurṇamāsi*). *Upāgrahāyaṇam* or *upāgrahāyaṇi*.
[This applies] after a *jhay* consonant.
The suffix *ṭac* may optionally follow a word ending in a *jhay* sound (any consonant except *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*, and nasals). For example: *pratisamidham* or *pratisamid*; *upadṛṣadam* or *upadṛṣad*.
According to Senaka, this also applies after the word *giri*.

According to the opinion of Senaka, the suffix *ṣṭac* may optionally be applied after the word *giri*. [The forms] *anugiram*, *anugiri*, *upagiram*, or *upagiri* denote "that which is being performed near a mountain" (*anugiri*) or "near a mountain" (*upagiri*). Thus, the suffixes for the compound-ending (*samāsānta*) in the case of an *avyayībhāva* have been explained.
Now, regarding the *bahuvrīhi*: the suffix *ṣac* is applied after the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṣac* is applied after the words *sakthi* (thigh) and *akṣi* (eye) when they denote one's own limbs (*svāṅga*). Examples: *dīrghasakthaḥ* (long-thighed); because of the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added—thus *dīrghasakthī*; *sahasrākṣaḥ* (thousand-eyed); *viśālākṣaḥ* (large-eyed); *āyatākṣī* (long-eyed).
Why "when denoting one's own limbs"? [Consider] *dīrghasakthi śakaṭam* (a cart with long poles). This rule is prescribed for *bahuvrīhi* compounds up to the end of the chapter.
[The measurement] of fingers [is applied] to wood.

The suffix *ṣac* is added to *aṅguli* in the sense of "wood. Examples: *dvyaṅgulam* ("two-finger wood"), *pañcāṅgulam*. This refers to a wooden tool for lifting grain or similar items, consisting of parts equal in measure to fingers.
After the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *ṣan* is added to *mūrdhan*.
The suffix *ṣat* (which functions as *a*) is applied after these two [words, *dvi* and *tri*], when followed by *mūrdhan*. Examples: *dvimūrdhaḥ*, *trimūrdhaḥ*.
Why "after *dvi* and *tri*" (*dvitribhyām*)? [Counter-example: *bahumūrdhnor dvimūrdhāṃś ca trimūrdhāṃś cāhatāṃ mṛdhe*.
Also, [the suffix *ṣat* is applied] after a feminine ordinal number (*pūraṇī*) and after a word denoting measure (*pramāṇī*).

The suffix *cāp* (i.e., *ān*) is added after a feminine word ending in a superlative suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) and after the word *pramāṇī* when forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For example: *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ* ("the nights of which the fifth is auspicious"); *bhāryāpramāṇāḥ kuṭumbinaḥ* ("householders for whom the wife is the authority"). There is an extension [of this rule] to words preceded by the name of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) when used with *netṛ* ("leader"): *mṛganetrā rātrayaḥ* ("the nights of which the leader is Mṛga"); *puṣyanetrāḥ*. [The suffix *cāp* is also applied] after *loman* ("hair") when preceded by *antar* or *bahiḥ*: *antarloma*, *bahirloma*.
From these two [words], *loman* (hair) takes the suffix *ap*. *Antarlomaḥ prāvāraḥ* (a cloak with hair on the inside); *bahirlomaḥ kambalaḥ* (a woolen blanket with hair on the outside).
After the word *nāsikā* (nose), when used as a name (*saṃjñā*) and provided it is not preceded by *sthūla*, the suffix *añ* is applied and *nāsikā* is replaced by *nas*.

The suffix *ac* may be applied after the word *nāsikā*, and the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* should be made. Examples: *druṇasaḥ* (a snake), *gonasaḥ* (a snake). Why "not after *sthūla*"? Example: *sthūlanāsikaḥ varāhaḥ* (a boar with a thick nose). Why "in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*)"? Example: *tuṅganāsikaḥ* (one with a prominent nose). Furthermore, it should be stated that *nas* is substituted after *khara* and *khura*. Examples: *kharaṇāḥ*, *khuraṇāḥ*.
The *ac* suffix is also desired [after these words]: *kharaṇasaḥ*, *khuraṇasaḥ*.
And [the suffix is applied] after a prefix as well.

After the prefix *pra* and others, the substitute *ac* (a vowel) shall be used for *nāsikā*, and the form *nas* shall also be substituted. Examples: *unnasam dadhatī vaktram* ("holding her face with the nose raised"), *vinasā hatabāndhavā* ("with nose [and other limbs] destroyed, her kinsmen slain"). However, the word *anunāsika* is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). It should be stated that *gr* replaces *v* [in certain compounds]; thus, *vigraḥ*. But tradition holds that this [usage of *vigraḥ*] belongs to the Vedic language (*naigama*). [The following are irregular formations: *suprāta-*, *suśva-*, *sudiva-*, *śārikukṣa-*, *caturaśra-*, *aiṇīpada-*, *ajapada-*, and *proṣṭhapada-*.

These eight words ending in *an* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*). *Suprātaḥ*: he whose morning is beautiful. *Suśvaḥ*: he whose tomorrow is beautiful. *Sudivaḥ*: he whose day is beautiful; as in *sudivevāravindinī* (a lotus pond on a beautiful day). *Śārikukṣaḥ*: his belly is like that of a *śārī* bird. *Caturaśraḥ*: he who has four corners. *Eṇīpadaḥ*: her feet are like those of a female deer (*eṇī*); likewise *ajapadaḥ* and *proṣṭhapadaḥ*. The suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied after *halin* and *sakthi* when preceded by *nañ*, *dur*, or *su*.

After these [words] *hali* and *sakthi*, the suffix *aj* may optionally occur. For example: one for whom a plough (*hali*) does not exist is *ahalaḥ* or *ahalī*; likewise, one without thighs is *asakthaḥ* or *asakthiḥ*. Similarly, one with a good plough is *suhalaḥ* or *suhālī*; one with a bad plough is *durhalaḥ* or *durhalī*; one with beautiful thighs is *susakthaḥ* or *susakthiḥ*.
However, the suffix *asic* is compulsory after the words *prajā* and *medhā*.

The suffix *as* occurs after the words *prajā* and *medhā* when preceded by *nañ* (the negative particle) and others. Examples: *aprajāḥ*, *duṣprajāḥ*, *suprajāḥ*; *amedhāḥ*, *durmedhāḥ*, *sumedhāḥ*. "Alas, the dull-witted are destroyed! Because of the inclusion of the word *nitya* [in the rule], Jayāditya maintains that the form *alpamedhasaḥ* is also valid. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the form *bahuprajāḥ* is used.
The *chandas* [section] is the *sūtra*:
"The suffix *an* is applied after a single *dharma*."

The suffix *an* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) after the word *dharma*. Examples are *priyadharma* ("one who loves dharma") and *kalyāṇadharma* ("one whose nature is auspicious"). Regarding the usage in the *Bhāṣya*: "those by whom dharma has been realized are *sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇaḥ*, the sages. Why [is it said] "after [the word] alone"? It should not apply when *dharma* is compounded with another word; for example, *kuladharmaḥ* ("the dharma of the family") and *kṛtakuladharmaḥ* ("one by whom the family-dharma has been performed"), as well as *darśitasvadharmaḥ* ("one who has shown his own dharma").

But when it is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*—meaning "for whom his own duty (*svadharma*) is supreme"—then the word *dharma* alone [is used], and thus it becomes simply *paramasvadharmā*. However, according to Jayāditya, this is not so; [the rule applies] after *jambha*, *su*, *harita*, *tṛṇa*, and *soma*.

After the words *su* and others, the word *jambha* becomes *jambhā* when it does not end in the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *sujambhā*, *haritajambhā*, *tṛṇajambhā*, *somajambhā*. The word *jambha* means "eating" and also "the separation of the teeth. [The word] *dakṣiṇermā* [is used] in connection with a hunter.
If this [suffix] *lub* is elided here due to connection with a hunter (*lubdha*), then [the word] *dakṣiṇermā* refers to a deer whose right flank has been wounded by a hunter.
What is the purpose of the connection with a hunter? [Consider: *dakṣiṇermam*.
[The suffix] *ic* is applied when there is a mutual exchange of actions.

The suffix *ic* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound when there is a mutual exchange of actions. Examples: *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (stick against stick), *keśākeśi* (hair against hair), *bāhūbāhavi* (arm against arm), *nakhānakhi* (nail against nail), *musalāmusali* (club against club), and *jalpājalpi* (mutual chatter) among disputants.
[The suffix is also applied] after the group beginning with *dvidaṇḍi*.

The fifth case is used in the sense of the first case. Words such as *dvidaṇḍi* and others ending in the suffix *ic* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*). In *dvidaṇḍi praharaṇam*, there are two staffs in this weapon; [similarly] *dvimusali*. *Ubhāyāñjali*, *ubhayāhasti*; with his hands joined together (*prahasta*), he crushed the chariots and their drivers with both hands (*ubhayāhasti*). *Ekapadi*, *ubhayapadi*, *ubhayādanti*. Because they are listed in the *gaṇa*-list, they also form *tatpuruṣa* compounds: *nikucyakarṇi dhāvati* (he runs with ears flattened), *prohyapadi* (with feet extended). These belong to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. After *pra* and *sam*, the word *jānu* becomes *jñu*: *prajñu*, *saṃjñu*.
In place of *jānu* ("knee"), the substitute *jñu* shall occur after these two [prefixes]. Examples: *prajñuḥ*, *saṃjñuḥ*. After *ūrdhva*, it is optional.

After the word *ūrdhva*, the term *jānu* may optionally become *jñu*; thus, one may say *ūrdhvajñuḥ* or *ūrdhvajānuḥ*. [Furthermore,] after the word *ūdhas*, the substitution *anaṅ* occurs [in place of the final syllable].

The substitution of *anaṅ* and so forth is prescribed for a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas*. Examples: *kuṇḍodhnī*, *ghaṭodhnī*. Because this is taught specifically for the feminine gender—*mahodhāḥ parjanyaḥ* (the great rain-cloud), *gavāṃ gaṇāḥ prasrutapīvarodhasaḥ* (herds of cows with flowing, full udders)—it does not apply to the masculine. [It also applies] after *dhanus*.
The word *anaṅ* is prescribed [in place of the final vowel of the first member]. Thus: *śārṅgadhanvā*, *gāṇḍīvadhanvā*, *gṛhītadhanvā*.

One should consider [the form] *dhṛtadhanuṣam* as having *puṣpāyudha* [as its second member]. Alternatively, the rule for the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not mandatory; thus, by the rule "optionally when it is a proper name" (*vā saṃjñāyām*), [the form *dhṛtadhanvā* is also valid].
*Puṣpadhanvā*, or *puṣpadhanuḥ*.
[The suffix] *niṅ* is substituted for the word *jāyā*.
The suffix *niṅ* is prescribed after the word *jāyā*. There is elision of the *y* in the case of *vali*. One whose wife is young is called *yuvajāniḥ*; likewise, *priyajāniḥ* and *kamalājāniḥ*.
[The suffix *ic* is added] to the word *gandha* when preceded by *ut*, *pūti*, or *susurabhi*.

The *i* of the word *gandha* following *ud* and others shall be replaced by *it*. Examples: *udgandhiḥ* (one from whom a fragrance has gone out), *pūtigandhiḥ* (having a foul odor), *sugandhiḥ* (having a good odor), *surabhigandhiḥ* (having a fragrant odor). Because the rule applies only when [the odor] is inherent (*samaveta*), it does not apply here: *subandha āpaṇikaḥ* (a merchant with a good scent).
[The suffix *it* is applied] when expressing "smallness" (*alpākhyāyām*).

The suffix *gandhi* may be used after this [word *sūpa*]. A pot in which there is little soup is called *sūpagandhi*; a meal with a trace of curd is *dadhighandhi*; a statement with a hint of affection is *premagandhi*.
[The suffix *gandhi* is also applied] after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

[The suffix *ini*] may be used after the word *gandha*. For example: "having the scent of a lotus" is *padmagandhiḥ*; "having the scent of a water-lily" is *kumudagandhiḥ*. [In these cases], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final syllable of *pāda* when it follows words such as *hastin* and others.

The suffix *samāsānta* (compound-final suffix) *lopa* (elision) shall apply to the word *pāda* when it follows a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Examples: *vyāghrapāt* ("tiger-footed"), *siṃhapāt* ("lion-footed"). Why "not after *hastin* and so forth"? Examples: *hastipādaḥ* ("elephant-footed"), *ślīpādaḥ* ("club-footed"), *gaṇḍolapādaḥ* ("having swollen feet"). Also [the suffix *lopa* applies] in the case of *kumbhapadī* and similar forms.

Words such as *kumbhapadī* and others, which have undergone the elision of the suffix *ṅīp*, are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) with the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Examples include *kumbhapadī* and *śatapadī*. The word *ekapadī* refers to a path where there is one undivided foot for all; here, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *pādo 'nyatarasyām*. Furthermore, by the rule *pādaḥ pat*, the word *pāda-* becomes *pat-* when preceded by a numeral or the word *su-*. This is governed by the rule *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya*.

There shall be elision of the first member [of the compound] in this case. Examples: *dvipāt* (two-footed), *supāt* (well-footed), *dviradanāsorūḥ* (having thighs like the trunk of a two-tusked elephant).
In the sense of age (*vayas*), the word *danta* (tooth) is replaced by *datṛ*.

The word *danta* (tooth) is replaced by *dat* when preceded by a numeral or the word *su*. Examples: *dvidan vatsaḥ* (a two-toothed calf); *ṣoḍaśadan vayasthaḥ* (a sixteen-toothed youth); *ṣoḍan gauḥ* (a six-toothed ox); *sudant kumāraḥ* (a handsome-toothed boy); *sudatī taruṇī* (a beautiful-toothed young woman). Why specify "in the sense of age"? [Because] *dvidanto gajaḥ* (a two-toothed elephant).
And [this substitution occurs] in the Vedic language as well.
The *chandas* (Vedic) sūtra:
[the suffix *aṇ* is applied] in the feminine when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*).
In a feminine name, *datṛ* shall be substituted for *danta*; for example, *sudatī*. A certain woman is called *phāladatī*. [The substitution] is optional after *śyāva* and *aroka*.
After these two [words], the suffix *datṛ* may optionally be substituted for *danta*. For example: *śyāvadan*, or *śyāvadanta*; *arokadan*, or *arokadanta*. *Aroka* means "lusterless" (*adīpti*).
[The suffix *datṛ* is also applied] after *agra*, *anta*, *śuddha*, *śubhra*, *vṛṣa*, and *varāha*.

The suffix *datṛ* may optionally be applied to these words after *danta*. From words ending in *agra*: *kundakuḍmalāgradan* or *kundakuḍmalāgradantaḥ*. Similarly, *śuddhadan* or *śuddhadantaḥ* [referring to] a Brahmin.

Because of the word *ca*, Jayāditya states that it is also applied after *ahi*, *mūṣika*, *gardabha*, and *śikhara*: *ahidantaḥ* or *ahidan*; *śikharadatī*. There is elision of *kakuda* when expressing a particular state.

In the sense of a state (avasthā), there shall be elision of the final syllable of *kakuda*. For example: *ajātakakud* "a calf that has not yet grown a hump," and *sthūlakakut* "a young bull with a large hump. Why "in the sense of a state"? [Consider: *śvetakakuda* "a white bull" [where it refers to the animal itself]. Also, *trikakud* "a mountain" [is an exception].
In this context, [the suffix] is elided;
[it is also elided] after the words *ut* and *vi* when they precede *kākuda*.

By these two [suffixes], there is the elision of the final syllable of *kākuda*. For example: *utkākut* (one whose palate is raised) and *vikākut* (one with a deformed palate). When preceded by *pūrṇa*, it is optional.

In the word *pūrṇa*, when it precedes *kākuda*, the final syllable may optionally be elided. Thus, one says either *pūrṇakākut* (having a full palate) or *pūrṇakākudaḥ*. The words *suhṛd* and *durhṛd* denote a friend and an enemy, respectively.
These two [suffixes] are elided after these two [words]: *suhṛt* means "friend" (*mitra*) and *durhṛt* means "enemy" (*śatru*).
Why [specify] "of friend and enemy"? [Because otherwise] *suhṛdayaḥ* would mean "a good-hearted person" and *durhṛdayaḥ* would mean "a thief.
[The suffix] *kap* [is added] after words beginning with *uras*.

The suffix *kap* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with "chest" (*uraḥ*) and ending with a case-ending. For example: *vyūḍhoraskaḥ* (one whose chest is broad), *priyasarpiṣkaḥ* (one who likes clarified butter), *priyayaśaskaḥ* (one who likes fame). After the word *artha*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, [the suffix *kap* is applied]: *anarthakaḥ* (meaningless).

In this *gaṇa*, the words *lakṣmī*, *anaḍvān*, *payas*, *nau*, and *pumān* are recited ending in the nominative singular. Consequently, according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*, the suffix *kap* may optionally follow these when they end in the dual or plural: *bahulakṣmīḥ* or *bahulakṣmīkaḥ*; *dvipumān* or *dvipuṃskaḥ*, according to Jayāditya.

Because of the prohibition against *tadantavidhi* (extension of a rule to that which ends with the word specified) when the base is accompanied by a suffix (*grahaṇavatā prātipadikena*), the suffix does not apply here: *plavaṅganakhakoṭibhiḥ kṣatadṛḍhoraso rākṣasāḥ*.
[The suffix *kap* is also applied] after *inaḥ* when it occurs in the feminine.

The suffix *kap* shall be applied after a stem ending in *innanta* when forming a feminine noun. Examples: *bahudaṇḍikā śālā* (a hall with many staff-bearers), *bahuvāgmikā sabhā* (an assembly of many eloquent speakers).
[The suffix *kap* is also applied] after a word ending in *nadī* and after a word ending in *ṛt*.

The suffix *kap* shall be applied after a feminine noun ending in *nadi* (the *nadi*-class) or a feminine noun ending in long *ā*. Examples: *bahustrīkaḥ* nṛpaḥ ("a king who has many wives"), *bahukumārīkaḥ* deśaḥ ("a country with many young girls"), *bahudhībandhūkaḥ*, *bahuvīrabandhūkaḥ*, *bahubrahmabandhūkaḥ*, *bahudātṛkaḥ*, *bahumātṛkaḥ*. It is not desired that *kap* be applied after a feminine noun formed by a *kṛt* suffix, because the term "feminine" (*strī*) here refers to those [words] prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*stryadhikāra*). Therefore, by the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*, *kap* is optionally applied: *bahutantrī* or *bahutantrīkaḥ*; *suvadhūḥ* or *suvadhūkaḥ*, and so forth. [The rule: *śeṣād vibhāṣā* ("Optionally after the remainder").

Since no suffix is prescribed for the Bahuvrīhi compound [in these cases], the suffix *kap* may optionally be applied. Thus: *bahukhaṭvākaḥ*, *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, or *bahukhaṭvaḥ*; *bahudaṇḍī rājā* or *bahudaṇḍikaḥ*. Why "from the remainder" (*śeṣāt*)? [Consider: *priyapathaḥ*, *priyadhuraḥ*. Here, because of the force of the rule prescribing the long vowel in *ūṅutaḥ*, or by means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the suffix *kap* does not apply. Therefore, it is obligatory: *brahmabandhūḥ*. [This does not apply] when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *kap* shall not occur after a *bahuvrīhi* compound when it ends in a name. For example: *viśve devā asya* (all the gods belong to him) becomes *viśvadevaḥ*; likewise, *viśvayaśāḥ* (one who possesses universal fame).
[This also applies] after a word ending in the superlative suffix *īyas*.

In the case of words ending in *īyas*, there is no *kap* suffix; for example, *bahuśreyān*. Although the rule *śeṣāt* would have applied [to add *kap*], it does not because of the inclusion of the forms qualified by gender—namely, *bahuśreyasī* and *bahupreyasī*. Furthermore, although the rule *nady-ṛtaś-ca* would have applied [to add *kap*], it does not.
[The suffix *kan* is added] after *bhrātṛ* when it is used in the sense of "one who is praised."

The suffix *kap* shall not be applied after the word *bhrātṛ* when it signifies praise. For example: *subhrātā lakṣmaṇaḥ* ("Lakṣmaṇa is a good brother" / "one who has a praiseworthy brother"). Why [is it] said "when praised"? [Consider: *caurabhrātṛkaḥ* ("having a thief as a brother") and *pāpabhrātṛkaḥ* ("having a wicked brother as a brother").
[In Vedic usage, however, the suffix *kap* is applied] after words ending in *ṛ*.
The word *chandas* [is used] in the sense of a Vedic hymn;
[the word *tantrī* is used] in the sense of a vein or a string when referring to one's own body.

The suffix *kap* is not applied after the words *nāḍī* and *tantrī*. [The suffix *ka* is applied] to form *bahunāḍiḥ* (having many veins) for the body (*kāya*), and *bahutantrīḥ* (having many strings) for the neck (*grīvā*).
Why [is it said] "in reference to one's own limbs" (*svāṅge*)? [Because] *bahutantrīkā* (having many strings) refers to a lute (*vīṇā*).
Also, [the suffix *ka* is applied] after *niṣpravāṇi*.

It is elided. That from which the *pravāṇī* (the finishing comb) has been removed is *niṣpravāṇi*: a new cloth from which the pins have been taken out. The section on suffixes (*pratyaya*) is complete. [Now begins: "A single-vowel root becomes double for the first [suffix]."

The rule "the first monosyllabic [element] becomes doubled" is governed until the section on *samprasāraṇa*. He will state [later]: "in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], [doubling occurs] for the root. Examples: *papāca*, *jajāgāra*.
[The rule] "of the second [syllable] of that which does not begin with *a*" [is now introduced].

The governing rule "the second monosyllabic vowel (*ekāc*) of a root beginning with a non-j letter (*ajādi*) becomes doubled" is now in force. As he will state [later]: "in the case of *san* and *yaṅ*" (*sanyaṅoḥ*). Examples: *aṭiṭiṣati*, *pratīṣiṣati*. [Exception: "Consonants other than *n* and *r* that are the first members of a cluster (*saṃyoga*) are not doubled. (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*)

In the case of roots beginning with *aja* and others, the *na*, *da*, and *ra* that constitute the initial conjunct are not reduplicated. Examples: *undidiṣati*, *aḍiḍaḍiṣati*, *arciciṣati*. This prohibition applies to the letter *va* as well: *ubjijiṣati*.
There is no prohibition for the *ya* and *ra* [of the root *ar*]: *arāryyate*; here, there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "after *arti*, when *yaṅ* follows."
Regarding the third [root] *irṣyati*: there are two forms of the third [root] *irṣyati*.
According to some, for a third [root] that has a single vowel (*ekāc*), [the suffix -san is added]—thus *irṣiṣiṣati*.
According to others, [it is added] after a consonant (*vyañjana*)—thus *irṣyiyiṣati*.

The Cāndra Sūtra states: "When there is a desire for repetition, whether it be once or twice," and also regarding the *kaṇḍvādi* group: "The third monosyllabic element (*ekāc*) becomes doubled. Examples: *kaṇḍūyiyiṣati*, *asūyiyiṣati*.
Regarding denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*), it is optional: "The third monosyllabic element may be doubled. Examples: *aśvīyiyiṣati* or *aśiśvīyiṣati*.

Others [hold that] for verbal roots ending in a name (nāman), it may be as desired: *puputrīyiṣati*, *putitrīyiṣati*, or *putrīyiyiṣati*. However, *puputitrīyiyiṣati* is not based on the sacred tradition (*anārṣa*). The preceding portion is the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Of that which is reduplicated, the first part shall be designated as "abhyāsa" (the reduplicated syllable). *ditsati*, *dhitsati*, *jñīpsati*, *irrtsati*, *dhipsati*, *dhipsuḥ*. Here, the operation on the reduplicated syllable is according to the rule "lopo'bhyāsasya" (elision of the reduplicated syllable).
Both [halves] together are called "abhyasta" (the reduplicated stem).

Both [verbs] that are repeated (dvirukta) shall have the designation "abhyasta" (repeated). [The rule] *adabhyastāt*—as in *dadati* and *bibhyati*. [The rule] *nābhyastāc chatuḥ* prohibits the augment *num*—as in *dadat* and *bibhyat*. Why "both"? [Consider] *īpsati* and *aipsat*.
The six beginning with *jakṣ* are also designated as *abhyasta*.

The root *jakṣ* (to eat), as well as six others beginning with it, shall be designated as "abhyasta" (reduplicated). These are: *jakṣati*, *jāgrati*, *daridrati*, *cakāsati*, *śāsati*; and *dīdhī* and *vevī*, which are Vedic. Regarding these seven—*jakṣ*, *jāgṛ*, *daridrā*, *cakās*, *śās*, *dīdhī*, and *vevī*—the designation "abhyasta" applies starting from *jakṣi*. [Commentary: The term *upagraha* here refers to the technical name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, for the seven roots beginning with *jakṣi*, the status of being "abhyasta" is established. The mention of *śās* is necessary because, although it is included among the roots ending in *ā*, it is specifically listed here to ensure its inclusion even when it appears in forms other than those ending in *ā*. The roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* are mentioned because they are not included in the list of roots ending in *ī*. The word *ca* ("and") is used to include the two roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* along with the others. The particle *eva* ("only") is used to restrict the application of the designation to these specific roots. The word *saptānām* ("of the seven") is used to indicate that the designation applies collectively to all seven. The word *jakṣityādau* ("starting from *jakṣi*") indicates that the sequence begins with *jakṣi*. The word *upagrahaḥ* ("designation") confirms that this is indeed a technical term. Thus, the meaning is that the designation "abhyasta" applies to these seven roots beginning with *jakṣi*. This is stated so that the rules governing abhyasta roots, such as the substitution of *śnu* for *śap* in the present tense, may apply to them. For example, in the case of *daridrā*, the rule *daridrāteḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.59] applies, whereas for *śās*, the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.34] applies. The mention of *dīdhī* and *vevī* is for the sake of their inclusion, as they are not part of the group of roots ending in *ī*. The particle *ca* serves to bring together the two roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*. The word *saptānām* is used to show that the designation applies to all seven simultaneously. The phrase *jakṣityādau* indicates that the enumeration starts with *jakṣi*. The word *upagrahaḥ* signifies that this is a formal technical designation. Therefore, the sense is that the seven roots beginning with *jakṣi* receive the name "abhyasta. This is stated so that the grammatical operations prescribed for abhyasta roots, such as the addition of the suffix *śnu* in the present tense, may take effect upon them. For instance, in the case of *daridrā*, the rule *daridrāteḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.59] is applicable; for *śās*, the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.34] is applicable; and *dīdhī* and *vevī* are mentioned to ensure their inclusion, as they do not belong to the class of roots ending in *ī*. The particle *ca* brings together the two roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*. The word *saptānām* indicates that the designation applies to all seven at once. The expression *jakṣityādau* shows that the list begins with *jakṣi*. The term *upagrahaḥ* confirms that this is a formal technical name. Consequently, the meaning is that the seven roots beginning with *jakṣi* are designated as "abhyasta. This is stated so that the grammatical operations prescribed for abhyasta roots, such as the insertion of *śnu* in the present tense, may be applied to them. [The rule] "liṭi dhātoranabhyāsasya" [applies].

Why "preceded by *pra*" (*prapūrvasya*)? [So that it does not apply here: *saṃstyānaḥ*, *saṃstyānavān*. Why the mention of "preceding" (*pūrvagrahaṇam*)? So that it may also apply in this case: *prasaṃstītaḥ*, *prasaṃstītavān*.

And also in the causative (*ṇic*), as well as in the *saṃc* (the *san* and *ciṇ* affixes).

And [vocalization occurs] for a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) as well.

In what sense does "not pertaining to the other world" (*apāralaukika*) apply? As in *tapas tāpasam sedhayati*, which means "he causes the ascetic to attain a specific knowledge. According to tradition (*smṛti*), the mention of "pertaining to the other world" is intended to indicate "specific knowledge.
[The rule continues: The substitution of *ā* also occurs for the roots *mīnāti*, *minoti*, and *dīṅ* before the affix *lyap* and [before *ṇic*].

In the case of the roots *mīñ*, *ḍumiñ*, and *dīṅ*, there shall be substitution of *ā* (āttva) for the final vowel when followed by the suffix *lyap*, and also in the scope of the suffix *eñ*. Examples: *pramāya*, *pramātavyam*; *nimāya*, *nimātavyam*; *upadāya*, *upadātavyam*. With the suffix *ghañ*: *upadāyaḥ* exists. With the suffix *yuc*: *īṣadupādānam*.

There is a prohibition [of the substitution of *i* for *ya*] after the roots *mīl* and *mīl* when followed by the suffixes *khal* and *ac*. Examples: *irṣallayaḥ*, *vilayaḥ*; *irṣannimayaḥ*, *nimayaḥ*, *nilayaḥ*.
[The substitution of *i* for *ya* occurs] after the root *khid* in the Veda.

[The substitution of] *ṇamul* occurs after the root *apagur*.

When the suffix *ṇamul* follows, the long vowel *ā* may optionally replace the diphthongs *e* and *o* of this [root *as*]. Examples: *asyapagāram* or *asyapagoram* yudhyante (they fight, having thrown aside their armor). The suffix *ṇamul* is applied here by the rule *dvitīyāyāṃ ca*. Examples: *pallavagāram* or *pallavagoram* nṛtyanti (they dance, having taken up sprouts). The suffix *ṇi* is applied to the roots *ci* and *sphur*.

In these two cases (*ṇau*), there is optionally the substitution of *ā* for the vowel. In the case of *ciñ* (to gather), when the *ā*-substitution applies, the augment *puk* is added: *sañcāpayati*. [Similarly from *sphāy*: ] *sphārayati*. In the alternative case, the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions apply: *cāyayati*; *sphorayati*. [The substitution of *ā* occurs] for the root *vī* in the sense of procreation (*prajane*).

The substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the root *vī* (meaning "procreation") occurs optionally after the causative suffix *ṇic*. For example: *purovāto gāḥ pravāpayati* ("the east wind causes the cows to conceive"). In the alternative case—*pravāyayati*—the meaning is "he causes them to take their first pregnancy.
They say that the mention of the letter *y* in the rule is intended to include the root *aj* as well, as in *ajervī*.
[The next rule is: *bibheterhetubhaye* ("the substitution of *ā* occurs for the root *bhī* when fear is caused by a specific agent").

When fear arises from an instigator (*prayojaka*), the substitution of *ā* for the root *bhī* may optionally occur before the causative suffix *ṇic*, provided that the root *īkṣ* does not intervene. Examples: *muṇḍo bhāpayate* (the bald man causes fear) or *muṇḍo bhīṣayate*.
Why "when there is fear from an instigator"? Consider: *ahinā bhāyayati* (he causes fear by means of a snake); here, the fear arises from the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The substitution of *ā* for *smi* occurs invariably [before *ṇic*].

In the *ṇic* suffix, the root *smi* always undergoes the substitution of *ā*. Example: *jaṭilo vismāpayate* ("The matted-hair ascetic causes amazement"). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *bhīsmyorhetubhaye*. This applies only when there is fear caused by a specific cause; it should not apply to amazement caused by an instrument—as in *rūpeṇa vismāyayati trilokīm* ("He causes the three worlds to marvel at his form").
[Furthermore, the rule] *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* [applies].

The augment *am* is added after the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś* before an affix beginning with a *jhāl* consonant that is not marked with *k* (akit). This is an exception to *guṇa*. Examples: *sraṣṭā*, *draṣṭā*; *asrākṣīt*, *adrākṣīt*. When *am* has been applied, *vṛddhi* occurs. Why "not marked with *k*" (*akiti*)? [Because in these cases *am* does not apply]: *sṛṣṭaḥ*, *dṛṣṭaḥ*, *dṛṣṭiḥ*. [In the desiderative forms] *sisṛkṣati* and *didṛkṣate*, [the *am* is applied]. Why "before a *jhāl* consonant" (*jhali*)? [Because in these cases the following consonant is not *jhāl*]: *sasṛjitha*, *dadṛśitha*.
[The rule] *anudāttasya cardupadhasyānyatarasyām* [is also relevant here].

The augment *am* may optionally be added after a root that has an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) as its penultimate letter and ends in *ṛ*, provided it is followed by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant and is not marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Examples: *traptā*, *tṛptā*, or *tarpitā*; *rdaptā*, *draptā*, or *darpitā*. Why "unaccented" (*anudātta*)? Consider the root *vṛhū*, which is taught as having an accented (*udātta*) initial vowel: *varḍhā*, *varḍhum*. In the Veda, the word *śīrṣan* [is used].
And [the rules] concerning those [suffixes] ending in *taddhita* [apply].

At the beginning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), by virtue of semantic proximity, *śīrṣan* shall be substituted in place of *śiras*. [Example: that which is on the head (*śirasi bhavaḥ*) is *śīrṣaṇyaḥ* sound.
Optionally, when referring to hair (*keśeṣu*): hair is either *śīrṣaṇyāḥ* or *śirasyāḥ*.
Before a vowel suffix (*aci*), it becomes *śīrṣaḥ*.

In a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel (other than *a*), the word *śiras* shall become *śīrṣa*. The mention of *an* [in the rule] is so that the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) does not apply. Examples: *hāstiśīrṣaḥ putraḥ* (a son with an elephant's head); *sthaulaśīrṣaṃ vapuḥ* (a body with a large head); *mārgaśīrṣī tithiḥ* (the lunar day joined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras). [This applies] in the case of *paddan*, *nomās*, *hṛn*, *niśas*, *nyūṣan*, *doṣan*, *yakan*, *śakan*, *udan*, and *āñchan*, etc.

In place of *pāda*, *danta*, *nāsikā*, *mās*, *hṛdaya*, *niśā*, *srak*, *yūṣa*, *doṣ*, *yakṛt*, *śakṛt*, *udaka*, and *āsana*, the substitutes *pad* and so forth shall apply respectively. In this regard, the traditional authority (*āgama*) states that the word *chandasī* ("in Vedic usage") is understood to carry over into the rule *paddannomās* (Pāṇini 6.1.63). Furthermore, the usage of *pad*, *dat*, and so on is observed in the sense of *pāda*, *danta*, and the rest—for example: *padbhyām udvartitasya* ("rubbed with the feet"), *dato dhāvati sudatī* ("the fair-toothed woman cleanses her teeth"), *hṛdi vinihitarūpaḥ* ("whose form is placed within the heart"), *apraśastaṃ niśi snānam* ("bathing at night is not recommended"), *pīte yūṣṇi nirāmayaḥ* ("free from disease when the soup has been drunk"), and *yad doṣṇāṃ bhāti viṃśatiḥ* ("that which shines as twenty arms"), and so forth.
Regarding this, some say these are words of the Vedic apocrypha (apaya); others say they are different words altogether; others say that the rule "in the Veda" (chandasī) does not apply here;
and still others say that even Vedic forms are occasionally employed in the common language (bhāṣā).

In the case of the word *nāsikā*, when it occurs before the words *kṣudra* and *avarṇanagara*, the substitute *nas* shall take the place of *nāsikā*. Thus: *nasyam*, *nasyā*, *nastaḥ patitaḥ*, *naḥ kṣudraḥ*. It is not so here: *nāsikyo varṇaḥ* (a nasal sound), *nāsikyaṃ nagaram* (a city of the nose).
[Also,] the *ṣ* at the beginning of a verbal root is replaced by *s*.

"Upadeśa" (original enunciation) means this: the initial *ṣ* of a verbal root (*dhātu*) should be dental (*dantya*). Thus, one says *ṣaha* (to endure) as *sahate*, and *ṣica* (to sprinkle) as *siñcati*. Roots are taught with an initial *ṣ* for the purpose of establishing the rule of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) according to the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ. As stated in the Bhāṣya: "Roots beginning with *sa* followed by *ja*, *da*, *ta*, or *pa* are taught with an initial *ṣ*; so too are *smiṅ*, *śvi*, *adi*, and *śvas*, with the exception of *sṛpi*, *mṛj*, *stṛ*, *styai*, *seka*, *sṛ*, and *sṛ*. There is an exception for the roots *subdhātu*, *ṣṭhīvu*, and *ṣvaṣkati*: *ṣoḍīyati*, *ṣṭhīvyati*, *ṣvaṣkate*. [The rule] "ṇo naḥ" [follows].

The initial *ṇ* of a root and so forth shall become *n*. Roots are listed with an initial *ṇ* for the purpose of establishing the rule of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*). As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "All roots beginning with *n* are taught with an initial *ṇ*, with the exception of *nṛt* (to dance), *nand* (to rejoice), *nard* (to roar), *nak* (to reach), *nāṭ* (to dance), *nāthṛ* (to seek protection), and *nādhṛ* (to trouble). Examples: *nayati* (he leads), *namati* (he bows), *praṇayati* (he leads forward), *praṇamati* (he bows down), *pariṇayati* (he marries). This prohibition applies to roots that begin with a *sub-dhātu* (a consonant cluster). Example: *ṇakārīyati* (he acts like one who possesses the letter *ṇ*). [Note: *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) applies here.]

There shall be elision (*lopa*) of *v* and *y*. In that context, the elision of *v* occurs only in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Examples: from *div*, *didivān* and *didivāṃsau*; from *jīv* with the suffix *adānuk*, *jīradānuḥ*. However, there is a prohibition in the case of *vraśc*, *kvañc*, *vrīhi*, *vraṇa*, and so forth. Regarding the elision of *y*: from *knūyī*, *knūtaḥ* and *knūtavān*; *godheraḥ*; *paceyuḥ*. Here, after the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*), the elision of *v* is desired: *kaṇḍūḥ*, *lolūḥ*. Why "after *v*" (*vali*)? [Consider: *bhaveyuḥ*. [The rule] *verapṛktasya* [follows].
There shall be elision (*lopa*) of a *vel* suffix that is designated as *apṛkta*. Examples: with *kvip*—*ghṛtaspṛk*; with *kvip*—*grāmaṇīḥ*; with *ṇviḥ*—*pādabhāk*.
Why "of an *apṛkta*" (*apṛktasya*)? [Consider] *jāgṛviḥ*. [And:
after a word ending in a consonant (*hal*), a long vowel (*dīrgha*), or a feminine suffix (*āp*), the *apṛkta* suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si* are elided if they are consonants (*hal*).

There shall be elision (*lopa*) of the *su*, *tip*, and *sip* suffixes when they are not followed by a vowel (*apṛkta*) and are attached to a consonant (*hal*). The elision of *su* after a word ending in a consonant: *rājā* (king), *takṣā* (carpenter). After words ending in long vowels—namely those in *ṅī* and *āp*: *kumārī* (young girl), *bahupreyasī* (one who has many beloveds), *nṛpaḥ* (king), *khaṭvā* (bedstead). Why "after long vowels"? [To exclude cases like] *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī) and *atikhaṭvaḥ* (one who has surpassed a bedstead). Why "after consonants, *ṅī*, and *āp"? [To exclude cases like] *grāmaṇīḥ* (leader of a village). The elision of *tip* and *sip* occurs only after words ending in consonants. In the *laṅ* tense, after the roots *bhṛ* (to carry) and *jāgṛ* (to wake): *abibharbhavān* (you carried), *ajāgarbhavān* (you woke). Another man there woke up later. *abhinastvam* (you pierced), *acchinastvam* (you cut).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "when not followed by another suffix" (*apṛktasya*)? [Consider: *jāgarti*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "consonant" (*hal*)? [Consider: *bibheda*. [The rule continues: "After *eṅ* (e, o) and a short vowel, when the vocative case ending follows."

After a short vowel (eṅ) and a short vowel (hrasva), there shall be elision (lopa) of the *hal* [the consonant] following the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*). Examples: *he agne*, *he vāyo*, *he paṭo*. Regarding the rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*): *he nātha*, *he vṛkṣa*, *he nadi*. In the case of *he vana*, once the substitution of *ām* for the vocative suffix has been applied (*ami pūrvatve*), there is elision of the *m* alone.
[The rule] *śeśchandasi bahulam* [states that in Vedic usage, the remainder is frequently retained].
This is Vedic.
[In the Veda], the augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a suffix beginning with *p* when it is a *kṛt* suffix.

The augment *tuK* is added after a verbal root ending in a short vowel before a *kṛt* suffix containing *p*. Examples: *agnicit*, *prakṛtya*, *saṅgatya*. Why "short vowel"? Consider *grāmaṇīḥ* and *āhūya*. It does not apply here: *grāmaṇi-kulam*, because the short vowel [in *grāmaṇi-ka-*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to being external (*bahiraṅga*). Why "containing *p*" (*pit*)? Consider *citam* and *stutam*. Why "*kṛt* suffix"? Consider *paṭutaraḥ*. [This rule applies] in *saṃhitā*.
This governing rule (adhikāra) extends up to the sūtra *anudāttaṃ padam* (VI.1.158). [Now follows: *che ca*.
It might appear that the augment *tuK* should occur after a short vowel: as in *icchati*, *gacchati*, *ciccheda*, *cicchidatuḥ*, and *dadhi-chatram*.

[The rule applies] only when there is *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination)—as in *dadhi chatram* [without *saṃhitā*]. *Saṃhitā* is obligatory within a single word and obligatory between a verbal root and a prefix.
"Even in the Sūtras, that [rule] is likewise eternal; elsewhere it is by way of the Vibhāṣā"—such is the traditional teaching (smṛti).
And [the same applies] after the prefixes *āṅ* and *māṅ*.

The augment *tuk* shall be inserted after the vowels *ā* and *mā* when followed by the letter *ch*. This supersedes the rule "optionally [inserted] after a word-final [vowel]. Examples: *ācchādayati*; *mā cchaitsīt*.
[This applies] after a long vowel.
The suffix *tuk* shall be applied after a long vowel. Examples: *hrīcchati*, *mlecchati*. After the root *cho*, it becomes *cācchāyate*; after *chupa*, it becomes *cocchupyate*.
Optionally, this applies when the [long vowel] is at the end of a word (*padānta*).

After a long vowel at the end of a word, a *tuk* augment may optionally be inserted before *cha*. Thus: *nadīcchayā* or *nadīchāyā*; *vadhūcchāyā* or *vadhūchāyā*. [Furthermore: *yaṇ* replaces an *ik* vowel when followed by a vowel (*aci*).

In place of an *ik* vowel, when followed by an *ac* vowel, a *yaṇ* substitute shall occur. For example: *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*, *kartṛ atra*. This applies only in *saṃhitā* (continuous utterance); otherwise: *dadhi atra*, *madhu atra*, *kartṛ atra*.

It should be stated that for Vyāḍi and Gālava, there may be intervention by a semi-vowel (*yan*) between the *ik* vowels and the following vowel: *dadhiy atra*. [The list of roots] beginning with *bhū* and so on;
the term *aci* (after a vowel) continues in force until the rule *samprasāraṇācca*.
The sounds e, o, ay, āv, and āv [are called guṇa].

In place of *eta*, *ot*, *aita*, and *aut* when followed by a vowel (*ac*), the substitutes *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* respectively shall occur. Examples: *cayanam*, *lavanam*; *cāyakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*; *kāyati*; *gavityāha*; *asmāyācaṣṭe*; *asāvatra*. [Also]: *vānto yi pratyaye* (when followed by a suffix beginning with *y*, the final *au* and *av* are substituted by *āv*).

When a suffix beginning with *e* or *o* follows, the substitution of *vānta* (the sounds *au*, *ai*, and *o*) shall take place. Examples: *gavyam*, *śaṅkavyam*, *nāvyam*. [The suffix *kyac* is applied: one who desires a cow (*gām icchati*) is *gavyati*. Why "ending in *vānta*"? To prevent it from applying to that which ends in *yānta*: one who desires wealth (*rāyam icchati*) is *raiyati*. Why "when a suffix follows"? [To exclude cases where no suffix follows: *goyānam*.
As for the word *gavyūti*, however, it is simply an unanalyzed (irregular) formation, like *krośa* and *yojana*.
Of the root, which has that very [suffix] as its cause.

In the presence of an affix beginning with *y*, there shall be the substitution of *vānta* (the sounds *o* and *au*) for the vowel of a verbal root that is the cause of that very affix. Examples: *lavyam*, *pavyam*, *avaśyalāvyam*.
Why "caused by that"? [Consider] *laūyamāniḥ* as a son.
[The forms] *kṣayya* and *jayya* are used in the sense of "possible."

These two [suffixes] are prescribed as substitutes when the sense is "capable of. That which is capable of being destroyed is *kṣayya*; that which is capable of being conquered is *jayya*. In cases other than "capable of," [the forms are] *kṣeya* and *jeya*.
[The suffix -yañ is used] in the sense of "to be bought" (*krayya*).
When an object is displayed for the purpose of sale, the suffix *kraya* is applied; otherwise, the form is *kreya*.
Furthermore, the forms *bhayya* and *pravayya* occur in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
This is Vedic usage.
[The rule] "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" [applies].
It should be stated that there is a single substitution for the preceding and following sounds. This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending up to the sūtra *parasya* (P.
6.1.83). He will state: "There is *guṇa* substitution for [the final vowel] *ā* and the following vowel"—that is, a single substitution occurs for the two: *khaṭvendraḥ*. And:
"The substitute is treated like the end of the preceding and the beginning of the following."

A single substitute (ekādeśa) should be understood as being like the final letter with respect to what precedes it, and like the initial letter with respect to what follows it. For example: *dhībandhūḥ* and *dhībandhūbhyām*. When it is treated as the final letter of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavattva*), the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) apply, as in *vṛkṣau* and *paṭau*. When it is treated as the initial letter of the following element (*parādivattva*), the status of being a word (*padatva*) applies by virtue of the suffix *su*, as in *varṇāśraye nāntādivat* (in matters depending on individual phonemes, the substitute is not like the final or initial). Thus, in *khaṭvābhiḥ*, the ending *ais* does not occur. Furthermore, regarding the rules for *ṣatva* and *tuka*, [the preceding rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

When the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) or the insertion of *t* (tuṅ) is to be applied, that single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*). For example: *ko'sicat*, *yo'sicat*; *ko'sya*, *yo'sya*. Because the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* is treated as non-existent, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *iṇaḥ* does not occur. In *adhītya* and *pretya*, the *t* (tuṅ) is applied according to the rule for a short vowel.

A prohibition must be stated regarding *samprasāraṇa*, the *ṅī* suffix, and the *iṭ* augment, so that the change to *ṣ* and the optional *tuk* augment may occur. For example: *śakaṃ hvayati* (he calls the Śakas); *śakahūṣu*—here there is *samprasāraṇa* when the *kvip* suffix is applied. *vṛkṣecchatram*, *vṛkṣechatram*. With the *iṭ* augment: *apacecchatram*, *apace chatram*;
[in the latter case] there is *guṇa* substitution for the initial vowel (*ād guṇaḥ*).

When a vowel follows a non-final *a*, there shall be a single substitute for the two [sounds], namely the *guṇa* [vowel]. Examples: *tavedam* (your this), *dhanendraḥ* (wealth-Indra), *dhaneśaḥ* (wealth-lord), *khaṭveyam* (this bed), *khaṭvendraḥ* (bed-Indra), *khaṭveśaḥ* (bed-lord), *khātodakam* (water from a well), *gaṅgodakam* (Ganges-water), *tavarṣiḥ* (your sage), *tavaiśyaḥ* (your Vaiśya), *khaṭvaiśyaḥ* (bed-Vaiśya), *maharṣiḥ* (great sage), *tavalkāraḥ* (your maker), *khaṭvallakāraḥ* (bed-maker).
[Next rule: *vṛddhir eci* (there is *vṛddhi* when *eC* follows).

When a vowel other than *a* (i.e., any vowel except *a*) precedes and an *e*-vowel (*ec*) follows, *vṛddhi* (the corresponding *guṇa* vowel) shall occur. Examples: *tavaiḍakā*, *khaṭvaiḍakā*, *tava-aitikāyanaḥ*, *gaṅgaughaḥ*, *mama-upagavaḥ*.
[This rule applies] before the suffixes *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*.

When a vowel other than *a* precedes, and *e* or *ai* (the substitutes for *i* and *ī*) followed by a vowel occurs before *ṛ*, *ḍh*, *dy*, *ṭh*, or *i*, there shall be *vṛddhi*. Examples: *upaiti*, *uṣaiṣi*, *praiti*, *praidhate*, *paraidhate*, *dhautam*, *dhautavān*, *praṣṭhauhaḥ*.
The rule applies only when a vowel follows (*ecīti*): *upetaḥ*, *upethaḥ*, *avehi*, *apehi*.

In the presence of *pra* and the words beginning with *ūḍha*, *ūḍhi*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*, there shall be *vṛddhi*. Thus: *prauḍhaḥ*, *prauḍhiḥ*, *praiṣaḥ*. [The suffix] *ghañ* occurs after the root *iṣ* (to send).

In the presence of *sva* and the words *īra* and *erina*, there shall be *vṛddhi*. Thus: *svairam*, *svairī*; *svairiṇī* means an unchaste woman (*bandhakī*). In the case of *ṛta*, when it follows a word in the instrumental case in an uncompounded form, there shall be *vṛddhi*. Thus: *sukhārtaḥ*, *duḥkhārtaḥ*, *kṣudhārtaḥ*, *kāmārtaḥ*.

In the case of *ṛṇa* (debt) following *prava*, *vatsatara*, *kambala*, *vasana*, *daśārṇa*, and *ṛṇa*, the suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied. Examples: *prārṇam*, *vatsatarārṇam*, *kambalārṇam*, *vasanārṇam*, *daśārṇam*, *ṛṇārṇam*.

However, the word *akṣauhiṇī* is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for a specific measure; the etymological derivation *akṣād ūhinyām* is merely formal and lacks actual semantic connection. [The rule] *āṭaś ca* [also applies].
Before a vowel (aci), there is vṛddhi substitution for the augment āṭ. Examples: *aikṣata*, *aikṣiṣṭa*, *aumbhīt*, *praurṇāvīt*, *prārdhnot*.
[This rule applies] when a root beginning with ṛ follows a prefix (*upasarga*).
Vṛddhi shall occur for a root beginning with the vowel ṛ when preceded by a prefix ending in a non-vowel (a consonant). Examples: *prārcchati*, *upārcchati*, *ārttaḥ*.
According to Āpiśali, this substitution may optionally occur when the prefix ends in a vowel (*suP*).
When a root beginning with *ṛ* follows a prefix, a vṛddhi vowel may optionally be substituted. Thus: *upārṣabhīyati*, *uparṣabhīyati*.
Because *ṛ* and *lṛ* are identical (*sārvaṇya*), we also have: *upālkārayati*, *upalkārīyati*.
The mention of Āpiśali is for the sake of honor.
The substitution of *ot* occurs in place of the case endings *am* and *śas*.

The *o* sound [at the end of a word] becomes *ā* when followed by the case endings *am* or *śas*. Examples: *gāṃ paśya* (look at the cow), *gāḥ paśya* (look at the cows); *dyāṃ paśya* (look at the sky), *dyāḥ paśya* (look at the skies).
Only when followed by a *sup* suffix [is this rule applied]—as in *acinavam* (I gathered) and *akaravam* (I did).
Why "of the *o* sound"? [Consider: *glāvam* (the tired one).
When *eṅ* follows, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is substituted.

When a verbal root beginning with *e*, *ai*, or *o* follows a prefix ending in *a* or *ā*, the single substitute shall be the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). This serves as an exception to the rule for *vṛddhi*. Examples: *prelayati*, *prokhayati*. Some maintain that the phrase "optionally before a nominal stem (*sup*)" from a previous rule should also apply here, for the sake of optionality regarding nominal roots (*subdhātu*): *upaiḍakīyati*, *upeḍakīyati*. In the group of words beginning with *śakandhu*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) should be stated [as an exception]. Examples: *śakandhuḥ*, *karkandhuḥ*, *kulaṭā*, *sīmantaḥ* (in the sense of hair). *Sīmāntaḥ* is used in another sense. *Gandharvaḥ*, *ardhaśanam*, *samaśanam*, *halīṣā*, *lāṅgalīṣā*. There is also elision (*lopa*) of the vowel in *manas*: *manīṣā*. *Kena ubhyate kumbhaḥ* (by whom is the jar carried?), *śuddhodanaḥ*.

In a compound, the substitution [of *u* for *o*] is optional before the words *oṣṭha*. Examples: *sūkṣmautoḥ*, *sūkṣmauṣṭhaḥ*; *bimboṣṭhī*, *bimbauṣṭhī*. Why "in a compound"? Consider: *paśyauṣṭham*. Also, when *eva* is used except in the sense of restriction (*aniyoga*), the substitution is optional: *ihaiva*, *iheva*; *adyeva*. But in the sense of restriction (*niyoga*), it is not optional: *ihaiva bhava mā gāḥ* ("Stay right here, do not go");
*adyaiva nādhiśayito rudhirārdraśayyām* ("He did not lie down today upon a bed wet with blood").
And [the substitution of *guṇa* occurs] for the vowels *o* and *āṅ*.

When a vowel other than *a* (avarṇa) ends a word and is followed by *om* or *āṅ*, the single substitute shall be the form of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*). Examples: *kā om iti* becomes *komiti*; *sā om iti avocat* becomes *somityavocat*. Regarding *āṅ*: *ā ṛśyate* becomes *arśyate*; *upa ṛśyate* becomes *urpaśyate*. Here, however, this rule supersedes the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel for homogeneous vowels). When *us* follows a short vowel (*avarṇa*) that does not stand at the end of a word (*apadānta*), a single substitute in the form of the subsequent sound (*pararūpa*) shall take the place of both the preceding and the following sounds. This is an exception to the rule for *guṇa* substitution (*ādguṇa*). Examples: *bhindyāt* + *us* = *bhindyuḥ*; *chindyuḥ*; *aduḥ*; *adhuḥ*. Why "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntāt*)? Consider: *kā usrā* = *kosrā*; *koṣitā*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "There is a prohibition [of this rule] when *us*, *om*, or *āṅ* follow. Examples: *usrām aicchat* = *ausrīyat*; *aum* = *auṅkārīyat*; *āṅi* = *auḍhīyat*.
Therefore, [the suffix] is applied to a quality.
When a vowel follows a non-final *a*, there shall be the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) before a *guṇa* vowel. Examples: *pacanti*, *pace*, *yaje*.
Why "after *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider: *yānti*, *yātaḥ paśya*. Why "before a *guṇa*" (*guṇe*)? Consider: *apace*. It must be "non-final" (*apadāntāt*); otherwise, consider: *daṇḍāgram*.
In the case of an imitation of an indistinct sound, the suffix *it* is applied after the syllable *at*.

When the word *iti* follows, the single-substitute (pararūpa) form shall apply to an indistinct imitation (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) that does not end in a consonant. For example: *paṭat* becomes *paṭiti*; *damat* becomes *damiti*.
Why "indistinct imitation"? Witness *jagaditi*. Why "not ending in a consonant"? Witness *maruditi*. Why "when followed by *iti*"? Witness *paṭad atra*.
There is no such form as *śrat*, because it is not so prescribed.
How is it that "ghaṭat" is an imitation of the deep roar of clouds? It is an imitation of a sound. However, for the final syllable of a reduplicated word, [the substitution] is optional.

The preceding rule shall not apply to an *āmreḍita* (repeated word). For an *avyaktānukaraṇa* (imitation of an indistinct sound), the single-substitute *pararūpa* (the form of the subsequent vowel) shall not occur for the vowel *a* that constitutes the *āmreḍita*; however, it may optionally occur for the final *t*. Examples: *paṭat-paṭad iti karoti* or *paṭat-paṭeti karoti*. The reduplication is by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*.
[Furthermore,] when *ḍāc* follows an *āmreḍita*, [the substitution of *ḍāc* for *iti* is obligatory].

When the suffix *ḍāc* follows an unmanifested (*avyakta*), soundless (*aśabda*), and final (*antya*) vowel, there shall always be a single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*) when it is reduplicated (*āmreḍita*). For example: *paṭapaṭākāraḥ*, *paṭapaṭākṛtya*, *damadamākṛtya*. The reduplication occurs by the rule "optionally in *ḍāc*" (*ḍāci bahulam*), followed by the elision of the feminine suffix *ṭi*. Then, by the rule "a long vowel replaces [two] homogeneous vowels" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), a long vowel is substituted for a vowel of the *ak* class (*ak*) before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa-ac*). When a homogeneous vowel (*aci*) follows, a long vowel is the single substitute for both the preceding and following vowels. Examples: *daṇḍāgram*, *śailāgram*, *vanāgram*, *tavāsyam*, *latāgram*, *yoṣāsyam*.

*Mahīndraḥ*, *nadīhate*, *madhūṣṇam*, *madhūpamam*, *vadhūḍhā*, *hotṝśyaḥ*. Why "before a homogeneous vowel" (*savarṇe*)? [As in] *dadhyatra*. Only when "before a vowel" (*aci*) is it so—[as in] *kumārī śete*. *Ṛti rṛrvā*: When a homogeneous *ṛ*-vowel follows, the substitute *ṛ*—which consists of two *ṛ*-mātrās and is joined with two *r*s—may optionally occur. *pitṛ ṛṇam* → *pirtṛṇam*. In the other case, there is only a single long *ṛ* (with one *r*): *pitṝṇam*. *Lṛti llṛrvā*: When a homogeneous *lṛ*-vowel follows, the substitute *llṛ*—which is joined with two *l*-parts—may optionally occur. *hotṛlṛkāraḥ* → *hotllṛkāraḥ*. In the other case, since there is no long *lṛ*, [the substitution is as before for] *ṛ* and *lṛ*.
Because it is universal, the single letter *repha* alone becomes a long *ṛ*-vowel—namely, *hotṝkāraḥ*.
[In the case of] the first two [vowels], there is the *pūrvasavarṇa* (the homogeneous preceding vowel).
When an *ac* vowel follows the first or second case endings, there shall be a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one. Examples: *vṛkṣāḥ*, *vṛkṣān*; *agnī*, *vāyū*; *agnīn*, *vāyūn*; *buddhīḥ*.
Only when an *ac* follows—e.g., *vṛkṣaḥ*. Only when an *ak* follows—e.g., *nāvau*.
Therefore, [the substitution of] *na* occurs for *śas* in the masculine.

The substitute *na* shall take the place of the final vowel of a stem ending in *ā*, when followed by the case-ending *śas* (accusative plural), provided that the *ā* is not separated from the preceding consonant by more than one intervening letter. Examples: *vṛkṣān*, *ghaṭān*, *māṇavakān*, *parvatān*, *plakṣān*, *agnīn*, *girīn*, *paṭān*, *pitṝn*, *kartṝn*.

Why is it said "from that [stem]" (*tasmāt*)? Consider: *gāḥ paśya* ("look at the cows"). Why is it said "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*)? Consider: *cañcāḥ*, *vadhrikāḥ paśya*, *buddhīḥ*, *dhenūḥ*, *mātṝḥ*.
Not in the case of *nādi*.

The substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (pūrvasavarṇadīrgha) should not be applied to the first two case endings (*au* and *śas*) when they follow a vowel other than *a*, or when they follow the letter *j*. [Examples: *vṛkṣau*, *khaṭve*, *kuṇḍe*.
Why "after a vowel" (*āt*)? [Counter-example: *agnī*. Why "before *au* and *śas*" (*ici*)? [Counter-example: *vṛkṣāḥ*.
[Also, the substitution does not occur] after a long vowel before the ending *jas*.
In the case of *dīrghā* and so forth, when followed by *jas*, there would not be a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). [Examples: *padyau*, *dhībandhvau*.
With *jas*: *nadyaḥ*, *dhībandhvaḥ*. In the case of "the beds stand" (*khaṭvāstiṣṭhanti*), there is a long vowel homogeneous with a vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*).
[This rule applies] optionally in the Veda (*vā chandasi*).
This is Vedic.
[In the case of] *ami*, the preceding [vowel] is [lengthened].

If the single substitute [for the vowel and semivowel] were to take the form of the preceding [element], then one would see: *vṛkṣam*, *khaṭvām*, *agnim*, *nadīm*, *vayum*, *vadhūm paśya*. [This is prevented by the rule:
"And [the substitution of the semivowel] from *samprasāraṇa* [is not so]."

When a vowel follows a *samprasāraṇa* [vowel], there shall be a single substitute for the two [sounds] consisting of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). Examples: *iṣṭam*, *uptam*, *ḍhaukitaḥ*, *āhūtam*, *gṛhītam*.
How is *śakahvartham* [formed]? Because the word refers to a genus (*jāti*), the grammatical operation applies due to its being produced [as such].
[Next: *eṅ* [is substituted] for a final *eṅ* when followed by *ati*.

When followed by *eṅ*, there shall be a single substitute for both [the preceding and following sounds] consisting of the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*). Examples: *agne'tra* (agne + atra), *paṭo'tra* (paṭaḥ + atra), *vāyo'tra* (vāyoḥ + atra).

Why "after a word-final [sound]"? [Counter-example: *nayanam*, *lavanam*. Why "followed by *eṅ*"? [Counter-example: *paṭaviha* (paṭaḥ + iha). Why "followed by a *t*-marker"? [Counter-example: *vāyavāyāhi* (vāyo + āyāhi). And [the same applies] after the case-endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas*.

When *eṅ* (e, o) or *ṅasiṅas* (the fifth and sixth case endings) follow, there shall be a single substitute of the *pūrva-rūpa* (the form of the preceding vowel). *girer āgatam* (come from the mountain); *gireḥ svam* (belonging to the mountain). *guror āgatam* (come from the teacher); *guroḥ svam* (belonging to the teacher).
[In the case of *ṛt*,] *ut* [is the substitute].

When *ṛ*-ending stems are followed by the case endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas*, if the vowel *a* follows, there shall be a single substitute for both the preceding and following sounds, and this substitute shall be *u*. Examples: *hotur āgacchati* (the priest comes), *pitur ājñā* (the father’s command).
[Furthermore, this substitution occurs] when *u* or *ṛ* (*khyat*) precedes.

The words *khi* and *ti* are short, while the forms *khī* and *tī*—which have undergone the *yaṇ* substitution—are long; these are called *khyatya*. After these, the vowel *a* of the case-endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas* is replaced by *u*. Thus: *sakhyur āyāti* (the friend approaches), *sakhyuḥ svam* (the friend's own); *patyur āgatam* (received from the husband/master), *patyuḥ svam* (the husband's/master's own). From the denominative root *sakhīyati* (derived with the suffix *kyac*), the suffix *kvip* is applied, resulting in *sakhīḥ* (friend) and *sakhyuḥ*; likewise, *patīḥ* and *patyuḥ*. How is it that *lūnyuḥ*, *pūnyuḥ*, and *kṣāmyuḥ* are formed? [The answer is: the rules for *natva* (nasalization) and *atva* (substitution of *a*) are considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to what precedes them.
Therefore, [the substitution of *u* occurs] for *roḥ* (the final *r*) when it follows a non-protracted vowel and precedes a non-protracted vowel.

"ati" (after) is understood [from the previous rule]. Therefore, when *at* follows, the *u*-vowel (*ukāra*) shall replace the *r* of a preceding *roḥ*. Examples: *vṛkṣo'tra*, *nabho'tra*. Because of the [different] substratum, the *roḥ* is not considered *asiddha*. Why "ataḥ"? Example: *agniratra*. Why "taparaḥ" (followed by *t*)? Example: *vṛkṣā atra*. Why "roḥ"? Example: *svaratra*, *prātaratra*. "ati" is understood—example: *vṛkṣaḥ + atha*. Again, why "taparaḥ"? Example: *vṛkṣa āśritaḥ*. And [the substitution occurs] before a *haś* (voiceless consonant).

When followed by *haś* (any consonant except *y*, *v*, *r*, or *l*), the *u* of *at* (the short vowel *a*) following *ra* shall be replaced by *utva* (the sound *u*). Examples: *vipraḥ hasati* (the Brahmin laughs); *vipraḥ yāti* (the Brahmin goes); *devaḥ varṣati* (the god rains). [Exception:
Within a *pāda* (verse-quarter), the *visarga* remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*) unless it is followed by *a* or *va*.

"By nature" (*prakṛtyā*) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). "The remainder" (*śeṣaḥ*) refers to Vedic usage (*chāndasaḥ*). Here, "Vedic usage" (*chandaḥ*) refers to these six sūtras. These are the six sūtras: *avyāt*, *avadyāt*, *avakramuḥ*, *avrata*, *ayam*, *avantu*, and *asyuṣu*.
In the Yajurveda, [the measurement] is the chest.
O Waters, you who delight in the bull, in the most excellent, in the womb, in Ambā, and in Ambikā, [be] foremost!
And [the same applies] in cases such as *aṅga* and so forth.
And [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] before an unaccented vowel when followed by *k* or *dh*.
And you shall fall down.
In all cases, there is an option regarding the word *go*.

The word *sarvatra* (everywhere) is for the purpose of terminating the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *chandas* (Vedic). By the "frog-leap" principle (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the rule *eṅaḥ ati* (Pāṇini 6.1.94) continues to apply. When *ati* follows, the *eṅ* vowels of *go* may optionally remain in their original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Thus: *go asthi*, *go'sthi*, or *gavāsthi*; *go agram*, *go'gram*, or *gavāgram*.
[In this context,] the substitution of *avaṅ* occurs according to Sphoṭāyana.
The word *ati* has ceased [to apply]. The word *aci* continues [to apply]. When followed by a vowel (*ac*), *go* may optionally become *avaṅ*. Examples: *gavājinaṃ* (cow-hide), *gavoṣṇaṃ* (cow-warm).

In the alternative case—*go'jinaṃ*, *go'jinaṃ*; *ga'uṣṇaṃ*, *ga'uṣṇaṃ*. Here, the optional elision of the *v* sound occurs according to the rule "the elision of *v* is optional for Śākalya. By means of a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*)—*gavākṣaḥ* (cow-window) is always [formed with *avaṅ*].
In the *Vibhāṣā-anuvṛtti*, the mention of Sphoṭāyana is for the sake of honor;
and [the rule] applies invariably before Indra.
In the word *gorindra*, the substitution of *avaṅ* occurs invariably. Thus: *gavendraḥ*.
[Furthermore: *pluta* and *pragṛhya* vowels are invariably [retained] before a vowel (*aci*).

The term *pluta* refers to a protracted vowel (*svarabhāga*). Those vowels designated as *pragṛhya* shall always remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) before a vowel. Examples: *agnī atra*, *vāyū imau*, *pacete imau*.
Why is there a constant recurrence (*nityānuvṛtti*) of this rule here? [To ensure] that the substitution of a short vowel for *ik* before a non-homogeneous vowel (*asavarṇa*) does not occur.
[Furthermore: In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the nasalized form (*anunāsika*) of *āṅ* [is used].
This is Vedic. [The rule] "iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca" applies.

The rule *padāntāt* (from the end of a word) applies here as well. An *ik* vowel at the end of a word retains its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) before a non-homogeneous *ac* vowel; furthermore, according to Śākalya, a short vowel is also permitted. Examples: *dadhi atra*, *kumāri api*, *nadi āyāti*, *vadhu ṛtuḥ*. Why is the term *padānta* (end of a word) repeated? [To exclude cases where it is not at the end of a word: *kumāryau*, *kumāryaḥ*. There is a prohibition of the Śākalya rule in the case of the particle *si* and in eternal compounds (*nityasamāsa*). Examples: *ṛtviyaḥ*; in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is the form *ghas*. In an eternal compound: *vyākaraṇam*, *kumāryartham*.
The *ṛti* [vowel] is replaced by *ak*.

According to the opinion of Śākalya, when followed by *ṛ*, the vowels *a* and *ka* (i.e., all simple vowels) remain in their original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and they also become short. Examples: *sthūla ṛśyaḥ* [becomes *sthūlaṛśyaḥ*]; *himartau api tā bhṛśasvidaḥ*; *uccāritarucira ṛcāñcānanānāṃ caturṇām*; *khaṭva ṛśyaḥ* [becomes *khaṭvaṛśyaḥ*]; *hotṛ ṛśyaḥ* [becomes *hotṛṛśyaḥ*]. Why "of *a* and *ka*"? Consider *vṛkṣe ṛśyaḥ* [which becomes *vṛkṣeṛśyaḥ*].
[Furthermore,] when a word follows immediately after another, it is treated as if it were not protracted (*aplutavat*).
The third [verse] belongs to Cākravarmaṇa.
The two sūtras are Vedic;
[the rule] "diva ut" [applies].

The term *padānta* (end of a word) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. For the word *div*, when it is at the end of a word (*padānta*), *ut* shall be substituted [for the final *v*]. Examples: *vimaladyu dinam* (a day with a clear sky). Because of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is treated as being at the end of a word in the following cases: *dyukāmaḥ*, *dyumanāḥ*, *dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ*. Because the rule refers to the form without the *anubandha* (the vowel *u*), this substitution does not occur here: *akṣadyubhyām*, *akṣadyūbhiḥ*. Why "at the end of a word"? Observe: *divau*, *divaḥ*. [Furthermore:

There is elision of the *su* (nominative singular suffix) after *etad* and *tad* when followed by a consonant (*hal*), provided they are not part of a negative compound (*anañ-samāsa*) and do not contain the augment *ak*.

In place of *etad* and *tad*, there shall be elision (*sulopa*) before a consonant (*hal*). Examples: *eṣa dātā* (this giver), *sa bhoktā* (that eater). Why "not when followed by *ak*" (*akoḥ*)? *eṣako dātā* (this very giver), *sako bhoktā* (that very eater). Why "not in a compound with *nañ*" (*anañ-samāse*)? *anaṣo dadāti* (he gives without a net). That [suffix] is also understood by others as being present even in this case. Why "before a consonant" (*hali*)? *eṣo'tra* (this here). Here, two Vedic metrical rules (*chandaḥ-sūtra*) apply.
The suffix *sya* is frequently applied after a word ending in *chandas*.
That [substitution of *ay* for *i*] occurs before a vowel (*aci*), provided that the elision (*lope*) serves to complete the metrical foot (*pādapūraṇam*).
In this context, both the completion of a quarter of a *ṛc* verse and the completion of a quarter of a *śloka* are included. By that [principle], for example:
"This is that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; this is that King Yudhiṣṭhira;
this is that Karṇa, the great renouncer; this is that Bhīma, possessed of great strength."
Thus, even in common usage, some maintain that there is elision of the *su* in *saḥ* before a vowel;
the augment *suṭ* is placed before the root-final consonant.
[The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] even when there is an intervention by a non-reduplicated (*aḍ*) prefix or a reduplicated (*abhyāsa*) syllable.
These two [prefixes] are governed [by this rule]. The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of specification in the rule *ṭakāraḥ sahasuṭstusvaññjām*.
[The prefix *sam* is used] with the root *kṛ* when it means "adornment," following *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*.

The augment *suṭ* is placed before the root *kṛ* when it follows these [prefixes] in the sense of "adornment" (*bhūṣaṇa*). Examples: *saṃskaroti*, *pariṣkāraḥ*, *upaskriyate*, *upaskāraḥ*, *upaskartavyaḥ*. Even when there is an intervention by the augment *aṭ* or the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), [the rule applies]: *samaskārṣīt*, *sañcaskāra*. Why "in the sense of adornment"? [Consider: *upakaroti* (he assists).

As for the statement—"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is impermanent"—here the word *saṃskṛta* is used as a synonym for "effect" (*kārya*) and is simply an unanalyzed (irregular) form.
And in the case of inherence as well.
In this context, the augment *suṭ* is added before the root *kṛñ* after those [prefixes]. Examples: *saṃskṛtam*, *pariṣkṛtam*, *upaskṛtam*. The meaning is "assembled" (*samaveta*).
[The augment *suṭ* is also applied] after the prefix *upa-* in the senses of refinement (*pratiyatna*), transformation (*vaikṛta*), and supplying an ellipsis in a sentence (*vākyādhyāhāra*).

The suffix *suṭ* is applied before the root *kṛ* when used with the prefix *upa*, provided it signifies "improvement" (*pratiyatna*). For example: *edho dakasyopaskurute* ("He improves the water by means of fuel"). *Vaikṛta* means that which is modified (*vikṛta*). Example: *upaskṛtaṃ bhuṅkte* ("He eats [food] that has been prepared"). The "supplying of a sentence" (*vākyādhyāhāra*) refers to the introduction of a sentence whose meaning is merely implied. Example: *upaskṛtaṃ jalpati nityameṣaḥ* ("This man always prattles on [about] what has been prepared"). How indeed, O sir, shall we determine the meaning of a word? [The suffix *suṭ* is also applied] before the root *kṛ* (in the form *kira*) when it means "cutting" (*lavana*).

The augment *suṭ* is placed before the root *kṛ* (kirati) when preceded by *upa*. Example: *upaskīrya lunanti* ("having scattered [the grass], they cut it"). Why "in the sense of cutting"? Consider: *upakirati puṣpam* ("he scatters flowers").
[The augment *suṭ* is also applied] after *prati* when the sense is injury (*hiṃsā*).

The suffix *suṭ* is applied after the prefixes *prati* and *upa* when the root *kṛ* (kirati) means "to injure. Examples: *pratiskīrṇaḥ*, *upaskīrṇo vipraḥ*. [In the phrase] *urovidāraṃ praticaskare nakhaiḥ* ("he tore open his chest with his claws"), [the form is] *upaskīrṇo dasyuḥ* ("the bandit has been injured"). The meaning is "scattered" preceded by injury. [Next:
*apāccatuṣpācchakuniṣvālekhane* ("after *apa*, [the suffix *suṭ* is applied] when referring to quadrupeds and birds in the sense of scratching").

The suffix *suṭ* is applied to the root *kirati* when it refers to lower animals (*apād*), quadrupeds (*catuṣpād*), or birds (*śakuni*), provided that the action involves scratching (*ālekhanam*). This denotes joy (*harṣa*), livelihood (*jīvikā*), or making a nest (*kulāyakaraṇa*). An ox scratches itself out of joy: *apaskirate vṛṣabho hṛṣṭaḥ*. A cock scratches for the sake of food: *apaskirate kukkuṭo bhakṣārthī*. A dog scratches for the sake of a shelter: *apaskirate śvā āśrayārthī*. "The suffix *tum* is optionally used after the words *avaśyam*, *kṛtya*, *kāma*, and *manas*; likewise, it is optional after the word *sama* when followed by *hita* or *tata*; and the suffix *yu* is used after *māṃsa* before the suffixes *pac* and *ghan*.
