The initial sound of the following member [is unmodified].
Karṇa [is so called] because of his color and characteristic marks.
And [the same applies] to the case of *saṃjñā* (a name) and *aupamya* (a comparison).
And [the same applies to] the back of the head, the neck, and the shanks.
And [it exists] in the state of the peak.
No other [friend] is equal to one who is undecaying, immortal, and deathless.
Possessing beautiful thoughts, devoid of greed.
And [the terms] *kratvādi* and so forth.
In the Vedic language, a two-syllable word has its first syllable acute-accented.
And [the suffixes] vīra and vīya.
In an *avyayībhāva* compound, [the word] *kūla*, *tīra*, *tūla*, *mūla*, *śāla*, and *akṣa* take the neuter gender.
In a *dvigu* compound, the words *kaṃsa*, *mantha*, *śūrpa*, *pāyya*, and *kāṇḍa* [retain their original forms].
In a Tatpuruṣa compound, the word "śālā" becomes neuter [when it denotes a dwelling].
And a patched cloak.
The beginning [of the list] refers to Cihaṇa and the others.
The words *cela*, *kheṭa*, *kaṭuka*, and *kāṇḍa* are used in the sense of reproach.
Bark-cloth is the comparison.
In the case of *palala*, *sūpa*, and *śāka*, [the compound is] *miśra*.
The words *kūla-sūda-sthala-karṣa* [form a Tatpuruṣa compound] when used as a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*).
The word *rājya* [is used] except when it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
And [the suffixes] beginning with *varg* [are also used].
The word *putra* [is substituted] for masculine words [ending in the sixth case].
Nor [should one give] to those designated as teachers, kings, officiating priests, or kinsmen.
Powders and so forth [are permissible] provided they do not contain sixty living beings.
And there are six sections and so forth.
The grove is the sacrificial pit.
By nature, it is a skull.
In a bahuvrīhi compound, [the word] *śita* is optionally [placed first], except when it is accompanied by *bahu*.
The suffix *kṛt* follows a verbal root when preceded by a word denoting a destination (*gati*), a grammatical participant (*kāraka*), or a secondary word (*upapada*).
In the case of the Vanaspati and other offerings, both [the oblation and the formula] occur simultaneously.
And [the first vowel retains its original accent] in a copulative compound of deities.
The first syllable of the first member of a compound is acute when the second member begins with an unaccented vowel and is one of the words *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, or *manthin*.
End.
The suffixes *tha*, *thaK*, *ghaÑ*, *kta*, *aca*, *trC*, and *ka* [are applied after verbal roots].
The suffix *kta* is applied after a word denoting a standard of comparison.
In a compound denoting a name, the elision of *an* does not occur after words such as *anācita*.
And [the same applies] to those who have increased [their faculties] and so forth.
After a word denoting an agent, the suffix *kta* is used only with the words *datta* and *śruta* when expressing a blessing.
And [the rule] "done by one who is in such a state."
The other [term] expresses the action of becoming.
Those obtained through bartering, explaining [the scriptures], lying down, sitting, standing, officiating as a priest, and so forth, or by purchase.
The merit of the seventh [stage].
A quarrel concerning a deficiency of wealth results from the third lunar day.
And a compound containing a prefix [ending in a vowel] followed by a word beginning with a vowel, provided there is no sandhi-conjunction.
In the negation of a quality, the taddhita suffixes having the senses of "to be accomplished," "worthy of," "beneficial for," and "capable of" do not apply.
And [the suffix *cha*] is applied after *yayāti* in the sense of "not that."
In the case of inability to speak.
And also in the case of verbal abuse.
In the case of perception (saṃjñā).
The words *kṛtya*, *ukeya*, *uṣṇika*, *cāru*, and so forth [are also formed with the suffix *kyap*].
The suffix *tṛn* is optionally applied [after a verbal root] before the words *anna*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *śuci*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* (ṣaṣ) is applied after the words *idam*, *etad*, and *tad* when they denote the first [in order] or a fraction used in counting actions.
The word *stana* [is used] after a numeral.
In the Vedic language, there is optionality.
In the case of a name, [the suffix -in] is applied after the words *mitra* and *ajina*.
The interval between those that are separated.
One's own limb is pleasant.
[The suffix *ka*] is not applied after indeclinables, words denoting direction, or the words *go*, *mahat*, *sthūla*, *muṣṭi*, *pṛthu*, and *vatsa*.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* may optionally be used after a word that serves as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

The suffix *kta* is applied after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), happiness (*sukha*), and so forth, provided they have not been covered [by another word], and it denotes those things which are unmade (*akṛta*), measured (*mita*), or attained (*pratipanna*).
or when [the child] is born.
[The suffix *naṅ* is applied] after [the words] *anya* and *ubha*.
The *kapi* [affix] occurs after [a verbal root] preceded by *pūrva*.
In the case of a short vowel at the end, [the augment *ṭi* is placed] before the final letter.
After *bahu*, when it does not have the sense of a negative particle (*nañ*), [the suffix *īyasun*] is applied to express excellence in relation to the subsequent word (*uttarapada*).
Qualities and so forth are not constituent parts.
After a prefix, the word *dhruva* ending in a vowel, except for *parśu*, takes the suffix *ka*.
The word *vana* is a compound.
End.
And at the end.
Not after the words *ni* and *vi*.
The mandala is formed by surrounding it on all sides.
The word *prāda* [is used] before a body part (*svāṅga*) when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*).
And [the rules concerning] waterless places and so forth.
Facing north.
And [the suffix] *ap* [is applied].
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after *sphic*, *pūta*, *vīṇā*, *anyoḥ*, *ūrdhva*, *kukṣi*, *sīra*, and *nāman*.
Seated upon an ādhāra.
It is smaller than the smallest and more subtle than the subtlest.
And the Puruṣa is subsequently assigned.
Aterakṛt is the pada.
In the case of a treasure-trove.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, words such as *prateraśva* [and others] [are used].
From the prefix *upa*, [the suffix *kvun*] occurs after the two roots *ji* and *mṛ*, as well as after *gaura* and others.
In the case of throwing down a corpse.
The term *vibhāṣā* is used when the tail is raised.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *pāda* becomes *pad* when it follows *dvi*, *tri*, or the words *pāda*, *dan*, and *mūrdhan*.
And [the vowel] of the word *saktha* [is long] when it follows the root *kram*.
In the Vedic language, there is frequently the substitution of the subsequent element for the preceding one.
When the subsequent word begins with a vowel.
The absence of elision (*aluk*) should be stated when a subsequent member follows. This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending to the end of the chapter.
[The elision of] the fifth case-ending does not occur after words such as *stoka*.
The elision of the genitive case-ending (*ṅasi*) shall not occur after the words *stoka*, *antika*, *dūra*, and *kṛcchra*. Examples: *stokānmuktaḥ* ("freed with little effort").
This applies only when [the word] is the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*); thus, *niḥstokaḥ* ("departed from a little") is derived as *niṣkrāntaḥ stokāt*.
How is it that *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* is an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? It is due to a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
The forms *ojaḥ*, *sahaḥ*, and *ambhaḥ* are substituted for the third case ending of the word *tamaḥ*.

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall not be elided after these [words]. *ojasābhūtaḥ* (born through vigor). His offspring is *aujasābhūtiḥ*. *ojasākṛtam* (done by vigor). *sahasākṛtam* (done by force). *ambhasāvyāptam* (pervaded by water). *tamasāvṛtam* (covered by darkness). Because the non-elision (*aluk*) is prescribed when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the non-elision occurs where *tamas-* is the prior member (*pūrvapada*), but not where a word ending in *tamas-* is the prior member. Therefore, in the expression *satatanaiśatamovṛtamanyataḥ* ("covered on the other side by constant nocturnal darkness"), there is no non-elision.

There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *añjas-*. The non-elision shall occur: *añjasākṛtam* (done straightway). By the addition, [we have] *puṃsānujaḥ* (younger than a male) and *januṣāndhaḥ* (blind from birth). "Birth" (*januḥ*) means "birth" (*janman*).

In this context, some have stated that the word *tamas* means "asceticism" (*tapas*). Thus, Vyāsa says: "Seeing [the demon] standing on his chariot, having attained perfection through asceticism, and having conquered the king of the gods by his splendor"; and Bhaṭṭi says: "Those emaciated by asceticism, with water-pots for pacification in their hands.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the word *manas* when it denotes a name.
In a proper name, there shall be no elision (aluk) of the third case ending of the word *manas*. For example: *manasāguptā* ("protected by mind") and *manasādevī* ("the goddess Mind").
This also applies when [the second member] means "obedient."

In this case, there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending of *manas-* when it occurs as the first member of a compound with a word beginning with *uttara-pada*. Examples include *manasājñāyī* (one who knows with the mind) and *yogin*.
Furthermore, there is no elision of the genitive case-ending of *ātman-* when used in the sense of a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*).

The elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending of the word *ātman* shall not occur when followed by a word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*). Examples: *ātmanāpañcamaḥ* (the fifth with oneself), *ātmanāṣaṣṭhaḥ* (the sixth with oneself).
However, in the case of *ātmacaturthaḥ*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Furthermore, there is no elision of the genitive case-ending of *caturthī* when used in the sense of designating a grammarian.
And for another as well.

The elision of the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) after *ātman* and *para* shall not occur when the word is a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *ātmanebhāṣaḥ*, *ātmanepadam*; *parasmaibhāṣaḥ*, *parasmaipadam*.
[Furthermore,] the elision of the seventh case-ending does not occur after a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*, when it is a technical grammatical term.

There shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending after a word ending in a consonant (*halanta*) or the letter *a* (*adanta*). Examples: *tvacisāraḥ* (the core of the bark), *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ* (firm in battle). In the case of the word *ap-* (water), there is no elision before the suffixes *yoni*, *yoni-mati*, and *mati*. *apsuyonir agniḥ* (fire whose origin is in the waters); here the suffix *yat* is applied because the word belongs to the *digādi* group, resulting in *apsavyaḥ* (born in the waters). *apsumatiḥ* (possessing water); this is a compound formed by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. It should be stated that there is no elision of the locative singular ending (*ṅeḥ*) after the words *hṛd-* (heart) and *div-* (heaven). Examples: *hṛdispṛk* (touching the heart), *diviṣado devāḥ* (the gods who dwell in heaven).
How is one called *dyukāma* (one whose desire is for heaven)? Because of the rule concerning future frequent usage (*bhāvibahula-vacana*).
And [the suffix *aṇ*] occurs after a word ending in a consonant (*hal*) when it is the name of a cause, according to the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*).

The term *kāra* is a technical designation for a restrictive rule (*niyama*). According to that rule, when a word ending in the name [of a place] follows a word beginning with a consonant, the seventh case suffix (*saptamī*) shall not be elided according to the usage of the Easterners (*prācām*). Examples: *haledvipadikā* (a two-pence coin at the plough), *kūpeśāṇaḥ* (a stone in the well). Only after a word ending in *hal* or *adanta* [is this applied]—for example, *nadyāṃ dohanī* (a milking vessel in the river) becomes *nadīdohanī*. Why is it a restrictive rule? Consider *avikaṭe uraṇaḥ* (a goat in a narrow space); [if it were not a restrictive rule, the elision would apply here as well, resulting in] *avikaṭoraṇaḥ*.
In the middle, [there is] Jupiter.

In a Bahuvrīhi compound, there shall be no elision (aluk) of the seventh case-ending after the word *madhya* when it follows *guru*. Thus: *madhyeguruḥ*. [There is also no elision] after *anta*: *anteguruḥ*.
[The rule] "after a word denoting a body part (*svāṅga*), except for *mūrdhan* and *mastaka*, provided it does not mean 'desire' (*kāma*)" [applies here].

There shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending after a word denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*). Examples: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (one whose throat is black), *urasilomā* (one who has hair on the chest), *udaremaṇiḥ* (one who has a jewel on the belly). [Also]: "He quickly struck the enemy with a sword and an arrow. Why say "not after *mūrdhan* or *mastaka*"? Consider: *mūrdhaśikhaḥ* (one whose crest is on the head), *mastakaśikhaḥ* (one whose crest is on the skull). Why say "when not meaning desire" (*akāme*)? Consider: *mukhakāmaḥ* (desiring the face). Why say "after a word for one's own limb"? Consider: *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* (skilled at dice).
Only when the word ends in a consonant or the letter *a* (*haladantāt*)—as in: *aṅgulitrāṇaḥ* (a finger-guard).
And there is an option regarding the compound.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *bandha*, there may optionally be no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending when it follows a word ending in *hal* (a consonant) or a short vowel (*adanta*). Examples: *hastebandhaḥ* or *hastabandhaḥ*; *cakrebhandhaḥ* or *cakrabandhaḥ*.
This applies only after words ending in *hal* or a short vowel—as in *guptibandhaḥ*—but in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt*-suffix, the non-elision occurs diversely (*bahulam*).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix follows as the final member (*uttarapada*), there is generally (*bahulam*) no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*). Examples: *vanecaraḥ* (forest-dweller), *stamberamaḥ* (elephant), *paṅkeruhaḥ* (lotus), *hṛdisthaḥ* (situated in the heart).
And it does not occur: *kāyasthaḥ* (situated in the body), *kurusthaḥ* (situated in Kuru), *kurucaraḥ* (wandering in Kuru).
In some cases, it is optional: *sarojam*, *sarasijam* (lotus).
The lotus blooms during the day in the seasons of the rainy season and autumn.
In these cases, there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*). Examples: *prāvṛṣijaḥ*, *śaradijaḥ*, *kālejaḥ*, *divijaḥ*.
Why "in these cases"? [Counter-example: *grīṣmajaḥ*. [There is] optionally (*vibhāṣā*) [no elision] after the words *varṣa*, *kṣara*, *śara*, and *varā*.

After these [words], the elision (*aluk*) of the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) may optionally not occur before the suffix *ja*. Examples: *varṣejaḥ* or *varṣajaḥ*; *kṣarejaḥ* or *kṣarajaḥ*; *śarejaḥ* or *śarajaḥ*; *varejaḥ* or *varajaḥ*.
[This rule applies] when a word denoting time is followed by the suffix *gha*, as well as by *kāla* and *tana*.

In compounds ending in *gha* and others, there may optionally be no elision (*aluk*) of the seventh case-ending of a word denoting time. Examples: *pūrvāhṇetarām*, *pūrvāhṇatare gāyati*, *pūrvāhṇekālakṛtam*, *pūrvāhṇakālakṛtam*, *pūrvāhṇetane*, *pūrvāhṇatena gāyati*. [The rule applies] only when the preceding word ends in a consonant or the letter *a*: *rātritarāyāṃ jāgarti*. [An exception:
There is no elision after a word that is not a time-denoting term before the words *śaya*, *vāsa*, and *vāsin*.

In compounds such as *śaya* ("lying"), there may optionally be non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending when it does not denote time. For example: *kheśayaḥ* or *khaśayaḥ* ("lying in the sky"); *vanavāsaḥ* ("dwelling in the forest"). Similarly: *grāmevāsī* or *grāmavāsī* ("residing in the village"). Why "not denoting time"? Consider: *pūrvāhṇaśayaḥ* ("lying in the forenoon"). Only when [the preceding word] ends in a consonant or the vowel *a*—as in *bhūmiśayaḥ* ("lying on the ground")—does this rule apply.
And in the case of the roots *nind*, *sidh*, and *badh*.

Furthermore, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending before the words *innanta*, *siddha*, and *badhnāti*. For example: *sthaṇḍilaśāyī* (one who sleeps on the bare ground), *sāṅkāśyasiddhaḥ* (one perfected at Sāṅkāśya), and *cakrabandhaḥ* (binding with a wheel).
How is it that we have *cakrebandhaḥ*? The option has been stated regarding forms ending in the suffix *ghañ*; moreover, the rule *sthe ca bhāṣāyām* applies here.
When followed by *stha*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. Examples: *samasthaḥ*, *kūṭasthaḥ*, *kāyasthaḥ*, *udarasthaḥ*.
How is *hṛdisthaḥ* explained? By virtue of its frequent usage (*bāhulyāt*).
The mention of "colloquial usage" (*bhāṣā*) is intended for application in a single grammatical rule (*ekavṛttau*).
The sixth case [is used] in the sense of abuse.

In the sense of "insulting," there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the sixth case-ending. Examples: *caurasya kulam* ("the family of a thief"), *mātuḥ sutaḥ* ("the son of a mother"), *vṛṣalyāḥ patiḥ* ("the husband of a low-caste woman").

Why "in the sense of insulting"? [Counter-example: *brāhmaṇakulam* ("a Brāhmaṇa family"). After the words *vāc*, *diś*, and *paśyat*, there shall be no elision of the sixth case-ending when followed by *ukti*, *daṇḍa*, and *hara*, respectively. Example: *keyaṃ vācoyuktiḥ* ("what is this verbal artifice?"), *diśodaṇḍaḥ* ("a punishment directed toward a quarter"), *paśyatoharaḥ* ("one who steals while others look on").

In the forms *āmuṣyāyaṇa*, *āmuṣyaputrikā*, and *āmuṣyakulikā*, there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the sixth case ending. [The suffix] *phak* is applied after [stems] beginning with *naḍa*. Thus: *āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ*.
[The suffix] *vuñ* is applied because [the word *amuka*] belongs to the *manojñādi* group. Thus: *āmuṣyaputrikā* and *āmuṣyakulikā*.
In the expression *devānāṃ priyaḥ*, there shall be no elision of the sixth case ending. Thus: *devānāmpriyaḥ*.

In the case of the names Śepa, Puccha, and Lāṅgūla following the word *śvan*, there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the sixth case ending. For example: the sage named Śunaḥśepa; Śunaḥpuccha; Śunolāṅgūla.
The form Divodāsa is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is optionally applied after the word *putra*.

In the sense of "insulting," the sixth case may optionally be used after the word *putra* when it follows *alaka*: *dāsyāḥ putraḥ* or *dāsīputraḥ*. [The sixth case is also used] after words denoting knowledge (*vidyā*) or kinship through the womb (*yoni*).

The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not elided after a word ending in *ṛt* that denotes a relationship based on learning (*vidyā*) or procreation (*yoni*). Examples: *pituḥ putraḥ* (the son of the father), *hotur antevāsī* (the pupil of the priest). This does not apply when both members of the compound denote such a relationship, as it is not so prescribed in this context—for example, *pitṛdhanaṃ* (the father's wealth).
[There is] optionally [no elision] in the case of *svasṛ* and *pati*.

After a word ending in *ṛ*, there may optionally be no elision (*aluk*) of the sixth case-ending before these two [suffixes]. For example: *mātuḥṣvasā* or *mātṛṣvasā*; *pituḥṣvasā* or *pitṛṣvasā*; *duhituḥpatiḥ* or *duhitṛpatiḥ*. The non-elision has been explained. The section concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) extends up to before the rule for *aṅga*. In a *dvandva* compound, the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs in place of the final vowel *ṛ*.

In a *dvandva* compound consisting of words related by learning (*vidyā*) or by blood (*yoni*), which end in the vowel *ṛ*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs before the first member. The letter *n* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *r* (in place of *ṇ*). Examples: *hotāpotārau* (the Hotṛ and Potṛ priests), *mātāpitarau* (mother and father).

Why "in a *dvandva* of words ending in *ṛ*"? [Observe: *pitṛpitāmahau* (father and grandfather). How then is the form *pitāputrau* (father and son) or *mātāputrau* (mother and son) formed? [It is so] because the word *putre* (before the word "son") is understood as a governing rule from the previous sūtra.
Furthermore, this applies to *dvandva* compounds of deities.
In this context, the substitution *anaṅ* shall occur for the first member of the compound. Examples: *indrābṛhaspatī*, *sūryācandramasau*.

Because of the repeated mention of "dvandva" (copulative compound), the designation applies only to those [deities] who are associated together in common worldly usage or in the Veda. Therefore, it does not apply here: *śivavaiśravaṇau*.
How is it that *ravicandrau* is also not included? This must be considered further.

The prohibition applies to the word *vāyu* in both cases: *vāyvagnī* and *agnivāyū*. [Furthermore,] the long vowel *ī* is substituted for the final vowel of *agni* when followed by *soma* or *varuṇa*: *agnīṣomau*, *agnīvaruṇau*.

In the case of *varuṇa* following *agni*, there may be *ī*: *agnīvaruṇau*. Although the long vowel *ī* (*ītvam*) would be established even by the rule for homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*), they say that the explicit mention of *ī* is for the sake of other instances; thus, the usage of Vālmīki, *kuśīlavau* (meaning "Kuśa and Lava"), is justified.
[The suffix] *id* occurs when there is an increase (*vṛddhi*).

When the following member of a compound is *vṛddhi*-strengthened, the substitution of *it* (i.e., *ī*) occurs for the final vowel of *agni*. Examples: *āgnivāruṇam*, *āgnimārutam* (a ritual). In these cases, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening of both members due to the rule "in a *devatā*-dvandva. However, not before *viṣṇu*: here the substitution of *it* for *agni* does not occur. Example: *āgnāvaiṣṇavam*. [In the case of *div*, the form becomes] *dyāvā*.
In a dvandva compound of deities, the word *div* becomes *dyāvā*. [Examples: *dyāvābhūmī*, *dyāvāpṛthivyau*;
and [the substitution occurs] for *divas* when followed by *pṛthivī*.

In the place of *div*, there shall be the substitution of *divas* when followed by *pṛthivī*; and [the form] *dyāvā* [is also used]. The pronunciation of the vowel *a* at the end of the word is for the purpose of preventing the application of *ru*-substitution (*visarga*) and other such changes. Examples: *divaspṛthivyau* (Heaven and Earth) or *dyāvāpṛthivyau*.
[The same applies to] *uṣas*: *uṣāsoṣasaḥ*.

In a Dvandva compound of deities, the word *uṣas-* shall undergo the substitution *uṣās-*; for example, *uṣāsāsūryam* and *uṣāsānaktam*. According to the Eastern grammarians, the words *mātṛ-* and *pitṛ-* also undergo such substitution [in a Dvandva of deities], as in *mātāpitarau*.

The parents of others [are expressed as *mātāpitarau*]. Because it is not a rule ending in a dental, some say that by the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [of *mātāpitṛbhyām*], it becomes *mātarapitarābhyām*; others say *mātarapitṛbhyām*. And in the Veda, [the forms] *pitarāmātarā* and *mātāpitarā* also occur.
This is Vedic usage.

[A feminine word] ending in a suffix other than *ūṅ*, which has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), takes the masculine form when it is in grammatical apposition with another feminine word, provided it is not a term for a female ordinal number or one of the group beginning with *priya*.

A feminine word ending in *ūṅ* (other than *ūṅ*) shall take the form of the masculine when in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Example: *paṭvī bhāryā asya* → *paṭubhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is clever"); *śobhanabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is beautiful"); *dīrghajaṅghaḥ* ("one with long shanks"); *dīrghajaṅghabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife has long shanks"). Why "from a word that has a corresponding masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*)? Example: *khaṭvābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a bed"). Why "not ending in *ūṅ*" (*anūṅaḥ*)? Example: *dhībandhūbhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a female relative"). Why "in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇe*)? Example: *kalyāṇyā mātā* → *kalyāṇīmātā* ("the mother who is auspicious"). This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*). Why "when [the compound] refers to a female" (*striyām*)? Example: *kalyāṇīpradhānā ime* ("these [people] have an auspicious woman as their leader"). Why "not a superlative suffix" (*apūraṇī*)? Example: *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ* ("the nights of which the fifth is auspicious").

And here, in the rule prescribing the compound-ending suffix [ṭac] for "pūraṇī" (ordinal) and "apramāṇī" (non-measure), because of the inclusion of the *pradhāna* (principal) ordinal, the suffix does not apply when the meaning of the ordinal is other than the meaning of the compound itself—as in the example: *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("a fortnight having the auspicious fifth day"). What about in the case of words beginning with *apriya*? For example: *kalyāṇīpriyaḥ* ("one whose beloved is beautiful"), *kalyāṇīkāntaḥ* ("one whose beloved is beautiful").

[The words are: *priyā*, *bhakti*, *kāntā*, *subhagā*, *durbhagā*, *duhitā*, *capalā*. How is it that we have *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* ("firm devotion")? It is because in the expression *dṛḍhaṃ bhaktir asya* ("his devotion is firm"), the first member (*dṛḍha*) is intended to be expressed as non-feminine.
However, cases such as *śliṣṭapriyaḥ* ("one who loves embracing") and *vimuktakāntaḥ* ("one who has abandoned his beloved") are to be considered;
[the rule] applies to suffixes beginning with *tasil*, excluding *kṛtvasuc*.

In the context of suffixes beginning with *tasil* and others, the feminine form should be treated like the masculine. In this regard, there is the following enumeration: *tral*, *tas*, *tasi*; *tarap* and *tamap*; *caraṭ* and *jātīyar*; *kalpap*, *deśya*, and *deśīyara*; *rūpap* and *pāśap*.

*tham*, *thāl*, *au*, *dārhilau*, and *til-thyanau*. In that [feminine base], there [is the suffix] *tatra*; from that, *tataḥ*. *Ramyatarā*, *ramyatamā*; *paṭutarā*, *paṭutamā*. *Paṭucarī*, *paṭujātīyā*, *mṛdujātīyā*. *Vṛddhakalpā*, *paṭukalpā*, *mṛdukalpā*. *Paṭudeśyā*, *paṭudeśīyā*, *paṭurūpā*, *vṛddharūpā*, *vṛddhapāśā*. By what nature? *Katham*. By that nature, *tathā*. At that time, *tasyāṃ velāyām*, *tadā*. Then, *tarhi*. *Til* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *Ajathyā*. In the *śas* [case-ending], for words meaning "much" or "few," it should be like the masculine (*puṃvat*). Give to many women: *bahuśaḥ*. Few: *alpaśaḥ*.

In the case of words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), when the suffixes *tva* or *tal* are added, the word takes the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Examples: *paṭutvam*, *paṭutā*, *mṛdutā*. Why "of a word denoting a quality"? Consider *daṇḍinītvam* (the state of being a woman with a staff) and *kaṭhītvam* (the state of being a female follower of the Kaṭha school).
How then is it that one speaks of "the variability of arguments" (*vyabhicāritvam yuktīnām*)? This is because the reference is made to the general category (*sāmānyopakrama*).
However, the form *tanvītvam* (the state of being a slender woman) requires further consideration.

In the case of a *taddhita* suffix following a base termed *bha*, the feminine form shall be treated as masculine (*puṃvat*). For example: *hastinīnāṃ samūhaḥ* (a collection of female elephants) becomes *hāstikam*. Why "not when followed by *aḍha*"? Consider *śyaineyaḥ* (descendant of Śyenī) and *rauhiṇeyaḥ* (descendant of Rohiṇī).

Also, when the suffixes *ṭhak* or *chaś* follow, the feminine form shall be treated as masculine. For example: *bhavatyāḥ chātrāḥ* (the students of your ladyship) becomes *bhāvatkāḥ*; likewise, *bhavadīyāḥ*.

The statement "the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be prescribed for all pronominal bases in every type of compound formation" is the *bhāṣya* on the rule *diṅnāmāny antarāle*. Examples include: *sarvāsāṃ dhanaṃ* = *sarvadhanam*; *anyasyāstanayaḥ* = *anyatanayaḥ*; "she who is not proud does not tolerate union with another" = *na māninī saṃsahate 'nyasaṅgamam*; and "her face" = *tasyā mukham* = *tanmukham*. However, the example *bhavatīprasādāt* (by your grace) should be considered [as a separate case]. This also applies in the presence of the *kyaṅ* suffix and the suffix *mānin*.

Furthermore, in the case of a feminine word ending in the suffix *mānin*, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) may optionally be used. For example: *enīm* (a beautiful woman) becomes *enī-mānī* (one who considers herself beautiful), or *etām* (a white woman) becomes *etā-mānī* (one who considers herself white). Similarly, *darśanīyām* (a beautiful wife) becomes *darśanīya-mānī* (one who considers her wife beautiful).
However, this does not apply to words whose penultimate vowel is long (*kopadhā*).

The feminine word ending in *kopadha* (having *k* as its penultimate letter) shall not undergo the *puṃvat* (masculine-like) transformation. Examples: *madrikābhāryaḥ*, *pācikābhāryaḥ*, *dāhikāśaktiḥ*, *pācikākalpā*, *pācikāyate*, *pācikāmāninī*. In the prohibition regarding words ending in *kopadha*, the term "taddhita" (secondary suffix) and "vuñ" (the specific suffix *vuñ*) must be included [in the rule]. This is so that the following do not occur: *ekabhāryaḥ*, *pākabhāryaḥ*, *pākakalpā*.
And [the shortening of the penultimate vowel does not occur] in the case of a name or a feminine suffix used for filling out a meter.

In these two cases, the feminine form shall not be replaced by the masculine form. *dattābhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is named Dattā). *mandodarībhāryam atītya reje* (he shone, surpassing those whose wives are Mandodarī). *dattāmāninī* (one who considers herself Dattā). *pañcamībhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is Pañcamī). *dvitīyākalpā* (one who is almost like Dvitīyā). *pañcamīkalpā* (one who is almost like Pañcamī).
And [the feminine suffix] of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) caused by *vṛddhi* is not replaced by the masculine form, except when it denotes a colored product or a modification.

The masculine form is not substituted for a feminine word ending in a *taddhita* suffix that causes *vṛddhi*, [when it occurs in a compound with] a word denoting a wife (*bhārya*), the suffix *-mānin*, or the suffix *-kalpa*. Examples: *aupagavībhāryaḥ*, *māthurībhāryaḥ*, *māthurīmāninī*, *māthurīkalpā*. Why "causing *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddhihetu*)? Consider: *madhyamabhāryaḥ*. Why "not when denoting a colored object" (*arakte*)? Consider: *kāṣāyabṛhatikaḥ*, *hāridrapatākaḥ*. Why "not when there is no modification" (*avikāre*)? Consider: *lauheṣo rathaḥ* ("an iron chariot").
[Also excluded is] a word denoting a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*) ending in the suffix *-cetaḥ*, except when followed by the suffix *-mānin*.

That which follows an *īkāra* belonging to its own stem (*svāṅga*)—the feminine word ending in it—does not undergo the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Examples: *dīrghakeśī-bhāryaḥ*, *sumukhī-bhāryaḥ*, *sumukhī-kalpā*. Why "not [ending] in *-mānin-*"? Example: *sukeśa-māninī*.
And [this rule does not apply] to words denoting a genus (*jāti*).

In the case of a feminine word denoting a genus (*jāti*), the masculine form shall not apply. Examples: *kumbhakārī-bhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is a potter-woman), *kaṭhī-kalpā* (one who is almost a Kaṭhī), *kaṭhī-pāśā* (one who is like a Kaṭhī), *bahvṛcī-yate* (she behaves like a Bahvṛcī).

This is not desired for that which is taught by supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*): *hāstikam* (a herd of female elephants). It applies only when the suffix *-mānin-* is not present: *kaṭha-māninī* (one who considers herself a Kaṭhī).
The masculine form applies in *karmadhāraya* compounds and with the suffixes *-jātīya-* and *-deśīya-*.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound and similar formations, the feminine form following a word that has already expressed the masculine gender (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) shall be treated like the masculine (*puṃvat*), provided it does not end in the suffix *ūṅ*; this is not a prohibition. Examples: *mahāpañcamī* (great fifth woman) *puṇyaṣaṣṭhī* (virtuous sixth woman) *mahāṣaṣṭhī* (great sixth woman) *priyaduhitā* (one who has a beloved daughter) *mṛgacapalā* (as fickle as a deer) *pācakavṛndārikā* (a young woman who is a cook) *kārakavṛndārikā* (a young woman who is an agent) *kākavandhyā* (a woman whose children die like a crow’s offspring) *kārakajātīyā* (of the nature of an agent) *kārakadeśīyā* (almost an agent) Similarly: *dattavṛndārikā* (a young woman to whom something was given) *pañcamavṛndārikā* (a fifth young woman) *māthuravṛndārikā* (a young woman from Mathurā) *māthurajātīyā* (of the type from Mathurā) *māthuradeśīyā* (almost from Mathurā) *sukeśavṛndārikā* (a young woman with beautiful hair) *kaṭhadeśīyā* (almost a follower of the Kaṭha school) The rule applies only when the word refers to a female (*striyām*). Thus, there is no substitution in: *kaṭhīprakāṇḍam* (an excellent female follower of the Kaṭha school) *māninījanaḥ* (a group of proud women).

The masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) should be stated for *kukkuṭī* and other such words when used with *aṇḍa* and so forth: *kukkuṭyā aṇḍam* becomes *kukkuṭāṇḍam*; *mṛgyāḥ padam* becomes *mṛgapadam*; *mṛgyāḥ kṣīram* becomes *mṛgakṣīram*; *kākyāḥ śāvaḥ* becomes *kākaśāvaḥ*. Due to the application of the masculine form, shortening occurs by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) in the case of suffixes beginning with *khid* and *gha*, etc.: *kālimmanyā*, *hariṇimmanyā*, *paṭvitarā*, *mṛdvitamā*. The rule for the masculine form has been explained. [Now follows:

In the presence of the suffixes *gha*, *rūpa*, *kalpa*, *celaṭ*, *bruva*, *gotra*, *mata*, and *hata*, the final vowel of a word ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī* that consists of more than one syllable is shortened.

In the case of words ending in *gha* and others, as well as those with more than one vowel (*anekāc*) and those ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, there shall be shortening (*hrasva*) when followed by [the superlative suffixes] *tara* or *tama*. Examples: *brāhmaṇitarā*, *sundaritamā*, *gaurirūpā*, *bhujaṅgikalpā*, *vṛṣalicelī*, *paṭvibruvā*, *taruṇigotrā*, *kumārimatā*, *gaurihatā*. The rule applies only when the word has been previously mentioned as having a masculine form (*uktapuṃska*). For example: *badarītarā* (where *badarī* is not of the feminine class). The word *bruvaḥ* is derived from the root *brūñ* with the suffix *ac*. The words *celaṭ*, *bruva*, and *gotra* are used here in a derogatory sense (*kutsanārtha*). [The following rule applies:
"For a river-name (*nadī*), the shortening of the remaining [final vowel] is optional. (Pāṇini 6.3.62)

In the case of words beginning with *gha* and others, the short vowel may optionally take the place of the remaining *nadī* [vowel]. What is the "remainder"? A *nadī* that is a feminine suffix (*aṅī*) consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*), such as *ṅīp* or *ṅīṣ*. Examples: *dhībandhutarā* or *dhībandhūtarā*; *strītarā* or *stritarā*. There is a prohibition for a *nadī* formed by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*). Example: *lakṣmītarā*, *tantrītarā*. Also, this applies to a *nadī* ending in an *ugit* suffix.

In the case of words ending in *ūṅ*, such as *nadī*, there may optionally be a short vowel before suffixes beginning with *gh* (the *gh-kāra-pratyāhāra*). For example: *śreyasītarā* or *śreyasitarā*; *viduṣītamā* or *viduṣitamā*; *mahatītamām* or *tām*. Here, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is also desired: *śreyastarā*, *vidvattamā*.
[Furthermore, the rule] *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ* [applies].

In the case of words in apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) and for the word *jātīya*, there may optionally be substitution of the masculine form after the word *mahat*. [This is] the "great fifth" (*mahāpañcamī*), the "great sixth" (*mahāṣaṣṭhī*), "great king" (*mahārājaḥ*), "great-armed" (*mahābhujaḥ*), and "of great birth" (*mahājātīyaḥ*). In the presence of *ghāsa*, *kara*, and *viśiṣṭa*, there is also the masculine form: "grass from a large [quantity]" (*mahāghāsaḥ*), "tax from a large [amount]" (*mahākaraḥ*), and "greatly distinguished" (*mahāviśiṣṭaḥ*).

The word *aṣṭan* [takes the substitution of *aṣṭā-*] before the suffix *kapāla* when it refers to an oblation (*havis*). For example: *aṣṭākapālaṃ haviḥ*. It also occurs before *go* when it means "yoked. For example: *aṣṭāgavaṃ śakaṭam*. Why "when yoked"? [Counter-example: *aṣṭagavaṃ viprasya*.
[Furthermore, the substitution of *aṣṭā-* for *aṣṭan* occurs] before a numeral, except in a *bahuvrīhi* compound or when followed by *aśīti*.

The vowel *ā* is substituted for the final vowel of the numerals *dvi* and *aṣṭan* when they are followed by another numeral. Examples: *dvādaśa* (twelve), *dvāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-two), *dvātriṃśat* (thirty-two); *aṣṭādaśa* (eighteen), *aṣṭāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-eight), *aṣṭātriṃśat* (thirty-eight).
Why specify "when followed by a numeral"? [To exclude cases such as] *dvaimāturaḥ* (born of two mothers).
Because of the rule stating "before one hundred" (*prākśatāt*), it does not apply here: *dviśatam* (two hundred), *aṣṭasahasram* (eight thousand).
Why [is the rule] not applied to non-bahuvrīhi compounds and to the word *aśīti*? For example: *dvidaśāḥ*, *dvitrāḥ*, *dvyaśītiḥ*.
[In the case of *tri*,] *trayaḥ* [is substituted].
The substitution of *tre-* for *tri-* should occur [before a word beginning with a vowel]. Examples: *trayodaśa* (thirteen), *trayoviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-three), *trayastriṃśat* (thirty-three).

[This applies] only when referring to a number—e.g., *traimāturaḥ* (born of three mothers). [This applies] only when it is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound and not before *aśīti*—e.g., *tricaturāḥ* (three or four), *tryaśītiḥ* (eighty-three). [This applies] only before *śata*—e.g., *triśatam* (three hundred), *trisahasram* (three thousand).
According to the Vibhāṣā, for all [the factors] beginning with forty, [this applies].

Regarding the words *dvyaṣṭa*, *tri*, and *śabda*, that which has been stated may optionally occur when followed by *catvāriṃśat* and so forth, up to *navati*. Thus: *dvācatvāriṃśat* or *dvicatvāriṃśat*; *aṣṭācatvāriṃśat* or *aṣṭacatvāriṃśat*; *trayaścatvāriṃśat* or *tricatvāriṃśat*. Likewise, *dvānavati* or *dvinavati*; *aṣṭānavati* or *aṣṭanavati*; *trayonavati* or *trinavati*. How is *ekādaśa* (eleven) formed? It is through the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) from *kusīda* and *daśaikādaśāt*.
[Also, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs] before *lekha*, *ya*, *daṇ*, and *lāsa*.

When followed by words such as *lekha* and others, the word *hṛdaya* becomes *hṛd*. *Hṛllekhaḥ* means consumption (tuberculosis); [here] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) because it "writes upon the heart. *Hṛdyam* means dear to the heart; *hārdam* means belonging to the heart. *Hṛllāsaḥ* [is formed with *ghañ*].
[The suffix] *śyañ* is optionally used after *hṛd* when expressing grief or disease.
In these cases, the word *hṛdaya* may optionally become *hṛd*: *hṛcchokaḥ* or *hṛdayaśokaḥ*; *sauhārdyam* or *sauhṛdayyam* (some say *sauhṛdyam*); *hṛdrogaḥ* or *hṛdayarogaḥ*.
[The substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs] before the words *āj*, *ati*, *go*, and *upahata*.
In the case of words such as *ājya* and others, the substitute *pada-* shall take the place of *pāda-*. Examples: *padājiḥ*, *padātiḥ*, *padagaḥ*, *padagaiḥ bahubhiḥ stutam*, *padopahataḥ*.
[The substitution of] *pada-* occurs before the suffix *yat* when it does not have its own inherent meaning (*atadarthe*).

In the word *pāda*, when it ends in a consonant (*hal*), the substitute *pat* shall take its place. Examples: *padyāḥ kaṇṭhakāḥ* (thorns that pierce the feet). Why "not having that meaning" (*atadarthe*)? [Counter-example: *pādyaṃ jalam* (water for washing the feet).

[The suffix] *ika* is added after *pāda* in the sense of "moving by means of. Example: *padikaḥ* (one who moves on foot). [The suffix] *ṣṭhan* is applied because the word belongs to the *parpādi* group. And [the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied] after *pāda* when combined with *himakaṣi* and *hati*.

In these [compounds], *pāda* becomes *pad*. Examples: *paddhimam*, *mānuṣaḥ nāma padkāṣī*, *paddhatiḥ*. Because of the word *ca* (and), [the forms] *padgāḥ* [are included]. [The suffix] *śas* is applied after *ṛc* when [referring to] the sage Bharadvāja together with his disciples.

The suffix *śas* shall be applied after the word *ṛc* when it denotes a quarter (*pāda*). [For example: "They recite the Gāyatrī verse by quarters" (*paccho gāyatrīṃ śaṃsanti*). [The suffix] *śas* is used here in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Why "after *ṛc*" (*ṛcaḥ*)? [Observe: "He gives a kārṣāpaṇa coin by the quarter" (*pādaśaḥ kārṣāpaṇaṃ dadāti*).
[The suffix *śas* is also applied] optionally (*vā*) when the words are mixed with sounds of shouting (*ghoṣamiśraśabda*).
In these [compounds], *pāda* may optionally become *pat*: *padghoṣaḥ* or *pādaghoṣaḥ*; *panmiśraḥ* or *pādamiśraḥ*; *pacchabdaḥ* or *pādaśabdaḥ*.
Also before *niṣka*: *panniṣkaḥ* or *pādaniṣkaḥ*.
In a name (*saṃjñā*), *udaka* becomes *uda*: [e.g., *udameghaḥ*].
In a name, *udaka* becomes *uda*. For example: *udamegha* (name of a person).
And [the substitution occurs] for the final member of a compound as well: *lohitoda* (name of a sea), *kṣīroda*, *lavaṇoda*.
Also before the words *peṣam*, *vāsa*, *vāhana*, and *dhi*: [e.g., *udapeṣam*, *udavāsa*, *udavāhana*, *udadhi*].

In these cases, *uda* shall be substituted for *udaka*. He grinds ginger with water (*udapeṣam*). She is intent on staying overnight in water (*udavāsa*). One who carries water (*udavāhanaḥ*). The ocean (*udadhiḥ*).
When a single plow or similar object is to be filled, the substitution may optionally take place.

When a dissyllabic word beginning with *hal* (a consonant) follows as the second member, the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* may optionally take place. For example: *udakumbhaḥ* or *udakakumbhaḥ*; *udapātram* or *udakapātram*.
Why "beginning with a single consonant"? [Consider: *udakasthānam*. Why "when it is to be filled"? [Consider: *udakagiriḥ* ("a mountain full of water").
Furthermore, this substitution occurs before *mantha*, *odana*, *saktu*, *bindu*, *vajra*, *bhāra*, *hāra*, *vīvadha*, and *gāha*.

In these cases, there may be the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-*. Examples include: *udamanthaḥ* (barley gruel with water), *udaudanaḥ* (rice with water), and *udasaktuḥ* (flour with water). [The text mentions: "shattering the heart with drops of water resembling snow-flakes" (*himalava-sadṛśa-śrama-udabindūn bhindānaḥ hṛdayam asāhi nodavajraḥ*).
The terms *bhāra-hāra-gāhāḥ* include those ending in the suffix *-aṇ* (kṛtya) and those ending in *ghañ*: *udabhāraḥ* (a load of water) and *udabhārī* (a woman carrying a load of water).

*Udahārī* is a woman who draws water; *udavīvadhaḥ* is a water-skin. [In the sense of] "of women (*rāmāṇām*) who resort to constant deep immersion (*anavaratodagāhabhājām*)," there are forms such as *udakamantha* and others. The substitution of *uda-* has been stated. [Now follows:
"In place of *ika*, a short vowel is substituted before a non-ṅit suffix, according to Gālava."

For words ending in *i* or *u*, there may optionally be a short vowel [before the suffix *ap*]. Examples: *grāmaṇiputraḥ* or *grāmaṇīputraḥ*; *jambulatā* or *jambūlatā*; *dhībandhūsutaḥ* or *dhībandhusutaḥ*. Why say "ending in *i* or *u*"? Consider *gārgīputraḥ*. By virtue of the rule of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), this does not apply here: *kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*.
A prohibition must be stated for those [words] that undergo the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions, as well as for indeclinables: *śrīkulam*, *bhrūkulam*, *śuklībhūtam*.
The forms *bhrūkuṃsa* and so forth are accepted. Thus, one may have *bhrūkuṃsaḥ* or *bhrukuṃsaḥ*; *bhrūkuṭiḥ* or *bhrukuṭiḥ*.

Some maintain that the vowel *a* is also [an optional substitute], as in *bhrakuṃsaḥ* and *bhrakuṭiḥ*. However, in this case, in the expression *alābukarkandhudṛmphuphalam*, [the elision occurs] at the very end of the entire compound.

Because of common usage in the world regarding the final member of a compound, the shortening applies only to *dṛmphū*, and not to the two preceding ones. In that case, another compound must be assumed: *alābū* and *karkandhū* are "the two *alābukarkandhvau*"; these and *dṛmphū* are "those *alābukarkandhudṛmphvaḥ*. This belongs to the *rājadantādi* group. "The fruit of those is likewise" (*tāsāṃ phalaṃ tathā*). [This is established by] the rule *eka taddhite ca*.

In a *taddhita* suffix, the word *eka-* shall take a short vowel. Examples: *ekarūpyam* (that which has come from one), *ekamayam*, *ekatvam*, *ekatā*. And when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*): *ekakṣīram* (the milk of one).
[This substitution occurs] diversely (*bahulam*) after feminine stems ending in *ṅī* or *āp* in names (*saṃjñā*) and in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

A short vowel shall be substituted for a feminine stem ending in *ī* or *ā* when it forms part of a proper name (*nāman*). Examples: *revatiputraḥ*, *rohiṇiputraḥ* (the son of Revatī, the son of Rohiṇī)—these are names of certain individuals. *śilavahaṃ* and *śilaprastham* are names of a city. Because of their frequency, [names like] *nāndīghoṣaḥ* are included.
Also when not forming a compound name (*asaṃjñāyām*): *kalajñaḥ*, *mandurajaḥ*, *susūkṣmajaṭakeśo vratī*. And also before the suffix *tva*.
The particle *ca* may optionally follow *tve* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

The long vowel *ī* is substituted for the final vowel of the words *iṣṭakā*, *iṣīkā*, and *mālā* when they appear as the first members of a compound denoting a "pile," "tuft," or "wreath" respectively.

In compounds such as *iṣṭakā-cita* (built with bricks) and the like, the final vowel of the first member shall be short. Examples: *iṣṭakacitam*, *iṣīkatūlam*, *mālabhāriṇī*. And this rule applies to words ending in those [terms]—for example: *pakveṣṭakacitam*, *navahāṭakeṣṭakacitam*, *muñjeṣīkatūlam*, and "a girl who wears a garland of lotuses" (*utpalamālabhāriṇī*).
[This also applies] when a word ending in a *khit* suffix is not an indeclinable.
In the case of a non-indeclinable [first member], the *khidanta* [second member] shall have a short vowel. Examples: *kālimejayaḥ*, *kālimmanyā*.

Why "of a non-indeclinable"? Consider: *divāmanyā rātriḥ katham api na padmair vikasitam* ("The night was considered as day; yet somehow the lotuses did not bloom"). [Also: *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*. (The augment *mum* is added after *aru*, *dviṣat*, and words ending in *ac* when followed by a word beginning with a vowel).

The suffix *mum* is applied after these [words ending in *khi*]: *aruntudaḥ*, *dviṣantapaḥ*, *dviṣamejayaḥ*. For words ending in vowels (*ajanta*): *paṇḍitammanyaḥ*, *subhagammanyā*, *harimmanyaḥ*, *mahimmanyā*, *kālimmanyā*, *vidhummanyaḥ*, *vadhummanyā*, *subhrummanyā*. When there is elision of *n* (*nalopa*), as in *rājammanyaḥ*, *surājambhavam*, *guṇimmanyaḥ*.
What [is the result] for these? *vidvanmanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself learned"), *śrīmanmanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself prosperous"). [The rule is:
"In place of *iC*, there is substitution of a single-vowel [vowel], as if it were the suffix *am*."

In place of a monosyllabic stem ending in an *ij* suffix before a *khit* affix, there shall be the substitution of *am*. And that [substitution] is like the *am* augment (*am-pratyaya-vat*). The meaning is that it is like the second case singular. Examples: *striyam-manyaḥ*, *strīm-manyaḥ*; *bhruvam-manyaḥ*, *bhrūm-manyaḥ*; *naram-manyaḥ*, *nṛm-manyaḥ*; *gām-manyaḥ*, *gom-manyaḥ*; *nāvam-manyaḥ*, *nāvum-manyaḥ*.
Also, the forms *vācaṃyama-* and *purandara-* are established.
These two [suffixes] are elided when followed by the word *kāra*,
provided it refers to something other than a true promise (*satyāgada*).
The suffix *mum* shall be applied after these two [words] before the word *kāra*. *satyaṅkāraḥ* (one who makes a promise); *agadaṅkāro vaidyaḥ* (a physician who dispels disease).
Also after *astu*: *astuṅkāraḥ*. After *dhenu* before the word *bhavyā*: *dhenumbhavyā gauḥ* (a cow that is likely to become a milch-cow).

In the sense of "filling the world," *lokaṃpṛṇa* refers to the moon. In the sense of "kindling," *bhrāṣṭrāgnīndha* refers to one who kindles a frying pan and one who kindles fire. In the sense of "making," *uṣṭraṃkaraṇa* and *bhadraṃkaraṇa* refer to the making of a camel and the making of something auspicious. In this same way, other types of technical names (*saṃjñā*) such as *timiṅgila*, *dīpaṅkara*, and *sarvaṃdada* are also to be inferred through the application of the rule by splitting the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*), namely that the suffix *mum* is added.

The suffix *putraṅ* is optionally applied after the words *sūta*, *ugra*, *rājan*, *bhojaka*, and *meru* when followed by the word *duhitṛ*. After these, the word *duhitṛ* may optionally take the suffix *putraṅ*. Examples: *sūtaputrī* or *sūtaduhitā*; *ugraputrī* or *ugraduhitā*. It is also seen elsewhere: *śailaputrī*. Māgha says: "Beholding the mark of saffron on the breasts of the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, [he thought], 'This is the consort of Acyuta. According to Vāmana’s commentary, some read the word *putra* in the list beginning with *śārṅgarava*. By this, the following is established: "I give to you the daughter of Kṛṣṇadāsa. The suffix *ñ* is applied after *śyena* and *tila* when followed by *pāta*.

The augment *mum* shall be inserted after these two [words] when followed by the suffixes *ñā* and *ante*, as well as by *pāta*. Examples: *śyenampātā mṛgayā* (a hunt conducted by means of a hawk), *tailampātā kriyā* (an action performed with oil).
Regarding the word *rātri*, the augment is optional before a *kṛt* suffix.

When a *kṛt* suffix follows, the augment *mum* may optionally be inserted after the word *rātri*. Thus, one may say either *rātricaraḥ* or *rātriñcaraḥ*, or *rātryaṭaḥ* or *rātrimaṭaḥ*. However, when a *khit* suffix follows, the insertion of *mum* is required by the preceding rule; for example, *rātrimmanyamahaḥ*. The *mum* has been explained.
Now, the elision of the *n* of the negative particle *nañ*: [The *n* of *nañ* is elided before a following vowel.]

When a subsequent member of a compound follows, there shall be the elision of the *n* of the negative particle *nañ*. Examples: *abhikṣuḥ*, *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, *avijñaḥ*, *aśocyaḥ*. How is it that [the forms] *naikakīrttiḥ* and *naikayaśāḥ* are not [examples of this rule]? In a compound, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is that which ends the entire compound; and that [condition] does not exist here [in these cases].
There is an extension of the rule to include finite verbs (*tiṅ*) when used in a sense of contempt (*avakṣepa*). Examples: "O fool, you do not cook! You do not do it! / "It is utterly laughable."
Therefore, *nuṭ* [is inserted] before a vowel.
The augment *nuṭ* shall be applied after the negative particle *nañ* when it loses its *n* before a vowel-initial suffix. Examples: *anaśvaḥ*, *anuṣṭraḥ*, *anūruḥ*.

In the words *nabhrāj*, *naptṛ*, *nava*, *veda*, *nāsatya*, *namuci*, *nakula*, *nakha*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *nakra*, and *nāka*, the negative particle *nañ* remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*).

In these eleven cases, the negative particle *nañ* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). *Na bhrājate* = *nabhrāṭ* (one who does not shine). *Na pāti* = *napāt* (a grandson; ending in the suffix *śatṛ*). *Na vetti* = *navedāḥ* (one who does not know; ending in the suffix *asun*). *Nāsatyāḥ* (the truthful ones; the virtuous).
Words such as *namuci* and others, which are technical names (*saṃjñā-śabda*), are to be inferred in whatever way appropriate.
And in the case of *ekādi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the word *eka*.

A compound beginning with *eka-* and followed by a negative particle (*nañ*) shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*), and the augment *ad* is added to *eka-*. Thus, "not twenty by one" is *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*; "not a hundred by one" is *ekānnaśatam*. Here, the negative particle has the sense of "deficient" (*ūna*).
Furthermore, in the case of "mountain" (*naga-*) when referring to non-living beings, it is optionally [treated as such].

The word *naga* may optionally be treated as a *nañ*-compound by its very nature. Examples: *śailanagau* (mountains) and *vṛkṣanagau* (trees). Why "not referring to living beings"? Consider: *ago vṛṣalaḥ śītena* (the low-born man is [like] a non-cow because of the cold).
In the case of the word *sahasra*, it becomes *sa-* when used as a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *khañ* (īya) occurs after the word *sahasya* when it denotes a name; likewise after *sāśvattha*.
Why "when it denotes a name"? [Consider] *sahayudhvā* ("one who has fought together").
It also occurs when there is an addition at the end of a book.

At the end of a book, and when there is an addition, that [compound] occurs; for example, *sakalaṃ jyautiṣam adhīte*—the meaning is "he studies the entire science of astronomy" (*kalāntam*). *Samuhūrtam adhīte*. *Sasaṅgrahaṃ vyākaraṇam adhīte*. When expressing the "end," it is an *avyayībhāva* compound. Regarding "in excess": *sadroṇā khārī*; the meaning is "a *khārī* with an additional *droṇa*" (*droṇādhikā*).
And [this applies] in the second case when the object is indefinable (*anupākhye*).

The term *upākhya* means "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*); that which is other than this is *anupākhya*—the second relative (*sambandhin*), namely, that which is inferable (*anumeya*). When a word expressing such [an inferable entity] is used as an *upapada*, the substitute *sa-* shall take the place of *saha*. Examples: *sāgniḥ kapotaḥ* ("a pigeon accompanied by fire"), *sapiśācikā vātyā* ("a whirlwind accompanied by a female Piśāca"). Because of the falling of a pigeon at home, its second correlate, fire, is inferred.
Furthermore, in an *avyayībhāva* compound, [the substitution occurs] except when referring to time.

In this context, *saha* may optionally become *sa-* [before a following vowel]. [Examples: *sacakraṃ nidhehi* (place it with the wheel), *sadhuraṃ vraja* (go with the yoke-pole). Why "not at the end of a compound"? [Counter-example: *sahāparāhṇam*. [The rule] *vopasarjanasya* applies.

In a compound where every element is subordinate (sarvopasarjana), the word *saha* may optionally become *sa-* before a final member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *saputraḥ* or *sahaputraḥ*; *saparivāraḥ* or *sahaparivāraḥ*.
[The substitution of *sa-* for *saha*] is by rule (*prakṛtyā*) when the following words are *āśis*, *go*, *vatsa*, or *hala*.

In the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the word *saha* may optionally remain in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *svasti te sahaputrāya* (May it be well with you and your son); *sahabandhave* (with your kinsmen). Why not in the case of *go*, *vatsa*, and *hala*? [Counter-examples: *sagave*, *savatsāya*, *sahalāya*. In the alternative—*sahagave*, *sahavatsāya*, *sahahalāya*. In Vedic usage (*chandas*), the word *samāna* remains in its original form before words beginning with *amūr-dha* and ending with *udarka*.
This is a Vedic rule:
[the final *i* of a word ending in *i* or *ī* becomes long] before the words *jyotis*, *janapada*, *rātri*, *nābhi*, *nāman*, *gotra*, *rūpa*, *sthāna*, *varṇa*, *vayas*, *vacana*, and *bandhu*.

In these twelve subsequent compounds, *samāna* (common) becomes *sa*. [Examples: *sajyotiḥ*, *sajanapadaḥ*, *sarātriḥ*, *sanābhiḥ*, *sanāmā*, *sanāmnī kanyā* (a girl of the same name), *sarūpaḥ*, *savayāḥ*, *savacanaḥ*, *sabandhuḥ*. Regarding this, Vāmana’s commentary states that there is a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) for *samāna*; by this, forms such as *sapakṣa*, *sadharma*, and *sajātīya* are established. However, this separation of the rule is not original to the tradition (*anārṣa*). For indeed—since indeclinables have multiple meanings—these usages are instances of the word *saha* meaning "similar" (*sadṛśa*). How else could forms such as *samānapakṣa* and so forth also occur? Thus says the Bhāgavṛtti.
The Cāndras, however, state that there is an optional substitution of *sa* for the initial [of the second member] in words such as *nāman*.
In the case of *caraṇa*, meaning a Vedic school (*brahmacārin*), when it refers to one who has attained proper conduct (*ācāra*), the *sa* of the compound shall occur; thus, *sabrahmacārī*.
Those who [are] at the sacred ford.
The suffix *uda* is substituted for *udara* when preceded by *vibhā*.

The suffix *yat* occurs at the end of a compound with *samāna* when it means "fellow-student" (*satīrthya*), as in *samānatīrtha*; likewise, those who have the same teacher are called *ekaguru*. When combined with *udara*, it forms *samānodarya* or *sodarya*, meaning "uterine brother.
[The suffix *vatup* is applied] after words ending in *dṛś* or *dṛk*.

In these cases, the substitute *sa-* shall be used for *samāna-*. [The forms] *sadṛk*, *sadṛśaḥ*, and *sadṛkṣaḥ* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). The mention of the suffix *-vat* is for the sake of what follows. The substitution of *sa-* has been explained. Now, for *idam* and *kim*, there are the substitutes *īś* and *kī*.

The substitute *idam* becomes *īd-* and *kim* becomes *kī-* when followed by those [suffixes] beginning with *īdṛk* and *īdṛśaḥ*. Thus: *īdṛk*, *īdṛśaḥ*; *iyān*, *iyatī*; *kīdṛk*, *kīdṛśaḥ*; *kiyān*, *kiyatī*.
[Furthermore,] the substitution of *ā-* occurs for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) [before these suffixes].

In these [words], the long vowel *ā* shall replace the final syllable of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). For example: *tādṛk*, *tādṛśaḥ*; *tāvān*; *etāvān*; *etādṛśaḥ*, *etādṛk*; *yāvān*; *yādṛk*, *yādṛśaḥ*; *anyādṛk*, *anyādṛśaḥ*; *yuṣmādṛk*, *yuṣmādṛśaḥ*; *bhavādṛk*, *bhavādṛśaḥ*; *amūdṛk*, *amūhag* (variant: *amūhāk*), *asmādṛk*, *asmādṛśaḥ*.
Furthermore, when the suffix *vap* follows, the *ṭi* (the last vowel and following consonant) of the words *viṣvak* and *deva* becomes *adri* before the suffix *añcu*.

The *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the words *viṣvak* and *deva* is replaced by *adri* when followed by the suffix *añcu* with the augment *vap*. Thus: *viṣvagañcati* becomes *viṣvadryaṅ* and *viṣvadryañcau*;
*devadryaṅ*; *yadryaṅ*; *tadryaṅ*; *kadryaṅ*; and *kadrīcī*. Why "with the suffix *vap*"? [Observe: *viṣvagañcanam*.
The letter *sa* [is a position of contact] when followed by *sa*.
The word *samyañc* is prescribed as *sam-*, etc., when followed by a vowel-initial suffix. Thus: *samyaṅ*, *samyañcau*, *samīcī*.
[Also,] *tiras* becomes *tiri* when the syllable *a* is elided.

The word *tiras* is replaced by *tiri* when the *al* suffix is elided; for example, *tiryaṅ*. Why "when the *al* is elided"? To prevent it from applying when there is no elision, as in: *tiraścaḥ paśya* ("look at the crosswise ones") or *lajjā tiraścāṃ yadi cetasi syāt* ("if shame were present in the hearts of animals").
[Furthermore,] *sahas* is replaced by *sadhri*.

In that [context], *sadhri* may be used for *sahasya*. *Sadhryaṅ* is used when one is intent on the highest good; as in *lakṣmaṇo’bhūt sadhryaṅ*. The forms *sadhryañcau* and *sadhrīcā* occur when the lotus-stalk fiber is coiled. *Sadhrīcī* is likewise used. [The rule] *sadhamādasthayoś chandasi* applies in the Vedic language.
This is Vedic. The word *apa* is elided after dual endings and after the suffix *uṣasarga*.
After these [prefixes], *ī* shall be substituted for the initial vowel of the following word, such as *apa*. Examples: *dvīpam*, *antarīpam*.
Regarding prefixes beginning with *pra* that do not end in a nasalized vowel (*anavarṇa*), there is specific designation: *samīpam*, *nīpam*.
But not here: *prāpam*, *parāpam*.
In the region north of the [Vindhya] mountains.
After *anu*, the word *ap* shall become *ūt*. Thus, *anūpa* means "a marshy region. Elsewhere, it is *anvīpam*.

[Furthermore,] for any other word not standing in the genitive or instrumental case, its final vowel is replaced by *dug* before the following words: *āśis*, *āśā*, *sthās*, *sthita*, *utsuka*, *uti*, *kāraka*, *rāga*, and *ccheka*.

The augment *duk* is applied to another [word] ending in a vowel other than the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or third (*tṛtīyā*) case, when followed by *āśis* and so forth. Examples: *anyā āśīḥ* → *anyadāśīḥ*; *anyadāśā*; *anyadāsthā*; *anyadāsthitaḥ*; *anyadutsukaḥ*; *anyadūtiḥ*; *anyadrāgaḥ*. Why "not ending in the sixth or third case"? Consider: *anyasyāśīḥ* → *anyāśīḥ*; *anyenāsthitaḥ* → *anyāsthitaḥ*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states that the augment *duk* applies without distinction to both the agent (*kāraka*) and the object (*chaya*). Example: *anyenānyasya*.

Or [it may mean] one who performs another action; or "belonging to another" (*anyadīya*), meaning that which exists in another or that which belongs to another—the suffix *cha* is applied as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) because [the word *anya*] belongs to the *gaha*-class.
[The suffix is applied] optionally when the sense is "for the sake of" (*arthe*).
When *artha* follows, it may optionally become *dugdha*. [The forms] *anyadarthaḥ* or *anyārthaḥ* are examples.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, *ku-* becomes *kat* before a vowel-initial suffix.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when a vowel (*ac*) follows, the substitute *kat* shall take the place of *ku*. Examples: *kadannaṃ*, *kadindhanaṃ*, *kaduṣṇam*. Why "when a vowel"? Consider *kubrāhmaṇaḥ*. An addition should be made for the case of *tri*: *kutsitās trayaḥ* becomes *kat-trayaḥ*.
One who has mastered weapons but is not victorious, one who is wealthy yet indifferent to sacrifice,
and one who is lustful despite being old— these three are outcasts within the lineages of the Kshatriyas.
And [the same applies] to the chariot and so forth.
In these two cases, *ku-* becomes *kat*: *kadrathaḥ* (a bad chariot), *kadvadaḥ* (one who speaks badly). Also [before the word] *tṛṇa*, when it denotes a genus (*jāti*).
In this context, *ku-* becomes *kat* [before a following vowel]. *Kattṛṇam*. Why [is it said] "in the sense of a genus"? [Consider: *kutṛṇāni*.
[The substitute] *kā* [occurs for *ku-*] before the words *pathin* and *akṣa*.
What would be the substitute for *ka-* in these two cases? *kāpathaḥ*, *kākṣam*, and *kākṣeṇānādarekṣitaḥ* [are examples where] *ka-* occurs in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*).

In this context, what should be the substitute for *ku-*? [The answer is: *kāma-dhuram*, *kā-tantram*, *kā-mlam*. In the expressions *deva-ākāni-nikā-vāde*, *vāhikā-sva-svakā-hi vā*, and *kākāre-bha-bhare-kākāni-sva-bhavya-vya-bhasvani*, [the same applies].
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies when referring to a person (*puruṣa*).
In the word *puruṣa*, what [sandhi] might occur for *koḥ*? It would be either *kāpuruṣaḥ* or *kupuruṣaḥ*.
[The suffix] *kavañc* occurs in the sense of "hot."
In the sense of "slightly," *ku-* may optionally become *kā-*, *ka-*, or *kava-* before the word *uṣṇa*. Thus: *koṣṇam*, *kavoṣṇam*, or *kaduṣṇam*.
And in the Vedic language (*chandas*), this substitution also occurs before the word *pathin*.
Vedic forms;
and words such as *pṛṣodara* and others, as they are traditionally taught.

Words of the *pṛṣodara* type are correct (*sādhu*) as they are employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). The definition of the learned, however, is to be understood from the *Bhāṣya*. One whose belly is speckled is a *pṛṣodara*. One who carries water is a *valāhaka* (cloud). That upon which those speaking sit is a *bṛsī* (grass mat). It cries in the earth, thus it is a *mayūra* (peacock). Bodies (*deha*) are filled and they dissolve; thus they are *pudgala*.

*Tathatā* is the state of being as it truly is (*tathya*). A *ratna* (jewel) is that which radiates light (*ratana*). One by whom evil has been removed is a *brāhmaṇa*. One by whom sin (*enaḥ*) has been conquered is a *jina*. One who cries out fame (*yaśas*) is a *yakṣa*. That which decays in the earth (*kau*) is an *elephant* (*kuñjara*). One who destroys (*hinasti*) is a *lion* (*siṃha*). That in which beings move is a *courtyard* (*aṅganam*). The resting place of corpses is a *cemetery* (*śmaśānam*). That whose mouth is turned upward is a *mortar* (*ulūkhalam*). One who eats flesh is a *piśāca*. Thus also: *ṣoḍan*, *ṣoḍaśaḥ*, *ṣoḍhā*, *ṣaḍdhā*, and so forth. [The causes of phonetic change are:
the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*), the transposition of a phoneme (*varṇaviparyaya*), and two others: the modification of a phoneme (*varṇavikāra*) and its elision (*varṇanāśa*).
The connection of a verbal root with its meaning through an excellence [of that meaning] is called the fivefold *nirukta*.
In the locative case (ṅi), the word *ahan* may optionally replace *ahna*, when it follows a numeral or the word *viṃśati*.

For a word beginning with a numeral followed by *ahna*, the substitution of *ahan* for *ahna* may optionally occur before the locative suffix *ṅi*. Thus: *dvyahne*, *dvyahani*, or *dvyahe*; *tryahne*, *tryahani*, or *tryahe*; *vyahne* or *vyahni*; *sāyāhni*, *sāyāhne*, or *sāyāhani*. Why "before *ṅi*"? Consider *dvyahnaḥ*, meaning "born on two days" (*dvayor ahnor bhavaḥ*). This is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). In *vyahnaḥ*, meaning "one from whom a day has departed," it is a *prādi*-compound. In all these cases, the suffix *ṭac* is added after *ahnaḥ*. In *sāyāhnaḥ*, meaning "the evening of the day" (*sāyo 'hnaḥ*), it is a part-whole compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*). [Note:
In the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ*, when *ḍha* or *ra* is elided, the preceding vowel *aṇ* is lengthened.]

When there is elision of both *ḍha* and *ra*, a long vowel should replace the preceding *aṇ*. Examples: *līḍham*, *gūḍham*, *nīraktam*; *indūrājate*; *punāramate*; *punāraktam*; *punāroḍhum*; *dhātūrajaḥ*. The inclusion of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for the purpose of lengthening the vowel of the preceding member alone, even when it is not followed by a *pada*.

Here, because the elision of *ra* following *ri* is understood as being accompanied by the elision of *ḍha*, there is no lengthening in the case of the elision of *ra* after *r* in *darśanīyaḥ paṭaḥ*.

In place of the vowel *a* of the roots *sah* and *vah*, *au* shall be substituted when the suffix *ḍha* is elided. Examples: *soḍhā*, *soḍhum*, *soḍhavyam*; *vanoḍhā*, *voḍhum*, *voḍhavyam*.

The mention of "the vowel" (*avarṇasya*) is for the sake of ensuring the substitution occurs even when *vṛddhi* has already taken place. Example in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *tas*: *udavoḍhām*. Why "of the vowel"? [To exclude cases where it is not a vowel, e.g.,] *ūḍhaḥ*, *ūḍhavān*.

In the Saṃhitā.

Why "not for *viṣṭa* and others"? [Counter-examples: *viṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *aṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *svastikakarṇaḥ*. [Also, the long vowel occurs] before the suffix *kvip* following the roots *nah*, *vṛt*, *vṛṣ*, *vyadh*, *ruc*, *sah*, and *tan*.

Due to the general rule (*bāhulyāt*), it does not occur in some cases—e.g., *vihāraḥ*, *nihāraḥ*.

[The suffix] *ika* occurs after *kāśa*.

In the word *kāśa*, there is lengthening of the vowel of a prefix that ends in *i*. Examples: *pratīkāśaḥ*, *nīkāśaiḥ* (be attached with those which are near), *anūkāśaḥ*. Why "ending in *i*"? Consider *prakāśaḥ*.

Why "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *prattam*.

This [substitution] also occurs in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

In this mantra, there are six rules; they are as follows:
"In a mantra, [the long vowel occurs] for *soma*, *aśvin*, *indrī*, and *viśvadevya*, when [the word] follows *mata*."
And [the substitution of *oṣadhi* for *oṣadhī* occurs] before a case-ending other than the first.

One is empty.

Also: *śvākarṇaḥ*, *pūrvāmukhaḥ*, *uttarāmukhaḥ*, *dakṣiṇāmukhaḥ*.
According to Vāmana’s commentary (*vṛtti*), because of the inclusion of the root *dṛś* [in the rule], this lengthening also occurs here in words such as *pūruṣaḥ* and *nārakaḥ*.

The *Bhāgavṛtti* states: "Because this prescribes the final member [of the compound], it is not otherwise obtained; therefore, words such as *puruṣa* and others are technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) taught with a long vowel.

When the suffix *añc* has its vowel *a* and its consonant *k* elided, a long vowel shall be substituted [for the remaining *i*]. Examples: *dadhīcaḥ paśya* (behold Dadhyañc), *dadhīcā*, *sadhrīcā*, *sadhrīcaḥ*, *sadhrīcī*, *madhūcaḥ*, *madhūcā*, *viṣvadrīcaḥ*, *viṣvadrīcīr vikṣipan sainyavīcīḥ* (scattering the waves of the army in all directions), *sadhrīcā valayitapadmanālasūtraḥ* (with his arms joined like a lotus-stalk thread).
[This rule applies] to the *samprasāraṇa*.

In a compound where the final member begins with a vowel, there shall be a long vowel for a penultimate *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) ending [stem]. Examples: *kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, *kaumudagandhīputraḥ*; *kārīṣagandhīpatiḥ*, *kaumudagandhīpatiḥ*. The section concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is complete. Now follows the rule regarding the stem (*aṅga*).
This is a governing heading (adhikāra). The operation concerning an *aṅga* is to be stated in the section beginning with "pañcapādī. [The next rule is: "After a consonant (*hal*)."
There shall be a long vowel for a consonant-final *aṅga* that ends in a *samprasāraṇa*. [Examples: *saṃvītam*, *āhūtam*.
Why "of the *aṅga*"? [Counter-example: *niruktam*. How [is the form] *tṛtīyā* [formed]? By means of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

In the case of *nāmi* (stems ending in long vowels), there shall be lengthening of the vowel of the preceding member (*aṅga*) before the genitive plural suffix *nām*. Examples: *agnīnām*, *vāyūnām*, *mātṝṇām*, *bhrātṝṇām*.
This does not apply to *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*.
In these two cases, the long vowel does not occur: *tisṛṇām*, *catasṛṇām*.
In the Veda, it is both ways.

and [the substitution of] *nṛ* for *naḥ*.
The long vowel is optionally substituted for the *nṛ* [of *nṛn*] before a case-ending beginning with a vowel.
Some say this applies even in the secular language (*bhāṣā*). Thus, one may have either *nṛṇām* or *nṝṇām*.
[This rule applies provided that] the penultimate vowel is not *n*.

The long vowel does not occur for the penultimate (upadhā) of a stem ending in *n* when followed by a *nām* suffix. For example: *pañcānām*, *saptānām*, *daśānām*. Only when followed by a *nām* suffix—such as *varmaṇām* or *carmaṇām*—does this apply. Furthermore, [the long vowel occurs] before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, except in the vocative singular.

*Śi* is the technical term *suṭ* for the case-endings of the strong cases (*sarvanāmasthāna*); when these follow, there shall be lengthening of the vowel preceding the penultimate letter (*nopadhā*). Thus: *rājā*, *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*; *sīmā*, *sīmānau*, *sīmānaḥ*; or "the *sāman*-hymns exist, look!"; *kuṇḍāni*. Why say "except in the vocative singular" (*asambuddhau*)? [Because in that case it is not lengthened]: *he takṣan*.
Or [the substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] in the Vedic texts (*nigama*) when preceded by *ṣ*.
There is one rule for the *chandas* (Vedic) sūtras:
[the elision of] a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) ending in *m* or *h*, provided it follows a long vowel (*mahat*).

In the case of a word ending in a conjunct consonant that begins with *s* or *m*, and also for the word *mahat*, there shall be lengthening of the penultimate vowel as before. Examples: *śreyān*, *vidvān*, *śreyāṃsi*, *payāṃsi*, *sarpīṃṣi*, *mahān*, *mahānti*.
This applies only when not in the vocative singular: *he śreyaṃs*.
[This rule also applies] to the stems *ap*, *tṛn*, *tṛc*, *svasṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *naṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣattṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ*.

In the presence of a *sarvanāmasthāna* (nominal suffixes of the nominative and accusative cases), there shall be lengthening of the penultimate vowel of the word *āp*, of words ending in the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*, and of the eight beginning with *svasṛ*.

Examples: *āpaḥ santi* ("the waters exist"). In a compound, because *āp* is not part of a nominal stem (*anaṅga*), there is no lengthening: *bahvapāni taḍāgāni sārasāḥ samupāsate* ("cranes frequent the many waters of the ponds"). Some say that because the rule for compound-final suffixes is not universal (*anitya*), the form *bahvāmpi* also occurs.

With the suffix *tṛn*: *karttāraḥ kaṭān* ("those who make mats"). With the suffix *tṛc*: *śrotāraḥ śāstrāṇām* ("hearers of the scriptures"). *svasārau*, *svasāraḥ*. Likewise up to: *praśāstārau*, *praśāstāraḥ*.
The same applies when [the word] is not followed by *asambuddhau* (i.e., in non-vocative singular forms): *he karttaḥ*, *he svasaḥ*, *he naptaḥ*.
[Furthermore, the long vowel is substituted for the final vowel] of stems ending in *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman* before the nominative-accusative dual suffix *śi*.

In these [words], a long vowel should occur only for the penultimate (*upadhā*) before the suffix *śas* (the nominative-accusative plural ending), and not elsewhere. Examples: *bahudaṇḍīni*, *bahuvāggamīni*, *suvṛtrahāṇi*, *supūṣāṇi*, *bahvaryamāṇi*. Why specify "before *śas*"? Consider: *vṛtrahaṇau*, *daṇḍinau*, *bhrūṇahanau*, *pūṣaṇau*, *aryamaṇau*. And one hundred.

Only when not in the vocative (*asaṃbuddhau*)—as in *he aryaman* and *he pūṣan*. [This applies] to that which ends in *at* or *as*, provided it is not a verbal root (*adhātoḥ*).

There shall be lengthening of the penultimate vowel of a stem ending in *at*, *an*, or *as* before the nominative singular suffix *su*. Examples of stems ending in *at*: *bhavān*, *kṛtavān*, *gomān*. Examples of stems ending in *as*: *suyaśāḥ*, *candramāḥ*, *sumedhāḥ*.
Why "not after a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*)? [Consider: *piṇḍagraḥ* (one who swallows a ball).

A nasalized vowel (anunāsika) is replaced by its corresponding non-nasalized counterpart before the suffix *kvi* and before consonant-initial affixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*.
