In the case of roots ending in vowels, as well as for *han* and *gam*, there is lengthening of the vowel before a suffix beginning with *jhal* when the desiderative suffix (*san*) follows. Examples: *cicīṣati* (he wishes to collect), *cikīrṣati* (he wishes to do), *jihīrṣati* (he wishes to take), *jighāṃsati* (he wishes to kill). *Adhijigāṃsate śāstram* (he desires to study the scripture).

Because the rule refers to the substitute form *iṅ* for *gam*, it does not apply here: *sañjigaṃsate vatsaḥ mātrā* (the calf desires to go with its mother). Regarding the root *tan*, there is an option.
Alternatively, there may be a lengthening of the vowel in the root *tan* when preceded by *saṇ*: *titāṃsati* or *titaṃsati*. This occurs only before a *jhal* consonant—thus, *titaniṣati*.
And the same applies to the root *kram* when followed by the suffix *ktvā*.
In the case of the root *kram*, there may optionally be a long vowel before the suffix *ktvā*; thus, either *krantvā* or *kramitvā*.
This applies only when a *jhal* consonant follows—hence *kramitvā* [in other cases].
Furthermore, for the sounds *ch* and *v*, the substitutes *śū* and *ūṭ* respectively occur before an affix beginning with a nasal or a *jhal* consonant.

When *kvip* follows, and when a *jhal* (consonant) beginning with a *kṅit* suffix follows, as well as when an *anunāsika* (nasal) follows, the *ś* of *satuk* *ch* and the *ś* of *vas* become *ṣ*. Examples: *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*, *pṛṣṭaḥ*, *pṛṣṭvā*, *śabdaprāśau*. In this rule, the term *kṅiti* does not carry over [from the previous sūtra]. Furthermore, the carry-over of *kvip*, *jhal*, and so forth is for the sake of the letter *v*; according to some, it is not for the sake of the letter *ch*. According to that opinion, the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch* occurs by the rule *vraśca-ādi-sūtra* itself, both before a *jhal* and at the end of a word (*padānte*).

[The form] *pṛṣṭaḥ* [is derived from the root] *praś*. [The form] *pṛṣṭvā* [is derived from the same root with the suffix] *ktvā*. [From the root] *prach*, we have *śabdaprāṭ*; [in the dual] *śabdaprāḍbhyām*; but when beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*), it is *śabdaprācchau*. Now, regarding the substitution of *uṭha* for *vas*: [from the root] *siv*, there is the *na*-suffix by the *uṇādi* rule; thus, *akṣadyūḥ*, *hiraṇyaṣṭhyūḥ*, *vastrasyūḥ*, *ratnasyūḥ*. [The forms] *dyūtam* and *dyūtvā* [are derived from the root] *div*.

However, for those who do not carry forward the condition *kṅiti*, according to them, when there is *yaṅluk* of the roots *dhāv* and *dyut*, even before a *pit* suffix that is not *kṅit* but a *jhal* [consonant], there is the substitution of *uṭha* for *vas*: *dādhauti*, *dedyoti*.

In the case of the elision of *val* in other [roots], there is *dādhāti* and *dedeti*. [This applies to] the roots *jvar*, *tvar*, *śriv*, *yav*, and *mav*, as well as the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

For these roots, as well as for the root *vas*, the substitution of *uṭ* (the vowel *u*) shall take place before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*, when the suffix *kvip* follows. Thus: *jaḥ*, *jūrau*, *jūrṇaḥ*, *jūrttiḥ*; *tūḥ*, *tūrau*, *tūrṇaḥ*, *tūrttiḥ*; *śrūḥ*, *śruvau*, *śrūtiḥ*; *ūḥ*, *uvau*, *ūtiḥ*; *mūḥ*, *muvaḥ*, *mūtiḥ*.
[In the case of roots ending in *r* or *l*,] there is elision (*lopa*) of the *r* or *l*.

The *repha* (the letter *r*) is elided before the suffixes *kvip*, *śa*, and *vyañjanas* beginning with *jhal* that are marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Examples: from *mūrch*—*mūḥ*, *murau*, *mūrtiḥ*; from *urvī*—*ūḥ*, *ūrtiḥ*; from *turvī*—*tūḥ*, *turau*, *turaḥ*, *tūrtiḥ*.
In this [section], up to the end of the *abhyaḥ* section, what is taught is to be treated as if it were not established (*asiddhavat*).

Up to the rule *ā bhāt* (P. 6.4.63), operations that are mutually unestablished (*parasparam-asiddha*) must be understood. *edhi* (from √*as*); *śādhi* (from √*śās*). After a root ending in a *jhal* consonant, *hi* is substituted for *hi*. [In *jahi* (from √*han*),] the elision of *hi* does not occur. Why is "here" (*atra*) specified? So that it does not apply in cases of different bases (*vyāśraya*): *praṇamayya gataḥ*. In this case, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] before the causative suffix *ṇic* is not established (*asiddha*) with respect to the substitution of *ay* for *e* [in *praṇamaya-ya*]. Why "up to *ā bhāt*"? Consider *abhāji rāgaḥ* (the passion was divided).
Here, the *vuk* augment and the *yuṭ* augment are to be stated as established (*siddha*) with respect to the *uvaṅ* and *yaṇ* substitutions respectively. Thus: *babhūva*; *upadidīye*.
There is elision of the *n* after a suffix ending in *ś*.
There is the elision of the *n* of the suffix *śnam*. [Examples: *anakti*, *hinasti*.
[The rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* applies.]

When followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *n* of roots ending in a consonant that have *n* as their penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel. Examples: *srastaṃ* (past passive participle); *sanīsrasyate* (desiderative). Why "of roots not having *i* or *t* as it" (*aniditām*)? Consider *vand*—*vandyate*. Why "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? Consider *nīyate*. Why "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*)? Consider *nahyate*. Why "when followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅiti*)? Consider *sraṃsitā* (future active participle). The elision of *n* occurs after the root *lag* and *kap* when followed by the suffix *laṅ* (the *kṛt*-suffix *-it*, i.e., *-ta*), provided that the meanings are "affliction" (*upatāpa*) and "bodily change" (*śarīravikāra*) respectively. Examples: *vilagitaḥ*; *vikapitaḥ*.
The substitution of *sa* for the root-final consonant occurs before the suffix *śap* in the case of the roots *daṃś*, *sañj*, and *svañj*.
The *n* of these [roots] is elided before the suffix *śap*. Examples: *daśati*, *prasajati*, *pariṣvajate*.
And also for the root *rañj*.

When the suffix *śap* follows, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the nasal (*na*). Thus: *rañjati*, *rañjanti*. In the sense of "pleasing deer" (*mṛgaraṇe*), when the causative suffix *ṇic* follows the root *rañj*, [the nasal is elided]: *rañjayati mṛgān*; *rañjitā mṛgāḥ*. Why "in the sense of pleasing deer"? [Consider: *rañjayati vastram* ("he dyes the cloth"). However, in the case of the suffix *ghinuṇ*, the elision of the nasal occurs by virtue of the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) "tyajarāja": *rāgī*.

But here, in the cases of *rajakaḥ*, *rajanam*, *rajatam*, and *rajaḥ*, the elision of the nasal occurs by the rule "aniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24), because the suffixes beginning with *uṇādi* are treated as having a *k*-marker (*kit*) or a *ṅ*-marker (*ṅit*).
And the suffix *ghañ* is used in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
In these two cases, there shall be the elision of the *n* of the root *rañj* when followed by the suffixes *ghañ* or *ni*. Thus: *rāgaḥ varttate* (passion prevails) and *rāgaḥ kuṅkumam* (saffron).
Why "in these two cases"? [Because otherwise it would be] *raṅgaḥ* (a stage or color). [Also, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *syand* in the sense of speed: *syadaḥ jave* (speed in running).
The suffix *syad* occurs after the root *vep*; otherwise, the suffix is *syanda*. [The forms] *avoda*, *aidha*, *udma*, *praśratha*, and *himaśratha* are irregularly formed.

The form *odman* is derived with the suffix *manin*. Other forms ending in *ghañ* are also treated as irregular (*nipātita*). From the root *undī*: *avodaḥ*, meaning "slightly moist. From the root *indhī*: *edhaḥ*, meaning "firewood. With the suffix *manin* after *undī*: *odman*, meaning "moisture. Regarding the phrase "wandering in battle like a loosened [rope]," there is the word *vyoṣaḥ*. The moon is called *himaśratha* because it "loosens" (*śrathnāti*) or releases the frost (*himam*). The usage of Bhaṭṭi in the *Luṭsarga* chapter is: *nirākṛtahimaśrathāḥ*. [The suffix *ghañ* is not applied] after the root *añc* when expressing honor (*pūjā*).

There shall be no elision of the final *n* of the root *añc* when it has the sense of "reverence. Examples: *añcitā guravaḥ* ("the teachers have been honored") and *añcyate* ("he honors"). Why specify "in the sense of reverence"? Observe: *udaktam udakam kūpāt* ("the water has been drawn up from the well"). [The rule applies] before the suffix *ktvā*, except in the case of the roots *skand* and *syand*.

In these two cases, the elision of *n* before the suffix *ktvā* shall not occur: *skantvā*, *syantvā*; *praskandya*, *prasyandya*. [However,] for roots ending in *j* or *n*, and for the root *naś*, the elision is optional.

The elision of the nasal (n) may optionally occur after roots ending in *j* and after the root *naś* before the suffix *ktvā*. Thus: *raṅktvā* or *raktvā*; *bhaṅktvā* or *bhaktvā*; *naṃṣṭvā* or *naṣṭvā*.
Furthermore, the elision of the nasal occurs for the root *bhañj* in the *ciṇ* formation.
In the case of the root *bhañj*, there may optionally be elision (*lopa*) of the nasal. Thus, one says either *abhāji* or *abhañji*.
In the case of the root *śās*, the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final *s*] before the affixes *aṅ* and *hal*.

The vowel *it* is substituted for the penultimate vowel of the root *śās* before the affix *aṅ*, as well as before *hal*-beginning *kiṭ* and *ṅiṭ* suffixes. Examples: *anvaśiṣat*, *śiṣṭaḥ*, *śiṣṭavān*, *śiṣyaḥ*. [In the Vedic plural] *vayaṃ śiṣmaḥ*. Why specify "before *aṅ* and *hal*-beginning suffixes"? Consider *anuśāsatam* (from *śās*), which is used in the sense of "without confusion. The substitution is not desired after the prefix *āṅ*: *āśāste*.

How is it formed with the suffix *kvip*? [The form] *āśīḥ* [is derived] by virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [stated in Pāṇini 6.4.32]: "In the case of commands to servants, [the word] *kṣiyā-āśīḥ* [is used].
[And] *śā* [is the substitute] for *hau*.
When followed by *ha* or *au*, the substitute *śā* occurs in place of the root *śās*. [Examples: *śādhi naḥ*, *karavāma kim*.
In place of the root *han*, the substitute *jahi* occurs.

The suffix *han* may optionally take the substitution *jaś*. [Thus: *jahi śatrūn*. There is elision of the nasal in roots taught with an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), as well as in *van*, *tan*, and others, when followed by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*.

When followed by a *jhal* consonant, the nasal (*anunāsika*) of these [roots] is elided before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. The roots *yam*, *ram*, *nam*, *gam*, *han*, and *man* are taught as having anudātta (low-pitched) vowels in their original enunciation. Before an affix marked with *k*: *yatam*, *yatvā*, *yatiḥ*. Before an affix marked with *ṅ*: *hataḥ*, *hathaḥ*. From the root *van* with the suffix *ktin*: *vatiḥ*. From the group of roots beginning with *tan*: *tantatiḥ*. *tatam*, *tatvā*. From the root *kṣaṇ*: *kṣatam*, *kṣatvā*, *kṣatiḥ*. Before an affix marked with *ṅ*: *atata*, *atathāḥ*. Why "before a *jhal* consonant"? [Observe: *gamyate*, *ramyate*, *ramitvā*. Why "before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*"? [Observe: *gantā*. [The nasal is optionally elided] before the suffix *lyap*.

For these [roots], the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) may optionally occur when the suffix *lyap* follows. Examples: *udyatya khaḍgam arjunaḥ* (Arjuna having raised his sword) or *udyamya*; *āgamya* or *āgatya*; *viramya* or *viratya*. By means of the "restricted option" (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), the elision of the nasal is indeed obligatory in certain cases: *āhatya*, *avamanya*, *pratatya*. [Question: How is it that [the form] *caturdigīśānavamanya māninī* occurs? [Answer: In that case, let it be so for the root *man* meaning "to obstruct," which belongs to the *curādigaṇa* and is not invariably accompanied by the causative marker *ṇic*.
And there is no lengthening [of the vowel] before the suffix *ktic*.

When the suffix *kvip* follows, there is the substitution of *gam*, as well as the elision of the nasal (*anusvāra*). Examples: *aṅgagat*, *kaliṅgagat*.
It should be stated that this applies to *yam* and the others: *saṃyat*, *ānat*, *parītat*, *suvat*.
Furthermore, for *gam* and the others, the suffix *ḍu* is applied, and the final syllable is replaced by *yaṅ*: *agregūḥ*.
The nasalized *an* and *u* [of the suffixes] become *a* when followed by *viṭ*, *van*, or *an*.
The two rules beginning with *anunāsikasya aditi* are governed [by this]. *Viṭ* and *van* are Vedic; [the forms] *avāvā* and *avāvarī*.
[The rule] *janasanakhanām saññalau* [is also governed by this].

The substitution of these [roots] for their original forms occurs before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant when followed by *san*, and also before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Examples: *siṣāsati* (desires to obtain); *sātaḥ* (past participle). Likewise, after roots beginning with *tan*, the *s* of *liṭ* (*as*) is elided—resulting in *asāta*, *asāthāḥ*. Examples: *khātam*, *jātam*, *jātiḥ*. Only before a *jhal*-beginning suffix:
*jijaniṣati*, *cikhaniṣati*, *sisaniṣati*. In the case of *ya*, it is optional (*vibhāṣā*).

Before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*, there shall optionally be the augment *āT* for those [roots] beginning with *ya*. *jāyate* or *janyate*; *jājāyate* or *jañjanyate*; *sāyate* or *sanyate*; *sāyāt* or *sanyāt*; *khāyate* or *khanyate*; *cākhāyate* or *caṅkhanyate*.
[This applies] to the root *tan-* before the suffix *yak*.
[The substitution of *ta* for the root *tan*] may optionally occur when the suffix *yaK* follows; [the forms] *tāyate* or *tanyate* [are thus derived].
Why mention *yaK*? [To show that it does not apply here: *tantanyate*. When the suffix *ktic* follows *san*, there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of this [augment *iK*].

After the root *san*, there may be elision [of the *n*] when the suffix *ktic* follows; alternatively, there may be the substitution of long *ā* [for the radical vowel]. Thus, the forms are *satiḥ*, *sātiḥ*, or *santiḥ* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

This governing rule extends up to the word *lyap*. [Now follows: *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām* (P. 6.4.47). "In place of the *r* and the penultimate *o* of the root *bhrasj*, *ram* is optionally substituted."

Before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the augment *ram* may optionally be inserted after the root *bhrasj*, which causes the elision of both the letter *r* and the penultimate vowel. Thus, one forms either *bhraṣṭā* or *rbhraṣṭā*; likewise, *bhrajjanam* or *rbhajjanam*. How is *bhṛṣṭam* formed? It is due to the greater force of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution).
Then follows the elision of the *a* by *ato lopaḥ*.

In an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, there shall be the elision (*lopa*) of the short vowel *a*. Examples: *cikīrṣitā*, *dhinutaḥ*, *kṛṇutaḥ*. By the rule of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), this elision of *a* takes precedence over *vṛddhi* and *dīrgha*: *cikīrṣakaḥ*, *jihīrṣyate*. Only when it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix does this apply—not so in *vṛkṣatvam* or *vṛkṣavān*.
Of that which has a consonant [as its penultimate].

There shall be elision of the letter *y* that follows a consonant (*hal*). Examples: *bebhiditā*, *cecchiditā*. Because the rule refers to the compound *ya* (in *yasya*), it does not apply here: *īrṣyitā*. Why "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? [Observe: *lolūyitā*.
There is an option regarding the word *kya*.

There may be the elision of the suffix *ky* following a consonant (*hal*). Thus: *samidhitā* or *samidhyitā*; *samidhitum* or *samidhyitum*; *namasitum* or *namasyitum*; *namasitā* or *namasyitā*. [This applies] by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*.

The elision of *ṇi* should occur before an *ardhadhātuka* suffix that does not take the augment *iṭ*. Examples: *pāktiḥ*, *yāṣṭiḥ*. Even in the presence of *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, or *dīrgha*, the elision of *ṇi* occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Examples: *atatakṣat*, *āṭiṭat*, *kāraṇā*, *kārakaḥ*, *kāraṇam*, *kāryate*. Why "before one that does not take *iṭ*"? [Consider: *kārayitavyam*.

In this context, since the root *gaṇ* takes the suffix *yat*, we have *gaṇeyam*; and since the root *cint* takes the suffix *rañj*, we have *cintiyā*. This elision of the *ṇi*-affix does not occur here, as it has been stated that this is due to the application of the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
[This applies] when the suffix is a *niṣṭhā* ending with the augment *iṭ*.

In the case of a *niṣṭhā* suffix that has an indicatory *i* (*seṭ*), there shall be the elision of the *ṇi* augment. Examples: *kāritam*, *gaṇitam*, *lakṣitam*. Why "with an indicatory *i*" (*seṭ*)? [Counter-example: *saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ* ("the animal was slaughtered"). [Exception: In the case of the root *jan*, the *ṇi* is not elided when used in a mantra; [e.g.,] *janitā*.
The pacifier at the sacrifice.
The two *sūtra*s [are applied] to the *mantra*;
[the suffixes] *ay*, *ām*, *ant*, *āl*, *vāyi*, *tnu*, and *iṣṇu* [are applied] to [the words] *viṣṇu* and others.

The substitution of *ṇi* for *āmi* (the causative suffix) occurs in the following forms: *Ām*: *kāmayāmāsa*, *kārayāmāsa*. *Anta*: *gaṇḍayantaḥ*. *Ālu*: *spṛhayāluḥ*. *Ayya*: *spṛhayāyyaḥ*. *Itnu*: *stanayitnuḥ*. *iṣṇuc*: *pārayiṣṇuḥ* (Vedic). [The substitution of *ṇi* for *āmi* does not occur] before *lyap* when the preceding syllable is light (*laghu*).

When *lyap* follows, there shall be the substitution of *ay* for the causative suffix *ṇi* after a root that has a light vowel (*laghu*) as its penultimate (*pūrva*). Examples: *praṇamayya gataḥ*, *prabebhidayya gataḥ*, *parigaṇayya*. Why "after a light penultimate"? [Consider: *prabodhya*, *prayācya*, *pravācya*.
[The substitution is] optional after the root *āp*.
After the causative suffix *ṇic*, the substitution of *ay* for the final vowel of the root *āp* may optionally occur even when followed by *lyap*. Thus, one may say either *prāpya* or *prāpayya*.
In Vedic usage, a long vowel is substituted for the finals of the roots *yup* and *plu* before *lyap*.
Chandas is one Sūtra;
Kṣiya is [another].
The vowel of the root *kṣi* becomes long before the suffix *lyap*. For example: *prakṣīya*.
[Furthermore, the vowel becomes long] before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktavatu*), except when they have the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

In the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, there is lengthening of the vowel for the root *kṣi*. In the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*): *upakṣīṇaḥ* (wasted away). In the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*): *idameṣāṃ kṣīṇam* (this has been consumed by them). The meaning of the causative suffix *ṇyat* consists of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); in those cases, the rule is prohibited. *kṣitam asya jātam* (his wasting has occurred)—here the *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve ktaḥ*).
Optionally, [the vowel is lengthened] when expressing abuse (*ākrośa*) or dejection (*dainya*).

In the case of verbal expressions denoting abuse or dejection, the immediately preceding rule may optionally apply. For example: *kṣīṇāyuḥ* or *kṣitāyuḥ*. Regarding dejection: *kṣīṇo varākaḥ* or *kṣito varākaḥ*; *kṣīṇakaḥ* or *kṣitakaḥ*.

[Furthermore,] before the affixes *sy*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*, when the sense is that of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or passive (*karman*), for roots taught with an initial vowel (*aj-*) or containing *han*, *grah*, or *dṛś*, there is optionally the substitution of *ciṇ* and the augment *iṭ*.

In the case of roots ending in vowels, as well as for the roots *han*, *grah*, and *dṛś*, when used in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or the passive (*karman*), the grammatical operations should optionally be like those of *ciṇ*. Furthermore, the augment *iṭ* occurs after these [roots]. In the impersonal: *śayiṣyate* or *śāyiṣyate* (he will lie down). In the passive: *dāsyate* or *dāyiṣyate gaur* (the cow will be given). With the suffix *sic*: *adiṣātām* or *adāyiṣātām* (they two ate). With the suffix *sīyuṭ*: *dāsīṣṭa* or *dāyisīṣṭa* (may he be given). With the suffix *tāsi*: *dātā* or *dāyitā* (the giver);
likewise *dhātā* or *dhāyitā* (the placer). Similarly for the root *han*: *haniṣyate* or *ghāniṣyate* (he will kill); *vadhiṣīṣṭa* or *ghāniṣīṣṭa* (may he kill).
From the root *grah*: *grahīṣyate* or *grāhiṣyate*; *grahīṣīṣṭa* or *grāhiṣīṣṭa*. From the root *dṛś*: *drakṣyate* or *darśiṣyate*; *dṛkṣīṣṭa* or *darśiṣīṣṭa*; *draṣṭā* or *darśitā*.

Here, in the section concerning the stem (*aṅga*), it is the stem itself that is extended by the rule of *ciṇvadbhāva*. Consequently, [the following forms occur]: *haniṣyate* or *ghāniṣyate*; *adhyāyiṣyate* or *adhyeṣyate*; *eṣyate* or *āyiṣyate*. For the roots *han*, *ni*, and *ṅī*, the substitutes *vadh*, *gā*, and *āṅ*—which are prescribed in other sections—are not applied here.
The augment *yuṭ* is applied after the root *dīṅ* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

The augment *yuṭ* is applied to the root *dīṅ* before suffixes beginning with a vowel other than *a*, as well as before those marked with *k* or *ṅ*. [Examples: *upadidīye*, *upadidīyire*. Why "before *k* or *ṅ*"? [Counter-example: *upadānam*. [Also: "There is elision of the final *ā* when followed by an *iṭ* augment or a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*."

In the case of roots beginning with *iṭ* (the augment) or *yaj*, and before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ* or when beginning with a vowel (*at*), there is elision of the long *ā*. Examples: *papitha*, *tasthitha*; *papatuḥ*, *papuḥ*; *godah* (cow-giver), *sarvadah* (all-giver); *gojnaḥ* (cow-knower), *sarvajñaḥ* (all-knower).
Before the suffix *yat*, *īr* is substituted [for the final *ā*].
The augment *īT* shall be applied after roots ending in long *ā* when followed by the suffix *yaT*. Examples: *deyam*, *dheyam*, *geyam*, *gleiyam*.

[Furthermore,] *yaṇ* is substituted for *iṇ* (the vowels *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*).

In place of the root *iṇ*, *yaṇ* shall be substituted before a vowel. Thus: *yanti*, *yantu*, *iyuḥ*. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *iyaṅ*. This *yaṇ* is superseded by *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* because it is an intermediate exception (*madhye'pavāda*) and because those two rules are subsequent (*paratvāt*). Examples: *ayanam*, *āyakaḥ*, *iyāya*.
[The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] in place of a single vowel that is not preceded by a conjunct consonant.

The *yaṇ* substitute shall take the place of the vowel *i* at the end of a multi-syllabic (*anekāc*) stem before a vowel. Examples: *ninyatuḥ*, *ninyuḥ*, *ninyire*; *unnayau*, *praṇyau*, *senānyau*, *senānyaḥ*, *grāmaṇyau*. This substitution is desired only for a *kvip*-derived stem that is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka (case-relation). Therefore, it does not apply here: *paramaniyau*, *paramaniyaḥ*. Because of the association with a prefix (*gati*), it is also accepted as applying only when the kāraka is part of a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*); therefore, it does not apply here: *śravaṇadhiyā* (meaning "by one whose intellect is in the ear"). Only when followed by a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* (i.e., *kṅit*) does this not apply—as in *karoti*.
[Next rule: There is elision (*lopa*) of the *a* of the roots *śn* and *as*.

The elision of *a* occurs after [the suffix] *śna* and *as* before a *sārvadhātuka* affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Thus: *bhindati*, *bhindyāt*, *bhindyuḥ*; *chindanti*. From *as*: *staḥ*, *santi*, *syāt*, *edhi*.
How is it that there is *asyati*? Because here the root *as* is taken [by the rule], as it is without an *anubandha*.
The substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) for *śna-as* is due to the fact that this is a Vedic (Pāṇinian) aphorism (*sautratvāt*).
The *ā* of the roots *śnā* and those ending in reduplication (*abhyasta*) is elided [before an affix beginning with *a*].

The *ā* of the root *śnā* and of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) roots is elided before a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a *k* or *ṅ* (i.e., having an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*). [Examples: *lunanti*, *lunate*, *lunāna*; *punate*; *dadati*, *dadat*.
[Next rule: *ir halyaghoḥ*.

In place of the long vowel *ā* of the roots *śnā* and *abhyasta*, *ir* shall be substituted before an affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ* (i.e., a *sārvadhātuka* affix). Examples: *lunīte*, *mimīte*, *jihīte*.
Why "not of *aghū*" (*aghoḥ*)? [Because in] *datte*, *dhatte*, the substitution does not apply. [Furthermore,] *id* is substituted for the final vowel of the root *daridra*.
The suffix *it* shall be applied after the root *daridrā-* when that [suffix] follows. Thus: *daridritaḥ*, *daridrithaḥ*. Only when a consonant (*hal*) follows—[as in] *daridrati*.

There is elision of the root *daridrā-* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; and this elision is established even when the suffix is being prescribed. Thus: *daridraḥ* (by adding *ac* according to the rule for *pacādi*). The suffix *ṇa* does not apply here by the rule *śyādvyadhā-*. In the *adyatanī* (imperfect), there is an option: *adaridrīt*, *adaridrāsīt*, *adaridri*, or *adaridrāyi*.
The elision [of the penultimate vowel] is not desired after *daridrāyaka* or *daridrāṇa*;
some say that the form is *didaridrāsati*, while others say it is *didaridriṣati*.

*bhiyo'nyatarasyām* | Before a *hal*-beginning *sārvadhātuka* affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, the root *bhī* may optionally take the substitute *it*. Thus, *bibhitaḥ* or *bibhītaḥ*. "At that time, we were not ourselves afraid" (*na tadā bibhimaḥ* or *bibhīmaḥ*). "On the road, we two, fearing one another, were terrified" (*anyonyataḥ pathi vatābibhitāvibhoṣṭrau*). And [the substitution of *it* applies] also to the root *jahāti*.
The forms *jahāti* and *jahati* are as before; [the forms] *jahitaḥ* or *jahītaḥ* [are also formed].
And [the substitution of *ī* for *e* occurs] before the suffix *hi*.
The root *hā* (to abandon) may optionally take the form *icca* [i.e., *ihi*]. Thus, one may say *jahāhi*, *jahihi*, or *jahīhi*.
[In the case of the suffix] *yi*, there is elision [of the penultimate vowel].
In the presence of an affix beginning with *k* or *ṅ* that has an indicatory *i* (kṅit), there shall be elision of the [root] *hā* (*jahāti*). Thus: *jahyāt*, *jahyuḥ*.
This has been stated regarding the *sārvadhātuka* affixes.
In the case of *ghu*, *sū*, and *ṛdha* roots, there is the elision of the reduplication.
In the case of the roots *ghu* and *as*, there shall be the elision of the reduplication when followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ* or *k*. *Ghu*: *dehi*, *dhehi*; *as*: *edhi*.

[Furthermore,] in the Perfect (*liṭ*), there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel *a* when it stands between two single consonants and is not the result of a grammatical substitute (*anādeśādi*).

In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, for a single vowel *a* situated between single consonants, there shall be the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication. Examples: *reṇatuḥ*, *reṇuḥ*; *rebhe*; *pece*. Why does it say "of a stem (*aṅga*) that does not begin with a substitute"? Consider: *babhaṇatuḥ*, *babhaṇuḥ*. How is it that we have *nematuḥ*, *nemuḥ*, and *sehe*? One must exclude those that begin with a substitute in the *liṭ* tense. Why does it say "between single consonants" (*ekahalmadhye*)? Consider: *tatakṣatuḥ*, *tatakṣuḥ*; *tatsaratuḥ*, *tatsaruḥ*. The rule applies only when followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ* (i.e., *kṅiti*). For example: *ahaṃ papaca* ("I cooked"). Why does it say "of *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider: *rarāse*.

In some instances, the substitution of *et* for the root vowel of *naś* and *man* occurs in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense: *aneśam*. In the *luṅ* (aorist), there is the *aṅ* suffix after roots beginning with *puṣ*: *amenakā*. In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), there is the suffix *vun*; it belongs to the *kṣipakādi* group, which is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, and therefore the substitution of *it* does not occur. [The rule] *thali ca seṭi* [also applies].

As before, the substitution of *e* for *ai* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*) shall apply here. Examples: *pecitha*, *śekitha*. Why "before a suffix marked with *ṣ* (seṭ)"? Example: *papaktha*.

From this point forward, the conditions "before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅit*), "in the perfect tense" (*liṭ*), "elision of the reduplicated syllable," and "before a suffix marked with *ṣ*" (*seṭ*) are understood to carry over.
[The rule applies to] the roots *tṛ*, *phal*, *bhaj*, and *trap*.

In these cases, there shall be the substitution of *et* (e), and in that [substitution], there is also the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*). Examples: *teratuḥ*, *teruḥ*, *teritha*; *phelatuḥ*, *pheluḥ*, *phelitha*; *bhejatuḥ*, *bhejuḥ*, *bhejitha*; *trepe*, *trepire*. This statement is made for the sake of *guṇa* in the case of the root *tṛ*, for the sake of the specific substitutes in the case of the roots *phal* and *bhaj*, and for the sake of the rule regarding vowels situated between more than one consonant in the case of the root *trap*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the sūtra, we have: *śrethutuḥ*, *śrethuḥ*; *debhatuḥ*, *debhuḥ*. Even in the case of the root *dambh*, it would not have been obtained by the preceding rule, because the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of that rule.
The root *rādha* is used in the sense of injury.
The substitution of *et* (e) occurs for the root *rādh* when it is situated between two single consonants (*ekahalmadhya*). Examples: *aparedhatuḥ*, *aparedhuḥ*, *aparedhitha*.
Why "in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsāyām*)? [Counter-example: *ārarādhur devatām* ("they propitiated the deity").
Optionally so for the roots *jṛ*, *bhram*, and *tras*: [jṛ—*ajaritar/jaritar*; bhram—*abibhramur/ababhramur*; tras—*atrasthur/atrasur*].

For these [roots], the substitution of *et* may optionally occur in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. Thus: *jeruḥ* or *jajaruvā*; *jeritha* or *jajaritha*; *bhremuḥ* or *babhramur vā*; *tresasuḥ* or *tatrasatur vā*. [The same applies] for the seven beginning with *phaṇ*.

For the roots *phaṇ*, *rāj*, *bhrāj*, *bhrās*, *bhlās*, *syam*, and *svan*, there may optionally be the substitution of *iṭ* (the augment *i*). Thus: *pheṇuḥ* or *paphaṇuḥ*; *pheṇitha* or *paphaṇitha*. *reje* or *rarāje*; *bhreje* or *babhrāje*; *bhrejire* or *babhrājire*; *bhleśe* or *babhlāśe*; *bhleśire* or *babhlāśire*; *syematuḥ* or *sasyamatuḥ*; *syemuḥ* or *sasyamuḥ*; *svenatuḥ* or *sasvanatuḥ*; *svenuḥ* or *sasvanuḥ*. [The substitution occurs] only when a *kṅit* suffix follows—thus: *rarāja*. Why mention "of the seven"? [Because it does not apply to others, as in: *dadhvanatuḥ*, *dadhvanuḥ*. [Also excluded are: those roots ending in *śas*, *das*, and *davadi*, and those that undergo *guṇa* substitution.

If [the rule] were *śasidadyoḥ dantoṣṭhyavakārādīnāṃ guṇaḥ*, then for that which has been produced by the guna [substitution], the substitution of *et* would not occur in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. For example: *viśaśasatuḥ*, *viśaśasuḥ*, *viśaśasitha*; *dadade*, *dadadāte*; "the Daityas vomited blood" (*vavamuḥ*), *vavamitha*. Regarding the guna [substitution]: *viśaśaratuḥ*, *viśaśaruḥ*, *viśaśaritha*; *lulavitha*. The mention of *śasidadi-* is for the purpose of making known that the substitution of *et* is not understood [to apply] when there is no difference in form due to a phonetic replacement (*ādeśa*). By this, the substitution of *et* is established even in cases such as *pecatuḥ* and *celuḥ*.
[The sūtra continues: *arvaṇas tṛ maghonaśca anaṅ ṅau*.
Maghavā is frequently [used].
Here are two Vedic (chāndasa) sūtras [from the *Vārttika*] which are stated in the Bhāṣya: "The forms *arvaṇas-tṛ* and *maghonas-tṛ* need not be taught as exceptions, for they are Vedic.

How then do we explain Māgha’s usage of *ślathīkṛtapragrahamarvatāṃ vrajam* ("the pen of horses whose reins have been loosened") and Vyāsa’s usage of *maghavadvajralajjānidānam* ("the cause of shame for Indra, who possesses the thunderbolt")? Poets employ even Vedic words in the common language (*bhāṣā*) because they function as proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*). For example: *paripanthin*, *adhvaryu*, *dīdhiti*, *turāṣāṭ*, *pṛtanāṣāṭ*, and so forth. [This applies to] the base (*bha*).
This heading [of authority] extends to the end of the chapter.
A *pāda* is a quarter-verse.
The substitute *pat* shall take the place of *pāda* at the end of a word. Examples: *dvipadaḥ*, *dvipadā*, *dvipade*, *dvipadikā*, *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*.
Why "of a *bha*-stem"? [Observe: *dvipādaṃ paśya*. [Next sūtra:
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowel in *vasu*.

There may be [the following examples]: *kvasuḥ*—in *upeyuṣām api divam* ("even of those who have gone to heaven") and *dhāvuṣām* ("of those who have run"); *vasuḥ*—in *viduṣā* ("by the wise man") and *viduṣī* ("a wise woman");
*vāh*—in *ḍhadyaṣṭh*.

This is Vedic; for the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed after the root *vah* in the Veda [by Pāṇini 3.2.178], and [the rule] "of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* when not followed by a *taddhita*" [applies].

For these [words], there shall be *samprasāraṇa*. [Examples: *śunā*, *śune*; *yūnā*, *yūne*; *maghonā*, *maghone*. How is it that one says *yuvatīḥ paśya*? It is because the inclusion of the specific gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇa*) is not intended here. Why say "provided it is not a *taddhita* suffix"? [Consider: the suffix *añ* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*): *śauvaṃ māṃsam* ("dog meat"). [Next rule: *allopo'naḥ* ("there is elision of the *an* of *anaḥ*").
In a *bha* suffix, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel of the word *anna*. Examples: *rājñā*, *rājñe*, *rājñī*; *takṣṇaḥ*, *takṣṇā*;
*ahnā nirvṛttam āhnikam* ("produced by the day").

Here, because the governing rule for the "body" (*aṅga*) applies, in the cases of *vṛṣaṇaśvaḥ* and *vṛṣaṇvasuḥ*, even though they possess the status of *bha*, the elision does not occur due to the absence of the status of being a "body" (*aṅgatva*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words preceded by *ṣat*, *pūrva*, *han*, *dhṛta*, and *rājan*.

The elision (lopa) of these [suffixes] occurs before the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *aukṣṇaḥ*, *tākṣṇaḥ*, *bhrauṇaghnaḥ*, *vārtraghnaḥ*, *dhārtarājñaḥ*. In cases other than these—such as *sāmanaḥ*—the elision does not occur.
Why "before *aṇ*"? Consider *tākṣaṇyaḥ* (where the suffix is *nya*).
Optionally so before the locative singular (*ṅi*) and the nominative/accusative dual (*śi*).

The elision of the vowel *a* may optionally occur before the locative suffixes *ṅi* and *śi*. Thus: *rājñi* or *rājani*; *dadhni* or *dadhani*; *sāmnī* or *sāmanī*; *dāmnī* or *dāmanī*. [However, this does not apply] after a conjunct consonant ending in *v* or *m*.

After a conjunct consonant that begins with *v*, the *l* of the suffix *an* is not replaced by *ap*. Examples: *parvaṇā*, *parvaṇe*; *carmaṇi*, *varmaṇi*; *śarmaṇā*, *śarmaṇi*; *varmaṇā*, *karmaṇā*, *karmaṇi*; *suparvaṇaḥ*; *atharvaṇā*, *atharvaṇaḥ*. [This applies] after a vowel.

There shall be elision (*al-lopa*) of the *n* of the root *añc* when it is part of a *bha*-stem that has lost its *n*. Thus: *dadhīcā*, *dadhīcaḥ*; *madhūce*, *madhūcaḥ*; *pratīcī*, *pratīcyam*; *samīcī*, *samīcīnam*.
[The suffix] *ut* [is also added].
The vowel *i* shall be substituted for the final vowel of a verbal root ending in *ud*. Examples: *udīcaḥ paśya* (look toward the north), *udīcā*, *udīcām*, *udīcī*, *udīcyam*.
[This rule applies] to a verbal root ending in *ā*.

The suffix *śas* is elided after this verbal root (*dhātu*). Examples: *śaṃsthaḥ paśya* ("look at the one standing well"), *śaṃsthā kṛtam* ("the act of standing well"), *śaṃstha idam śāṃstham* ("this is well-standing"). [In the case of] *somapāḥ* and *somape*, [the elision occurs] because it follows a verbal root.
Why? Because of the rule "after a verbal root.

Why [is there no elision in] *ktvo lyap* and *kramaśca ktvi*? Because they are irregular forms (*nipātana*), or because they are imitations of a part [of a word], just as in the case of the suffix *aṇ* [which applies] "before the suffix *dīvyat*" (Pāṇini 4.1.83).
Some say that this is due to a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). Alternatively, it should be stated as "āto 'nāpaḥ" (after a long vowel, except for *āp*, there is elision);
[this applies] to the *ātmanepada* endings following the prefix *ā* in mantras.
This is Vedic usage; for [the rule] states: "After *viṃśati*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *ḍ*."

When a suffix marked with the marker *ḍ* follows, the letter *ti* of the word *viṃśati* is elided. With the suffix *ḍun*: *viṃśakaḥ aśvaḥ* (a horse worth twenty), *dvāviṃśakaḥ*. With the suffix *ḍa*: *viṃśaṃ śatam* (one hundred less twenty).
Why "when marked with *ḍ*"? Consider *viṃśatikaḥ aśvaḥ* (a horse bought for twenty).
[The rule applies] to the final syllable (*ṭeḥ*).
When a *ḍit* suffix follows, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the final letter of a *bha*-stem. [Examples: *triṃśakaḥ*, *ekādaśaḥ sargaḥ*.
How is *kumudvān* [formed]? Even though it is not a *bha*-stem, the elision of the final letter occurs by virtue of the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) *ḍ*.
[This is governed by the rule: *na-staddhite* ("*n* is elided before a *taddhita* suffix").

In a *taddhita* suffix, there shall be elision (*ṭilopa*) of the final vowel of this [stem] when it ends in *an*. Examples: *āgniśarmiḥ*, *aurdhvalomiḥ*. Here, the suffix *iñ* is applied because they belong to the *bāhv-ādi* group.

Regarding the rule "of *sabrahmacārin*, *pīṭhasarpi*, *kalāpin*, *kuthumin*, *taitilin*, *jājalin*, *lāṅgali*, *śilālin*, *śikhaṇḍin*, *śūkara*, *sadman*, and *suparvan*": for these, there shall be elision of the final vowel as an exception to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Examples: *ime sabrahmacāriṇaḥ* → *sābrahmacārāḥ* (these are fellow students). *paiṭhasarpāḥ* (descendants of Pīṭhasarpi). *kālāpāḥ*: those who study what was taught by Kalāpin. *kauthumāḥ* (followers of Kuthumin). *taitilāḥ* (followers of Taitilin). *jājalāḥ* (followers of Jājalin). *lāṅgalāḥ* (followers of Lāṅgali). *śailālāḥ* (followers of Śilālin). *śaikhaṇḍāḥ* (followers of Śikhaṇḍin). *śaukarasadmāḥ* (followers of Śūkara-sadman). *sauparvāḥ* (followers of Suparvan).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *carman* when the sense is "in the sheath [made] of leather": *cārmaḥ kośaḥ* ("a leather sheath"). It is not applied after *carman* in any other sense. It is applied after *aśman* when the sense is "a modification [of stone]": *āśmaḥ prāsādaḥ* ("a palace made of stone"). In other cases, it is *āśmanaḥ*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied [after *aśman*] in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*). It is applied after *śvan* when the sense is "contraction": *śauvaḥ saṅkocaḥ* ("a contraction of a dog").

The elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) of indeclinables (*avyaya*) occurs before any suffix beginning with *bha*; this is for the sake of forms such as *sāyamprātika*. Examples: *sāyamprātikaḥ*, *paunaḥpunikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after a word denoting time (*kālāt*). Why "for the sake of *sāyamprātika* and others"? [Consider: *ārātīyaḥ*—here the suffix *cha* is applied after a *vṛddha* stem. [Also consider: *sandhivelādyaṇ*—*śāśvataḥ*. However, *śāśvatikaḥ* is derived by means of a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
[Furthermore, the rule] *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* applies.

The elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) occurs after the word *ahan* when followed by the suffixes *ṭa* or *kha*. The aggregate of two days is *dvyahaḥ*; [likewise] *tryahaḥ*. That for which two days have been hired, or which has lasted, or will last for two days, is *dvyahīnaḥ*.
Why "after *ṭa* or *kha*"? Consider: that which is accomplished in a day is *āhnikaṃ*. [Now follows: *orguṇaḥ* (P. 1.1.2).

In a *taddhita* suffix, there shall be *guṇa* substitution for a *bha*-stem ending in the vowel *u*. For example: *aupagavaḥ* (son of Upagu), *bābhravyaḥ* (descendant of Babhru). Because a rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably obligatory, we have: *dhāma svāyambhuvaṃ yayuḥ* (they went to the abode of Svayambhū).
[Furthermore,] when the suffix *ḍha* follows, there is elision of the final vowel of a stem, except for *kadrū*.
There shall be elision of the final vowel of a word ending in *u* before the suffix *ḍha*. Examples: *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *jāmbeyaḥ*.
Why "not ending in *ka* or *dra*"? [Counter-example: *kādraveyaḥ*. And [the elision applies] to that which is designated by the term *yasya*.

The *lopa* (elision) of the final vowel of a *bha*-stem ending in *i* or *ya* occurs when a *taddhita* suffix follows. Examples: *sakhī*, *gārgī*, *dākṣī* (referring to a young girl). Regarding *taddhita* suffixes: *valiḥ*; *vāleyāḥ taṇḍulāḥ* (rice grains belonging to Vali); *dākṣiḥ*; *cauṅiḥ*. There is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) before the suffix *śyaṅ*: *kāṇḍe*, *kuṇḍe*. The elision (*lopa*) takes precedence over the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Example: *vatsaprīḥ* is a cow; its offspring is *vātsapreyaḥ*—[formed with] *ḍhañ* after words denoting four-footed animals. *Laikhābhreyaḥ*—[formed with] *ḍhak* after words such as *śubhra*.
The penultimate vowel of the words *sūrya*, *tiṣya*, *agastya*, and *matsya* [is replaced by *i* when followed by a suffix beginning with *t*].
The *upadhā* vowel of these [words] is elided.
[This occurs] after *sūrya* when followed by a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or the suffix *cha*. *Saurī balākā* (the female crane of Sūrya); *saurīyās taṇḍulāḥ* (the rice grains belonging to Sūrya).
After *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, when referring to asterisms (*nakṣatra*), [the *upadhā* is elided]. *Taiṣaḥ*; *pauṣaḥ*.

In the case of *āgastya*, [the final syllable is elided] before a feminine suffix ending in *ṅī* and before the suffix *ccha*: *āgastī*. With the *ṛṣyaṇ* suffix, there is the *ṅīp* suffix: *āgastīyāḥ*.

In the case of *matsya*, [the elision occurs] only before a feminine suffix ending in *ṅī*: *matsī*. Why "before a feminine suffix ending in *ṅī*" (*ṅyām*)? [Observe: *mātsya* logic prevails. Why "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*)? [Observe: *matsyacarī*.
Here, in the suffix *tasi* after *antika*, the elision of the *kādi* group [of sounds] is frequent: *antikaḥ*; *antitaḥ*.

[The suffix] *tama* is substituted for *tad* and its derivatives. *Antamaḥ* (the nearest). They also accept *antikātamaḥ* in the common language (*bhāṣā*). When the initial *ka* is elided, it becomes *antitamaḥ*.
[The rule] *halastaddhitasya* applies.

There is elision of the *yakāra* of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix that follows a consonant when the feminine suffix *ī* follows. Examples: *saumī iṣṭiḥ* (a sacrifice belonging to Soma), *ānupūrvī* (succession), *vaidagdhī* (cleverness), *aucitī* (propriety), *vārkeṇī* (a female descendant of Vṛka), *gārgī* (a female descendant of Garga), *vātsī* (a female descendant of Vatsa). Why "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? Consider *kārikeyī* (the wife of Kārikeya).
Why "of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitasya*)? Consider *vaidyī*, which means "the wife of a physician" (*vaidyasya bhāryā*). Here, the suffix is not a *taddhita*.
And [the final phoneme] of a patronymic suffix is elided before a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), except when that suffix begins with *ā*.

The *apatya* (patronymic) suffix *k* shall be elided before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel other than *ā*. Examples: *gārgīyaḥ*, *vātsīyaḥ*. Before a suffix denoting a collection (*samūha*), the suffix *vuñ* is added after a *gotra* (lineage) name: *gārgakam*. Why "of the *apatya*"? Consider *sāṅkāśyakaḥ*. Why "before a suffix other than *ā*"? Consider *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, where the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *yaññiññośca*. [The elision occurs] only after a consonant: *kārikeyiḥ*. [The suffix *k* is also elided] before the denominative suffixes *kyac* and *kyan*.

There shall be elision of the letter *k* that forms part of a secondary derivative (*apatya*) after [stems ending in] *kyac* and *vyañ*. Examples: *vātsīyati*, *vātsāyate*; *gārgībhūtaḥ*, *vātsībhūtaḥ*. Only when [the stem ends in] a consonant (*hal*) does this apply—thus, *ātreyīyati*. Why "of a secondary derivative" (*āpatyasya*)? [Observe: *sāṅkāśyīyati*.
There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha* after [stems beginning with] *bilvaka* and others.

From these words ending in the suffix *ccha*—namely *naḍa* and so forth—the suffix *ccha* alone is elided when a *taddhita* suffix follows, provided that the suffix *ku* is added. For example: *bilvā yasyāṃ santi* (in which there are *bilva* trees) results in *bilvakīyā*; those who exist on the ground of *bilvakīyā* are *vailvakāḥ*. Similarly, *baiṇukāḥ*. [The rule] *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu* [applies here].
The term *iva* is introduced as a governing heading for the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun*. The word *tu* indicates that this is a portion of the Vedic meter (*chandas*).
For a *bha*-stem, the final *ṭi* (the last vowel with its following consonant) is elided before these suffixes, *iṣṭhan* and so forth. Thus: *paṭuḥ*, *paṭiṣṭhaḥ*, *paṭimā*, *paṭīyān*.
The operations of the *iṣṭhan* suffix are not to be applied to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

This statement is made for the sake of [achieving] the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), the substitution of *ra* (*rabhāva*), the elision of *ṭi*, the elision of *yaṇ* and so forth. For example: from *enī* (feminine), one says *etayati*; from *prathā*, *prathayati*; from *dūṣad*, *dūṣayati*; from *dūra*, *dūrayati*.
The prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) are also desired [to undergo these operations]: from *priya*, *prāpayati*; from *sthira*, *sthāpayati*.

In the case of *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *yaṇ* (semivowels) and so forth, the subsequent portion beginning with *yaṇ* is elided, and there is *guṇa* substitution for the preceding vowel. Among these, in the words beginning with *sthūla*, the subsequent portion starting with *yaṇ* is dropped, and *guṇa* is substituted for the preceding [vowel]. Thus: *sthaviṣṭhaḥ*, *sthavīyān*; *daviṣṭhaḥ*, *davīyān*; *yaviṣṭhaḥ*, *yavīyān*. *Hrasva* and *kṣipra* belong to the *pṛthvādi* group. [Thus]: *hrasiṣṭhaḥ*, *hrasimā*, *hrasīyān*; *kṣepiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṣepimā*, *kṣepīyān*; *kṣodiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṣodīyān*. The mention of "the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is for the sake of clarity.

In place of the words *priya*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *uru*, *bahula*, *guru*, *vṛddha*, *tṛpra*, *dīrgha*, and *vṛndāraka*, there are substituted respectively: *prastha*, *spha*, *vara*, *baṃhi*, *garva*, *ṛṣi*, *trapa*, *drāghi*, and *vṛnda*.

Among those [words], for the ten beginning with *priya*, there are exactly ten suffixes beginning with *pra*. These are: *priya*, *uru*, *laghu*, *guru*, *bahula*, *dīrgha*, *pṛthu*, and so on. From these very [bases], the suffixes *iman* and *iyas* are to be illustrated: *preman*, *preṣṭhaḥ*, *preyān*. Likewise: *stheṣṭhaḥ*, *spheṣṭhaḥ*, *variṣṭhaḥ*, *gariṣṭhaḥ*, *trapiṣṭhaḥ*, *drāghīyān*, *drāghimā*, *drāghiṣṭhaḥ*, *vṛndiṣṭhaḥ*, *vṛndīyān*. In *baṃhi*, the letter *ṃ* is for the sake of pronunciation; thus: *baṃhiṣṭhaḥ*, *varṣiṣṭhaḥ*.
[In the case of *bahu*,] there is elision of the final part of *bahu* and *bhū* is substituted for *bahu*.
And for the root *iṣ*, there is the substitution of *yiṭ*.

There shall be elision of the initial [vowel] of *iṣṭha* and the others, and for *bahu*, the substitute *bhū* is applied. Thus: *bhūyān* (comparative), *bhūmā* (superlative). The applications of *bhūman* and *rasan* are profound. Furthermore, there is the augment *yiṭ* for *iṣṭha*: *bhūyiṣṭhaḥ*.
[And] for *jyā*, *āt* is substituted before *īyasun*.
After the comparative suffix *jyās*, *āt* (the long vowel *ā*) shall be substituted for *iyas*. Thus: *jyāyān*, *jyāyāṃsau*.
The mention of *āt* is for the sake of variety; for when the initial [vowel] is elided, the long vowel remains even though the *yakāra* has not been applied. [Furthermore, by Pāṇini 6.4.161:
*ra* is substituted for a light *ṛ* that is followed by a consonant-initial [suffix].

In the place of the light *ṛ* sound belonging to a stem beginning with *hal* (any consonant), there shall be *r*. Examples: *prathiṣṭhaḥ*, *prathimā*, *prathīyān*. Since the rule applies specifically to the words *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *bhṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha*, it does not apply here: *kṛtam ācaṣṭe* → *kṛtayati*; *kṛtiṣṭhaḥ*; *mātayati*; *pitayati*; *bhrātayati*. One should remember these six—*pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *bhṛśa*, *kṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha*—in the context of the rule for the substitution of *r*.
The suffix *jaras* is optionally substituted for *jara* in the Vedic language.
Vedic;
[a word] consisting of a single syllable is its own base form.

Among those [suffixes], that which has a single vowel (ekāc) and is designated as *bha* shall remain in its original form (*prakṛtyā*). Examples: *srajiṣṭhaḥ*, *srajīyān*; *tvaciṣṭhaḥ*, *tvacīyān*. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *mat* before the suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyas*. Examples: *preṣṭhaḥ*, *premā*. Why "having a single vowel"? [Consider] *paṭiṣṭhaḥ*.
In cases other than *iṣṭha* and so on: *asyāpatyam iḥ* ("the offspring of this one is *iḥ*"); *jñā devatāsya jñaḥ* ("Jñā is his deity; he is *jñaḥ*").

The suffix *ka* is applied after *rājanya* and *manuṣya* when they denote a youth by nature; thus, *rājanyakam* and *mānuṣyakam*. [This is stated] so that there may not be the elision of the patronymic suffix (*apatyaya-lopa*). The form *yauvanikā* is derived with the suffix *vuñ* because [the base] belongs to the *manojñādi* group; [this is stated] so that there may not be the elision of the final *a* by the rule *na-staddhite*.
[Furthermore, the suffix *ka* is applied] after words ending in *ina*, provided it is not a patronymic suffix (*anapatye*).

The suffix *ini* (forming adjectives) would naturally apply to words ending in *an*, provided they do not denote offspring (*anapatya*). Examples: *sāṃrāviṇam*, *sāṃkūṭinam*, *sāṃmārjinam*; and from *sragvin*, *srāgviṇam*. Why "provided they do not denote offspring"? Consider: the offspring of *medhāvin* is *maidhāvaḥ* [meaning] a son.
[Also included are: *gāthin*, *vidathin*, *keśin*, *gaṇin*, and *paṇin*.

This undertaking is for the sake of offspring. These [words] shall remain in their original form even when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to denote offspring: *gāthinaḥ*, *vaidathinaḥ*, *kaiśinaḥ*, *gāṇinaḥ*, *pāṇinaḥ*; likewise, those beginning with a conjunct consonant.

When the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "offspring," a word beginning with a conjunct consonant and ending in *ṛn* shall remain in its original form (*prakṛtyā*). Examples: *śāṅkhaṇaḥ*, *vājriṇaḥ*, *vāgminaḥ*, *nāndinaḥ*.
[The suffix] *an* [is also applied].
In the case of *annantam*, it would be by its very nature [the feminine suffix *ī*]. For example: *sāmanaḥ*, *sautvanaḥ*.
And those [suffixes] which do not express an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*).
In the beginning, before a *taddhita* suffix, the word *an* shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *sāmanyaḥ*, *adhvanyaḥ*, *śīrṣaṇyaḥ*, *brahmaṇyaḥ*.

Why "not denoting state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*)"? [Because in those cases the rule does not apply]; for example, the state or action of a king is *rājyam*, as is the case with *purohita* and others.
The self and the paths are in the void.
These two [suffixes] occur after the word *kha* by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*): *ātmanīna* and *adhvanīna*.
Why "after *kha*"? [Consider: *adhyātmam*, *pratyātmam*, *prādhvam*. [The suffix *khañ* is applied] not after a word preceded by *m* when denoting offspring, except for the word *varman*.

The term *anitya* applies here. The word *anna*, when preceded by the letter *m*, shall not remain in its original form (*prakṛtyā*). Examples: *bhādrasāmaḥ*, *sauṣāmaḥ putraḥ*. Why "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*)? Consider: *cārmaṇo rathaḥ* ("a chariot made of leather"). [The rule applies to] that which is surrounded by it. Why "not preceded by *avarman"*? Consider: *cāndravarmaṇaḥ*, *cākravarmaṇaḥ putraḥ*. Optionally so for *hitanāman*: *haitanāmaḥ putraḥ*, or *haitanāmanaḥ putraḥ*.
The term *brāhma* [is used] except when referring to birth.
The suffix *aṇ* is elided. Thus, we have *brāhmo daṇḍaḥ* (the staff of Brahmā) and *brāhmī oṣadhiḥ* (the herb of Brahmā).

According to traditional teaching, there is a prohibition [of this elision] when the offspring (*apatya*) denotes a genus (*jāti*). Thus, the offspring of Brahmā that constitutes a genus is a *brāhmaṇa*.
However, they say that when referring to offspring in general, the form is *brāhmaḥ*, as in *brāhmaḥ nāradaḥ* (Nārada, the son of Brahmā).
The suffix *kārmast* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
*Karmaśīla* means "one whose nature is action"; *kārma* refers to a parasol and so forth; *kārmaṇa* occurs in other senses;
and *aukṣa* is used when not referring to offspring.
This is what is prescribed here: *aukṣaṃ padam* (the footprint of a bull). Why "not in the sense of offspring"? [Answer: *aukṣṇo vatsaḥ* (the calf of a bull). [The following are also included:
*dāṇḍināyana*, *hāstināyana*, *ātharvaṇika*, *jaihmāśineya*, *vāsināyani*, *bhrauṇahatya*, *dhaivarya*, *sārava*, *aikṣvāka*, *maitreya*, and *hiraṇyamaya*.

The original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of five [words] is maintained, the true form (*tattva*) of two, and the elision (*lopa*) of four is prescribed by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Daṇḍin* and *hastin* belong to the *naḍādi* group. *Atharvan* belongs to the *ukthādi* group. *Jihmāśin* belongs to the *śubhrādi* group. From *vāsin* with a *vṛddhi*-strengthened stem, the suffix *phiñ* is applied. *Bhrūṇahan*. *Dhīvan*. The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*); thus, *dhaivatyaṃ*.

Some say it is Vedic; others say no. From *sarayū*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied with the elision of *y*: *sāravaḥ*. From *ikṣvāku*, the suffix [denoting offspring] is applied with the elision of *u*: *aikṣvākaḥ*, *aikṣvākau*. From a *kṣatriya* name, the suffix *añ* is applied; in the plural, there is elision (*luk*): *ikṣvākavaḥ*. This is the *aikṣvāka* lineage of them. From *mitrayu*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after *gṛṣṭi* and others; there is elision of the *yādi* portion: *maitreyaḥ*. From *hiraṇya*, when the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied, there is elision of *y*: *hiraṇmayaḥ*. [The forms] *ṛtvyá*, *vāstvá*, *ātvá*, *ayavá*, *mādhvī*, and *hiraṇyayá* occur in the Veda (*chandas*).
This is Vedic.
[The rule] "yuvoranākau" [applies].
The suffixes *yu* and *vu* are prescribed [after the root *tan*]. Examples: *yuvan-danaḥ*, *sāman-tanaḥ*, *ciran-tanaḥ*. With *vu*: *kā-rakaḥ*, *hā-rakaḥ*, *gārg-akam*.
Here, because of the inclusion of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) *yaṇ*-substitutes and suffixes, it does not apply in these cases: *ūrṇā-yuḥ*, *kaṃ-yuḥ*, *śaṃ-yuḥ*, *yudhyate*, *vusyati*.
The elision of the *v* in *yuvuḥ* occurs because it is a Vedic (Sautra) usage.
The substitutes *āyan*, *eyan*, *īyan*, and *īy* take the place of the initial sounds of suffixes, while *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, and *gha* take the place of the final sounds of suffixes.

The letters *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, *gha*, *mā*, *ya*, *nn*, and so forth, are [substitutes]. In the case of *ph* and the others, the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Substitutions ending in consonants apply only to those [bases] that end in consonants. *Phak*: *nāḍāyanaḥ*. *Ḍha*: *vainateyaḥ*. *Kha*: *kulīnaḥ*. *Cha*: *gārgīyaḥ*. *Gha*: *kṣatriyaḥ*. *Kiyān*. *Iyān*. Why is it said "affix" (*pratyaya*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to verbs: *phakkati*, *ḍhaukate*. Why is it said "initial" (*ādi*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to words like] *jānudaghraḥ*. However, words such as *śepha*, *śaṅkha*, *ṣaṇḍha*, *puccha*, and so forth, are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.
Immediately after the pronunciation of *kha*, *śa*, *ghañ*, *ña*, and so forth, there is no substitution because of elision (*lopa*) once the designation *it* has been applied.
[Pāṇini 1.1.52: *jho'ntaḥ* (the substitute *ant* takes the place of *jh*).
The substitute *jha* shall be applied in place of the final phoneme of a pratyaya ending in *jh*. Examples: *navanti*, *kurvanti*. For *jha*: *jarantaḥ*, *veśantaḥ*.
[The suffix *ad* is applied] after a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*).

After a reduplicated stem (abhyasta), the substitute *āt* shall take the place of the *jh* [the first person plural ending]. Examples: *dadati*, *dadhati*, *jāgrati*, *cakāsati*, *śāsati*, *bibhyati*.

In the *ātmanepada*, after a stem that does not end in *a*, the substitute *āt* shall take the place of the *jh* [the first person plural ending] when it is marked with *taṅ*. Examples: *āsate*, *cinvate*, *bhuñjate*, *lunate*, *punate*, *vyativāte*.
What [is the purpose] of [specifying] that which does not end in the vowel *a*? [Examples: *cyavante*, *plavante*.
[The augment] *ruṭ* is applied after the root *śīṅ*.
The augment *ruṭ* shall be added after the root *śīṅ* before a substitute *jha*-class suffix beginning with a vowel. [Thus: *śerate*, *aśerata*. [After the root] *vid*, it is optional.
After the root *vid* (in the sense of "to know"), the augment *ruṭ* may optionally be inserted before the suffix *a* of the present indicative. Thus: *saṃvidrate* or *saṃvidate*.
In the Vedic language, this occurs frequently.
This is Vedic.
Hence, *ais* replaces *bhis*.
After a word ending in a non-dental [dental stop], *bhisa* shall be replaced by *ais*. For example: *vṛkṣaiḥ*, *vanaiḥ*, *dhanaiḥ*, *dāraiḥ*, *vipraiḥ*.

Why is it specified that the dental is followed by *t* (i.e., *tatpara*)? [To exclude cases such as: *khaṭvābhiḥ*, *mālābhiḥ*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), this substitution occurs diversely (*bahulam*).
This is Vedic.
[The rule] "nedamadasor akoḥ" [applies].
The substitution of *ais* for the case endings *bhisa* of the words *idam* and *adas* does not occur. [Examples: *ebhiḥ*, *amībhiḥ*.
Why say "of *aka*" (i.e., those ending in *a*)? [Counter-examples: *idakaiḥ*, *amukaiḥ*.
[Furthermore, the following substitutions apply: *ṭā*, *ṅasi*, *ṅas*, *ām*, *ina*, *āt*, and *syāḥ*.

In place of the case endings beginning with *ṭ* (i.e., the third through seventh cases) following a stem ending in a consonant (*adanta*), *in* and so forth shall be substituted. [Examples: *vṛkṣeṇa*, *vṛkṣāt*, *vṛkṣasya*.
[Furthermore,] *ya* is substituted for the dative singular marker (*ṅe*).
After a stem ending in *a* that is not a pronominal (*adanta*), *ṅe* shall be replaced by *ya*. [Examples: *vṛkṣāya*, *kalatrāya*, *viprāya*, *vanāya*, *dhanāya*.
After a pronominal stem, [the same case ending] is replaced by *smai*.

After a non-final pronoun, *ṅe* is replaced by *smai*. [Examples: *sarvasmai*, *asmai*, *yasmai*, *tasmai*, *kasmai*. Only after a stem ending in *a*—as in *bhavate*. For *ṅasi* and *ṅi*, *smāt* and *smin* are substituted respectively.

After a non-final pronominal stem, *smāt* is substituted for the fifth case ending *ṅasi*, and *smin* is substituted for the seventh case ending *ṅi*. Thus: *sarvasmāt*, *sarvasmin*; *yasmāt*, *yasmin*; *tasmāt*, *tasmin*;
*kasmāt*, *kasmin*.
After the stems beginning with *pūrva*, these substitutions are optional.
After the words *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *adhara*, *apara*, *sva*, and *antara*, the suffixes *tas* and *smin* may optionally occur [in place of the fifth case ending].
Thus: *pūrvāt* or *pūrvasmāt*; *pūrve* or *pūrvasmin*. [In the neuter plural,] *jaś* is replaced by *śī*.
After a non-dental (adanta) pronominal stem, *śī* shall be substituted for *jaś*. [Examples: *sarve*, *viśve*, *ye*, *te*, *ke*.
After a pronominal stem ending in *āp*, *auṅ* is substituted.

After a neuter stem ending in *ā*, the substitute *śī* shall take the place of *auṅ*. Examples: *khaṭve tiṣṭhataḥ* (the two beds stand), *khaṭve paśya* (look at the two beds), *te dve paśya* (look at those two).
The term *auṅ* is a technical designation for both *au* and *auṭ*.
[This rule applies] also after a neuter [stem].

After a neuter stem ending in /a/, the substitute *śī* shall occur in place of the dual case endings *auṅ*. For example: *kuṇḍe staḥ* (two pots are), or *paśya* (behold). [Similarly: *śucinī*, *dadhinī*, *paṭunī*, *madhunī*, *payasī*. [Furthermore:
the substitute *śi* occurs in place of the case endings *jas* and *śas*.

After a neuter stem, *śi* shall be substituted for the nominative-accusative plural suffixes *jas* and *śas*. Examples: *kuṇḍāni*, *payāṃsi*—they stand or behold them; *yaśāṃsi*. [The rule] *aṣṭābhya auś* [applies].

For the word *aṣṭan* that has undergone the change to *āt*, the substitutes *auś* shall take the place of the nominative-accusative plural endings (*jas* and *śas*). Examples: *aṣṭau santi* (there are eight) or *paśya* (look). Here, because of the rule stating "in the context of the designation of a stem (*aṅga*), [the substitute applies] to that [stem] and its subsequent member," we have *paramāṣṭau* (the highest eights) and *uttamāṣṭau* (the best eights).
Why specify "that which has undergone the change to *āt*"? [Consider: *aṣṭa santi* or *paśya*.
There is elision [of the case-ending] after the six [cases].

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jaś* and *śas* after stems designated as "six" (*ṣat*). [Examples: *pañca*, *ṣaṭ*, *sapta*, *nava*, *daśa*, *ekādaśa*, *kati*—see whether they exist. [The rule] *svamornapuṃsakāt* [applies].
The *luk* elision of the nominative-accusative singular suffixes (*svam*) occurs after neuter stems. For example: *dadhi*, *madhu*, *kartṛ*, *karma*, *tiṣṭhati*, or *paśya*.

Here, in the case of *tatkulam*, this *luk* elision occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), or because it is obligatory (*nitya*).
From this [stem ending in *a*], the suffix *am* is applied.
After a neuter stem ending in a vowel other than *a*, the suffixes *su* and *am* may optionally be replaced by *adḍ*. For example: *dhanam asti* or *paśya*; *vanam asti* or *paśya*.
After the five beginning with *katara*, the suffix *adḍ* is substituted [for *su* and *am*].

After the five beginning with *katarad*—namely, *klība*, *katarad*, *katamad*, *anyat*, and *anyatarat*—the suffixes *adḍ* and so forth are prescribed in place of *svam* (the nominative-accusative dual and plural endings). Examples: *katarat*, *katamat*, *anyat*, *anyatarat*, or *itarat* [stands] or "look. The form *ekatarāt* is not desired; however, *ekatarām* exists. But in the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the suffix *adḍ*] does not follow *itara*.
This is Vedic grammar.
From the rule *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso'ś*:
after these two, *aś* is prescribed in place of *ṅasi*. [Examples: *tava*, *mama*.

In this context, because of the qualification by the *aṅga* (stem), even when [the suffix] ends in that [vowel], substitutes occur for the element being designated, according to the rule: "Substitutes occur for the element being designated. Thus: *atitava*, *atimama*; likewise, *atiyuṣmākam*, *atyasmākam*; *susakthnā vipreṇa* (by the Brahmin with beautiful thighs); *priyānaḍvān* (one who has a dear ox), and so forth.

But here, in cases such as *bahuvanā girayaḥ* (many forests are the mountains), *suvanau śailau* (two beautiful mountains), *bahutrapur grāmaḥ* (a village with many wells), and *sutrapor viprasya* (of the Brahmin with a beautiful well)—because the neuter gender is qualified by the *aṅga* itself, the rules for *śi*, *luṅ*, and *num* do not apply.
[The rule *ṅeprathamayoram* follows.]

After these two [words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*], the ending *ṅe* (dative singular) and the first and second case endings shall be replaced by *am*. Regarding *ṅe*: *tubhyam*, *mahyam* (is given). Regarding the first two cases: *tvam*, *aham*; *aham* (and) *yuvām*, *āvām*; *yūyam*, *vayam*; *tvām*, *mām*; *yuvām*, *āvām*.
[The rule for] *śas* (nominative/accusative plural): it is replaced by *naḥ*.

After these two [yuṣmad and asmad], the suffix *śas* shall become *naḥ*. [By the rule] "of the following, the first [element]," there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). [Examples: *yuṣmān nadīḥ paśyāmi* (I see you rivers); *asmān kulāni paśya* (see our families).
After [the suffix] *bhyas*, [the substitute] *bhyam* [is applied].
The suffix *bhyam* is substituted for *bhyas* after these two [stems]. [Examples: *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam* "give to you" and "give to us. For the fifth case (*pañcamī*), *at* is substituted.

After these two [pronouns], when followed by the fifth case ending *bhyas*, *at* shall be substituted. [Examples: *yuṣmad-bhītaḥ* (fearful of you), *asmad-patitaḥ* (fallen from us). And [the substitution applies] after the singular [forms].
In the singular, *āt* shall be substituted for [the ending] *si*. *tvad gacchati* (you go); *mad bibheti* (he fears me).

*Ākam* [is substituted for *ām*]: after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *ākam* shall be the substitute for *ām* when it is accompanied by the augment *suṭ*. *yuṣmākam*, *asmākam*. [Examples with qualifiers: *priyayuṣmākam*, *atyasmākam*, *priyāsmākam*.
The substitution of *au* for *ā* occurs before the suffix *ṇal*.

The substitution of *aur* is prescribed for the *ṇal* suffix following a verbal root ending in a vowel. Thus: *dadau*, *jaglau*, *mamlau*, *tasthau*, *papau*. The sequence is as follows: the substitution of *au*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), and then reduplication (*dvirukti*).
[In the Vedic language,] the substitution of *tāt-aṅ* is optionally applied for *tu* and *hi* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

In place of the suffixes *tu* and *hi*, *tātaṅ* may optionally be substituted when expressing a benediction (*āśis*). Examples: *jīvatu* or *jīvatāt* "may you live"; *jīva* or *jīvatāt* "may you live. Because [the substitute] is marked with the *ṅ*-sign, there is no substitution of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. Examples: *brūtāt*; *mṛṣṭāt*. By the rule *allopaḥ*, [we have]: *bhintāt*; *stāt*. By the rule *ittvam*: *śiṣṭāt*. By the rule *irtvam*: *lunītāt*. By the rule *uttvam*: *kurutāt*. [The rule] *videḥ śaturvasuḥ* [is also applicable].

The substitute *vasu* is optionally prescribed for the suffix *śatṛ* following the root *vid*. Thus: *vidvān*, *vidvāṃsau*, *vidvāṃsaḥ*; and for the feminine: *viduṣī*. In the alternative case: *vidan*, *vidantau*, *vidantaḥ*; and for the feminine: *vidatī*.
In a compound that is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*.

In a compound not preceded by *naÑ*, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Examples: *prakṛtya*, *prasthāya*, *vijitya*, *praṇīya*, *pradāya*, *ḍhaukṛtya*, *nānākṛtya*, *pārśvataḥkṛtya*. Why "not preceded by *naÑ*"? [Counter-example: *akṛtvā*. Why "preceded by *naÑ*"? [Counter-example: *akṛtvā*.

The suffix *ktvā* does not occur even in a negative (*nañ*), a privative (*paryudāsa*), an adverbial (*avyaya*), or a compound (*samāsa*)—as in *paramakṛtvā*, *uttamakṛtvā*, and *apakṛtya*. In the view that favors word-formation (*padasaṃskāra*), the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) occurs later.
Here, there are twelve Vedic rules (*chandaḥsūtra*). They are as follows:
"In the Veda, *ktvā* also [is used]."
In place of the case endings (sup), there may occur *suluk*, *pūrvasavarṇa*, *śī*, *nā*, *ḍā*, *ḍe*, *yā*, *āt*, *yāc*, *jhal*.
I am Maś.
