[The suffix *kyac* is applied] after the words *aśva*, *kṣīra*, *vṛṣa*, and *lavaṇa* when the sense is "one's own pleasure" (*ātmaprīti*).

The augment *asu* is added after words such as *aśva* when the suffix *kyac* follows, provided that there is no sense of affection; furthermore, this occurs if there is a desire for sexual intercourse on the part of a horse or a bull, or a craving for milk or salt.

Examples: *Aśvasyati vaḍavā*—the mare desires [sexual intercourse with] the stallion. *Sā vṛṣasyantī lakṣmaṇam*—she, desiring a bull, [approaches] Lakṣmaṇa. *Kṣīrasyati vaṭuḥ*—the boy craves milk. *Lavaṇasyaty uṣṭraḥ*—the camel craves salt. It should be stated that *asu* is added after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) when expressing a craving. Examples: *Dadhyasyati*—he craves curd. *Madhvasyati*—he craves honey.

Others say it is *sugit*. Examples: *dadhisyati*, *madhusyati*, *patiṣyantī varāṅganā*. Why [is it] not so in the case of *lālasā*? Example: *dadhīyati*. [The augment] *suṭ* is applied after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) before the suffix *ām*.

The augment *suṭ* is added to the suffix *ām* following a pronominal stem that ends in a vowel other than *ā*. Examples: *sarveṣām*, *viśveṣām*, *yeṣām*, *teṣām*, *keṣām*; *sarvāsām*, *yāsām*, *tāsām*, *kāsām*. This occurs only after [stems ending in] *ā*: e.g., *bhavatām*. Also: *ubhayīnām*, *traiśabdyaḥ*.
The forms *trerbhām* and *trayāṇām* are derived from *tri*.
[In the formation of the genitive plural], the augment *nuṭ* is added after a short vowel, as well as after the words *nadī* and *āp*.

The augment *nuṭ* shall be added to the genitive plural suffix *ām* after words ending in a short vowel, after feminine words ending in *nadi*, and after words ending in *ā*. Examples: *vṛkṣāṇām*, *viprāṇām*, *mālānām*, *khaṭvānām*, *bahurājānām*, *agnīnām*, *dīnām*, *lakṣmīṇām*, *vāyūnām*, *bandhūnām*, *vadhūnām*, *kartṛṇām*. In cases other than these—such as *grāmaṇyām* (the genitive singular)—[the augment does not apply].
And [the augment *nuṭ* is also applied] after the words *ṣaṣ* and *catur*.
After those [stems] designated as "ṣat" (six), the augment *nuṭ* shall be inserted before the genitive plural ending *ām*. Thus: *ṣaṇṇām*, *saptānām*, *daśānām*, *caturṇām*.
Here—
The words *śrī* and *grāmaṇī* [take the suffix *ṣyaṅ*] in the Vedic language.
At the end of the word "go" (cow).
Two sūtras on *chandas*:
"The augment *num* is added to a verbal root ending in an *it*-letter."
The augment *num* shall be added after a verbal root ending in the letter *i*. [Examples: *nandati*, *vandate*, *kuṇḍā*, *huṇḍa*.
[Vārttika: The augment *num* is added to roots belonging to the *muc*-class and others.

Furthermore, the augment *num* shall be applied to the roots beginning with *muc* when followed by a suffix beginning with *ś*. Thus: *muñcati*, *siñcati*, *limpati*, *lumpati*, *nikṛntati*, *vindati*.
And [the augment *num* is applied] to the roots beginning with *tṛph*. Thus: *tṛmphati*, *gumphati*. Here, due to the specific force of the rule prescribing *num*, there is no elision [of the nasal].
[Also, the augment *num* is applied] to the roots *masj* and *naś* before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant.

The augment *num* shall be applied after the roots *masj* and *naś* before a *jhal*-ending suffix. Examples: *maṅktvā*, *naṃṣṭvā*. Why "before a *jhal*-ending suffix"? Observe: *majjanam*, *naśanam*. [Also, the augment *num* is applied after the roots *radh* and *jabh* before a vowel. *radhijabhor aci*.

The augment *num* shall be applied to these two roots when followed by a vowel (*ac*). Examples: *randhanam*, *randhakaḥ*, *randhayati*; *jambhanam*, *jambhayati*, *jambhakaḥ*. The obligatory *num* overrides the *vṛddhi* [substitution]. Why "when followed by a vowel"? [Observe: *raddhā*, *jabhyam*. [Note:
The augment *iṭ* is not applied to the root *radh* in the *liṭ* [perfect tense].

The augment *num* does not occur after *radh* except when followed by *aliṭ*. [Examples: *radhitā*, *radhitum*. Why "except when followed by *aliṭ*"? [Counter-examples: *rarandhiva*, *rarandhima*. [The rule *rabher aśabliṭoḥ* applies as well.]
And from gains.

The augment *num* is added after the roots *rabh-* and *labh-* when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel. Examples: *ārambhayati*, *ārambhakaḥ*, *ārambhaṇam*, *ārambhī*. *lambhayati*, *lambhanam*, *lambhakaḥ*. Why "except for the [affix] *aṅ* and the *liṭ* [perfect]? Consider: *ārabhate*, *ārebhe*; *labhate*, *lebhe*.
[Also, the rule applies] after *āṅ* before the affix *ya*.

The augment *num* shall be inserted before a root beginning with *y* when preceded by the prefix *ā*. Thus, *ālambhyaḥ paśuḥ* ("an animal fit to be sacrificed"). In the form *ālabhyate*, there is elision of the nasal (*n*) according to the rule *aniditām*.
[Furthermore, *num* is inserted] after the prefix *upa* when expressing praise.
The augment *num* shall be inserted after the root *upalabh* when followed by the suffixes *yak* and others. For example: *vidyā upalambhyā* (knowledge to be acquired).

Why "in the sense of praise"? Consider: *kiñcid upalabhyam vṛṣalāt* (something obtainable from a low-born person). [This rule applies] after a prefix (*upasarga*) when followed by the suffixes *khal* or *ghañ*.

The augment *num* shall be inserted before the root *labh-* when it is preceded by a prefix (*upasṛṣṭa*), both in the case of the suffix *khal* and the suffix *ghañ*. With *khal*: *supralambhaḥ*. With *ghañ*: *vipralambhaḥ*. Why "only when preceded by a prefix"? Consider: *īṣallabhaḥ*; here the sense of obtaining (*lābha*) prevails. How then is *rāṣṭralambhaḥ* explained? In that case, it must be considered [as a separate matter].
By the rule that [the suffixes] apply only when there is an object of affliction (*upasṛṣṭa*), the suffixes *khal* and *ghañ* would otherwise occur even in other cases—as in *pralambhanam*.
However, they do not occur with the prefixes *su-* and *dur-* used alone.

When these two [prefixes *su-* and *dur-*, meaning "easy" and "difficult"] follow *nabh* (to obtain), the augment *num* does not occur before the suffixes *khal* or *ghañ*. Examples: *sulabhaḥ* (easy to obtain), *durlabhaḥ* (difficult to obtain); *sulābhaḥ*, *durlābhaḥ*. Why specify "only by these two"? Consider *atisulambhaḥ* (extremely easy to obtain). When *su-* is used in the sense of praise (*pūjā*) and *ati-* as a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of exceeding (*atikramaṇa*), and thus *ati-* is not a verbal prefix (*upasarga*), then the form *atisulabham* also occurs.
[The rule] *vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ* applies here.

The augment *num* may optionally be inserted before the suffixes *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* following the root *labh*. Thus, one says either *alābhi* or *alambhi*, and *lambhaṃlambham* or *lābhaṃlābham*. This option applies when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). However, when a prefix is present, it is obligatory—as in *prālambhi* and *pralambham*.
[Furthermore, the rule] *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne'dhātoḥ* [applies].

The augment *num* shall be added after stems ending in long *ū*, *ṛ*, or *ṝ*, as well as after those ending in *añc*, when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. Examples: *bhavān*, *bhavantau*, *bhavantaḥ*; *śreyān*; *vidvān*; *upeyivān*; *pacan*; *paṭhan*. Regarding those ending in *añc*: *prāṅ*, *prāñcau*, *prāñcaḥ*. Why "when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix"? Consider: *bhavataḥ paśya* (see the two of you), *bhavatā kṛtam* (done by you). Why "not after a verbal root"? Consider: *ukhāsrat* (one who has fallen from the pot), *parṇadhvat* (one who has fallen from the leaf).
[The augment *num* is added] after the root *yuj* when not in a compound.

The augment *num* shall be added after the root *yuj* when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. [Examples: *yuñjau*, *yuñjaḥ*. Why "not in a compound"? [Counter-example: *aśvayuk*, *aśvayujau*, *aśvayujaḥ*.
[The rule applies] to neuter stems ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or *ac*.

The augment *num* shall be added to a neuter noun ending in a *jhal* consonant or a vowel, when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. Examples: *udaśvinti*, *payāṃsi*, *kuṇḍāni*, *vārīṇi*, *madhūni*.
Why specify "ending in a *jhal* or a vowel"? Consider *vimaladivi* (locative singular), *catvāri*, and *ahāni*.

Even for a neuter noun ending in a *jhal* that also possesses the *uṅ* marker (i.e., ends in *ū*), this *num* applies because it is taught later [in the sequence of rules]—as in *śreyāṃsi* and *kurvanti*.
There is a prohibition against the plural form *bahūrji*.

Some [teachers] hold that the augment *num* occurs before the final letter; others hold that *num* occurs after the letter *r*. Examples include *bahūrñji viprakulāni* or *bahūrji vā*; elsewhere than after *bahu*, as in *atyūrnji* and *sūrnji*. [The rule] *iko'ci vibhaktau* [applies].
The augment *num* shall be added to a neuter stem ending in an *ik* vowel when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel. Examples: *dadhinī*, *madhunī*, *trapuṇī*; *trapuṇe*; *trapuṇaḥ*.

Why "ending in an *ik* vowel"? Consider: *kuṇḍe* (two pots). According to Gālava, a neuter stem that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) takes the masculine form in the third case and those following.

According to the opinion of Gālava, a neuter word ending in *i* that has been stated as having masculine forms may optionally take the masculine form before suffixes beginning with *ṭa* and before vowel-initial suffixes. For example: *grāmaṇye kulāya* (to the village-chief family) or *grāmaṇyāṃ kule* (in the village-chief family).

According to others, this does not apply: *grāmaṇine* (to the village-chief) or *grāmaṇini* (in the village-chief). Similarly: *śucaye* or *śucine* (to the pure one); *paṭave* or *paṭune* (to the clever one).
[In the case of the words] *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the substitute *anaṅ* is applied, and it is udātta-accented.
In the case of words such as *asthi* and others, the substitution of *anaṅ* is prescribed before vowel-initial suffixes beginning with *ṭ*. Thus: *asthnā*, *dadhrā*, *sakthnā*, *akṣṇā*.
This substitution is also desired for words ending in *guṇa* vowels: *susakthnā vipreṇa*.
What is the purpose of [the mention of] *aci*? [Examples are: *akṣibhyām*, *asthibhyām*. It is also seen in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
And [the substitution of *au* for *as*] occurs in the dual; these are two Vedic sūtras. [The following is:
"Not after a reduplicated stem, before the suffix *śatṛ*."
The augment *num*—prescribed by the rule *ugidacām*—does not occur after a *śatṛ* suffix that follows a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*). Examples: *dadat*, *dadatau*, *śāsat*, *cakāsat*, *jāgrat*.
[Alternatively: *vā napuṃsakasya* (the *num* is optionally applied for the neuter gender).
The prohibition [of the augment *num*] may apply to the neuter [noun]. For example: *kulāni dadati* or *dadanti*; *jāgrati* or *jāgranti*.
[This is governed by the rule: *ācchīnadyornum*.

The augment *num* is optionally inserted after a śatṛ-pratyaya that follows a vowel other than *a*, when followed by the feminine suffixes *śī* or *nadyām*. Examples: *tudantī* or *tudatī*; *kariṣyatī* or *kariṣyantī* in a Brahmin family (*viprakule*). In the case of *nadyām*: *tudatī* or *tudantī*; *bhātī* or *bhāntī*; *brāhmaṇī*. Why is it said "after [a vowel] other than *a*" (*āditi*)? [Because in these cases, *num* is not added: *adatī*, *dhnatī*, *bibhratī*, *cinvatī*, *rundhatī*, *lunatī*.
The substitution of *śya* for *śyan* occurs invariably.

The augment *num* is always applied after the suffix *śatṛ* that follows a verbal root ending in *ś*, *śyan*, or a vowel other than *a*. [Examples: *pacantī*, *corayantī*, *dīvyantī*—whether it refers to a family (*kula*) or a woman (*strī*).
[Furthermore: *sāvanaḍuhaḥ* (the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added to *anaḍuh* in the nominative case).
Could there not be [the form] *anaḍvān*? [As in] "O *anaḍvan*. Why [specify] *sau* (in the nominative singular)? [Because it does not apply] in *anaḍvāhau*.
[The rule applies to] *dṛś*, *svavas*, and *svatavas* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
This is Vedic.
[The rule] "diva aut" [applies].
After the word *div*, *au* should be substituted [for the nominative singular suffix]. *dyauḥ*. [In the vocative:
*he dyauḥ!* Why [specify] "after *div*"? [Observe: *divaṃ paśya*.
[The rule continues: For *pathin*, *mathin*, and *ṛbhukṣan*, [the final consonant is replaced by] *ā*.
The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of these [words] occurs before the nominative singular suffix *su*: *panthāḥ*, *manthāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣāḥ*. [In the vocative: *he panthāḥ*.
[The rule] "from here onwards, *at* [is substituted] in the place of a *sarvanāmasthāna*" [applies].

The suffix *at* shall replace [the final vowel] of words such as *pathin* and others before a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending. Thus: *panthāḥ*, *panthānau*, *panthānaḥ*; *manthāḥ*, *manthānau*, *manthānaḥ*; *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣāṇau*, *ṛbhukṣāṇaḥ*, *ṛbhukṣāṇām*, *ṛbhukṣāṇau*. [In these forms,] *tha* becomes *ntha*.

The *tho* and *ntha* [suffixes] of those [words ending in *an*] become [the substitute] in the place of a *sarvanāmasthāna*; this has been illustrated in the same manner. There is elision of the *ṭi* of a *bha* [stem].

There shall be elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of those [stems] termed *bha*. [Examples: *pathaḥ*, *paśyaḥ*; *pathā*; *pathe*; *mathaḥ*; *mathā*; *ṛbhukṣaḥ*; *ṛbhukṣā*; *ṛbhukṣi*.
[In the case of the stem] *pums*, [the substitution] *asuṅ* [occurs].
The suffix *asuṅ* shall be substituted for this [stem]. Thus: *pumān*, *puṃmāsau*, *puṃmāsaḥ*; *he puman*. Only when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows—thus: *puṃsaḥ*, *puṃsā*, *puṃsām*.
[The suffix] *ṇit* follows after *go*.
A *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix related to the word *go* shall be treated as having the marker *ṇ*. Thus: *gauḥ*, *gāvau*, *gāvaḥ*; *he gauḥ*. And for *dyau*: *dyauḥ*, *dyāvau*, *dyāvaḥ*; *he dyauḥ*.
[In the case of the first person endings,] the final syllable of the *uttama* (first person) is optionally treated as having the marker *ṇ*.

The suffix *ṇal* would be the best [to indicate the agent]; for instance, "I indeed did" would be expressed as *cakara* or *cakāra*, *cukuṭāham* or *cukoṭa*, and *ahaṃ vivica* or *vivyāca*. [This applies] to the word *sakhi* when it is not in the vocative case.

The *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes following the word *sakhi* shall be treated as having the marker *Ṇ* (ṇit). [Thus we have] *sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*. Why "except in the vocative singular"? [Because in that case we have] *he sakhe*. [In the nominative singular, the rule] *anaṅ sau* applies.
The substitution of *anaṅ* occurs for the final vowel of *sakhi* before the nominative singular suffix *su*.
This applies only when it is not the vocative singular—thus, *he sakhe*.
Furthermore, the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs for the final vowel of words ending in *ṛ*, as well as for *uśanas*, *purodas*, *anehas*, and [words ending in] *as*.

For stems ending in *ṛ* and for the word *uśanas*, the substitute *aṅ* shall apply in place of the nominative singular suffix (*su*). Examples: *karttā*, *harttā*, *bharttā*, *mātā*, *pitā*; [also] *thaśanā*, *purodaṃśā*, *anehā*. Why "in the nominative singular (*sau*)"? [Because it does not apply here: *karttārau*, *anehasau*.
The rule applies only when it is not the vocative singular (*asambuddhau*): [e.g.,] *he karttaḥ*, *he anehaḥ*.
In the vocative case, they maintain that *uśanas* has three forms: ending in *-s*, ending in *-n*, and ending in *-a*.

Thus: *he uśanaḥ*, *he uśanan*, and *he uśana*. Accordingly, the *Ślokavārttika* states: "But in the vocative, *uśanas* has three forms: ending in *-s*, as well as ending in *-n*, and also ending in *-a*."
The son of Mādhyandina taught the suffix *guṇa* [in the case of the word *kroṣṭu*]; the most excellent among the Vyāghrapadas [taught] it as neuter. Thus ends the rule *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*.

The word *kroṣṭu* should behave like a word ending in the suffix *-tṛ*. That is to say, it should follow the paradigm of the word *kroṣṭṛ*: *kroṣṭā*, *kroṣṭārau*, *kroṣṭāraḥ*. This applies only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]—as in *kroṣṭūn*. This applies only when not in the vocative singular—as in *he kroṣṭo*.
And likewise in the feminine.
In the feminine, the word *kroṣṭṛ* should behave like *tṛjvat* (i.e., like a word ending in the suffix *tṛc*). Thus: *kroṣṭrī*, *kroṣṭrībhiḥ*.
[Thereafter,] there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the vowel-beginning case endings from the third case on.

In the case of vowels beginning with those starting with *ṭa* (i.e., the *ṭā* case-ending and following), the word *kroṣṭu* may optionally be treated like a word ending in *tṛc*. Thus: *kroṣṭrā* or *kroṣṭunā*; *kroṣṭari* or *kroṣṭau*. Why "before a vowel"? [Observe: *kroṣṭubhyām*, *kroṣṭubhiḥ*.

By the rule of prior prohibition (*pūrvapratiṣedha*), the augment *num* and the augment *nuṭ* take precedence over the application of *num*, the long vowel *ī* (*aci raṅ*), and the treatment as *tṛjvat*. Thus: *trapūṇām*, *tisṛṇām*, *kroṣṭūnām*.
In the word *caturanaḍuh*, the suffix *ām* is udātta.

The suffix *ām* shall occur after these two [words]. *catvāraḥ*, *catvāri*; *anaḍvān*, *anaḍvāhau*, *anaḍvāhaḥ*. And also after that which ends in this [suffix]: *sucatuḥ*, *sucataḥ*, *sucatvārau*. *priyānaḍvān*, *priyānaḍvāhau*.
Only when a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix] follows—[as in] *caturaḥ paśya*.
It should be stated that for the feminine of *anaḍuh*, there is an option: *anaḍuhī* or *anaḍvāhī*. [The latter belongs to] the *gaura*-group.
[The suffix] *am* is used in the vocative singular.
In the case of the two perfect participles (*sambuddhau*), there would be *am*: *he priyacatvaḥ*, *he anaḍvan*, *he priyānaḍvan*.
By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* ("*it* is substituted for *ṛt* of a root"):
*ṛt* at the end of a root is replaced by *it*. Thus: *kirati*, *girati*, *visṛtīrṇam*, *cikīrṣati*.
Why [is it specified] "of a verbal root"? [Consider] *mātṛṇām*.
And [the substitution applies] to the penultimate vowel as well.
The vowel *ṛ* of a verbal root, when it is an *upadhā* (penultimate), shall be replaced by *i*. [Thus: *kīrttayati*, *kīrttanam*.
[Furthermore, by the rule] *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*: [the *ṛ* of a root ending in *u* or *ū* is replaced by *u* when followed by a labial].

The vowel *ṛ* preceded by a labial consonant is replaced by *u*. For example: *pṛ* becomes *pūrtam*; *puṣūrṣati*; *susmūrṣate*; *prāvuvūrṣati*; *mumūrṣa*; *vuvūrṣati*. By the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the substitution of *it* and *ut* takes precedence over *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. For instance: *āstaraṇam*, *āstārakaḥ*; *niparaṇam*, *nipārakaḥ*. How is *udagiraṇam* justified? It is correct due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *o* for *as*] occurs frequently.
This is Vedic.
[In the rule] "vṛddhi occurs before *sic* in the case of *parasmaipada* endings," [the term *parasmaipada* refers to the *ātmanepada* endings as well].

When a *sic* suffix follows, there shall be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of a stem ending in *i* or *u*, provided that the *sic* occurs in a *parasmaipada* context. Examples: *acaishīt*, *anaishīt*, *astāvīt*, *alāvīt*, *apāvīt*, *akārṣīt*, *ahārṣīt*.
Why "in *parasmaipada* contexts"? [Consider: *acyoṣṭa*, *aploṣṭa*. This rule applies within this section of seven sūtras concerning *parasmaipada* endings.
Therefore, [the rule] applies to that which ends in *lṛ*.

When the *sic* affix follows in the *parasmaipada*, there shall be *vṛddhi* of the vowel *a* belonging to a verbal root (*aṅga*) ending in *lṛ* or *r*. Examples: *acālīt*, *ajvālīt*, *akṣārīt*; "the moonstone gems flowed" (*akṣāriṣuś candrakāntā maṇayaḥ*); *acārīt*. How [is it that] *ababhrīt*? Because of the intervention of more than one consonant after the *a*. [The rule applies to roots] ending in *va*, *dra*, *vraja*, or a consonant other than *ha*.

In these cases, there shall be *vṛddhi* [substitution] for the vowel *a* before that [suffix]. Examples: *avādīt*, *avrājīt*. For roots ending in consonants: *apākṣīt*, *abhaitsīt*, *arautsīt*, *atārpsīt*. Even when there is intervention by more than one letter, the desired result occurs: *arāṅkṣīt*, *abhāṅkṣīt*.
Not so.

In the case of the *sic* suffix following roots beginning with *iḍ* (the augment) and those ending in a consonant, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening. Examples: *adevīt*, *asevīt*, *vyaraṃsīt*, *amoṣīt*.
[This applies] to roots ending in *h*, *m*, or *y*, as well as *kṣaṇ*, *śvas*, *jāgṛ*, *ṇi*, *śvi*, and those ending in long *e*.

There is no vṛddhi substitution for roots ending in *h*, *m*, or *y*, nor for *kṣaṇ* and the like, when followed by the *sic* suffix with the augment *iṭ*. Examples: *agrahīt*, *avamīt* (from *vye*), *avyayīt*, *akṣaṇīt*, *aśvaśīt*, *ajāgarīt*. An example of a root ending in a *ṇat* (nasal) occurs in the Vedic language: *aśvayīt*. For roots ending in *e* or *o*, examples are: *aragīt*, *alagīt*. This applies only when the *iṭ* augment is present—thus, *adhākṣīt*.
There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the root *ṛṇoti*.
In this case, there may optionally be *vṛddhi* for the root *ūrṇu* before that [affix]. Thus, one says either *praurṇāvīt* or *praurṇavīt*.
In the alternative where the affix is treated as having the *ṅit* designation, *uvaṅ* is substituted: *praurṇuvīt*.
[This applies] by the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ*.

In place of a light vowel of a root beginning with *hal*, there may optionally be *vṛddhi* before a *sic* that has an *iṭ* augment. Thus: *arāṇīt* or *araṇīt*; *atrāsīt* or *atrasīt*; *atānīt* or *atanīt*.

How is it that we have *avādīt*, *ajvālīt*, and *agrahīt*? Because of the prohibitive rule in the *vadavraja-* sūtra (*Pāṇini 7.2.3*) and others. How then is *acakāsīt* formed? Because of the intervention of more than one consonant after the vowel *a*. Vṛddhi has been explained.
He is not subject to the power of others.

In the case of roots beginning with *vaś*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after a *kṛt* suffix. It is better [to state this] as an exception (*apavāda*) rather than as a general rule (*utsarga*). Examples: *īśvaraḥ*, *dīpraḥ*, *bhasma*, *yācñā*.
Why "after a *kṛt* suffix"? Consider: *rurudiva*, *rurudima*.
Also, [the augment *iṭ* is not applied] before the suffixes *ti*, *tu*, *ta*, *tha*, *si*, *su*, *sa*, *ra*, and *ka*.

In these cases, the suffix *iṇ* does not occur. *k-tin*: *dīptiḥ* (light). *k-tic*: *tant-iḥ* (thread). *tun*: *sak-tuḥ* (groats). *ṣṭran*: *pat-traṃ* (leaf). *tan*: *hastaḥ* (hand), *garttaḥ* (pit). *than*: *kuṣ-ṭhaḥ* (costus), *kāṣ-ṭham* (wood). From the root *kuṣ*, with the suffix *ksi*: *kuk-ṣiḥ* (belly). From the root *iṣ*, with the suffix *suk*: *ik-ṣuḥ* (sugarcane). From the root *aś*, with the suffix *ksaran*: *ak-ṣaraṃ* (syllable). From the root *śal*, with the suffix *kan*: *śalk-aḥ* (splinter). From the root *vad*, with the suffix *sa*: *vat-saḥ* (calf).
It should be stated that this applies to the group beginning with *agraha* (non-grasping): *nigṛh-itiḥ* (restraint), *nipaṭh-itiḥ* (recitation), *bhaṇ-itiḥ* (speech).
A monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its original enunciation [does not take *iṭ* in the formation of the perfect].
In the *Upadeśa*, there is no *iṇ* augment for a root that has a single vowel (*ekāj*) and is *anudātta*.
In that regard, all roots ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) are *aniṭ*. Examples: *dātā*, *dātum*, *dātavyam*; *netā*; *cetā*; *stotā*; *karttā*; *harttā*; *akārṣīt*;
*cinīṣati*; *ninīṣati*.
The roots with a penultimate *iṭ* (seṭ) are now written:

those ending in *ū*, *ṛ*, and *a*; furthermore, *ṇu*, *snū*, *kṣṇu*, *yu*, *kṣu*, *ru*, *ru*, *vṛṅ*, *vṛñ*, *śīṅ*, *śri*, as well as *ḍīṅ* and *iṣyā*—these they declare to be *seṭ* among the vowel-ending roots. (1)

Stems ending in *ū*: *bhavitā*, *lavitā*. Stems ending in *ṛ*: *taritā*, *nigaritā*, *āstaritā*. Stems ending in *ad* (consonants): *han-* becomes *vadha-* [in the future]; *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*; *āvadhiṣṭa*; *avadhīt*; *navitā*; *prasravitā*; *kṣṇavitā*; *yavitā*; *kṣavitā*; *prorṇavitā*; *ravitā*; *nivaritā*; *prāvaritā*; *śayitā*; *śrayitā*; *uḍḍayitā*; *āśvayitā*. However, all stems ending in consonants (*hal*) are necessarily *seṭ* (taking the *iṭ* augment): *śaṅkitā*, *kuṇḍitā*.
The roots that are also *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) are written here:
*śaki* alone ends in *k*; *śakta*. Similarly, there are six ending in *c*: *paci*, *vaci*, *vic*, *ric*, *sic*, and *nuci*. *Pracchi* alone ends in *ch*.

The roots *rañj*, *bhañj*, *tyaj*, *yaj*, *bhaj*, *ay*, *sañj*, *svañj*, *sṛj*, *yuj*, *ruj*, *ay*, *masj*, *bhrasj*, *bhuj*, *nij*, and *vij*—these, indeed, are aniṭ (lacking the augment *i*) when followed by the affixes of the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
*adi*, *hadi*, *skandi*, *bhidi*, *chidi*, *kṣudi*, *sadi*, *śadi*, *svidyati*, *padyati*, *khidi*,
*tudi*, *nudi*, *vidyati*, and also *vinti*.
Know that there are fifteen [types of] tamed ones. || 3 ||

*rudh*, *sarādh*, *yudh*, *bandh*, *sādh*, *krudh*, *kṣudh*, *śudhyati*, *budhyati*, and *vyadhi*—these ten roots ending in *dh* are considered to be *aniṭ* (not taking the *iṭ* augment); after these, only *sidhyati* is [so considered], and no others.

Know that there are thirteen roots ending in *p* taught here: *han*, *man*, *yat*, *dvi*, *nā*, *ant*, *tap*, *tip*, *piñ*, *math*, *vap*, *svap*, *lip*, *lup*, *tṛp*, *dṛp*, and *sṛp*; as well as *śāp*, *chup*, and *kṣip*, which are to be recognized by their low-pitched accent (*anudātta*).
The three roots *rabh*, *labh*, and *bhās* end in *bh*.
The four roots *yam*, *ram*, *nam*, and *gam* end in *m*.
Then there are *diś*, *dṛś*, *daṃś*, *mṛś*, *spṛś*, *riś*, *ruś*, *kruś*, and the eighth, *viś*.
And those who recite the Purāṇas read "liśim" as the tenth among the peaceful fires in their recitations, and not others.

Śiṣ (to sharpen), piṣ (to grind), śuṣyati and puṣyati (to dry/to nourish), tviṣ (to shine), viṣ (to pervade), śliṣ (to embrace), tuṣyati and duṣyati (to be satisfied/to be corrupted), and dviṣ (to hate)—these ten they teach as ending in ṣ in the [curādigaṇa] groups, excluding the root vadh; likewise kṛṣ (to draw/to plow). ||7||
*ghas* and *vas* (in the sense of dwelling)—these two end in *s*.
*dih*, *duh*, *mehati*, *rohati*, *vah*, *nah*, and likewise the sixth, *dahati*, as well as *lihi*:
these eight, which do not take the augment *iṭ*, have been proclaimed here in the lists of roots, distinguished by their ending in *h*, with all doubt removed.

The eleven *aniṭ*-kārikās composed by Vyāghrabhūti are presented here; some are complete, while others are extracted in part. The verse beginning with "ūdantam ṛdantam" does not belong to Vyāghrabhūti. Thus, there are eight ending in *ha*.
[The rule] "śryukaḥ kiti" [is now discussed].
The suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*) does not occur after roots ending in *śri*, nor after those ending in *u*. *śritam*, *śritvā*; *yutam*, *yutvā*;

*prasrutaḥ*; *prabhūtaḥ*; *lūnaḥ*, *lūnavān*; *lūtvā*; *tīrṇam*, *tīrtvā*—having crossed the ocean, terrible with its leaping crocodiles; *pūrtam*, *pūrtvā*. Why say "before *kit*" (*kiti*)? [Observe: *āśrayitā*, *lavitā*. The rule "after a monosyllabic root" (*ekācaḥ*) applies here as well: *jāgaritaḥ*.
The substitution of *nu* for the root *ūrṇu* should be stated. [Thus we have] *ūrṇutvā*. [And the rule applies] to the root *grah* and *guh* as well when followed by the suffix *san*.
The suffix *san* does not occur after roots ending in long vowels (*gṛ*, *guh*, *ūrg*), nor after the following roots: *jighṛkṣati*, *jughuksati*, *rurūṣati*, *lulūṣati*, and *pūñ*—as in *pupūṣati*.
[Furthermore, there is no *liṭ* *samprasāraṇa*] for the roots *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru* when followed by *liṭ*.

The substitution of *iṇ* for *liṭ* occurs only after roots beginning with *kṛ*, and not after others: *cakṛ*, *cakṛma*; *cakṛṣe*; *cakṛḍhve*; *sasṛva*, *sasṛma*; *babhṛva*, *babhṛma*; *vavṛma*; *vavṛvahe*, *vavṛmahe*; *tuṣṭuva*, *tuṣṭuma*; *dudruva*, *dudruma*; *susruva*, *susruma*; *śuśruva*, *śuśruma*. What is the purpose of this restriction? [To exclude cases such as: *bibhidiva*, *bibhidima*; *luluviva*, *luluvima*; *sedivān*; *ūṣivān*.
This prohibition applies even in the case of *thal*: *cakartha*; *tuṣṭotha*; *dradrotha*.
How is *vavaritha* formed? It is due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) taught in the *Nigama*.
It should be stated that [the substitution of *iṭ*] applies to the root *kṛ* when it is not preceded by the augment *suṭ*: thus, *sañjaskaritha*, *sañcaskariva*, *sañcaskarima*.
[The rule] "after a root ending in *śū* or one marked with *it*, before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes... [applies].

The augment *iṭ* does not occur before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktavatu*) after roots marked with *śvi* or those that have an indicatory *ṛ*. Examples: *śūnaḥ*, *śūnavān*; *udvignaḥ*, *udvignavān*; *nagnaḥ*; *dīptaḥ*. They also explain the absence of *iṭ* for the root *ḍīṅ*: *uḍḍīnaḥ*, *uḍḍīnavān*.
The recurrence of the rule regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes applies prior to the prohibition of *iṭ*.
Of that for which there is an option.

For that verbal root (*dhātu*) for which the augment *iṭ* is optionally prescribed in certain instances, there is no *iṇ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. Regarding the rule *dhūñ ñ-udito vā*: *dhūtam*, *gūḍham*; or regarding *udito vā*: *vṛttam*, *vṛttavān*, *vṛddhaḥ*.

The designation *iṭ* for the roots *kṛtī*, *vṛtī*, and *nṛtī*—which otherwise would be optional according to the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*—is for the purpose of making known that the prohibition [of *iṭ*] is not universal (*anitya*). By this, from the root *dhāv* in the sense of "motion," we have *dhāvitaḥ* and *dhāvitavān*; and from *pat*, *patitaḥ* and *patitavān*. Here, in the rule *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām*, because of its association with *viś* belonging to the *tudādigaṇa*, the root *vid* with the *śap* suffix is understood; thus, for *vid* with the *luk* suffix, we have *viditaḥ* and *viditavān*. Only when the root has a single vowel (*ekāc*) do we have *saṃjñapitaḥ* and *daridritaḥ*. Also, [the rule applies] to those roots marked with *ādi* (indicating the optional presence of *iṭ*).

From the beginning, the augment *iṇ* is not present in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Examples: *minnaḥ*, *kṣviṇṇaḥ*. Due to the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], also: *āśvastaḥ*, *vāntaḥ*. [The augment *iṇ* is] optional in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) or a reflexive action (*ādikarman*).

Alternatively, [the suffix *kta*] is applied after the roots *mī* (to measure) and *mī* (to destroy) when used with the prefixes *pra-* and *vi-*, respectively, in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the beginning of an action (*ārambha*). Thus, one says *praminnaḥ* or *prameditaḥ* (measured or destroyed by him), or *praminnaḥ* or *prameditaḥ* (this one has been measured or destroyed). Regarding the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object (*karman*), the followers of Śākalya (*saunāgāḥ*) maintain that the augment *iṭ* is optional after the root *śak*. Thus, one says either *śaktaḥ* or *śakitaḥ* (capable) regarding a jar (*ghaṭaḥ*) to be made. The words *kṣubdha*, *svānta*, *dhvānta*, *lagna*, *mliṣṭa*, *viribdha*, *phāṇṭa*, and *bāḍha* are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) to mean, respectively: churning (*mantha*), mind (*manas*), darkness (*tamas*), clinging (*sakta*), indistinct (*avispaṣṭa*), sound (*svara*), and excessive effort (*anāyāsa*) or intensity (*bhṛśa*). Specifically: *kṣubdha* means "churned"; *svānta* means "mind"; *dhvānta* means "darkness"; *lagna* means "clinging"; *mliṣṭa* means "indistinct"; *viribdha* means "sound"; *phāṇṭa* means "effortless" (referring to a decoction made without heating); and *bāḍha* means "intense. These forms are established as exceptions to the general rules for the application of *kta*.

The forms *kṣubdha* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of "churning" (*mantha*) and so forth. *kṣubdhaḥ* means churning; that is, a stirring-stick. *svāntam* means the mind (*manaḥ*). *dhvāntam* means darkness (*tamaḥ*). *lagnam* means stuck or attached (*saktam*). *mliṣṭam* means indistinct. *viribdhaḥ* refers to a tone such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth. *phāṇṭaḥ* refers to a person or something else who is effortless. *phāṇṭāḥ* refers to those whose hands hold various weapons. *bāḍham* means excessively or intensely. In other senses, the forms are *kṣubhitam*, *svanitama*, *dhvanitam*, *lagitam*, *mlecchitam*, *virebhitam*, *phaṇitam*, and *bāhitam*.
The roots *dhṛṣ* and *śas* are used in the sense of impudence (*vaiyātya*).

In these two cases, when the sense is "boldness" or "completion," the suffix *iṇ* does not occur. [Examples: *dhṛṣṭaḥ*, *viśastaḥ*. Why [is the rule] stated as "in the sense of impudence"? [Counter-examples: *dharṣitaḥ*, *viśasitaḥ*. [The word] *dṛḍhaḥ* [is formed with *kta*] in the senses of "thick" and "strong."
The form *dṛḍha* is substituted for the root *dṛh* when preceded by *sthūla*, *balavat*, or *dṛha*;
and *parivṛḍha* is used in the sense of "lord" (*prabhu*).
In this context, the following [suffix] is prescribed:
the suffix *kta* is applied after the root *kaṣ* when used with the words *kṛcchra* and *gahana*.

In the sense of "difficult," [the suffix *khal*] is applied after the roots *gaha*, *kaṣi*, and *agni*; for example, *kaṣṭaṃ duḥkham* ("a difficult suffering"), *kaṣṭaṃ gahanam* ("a difficult thicket"), and *kaṣṭo 'gniḥ* ("a painful fire"). The root *ghuṣi* is used in the sense of "not making a sound."

The suffix *iṇ* does not occur after the root *ghuṣ* when followed by a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Examples: *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* (the rope has been sounded), *śastraghuṣṭakarān kapīn* (monkeys whose hands were struck by weapons), *udghuṣṭo 'yamarthaḥ* (this matter has been proclaimed), *udghuṣṭaṃ parapuṣṭayā* (proclaimed by the cuckoo). Why say "not in the sense of sound"? [Observe: *avaghuṣitaṃ vākyam āha* (he spoke a word that was not sounded); the meaning is that it was improper or ungrammatical. [Now for the rule: After the root *ard*, [the suffix *iṇ* is not used] when preceded by *sam*, *ni*, or *vi*.
The augment *iṇ* is not applied to the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) after these prefixes: *sam-arṇaḥ*, *ni-arṇaḥ*, *vi-arṇaḥ*; that is to say, when the root is *pīṅ*.
Also, [the augment is not applied] after *abhi* when there is no sense of proximity (*avidūrya*).

In the sense of "nearness," the suffix *iṇ* does not occur after the root *ṛd* when followed by the prefix *abhi* and ending in a *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffix. Thus, *abhyarṇā senā* ("the army is near").
[Furthermore,] the suffix *ṇa* is applied to the root *vṛt* when preceded by *adhi* in the sense of "occurrence" (*vṛtta*). Thus, *adhyātma-vṛtta*.

From the root *vṛt* with the causative suffix (*ṇi*), the form *vṛtta* occurs in the sense of study; for example, "the *pārāyaṇa* has been completed by him. In other senses, it is *vartita*. Furthermore, the forms *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *channa*, and *jñapta* are optionally formed [with the suffix *kta*].

The seven roots beginning with *dam* (Dami-ādi), when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, optionally take the suffix *am*; in the alternative case, they form *damitaḥ*, *śamitaḥ*, *pūritaḥ*, *dāsitaḥ*, *spāśitaḥ*, *chāditaḥ*, and *jñapitaḥ*.
[This applies] to the roots *ruṣ*, *am*, *tvar*, *saṃghuṣ*, and *asvan*.
For these [roots], there may optionally be *iṭ*: *ruṣṭaḥ* or *ruṣitaḥ*; *abhyāntaḥ* or *abhyamitaḥ*;
*tatūrṇaḥ* or *tvaritaḥ*; a sentence that is *saṃghuṣṭam* or *saṃghuṣitam*; a drum that is *āsvāntaḥ* or *āsvanitaḥ*. [The suffix *kta* is used] after the root *hṛṣ* when referring to body hair.

From the root *hṛṣ* in the sense of "to be pleased," the suffix *iṭ* may optionally be applied when the agent is body hair (*loman*). Thus, one says *hṛṣṭam* or *hṛṣitam* [of the hair]. With reference to the hair: *hṛṣṭam* or *hṛṣitam* by the hairs; *bhayasaṃhṛṣṭalomānaḥ* ("those whose body hair has bristled with fear").
Why "in the case of body hair"? [Consider: *hṛṣito vipraḥ* ("the Brahmin is delighted").
And also in the senses of "astonishment" and "resistance," the suffix *iṭ* may optionally be applied. Thus, *hṛṣṭaḥ* or *hṛṣitaḥ*, meaning "astonished" or "resisted."
And he was honored.
Alternatively, the substitution of *ci* for the root *apacāyati* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Thus we have *apacitaḥ* or *apacāyitaḥ*.
It should be stated that the substitution of *ci* is obligatory when the suffix *ktin* follows. [The phrase] "honouring was performed by the kings" is an example.
Here, there are four metrical rules (*chandaḥ-sūtra*). They are as follows:
Hra hvarēś chandasi.
And they are not subject to defeat.
Some are crooked.

And [the following are also used]: *grasiti*, *skabhiti*, *stabhiti*, *uttabhiti*, *cattavi*, *kastāvi*, *śaṃstṛ*, *śaṃstṛ*, *jñāstṛ*, *tarutṛ*, *tarūtṛ*, *varutṛ*, *varūtrī*, *ujjvaliti*, *kṣariti*, *kṣamiti*, *vamiti*, and *amiti*.
The augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant of the *val* class.
The augment *iṭ* shall be added to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix that begins with a consonant (*valādi*). Examples: *bhavitā*, *lavitā*; *lavitum*; *laviṣyati*; *alaviṣyat*; *lulavitha*; *laviṣīṣṭa*.

Why "beginning with a consonant" (*valādeḥ*)? [Because in cases like] *lavyam* and *lavanīyam*, it does not apply. This rule for the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix applies up to the rule beginning with *rudādi*.

The rule for the augment *iṭ* after roots beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) is prescribed for the following: the *liṭ* affixes *thava*, *mas*, and *dhv*; the *syasīyuṭ* and *tās* affixes; the *san* affix;
and the *tṛc*, *tumun*, *tavyat*, and *niṣṭhā* (kta/ktavatu) affixes. This applies until the point where the elision of the *sa* of *sas* is taught.
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the roots *snū* and *kram* occurs when they do not have a cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

The suffix *iṭ* shall be added after the roots *snu* and *kram*. [Examples: *sravitā*, *kramitā*; *sravitum*, *kramitum*. This prohibition applies where *snu* and *kram* are causes for the *ātmanepada* voice; for instance, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*): *prasrīṣīṣṭa*, *prakraṃsīṣṭa*.

There is a prohibition [of the *yaṅ* suffix] after the root *kram* when it occurs in the *ātmanepada* and is followed by a *kṛt* suffix. After the roots *pra* and *upa*, when they are semantically connected [with *kram*], [the forms are] *prākrāntā* and *upakrāntā*. Why "in that domain" (*tadviṣayāt*)? [Counter-example: *niṣkramitā*. Why "after *kram*" (*krameḥ*)? [Counter-example: *vyatisraviṭā*; *prasravitrī gauḥ svayameva* ("the cow flows forth by herself").
In the case of the root *grah*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] except in the *liṭ* [perfect tense].

The augment *iṭ* is long after the root *grah*, except when it is *liṭ*. [Examples: *grahītā* (the agent), *grahītum* (infinitive), *grahītavyam* (gerundive). Why "except when it is *liṭ*" (*aliṭi*)? [Counter-examples: *jagṛhiva*, *jagṛhima* (perfect forms). Even for the *iṭ* that follows the rule of *ciṇvat*, the lengthening does not occur, because that is not the subject under discussion here. [Example: *grāhiṣyate* (future passive participle).
It does not occur after a stem with a *yaṅ* elision (*yaṅluk*), because it is understood that the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for the root *grah*. [Examples: *jarīgṛhitā*.
[The rule] *vṛto vā* [applies].

A long vowel may optionally be substituted for the *iṭ* augment after these roots: *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*. Thus, one may say either *varitum* or *varītuṃ*; *varitā* or *varītā*; *āstaritum* or *āstarītuṃ*; *jaritvā* or *jarītvā*. The restriction "except in the *liṭ*" applies here as well; thus, [in the *liṭ*] one says *teritha* or *ātastaritha*.
Why specify "after *vṛta*"? [To exclude: *kariṣyati*. This does not apply in the *liṅ* (optative).
The long vowel [substitution] in the *liṅ* (optative) after a root ending in *vṛt* would not occur; for example: *prāvariṣīṣṭa*, *tariṣīṣṭa*.
Also, [the substitution of *iṭ*] does not occur in the *sic* (aorist marker) when followed by *parasmaipada* endings.
The lengthening of the vowel does not occur when *sic* follows after a root ending in *vṛ*. Examples: *prāvāriṣṭām*, *āstāriṣṭām*.
Why "in the parasmaipada endings"? [Observe: *āvarīṣṭa* or *āvariṣṭa*; *atarīṣṭa* or *atariṣṭa*.
[In the case of the suffix] *san*, the augment *iṭ* is optional.

The suffix *san* (desiderative) may optionally take the augment *īṭ*: *prāvuvūrṣuḥ*, "desiring to cause to flow," from the root *vṛ* (to flow), when it is called upon by the Lord who desires to issue a command (*ājñām vivariṣoḥ*). Or: *prāvivarīṣuḥ*. From roots ending in *ṛ*—*titīrṣuḥ*, "desiring to cross" the difficult-to-cross ocean with a raft due to delusion (*mohāt*), [from the root *tṛ*]. Or: *titariṣuḥ*, *titarīṣuḥ*. Because these are technical forms (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*), it is not included here: *cikīrṣati*, "he desires to do. [The augment *īṭ* is optional] before the suffixes *liṅ* (optative) and *sic* (aorist) when the *ātmanepada* endings follow.

After the root *vṛ*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally occur before the suffixes *liṅ* (optative) and *sic* (aorist). Thus: *vṛṣīṣṭa* or *varīṣīṣṭa*; *āstīrṣīṣṭa*, *āstīrṣīṣṭa*, *āstariṣīṣṭa*, or *āstarīṣīṣṭa*. With *sic*: *avṛta*, *avariṣṭa*, or *avarīṣṭa*; *āstīrṣṭa*, *āstariṣṭa*, or *āstarīṣṭa*. Why "in the Ātmanepada"? [Because in the Parasmaipada it is not optional: *āstāriṣṭām*, *āstāriṣuḥ*; *prāvariṣṭām*. In these cases, the *iṭ* is compulsory.
And [the substitution of *ṛ* occurs] for a root beginning with *ṛ* that has a conjunct consonant as its initial.

After a verbal root ending in ṛ and beginning with a conjunct consonant, the augment iṭ is optionally applied before the ātmanepada suffixes liṅ (optative) and sic (aorist). For example: *dhvṛṣīṣṭa* or *dhvariṣīṣṭa*; *stṛṣīṣṭa* or *stariṣīṣṭa*; *smṛṣīṣṭa* or *smariṣīṣṭa*. In the case of *sic*: *asmṛṣātām* or *asmariṣātām*; *adhvṛṣātām* or *adhvariṣātām*.
Because it is defined by its specific grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*), the augment does not apply here: *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, *samaskṛta*.
[The augment iṭ is also optional] after the roots *svarati*, *sūti*, *sūyati*, *dhūñ*, and those marked with the indicatory letter *it*.

After these roots, the suffix *iṭ* may optionally be applied: from *svar*, either *svaritum* or *svartum*; from *sū* and *sūyati*, either *sotum* or *savitum*; from *dhū*, either *dhotum* or *dhavitum*. After roots marked with a circumflex *ū* (*ūditaḥ*), it is optional: from *guh*, either *gāḍhum* or *gāhitum*; from *gup*, either *goptum* or *gopitum*; from *mṛj*, either *mārṣṭum* or *mārjitum*.

Because this section of prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) precedes [the rules for *ktvā*], it serves as a general exception (*sarvāpavāda*): hence *sūtvā*, *dhūtvā*, and *svṛtvā*. And [the suffix *iṭ* is not applied] after roots beginning with *radh*.

The augment *iṭ* may optionally be applied after eight roots beginning with *radh*. Thus: *rakṣitum* or *raṃdhum*; *naśitum* or *naṃṣṭum*; *tarpitum* or *tartum*. *radh*, *naś*, and *tṛp*, as well as *ip*, *druh*, *muha*, *snih*, and *snuh*—these are the roots beginning with *radh* belonging to the *divādi* (fourth) class.
In the case of *krādi* roots, there is no restriction: *rarandhiva*, *rarandhima*; [the substitution of] *niṛ* for *kuṣ*.
The root *niṣkuṣ* may optionally take the suffix *iṭ*: either *niṣkoṣitum* or *niṣkoṣṭum*. [This applies] when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows the root *iṇ*.

The augment *iṭ* shall be applied after the root *kuṣ* when the suffix of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) follows. Examples: *niṣkuṣitaḥ*, *niṣkuṣitavān*. [This rule applies to the roots] *tīṣ*, *sa*, *hal*, *lubh*, *ruṣ*, and *riṣ*.

The augment *iṭ* may optionally occur after these roots when followed by a suffix beginning with the letter *t*. Thus: *eṣṭā* or *eṣitā*; *soḍhā* or *sodhitā*; *lobdhā* or *lobhitā*; *roṣṭā* or *roṣitā*; *reṣṭā* or *reṣitā*.
Why "beginning with *t*" (*titi*)? [To exclude cases such as] *eṣiṣyati*, which is not desired for the root *iṣ* (meaning "to go"). In *praṣitum*, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory.
The suffix *ni* is applied after the roots √van, √tṛd, √bhrasj, √dambh, √śri, √svṛ, √ūrṇu, √bhṛ, √jñā, and √san.

The root *bhṛ* belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*: *bubhūrṣati*, or *bibhariṣati*. *Jñīpsati*, or *jijñapayiṣati*. *Siṣāsati*, or *sisaniṣati*.

[The augment *iṭ* is also applied] after the root *añc* when used in the sense of worship.

The suffix *iṭ* shall be applied after these two: *jaritvā* or *jarītvā*; *vraścitvā*.
However, for the root *jṛṣ* with its *anubandha*, it is *jīrtvā*.
[The suffix *iṭ*] is optionally applied after a root marked with *ud*.

The suffix *ktvā* may optionally take the augment *iṭ*. Thus: *dāntvā* or *damitvā*; *śāntvā* or *śamitvā*; *vṛttvā* or *vartitvā*; *syūtvā* or *sevitvā*; *ratvā* or *ramitvā*; *srastvā* or *saṃśritvā*; from the root *und*, *vuntvā* or *vunditvā*; *śiṣṭvā* or *śāsitvā*.
[The augment *iṭ* is applied] after the roots *kṛ*, *cṛ*, *chṛ*, *tṛd*, and *nṛt* when followed by *se* (the suffix *liṭ*) that does not have *sic*.

The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to the roots *kṛt*, *cṛt*, *chṛt*, *tṛd*, and *nṛt* before an affix beginning with *s*. Thus: *rkartsyati* or *karttiṣyati*; *rcartsyati* or *carttiṣyati*; and so on, up to: *rnartsyati* or *narttiṣyati*. Why "before *sic*"? [Observe: *akarttīt*, *anarttīt*.
The augment *iṭ* is added to the root *gam* before Parasmaipada affixes.

The augment *iṭ* shall be applied after the root *gam* when followed by an affix beginning with the letter *s*. Examples: *gamiṣyati*, *jigamiṣati*. The substitute form of the root *gam* is also included—e.g., *adhijigamiṣitā vyākaraṇasya* ("one who desires to learn grammar").

The mention of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is for the purpose of excluding the *ātmanepada* (middle voice). Examples: *sañjigaṃsate*, *adhijigāṃsate śāstram*. [This rule does not apply] after the four roots beginning with *vṛt*.
The suffix *iṇ* does not occur after the roots *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *śṛdh*, and *syandū* when followed by a word beginning with *s*. Examples: *rvatsyati*, *rvatsyan*, *vivṛtsati*, *vivṛtsitum*.

This restriction applies only to the *parasmaipada* endings—e.g., *vartiṣyate*, *vartiṣīṣṭa*. [The suffix *iṇ* is also absent] after the root *klṛp* when followed by the suffix *tās* (the future marker).
In the case of these roots, the suffix *iṇ* does not occur after *sādi* (the suffixes beginning with *sa*). [Examples: *kalptāsi*, *kalpsyati*, *ciklṛpsati*.
As before, when the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used: *kalpitāse* or *kalptāse*; *kalpsyate* or *kalpiṣyate*. [The rule] *acastāsvatthalyaniṭo nityam* applies.

For those roots that are invariably *aniṭ* (without the augment *iṭ*) and end in a vowel, there is no *iṭ* in the *thal* suffix, just as there is none in the *tās* suffix. This is because it is obtained by the rule beginning with *krādi*. Examples: *pātā*, *papātha*; *yātā*, *yayātha*; *netā*, *ninetha*; *jetā*, *jigetha*; *hotā*, *juhotha*. Why "ending in a vowel"? Consider *bhettā*, *bibheditha*. Why "invariably *aniṭ*"? Consider *dhūñ*: *dhotā*, *dhavitā*; *dudhavitha*. Why "in *tās*"? Consider *lūtvā*, *lulavitha*. However, this root (*dhūñ*) is invariably *aniṭ* before a *kit* suffix.
In an *upadeśa*, [the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*] does not take place for a stem ending in *at*.

In the recited text (*pāṭha*), there is no substitution of *iṇ* for a verbal root ending in the letter *a*, as in the previous rule. Examples: *śaśaktha*, *papaktha*, *iyaṣṭha*. Why is the term "having *t* as its marker" (*taparaḥ*) used? [To exclude cases like] *rarādhitha*. Why is it specified "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*)? [To exclude cases like] *cakarṣitha*. But how is it that [the forms] *papitha*, *yayitha*, *śekitha*, and *pecitha* are formed? He says:
The Ṛtu [Sāman] of Bhāradvāja.
According to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, this prohibition applies only to roots ending in *ṛ*. Thus, one forms *sasmartha* and *dadhvartha*.
However, from other roots, the suffix *-thas* would indeed occur—as in *papitha*, *yayitha*, *ninayitha*, and *śekitha*.

But how is it that we have *tuṣṭotha* and *dudrotha*? Because the prohibitive rule is stronger due to its placement prior to the section on the restrictive rule for roots beginning with *kṛ* (the *krādiniyama*).
"Babhūtha," "ātatantha," "jagṛmbha," and "vavārtha" [are forms] in the Veda.
This is Vedic usage.
[In the Veda,] there is optionally [the substitution of *i* for the final vowel] of the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*.

In these two cases, the augment *iṭ* may optionally be inserted: *sasraṣṭha* or *sasarjitha*; *dadraṣṭha* or *dadarśitha*. [The augment *iṭ* is applied] after roots ending in *ṛ*, as well as after *at* and *vyath*.
For these [roots], *thal* may optionally take the augment *iṭ*. Examples: *āditha*, *āritha*, *saṃvivyayitha*.
[The augment *iṭ* is applied] after roots ending in *vas*, after monosyllabic roots, and after the root *ghas*.
The substitution of *v* occurs for the final consonant of the roots *gam*, *han*, *vid*, and *viś* before the suffix *ghañ*.
One who has sighed and is sighing.

Regarding this, they say that the three rules beginning with *vasvekājādghasām* are Vedic (*chāndasa*), because the suffix *kvasu* is Vedic. Yet, the usage of learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*) is observed: *pavivān*, *tasthivān*, *gavi tasthivāṃsam*, *padamātasthuṣā tvayā*, *ūcivān*, *ūṣivān*, *dadṛśivān*, and so forth. Furthermore, Candragomin, the author of the *bhāṣāsūtra*, formulated a rule for the addition of the augment *iṭ* to *kvasu*: *vasvekājādghasām*; *vā gamahanavidaviśām*; and *dṛśeśca*.
Why [specify] "of these"? [To exclude forms like] *babhūvān*.
Or, from the root *gam* and others: *jagmivān*, *jaganvān*.
[The rule] "before the suffix *sya*, [the long vowel is substituted] for *ṛ* and *han*" [applies].

The augment *iṭ* is added after roots ending in long *ṝ* as well as after the root *han*, when followed by the suffix *sya*. [Examples: *kariṣyati*, *akariṣyat*; *haniṣyati*, *ahaniṣyat*. [The augment *iṭ* is also added] after the root *añj* when followed by *sic*.

When a Taddhita suffix beginning with ñ, ṇ, or n (or a Kṛt suffix beginning with k) follows, and there is the possibility of Vṛddhi for the first vowel of the stem *devikā* and others, the substitution of *ā* shall take place. *Śiṃśapāyā vikāraḥ* (a product of the Śiṃśapā tree) becomes *śāṃśapaḥ daṇḍaḥ* (a staff made of Śiṃśapā wood). *Dityavāṭ* is a Vedic form. *Dīrghasatre bhavam* (that which exists in a long sacrificial session) becomes *dārghasatram*. *Śreyasi bhavam* (that which exists in excellence) becomes *śrāyasam*. *Sa śrāyasena pramadena yuktaḥ* (he is endowed with that excellent joy). In the case of *kekaya*, *mitrayu*, and *pralaya*, the substitution of *iy* occurs for the vowel following the initial consonant.

In that [context], for these [words] beginning with *y*, there shall be the substitution of *iy* for the portion beginning with *y*, accompanied by the increase [of the preceding vowel]. [The rule] "not [after vowels] followed by *y* or *v* at the end of a word" does not apply here, because the vowels *ai* and *au* [are substituted] before those two [consonants].

A *vṛddhi* vowel does not occur after the final *y* or *v* of a word-base; however, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* do occur before those two [consonants]. For example: one who studies or knows grammar is a *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*; the offspring of *svaśva* is *sauvaśvaḥ*. And [the same applies] for words beginning with *dvāra*.

Among these, there is no subsequent *vṛddhi* for [the vowels] *y* and *v*; however, *ai* and *au* are substituted for the preceding [consonants] when followed by those two. *Dauvārikaḥ*: one appointed at the gate. *Śauvanam*: belonging to a dog (*śvan*). *Śauvastikaḥ*: that which will happen tomorrow (*śvas*). *Sauvaraḥ*: a treatise composed concerning accent (*svara*).
This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding the case where [the word] ends in a suffix (*apadānta*). [The substitution applies] also for the isolated (*kevala*) word *nyagrodha*.
And for this [suffix], it would likewise be so: *naiyagrodhaś camasaḥ* ("a cup made from a banyan tree").
What about when it is used alone? *nyagrodhamūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice growing at the root of a banyan tree").
[The suffix is not applied] in the sense of reciprocal action (*karmavyatīhāra*).
That which was stated regarding the reciprocal exchange of actions does not apply here: [it excludes] mutual abuse, mutual joking, and [the exchange of] greetings and the like.

Among these, that which was stated does not apply. *Svāgatika* means one who says "welcome" (*svāgata*). *Vyāvahārika* means one who conducts himself according to worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). *Vyāṅgiḥ* is the offspring of *Vyaḍa*.
