From the form *adīdapat*, it follows that even derivative (technical) forms are included: *adhyāpayati*, *adhyāpakaḥ*.
Furthermore, the augment *yuk* is added after the roots *śo*, *śā*, *so*, *hve*, *vyā*, and *veP*.

The augment *yuk* (i.e., *ya*) is applied to these roots when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*. *niśāyayati*, *adhicchāyayati*, *avasāyayati*, *hvāyayati*, *saṃvivyāyayati*. From the root *veñ* (to weave): *vāyayati*. From *pā* (to drink) and *pai* (to dry): *pāyayati*. It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the root *pā* (to protect): *pālayati*.

It should be stated that the augment *nuk* (i.e., *na*) is applied to the roots *dhūñ* (to shake) and *prīñ* (to please): *dhūnayati*, *prīṇayati*. How is it that [the forms] *dhāvayati* and *prāyayati* occur? They belong to two different roots.
The suffix *ju* occurs after the root *dhū* in the sense of shaking.

The augment *juk* shall be applied after the root *vā* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*. Example: *pakṣau vājayati* ("he fans the wings"). What if it does not mean "shaking"? Example: *keśān āvāpayati* ("he causes the hair to grow"). [The roots] *pai* and *ovai* are used in the sense of drying. After the roots *lī* and *līṅ*, the augments *nuk* and *luk* are optionally applied when the meaning is the trickling out of oil or fat.

The forms *lī* (from the root *līṅ*) and *lī* (the form derived from *lī* by the substitution of *atva*, as well as the root *lā*) are included here; after these two, when used with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the augment *nuk* or *luk* may optionally be applied when the meaning is "liquefying. Examples for *lī*: *ghṛtaṃ vilīnayati* or *vilāyayati* ("he causes the ghee to melt"). Examples for *lā*: *ghṛtaṃ vilālayati* or *vilāpayati* ("he causes the ghee to melt"). Why "when liquefying"? [Counter-example: *takraṃ vilāpayati* ("he causes the buttermilk to flow"). [Another example: *jaṭābhir ālāpayate* ("he causes himself to be addressed by means of matted locks"). [Now, regarding the rule: *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* ("after the root *bhī*, the suffix *ṣuk* is added when fear caused by a specific cause is expressed").
The augment *ṣuk* may optionally not be applied after the root *bhi*. Thus, *muṇḍo bhīṣayate* ("the shaven-headed one frightens").

Once the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) has been made, the augment *luk* and *ṣuk* are not desired. Thus, *ghṛtaṃ vilāpayati* ("he causes the ghee to melt") and *muṇḍo bhāpayate* ("the shaven-headed one frightens"). What is the purpose of the condition "out of fear caused by an agent" (*hetubhaye*)? [Consider: *ahinā bhāyayati* ("he frightens with a snake") and *śarair bhīrum abhāyayat* ("he frightened the coward with arrows"). In these cases, there is no *ṣuk*, no middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and no substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
Now begins the section on grammatical substitutions (ādeśa).
May it swell for you.
The suffix *va* shall be applied after the root *ṇau*. [Thus: *sphāvayati*. After the root *śad*, when not meaning "to go," the suffix *ta* is applied.

After the causative suffix *ṇic*, the substitute *ta* shall occur [in place of the root *śad*]. Example: *phalāni śātayati* ("he causes the fruits to fall"). Why "not meaning 'to go'" (*agatau*)? Example: *turagān śādayati* ("he saddles the horses") and *gāḥ śādayati* ("he settles the cows").
After the root *ruh*, the substitute *pa* occurs optionally.
After the causative suffix *ṇic*, the root *ruh* optionally becomes *p*. Thus, one forms either *ropayati* or *rohayati*.
Furthermore, when followed by the feminine suffix *āp* that is not part of a nominal stem (*asupaḥ*), the vowel *a* preceding a *k* situated within a suffix is changed to *i*.

The substitution of *i* for the vowel *a* preceding the letter *k* belonging to an affix (*pratyaya*) occurs when the feminine suffix *āp* follows. Examples: *ṇvul*-kārikā; *pācikā*. By the rule *prāgivāt kaḥ*: *muṇḍikā*; *jaṭilikā*. Why [is it said] "not after a *sup*" (*asupaḥ*)? So that the substitution does not occur when *āp* follows [a word] which is *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix) by virtue of the technical designation *pratyayalakṣaṇa*—as in: *bahuparivrājakā purī* ("the city with many wandering mendicants"). Why [is it said] "of *a*" (*ataḥ*)? [To exclude: *gokā*; *naukā*. Why [is it said] "followed by *t*" (*taparaḥ*)? [To exclude: *rākā*; *dhākā*. Why [is it said] "when *āp* follows" (*āpi*)? [To exclude: *kārakaḥ*; *pācakaḥ*. Why [is it said] "belonging to an affix" (*pratyayasthāt*)? [To exclude: *śakā*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the words *māmaka* and *naraka*: *mameyaṃ māmikā* ("this is mine"); *narān...* [narikā].
The suffix *kā* is applied after a word ending in *nṛ*, provided it does not end in *ap*. Examples: *dākṣiṇātyikā*, *amātyikā*. However, it is not applied after words ending in *yas* or *vas*.

The substitution of *it* for *yat* and *tat* does not occur here: *akac*—*yakā*, *asakā*, *yakām*, *takām*; [he] destroyed the city of the gods (*devapurīm*). [Examples with] *yakābhyām*, *takābhyām*.
There is also an addition [to the rule] regarding the benedictive (*āśis*): *vun*—*nandakā*, *jīvakā*.
And when there is elision of the final member of a compound (*uttarapadalopa*): *devakā*, *devadittakā*.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after *kṣipakā* and others. *Kṣipakā*, *dhruvakā*, *upatyakā*, *adhityakā*.
*Tārakā* when meaning "a star"; otherwise—*tārikā* (a woman). *Varṇakā* when referring to weaving; otherwise—*varṇikā*.
The word *varttakā* denotes a bird according to the Eastern grammarians; elsewhere, it is *varttikā*, meaning "a female.
The word *aṣṭakā* refers to a rite dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛdaivatyam*) and to a specific time (*kālaviśeṣe*).
This is a class of words (*ākṛtigaṇa*) beginning with *kṣipakā*.
[The suffix *kā*] is optionally applied after *sūtakā*, *putrakā*, *vṛndā*, and *kāṇā*: *sūtakā* or *sūtikā*; *putrakā* or *putrikā*; *vṛndārakā* or *vṛndārikā*; *kāṇā* or *kāṇikā*.
According to the Northern Grammarians, [the suffix *kā* is optionally applied] in place of the long vowel *ā* when it is preceded by *ya* or *ka*.

According to the opinion of Udīcya grammarians, the substitution of *it* (the feminine suffix *kāp*) shall not occur for the vowel *ā* that follows a word ending in *ya* or *ka*. Examples: *ibhyakā* or *ibhyikā*; *kṣatriyakā* or *kṣatriyikā*. For a word preceded by *ka*: *caṭakakā* or *caṭakikā*. Why "preceded by *ya* or *ka*"? [Consider: *aśvikā*.

Because the rule specifies "of a word denoting a female (*strīviṣaya*)," it does not apply here: from the root *śakaśakāyati* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *śakaśakāḥ*; then with the suffix *ka*, we get *śakaśakikā*. Also, *śubhaṃyikā*.
When preceded by *ya*, there is a prohibition [of the substitution of *ī*] for the *y* and *k* at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Examples: *sunayikā*, *aśokikā*, *suśayikā*, *supākikā*.
This prohibition applies even when preceded by *bhasra*, *eṣa*, *ajā*, *jñā*, *dvā*, *svā*, or *nañ*.

For the words *bhastrā* and others that are pure (i.e., not compounded), even when preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*) or by another word, the substitution of *it* does not occur according to the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*).

Thus: *bhastrakā* or *bhastrikā*; *abhastrakā* or *abhastrikā*; *bahubhastrakā* or *bahubhastrikā*. Also: *eṣakā* or *eṣikā*; *dvakā* or *dvikā*; *jñakā* or *jñikā*; *ajñakā* or *ajñikā*; *ajakā* or *ajikā*; *svakā* or *svikā*; *bahusvakā* or *bahusvikā*.
The forms *eṣā* and *dve*, however, are not used when preceded by the negative particle or by another word.
And [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a word that does not have a corresponding masculine form.

The substitution of *ām* for the vowel *a* in place of a feminine suffix that does not express the masculine gender does not occur according to the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*). Thus, one says either *khaṭvakā* or *khaṭivakā*, or *mālakā* or *mālikā*.
According to the Teachers (*ācāryāṇām*), however, the substitution of *ām* does occur.
According to the opinion of the teachers, the suffix *ā* should be applied [to the word *khaṭva*]. Thus: *khaṭvākā*, *mālakā*.
[The rule] "for *ṭha*, *ika*" applies.
The *ika* substitute shall take the place of the *ṭha* suffix when it follows a stem ending in *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, or *ṣ*. For example: *ṭhak*—*ākṣikaḥ*; *ṭhañ*—*lāvaṇikaḥ*.
Furthermore, the suffix *ka* is applied after stems ending in *is*, *us*, *uk*, or *t*.

What suffix would apply after these? It is *ka*, which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ika*. Examples: *sārpiṣkaḥ* (made from clarified butter), *dhānuṣkaḥ* (skilled with a bow). After a word ending in *u*: *ordeśe ṭaññ*—*naiṣādakarṣukaḥ* (a place where Niṣādas dwell), *audaśvitkaḥ* (made from buttermilk), *petṛkaḥ* (relating to a father). There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the word *doṣan*: *dauṣkaḥ* (one who crosses by means of his arms). For the consonants *c* and *j*, there is *ku* before the affixes *ghin* and *ṇyat*.
When the suffixes *ghit* or *ṇyat* follow, the consonants *c* and *j* are replaced by a *k*-class consonant (*kavarga*). Examples: *pākaḥ*, *bhogaḥ*; *pākyam*, *bhogyam*.
Also, this applies to the group beginning with *nyaṅku*.

In these cases, there would be the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *k* to *g*). For example: *nyaṅkuḥ*, *madguḥ*, *bhṛguḥ*, *takram*, *vakram*. With the suffix *ac* from the *pacādi* group: *vyatiṣaṅgaḥ*, *nidāghaḥ*, *meghaḥ*. With the suffix *aṇ* after the sense of "fit for the action" (*karmaṇyaṇ*): *śvapākaḥ*, *māṃsapākaḥ*.
[And] *ṇi* is substituted for the *h* of the root *han* before suffixes beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, or *e*.

When followed by a *ñ*, *ṇ*, *ṇit* suffix, or the letter *n*, the substitution of *k* (known as *kutva*) shall occur for the letter *h* of the root *han*. Examples: *dhātaḥ* (from *dhāt*), *ghātayati*, *ghātakaḥ*.
Regarding the letter *n*: *ghnanti*, *vṛtraghnā*, *vārtraghraḥ* (the descendant of Vṛtraghna). Also [after a reduplication].

The substitution of *k* for *h* occurs in the root *han*. [Examples: *jighāṃsuḥ* (desiring to kill), *jaṅghanyate* (is killed repeatedly). In the perfect tense, [the substitution occurs] as in *ahaṃ jaghana* (I struck). [This applies] except when *aṅ* follows.

The root *hi* (to send) likewise becomes *jighī*: *prajighāya*, *prajighīṣati*, *prajeghīyate*. Why "provided there is no *aṅ*" (*acaṅi*)? [Because] *prājīhayat* [is formed with *aṅ*]. [This rule applies] to the root *ji* before the suffix *sal* and in the periphrastic future (*liṭ*).

The substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*) shall occur for the root *ji* before the suffix *san* and also before the *liṭ* (perfect) affixes. Thus: *jigīṣati* (he desires to conquer), *jigāya* (he conquered).
[And] optionally so for the root *ci*.
Or [the augment *iṭ* is applied] after the root *ci* (to gather): *cicaiṣati*, *cikīṣati*. Or [it is applied] optionally: *niścikāya* or *niścicāya*.
But not after a root beginning with *kvā*.
It has been stated that the *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *c*) does not occur after the *ka*-group and so forth. Examples: *kūjaḥ*, *kūjayam*, *saṃkocaḥ*, *kharjaḥ*, *garjaḥ*.
By means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), it is not the case here: *romāñcaḥ*, *śocyam*.
And [it does not occur] after *aj* and *vraj*: *ajivrajyośca*.
In these two cases, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*) would not occur: *samājaḥ* and *parivrājyam*.
Because of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], we have *vājaḥ* and *pakṣaḥ*.
[The forms] *bhujam* and *nyubjam* are used in the senses of "hand" and "affliction," respectively.

These [suffixes] are elided in these two cases: *bhujaḥ* means "the hand," as it is that by which one eats (*bhujyate*); *nyubjaḥ* means "a disease," as it is that by which one is bent down (*nyubjyate*). In other instances: *bhogaḥ* ("enjoyment") and *samudgaḥ* ("a casket").
*Prayāja* and *anuyāja* refer to parts of a sacrifice.
These two are applied as suffixes in the context of sacrificial limbs (*yajñāṅga*); elsewhere, they are used in their general application. *Anuyāga*:
from the root *vañj*, meaning "to go."

There is no *kutva* [change of *v* to *u*]. [The forms] *vañcyam* and *vañcanti* mean "they deceive" (*vañcayanti*). [The form] *gantavyam* means "they go" (*yānti*). Why [is the rule] restricted to the root *gam*? [Consider] *vaṅgyam* as in "bent wood. [The suffix] *ke* follows the roots *uc* and *oka*.
This is a formal derivation (*nipātana*) for the word *uceñña* when the suffix *kap* follows, intended to preserve the accent;
[the suffix] *ṇya* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).
In other cases, there is no substitution of *ku*. For example: *apaśyapācyam*. Why [is the suffix] *ṇyat* used in the sense of necessity? Example: *pākyam*.
Also for the roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *ruc*, *pravac*, and *arc*: [the suffix *ṇyat* is applied].

And for these [roots], there is no substitution of *ku* (i.e., *guṇa*) before the suffix *ṇya*. Examples: *yājyam*, *yācyam*, *rocyam*, and the book named *pravācya*. Regarding *arcyam*: the suffix *ṇyat* is used; because of this very rule, the suffix *kyap* does not apply after the root *ṛc*. There is an addition [to the rule] for the root *tyaj*: *tyājyam*.
[The suffix *ṇyat* applies] to the root *vac* when it does not denote a grammatical technical term (*saṃjñā*).
In the case of the root *vac*, there is no substitution of *ku* (i.e., *v* becomes *u*). Thus, the form is *vācyam*.
Why is it said "except when it is a technical grammatical term (*aśabda-saṃjñā*)"? [Because in that case, *vākyam* is used].
The forms *prayojya* and *niyojya* are used in the sense of possibility (*śakya-artha*).

These two [suffixes, -ya and -anīya] are prescribed as irregular forms (nipātana) in the sense of capability. That which can be employed is *prayojya*; that which can be directed is *niyojya*. Otherwise, they are *prayogya* and *niyogya*.
[The suffix -ya is used after the root *bhuj*] in the sense of "that which is to be eaten": *bhojyam*.
[The suffix] is elided. "Rice is to be eaten" (*bhojya odanaḥ*).
Why "in the sense of what is to be eaten" (*bhakṣye*)? [Consider: "A woman is to be enjoyed" (*bhogyā strī*). [In the Vedic subjunctive (*leṭ*), there is optionally the elision of *ghu*.]
This is Vedic.
[The rule] "otaḥ śyani" applies.
There shall be elision of the root-final *s* when followed by the suffix *śyan*. Thus: *do-* becomes *dyati*; *ṣo-* becomes *syati* and *avasyati*.
[Furthermore, there is elision] of the final *s* of a root ending in *ks* before a vowel.

There shall be elision of the final letter of a *kṣa*-ending [root] when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel and ending in *t*. [Examples: *adhukṣātām*, *adhukṣi*. Alternatively, there is optional elision (*luk*) of the suffix after the roots *duh*, *hi*, *lih*, and *guh* when the *ātmanepada* endings beginning with a dental consonant follow.

For all these [roots], there may optionally be elision (*luk*) of the *ksa* affix before a *taṅ* substitute beginning with a dental sound. Thus: *adugdha*, *adhukṣata*; *adugdhāḥ*, *adhukṣathāḥ*; *adhugdhvam*, *adhukṣadhvam*.

The labiodental *v* is also included by the term "dental" (*dantya*). Because the root *vah* does not begin with a consonant other than a *jhal*, the substitution of *gh* for *d* does not occur. Hence: *aduhvahi*, *adhukṣāvahi*.
The long vowel is substituted for the eight roots beginning with *śam* before the suffix *śyan*.

In the presence of the suffix *śyan*, there is lengthening of the vowel in the eight roots beginning with *śam*. Thus: *śāmyati*, *tāmyati*, *dāmyati*, *śrāmyati*, *bhrāmyati*, *kṣāmyati*, *klāmyati*, *mādyati*. Why "in the presence of *śyan*"? [Observe: *bhramati* (where *śyan* is optional). *Śyan* is optionally applied after *bhrāś* according to the rule "vā bhrāśa". [Furthermore: "In the presence of a *śit* suffix, there is lengthening for the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *klam*, and *ācam*."
In these cases, the long vowel should be substituted for the short *i*. [Thus one says: *niṣṭhīvati*, *ācāmati*, *klāmati*.
In the case of the root *kram*, [the substitution occurs] when it is used with the *parasmaipada* endings.
The root *śit* (to go) becomes long [in the present tense]. Examples: *krāmati*, *utkrāman*. Not here: *kramate buddhiḥ*.
[In the case of the roots] *iṣu*, *gam*, and *yam*, [the substitute] *cha* is applied.
For these [roots], *cha* shall be substituted for *śit*. He desires (*icchati*). He goes (*gacchati*). He restrains (*yacchati*). He gave (*prāyacchat*).
Because of the specific mention of the letter *u*, it does not apply here: he wishes (*iṣyati*), he impels (*iṣṇāti*).

In place of the roots *pā* (to drink), *ghrā* (to smell), *dhmā* (to blow), *sthā* (to stand), *mnā* (to study), *dāṇ* (to give), *dṛś* (to see), *ṛ* (to go), *sṛ* (to flow), *śad* (to perish), and *sad* (to sit), there are substituted respectively: *piba*, *jighra*, *dhama*, *tiṣṭha*, *mana*, *yaca*, *paśya*, *vicha*, *dhau*, *śīya*, and *sīda*.

In the case of the eleven roots beginning with *pāghrā*, the substitutes *piba* and others shall occur when the suffix *śit* (indicating the present tense) follows. *pibati* (he drinks), *pibet* (he may drink); *jighrati* (he smells); *dhamati* (he blows); *tiṣṭhati* (he stands); *manati* (he thinks); *yacchati* (he restrains); *paśyati* (he sees); *ṛcchati* (he goes). Regarding the root *sṛt* (to go), when meaning "swift motion," [the substitute is *dhāv*]: *dhāvati* (he runs); otherwise—*abhisarati* (he approaches). *śīyate* (he lies down); *sīdati* (he sinks/sits).
Because of the Vedic (Sautra) rule "artisarti," there is an absence of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The substitution of *jā* occurs for the roots *jñā* and *jan*.
The root √jñā (to know) and √jan (to be born) may optionally take the affix *niC*. [Examples: *jānāti* (he knows), *jāyate* (he is born).
For roots beginning with *pū*, there is shortening of the vowel.
For these [roots], there shall be a short *śit* vowel: *punāti*, *lunāti*, *stṛṇāti*; and for the root *mī*, it occurs thus in the Veda (*nigama*).
Vedic grammar.
Now begins the section on secondary qualities (guṇa).
The quality of being middling.

For a root ending in a short vowel (śit), there shall be a single substitution of guṇa for the penultimate vowel. Thus: *medyati*, *medyataḥ*, *medyanti*. Only when [the suffix] is śit—[as in] *midyate*.
And also before the suffix *jus*.

In place of a single vowel at the end of a verbal base (*aṅga*), there shall be *guṇa* before the suffix *jus*. Examples: *abibhayuḥ*, *ajāgaruḥ*, *aiyaruḥ*. This *guṇa* is an exception to the *ṅit*-status based on *jus*; it is superseded by the *ṅit*-status of *yāsuṭ*—as in *cinuyuḥ*, *brūyuḥ*, *sunuyuḥ*. [This applies] by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*.

The *guṇa* substitution shall apply to the final vowel of these two roots when they function as *aṅga*s (bases). Examples: *jayati*, *nayati*, *cinoti*, *bhavati*, *karoti*; [in the benedictive] *karavāva*, *karavāma*; [with the suffix *kvip*] *vidhavati* (meaning "he acts like a widow"), *savitari*, *rātrayati*.
In the context of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes: *jetum*, *netum*, *bhavitum*, *kartum*, *taritum*, *vidhavitum*, *savitaritum*.
Why specify "these two"? [Because the rule does not apply to others: *agnikāmyati*, *bhūkāmyati*.
The substitution of *guṇa* for the root *jāgṛ* occurs before the affixes *a*, *vic*, *ṇi*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ*.

In the scope of both the prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the application of *guṇa*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the root *jāgarti*. Examples: *jāgarayati*, *nāgarakaḥ*, *jāgaritaḥ*, *jāgaritavān*. Regarding the substitution of *riṅ* as well, the *āgama* (augment) is applied as *guṇa* by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Example: *jāgaryate tvayā*. Why is it said "except in the case of *vin*, *ciṇ*, and *ṅit*"? — *vin*: *jāgṛviḥ*. — *ciṇ*: *ajāgāri*. — *ṇal*: *jajāgāra*. — *ṅit*: *jāgṛtaḥ*, *jāgṛthaḥ*.

How is it that *ajāgaruḥ* occurs? [The form] *jajāgara* results from the application of the rule *jāgarti* (Pāṇini 7.3.85), which is here prohibited. However, in this case, the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the two preceding rules:
*pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.86).

The *guṇa* substitution shall occur for roots ending in a consonant (*hal*) that have a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), before both *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Examples: *kropayati*, *hrepayati*; *hrepaṇam*; *vardhate*, *vartate*; *varttanam*; *bhedayati*, *bhettā*, *bhedanam*; *chettā*. How is it that [the form] *bibhitsati* occurs? Because of the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) prescribed by the rule *halantācca*. How is it that *likhanam* and *likhiṣyati* occur? Because the *guṇa* substitution is considered non-obligatory (*anitya*) when it is conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*).
Now follows the prescription for [suffixes] occurring after a verbal root (sārvadhātuka).
The substitution of *guṇa* does not take place for a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) before a *sarvadhātuka* suffix that begins with a vowel and has *p* as its *it*.

The guna substitute does not apply to a reduplicated root (abhyasta) before a sārvadhātuka affix beginning with *p* that has an initial vowel such as *a*. Examples: *nenijāni*, *anenijam*. Why "before an initial vowel"? Consider *nenekti*. In the *laṅ*: *anenek*. Guna occurs only when the penultimate vowel is light (*laghu*): *juhavāni cānale*. This rule applies up to the point where it is prescribed for sārvadhātuka affixes and also for *sup* endings.
The substitution of *bhū* for *as* occurs before an affix marked with *tiṅ*.
There is no *guṇa* [substitution]. [The forms are: *abhūt*, *abhūḥ*, *suvai*, *suvāvahai*, *suvāmahai*.
Furthermore, there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] when the suffix *luK* follows and a consonant (*hal*) begins the following element.

When a suffix beginning with a consonant and having an indicatory *p* follows, there is *vṛddhi* substitution for a stem ending in *ū* when the suffix is elided (*luk*). Examples: *yauti*, *rauti*, *stauti*, *staumi*. Why "before a consonant" (*hali*)? Consider: *stavāni*.
[There is] optionally [vṛddhi] for the root *ūrṇu*.
In the case of the root *ūrṇu*, there may optionally be *vṛddhi*. Thus: *praurṇauti* or *praurṇoti*. [The rule] "when a consonant follows" (*halīti*) applies here as well—thus: *praurṇavāni*.
[Furthermore,] there is *guṇa* when the suffix is not a single consonant (*apṛkte*).
In the case of the root *ūrṇu*, when followed by an *apṛkta* suffix, there shall be *guṇa*. This serves as an exception to *vṛddhi*. Thus: *prorṇot*, *prorṇoḥ*.
[The rule] *tṛṇaha im* [follows].

After the root *tṛh* (to strike), when followed by the affix *śnam*, there is the augment *im* for the form *tṛṇaha*, provided that a consonant-initial (*hal*) *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix follows. Thus: *tṛṇeḍhi*, *tṛṇekṣi*. "May Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, strike" (*tṛṇeḍhu*). [In the imperfect: *atṛṇeṭ*.
The rule applies only when a consonant follows—thus, *tṛṇahāni*.
After the root *brū*, the augment *ir̥t* is added.
The augment *ir* is optionally applied after the root *brūñ* when followed by a consonant (*hal*) in a position marked with *p*. Thus: *bravīti*, *bravītu*, *abravīt*.
Why "when followed by a consonant"? [Observe: *bravāṇi*. [This rule applies] optionally after the *yaṅ* suffix.

Since there is no *sārvadhātuka* affix *pit* following a root such as *halādi*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally occur after a *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive without *yaṅ*) stem. Thus, one says either *bobhavīti* or *bobhoti*; *lālapīti* or *lālapti*; or *vāvadīti*. The *Bhāgavṛtti* maintains that the *yaṅ*-luṅ is Vedic (*chāndasa*), while others disagree. Candragomin, the author of the *Bhāṣāsūtra*, has formulated the rule as *yaṅo vā* ("after *yaṅ*, [the augment *iṭ*] is optional").
The [substitution of] *tur*, *ustur*, *śam*, and *yam* occurs before an *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
*turustuśamyamaḥ* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) form;
[it is derived from the rule] *astisico 'pṛkte*.

The augment *iṭ* shall be applied after these two [roots] when followed by an uncombined (*apṛkta*) suffix. Examples: *āsīt*, *āsīḥ*. After the suffix *sic*: *akārṣīt*, *akārṣīḥ*. Why "uncombined"? [Observe: *asti*, *akārṣṭām*.
There is a prohibition of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitutional identity) regarding the *iṭ* augment in the case of the roots *āh* and *bhū*. Examples: *āttha*, *abhūt*.
In the Vedic language, it occurs diversely (*bahulam*).
Vedic;
and from *rudh*, after the fifth [suffix].

The augment *iṭ* shall be applied to a non-complex (*apṛkta*) suffix following these [roots]. In the case of *rud*, by the transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), *bhyas* becomes *ṅasi*. Thus: *arodīt*, *aśvasīt*, *asvapīt*, *aprāṇīt*, *ajakṣīt*.
According to Gārgya and Gālava, the augment *aṭ* is optional.
According to the opinion of these two [grammarians], *aṭ* should be inserted before these [suffixes]: *ādat*, *ādaḥ*, *adaḥ*;
[this applies] to all [schools].
When *ap* is followed by *uk*, the augment *aṭ* shall be applied to all [cases]. [Examples: *ādat*, *ādaḥ*. When *añ* follows, there is lengthening of the vowel after *at*.

Before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*yañ*), there shall be a long vowel for a stem ending in /a/. Examples: *pacāmi*, *pakṣyāmi*. Why "ending in /a/"? [Consider] *cinumaḥ*. Why "before a *yañ*" [suffix]? [Consider] *pacati*. It has been stated regarding the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.
And [the suffix] *suP* [is applied].

Therefore, when followed by a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with *yañ* or *ñī*, there shall be a long vowel. For example: *vṛkṣāya*, *vṛkṣābhyām*. [The rule] "when followed by *yañ* or *ñī*" applies only here; thus, [in the genitive singular] it is *vṛkṣasya*.
In the plural, when followed by a suffix beginning with *jhal*, *e* is substituted [for the final vowel].

In place of [the final vowel of] *adat*, there shall be *etva* (substitution by *e*) before a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant when followed by a plural ending. Examples: *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, *vṛkṣeṣu*, *sarveṣām*.
This applies only when a *sup* (nominal) suffix follows—as in *pacadhvam*—and also before the dual suffix *osi*.
In this context, *et* shall be substituted for a short vowel not ending in *ā*. Examples: *vṛkṣayoḥ*, *vanayoḥ*. Also, when *āṅ* follows, *et* is substituted for *āp*.
The substitution of *ā* for *āp* occurs when *aṅ* follows. [Examples: *khaṭvayā*, *khaṭvayoḥ*.

How is it that [the form] *atikhaṭvena* is not [obtained]? Some say that because the mention of *ṅy-āp* implies the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited. The *Bhāṣya* states that the mention of the long vowel is due to the splitting (*praśleṣa*) of the rule as *ā āpaḥ*.
*Āṅ* is the name for the third-case singular ending.
And also in the case of the word *sambuddhi*.

In the vocative case, the short vowel is substituted for words meaning "mother" and for feminine stems ending in *nadī*. Examples: he *amba*, he *akka*, he *kumāri*, he *dhībandhu*, he *vadhū*. There is also a prohibition for those [stems] containing *ḍa* or *la*: he *ambāḍe*, he *ambāle*, he *ambike*. For the word *mātṛ*, the substitution *mātac* occurs in the vocative when it denotes "one who deserves a son. This is an exception to the rule *nady-ṛtaś-ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.112) which prescribes the suffix *kāp*. Example: *gārgīmātaḥ*. When used in the vocative, *nātsīmātaḥ* refers to one who is praiseworthy.
The guna substitute occurs for a short vowel.

In the case of the vocative dual (*sambuddhau*), there shall be *guṇa* substitution for a short vowel. Examples: *he agne*, *he niṣkauśāmbe*, *he viṣṇo*, *he vāyo*, *he bandho*. [Question: Why is it not so in *he kartṛ kula*? [Answer: Because the rule applies to the short vowel that is dependent upon the suffix *jas*. And [there is *guṇa*] also before *jas*.
There shall be guṇa substitution for a short vowel at the end of a stem before the suffix *jas*. For example: *matayaḥ*, *bandhavaḥ*.
There is also guṇa substitution for the vowel *ṛ* at the end of a stem before the suffixes *ṅi* and *sarvanāmasthāna*.

A *guṇa* substitute shall occur for a stem ending in *ṛ*. In the case of the locative singular (*ṅi*), as in *mātari* and *kartari*; and in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* (nom./acc. dual/plural), as in *mātarau*, *mātaraḥ*, and *kartāraḥ*. In the form *he kartar*, since the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) takes precedence, the *guṇa* is applied first; then, by the rule *rātsasya*, there is the elision of the *t* [of the suffix]. How is it that we have *kartṛṇi* for "houses"? This is because the application of the augment *num* is desired by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
In the presence of *gher*.

There shall be *guṇa* substitution for a stem ending in a *ghu*-named vowel before a suffix marked with *ṅ*. For example: *agnaye*, *vāyave*, *paṭave*, *dhenave*. The rule applies only when the following word begins with a *su*-affix—thus, *paṭvī*.
[The rule] "before a suffix beginning with *ā*" applies to feminine stems ending in *āṅ*.
The augment āṬ is applied before a case-ending beginning with a Ṅ-letter (ṅit) after the feminine suffix ṅīp. For example: kumāryai, kumāryāḥ; dhenvai, dhenavām; vadhvai, vadhvām.
After the feminine suffix āP, the augment yāṬ is applied [before a case-ending beginning with a Ṅ-letter].
The augment *yāṭ* shall be applied after a feminine stem ending in long *ā* when followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ*. [Examples: *khaṭvāyai*, *khaṭvāyāḥ*, *mālāyāḥ*, *śāṇḍilāyāḥ*.
After a pronominal stem ending in long *ā*, the augment *syāṭ* is added and the vowel is shortened.

The augment *syāṭ* shall be added after a pronoun ending in long *ā* when followed by a case-ending marked with *ṅ*. Furthermore, the short vowel [of the stem] shall be substituted for that which ends in long *ā*. Thus: *sarvasyai*, *viśvasyai*, *viśvasyāḥ*, *yasyāḥ*, *tasyāḥ*.

In these cases, the substitutes *smas* and *smās* do not apply because they are intervened by *syāṭ*; moreover, since the endings *ṅe* and *ṅasi* follow a non-pronoun, [the rules for those endings would otherwise apply].
[However, there is an option: *vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyābhyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.115).
After these two [stems ending in] ṅī, *syāṭ* may optionally be inserted. [Thus: *dvitīyasyai* or *dvitīyāyai*; *tṛtīyasyai* or *tṛtīyāyai*.
After [stems ending in] *nadī*, *āp*, and *nī*, the suffix *ām* is substituted for the case-ending *ṅi*.

The suffix *ṅi* (locative singular) is prescribed as having the forms *ām* and so forth after these [stems]: *nadī*—in *kumāryām*, *vadhvām*, *dhenvām*; under the rule *ṅiti hrasvaśca*, when the *nadī* designation applies—in *kṛtyām*, *dhenvām*; *āp*—in *khaṭvāyām*, *bahurājānām*; *nī*—in *senānyām*, *dinapraṇyām*;
and after stems ending in *i* and *u*.
Or else.
The [suffix] GHI is substituted for *at*.

After stems ending in *i* or *u*, the substitute *aut* is applied for the nominative-accusative dual; e.g., *sakhyau*, *patyau*. For a stem ending in the vowel *e* (*gh*), the substitute *at* is also applied; e.g., *agrau*, *kṛtau*, *bhūmau*, *dhenau*.
After a stem ending in *ā*, the substitute *nā* is applied [in the locative singular], except in the feminine; e.g., *āṅo nā'striyām*.
The suffix *nā* shall replace the third-case singular ending of a word ending in *i*. Examples: *agninā*, *hariṇā*, *vāyunā*, *bandhunā*, *amunā*.
Why "not in the feminine"? [Counter-examples: *matyā*, *sūcyā*, *dhenvā*.
Thus ends the section in the *Bhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Puruṣottamadeva.
The third quarter of the seventh chapter is concluded;
and the section on the Devikās is finished.
When the affix *caṅ* follows *ṇi*, the penultimate vowel of the root is shortened.

In the *caṅ* (aorist) affix, there shall be shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of a verbal root that does not end in *ṇ*. Examples: *acīkarat*, *apīpacat*, *mā bhavān aṭiṭat*. Once the shortening has been applied here, reduplication (*dvirukti*) takes place as desired. Why "of the penultimate"? [Observe: *acakāṅkṣat*, *avavāṅkṣat*. [Exception: There is no shortening for roots that lose their initial vowel (*aglopi*), nor for *śās*, nor for those marked with *ṛt* (*udita*).

For these [roots], when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* and then the *caṅ* (reduplication) suffix, the shortening of the penultimate vowel does not occur. Regarding roots that do not elide a final *a*: - From *māl* (to garland): *amamālat* (he called him a garland-maker). - From *bhogin* (possessing enjoyment): *abubhogat* (he called him an enjoyer). - From *kṣmābhṛt* (earth-bearer, king): *acakṣmābhṛtat* (he called him an earth-bearer). - From *śās* (to rule): *aśaśāsat* (he ruled repeatedly). Regarding roots marked with an indicatory *ṛ* (*ṛdit*): - From *bādhṛ* (to oppress): *ababādhata* (he oppressed repeatedly). - From *yācṛ* (to beg): *ayayācat* (he begged repeatedly). - From *ḍhaukṛ* (to approach): *aḍuḍhaukat* (he approached repeatedly). The shortening is optional for the following roots: *bhrāj* (to shine), *bhās* (to shine), *bhāṣ* (to speak), *dīp* (to shine), *jīv* (to live), *mīl* (to close the eyes), and *pīḍ* (to press).

For these roots, when followed by the suffix *ṇic* and the *caṅ* (the reduplicated aorist marker), the vowel may optionally be short. *ababhrājat*, or *abibhrajat*; *ababhāsat*, or *abībhasat*; *ababhāṣat*, or *abībhaṣat*. *nyamīmilat*, or *nyamimīlat*; "The lotus-eyed one closed her eyes like a lotus. "Like the sun, she opened [her eyes] (*udamīmilat*). *adīdipat*, or *adidīpat*; *ajījivit*, or *ajijīvat*; *apīpiḍat*, or *apipīḍat*. And for *kāṇ* and the others: *acakāṇat*, or *acākaṇat*. *Kaṇ*, *raṇ*, *vaṇ*, and *bhaṇ* are the roots beginning with *kāṇ*.
There is elision of the root *pibati*, and the substitute *ī* is applied to the reduplicative syllable.

In the *caṅ* (reduplicated aorist) following the causative suffix *ṇic*, there shall be elision of the penultimate vowel of the root *pibati*, and the augment *i* shall be substituted for the reduplicated syllable. Example: *apīpyat*. They made him drink for a moment, even though he was solid (*mūrtam*). [The rule] "after *tiṣṭhati*" [is now stated].
The suffix *it* shall be applied to the root *sthā* when preceded by *caṅ* and an upadhā vowel; as in *atiṣṭhipat*.
Or, it may be applied to the root *ghrā*.
Before the suffix *caṅ*, the penultimate vowel may optionally become *i*. [Examples: *ajighripat* or *ajighrapat*.
[In the case of the root *ṛ*, it becomes *u*: *urṛt*.]

In the *caṅ* (the reduplicated aorist), the penultimate vowel *ṛ* may optionally be replaced by *ṛ*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules for *ir*, *ar*, and *ār*. Examples: *acakīrtat* or *acīkṛtat*; *avavartat* or *avīvṛtat*; *amamārjat* or *amīmṛjat*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), this substitution is obligatory.
The *chandas* [Vedic] *sūtra* is one;
from the root *dayati*, the form *digīliṭ* occurs.

The substitute *digya* shall take the place of *liṭ*. [In the form] *avadigye ambaraṃ nādaḥ*, reduplication is not desired here. Also, [the substitution applies] to a root beginning with a consonant cluster that has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel.

A root ending in *ṛ* that begins with a conjunct consonant shall undergo *guṇa* substitution before the *liṭ* suffixes, except in cases where such substitution is prohibited. Thus: *sasmaratuḥ*, *sasmaruḥ*. Regarding *sasmāra*, it is desired that *vṛddhi* takes precedence over *guṇa* by means of the "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) rule.
Why "beginning with a conjunct"? [Observe: *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*.
The mention of "having a conjunct as its penultimate" (*saṃyogopadhagrahaṇa*) must be made [to exclude forms like these]. Thus: *sañcaskaratuḥ*, *sañcaskaruḥ*.
He attains the Truth.

In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, there is *guṇa* substitution for the roots *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ṝt*. Examples: *ānarchatuh*, *ānacchuḥ*; *āratuḥ*, *āruḥ*. For roots ending in *ṝt*: *nicakaratuḥ*, *nicakaruḥ*; *nijagaratuḥ*, *nijagaruḥ*; *teratuḥ*, *teruḥ*.
For the roots *śṝ*, *dṝ*, and *pṝ*, there is optionally a short vowel.

When the *liṭ* suffix follows these [roots], a short vowel may optionally take the place of the long vowel that would otherwise be obtained by the preceding rule. Examples: *viśaśaratuḥ* or *viśaśratuḥ*; *vidadaratuḥ* or *vidadratuḥ*; *paparatuḥ* or *papraturvā*.
[The rule] *ke'ṇaḥ* [applies here].

When the suffix *kap* follows, the vowel of the *aṇ* [substitute] shall be short. Examples: *jñakā*, *kumārikā*, *vadhukā*, *naiṣādakarṣukaḥ*, *grāmaṇikā*. Why "of *aṇ*" (*aṇaḥ*)? [Counter-examples: *gokā*, *naukā*.
[The rule does not apply] when *kap* [itself] follows.
The word *kapi* does not exist when short [in its final vowel]. [The suffix] *bahukumārīkaḥ*.
[The word] *āpaḥ* optionally [takes the elision of the case-ending].

For a word ending in *āp*, the penultimate vowel may optionally be shortened: *bahumālākaḥ* or *bahumālakaḥ*. In the presence of the suffix *aṅ*, there is guṇa substitution for the vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*.
In these two cases, there shall be *guṇa* substitution when the suffix *aṅ* follows: *asarat*, *ārat*, *adarśat*, *ajarat*. [The word] *jarā* [is formed with this rule].
[Furthermore,] the augment *thuk* is added after the root *as* (to throw).
The augment *thuk* is added to the root *as* before the suffix *aṅ*. [Example: *nirāsthat*.
The augment *aṭ* is added to the root *śvi*.
The root *śvi* (to swell) takes the augment *aṭ* before the suffix *aṅ*; [the forms are] *aśvat*, *aśvatām*, *aśvan*.
[The root] *pat* becomes *pup*.
The augment *pu* is applied before the suffix *aṅ*. [Examples: *apaptat*, *apaptatām*.

It should be stated that in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*), the root *han* undergoes the change to *ghnī*: *jeghnīyate*. Why "in the sense of injury"? [Because otherwise] *jaṅghanyate*. [The rule] *ī ghrādhmoḥ* [applies].

Because of the statement "not an indeclinable," [the rule does not apply to] *divābhūtā rātriḥ* (the night became day) or *doṣābhūtam ahaḥ* (the day became evening). [The same applies] when the suffix *kyac* follows.

The forms *aśanāya*, *udanya*, and *dhanāya* are derived from the roots *aś*, *ud*, and *dhana* respectively when used in the senses of hunger, thirst, and greed.
These [roots] undergo elision before the suffix *kyac*: *aśanāyati* (he is hungry), *udanyati* (he is thirsty), *dhanāyati* (he is greedy). Otherwise: *aśanīyati*, *udakīyati*, *dhanīyati*.
Here, the *Pañcasūtrī* is the Vedic [portion]; it is as follows:
"In the Veda, however, there is no elision for [the root] *putra*."
Seeking to overcome the enemy and desiring wealth, he acts like a bull; he strives for nourishment.
From Aśvaghoṣa.
In the *kāṭhaka* recension of the *yajus*, there is elision of the vowel in *deva-sumna*, and of the vowels in *kavya*, *adhvara*, and *pṛtanasya* when followed by *ṛ*.
The suffix *ti* is applied after the roots *dyati*, *syati*, *māti*, and *sthā* when the suffix *kit* follows.

For these [roots], when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*, [the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs]. *do*—*ditam*; *ṣo*—*apavasitam*; *mā*—*mitam*; *sthā*—*sthitam*. Having stood: *sthitvā*. Standing: *sthitiḥ*.
[The substitution of *i* for the final vowel] optionally occurs for *śā* and *chā* [when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*].

Before an affix beginning with *k* that has an indicatory *i*, the substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the roots *śā* (to sharpen) and *chā* (to cut) may optionally take place. For *śā*: *niśitam* or *niśātam*; for *chā*: *chitam* or *chātam*. By virtue of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the substitution is compulsory in the case of *saṃśitavrataḥ*.

After the roots *dhā* (to place) and *dheṭ* (to suck), *hi* shall be substituted [for the suffix *ktvā*] when a *k*-or *i*-beginning suffix follows. Examples: *abhihitaṃ*, *abhihitavān*; *vihitaṃ*, *vihitavān*; *dvitvā*, *vihitvā*;
*avahitaṃ*. Why "of *dadhāti*"? [To exclude] *dheṭ*: *dhītaṃ*, *dhītvā*.
And [the substitution of *hi* for *ktvā* occurs] after *jahāti* when the suffix *ktin* follows.
For [the root √hi], it would be *hitvā*. But for √ohāṅ, it is *hātvā*. Why [mention] *ktvā*? [To show the difference from] *hīnaḥ*.
In the Vedic language, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*).
May I be well-established, may I cause the earth to be well-established, may I establish the rim [of the wheel], and may I be established in wisdom.
The two sūtras are Vedic:
*do dad ghoḥ*.

When a *kit* suffix follows, *dat* shall be substituted for the root *dā*. Examples: *dattaḥ*, *dattvā*, *dattavān*, *dattiḥ*. How is it that *pradāya* is formed? It has been stated that a *lyap*-affix, being *bahiraṅga*, overrides internal (*antaraṅga*) rules. Why [is the condition] "after *dyu*" specified? [To exclude: *dāp*—*dātaṃ dhānyam*; *daip*—*avadātaṃ vastram*.
In this context, the letter *t* [is substituted for *th*] after a prefix (*upasarga*).

When a *kit* suffix beginning with *t* follows a prefix (*upasarga*) ending in a vowel, the *ā* of the word *dā* is replaced by *t*. According to others, the entire word *dā* is replaced by *tta*. Examples: *prattam*, *parīttam*, *nīttam*, *vīttam*, *sūttam*. Why "ending in a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider *nirdattam*. Why "beginning with a prefix" (*prādeḥ*)?
Because *avadattam*, *nidattam*, and *pradattam* are used when referring to the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*).
It is intended that [the terms] *sudatta*, *anudatta*, and *vidatta* are used in this manner.

These particles are similar in form to prepositions (*upasarga*). Here, the substitution of *i* for the root *dyati*—as in *ditam* and *nirditam*—is superseded by this [rule], since it has already served its purpose in cases such as *itvā*. Examples include *avatto māraḥ* and *apo bhiḥ*.
The substitution of *ap* for *āp* occurs when followed by [suffixes] beginning with *bh*. Examples: *adbhiḥ*, *adbhyaḥ*. Why "beginning with *bh*"? [Counter-example: *apsu*.

Before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*, the *s* [of the root] shall be replaced by *t*. Examples: *vatsyati*, *vivatsati*, *adhyavātsīt*, *jighatsā*. Why "beginning with *s*" (*si*)? [Counter-examples: *pravāsaḥ*, *ghāsaḥ*. [Now follows: There is elision (*lopa*) of the *tās* [augment] and of the root *as*.

There is the elision of the *s* of the roots *tās-* and *rās-* before an affix beginning with *s*. [Examples: *karttāsi tvam* (you will do); *vyatise karttase* (you will do reciprocally). [In the case of *asi*: *ri ca*.

In the case of the two monosyllabic roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*.

In the case of these [roots], *i* and so forth are prescribed in place of the vowel (*ac*) when the suffix *san* follows. There is the inclusion of both *mīñ* (to loosen) and *ḍu-mīñ* (to loosen), after which the vowel has been lengthened in the presence of *san*. *mitsati* (he wishes to loosen). *Māṅ* (to measure): *mitsate*. *Meṅ* (to exchange): *apamitsate*. *Ghu* (the roots *dā*, *dhā*, etc.): *ditsā* (desire to give); *dhitsā* (desire to place); *ditsuḥ* (one who desires to give); *dhitsuḥ* (one who desires to place). *Ram* (to delight/to begin): *āripsate*; *āripsamānaḥ* (beginning). *Labh* (to obtain): *ālipsate*; *ālipsamānaḥ* (seeking to obtain). *Śak* (to be able): *śikṣate*. *Pat* (to fall): *pitsati*. *Pad* (to go): *prapitsate*. Only when preceded by *sī* (the root *pat* with *sa*) does it become *pipatiṣati*. Why "in *san*"? [Because in other cases: *dāsyati* (he will give).

In the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*), for the root *rādh*, *i* is substituted for the vowel (*ac*). *pratiritsati* (he injures). Why "in the sense of injury"? [Because otherwise: *ārirātsati* (he attains).
The root *ṛdh* (to prosper) takes the suffix *āpjñap*.

In place of the roots *āplṛ*, *jñapi*, and *ṛdh*, the vowel *ī* shall be substituted before the suffix *san*. Thus: *īpsati* (he desires to obtain); *jñīpsati* (he desires to make known—this person knows nothing); *īrtsati* (he desires to obtain). It is only when preceded by *s* that [the substitution applies]—as in *jijñapayiṣati* (he desires to cause to be made known). Also, *ardidhiṣati* (he desires to injure).
Furthermore, for the root *dambh*, the vowel *i* is also substituted.
