Now begins the section on the rules for reduplication (*abhyāsa*).
In this context, there is elision of the reduplicated syllable.

In this context, under the governing rule *sanīti*, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). This has been illustrated accordingly. The prescription for the reduplicated syllable extends until the conclusion of the chapter (*āpādaparisamāpteḥ*). [The following rule is:
"Short vowel" (*hrasvaḥ*).
The substitute for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) shall be short. Thus: *ḍuḍhaukiṣate*, *tutaukiṣate*.
[By the rule] "the remaining [consonant] is the first one beginning with a *hal*," [the result is as shown].

In the case of reduplication, a consonant (*hal*) that is not the first letter (*anādi*) is retained; a consonant (*hal*) that is the first letter (*ādi*) is elided. Thus: *papāca*, *cakāra*, *babhāra*, *jahāra*, *jaglau*, *āra*, *āṭa*, *āśa*.
The *khay* consonants (all consonants except semivowels and nasals) are preceded by *śar* (sibilants).

When *kh* sounds (k, kh, p, ph) preceded by *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s* are followed by a consonant (*hal*), the *kh* sounds remain as the substitutes for the preceding consonants. Thus: *cuścotiṣati*, *tiṣṭhāsati*, *pispandiṣate*.
It should be stated that this applies when the *kh* sounds are preceded by a *khar* (voiceless consonant). Thus: *ucicchiṣati*.
[And] *kuhoścuḥ*.

In place of the *k*-class and the sound *h*, the *c*-class shall be substituted. As in: *cakre*, *cakhāna*, *jaglau*, *jaghāsa*, *jaghāna*, *juhuve*, *juhāva*, *jahāti*. However, this does not apply when the root *kavati* occurs with the *yaṅ* suffix.

For the root *kuṅ* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, there is no change of *k* to *c* in the *yaṅ* suffix; thus: *kokūyate kharaḥ* (the donkey brays repeatedly) and *akokūyiṣṭa tatsainyam* (that army brayed repeatedly). Here, however, [the rule applies] to the root *kṛṣ* in the Vedic language.

*dādharti*, *dardharti*, *dardharṣi*, *bobhūtu*, *tetikte*, *laṣyāpanīphaṇat*, *saṃsaniṣyadat*, *karikrat*, *kanikradat*, *bharibhrat*, *davidhvate*, *avidyutat*, *aritrataḥ*, *sarīsṛpatam*, *varīvṛjat*, *marmṛjyāt*, *aganīt*—thus [they are formed].
The two sūtras are Vedic:
The vowel *a* shall be substituted for the reduplicated syllable ending in an *ṛ*-vowel. Examples: *vavṛdhe*, *cakāra*.
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the roots *dyuti* and *svāpi*.
In place of *yaṇ* (the semivowels), *ik* (the vowels) shall be substituted for these two [roots]. *vididyute*; *vididyotiṣate*. *svāpi* is followed by a suffix having *ṇi*.
*susvāpayiṣati*. In the case of *vyath*, [this substitution occurs] in the *liṭ* [perfect tense].
In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, there shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the root *vyath*. [Example: *vivyathe*.
Why "in the *liṭ*" [tense]? [Counter-example: *vāvyathyate*. [Furthermore,] there is lengthening of the vowel *i* when followed by a *kit* suffix.

A long vowel shall replace [the short *i*] of the root √*i* before a *liṭ* affix that begins with a *kit*. [Examples: *iryatuḥ*, *iryuḥ*. Why "before a *kit*"? [Counter-examples: *iyāya*, *iyayitha*. [The rule] *ata ādeḥ* [applies here].

Therefore, there shall be a long vowel for the reduplication (abhyāsa) when the suffix liṭ follows. [Examples: āṭa, āṭatuḥ, āṭuḥ. After that [reduplicated syllable], the augment nuṭ is added if the root has two consonants.

The augment *nuṭ* is added after a root consisting of two consonants (*dvihal*) that has been lengthened, when followed by the *liṭ* suffixes. Examples: *ānañja*, *ānañjatuḥ*; *ārnaccha*, *ārnacchatuḥ*.
Why "consisting of two consonants"? [Observe: *āṭa*, *āṭatuḥ*.
How is it that we have *ānṛdhatuḥ*? It is due to similarity.

The term *dvihala* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for multiple *hal*s. Therefore, when the augment *tuk* has been applied by the rule *arvaṇas tr-as* and the *guṇa* substitution has occurred, the form *trihala* is also desired.
And this applies to the root *aś*.

In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, the augment *nuṭ* shall be inserted after a long vowel and before this [the initial *a* of the root]. Examples: *aṃśu*—*vyānaśe diśaḥ kīrttiḥ*; *ānaśāte*. [And] for the root *bhū*, there is *ar*.
The root *bhu* (to be) shall lose its initial vowel *a* when followed by the reduplication in the *liṭ* tense; thus, *babhūva*. In the Vedic usage, it is also *anubabhūve* and *sasūva*.
Herein is one *chandas* sūtra:
"When *śl* follows, there is the triple guna of the three vowels."
In the case of the roots *ṇijir*, *vijir*, and *viṣ*, there shall be *guṇa* substitution when the suffix *ślau* follows. [Examples: *nenekti*, *vevekti*, *veveṣṭi*.
[The rule] "of *bhṛñ* and others... [applies].
The augment *am* shall be added after the roots *bhṛ*, *hā* (in the sense of abandonment), and *mā* when followed by the suffix *ślau*. [Examples: *bibharti*, *mijihīte*, *mimīte*, *mimāmaḥ*.
[The same applies] to the roots *ṛt* and *pipartī*.
The substitution of *ślu* for these two [roots] may occur: *iyarti*, *piparti*. In the Vedic language, this is frequent.
The Vedic form is *sanyataḥ*.

The augment *it* is applied after a reduplicated stem ending in a short vowel when followed by the suffix *san*. Examples: *pipakṣati* (desires to cook), *pipāsati* (desires to drink); *jijigayiṣati* (desires to cause to conquer). Why is it said "after [a reduplicated stem] ending in a short vowel"? Consider: *lulūṣati* (desires to cut), *susuṣate* (desires to purify). Why is it said "when followed by *san*"? Consider: *papāca* (he cooked).
[This rule applies] when the vowel *o* [of the reduplicated syllable] is followed by *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, or *j*, provided these are not followed by another vowel (*apare*).

The long vowel *ā* may optionally be substituted for a reduplicated syllable ending in *u*, provided that a semivowel (*yaṇ*) or the letter *ja* follows, with a short *a* preceding it. Examples: from *pū*—*pipaviṣate*; from *bhū*—*bibhāvayiṣati*; with a semivowel (*yaṇ*)—*yiyāvayiṣati*; with *ru*—*rirāvayiṣati*; with *lū*—*lilāvayiṣati*; with the letter *ja*—*jijāvayiṣati*. The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root. Here, because that which is formed by the suffix *ṇi* is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the reduplication occurs by means of the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) rule. What is the purpose of the word "optionally" (*kim*)? [To show that] in *bubhūṣati*, it does not apply. [The long vowel is optional] in the case of the roots *sravati*, *śṛṇoti*, *dravati*, *pravati*, *plavati*, and *cyavati*.

When followed by a *yaṇ* vowel that is not a letter of the *avarṇa* class, the augment *iṭ* may optionally be applied before the suffix *san*. Thus: *sisrāvayiṣati* or *susrāvayiṣati* (he wishes to cause to flow). The same applies to roots such as *śru* (to hear) and others. Only when preceded by something other than an *avarṇa*: *susrūṣati jalam* (he wishes to hear the water).
[In the case of reduplication,] there is *guṇa* substitution for the *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk* formations.

Furthermore, when there is elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), there should be *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus: *lolūyate*, *lolavīti*, *loluvaḥ*; *bobhūyate*, *bobhavīti*, *bobhūtiḥ*, *bobhuvaḥ*.
The application of the rules for *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk* continues up to the rule "like *san*" (*sanvallaghuni*). [Then follows: "Lengthening occurs for a vowel not followed by *kit*" (*dīrgho'kitaḥ*).

A long vowel should be substituted for a non-kiṭ (akita) reduplicated syllable. Examples: *pāpacyate*, *pāpacīti*; *pāpaṭhyate*, *pāpaṭhīti*; *pāpaṭhaḥ*. Why "non-kiṭ"? Consider *yaṃyamyate* and *raṃramyate*. [Objection: But surely the long vowel will be barred by the elision (*luk*) itself? [Response: In that case, the mention of "non-kiṭ" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, among modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), exceptions (*apavāda*) do not bar general rules (*utsarga*).
The [affixes] niṅ, vañcu, sraṃsu, dhvaṃsu, bhrasu, kasu, patu, and skandu [are added after a root ending in a vowel].

There shall be the augment *nu* after these eight [roots] when they undergo reduplication: *vanīvacyate*, *vanīvañcaḥ*; *sanīsrasyate*; *danīdhvasyate*; *banībhrasyate*; *canīkasyate*; *panīpatyate*, *panīpadyate*, *panīpardīti*; *canīskadyate*, *canīskandīti*.
[The augment *nu* is applied] after a root ending in a nasal that has undergone reduplication.

The augment *nuk* should be added to a reduplicated stem ending in a nasal (*anunāsika*). It should be stated that this [augment] is like [the rules for] a word-final position (*padāntavat*). The mention of *nuk* is for the purpose of indicating both *n* and *anusvāra*, so that it may apply even when there is no following *jhal* consonant in the case of the roots *yam* and *ram*. Thus: *yaṃyamyate*, *yaṃyamīti*; *jaṅgamyate*, *jaṅgamīti*; *jaṅgamaḥ*. Similarly, *cañcūryate*, *taṃtambyate*, *daṃdamyate*, *naṃnamyate*, *mamambyate*, *mamambate*, *mamabhate*, and so forth. By the rule *vā padāntasya*, there is optionally a *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the following sound). The inclusion of the long vowel marker *ta* (*tapara*) is for the purpose of excluding cases where the long vowel was previously present. From the root *bhām* in the sense of "anger": *bābhāmyate*.
And [the results of] *japa*, *jabha*, *daha*, *daśa*, *bhañja*, *paśa*, and *śāṃ* [are as follows].

For these [roots], there may be [the following forms]: *jañjapyate*, *jañjapīti*; likewise up to *pampaśyate*, *paṃpaśīti*. The elision of *na* in *daśa* is prescribed for the sake of the *yaṅlug* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix); thus, *dandaśaḥ*.
*Paśi* is a root from the *sūtra* (Vedic/technical) lexicon.
And [the same applies] to the *caraphala* [measure].
It should not be so. [The forms] *cañcūryate* and *cañcūraḥ*, as well as *paṃphulyate* and *paṃphulaḥ*, are derived from the rule *utparasyātaḥ*.
After the vowel *a*, when followed by the suffixes *cara* or *phala* used in the sense of repetition (*abhyāsa*), *u* shall be substituted for that *a*. This has been illustrated in the same manner.
And [the rule applies] before *ti* as well.

After the root *tṛ* and others, as well as after roots ending in *c* or *r*, the vowel *u* is substituted for the penultimate vowel when followed by the suffixes *ktin* or *kta*. Examples: *cūrtiḥ* (cutting) and *praphullam puṣpam* (a blossomed flower).
Furthermore, *rī* is substituted for the penultimate vowel of a root that has a light (*laghu*) vowel as its penultimate letter.

The vowel *a* of a reduplicated syllable that has a soft consonant (*ṛdupadha*) as its penultimate letter shall be replaced by *rī*. Examples: *narīnṛtyate*, *narīnṛtaḥ*; *darīdṛśyate*, *darīdṛśaḥ*. It should be stated that *rīg* is substituted for a root containing the sound *ṛ*. Examples: *varīvṛścyate*, *parīpṛcchyate*, *jarījṛmbhayate*, *jarījṛmbhaḥ*.
Furthermore, *ruk* and *rik* are substituted [for the *a* of the reduplication] when the suffix *yaṅ* is elided (*luki*).
When the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), the augment *ruk*, *rik*, or *rīk* may be applied after a root ending in *ṛ*. Thus: *narnarti*, *narinarti*, *narīnarti*.
[Also, the augment applies] after a root ending in *ṛ*.

For a root ending in *ṛ*, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), the augmentments *ruk*, *rik*, and *rīk* may optionally be inserted. Examples: *carkarti*, *carikīrti*, *carīkarti*; *carkraḥ*, *carikraḥ*, *carīkraḥ*.

Why is the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with a following *p*) specified? [To exclude cases like] *cākartti* and *cākiraḥ* from the root *kṝ* (*kirati*). Examples: *jāgarti*, *jāgiraḥ*. [The rule *sanvallaghuni caṅpare'naglope* applies as follows: When a *caṅ* suffix follows that has a light vowel in the penultimate position, the reduplication is treated like that of the *saN* suffix, provided there is no elision of *a*.

When a light vowel (laghu) occurs in a root-syllable (dhātu), the reduplicated syllable (abhyāsa) should undergo the same operation as before the suffix *san* when followed by *caṅ* (the aorist marker) after a causative (*ṇi*) affix. Examples: *apīpacat*, *acīkarat*. Why "when there is a light vowel"? Consider *ararakṣat*, *ajajāgarat*. Why "when there is no elision" (*anaglope*)? Consider *acakathat*, *mālām ākhyad amamālat*, *adadṛṣat*. How is it that in the case of *paṭum ākhyad apīpaṭat*, [the reduplication] becomes *it* (long *ī*)? Some say: since the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) in the causative is subsequent to the application of *vṛddhi*, once the *vṛddhi* has been applied, there is only the elision of the diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), and thus the status of being like *san* (*sanvadbhāva*) causes the *it* quality.

Others maintain that because of the force of employing the *pratyāhāra* "ag" in the rule *anaglope*, the elision of the *ṭi* occurs only when no *vṛddhi* has yet taken place—namely, in the case of the elision of an *ag* vowel—and thus, due to the prohibition of the *sanvadbhāva* treatment, the form is *apapaṭat*.
[The rule continues: "A long vowel replaces a short vowel."

In the scope of the preceding sūtra, there shall be a long vowel for a light penultimate syllable [of the reduplicated stem]. Examples: *apīpacat*, *acīkarat*, *alīlavat*, *acūcurat*. Why "light"? [Observe: *acikṣaṇat*, *acikvaṇat*. [The rule applies] only when the syllables are light—as in *ararakṣat*. [The following roots undergo the substitution of *at* for their penultimate vowel in the reduplication]: *smṛ*, *dṛ*, *tvar*, *prath*, *mrad*, *stṝ*, *spaś*.

The substitution of *ṇi* for *caṅ* occurs after these seven roots when followed by *caṅ*. Examples: *asasmarat*, *adadarat*, *atatvarat*, *apaprathat*, *amamradat*, *atastarat*, *apraspaśat*. The inclusion of the short vowel *a* (tapara) is for the purpose of excluding the long vowel. Example: *adadarat*. [Vārttika:
The substitution is optional for the roots *veṣṭi* and *ceṣṭi*.
When followed by *caṅ* which is itself followed by *ṇau*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally not be applied to these two roots. Thus: *avaveṣṭat* or *aviveṣṭat*; *acaceṣṭat* or *aciceṣṭat*.
And the root *gaṇ* also takes the augment *ī*.
In the *caṅ* affix, the *gaṇa* [root] takes the augment *iṭ* and the vowel *a*. Examples: *ajagaṇat* or *ajīgaṇat*.
The section on *aṅ* and the section on *abhyāsa* (reduplication) are hereby completed.
For everything there are two.
This is a governing rule (adhikāra). It should be stated that everything [subsequent] is repeated; the subsequent [term] is called *āmreḍita*.
That which follows a word repeated twice is called *āmreḍita*; for example, in "kānāmreḍite kāṃskān bhojayati" (whom does he feed again and again?).
And it is unaccented (*anudātta*).
The Vedic [grammar].
[The rule] "in the sense of continuity and distributive repetition" (Pāṇini 8.1.4).

A word that occurs in the sense of "perpetual" (nitya) or in the sense of "distribution" (vīpsā) shall be reduplicated; all such words take two forms. Perpetuity (ābhīkṣṇya) is a form of constancy, and it applies to verbal suffixes (tiṅ), indeclinables (avyaya), and primary derivatives (kṛt). Examples: *pacati pacati* ("he cooks repeatedly"), *prapacati prapacati* ("he cooks thoroughly again and again"), *bhuktvā bhuktvā yāti* ("having eaten, he goes [again and again]"), *nadīm avaskandam avaskandam upaspṛśati* ("he touches water by leaping from river to river"), *bhojaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes to every house where food is served"). Distribution (*vīpsā*) is the desire to pervade simultaneously; this applies to nominal suffixes (*sup*). Examples: *gṛhe gṛhe 'śvāḥ* ("there are horses in every house"), *nadīṃ nadīm avaskandam upaspṛśati* ("he touches water by leaping from river to river"), *grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ* ("every village is beautiful").

In this context, the reduplication of a word is desired when the suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*) has been added, as in *āḍhyataramāḍhyataram ānaya* ("bring him who is more and more wealthy"). However, according to some, because the rule for reduplication (*tiṅaśca*) takes precedence due to its higher status in the order of rules, the reduplication occurs first, and only then is the suffix of excellence applied; thus, one says *pacatipacatitarām* ("he cooks most excellently"). In certain instances within a compound formation (*vṛtti*), reduplication is dropped because the meaning has already been expressed, as in: *dvau dvau pādau dadāti* ("he gives two feet each") becomes *dvipadikāṃ dadāti*. *dvau dvau dehi* ("give two each") becomes *dviśo dehi*. *sapta sapta parṇāny asya* ("he has seven leaves on each [node]") becomes *saptaparṇaḥ*. *kulaṃ kulaṃ aṭati* ("she wanders from family to family") becomes *kulaṭā*.
In some cases, there is the usage of a word even when its meaning has already been stated—such as in "give one by one" (*ekaikaśo dehi*) or "mutually assisting one another" (*anyonyasahāyāḥ*).
The particle *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

In this case, two [forms] may occur here: it should be stated that "or when there is no compound. For example: *pari pari trigarttebhyaḥ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (It has rained all around the Trigarttas), or *pari trigarttebhyaḥ*. It would not occur when there is a compound—as in *paritrigarttam*.
What is excluded? [The following examples show it: *vṛkṣaṃ pariṣiñcati* (he sprinkles around the tree); *trigarttān pariṣiñcati* (he sprinkles around the Trigartas).
[The particles] *pra*, *sam*, *upa*, and *dus* are used for the purpose of completing the meter (*pādapūraṇe*).
Thus ends the Vedic (Chāndasa) Sūtra:
"The words *upari*, *adhi*, and *adhas* [are used] in the sense of proximity."

In these cases, two [instances] may occur: *upary-upari grāmam* (above and above the village), *adhy-adhi kulam* (over and over the family), *adho-adho grāmam* (below and below the village). Why "in the sense of proximity"? [Consider: *sarvasyopari candramāḥ* (the moon is above everything).
[The rule applies to] a vocative at the beginning of a sentence when expressing envy, approval, anger, censure, or reproach.

When a sentence begins with a word expressing censure (*asūyā*) and so forth, that vocative (*āmantrita*) at the beginning shall be doubled. For example: *bhīma bhīma riktaṃ tavābhijātyam* ("O Bhīma, Bhīma! Your nobility is empty"). In cases of approval (*sammata*), as in: *arjunārjuna śobhanaḥ khalvasi* ("O Arjuna, Arjuna! You are indeed excellent"). The same applies in cases of anger (*kopa*) and so forth.
The protracted vowel (*pluta*) prescribed by the rule "svaritamāmreḍite" is not illustrated here, because it is not in common usage in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*).
[The rule] "ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat" [is now stated].

The word *eka* is stated twice; it shall be treated like a *bahuvrīhi*. There shall be elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) and the masculine form (*puṃvat*) shall apply. Examples: *ekaikaḥ*; "the objects of the senses pierce one by one" (*ekaikaśo vinighranti viṣayāḥ*); "he mutters each syllable one by one" (*ekaikamakṣaraṃ japati*); "he offers with each oblation one by one" (*ekaikayāhutyā juhoti*). And [this applies] in cases of emphasis (*ābādhe*).
In the case of *pīḍā*, two [words] may occur as a compound like a *bahuvrīhi*; for example, *gatagatā* and *naṣṭanaṣṭā*. In subsequent cases, it is like a *karmadhāraya*.
In subsequent sūtras, the operation should be like that of a *karmadhāraya* compound;
[this applies] to a quality-word when it denotes a manner.

A word expressing a quality may be reduplicated when used in the sense of similarity. Examples: *paṭupaṭuḥ* (very clever), *mandamandam uditaḥ prayayau kham* (having risen very slowly, he went toward the sky), *paṭupaṭavī*, *paṇḍitapaṇḍitā*.
Because it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, it follows the rule of masculine substitution (*puṃvat*) even in cases where such substitution is otherwise prohibited: *kālakakālikā*.

Furthermore, this reduplication is desired both for words denoting a substance qualified by a quality and for those denoting the quality alone: *śuklaśuklaḥ paṭaḥ* (a very white cloth) and *śuklaśuklam asya rūpam* (its color is very white).

Thus, due to the addition of the verbal root *grahaṇa* (to grasp), it also occurs with a word denoting an action: "In spring, the cuckoo has warbled in the forest with great trepidation"; "The moon, as if trembling with cold."

The words *itaretara*, *anya*, *apara*, and *paraspara* are established as correct by virtue of their being technical nipātanas (irregular formations) when they refer to the reciprocal exchange of actions (*karmavyatīhāra*), singularity, and the neuter gender. Regarding these, there is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating that "after them, in the feminine and neuter genders, the suffix *ām* may optionally replace the case endings (*sup*). Examples: *itaretarām* [the two women] or the two kṣatriya clans vie with each other; or *itaretaram*. *itaretarām* [he] vies with the two women or with the women; or *itaretareṇa*. In the same way: *anyonyām* or *anyonyasya*; *parasparām* or *parasparasmin*.

Likewise—thus *anyonyām* or *anyonyaṃ*; *parasparām* or *paraspare*; *anyonyām*, *anyonyasya*; *parasparām*, or *parasparasmin*—this also applies in the neuter. In the masculine, however: *itaretaraṃ rājānau yudhyete* (the two kings fight with one another); *anyonyam āsūyataḥ* (they are jealous of each other). Regarding repetition for the sake of sequence (*ānupūrvye dve*): *mūle mūle sthūlā dantāḥ* (the teeth are thick at every root); *jyeṣṭhaṃ jyeṣṭhaṃ praveśaya* (let him enter according to seniority).

In the case of excess (*ādhikya*), there are two [words]. For example: *aho darśanīyāho darśanīyā* (oh, how beautiful! oh, how beautiful!), *mahyaṃ rocate mahyaṃ rocate* (it pleases me, it pleases me). Here, the excess of both the act of seeing and the pleasure is understood from the reduplication. In the case of agitation (*cāpala*), there are two [words] as long as the understanding lasts. For example: *ahirahirbudhyasva budhyasva budhyasva* (snake, snake, wake up, wake up, wake up!). In the sense of superiority (*atiśaya*) regarding "prior" (*pūrva*) and "first" (*prathama*): *pūrvaṃ pūrvaṃ puṣpyanti* (they flower earlier and earlier); *prathamaṃ bhuktam* (eaten first); *prathamaṃ prathamaṃ prathamaṃ paṭhyante* (they are recited first and first).
The comparative suffix is also desired [in the sense of frequency]: "they flower more and more frequently.
In the sense of ease, either of the two suffixes for "dear" (priya) and "pleasant" (sukha) may optionally be used.

In the case of these two [words], *akṛcchra* ("without difficulty") and *artha* ("object/purpose"), there may optionally be two [forms]. For example: *priyapriyeṇa*, *sukhasukhena*, *dadāti priyeṇa*, or *sukhena*.
Why "without difficulty"? [Answer: *priyaḥ putraḥ* ("a beloved son"); *sukho rathaḥ* ("a comfortable chariot").
*Yathāsve* means "according to one's own [nature]" (*yathāyatham*).

In this context, the following is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*): *yathāyatham*, meaning "according to each one's own" (*yathāsvīyam*), when used with those [words] joined together by sky-dwellers (*nabhaścaraiḥ*).
Furthermore, the term *dvandvam* is prescribed in the senses of secrecy, limit, transgression, and the manifestation of the use of sacrificial vessels.

In these five cases, the term *dvandva* is applied by nipātana (irregular derivation). Having become pairs (*dvau dvau*), they deliberate on secrets in *dvandva*. This continues until the manifestation [of the meaning]. *Rāmalakṣmaṇau dvandvam*: the meaning is that the two are manifested through their constant association (*sāhacaryeṇa*). Here, due to a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), it is observed that *sukhaduḥkhayoḥ dvandvam* is used in the sense of "and" (*cārthe dvandvaḥ*). [This applies] to a word (*padasya*).

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) prior to the rule concerning the substitution of the retroflex *mūrdhanya* [for *s*]. It will be stated: "There is elision of a final consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*). Examples: *paṭhan*, *pacan*. "The elision of *n*" (*nalopaḥ*): *rājabhyām*. "The substitute *n* for *m* when not part of a verbal root" (*mo nā dhātoḥ*): *praśān*. Why "of a word" (*padasya*)? [Consider: *pacantau*, *rājānau*, *praśāmau*.
[The rule applies] after a word (*padāt*).

This heading applies up to the section on "reproaches" (*kutsaneṣu*). He will state: "In place of the plural, *vas* and *nas* [are substituted]. [Examples: *pātu vaḥ* ("May he protect you all"), *pātu naḥ* ("May he protect us").

Why say "after a word" (*padāt*)? [Counter-example: *yuṣmān pātu* ("May he protect you"), *asmān dhinotu* ("May he satisfy us"). [The rule] "all [substitutes] are unaccented (*anudātta*) when not at the beginning of a verse-quarter" (*anudāttaṃ sarvamapādādau*) applies here as well.

The term *anudātta* (unaccented) is a Vedic usage, because accents do not function in the common language (*bhāṣā*). The phrase "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) that extends to the end of the chapter. He will state: "For the plural, *vas* and *nas* [are substituted]. As in: *grāmo vaḥ* ("the village is yours") and *putro naḥ* ("the son is ours"). Why "not at the beginning of a word"? So that it does not apply at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*pāda*), as in: *yuṣmākaṃ pālakaḥ śambhur asmākaṃ deśako jinaḥ* ("Śambhu is the protector of you all; the Jina is the teacher of us all").

The substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* must be stated to occur within a single sentence (*samānavākya*). They should not occur when there is a division of sentences (*vākyabheda*), as in: "Cook the rice; it will be yours," or "it will be mine. What, then, is a sentence? A sentence is a verbal root (*ākhyāta*) together with indeclinables, kārakas, or qualifiers. For example: with an indeclinable—*uccaiḥ paṭhati* ("he reads loudly");
with a kāraka—*grāmaṃ yāti* ("he goes to the village"); with a qualifier—*mṛdu pacati* ("he cooks softly").
And [the same applies] when one has been addressed.
Thus ends the Svarasūtra.
For the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when they stand in the sixth, fourth, or second case, the substitutes *vām* and *nau* [are applied].

When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in the dual case endings of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, they optionally take the substitutes *vām* and *nau*. Examples: *grāmo vām* (the village is for you two), *deśo nau* (the country is for us two); *grāmo vāṃ dīyate* (the village is given to you two), *deśo nau dīyate* (the country is given to us two); *śivo vāṃ rakṣatu* (may Śiva protect you two), *buddhir nau pātu* (may the intellect protect us two). Why is the word "fixed" (*stha*) mentioned? It is to prevent [the substitution] from occurring when the case ending is not actually heard—as in *sa yuṣmatputraḥ* (that son of yours) and *asmatputro 'yam* (this son of mine). When [the pronouns] are in the plural, the substitutes are *vas* and *nas*.

In place of those two [pronouns] when ending in the plural of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, *vas* and *nas* shall be substituted. For example: *grāmo vaḥ* ("the village is yours"), *putro naḥ* ("the son is ours"), and so on.
In place of the singular, *te* and *me* are substituted.
For those two [pronouns], when they end in the singular of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, *te* and *me* shall be used: *dhanaṃ te*, *grāmas te*, *putro me*, and so on.
For the second case (*dvitīyā*), *tvā* and *mā* are used.

But when those two [words *mām* and *tvām*] are in the second person singular, they become *mā* and *tvā* respectively: "I see you" (*ahaṃ tvā paśyāmi*) and "you see me" (*tvaṃ mā paśya*). However, this substitution does not occur when [the particle] *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *āha*, or *eva* is joined with them.

When used in conjunction with these five particles—*ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *aha*, and *eva*—the particles *vā* and *na* (and so forth) shall not be elided. For example: *grāmas tava ca svam* ("The village is yours as well") and *grāmo mama ca svam* ("The village is mine as well").

Here, the inclusion of the term *yukta* (conjunction) is for the purpose of [excluding] direct connection (*sākṣād yoga*). It should not apply to indirect connection (*yuktayukta*), as in *grāmaś ca te svam* ("The village is yours"). [Also, the particle *na* is not elided] when used with verbs meaning "to see" (*paśyārtha*), provided it does not mean "to look at" (*anālocane*).

In connection with words meaning "seeing" (*darśana*), the suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap* (i.e., *-tvā* and *-ya*) shall not be used. Examples: *vipras tava grāmam samīkṣyāgataḥ* ("The Brahmin came after looking at your village") and *vipro mama grāmam sandṛśya gataḥ* ("The Brahmin went after seeing my village"). Why is it said "not when there is no observation" (*anālocane*)? [So that] it does not apply to visual cognition (*cakṣur-jñāna*). Examples: *vipras tvā paśyati* ("The Brahmin sees you") and *vipraḥ gāḥ paśyati* ("The Brahmin sees the cows"). [The rule] is optional (*vibhāṣā*) when the first case ending (*prathamā*) is preceded by another word (*sapūrvāyāḥ*).

After a word ending in the first case that is preceded by another word, the suffixes *vān*, *naū*, and so forth may optionally be applied to those two [pronouns]. For example: *grāme kambalas te svaṃ* (the blanket in the village is yours) or *tava*. This applies everywhere in this context.

Here, all these suffixes—*vān*, *naū*, and so on—are to be stated as optional (*vibhāṣā*) when there is no subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*). Examples: *grāmas te* or *tava*; *grāmo me* or *mama*; *grāmas te dīyate* or *tubhyam*; *śivas tvā rakṣatu* or *tvām*; *viṣṇur mā rakṣatu* or *mām*. In the same way, one should understand forms such as *pātu vaḥ* or *pātu naḥ*, and so forth.

What is the purpose of excluding *ananvādeśa* (non-repetition)? Consider: *atho te grāmaḥ* ("Now your village"), *atho me grāmaḥ* ("Now my village"). Should it not then be stated? It must be stated that "the rule *sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā*" applies for the sake of *anvādeśa*. For example: *atho grāme kambalaste svam* ("Now in the village, the blanket is yours"); in the alternative case, it is *tava svam*. The phrase *padāt* ("after a word") has ceased to apply here.
From this point, beginning with "tiṅo gotrādīni," there are forty-five accentuation rules (*svarasūtra*).
They are as follows: *tiṅo gotrādīni kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ* ("The finite verb forms [ending in] *gotra*, etc., [are unaccented when used] in the sense of censure or repetition").
Thus it is said.
Not the periphrastic future.
When joined with the particles *yadi*, *yadiha*, *hanta*, *ku*, *vit*, *na*, *cet*, *iṇ*, *kaccit*, or *yatra*.
Not at the beginning of a new undertaking.
"Truth" [is used] in response to a question.
In the case of non-contrariety regarding the limbs.
And indeed.
In Vedic literature, even multiple [words] may be syntactically expectant.
By means of these two, as far as [is necessary].
There is no interruption in the performance of worship.
And [the suffix] -ññ- occurs when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*).
The suffixes *tup*, *aś*, *paśya*, and *paśyata* are used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*).
And oh!
In the remaining cases, there is an option.
And the word *parā* [is used] in the sense of desiring to obtain.
In the case of seeking permission, it is not [an offense].
What [is it] when there is a question regarding an action, provided it is not preceded by a prefix and is not prohibited?
In the case of elision, it is optional.
The suffix *lṛṭ* is used after [the particle] *ehi* when it expresses consent or derision.
Never before.
And the interrogative particle *kim* is followed by *cid* as its answer.
Or rather, [the particles] *āho* and *utāho* [occur] immediately after [the preceding word].
In the remaining cases, there is an option.
When an imperative verb (loṭ) expressing motion occurs, the future tense marker (lṛṭ) is not used, provided that no other kāraka (grammatical participant) differs from all others.
And the imperative suffix [is also used].
The unsurpassed [teaching] has been expounded along with its prefixes.
And indeed!
The vocative case ending is used for a single word that is not separated by another word and is situated nearby.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *ya* for *yat*] occurs when followed by a word beginning with a consonant.

Because there is no understanding [of the meaning] in the case of particles such as *cana*, *cit*, *iva*, *go*, *trā*, and so forth; in secondary derivatives (*taddhita*); and in reduplicated forms (*āmreḍita*).
And [the same applies] to the words beginning with *ca*.
The nominative case is used in connection with the particle *ca* (and).
The particle *heti* is used in the sense of reproach.
The particle *aha* is used in the sense of application (*viniyoga*).
The elision of *ca* and *ha* is optional.
When *ca* and the other particles are elided, the rule is optional.
And "vaivāva" is the *chandas*.
[The suffix *śas* is applied] after [a word ending in] the dual number *ekau* or *anyau*, when these two are semantically capable [of expressing the sense of "one or the other"].
Always [eating] from the food of such a person.
The word *pūjita* following *pūjana* is unaccented when it follows words such as *kāṣṭha*.
A finite verb (tiṅ) is also [called a word] when it has a preceding member (sagati).
And [the suffix *kha*] is used after a *sup*-ending word in the sense of reproach, provided it does not refer to one's lineage (*gotra*) and so forth.
The goal is in the goal.
And [the augment] *tiṅ* when it bears the acute accent (*udātta*).
An address placed at the beginning is treated like that which stands above the line.

An element ending in a vocative (āmantrita) shall be treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) when it precedes [another word]. Consequently, the case endings *vām* and *nau*, etc., which would otherwise be expressed by that [preceding] word, shall not occur. For example: *vipra tava svam* ("O Brahmin, this is your own"); *viprau yuvayoḥ svam* ("O two Brahmins, this is your own"); *viprā yuṣmākaṃ svam* ("O Brahmins, this is yours"). The same applies to the second and fourth cases.
Why specify "vocative"? [Observe: *kambalaste svam* ("The blanket is yours").
When not addressed, a word denoting a general class [is used] in grammatical apposition with another word.

When followed by another vocative in grammatical apposition, even a preceding general vocative shall not be treated as non-existent. Consequently, *vām*, *nau*, *vaḥ*, and so forth, shall indeed occur. For example: *chātrau guṇinau vāṃ svam* (O two virtuous students, this is your property);
*chātra guṇin te svam* (O virtuous student, this is your property). Why specify "general vocative"? [Consider: *devadatta jaṭila tava svam* (O matted-hair Devadatta, this is your property).
The plural number is used in the sense of expressing a distinction when there is a detailed explanation.

When a vocative with a specific attribute (viśeṣavacana) in grammatical apposition (tulyādhikaraṇa) follows, a plural-ending form may optionally be treated as non-existent (avidyamānavat). For example: *chātrā vaiyākaraṇā yuṣmākaṃ svam* ("O students, O grammarians, yours is the property"). In the alternative case: *vaḥ svam*, etc.
[The preceding rule is] not established for what follows.

This is an *adhikāra* (governing rule). When the rules of the first seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*) are to be applied, the rules of the final three quarters (*tripādī*) that are about to be stated shall be treated as *asiddha* (non-existent). Furthermore, within the *tripādī*, each subsequent rule is *asiddha* with respect to a preceding rule that is to be applied. Examples: In *asmā uddhara* and *dvā ānaya*, because the elision (*lopa*) of *v* and *y* is *asiddha*, no *sandhi* (euphonic combination) occurs. In *amuṣya*, *amuṣmai*, and *amuṣmāt*, because the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is *asiddha*, the case-endings (*syādi*) are applied. The elision of the *n* (in *an*), however, is not *asiddha* for the purposes of the following rules: the formation of *sup* (case endings), accentuation (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), the *tuṅ* augment, and rules concerning *kṛt* suffixes.

In these very instances, the elision of *n* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Regarding rules concerning *sup* suffixes: *rājabhyām*, *rājabhiḥ*, *rājasu*. Because [the rule for] lengthening applies when a *sup* suffix follows, [the long vowel] does not occur here. An example for accent (*svara*) is not cited. Regarding rules concerning technical designations (*saṃjñā-vidhi*): *pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ*. The designation "six" (*ṣat-saṃjñā*) applies, and consequently, there is the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Regarding rules concerning the insertion of the augment *tuk*: *vṛtrahabhyām*, *vṛtrahabhiḥ*. When a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *pi* follows, the *tuk* augment does not occur.

What is the purpose of the rule *kṛti*? [Consider] *vṛtrahacchatram*. By the rule *che ca*, the *tug* augment indeed occurs here. What is the purpose of the restriction *eṣveva* (only in these)? [Consider] *rājīyati*, *rājāyate*, *rājāśvaḥ*, and *rājehā*. [In these cases, the *tug* does not apply. Nor does it apply before *mu* or *na*.

A substitute (*mubhāva*) is not considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when an absence (*nābhāva*) is to be effected. By this [rule], the elision of *sij* is established as *siddha* (existent) for the purpose of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). [Example: *alāvīt*.

The substitution for the *niṣṭhā* suffix is established as *siddha* for the purposes of the rules concerning *ṣatva*, affixes, and grammatical operations. [Example: *vṛkṇaḥ*. Because of the condition "before a *jhal* [consonant]," the *ṣatva* does not occur here. [Example: *kṣībikaḥ*. The affix *ṭhan* occurs by the rule "after *nau* and a non-dvandva [compound ending in] a dissyllabic word. [Example: *kṣībaḥ*. In the alternative view where there is the elision of that [suffix] alone, the augment *iṇ* does not occur.
The substitution of *ś* for *s* is established before a *dhuṭ* [consonant]. In *raṭ ścyotati*, the rule *ṅaḥ si dhuṭ* does not apply.

The substitution of the *jaś* sounds, the substitution of *t* for *n*, and the substitution of *e* for *at* and *atuk* are established [as having taken effect]. Examples: *babhaṇatuḥ*; *dadhi cicchitsati* (this is the form of the root *chid* with the suffix *san*).
The substitution of the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇatva*) is established after reduplication. Examples: *sayam̐ yyantā*; *savam̐ vvatsaraḥ*.
Here follow three rules concerning accent (svara):
namely— "The svarita [is substituted] for an anudātta vowel following a yaṇ that represents either an udātta or a svarita."
When a single substitute takes the place of both [an udātta and a non-udātta vowel], that substitute is udātta.
Or, when followed by an unaccented word beginning with a syllable at the start of a pada, it may optionally be circumflex (svarita).
There is the elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
The letter *l* at the end of a stem (*prātipadika*) is elided. Examples: *rājā*, *rājabhyām*, *rājaputraḥ*, *rājatvam*, *rājatamaḥ*.

Regarding the word *ahan*: there is a prohibition of the elision of *n*. In *ahobhyām*, *aharatra*, and by the rule *ahan ro'supi*, the substitution of *ru* for *n* occurs; however, because *ru* and *repha* are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of this rule], the elision of *n* would otherwise apply. But [the elision of *n* does not occur] before the suffix *ṅi* or in the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*).

In these two cases, there is no elision of the *n* here. In the locative singular (*ṅi*)—one who behaves like a king is *rājanyati* (with reference to a teacher). [This is formed] by the suffix *kyac* according to the rule *adhikaraṇācca*.
In the vocative (*sambuddhi*)—*he rājan*.

How is it that *carmatilaḥ* ("one who has sesame seeds on his skin") is formed? [The answer is: "The prohibition must be stated for the locative case when it is not part of a compound," according to the *Bhāṣya*.
Or it should be stated: "or for neuter nouns. Thus: *he carman* or *he carma*; *he daṇḍin* or *he daṇḍi*.
[The suffix] *matup* becomes *va* after *m* or *a*, and after a vowel other than *y* and *v*.

The initial *va* shall replace the initial of the suffix *matup* after a word ending in *makāra* (m) or *akāra* (a), provided that *makāra* or *akāra* is the penultimate letter (*upadhā*). Examples: *kiṃvān*, *vṛkṣavān*, *khaṭvāvān*. And [the rule applies] when *makāra* or *akāra* is the penultimate letter: *lakṣmīvān*, *payasvān*, *yaśasvān*, *bhāsvān*. The forms *kaṃvān* and *śaṃvān* are established in both ways (by this rule or by the previous one). Why "after *ma* or *u* as the penultimate"? (Consider: *matimān*, *sarpiṣmān*, *āyuṣmān*. Why "not after *yava* etc."? (Consider: *yavamān*. The group begins with *yava*, *bhūmi*, *kṛmi*, *ūrmi*, *kakud*, and *garut*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
The letter jhaḥ.
The letter *va* is substituted for the final *m* of another word [ending in *matup*]. Examples: *agnicitvān*, *marutvān*.
[This substitution occurs] when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *mat* may occur after the word *nāmri* when it signifies "possessing" (*matorvaḥ syāt*). Examples are *ahīvatī*, *nadī*, *maṇīvatī*, and *śarāvatī*.
In these cases, the suffix *matup* is applied to the word *nadī*, and the vowel lengthening occurs according to the rule *śarādīnāñ ca*.
[Furthermore, there are] *āsandīvat*, *aṣṭhīvat*, *cakrīvat*, *kakṣīvat*, *rumaṇvat*, and *carmaṇvatī*.

These [suffixes] are applied by elision (*nipātana*) after the names of villages, animals, body parts, donkeys, sages, mountains, and rivers. Otherwise: *asanavān*, *asthimān*, *cakravān*, *kakṣyāvān*, *lavaṇavān*, *carmavatī*, and *udanvān* (which also occurs in the sense of "ocean").
This [suffix *matup*] occurs after *udadhi* (ocean) with the meaning "possessing water"; elsewhere, it means "possessing water.
Due to the word *ca* ("and"), it also occurs elsewhere according to specific designations: for example, a sage named *udanvat*.
It also occurs after *rājan* (king) in the sense of "good governance": *rājanvān*.
In a country with a good king, one should say *rājanvān*; elsewhere than that—*rājavān*.
Here, [the rule] *chandasīraḥ* applies.
The suffix *nuṭ* [is applied].
The substitution of *gh* occurs for *nā*.
The *chandas* [section] consists of three sūtras:
"kṛpo ro laḥ" [and the two following].

In the case of the root *kṛp*, the letter *r* may optionally become *l*. Thus: *kalptā*. Furthermore, due to the specific rule (*nipātana*) "and in the *luṭ* [future], after *kṛp*" (Pāṇini 7.4.62), even the vowel *ṛ* becomes *lṛ*: *klṛptaḥ*. [Examples of reduplication: *calīklṛpyate*, *caklṛpe*, *ciklṛpsate*. How is the word *kṛpā* formed? Because it is taught in the *Bhidādi* group with the rule "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) [of the *ṛ*] and [the substitution of *u* for the *ap* suffix]" (Pāṇini 3.3.104), it is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*); therefore, the substitution of *l* does not apply. However, words such as *kṛpāṇa*, *kṛpaṇa*, *kṛpīṭa*, and *karpaṭa* are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes by virtue of the "diversity" (*bāhulaka*) rule.
In the words *bāla*, *mūla*, *laghu*, *ara*, and *aṅguli*, the letter *r* may optionally become *l*. Thus: *bāraḥ* or *bālaḥ*; *mūram* or *mūlam*;

*raghuḥ* or *laghuḥ*; *aram* or *alam*; *aṅguriḥ* or *aṅguliḥ*. In the words *kapiraka* and others, the letter *r* may optionally become *l*. Thus: *kapilakā* or *kapirakā*; *roma* or *loma*; *pāṃśuram* or *pāṃśulam*; *karma* or *kalma*; *bhīruḥ* or *bhīluḥ*.

Some maintain that there is a recollection of the identity between *ra* and *la*; others say it is between *ḍa* and *la*. For example: *virocanaṃ* or *vilocanaṃ*; *vrīḍā* or *vrīlā*; *viḍālaḥ*, *virālaḥ*, or *vilālaḥ*; *cūḍā* or *cūlā*; *vaḍabhī* or *valabhī*, and so forth.
This entire range constitutes the manifold expansion of phonetic modification (*varṇavikāra*).
The [final] vowel of a preposition is lengthened before the root *ay*.

In the root *aya*, the *r* of a prefix shall be replaced by *l*. Examples: *plāyate*, *palāyate*, *palyayate*. Because it is not so expressed [by this rule], in the case of *prati* we have *pratyayate*. [Also,] *g* is substituted for *ru* when followed by *yaṅ*.
The substitution of *l* for the *r* of the root *girati* occurs when the suffix *yaṅ* follows. Example: *nijegilyate*.
Why "when *yaṅ* follows"? [Observe: *nigīryate*. [In the case of other suffixes beginning with a vowel (*ac*), the substitution] is optional.
The suffix *ac* may optionally take the form *lat* after the root *gṛ* (to swallow). Thus, one says either *girati* or *gilati*; likewise, *nigaraṇam* or *nigalanam*.

By virtue of the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), when referring to a limb of a living being, the form *gala* alone is used invariably; however, in the case of poison, it is *gara* alone. An operation prescribed for a verbal root applies only to that which is a suffix following the root; it does not apply here in *girau* or *giraḥ*.
And [the substitution of *gh* occurs] for *jha* and *ṅ*, when followed by another [consonant].

And when followed by *dha* or *ṅka*, there may optionally be the substitution of *la*. Thus, *parighaḥ* or *palighaḥ*; *paryaṅkaḥ* or *palyaṅkaḥ*. It should be stated that this also applies when followed by *yoga*. Thus, *pariyogaḥ* or *paliyogaḥ*.
[The rule] "there is elision of a final consonant following a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) [applies].
There shall be elision (*lopa*) of a word-final consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*). Examples: *gomān*, *śreyān*, *bhavan*, *pacan*, *kṛtavān*.

Here, in the cases of *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*, *kāky artham*, and *vāsy artham*, there is no elision of the final consonant of the cluster according to the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), because the elision of the semivowel (*yaṇ-lopa*)—which is caused by *saṃhitā*—is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) from the perspective of that external operation.
Of the grain at night.

The elision of *s* occurs only for a *s* that is part of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogānta*) following the letter *r*. Examples: *pituḥ*, *mātuḥ*, *he pitaḥ*, *kaṭacikīḥ*, *bhārajihīḥ*. It does not occur for any other [final *s*]: *ūrk* (from *ūrjas* with the suffix *kvip*), and *amārṭ* (from *mṛj* in the *laṅ* tense), where the elision of the two *j*s does not take place.
[Also, there is elision] before *dhi*.

When the letter *dh* follows, there is elision of *s*. Examples: *asahidhvam*, *ayācidhvam*, *apavidhvam*, *alavidhvam*. Here—some say that when *dh* follows *siC*, there is elision of *siC*; this is for the purpose of forms such as *cakāddhi*. Others say it applies generally to all cases. Examples: *cakādhi*, *vaserāseśca*—*nivadhvam*, *ādhvam*.

The rule applies only when [the word] *pada* is present—as in *payo dhāvati*; however, in *payodhiḥ*, it does not apply because of the continued application of the optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) mentioned previously.
Beyond this point, they say that only the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *sic* is intended.
[This concludes the section on] *jhalo jhali*.
The *sic* suffix following a root ending in a *jhal* consonant is elided when a *jhal* consonant follows. Examples: *abhittaḥ*, *abhitthāḥ*, *abuddhaḥ*, *abuddhāḥ*.
Why "when a *jhal* consonant follows"? [Observe: *abhitsātām*. [Also, the *sic* is elided] after a verbal base (*aṅga*) ending in a short vowel.

There shall be elision of the *sic* affix following a short vowel. Examples: *akṛta*, *akṛthāḥ*; *adita*, *adithāḥ*. Why "after a verbal base (*aṅga*)"? Observe: *alaviṣṭha*. Only when a *jhal* consonant follows—observe: *akṛṣātām*. Elision of *sic* other than this is not desired: *dviṣṭarām*, *dviṣṭamām*, *triṣṭamām*.
It goes to the desired place.

There is elision of the *s* of the suffix *sic* when it follows a root ending in *iṭ* (the augment *iṭ*) and when *īṭ* follows. Examples: *adevīt*, *aśvasīt*, *agrahīt*. Furthermore, there is elision of the *s* and *k* of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) at the end of a word.

When a conjunct consonant occurs before a *jhal* sound or at the end of a word (*padānta*), there is elision of the initial *s* and *k* sounds [of that conjunct]. *masj-* → *magnaḥ*, *sādhumak*. *takṣū-* → *taṣṭavyam*, *taṣṭaḥ*, *kāṣṭhataṭ*. [This applies] only when it is at the end of a word—e.g., *pṛthak sthātā*.
The *c* and *ch* sounds become *k* and *kh* [respectively].

Before a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word (*padānta*), the *ca*-class (*cavarga*) is replaced by the *ka*-class (*kavarga*). Examples: *vaktā*, *vaktum*, *vaktavyam*; *vāk*. In the *laṅ* [aorist]: *avak*. From *ruj*: *rugṇaḥ*. From *ghṛj*: *cakraghṛk*. How is *āññjīt* formed? Because the subsequent phoneme (*paramavarṇa*) is not established [as a cause for the change].

How then is it that from *kruñc*, with *kvip* after a root ending in *ñ*, we have *kruṅ*, *kruñcau*, *kruñcaḥ*? It is due to the specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*) stated as "after *yuj* and *kruñc*."
Ho ḍhaḥ.
Before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant and at the end of a word (*padānta*), *h* is replaced by *ḍh*. Examples: *soḍhā*, *leḍhā*, *madhuliṭ*, *aleṭ*.
For a root beginning with *d* or *dh*, *dh* is substituted [for the initial *h*].

In the *Dhātupāṭha*, when a suffix beginning with *t* follows, *gh* shall be substituted for *h* of roots beginning with *d*. Examples: *dogdhā* (milkman), *godhuk* (cow-milker); in the *laṅ* (imperfect): *adhok*; *dagdhā* (burner), *grāmadhak* (village-burner).
This substitution of *gh* for [the *ḍh* resulting from] *ḍhatva* is established by the force of this exception (*apavāda*). [The following rule applies:
"Or [there is optionally *gh*] for the roots *druh*, *muha*, *ṣṇuh*, and *ṣṇih*."
For these [roots], *gh* may optionally be substituted for *h*. Thus: *drogdhā* or *droḍhā*; *mitradhrug* or *mitradhruṭ*; *mogdhā* or *moḍhā*;
*srogdhā* or *sroḍhā*; *srik* or *sriṭ*; *snegdhā* or *sneḍhā*.
[In the case of the root] *nah*, *dha* is substituted [for *h*].
The substitution of *dh* for *h* occurs when that [root] follows. Examples: *naddham*, *naddhum*, *naddhā*, *naddhavyaḥ*, *upānat*, *āhasthaḥ*.
Or rather, does *tha* replace *ha* before a *jhal* [consonant]? As in *āttha*. Why "before a *jhal*"? [Observe: *āhatuḥ*, *āhuḥ*.
[Furthermore: In place of the [final] consonants of *vraśc*, *bhrasj*, *sṛj*, *mṛj*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *bhrāj*, and of *ch* and *ś*, there is *ṣ*.

The final *s* of a root becomes *ṣ* before a *jhal* consonant and at the end of a word. Examples: *vraṣṭā*, *mūlavṛṭ*; *bhraṣṭa*, *bhr̥ṣṭā*; *dhānyabhṛṭ*; *sraṣṭā*, *rajjusr̥ṭ*; *mārṣṭā*, *sthānamr̥ṭ*; *yaṣṭā*, *yaṣṭum*; *deveṭ*; *rāṣṭram*; *samrāṭ*; *bhrāṣṭram*; *vibhrāṭ*; *praṣṭā*; *śabdaprāṭ*; *praveṣṭum*; *viṭ*.

In the case of a root ending in a *jhaṣ* sound (any consonant except *y*, *r*, *l*, or *v*), when followed by a suffix beginning with *s* or *dhv*, the single-consonant substitute *vaś* (i.e., the third letter of each varga) is replaced by *bhaṣ* (the fourth letter of each varga).

In place of *baś* (the first three sounds of a class) belonging to a verbal root (*dhātu*) that consists of a single vowel (*ekāj*) and ends in a *jhaṣ* (a sound from the *jha* to *bha* group), there shall be *bhaṣ* (the fourth sound of the class, i.e., *bh*, *gh*, *ḍh*, or *dh*), provided it occurs before *se*, *dhve*, or at the end of a word (*padānte*). Examples: *√budh*: *bhotsyate*, *abhuṅdhvam*. *√guh*: *ghokṣyate*, *aghūḍhvam*. *varṇaghuṭ*. *√duh*: *dhokṣyate*, *adhugdhvam*; *godhuk*.

What is the purpose of taking recourse to the constituent elements of the verbal root (*dhātu*)? It is so that [the substitution] may take place even when *aṭ* has been applied—as in *adhok* and *adhugdhvam*. Likewise, from the roots *gardabhayati*, *ḍuṇḍubhayati*, and *abhyayati*, with the suffix *kvip*, we have *gardhab* and *ḍuṇḍhup*; and from *tuṇḍibhayati*, we have *tuṇḍhiv*. Why "of a monosyllabic root" (*ekācaḥ*)? [Consider] *dāmaliṭ*.
[The rule applies] also to *dadh-* before *t* and *th*.

In the case of the root *dadhāti* (to place), which has undergone reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the substitute *baṣ* shall take the place of *dha* when followed by *ta*, *tha*, *s*, or *dhv*. Thus: *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*, *dhatse*, *dhaṅghe*, *pidhaṅdhvam* (as in *pāṇibhir dṛḍhadaṃśaḥ*). This applies only when the root ends in a *jhaṣ* (a voiced aspirated stop); it does not apply in cases such as *dadhāti* or *dadhāsi*. Furthermore, at the end of a word, the *jaś* (voiced unaspirated stops) substitute takes the place of *jhal* (all consonants except semivowels and nasals).

At the end of a word (*padānte*), the *jaś* sounds (the voiced unaspirated stops) shall be the most similar (*antaratama*) to the *jhal* sounds (all consonants except *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *ha*). Examples: *vāg atra*, *ekāj atra*, *śvaliḍ atra*, *agnicid atra*, *triṣṭub atra*. [Examples of internal sandhi: *vāgbhyām*, *andhayug-gamanam*, *śvaliḍbhyām*, *bhavadbhyām*. Why "at the end of a word"? To prevent it from applying before a *jhal* sound; e.g., *vastā*. Here, when the final of a conjunct (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) is elided, the substitution of *jaś* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Thus, in *śreyān*, the substitution of *jaś* is not applied. However, in *payaḥ* and *yaśaḥ*, the substitution of *ut* for the *s* of the nominative singular (*su*) is established as valid. Why is this so? Because it is an exception (*apavāda*). [The rule continues: *jhaṣas tathor dho 'dhaḥ*.

The substitute *jhaṣ* (the entire consonant group) likewise occurs for the following two [consonants], as well as for the letter *ūrdhva* (*dh*). Examples: *labdhā*, *labdhum*, *labdhavyam*, *alabdha*, *alabdhāḥ*; *abuddha*, *abuddhāḥ*, *boddhā*; *leḍhā*; *alīḍha*, *alīḍhāḥ*; *dogdhā*, *adugdha*, *adugdhā*. Why "for *ūrdhva*"? To prevent it from applying to the root *dhā*/*dhāñ*: *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*. [Also:

In the *Saṃhitā*, [the rule] applies to those two vowels.

The term "in the *saṃhitā*" governs [the rules] up to the end of the chapter. *Saṃhitā* is obligatory between two words within a single compound, and it is obligatory between a verbal root and a prefix;
likewise, it is obligatory even in the *sūtras*. In other cases, however, it is optional.
In Vedic usage, the forms *mātuvas* and *ru* are substituted for the vocative case ending.

The term *ruḥ* is governed [as the subject] in the context of the vocative (*sambuddhau*). The remainder is Vedic (*chāndasaḥ*). [Rule: *vibhāṣā bhavadbhavadaghavatām occāvasya*. For these—namely *bhavat*, *bhagavat*, and *aghavat*—there is optionally the substitution of *ruḥ* in the vocative, and for the word *ava*, the substitution of the vowel *o*. Examples: *he bhoḥ* or *he bhavan*; *he bhagoḥ* or *he bhagavan*; *he aghoḥ* or *he aghavan*. The word *bhoḥ* is also an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Examples: *bho vipra*, *bho viprau*, *bho viprāḥ*. In the feminine: *bho brāhmaṇi*.
Here, there is an optional nasalization (*anunāsika*) of the preceding vowel.

The governing rule is established: "For that [vowel] after which *ru* has been substituted, the corresponding nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) may optionally take its place. This applies to the following: "Invariably before a vowel beginning with *a-ṭ*."
In the Chandas (Vedic literature), an anusvāra follows a nasalized vowel.

The word "anya" (other) is to be supplied here. It should be understood that for a *ru* (the letter *r*) other than one following an *anunāsika*, when the preceding [consonant] lacks an *anunāsika*, there is the augment *pari-anusvāra*. For example: *samaḥ suṭi*.

The *ru* [substitute] becomes *sam̐* when followed by *suṭ*; thus, one may say *saṃsskarttā* or *saṃsskarttā*. One may say *saṃsskaroti* or *saṃsskaroti*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "In the case of *sam*, there is elision of *m*. Even in the view that there is elision, both the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) and the anusvāra are desired; thus, one may say *saṃskarttā* or *saṃsakarttā*. Furthermore, regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "In the case of *sam*, *pum*, and *kān*, *s* should be prescribed [as the substitute for *m*]. Thus, one may say *saṃsskarttā* or *saṃsskarttā*; *pum̐skāmā* or *puṃskāmā*; *kāṃskān* or *kām̐skān*.

In the alternative where *ru* is applied, there would be either *visarga* by the rule *vā śari*, or the two forms *ḥka* and *ḥpa* by the rule *kupvoḥ ḥkaḥ pau ca*. According to Vāmana’s commentary (*vṛtti*), however, [the *visarga*] does not occur due to the restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in the rule *vā śari*.
In this matter, because of the difference of opinion between Kaiyaṭa and Śrutapāla regarding the root *saṃskṛ*, sixteen forms arise; these are not shown here for fear of excessive prolixity.
[The next rule is: *pumaḥ khayyampare*.

The word *pum̐s* becomes *pum̐* when followed by a *khay* consonant (any consonant except *y*) that is itself followed by an *am* vowel (a, i, u). Examples: *pum̐ścalī*, or *puṃścalī*; *pum̐skokilaḥ*, or *puṃskokilaḥ*; *pum̐skāmā*, or *puṃskāmā*; *pum̐stvam*, or *puṃstvam*. Why "followed by an *am* vowel"? Consider *puṃkhīram*. Why "when followed by a *khay* consonant"? Consider *puṃgavaḥ* and *puṃhāsaḥ*.
[The rule] *naśchavyapraśān* [is now introduced].

The *ru* substitute does not occur for the final syllable of a word before *ś*, *y*, or *ch-vi*. For example: *bhavāṃścinoti* or *bhavām̐ścinoti*; *bhavāṃśchādayati* or *bhavām̐śchādayati*; *bhavāṃṣṭīkate* or *bhavām̐ṣṭīkate*; *bhavāṃṣṭhakāraḥ* or *bhavām̐ṣṭhakāraḥ*; *bhavāṃstarati* or *bhavām̐starati*. Why "before *ch-vi*"? Witness: *bhavān karoti*. Why "except for *praśān*"? Witness: *praśāññcinoti*. Only when preceded by *am*—as in: *bhavān tsarukaḥ*. Only for a word-final [syllable]—as in: *bhavantau*, *pacantau*. Only in *saṃhitā* (continuous utterance)—as in: *bhavān cinoti*, *bhavān chādayati*.
How is it that there is an *antara* (intervening element) here? In this case, it does not occur because the *parasavarṇa* [substitution] is not established. For example:
*ubhayatharkṣu*.
The *dīrghāṭi* [sandhi] occurs when the same foot follows.
The two *chandas* sūtras:
"nṝn" and "pe".

The substitute *ru* occurs for the word *nṛn* when followed by a *pa*-sound. Thus: *nṛṃḥ pāhi* or *nṛḥ pāhi*; *nṛṃḥ prīṇīhi* or *nṛḥ prīṇīhi*. Why "before a *pa*-sound"? Observe: *nṛn bhojayati*. This applies only in *saṃhitā* (continuous speech); thus: *nṛn pāhi* [in a pause].
[The substitute *ru* also occurs] for *svatavān* before the root *pā*.
This is according to the Vedic usage (*cchāndasa*).
Regarding *kān* when followed by a reduplicated form (*amreḍita*):
the substitute *ru* occurs for the *n* of *kān* when a reduplicated form follows. Thus, one says either *kāṃskān* or *kām̐skān* [in the sense of] "he feeds whom-whom."
The letter *ru* has been explained.
There is elision of the [augment] *ṭi* after the suffixes *ḍha* and *ḍha*.

When followed by a *ḍha*, there shall be the elision (*lopa*) of a preceding *ḍha*. Examples: *ūḍham*, *nirvyūḍhiḥ*, *līḍham*, *līḍhavān*, *līḍhvā*. Here, the substitution of *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ṣ* for *s* and *ṭ* for *t*) is established by virtue of this reference [to the rule].
[The next rule is: *ro ri* (R is elided when followed by R).

When a *repha* (the sound *r*) follows, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the preceding *repha*. Examples: *svārāṭ*, *punāraktam*, *punāramate*, *indūrājate*, *he karttā rājase*, *ahāramyam*, *nīraktam*, *agnīrathaḥ*.
How is *manorathaḥ* [formed]? Because the elision of the *repha* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *haśi ca*.
In the presence of a voiceless consonant (*khar*) or at the end of a pause (*avasāna*), the *visarjanīya* is substituted [for *r*].

The *visarjanīya* shall replace the final *repha* (the letter *r*) at the end of a word, before a *khari* consonant and at the pause (*avasāna*). Examples: *vipraḥ karttā* ("the Brahmin is the agent"), *vipraḥ sādhuḥ* ("the Brahmin is virtuous"). At the pause: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *prātaḥ*.

[In the case of] *nṛpater apatyam nārpatyam* ("the offspring of the king"), the substitution does not occur because the *vṛddhi* replacement is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for this rule. [This applies] when *su* follows *ru*.
When followed by the locative plural suffix (su), the visarga must be substituted for *ro* alone: as in *payaḥsu*, *sarpiḥṣu*. For *repha* [the rule applies]: as in *gīrṣu*, *caturṣu*, *dhūrṣu*.
[Furthermore, the substitution of *y* occurs] for the *bh-*, *bha-g-*, *a-gh-*, and *a-pūrv-a* [visargas] before any vowel (*aśi*).

The letter *y* shall be substituted for the *r* of this [word] *etad* when followed by a vowel (*aś*), provided it is preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, *aghō*, or a vowel. Examples: *bho atra* → *bhoyatra* *bho ātman* → *bhoyātman* *bhago atra* → *bhagoyatra* *aghō atra* → *aghoyatra* *bho dadāsi* → *bhōdadāsi* When preceded by a vowel other than *a* (i.e., *ā*): *ka āste* → *kayāste* *ka iha* → *kayiha* *narā āsate* → *narāyāsate* Why "preceded by *etad*"? [Counter-example: *vāyuratra* (the *r* here is not part of *etad*). Why "of *r*"? [Counter-example: *prātaratra* (here the *r* is not the *r* of *etad*). *priyacatvārasau* (here the *r* is not the *r* of *etad*). *vārbhyām* (here the *r* is not the *r* of *etad*).
The mention of *aś* is for the sake of what follows:
according to Śākaṭāyana, the [substitution] of *v* and *y* is one characterized by lighter effort.

The *y* and *v* at the end of words preceded by the word *bhoḥ* (and others) may optionally become slightly more touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭatara*) when followed by a vowel other than *a* (*aśi*). Examples: *bhoy atra*, *bhoy iha*, *bhoy idam*; *vṛkṣayiha*, *viprayāsate*, *asmāy uddhara*, *karavāy ānuṣṭubham*, *vaṭav āttha*, *dvāv ānaya*. In the alternative case—where they remain slightly touched—the elision (*lopa*) will be taught later; thus there are three forms. Regarding the rule "the [final] *o* is always elided" (*oto nityaṃ lopaḥ*), two forms will be established there through the application of the easier effort (*laghuprayatnatara*) and elision.
Then, "there is elision according to Śākalya" (*lopaḥ śākalyasya*).

According to the opinion of Śākalya, there is elision of the two vowels [when they meet]. For example: *ka āste* (Who sits?), *yasmā uddhara* (Lift it from whom?), *kasmā uddhara* (Lift it from whom?), *dvā ānaya* (Bring the two), *viprā āsate* (The sages sit), and *paṭa āste* (The cloth sits).
According to Gārgya, however, there is elision of the vowel *o*.
There shall be elision of the *pra* of the following *kāra*. This statement is for the sake of making it obligatory. Examples: *bho atra*; *agho idam*.
And [there is elision] when *uñ* follows within a word (*pade*).

The *u* [of *uñ*] is elided before a falling vowel (*nipāta*) and at the end of a word (*padānta*), when followed by *v* or *y*. Examples: *sa u paśyati*, *dvā u paśyataḥ*. In the alternative where the effort is lighter (*laghuprayatnatara*), the two forms *sayu paśyati* and *dvāvu paśyataḥ* occur. [This applies] before a consonant (*hal*) according to the opinion of all [grammarians].

The elision of *y* and *v* occurring at the end of a word, when preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, *agho*, or a vowel, before a consonant (*hal*), is universally accepted. Examples: *bho hasasi*; *bhago dadāti*; *agho yāsi*; *viprā hasanti*. Regarding the *v*: from *vṛkṣaṃ vṛścati* (he cuts the tree), we derive *vṛkṣavṛt*; from that, with the suffix *ṇic* and then *vic*, we get *vṛkṣav*. Examples: *vṛkṣaṃ gacchati*; *vṛkṣav karoti* (only when not followed by *ś*). Why "at the end of a word"? [Counter-examples: *śayyā*; *śaṅkavyam*.
The anusvāra is nasalized.
When followed by a consonant (haL), an anusvāra shall be substituted for the final *m* of a word (*pada*). Examples: *kuṇḍaṃ hanti*, *vanaṃ yāti*, *paṃbhyām*, *puṃsu*.

This applies only when it is the end of a word (*padasya*); thus, in *ramyate* and *gamyate*, no substitution occurs. Furthermore, when followed by a *jhal* sound, an anusvāra is also substituted for a *n* that is not at the end of a word.
Before a *jhal* consonant, an *anusvāra* shall be substituted for *n* and *m* that are not at the end of a word. Examples: *payāṃsi*, *yaśāṃsi*. For *m*: *ākraṃsyate*.
Why "before a *jhal*" (*jhali*)? [Counter-examples: *hanyate*, *gamyate*. [Sūtra:
*mo rāji samaḥ kvau* (Pāṇini 8.3.25).

When *kvip* follows, the *m* of *sam-* shall remain as *m* even when *rāj-* follows. Examples: *samrāṭ*, *sāmrājyam*. Why "when *rāj-* follows"? Consider *saṃyat*. Why "of *sam-*"? Consider *svayaṃrāṭ*. Why "when *kvip* follows"? Consider *saṃrājitā*.
Or else, it is otherwise.
When followed by another *ha* (hakāra), the *ma* of *kim* may optionally become *ma*. Thus: *kiṃ hlalayati* or *kiṃ hlalayati*.
When followed by *ya*, *va*, or *la*, the [substitutes] may optionally be *ya*, *va*, or *la* with nasalization (*sānunāsika*). Thus: *kiyam̐ hyaḥ* or *kiṃ hyo vā*;
*kiṃ hvalayati* or *kivam̐ hvalayati vā*; *kilam̐ hlādayati* or *kiṃ hlādayati vā*.
Not beyond us.
When followed by *ha*, the *m* of *kim* may optionally become *n*. Thus: *kiṃ hanti* or *kiṃ hanti*. [Also: *ṅ-ṇoḥ kuk-ṭuk śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.28).

After the final letters *ṅ* and *ṇ*, the augments *k* and *ṭ* (respectively) may optionally be added before a sibilant (*śar*). Examples: *adhyaṅk śastrabhṛtāṃ rāmaḥ* or *adhyaṅ śastrabhṛtāṃ rāmaḥ*; *prāṅ ṣaṇḍe* or *prāṅ kṣaṇḍe*. From the root *vaṇ* (derived from the verbal root *vaṇ*), we have *vaṇ śete*, *vaṇṭ śete*, or *vaṇṭc chete*; *vaṇṣ ṣaṇḍe* or *vaṇṭ ṣaṇḍe*. After the letter *ḍ*, the augment *dhuṭ* is added before *s*.
After a letter ending in *ḍ*, a *dhuṭ* (stop or sibilant) may optionally be inserted before the letter *s*. For example: *śvaliṭtsāye* or *śvaliṭsāye*.
Also, [a *dhuṭ* may be inserted] after *n*.
After a word ending in *n*, a *dhuṭ* (stop or sibilant) may optionally follow the letter *s*. Thus: *bhavāntsādhuḥ* or *bhavān sādhur vā*.
[The augment] *śi-tuk* [is applied].

The augment *t* may optionally be inserted after a final *n* before the letter *ś*. Thus: *bhavāññcśete*, *bhavāññcchete*, *bhavāññchete*, or *bhavāññśete*; likewise, *mahāññchete*, *mahāññcśete*, *mahāññcchete*, or *mahāññśete*. Furthermore, when a vowel follows a short vowel preceded by a *ṅ*-stop (*ṅama*), the augment *ṇ* is always inserted after that *ṅ*-stop.

After a short vowel, the final *ṅ*, *ṇ*, or *n* of a word shall be replaced by *ṅu*, *ṇṇu*, *ṇṇu*, or *ṇṭ* respectively, before a vowel. Examples: *udaṅ āste* (udaṅ + āste), *śvagaṇṇ iha* (śvagaṇ + iha), *yaṇṇ iha* (yaṇ + iha), *kurvann atra* (kurvan + atra).

Why "after a short vowel"? Observe: *prāṅ āste* (prāṅ + āste), *mahān avam* (mahān + avam). Because the rule depends on being at the end of a word (*padānta*), it does not apply here: *bhaṇati* (bhaṇat + i), *daṇḍinā* (daṇḍin + ā). However, forms such as those ending in *tiṅ*, those beginning with *ṇādi*, and those ending in *sanādi*, are established by specific grammatical exceptions (*nipātana*).
Or may I be inferior to you.

The word *mayaḥ* may optionally become *maḥ* before a following vowel (*aci*) or a semi-vowel (*uñ*). This is an exception to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by virtue of its being a *pragṛhya* due to the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*. Thus, we have *kimu ayam* or *kimvayam*.
[In the case of *kimu*,] the *visarjanīya* becomes *s*.
It may be so: *paṭuśchātraḥ* (a clever student), *vṛkṣaṣṣaṇḍe* (in a grove of trees), *viprassādhuḥ* (a virtuous Brahmin).
By means of the "frog-leap" [principle], it is just like *kharī*—namely, *vṛkṣaḥ*.
[The rule is: "The visarga remains when followed by a sibilant (*śar*) that is itself followed by a labial (*par*) sound."

Before a *khari* consonant followed by a *śar* consonant, the *visarjanīya* itself shall remain without undergoing modification: as in *ramyastsarukaḥ* and *vipraiḥpsātam*. Or, [the *visarjanīya* remains] before a *śari* consonant: as in *vāsaḥkṣaumam*.

Before a *śar* consonant, the *visarga* may optionally become *s*. *vṛkṣaśśete*, *vṛkṣaḥ śete* (the tree lies down). *vṛkṣaṣṣaṇḍe*, *vṛkṣaḥṣaṇḍe* (the tree [is] in the grove). *vṛkṣassādhuḥ*, *vṛkṣaḥ sādhuḥ* (the tree is good). *viprassādhuḥ*, *vipraḥ sādhuḥ* (the Brahmin is good).

Before a *khara* consonant followed by a *śar* consonant, there is optionally elision (*lopa*) of the *visarga*. *narā sthūlāḥ*, *narāḥ sthūlāḥ*, or *narās sthūlāḥ* (men who are stout). *svasthaḥ*, *svaḥsthaḥ*, or *svassthaḥ* (established in heaven/self). *nisspṛhaḥ*, *nispṛhaḥ*, or *niḥspṛhaḥ* (free from desire).
The sounds *k* and *p* [are substituted] for the sounds *c* and *v*, respectively, when followed by *a* or *ka*; and *a* and *p* are also substituted [for *c* and *v*].
Before *k* and *p*, the *visarga* may optionally become *ka* or *pa*; because of the word *ca* ("and"), it may also remain as *visarjanīya*.

The letters *k* and *p* are for the sake of pronunciation. [In the case of *k* and *kh*, there is the sound of a *ḍamaru* drum; in the case of *ph* and *ph*, there is the sound of an elephant's temple.
Examples: *vipraḥ karttā*, or *vipra-akarttā*; *ramyaḥ khaḍgaḥ*, or *ramya-akhaḍgaḥ*; *vipraḥ pacati*, or *vipraḥ pacati*; *śūdraḥ pibati*, or *śūdraḥ pibati*; *vṛkṣaḥ phalati*, or *vṛkṣaḥ phalati*.
He states the exception regarding the two *k* sounds: "That [substitution] does not occur when they are at the beginning of a word."

When *kup* (the letters *k* and *p*) follow a word-initial [consonant] and a *khari* (a voiceless consonant) follows, the *visarga* of the preceding word shall become *s*. This applies in the case of the suffixes *-pāśa*, *-kalpa*, *-ka*, and *-kāmya*. Examples: *rakṣas-pāśān*, *tamas-kalpān*, *ayas-kalpam*. It should be stated that this rule does not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*). Example: *prātaḥ-kalpam*, *punaḥ-kāmyati*. It should be stated that in the case of the suffix *-kāmya*, the change occurs only after the letter *r* and not after any other. Example: *yaśas-kāmyati*. It should not occur here: *gīḥ-kāmyati*, *dhūḥ-kāmyati*. Due to the restriction regarding *-kāmya*, it would indeed occur here: *ahas-kalpam*.
The *ṣ* replaces the final letter of the root *iṇ*.

After *k* or *p*, when followed by *v* or *r*, the *visarga* of a word-final syllable shall be changed to *ṣ*, provided it does not occur at the beginning of a subsequent word (*apadādau*). Examples: *jyotiṣkāmyati*, *sarpiṣkalpam*, *dhanuṣpāśam*, *dhānuṣkaḥ*, *dorbhyāṃ tarati* → *dauṣkaḥ*.
Why "not at the beginning of a word"? Consider: *agniḥ karoti*, *agriḥ karttā*. Only after *k* or *p*:
therefore, *vittaḥ* (from *vit-tas*) and *sarpiścaṇaḥ* (from *sarpis-caṇaḥ*).
From this point on, *sa* is the substitute for the visarga; however, *ṣa* is the substitute for a visarga followed by *isa*. The rules *khari* and *kupvoḥ* also carry over [from the previous sūtras].
[The rule] *namaspurasorgatyoḥ* [is now stated].

The visarga of the words *namas* and *puras*, when followed by a word beginning with a sibilant (*ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*), shall be changed to *s*. Examples: *namaskarttā* (one who pays homage), *namaskāraḥ* (homage), *namaskaroti* (he pays homage); *puraskartum* (to place before), *puraskaroti* (he places before).
Furthermore, the visarga of a word ending in *i* or *u*, provided it is not part of a suffix (*apratyaya*), is also changed to *s* under these conditions.

The *visarga* of a non-suffixal element that has *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* (short) as its penultimate letter shall be replaced by *ṣ* when followed by *k* or *p* (or their substitutes). The occurrence of *ni*, *dur*, *bahiḥ*, *prāduḥ*, and *āviḥ* [is as follows]: *niṣkulāni* (those from which the family has departed), *niṣkrīṇāti* (he buys out), *niṣkriyaḥ* (inactive). *duṣpītiḥ* (bad drinking), *duṣprajñaḥ* (of poor intellect), *duṣpītam* (badly drunk), *duṣkṛtam* (ill-deed). *bahiṣkṛtam* (cast out), *bahiṣpacati* (he cooks outside), *bahiṣkaroti* (he does outside). *prāduṣkṛtam* (made manifest), *āviṣkaroti* (he reveals). *catuṣpānam* (four-footed), *catuṣkapālam* (having four potsherds), *catuṣpārśvam* (four sides), *catuṣkāṇḍaṃ kṣipan rāmaḥ* (Rāma, throwing [arrows] in four sections).

What is the purpose of the condition *idudupadhasya* (the root must end in *i*, *u*, or *ū*)? [Consider: *doḥ karoti*. How then [is the form] *naiṣkulyam* or *dauṣkulyam* derived? Because the external *vṛddhi* substitution is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of this rule. What is the purpose of the condition *apratyayasya* (it must not be part of an affix)? [Consider: *agniḥ karoti*, *vāyuḥ pāti*. How then [is the form] *mātuḥ karoti*, *pituḥ karoti* derived? Since the word *bhrātuṣputra* is included in the *kaskādi* group for the sake of the *ṣatva* (retroflex sibilant) substitution, there is no *ṣatva* for the *visarga* following an *iṇ*-vowel that serves as the cause for a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).
Thus says the Bhāṣya:
there is a prohibition [of the substitution of *sa*] for the words *pum* and *muhuḥ*. [Examples: *paṃskāmā*, *muhuḥ karoti*, *muhuḥkāmyati*.
[Regarding the word *tiras*,] it is optional.

In the sense of disappearance (*antardhi*), the *visarga* of the word *tiras*, when it is designated as "motion" (*gati*), may optionally become *s*. Thus, one says either *tiraskarttā* or *tiraḥkarttā*.
Some do not carry over the mention of "motion" (*gati*) here, so that the change may occur even outside the context of motion, as in *tiraskāraḥ* meaning "insult" or "disrespect.
[The words] *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* [are used] in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*).

For these [words] ending in *kṛtvas* or having the sense of *su*, the substitution of *ṣ* may optionally take place. Examples: *dviṣ karoti*, *triṣ pacati*, *catuṣ kurvan*. In the alternative: *dviḥ karoti*, *triḥ pacati*, *catuḥ kurvan*. Why "in the sense of *kṛtvas*"? (Consider: *catuṣkāṇḍam*, *catuṣkaṇṭakam*.
[The substitution of *ṣ* occurs] for *is* and *us* when they express a common referent (*sāmānyārtha*).

Also: *suṣamam*, *niḥṣamam*, *viṣamam*. Why "after these"? [Counter-example: *abhisuptaḥ*. Why the mention of *sup*? [Counter-example: *susvapiti*. [The rule applies to] *snāti* after *ni-* and *nadī-* when meaning skillfulness.

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs after these two [prefixes] when the root *snā* signifies skill (*kauśala*) or attainment (*gati*). For example: *niṣṇātaḥ śāstre* (skilled in the scripture); *nadīṣṇaḥ* (one who has mastered the river), meaning one who knows the river. Why "skill"? [Counter-example: *nadīsnātaḥ* (one who has merely bathed in the river). Also: *pratiṣṇātam sūtram* (the sutra that has been thoroughly studied).

In the name *vṛtta*, there shall be the substitution of *ṣ* for the root *vi-stṛ*. [The suffix] *ghañ* [is applied]. Thus, the meter named *viṣṭārapaṅkti* is formed.
[The suffix] *ka* is added after *gavi* and *yudhi* when followed by *sthira*.

By these two [rules], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in the word *sthira*. Examples: *gaviṣṭhiraḥ*, *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ*. Precisely because of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending. [Also]: after *vi*, *ku*, *śami*, and *pari*, the word *sthalam* [undergoes the same change].

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs after these [words] before the word *sthalam*. Examples: *viṣṭhalam*, *kuṣṭhalam*, *śayānāṃ kuṣṭhale*, *śamiṣṭhalam*. In the case of *śamī*, the short vowel is substituted by the rule *ṅayāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63). Examples: *pariṣṭhalam*.

[The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] after *ambā*, *amba*, *go*, *bhūmi*, *savya*, *ap*, *dvi*, *tri*, *kuśe*, *kuśa*, *kaṅka*, *aṅgu*, *mañji*, *puñji*, *parame*, *barhis*, *divi*, and *agni* before the word *sthaḥ*.

The substitution of *ṣ* shall occur for the letter *s* of the word *stha* when it follows these [words]. Examples: *ambaṣṭhaḥ*, *āmbaṣṭhaḥ*, *goṣṭhaḥ*, *bhūmiṣṭhaḥ*, *savyaṣṭhaḥ*, *apaṣṭhaḥ*, *dviṣṭhaḥ*, *triṣṭhaḥ*, *kuṣṭhaḥ*, *śekuṣṭhaḥ*, *śaṅakuṣṭhuḥ*, *aṅaguṣṭhaḥ*, *maññjiṣṭhaḥ*, *puññjiṣṭhaḥ*, *parameṣṭhaḥ*, *barhiṣṭhaḥ*, *diviṣṭhaḥ*, *agriṣṭhaḥ*.

Because the term *sthaḥ* is used here as a formal citation (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), the rule does not apply in this case: *gosthānam*. How then are the forms *savyeṣṭhā*, *savyeṣṭhārau*, and *parameṣṭhī* explained? These are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes and should be understood as belonging to the *suṣāmādi* group.
And [the substitution of *su* for *sāt* occurs] in the case of the *suṣāmādi* group.

In these cases, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs: *suṣāmā*, *suṣāmnī* (in the sense of "possessing all splendor"), *niḥṣāmā*, *suṣedhaḥ*, *niṣedhaḥ*, *suṣandhiḥ*, *apaṣṭhu*, *suṣṭhu*, *duṣṭhu*. According to some, [it occurs] in *upaṣṭambha*.
[The word] *eti* [is used] when it refers to a name (*saṃjñā*) and has not moved away.

Hariṣeṇaḥ. Why [is it] *ekāre*? Harisiṃhaḥ. Why [is it] *saṃjñāyām*? Pṛthuseno rājā. Why [is it] *agaḥ*? Viṣvaksenaḥ. Only when following *iṇ* or *k*—as in Sarvasenaḥ. Or [the suffix applies] after a *nakṣatra* [name].

In the context of a name (*saṃjñā*), the *s* following a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) may optionally become *ṣ*. For example: *rohiṇiṣeṇaḥ* or *rohiṇisenaḥ*. In this manner, words such as *suṣāman* and others are treated according to what is observed.
[Furthermore, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] after a short vowel when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *t* follows.

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs after a short vowel before a *t*-initial taddhita suffix. Examples: *sarpiṣṭaram*, *sarpiṣṭamam*, *yajuṣṭamam*, *vapuṣṭamam*, *dīrghāyuṣṭvam*, *catuṣṭayam*, *sarpiṣṭā*. Why "before a *t*-initial [suffix]"? [Consider: *sarpissāt* becomes [the form]. Why "after a short vowel"? [Consider: *gīstarām*. A prohibition must be stated for verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*: *bhindyustarām*.
In the case of sitting, there is no fault if one does not practice it habitually.

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs after *ni* when followed by *tapati*, provided the action is performed only once (*sakṛt*). Examples: *niṣṭapati*, *niṣṭāpaḥ*, *niṣṭapanam*. Why "performed only once"? Consider *nistapati suvarṇaṃ suvarṇakāraḥ*; this means the goldsmith heats the gold repeatedly, touching it to the fire again and again.

Here, eight sūtras are Vedic (*cchāndasa*); they are as follows: 1. *niṣṭapati* 2. *niṣṭāpaḥ* 3. *niṣṭapanam* 4. *niṣṭarkyaḥ* 5. *niṣṭyānaḥ* 6. *niṣṭyānam* 7. *niṣṭyāvatī* 8. *niṣṭyāvan* (Note: These sūtras are traditionally cited as archaic forms found in the Vedas.)
The substitution of *yuṣmat* and *tad* occurs within the word (*antaḥpādam*) before the suffixes *tāt* and *kṣu*.
According to some, [the offering] is performed with the Yajus formula.
[The suffix *kvin* is applied] after the verbal roots *stu* and *stoma* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

[The substitution of *ṣ* occurs] for the *s* of the root *sic* when followed by *yaṅ*.

In the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur: *sesicyate*. Even rules such as "after a prefix, the root *su-* [becomes *ṣu-*]" are superseded by the *yaṅ* suffix: *kurvāṇāṃ parisesicām*. Why mention *yaṅ*? [Because it applies elsewhere]: *abhiṣiṣikṣati*.
The root *sedhati* is used in the sense of motion.
