Also, *soḍha*.

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur in the root *soḍhṛ* (the root of *sah*) when preceded by the prefixes *pari*, *ni*, or *vi*. Examples: *parisoḍhum*, *parisoḍhaḥ*, *parisoḍhā*; *nisoḍhyaḥ*, *nisoḍhaḥ*, *nisoḍhā*.
Why is it specified as *soḍha*? [To exclude forms derived from other roots, such as] *viṣahate*. [Also, the rule *stambhusivusahāññcaṅi* applies.]
And for these [roots], the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur after the augment *aṅ*. Examples: *paryatastambhat*, *paryasīṣivat*, *paryasīṣahat*, *vyasīṣahat*.

How is there the substitution of *ṣ* for the following [root-initial]? It should be stated that it occurs "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*); by this, the application [of the rule] from the prefix is prohibited, but not [the application] from the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsāt*).
[This applies] to the root *sū* (to press) in connection with the suffixes *syat* and *san*.

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur after the root *śru* (*sunoti*) when followed by the suffix *sya* or the suffix *san*. Examples: *parisoṣyate* (with *sya*), and from the causative form with *san*, *abhisusūḥ* (with *kyap*).
Why "after *sya* and *san*"? Observe: *abhisuṣāva* and *parisuṣāva* (where the substitution does occur). [The rule *sadisvaññjoḥ parasya liṭi* applies next.]
In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, there is no substitution of *ṣ* for the subsequent *s* in these two [roots]. Examples: *viṣasāda*, *pariṣasvañje*.

According to Vāmana’s commentary, they maintain that the *liṭ* optionally takes the *kittva* designation even after a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). By this, in one alternative, due to the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal), the form *pariṣasvaja* is established. [Also]: In the Vedic language, the augment *aṭ* may optionally intervene after the prefixes *ni*, *vi*, and *abhi*.
Vedic grammar:
After the letters *ra* and *ṣ*, *ṇ* is substituted for *n* within the same word.
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs after *ra* or *ṣ*, within the same word (*samānapada*). For example: *vistīrṇam* (spread out), *puṣṇāti* (he nourishes), *kuṣṇāti* (he tears).
Why "within the same word"? [Consider] *vārnidhiḥ* (the treasure of speech) and *pitṛnām* (of the fathers).
[The rule] also applies after a vowel containing *ṛ* (*ṛvarṇa*): *tisṛṇām* (of three), *catasṛṇām* (of four), *mātṛṇām* (of mothers), *pitṛṇām* (of fathers).
Even when there is an intervention by the letters *a*, *ṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, or *num*, [the substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs].

Even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* (vowels) and other such sounds, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall occur after *r*, *ṣ*, or *ṛ* within the same word (*samānapada*). Examples: *karaṇam*, *haraṇam*, *uraḥkeṇa*, *gṛhṇāti*, *vṛkṇaḥ*, *roṣaṇaḥ*, *bhūṣaṇam*, *vṛkṣeṇa*, *mūrkheṇa*, *bhṛṅgeṇa*, *darpeṇa*, *garbheṇa*. The mention of *num* is intended as an illustration for the *anusvāra*. Examples: *vṛṃhaṇam*, *vṛṃhaṇīyam*, *dṛṃhaṇam*, *dṛṃhaṇīyam*. Why "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and others"? To prevent it from occurring when there is an intervention by *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *u*, *l*, *r*, or *ś*. Examples: *raucanam*, *darśanam*, *kapardakena*. The rule applies only within a single word (*ekapada*). Example: *agnirānīyatām* (where *agniḥ* and *ānīyatām* are separate words).
The rule regarding the intervention of *aḍ* and other consonants continues as far as the state of being *ṇ*.
[Furthermore,] in a compound name (*saṃjñā*), a suffix beginning with *ṇ* is applied after a word ending in a vowel, provided it does not follow the letter *g*.

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs when a *n* follows letters *ra*, *ṣ*, or *ṛ* situated in the first member (*pūrvapada*) of a compound, provided that the compound is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *kharaṇasaḥ* (an ass-nosed one), *śūrpaṇakhā* (the demoness with ears like winnowing baskets), *nārāyaṇaḥ*.

Why "provided it is a name"? Consider *dīrghanayanā strī* (a woman with long eyes). How is it that we have *agraṇīḥ* (leader) and *grāmaṇi* (head of a village)? This is due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating "also after *agra* and *grāma*. Why "not after *aga*"? Consider *ṛgayanam* (the study of the Rigveda). The rule applies even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* (vowels and semivowels) and so forth—as in *ardhanasaḥ* (half-nosed). From here on, the rule concerns the substitution following *ra*, *ṣ*, or *ṛ* situated in the first member.
The forest [is derived] from *puragā*, *miśrakā*, *sidhrakā*, *śārikā*, *koṭara*, and *agra*.

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *v* of the word *vana* shall occur after these [words] when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *puragāvaṇam*, *miśrakāvaṇam*, *sidhrakāvaṇam*, *śārikāvaṇam*, *koṭarāvaṇam*, *agrevaṇam*. Since this was already established by the preceding rule, this present rule serves as a restriction (*niyama*) and does not apply here: *indravanam*.
Furthermore, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs after *pra*, *ni*, *antaḥ*, and the words *śara*, *ikṣu*, *plakṣa*, *āmra*, *kārṣya*, *khadira*, and *pīyūkṣā*, even when not forming a proper name.

In these cases, when the word *vana* (forest) follows, the *n* of the prefix [pra-, nis-, antar-, etc. shall be replaced by *ṇ*, whether the word *vana* is used as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or not. *Pravaṇam*: an excellent forest. *Nirvaṇam*: gone out from the forest. *Antarvaṇam*: within the forest. *Śaravaṇam*: a thicket of reeds. *Ikṣuvaṇam*: a field of sugarcane. *Plakṣavaṇam*: a grove of *plakṣa* trees. *Āmravaṇam*: a grove of mango trees. *Kārṣyavaṇam*: a grove of *kārṣya* trees. *Khadiravaṇam*: a grove of *khadira* trees. *Pīyūkṣāvaṇam*: a grove of date palms.
[This substitution is] optional (*vibhāṣā*) after words denoting medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) or large trees (*vanaspati*).

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* may optionally occur after these [words] before the word *vana*. After *oṣadhi*: *dūrvāvaṇam* or *dūrvāvanam*. In this context, *vanaspati* refers to any tree in general because of its broad application: *śirīṣavaṇam* or *śirīṣavanam*; *gambhārīvaṇam* or *gambhārīvanam*. By virtue of the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it does not apply here: *irikāvanam*, *timirāvanam*. It does not apply here because the words consist of two or three syllables when expressing a specific name: *devadāruvanam*, *sahakāravanam*. Only when there is intervention by *aḍ* (vowels) and so forth does the rule apply—as in *nyagrodhavanam*.
[The suffix *ṭyu* is applied] after [a word ending in] *ahan*, provided that it does not end in a short vowel (*at*).
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs after a word ending in *a* when followed by the word *ahnaḥ*. Examples: *pūrvāhṇaḥ*, *aparāhṇaḥ*. Why "after a word ending in *a*"? Consider: *nirahnaḥ*.
[Also, the substitution occurs] after the word *vāhana* when it follows a word [meaning] "placed upon."

The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not occur after a word denoting a vehicle (*vāhana*) when it follows a word denoting that which is to be carried (*voḍhavya*). Examples: *darbhavāhaṇo vaṭuḥ* (a student carrying *darbha* grass), *ikṣuvāhaṇo gauḥ* (an ox carrying sugarcane), *tārkṣyavāhaṇaḥ* (one whose vehicle is Tārkṣya). Why "after what is placed" (*āhitāt*)? Consider *gargavāhanam*, meaning a vehicle belonging to the Gargas. However, when Garga himself is the one to be carried, then it is *gargavāhaṇam*. [The suffix *khañ*] occurs after the word *pāna* when it refers to a country (*deśe*).

The substitution of *ṇ* shall occur for the *n* of the word *pāna* when it follows *ra*, *ṣ*, or *ṛ* situated in a preceding member of a compound, provided it refers to a place (*deśa*). *Pāna* means "that which is drunk" (*pīyate iti pānam*). Examples: *surāpāṇāḥ prācyāḥ* ("the Easterners who drink liquor");
*asṛkpāṇādhipaṃ tūrṇam* ("quickly [to] the lord who drinks blood"). Why "when referring to a place"? [Counter-example: *surāpāno manuṣyaḥ* ("a man who drinks liquor").
Or [the suffix *ktvā* is used] in the sense of the agent (*bhāvaka*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).

In the sense of the agent (*bhāve*) and the instrument (*karaṇe*), the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the suffix *pāna* may optionally occur. Thus: *pīyūṣapāṇam* or *pīyūṣapānam*; *kaṣāyapāṇam* or *kaṣāyapānam*; *surāpāṇam* occurs or *surāpānam*. In the sense of the instrument: *kṣīrapāṇaḥ kaṃsaḥ* (a bronze vessel for drinking milk) or *kṣīrapānaḥ*. How is it that *niṣpānam* and *duṣpānam* are formed? Because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 8.4.37] "after a sibilant at the end of a word. There is an extension of this rule to the class beginning with *giri-nadī*: *giriṇadī* or *girinadī*; *svarṇadī* or *svarnadī*.
And [the substitution of *n* for *m* occurs] before the final vowel of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), before the suffix *num*, and before case endings (*vibhakti*).

In these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* may optionally occur. At the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*): *māṣavāpiṇau*, or *māṣavāpinau*; *vrīhivāpiṇau*, or *vrīhivāpinau*. In the case of the augment *num*: *māṣavāpāṇi*, or *māṣavāpāni*; *vrīhivāpāṇi*, or *vrīhivāpāni*.
In the case of a case-ending (*vibhakti*): *paramāhiṇā*, or *paramāhinā*.
How is it that [the forms] *prapakvāni* and *kṣatriyayūnā* are formed? Because they belong to the *kṣubhnādi* group.
The rule "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and so forth" applies here as well—for example, *gardabhavāhinau*.
When the subsequent member of the compound consists of a single vowel (*ekāj*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied.

In those [compounds] where the final member consists of a single vowel followed by a consonant (*ekāj-uttarapada*), *ṇa* does not necessarily replace *na*. Examples: *vṛtrahaṇau*, *kṣīrapāṇi*, *kṣīrapeṇa*.
This applies only when there is an intervention by *aṭ* (the augment) and so forth—as in *vrīhijāni*.
The explicit mention of *ṇa* is for the sake of indicating that the substitution is obligatory.
And [the suffix] *kumati*.

When these [words] ending in *ka* etc. occur as the second member (*uttarapada*) following a word belonging to the *kavarga* (velar class), the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not necessarily occur. Examples: *nagarabakena*, *nagarakākena*, *dakṣamakheṇa*, *dakṣamukheṇa*, *vṛkamukheṇa*. In the case of the suffix *ghinuṇ* applied by the rule *yujākrīḍa* (Pāṇini 3.2.148): *vastrayogiṇau*, *puṣpayogiṇaḥ*, *puṣpayugāṇi*, *vṛṣabhayugāṇi*, *sarvāṅgāṇi*, *vṛkṣayugeṇa*, *varṣabhogyeṇa*, *mūrkhaugheṇa*. What about when there is intervention by letters such as *aḍ*? Examples: *vrīhityāginaḥ*. How is it that we have forms such as *śāstravākyāni*, *kurumukhyānām*, *praṣṭho'gragāmini*, *chātragāminā*, and *candragominā*? They belong to the *kṣubhnādi* group (which exempts them from the *ṇatva* rule).
The substitution of *ṇ* for the initial consonant of a root taught with an initial *n* occurs after a preverb, even when no compound is formed.

In both non-compounds (*asamāsa*) and compounds (*samāsa*), the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of a verbal root occurs after the prefixes *pra-* and so forth, as well as after *ṣ* and *ṛ*. Examples: *praṇamati*, *pratiṇanīṣati*, *praṇāyakaḥ*, *nirṇayaḥ*. What is the purpose of the condition "of that which is taught with an initial *ṇ* (*ṇopadeśasya*)"? [Consider: *pranardati*. How then is *durnayaḥ* explained? It is due to its inclusion in the *kṣubhnādi* group.
From this point forward, the rule applies to the *ṣ* and *ṛ* situated in a prefix (*upasarga*).
The fish and the tortoise.
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall occur in these two cases: *grahṇoti*, *prahiṇutaḥ*, *pramīṇāti*, *pramīṇītaḥ*. [The augment] *āṅ* is applied before the imperative (*loṭ*) suffix.

The substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* occurs in the imperative (*loṭ*) [when preceded by certain particles]. Examples: *pravapāṇi*, *parivapāṇi*. This applies only when there is an intervention by *aṭ* (the augment) or other such elements—as in *pradadāni*. Why "in the imperative" (*ānīti*)? Consider *pravapantu*. Why "of the imperative" (*loṭaḥ*)? Consider *pravapāṇi māṃsāni* (where the *n* is not changed because it is not part of the imperative suffix).
And [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] after the verbal roots *nargada*, *nad*, *patadaga*, *humāsyati*, *hanti*, *yāti*, *vāti*, *drāti*, *psāti*, *vapati*, *vahati*, *śāmyati*, *cinoti*, and *degdhi*.

In these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur. For example: *praṇigadati*. This is only when there is an intervention by *aṭ* (the augment) and so forth—as in *praṇyagadat*. Also not when the roots belong to the *ghu* class: *pratiṇadātā*, *pratiṇadhātā*. By the word "mā," both the roots *māṅ* and *meṅ* are included: *praṇimimīte*, *pratiṇamayate*. This continues up to *praṇidegdhi*.
In the remaining cases, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is optional when the root begins with a letter other than *k* or *kh*, provided that in its original form (*upadeśe*) it does not end in *ṣ*.

In the *dhātupāṭha*, for a root beginning with a consonant other than *ka* or *kha* and ending in a consonant other than *ṣa*, the *ṇ* of the prefix *ni* may optionally become *ṇ*. For example: *praṇipaktā* or *pranipaktā*; *praṇijānāti* or *pranijānāti*. Why is it said "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*)? To prevent [the substitution] in the case of roots such as *gad*, etc.: *praṇigadati*, *praṇigadanam*. Why is it said "beginning with a consonant other than *ka* or *kha*" (*akakhādau*)? To exclude cases such as: *pranikarttā*, *pranikhādati*. Why is it said "ending in a consonant other than *ṣa*" (*aṣānte*)? To exclude cases such as: *praṇipinaṣṭi*, *praniṣekṣyita*. Why is it said "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*)? To exclude cases such as: *praṇiveṣṭā* or *prativeṣṭā*. It should not apply here: *pranicakāra*, *pranicakhāda*, *pranipekṣyati*.
[The suffix] *ani* [is applied] after the root *an*.
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs when followed by a non-terminating (*anit*) affix. For example: *prāṇiti*. [The word] *antaḥ* [is used here].
Even for that [nasal] which has not been elided, there would be the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. [The suffix] *kvip* [is used here]: "he prāṇ".
However, in the *Keśavavṛtti*, an option is stated: "he prān" or "he prāṇ". Both [forms apply] when the reduplication is present.
Both *n* sounds of the root *han*, when preceded by an augment (*abhyāsa*), become *ṇ* [when followed by a sibilant]. For example: *prāṇiṇiṣati*.
[This applies] to *han* when it is not preceded by the vowel *a*.
The substitution of *ṇ* for *h* shall occur after the verbal root *han*. Examples: *prahaṇyate*, *parihaṇyate*, *prahaṇanam*.
Why "not preceded by *a*" (*atpūrvasya*)? [Counter-example: *praghranti*. Why "followed by *t*" (*taparaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *prāghāni*.
[The substitution is] optional when followed by *va* or *ma*: (*vamor vā*).

When preceded by *vam* (the vowels *u* and *ū*), the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *han* may optionally occur. Thus, one may say either *prahaṇvaḥ* or *prahanmo*; or *prahaṇmaḥ* or *prahanmo*.
[This applies] when there is an intervening region (*antaradeśe*).

In a non-locative context, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *han* occurs after the word *antar*. Examples: *antarhaṇanam*, *antarhaṇyate*. How is *antarhantā* formed? Because the substitution of *ṇ* is treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa* change, just as in the case of *kurvan*. Why "in a non-locative context"? Consider: *antarhanano deśaḥ* ("a region where killing occurs").
Also, [this applies] when followed by *ayana*.

When preceded by the word *antaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur in the word *ayana* when it does not denote a region (*adeśe*). Example: *antarayaṇaṃ varttate*. Why "not denoting a region"? Observe: *antarayano deśaḥ*. Here [the following rule applies]:
*chandasyṛdavagrahāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.26).
And [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs] after a root-final *n*, as well as after a *ru*, *uṣ*, or *u* that stands within a verbal root (*dhātu*).
The two sūtras concerning *chandas* [are as follows]:
"After a prefix, [the substitution of *n* for *ṇ*] occurs diversely."

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *nas* occurs after a prefix (*upasarga*). For example: *praṇasam mukham*, *pariṇasam mukham*. The inclusion of the term "extensively" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) is for the sake of Vedic usage. [This applies also to] a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix or a vowel.

There shall be the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of a suffix (*kṛt*) following a vowel that stands after a cause (the letter *ṛ*, *ṝ*, or *ṣ*) situated in a prefix (*upasarga*). This occurs in the case of the suffixes *-amāna*, *-anīya*, *-ani*, *-ini*, and the substitute of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Examples: *prayāṇam* (departure) *pramāṇam* (measure) *prayāyamāṇam* (being caused to go forth) *prayāṇīyam* (to be gone forth) *aprayāṇiḥ* (one who does not go forth) *prayāyiṇau* (two who have gone forth) *prahāṇiḥ* (abandonment) *parihāṇiḥ* (relinquishment) *prahīṇaḥ* (abandoned) *nirvāṇam* (extinction)

How is there *prakhyānam* (manifestation) and *paryākhyānam* (disparagement)? Effort must be made here [to justify these forms]. Alternatively, they are derived from the *kṣubhnādi* group. Why [is the word] *acaḥ* mentioned? [To exclude cases like] *pramagraḥ*. Only when following a prefix (*upasarga*)—as in *narayānam*. Only when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and so forth—as in *prayojanam*, *pratiyānam*, *pradānam*, *pradhānam*, and *prenvanam*. How is *nirviṇṇaḥ* explained? By means of an addition to the rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
After the root √nī, [the suffix -am] is optional.

Alternatively, there would be the application [of the suffix] by the rule *ṇyantāt kṛtyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.47). Thus, one would have either *prayāpaṇam* or *prayāpanam*, or *prahāpaṇīyam* or *prahāpanīyam*.
[This is governed by the rule] *halaścejupadhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

Or rather, there would be the application of the rule *halāderijupadhād vihitasya kṛtyacaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.56], resulting in either *pragopaṇam* or *pragopanam*, or *nirgṛhaṇam* or *nirgahanam*. [This applies] to roots beginning with *i* or *ā* that have the augment *num*.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* if it follows a root ending in a consonant that has a *num* augment; for example: *preṅkhaṇam*, *parīṅkhaṇam*, *preṅgaṇam*. Because the mention of *num* is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *anusvāra*, we have *prombhaṇam*.
Why "beginning with *ij*" (*ijādeḥ*)? [Observe: *pramaṅganam*. [There is also the rule:
"Optionally [the substitution of *ṇ* occurs] after the roots *niṃs*, *nikṣ*, and *nind*."

For these [roots], the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur after the prefix *pra-* and other such causes, or it may optionally occur. This optionality arises because the substitution of *ṇ* would otherwise apply by virtue of their being taught with an initial *ṇ*. Thus: *praṇiṃste* or *praniṃste*; *praṇikṣakaḥ* or *pranikṣakaḥ*; *praṇindati* or *pranindati*.
[However, this does not apply] to the roots *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, *kam*, *gam*, *pi*, *āpi*, and *vep*.

In these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) does not occur because they are preceded by a prefix (*prādi*) and end in a *kṛtya* suffix other than *ac*. Examples: *prabhānam*, *prabhānīyam*, *prabhavanam*, *prapavanam*, *prakamanam*, *pragamanam*, *prapyāyanam*, *pravepanam*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for *bhā* and others ending in *ṇyat* or *ana*. Examples: *prabhāpanam*, *prabhāpanīyam*. Although the rule "after a prefix and before a *kṛtya* suffix other than *ac*" would have applied, it is prohibited here; thus we have *prabhavāṇi* and *prabhāṇi*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "the *āni* of the imperative (*loṭ*)."
It has been stated [in Pāṇini 6.1.91]: "After a preverb (upasarga)."
[The substitution of *ṣ* occurs] for [the letter *s*] following a word-final [consonant].

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur after a *ṣ* at the end of a word. Examples: *sarpiṣpānam*, *yajuṣpānam*, *duṣpānam*, *duṣpīyamānam*, *niṣpīyamānam*, *duṣkheṇa*. Why "after a *ṣ*" (*ṣāt*)? [Consider: *nirṇayaḥ*, *durnayaḥ*.
[This applies] to the root *naś* when it ends in *ṣ*.
There is no *ṇatva* [substitution of *ṇ* for *n*]. [Examples: *pranaṣṭaḥ*, *pranaṅkṣyati*.
Why "ending in *ṣ*" (*ṣāntasya*)? [Counter-examples: *praṇaśyati*, *praṇāśaḥ*. [The rule applies] to that which stands at the end of a word (*padāntasya*).

The change of *na* to *ṇa* does not occur [after *pra*] in the following cases: *vṛkṣān*, *girīn*, *vrīhivāpān*, *kharamukhān*, *he kariṣyan*, *he kariṣyan*. [This rule applies] even when there is an intervention by a word (*pada*).

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur when there is an intervention by a word (*pada*). Examples: *vrīhikumbhavāpena*, *roṣabhīmamukhena*, *pravipānam*. It should be stated that this applies when it is not a *taddhita* suffix. Examples: *ārdragomayeṇa*, *śuṣkagomayeṇa*. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *kumati ca*. And [the substitution of *ṇ* is prohibited] in the *kṣubhna*-class of words.

In these cases, there is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. *kṣubhnāti*, *kṣubhnītaḥ*; *narīnṛtyate*, *narīnarti*; *nṛnamanaḥ* (the name of a certain person); *tṛpnoti*; *parinartanam*; *vārtraghnaḥ*; *punarnavā*; *daurbhāgineyaḥ*; *harinandī*; *brahmaghnaḥ*; *durnayaḥ*; *durnāma*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). The rules regarding the substitution of *ṇ* have been stated.
When *ś* or *c* follows *s*, *t*, or *th*, they are replaced by *ś* or *ch* respectively.

The *śa*-group [i.e., *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*] becomes the *ca*-group [i.e., *c*, *ch*, *j*, *jh*, *ñ*]. When? In conjunction with *ś* or *c*. Examples: *kaśśrūyate* (is heard by whom?), *kaścinoti* (he gathers by whom?), *kaśśete* (he lies down by whom?), *kaśchātraḥ* (which student?). *agnicicchete* (the fire-priest lies down), *bhavāññchete* (you lie down). Once the substitution of the *ja*-group (*jaś*) for the *jhal* sounds has been applied, the substitution of *ś* occurs;

then, by the rule *khari ca*, the substitution of *c* occurs. Examples: *taccinoti* (he gathers that), *tacchinatti* (he cuts that), *tajjayati* (he conquers that). *praśāñcinoti* (he gathers after having calmed), *praśāññcuṅuve* (he covered after having calmed).
Because of the use of the instrumental case in the rule *ścunā*, the substitution of *ś* occurs even in conjunction with the preceding sound—e.g., *yajñaḥ* (sacrifice), *yācññā* (request).

*masja-*—*majjati*; *lasja-*—*lajjate*. Here, because the substitution of *jaś* for *jhaś* is considered *asiddha*, the *s* [of *cinoti*] becomes *ś* by the rule of *ścutva*, and that [ś] becomes *j* by the rule of *jaśtva*. This applies only in *saṃhitā* (continuous speech)—as in *kaś cinoti* and *agrīc chete*. The governing term *padasya* (of a word) is applied only occasionally, as indicated by the "leap of the frog" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) principle.
In this context, although *stoḥ* and *ścuḥ* form a collective compound (*samāhāra*), they do not take the neuter gender because it is a Vedic (sūtra) usage.
[The rule] *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [applies].

*ṣasya ṣaḥ*: A *ṭavarga* (the retroflex class) shall be substituted for a *tavarga* (the dental class). When? In conjunction with *ṣ* and *ṭu* (the *ṭavarga*). Examples: *kaṣṣaṇḍe*, *kaṣṭīkate*, *eṣṭā*, *peṣṭā*, *aploṣṭa*, *acyoṣṭa*, *yaṣṭā*, *irṣṭe*, *irṭṭe*, *uḍḍīnam*, *taṭṭīkate*, *taḍḍhaukate*, *bhavāṇḍīnaḥ*, *abādayaṇḍhakkām*, *likhaṇṇakāraḥ*, *taṇṇakāraḥ*, *līḍham*, *gūḍham*. [Exception: *na padāntāṭṭoranām*: [The substitution does not occur] after a *ṭavarga* at the end of a word, nor before *r* and *n*.

It should be stated that [the substitution] does not apply to the word *anām* nor to cities (*nagarī*). After a final retroflex stop (*ṭavarga*) following a word-final consonant, the substitution of a retroflex for *s* or *t* (*ṣṭutva*) does not occur: *śvaliṭ sādhuḥ*, *śvaliṭ tarati*; *madhuliṭ sādhuḥ*, *madhuliṭ tarati*. It does not apply here: *ṣaṇṇām*, *ṣaṇṇavatiḥ*, *ṣaṇṇagarī*.
[The rule applies] when *ṣ* follows *t*.
The substitution of *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ṣ* and *ṭ*) does not occur when a dental consonant (*tavarga*) is followed by the letter *ṣ*. Examples: *agrīcic chaṇḍe*, *mahān chaṇḍe*, and *śāta*.
The substitution of *ś* for *t* after *ś* does not occur: *praśnaḥ*, *viśnaḥ*. The substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) occurs: *aśnāti*.
After a *yar* (a consonant other than a semivowel or nasal), before a nasal, a nasal may optionally be substituted: *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā*.
A letter at the end of a word may optionally become a nasal when followed by a nasal sound. For example: *vāgnnetā* or *vāṅanetā*; *tvaññ ññakāraḥ* or *tvajññakāraḥ*; *kakumnāthaḥ* or *kakubnāthaḥ*;
*śvaliṇnayati* or *śvaliḍ nayati*; *tanmātrā* or *tadmātrā*. Why is "end of a word" (*padānta*) repeated? [To exclude cases like] *vedmi*.
The rule for the suffix *pratyaya* is stated as being permanent: *vāṅmayam*, *ṣaṇṇām*, *madhuliṇmātram*, *śvaliṇmātram*, *tanmātram*. Now begins the section on doubling (*dvitva*).
After the letters *a* and *ra*, followed by *ha*, there is doubling [of the following consonant].

When *r* or *h* follow a vowel (*ac*), the following semi-vowel (*yar*) may optionally be doubled. Examples: *arkkaḥ* or *arkaḥ* *mūrkkhaḥ* or *mūrkhaḥ* *rsvaggaḥ* or *svargaḥ* *argdhyaḥ* or *ardhyaḥ* *nirjjharaḥ* or *nirjharraḥ* *artthaḥ* or *arthaḥ* *ārdraḥ* or *ārddraḥ* *vardhanam* or *varddhanam* *bahirnnayati* or *bahirnayati* *rdapyaḥ* or *darpaḥ* *nirbharaḥ* or *nirbbharaḥ* *rdabbhaḥ* or *darbhaḥ* *rdhamma* or *dharmaḥ*
*rśamma* or *śarma*; *kāryya* or *kārya*; *brahmā* or *brahmmā*; *apahnnute* or *apahanute*. Why "after a vowel"? [Consider: *hanute*.
And [the doubling occurs] even when not followed by a consonant (*anaci*).

A *yar* (any consonant except *h*) following a vowel (*ac*) may optionally be doubled. *ugraḥ*, or *ugro*; *vighnaḥ*, or *vighno*; *matsyaḥ*, or *mattsyo*; *putraḥ*, or *putro*; *yudhyate*, or *yudhyate*; *budhyate*, or *buddhyate*; *sidhyati*, or *siddhyati*; *dadhya-tra*, or *dadhyatra*; *madhu-tra*, or *maddhvatra*; *vadhyaḥ*, or *vadhyo*; *indraḥ*, or *innandro*; *ṛśyaḥ*, or *ṛśśyo*; *śiṣyaḥ*, or *śiṣṣyo*; *śasyam*, or *śassyaṃ*; *asthi*, or *assthi*. Why "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? [Consider: *smitam*. Why "not after a non-vowel" (*anaci*)? [Consider: *dadhi tiṣṭhati*.

*yaṇ* [is substituted] for *mayaḥ*. Or rather, there are two [possibilities]: *ulkā* or *ukkā*; *mayaḥ* and *yaṇ*, according to some. For example: *dadhyatra* or *dadhyyatra*; *śakyaḥ* or *śakyyo*; *madhvatra* or *madhvvatra*; *śuklaḥ* or *śukllo*. *śaraḥ* [is substituted] for *khayaḥ*. Or rather, there may be two [possibilities]: *sthālī* or *stthālī*; *sthānam* or *sththānam*.
Some say that *kha* and *ya* are *śara*. Examples: *vatsaḥ*, *vatsso* (or *vatsso*); *kṣīram*, *kṣṣīram* (or *kṣṣīram*); *apsarāḥ*, *apssarāḥ* (or *apssarāḥ*).
At the end of a word, two [consonants] may occur: *vāk*, *vākk* (or *vākk*). *ṣaṭ*, *ṣaṭṭa* (or *ṣaṭṭa*). Only when followed by *ya* or *ra*: *dadhi*.

According to Pauṣkarasādi, when a sibilant (śar) follows, the second letters [of each varga] may optionally be substituted for the first letters. That is to say, in place [of the first letters], the second letters are prescribed before a sibilant. For example: *vāk śete* or *vākh śete*; *apsarāḥ* or *apsārāḥ*; *apsu* or *apsu*; *kṣīram* or *khaṣīram*; *vṛkṣaḥ* or *vṛkṣaḥ*; *maghuliṭsu* or *maghuliṭhasu*;

*śvaliṭsu* or *śvaliṭhsu*; *vatsaḥ* or *vathsah*; *bhavatsu* or *bhavathsu*. According to others, the second letters following [the first] become augment-forms (*āgama*). For example: *kkhṣīram* or *kṣīram*.

*vatsaḥ*, *vatthso* or *vā*; *madhuliṭṭhsu*, *madhuliṭsu* or *vā*; *bhavatthsu*, *bhavatsu* or *vā*; *appasarāḥ*, *apsarāḥ* or *vā*. According to others, the second consonants are doubled: *kṣīram*, *kkhkhṣīram* or *vā*; *apasarāḥ*, *apphphsarā* or *vā*; *bhavatsu*, *bhavatththsu* or *vā*.
If a son reviles his mother-in-law, he shall pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas].

When the sense of "abusive" (ākrośa) is understood, there is no doubling of the word *putra* when followed by *ādinī*. For example: *putrādinī* ("one who devours her son," used as an insult). Why "when abusive"? [Answer: *putrādinī śiśumārī* ("the female porpoise devours her young"—this is a factual statement, not an insult). It should be stated that this applies when it is followed by that [same element]. For example: *putraputrādinī* ("one who devours her son's son").
And optionally so when followed by *hata* or *jagdha*: *putrajagdhī* or *puttrajagdhī*; *puttrahatī* or *putrahatī*.
A *śar* [consonant] is elided before a vowel (*ac*).

The [substitution of] *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s* would not occur before a vowel (*aci*) in two cases: *ādarśaḥ*, *karṣaḥ*, *varṣā*, and *kārsaram*. Why "before a vowel" (*aci*)? [Consider: *rdaśyate* or *rdaśśyate*; *irrṣyate* or *irrṣṣyate*; *irrśyā* or *irrṣṣyā*. According to Śākaṭāyana, this applies when three or more consonants occur.
According to this opinion, in cases of three or more [consonants], two [consonants] would not [be elided]. [Examples are: *indraḥ*, *rāṣṭram*.
Everywhere, according to Śākalya.
According to the opinion of Śākalya, doubling is not accepted in all cases. Examples have already been cited, such as *arkaḥ*, *brahmā*, *dadhyatra*, *yudhyate*, and *sidhyati*.
The mention of the teacher [Śākalya] is for the sake of honor, since the rule is established by the continued application of the word "optionally" (*vā*).
According to the teachers, [the vowel] following a long [vowel is pluta].
According to the opinion of the Teachers (ācāryāḥ), there shall be no doubling of a consonant following a long vowel: *pātram*, *dātram*, *sūtram*, *gotram*. [The rule] *jhalāñ ñaś jhaśi* [applies].
When followed by a *jhaś* sound, *jhal* sounds become *jaś* sounds. Examples: *labdhā*, *dogdhā*, *majjati*, *boddhā*.
In the case of reduplication (*abhyāsa*), *car* sounds [are substituted].

In reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the *jhal* sounds may become *ñcar* sounds, and they may also become *jaś* sounds. *ci-kha-ni-ṣ-a-ti* (desires to dig); *ti-ṣṭh-ā-s-a-ti* (desires to stand); *pi-pha-ṇ-i-ṣ-a-ti* (desires to expand). For original *car* sounds, there are original *car* sounds: *ca-cā-ra* (he walked); *pi-pā-s-a-ti* (he desires to drink). Furthermore, for *jaś* sounds: *ji-ghat-s-a-ti* (he desires to eat); *bi-bhar-ti* (he bears); *ḍu-ḍho-ke* (he was pleased).
For original *jaś* sounds, there are original *jaś* sounds: *da-da-u* (he gave); *bu-bud-he* (he woke).
And [the vowel] *khari* [is followed by a voiceless consonant].

Before a *khari* [stop or sibilant], the *jhal* sounds [consonants other than nasals] become *śar* [sibilants and *ha*]. Examples: *bhettā*, *chettā*, *yuyutsuḥ*, *āripsate*, *taccinoti*, *bubhutsate*, *bibhitsati*.
[Also, the *jhal* sounds become *śar*] optionally before a pause (*avasāna*).

At the pause (virāma), the *jhal* consonants may optionally become *ñ-cara* (nasalized). For example: *vāk*, *vāg* vā; *śvaliṭ*, *śvaliḍ* vā; *vṛkṣāt*, *vṛkṣād* vā; *kakup*, *kakub* vā. Furthermore, a non-*pragṛhya* vowel following an *aṇ* (a, i, u) becomes nasalized.

At the end of a word, a nasalized vowel (*aṇ*) may optionally become nasalized. For example: *karma* or *karmā*; *khaṭvā* or *khaṭvām*; *dadhi* or *dadhim*; *bhavati* or *bhavatim*; *kumārī* or *kumārīm*. Why "not a *pragṛhya*" (*apragṛhyasya*)? [Because in the following cases it does not apply: *agnī*, *vāyū*. Why "of a vowel" (*aṇaḥ*)? [Because in the following cases it does not apply: *kartṛ*, *hartṛ*. [The rule continues: After an *anusvāra*, when followed by a *yay* (any consonant except *h*), there is a substitution with the corresponding homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*).

It may be *śaṅkitā*, *uñchitā*, *kuṇḍitā*, *kurvanti*, or *kampitā*. Why [mention] *yayi*? [Because it does not apply here: *ākraṃsyate*. Or, [the rule applies] to that which is at the end of a word (*padāntasya*).

A *anusvāra* at the end of a word may optionally become a *parasavarṇa* (a sound homogeneous with the following consonant) when followed by a *yay* (any consonant except *h*, *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*). For example: *tvaṃ kathaṃ nayasi* or *tvaṅ kathannayasi*. Here, the semi-vowels (*antaḥsthā*)—*y*, *v*, *l*, and *r*—are each divided into two types: nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). Among these, when an *anusvāra* is followed by a *yay*...

A following homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) shall be the most similar [to the preceding sound], provided it is nasalized (*sānunāsika*). For example: *kiṃyuktaḥ* becomes *kiryyuktaḥ*; *puṃyatnaḥ* becomes *puyyam̐tnḥ* or *puṃliṅgaḥ* becomes *purlliṅgaḥ*; *dhānyaṃ lunāti* becomes *dhānyallum̐nāti*; *saṃvatsaraḥ* becomes *savvam̐tsaraḥ*; *grāmaṃ vahati* becomes *grāmavvam̐hati*; *gāṃ vahati* becomes *gāvvam̐hati*. [The rule continues: "In place of *t*, when *l* follows... (*torli*).

When a letter of the *tavarga* (the dental class) is followed by the letter *l*, it is replaced by its corresponding nasal (*parasavarṇa*). Examples: *tallunāti*, *tallikhati*, *bhavāllunāti*, *bhavāllikhati*.
[Exception: In the case of the roots *sthā* and *stambh* following the prefix *ud*, the preceding [nasal] is retained.

When preceded by *ud*, for these two [roots] (*sthā* and *stambh*), there shall be a substitute homogeneous with the preceding vowel in place of the initial *al*. Examples: *utthātā*, *utthitaḥ*, *uttambhitā*, *uttambhitum*.

It should be stated that this applies to the root *skand* when meaning "disease": *utkandaka* is the name of a disease. [In the case of the rule] *jhayo ho’nyatarasyām*: [The substitute *jaś* (the first letter of each varga) optionally occurs in place of *ha* following a *jhay* (consonant other than a nasal) at the end of a word.]

A *jh* (the consonants *j*, *bh*, *g*, *dh*, *d*) followed by another *h* may optionally become the same sound as its preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). For example: *vāghasati* or *vāgghasati*; *ajjhalaḥ* or *ajjhalo*; *taddhitam* or *tadhita*. [Furthermore,] *ś* becomes *ch* before a non-aspirate (*aṭ*) consonant.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] to *ami*. After a *jhay* consonant, the *ś* of *śas* may optionally become *ch*.

It should be stated that in the rule *aṭi*, it is *ami* [that follows]. Thus: *vākchete* or *vākśete*; *vākchokena* or *vākśokena*; *tacchete* or *tacśete*; *bhavāññchraraḥ* or *bhavāññśūro vā*. In the alternative where *tuk* is inserted after *śi*: *bhavāññchūraḥ* or *bhavāñññśūro vā*; *tacchlokena* or *tacślokena*; *tacchmaśānam* or *tacśmaśānam*.

What is the meaning of "these"? [The examples are: *tat ścyotati* (that drips), *vāk ścyotati* (speech drips). [This is governed by the rule: *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (there is elision of *yams* following a consonant when a *yam* follows).

There shall be the elision of *yama*s following a consonant (*hal*) when a *yama* follows; this occurs according to their respective order. For example: *āsye bhavam* becomes *āsyyam*, or *āsyaṃ*. Why "when a *yama* follows"? Consider: *kumāryyaḥ*.
A *jhar* (a consonant other than *y*, *v*, *r*, or *l*) is optionally elided before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) consonant.

A *jhar* (any consonant except *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*, and nasals) following a *hal* (consonant) may optionally be elided before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) *jhar*. There is no correspondence by position (*yathāsaṃkhya*) here; the elision occurs only before a homogeneous sound. Examples: *śiṇḍiḍha*, *śiṇḍi*; *piṇḍiḍha*, *piṇḍhi*; *rundadhi*, *rundhi*; *banddhum*, *bandhum*. Why "before a homogeneous sound"? Consider *rtaptā*.
Here—
after an acute (udātta) vowel, an unaccented (anudātta) vowel becomes circumflex (svarita).
An unaccented vowel followed by an udātta or svarita accent does not occur in the traditions of the Gārgyas, Kāśyapas, Gālavas, and Ānabhyas.
There are two [chapters] in the Chandaḥsūtra.

In the treatise, it is declared that the vowel *a* is taught as being open; however, in actual usage, it becomes closed. For example: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *siddhiḥ*. Thus [it is said].
